# PREFACE.

The Preliminaries, which I have placed at the head of each Part of this Work, will sufficiently inform the Reader of the sources where I have drawn from, and the character of the Authors from whom I have derived the History and the Doctrines of <term>MANICHAEUS</term> <note>original: MANICHÉE. Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the Persian founder of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion that once rivaled Christianity.</note>. It is only a matter of accounting to him what prompted me to treat this subject, and the method I have followed. I will add a general idea of what is contained in this Work, an Apology <note>Used here in the sense of a formal defense or justification of one's arguments.</note> for certain passages that might seem a bit too free to some Readers, and a kind of Introduction to Manichaeism.

I would never have thought to write the *Critical History of Manichaeus and his Errors* without the occasion I am about to describe. As it is pleasant to know the origin of great events, I wished to research that of the <term>Reformation</term>, of which one finds *attempts* in some of those Christian Societies that separated themselves from the Bulk of the Greek Church and the Latin Church, or whom the violence of the Bishops tore away from them. There were two famous ones in the West: one is that of the <term>WALDENSIANS</term> <note>original: VAUDOIS. A medieval movement that preceded the Protestant Reformation, emphasizing poverty and lay preaching.</note>, and the other that of the <term>ALBIGENSIANS</term> <note>original: ALBIGEOIS. A religious group in Southern France often accused by the medieval Church of being Neo-Manichaeans.</note>.

The origin of the *Waldensians* is so hidden that one cannot surely mark its Epoch. The name of

# PREFACE.

**Peter Waldo** (1) might well have been the occasion that caused them to be named *Waldensians*, but he was by no means the founder of their society. He found it already established, and only expanded it and carried its faith into countries where it was unknown. Regarding their dogmas, they have for a long time no longer been uncertain. The truth has made its way through calumny. Among so many indubitable monuments of their belief, we have the account of the conferences that *Claude de Seyssel*, Archbishop of Turin, held with them in their valleys, and which was printed in Paris after his death. But it is not the same for the *Albigensians*. They have perished, and the *Waldensians* still survive: They wrote, but their books have been suppressed: almost everything we know of their doctrine comes from their persecutors, who represent it as the most impious and monstrous that one could imagine.

The first members of this society who appeared in France were those fourteen persons from the nobility and the clergy of Orléans, against whom King *Robert* assembled a kind of council in the year 1022, and whom he had burned alive under the pretext of *Manichaeism* <note>Manichaeism was often used as a "catch-all" label by the medieval church for any group practicing dualism or opposing the established hierarchy.</note>. Historians agree that the ten canons who perished in this execution were regarded as among the most sanctified and

the most learned within the Clergy of Orléans. Their constancy did not belie this praise. They suffered their execution with a hope and a joy that astonished their Persecutors. I shall provide a Critical History <note>A "Critical History" refers to a scholarly approach that scrutinizes original sources and documents to separate fact from legend.</note> of them, God willing, after that of the <term>Paulicians</term> <note>A medieval Christian sect from Armenia and Byzantium often accused of dualism.</note> and the <term>Bogomiles</term> <note>A Bulgarian dualist sect that emerged in the 10th century and influenced later Western movements.</note>.

A few years later, a great number of Persons were discovered around Arras and Cambrai who held the same Belief, but who, it is said, did not possess the same firmness. At the same time, others were found in Toulouse and in neighboring Towns: And since the beginning of the eleventh century, they have been discovered everywhere in the West: in Spain, in France, in England, in the Low Countries, in Germany, and in Italy. There were nothing but Gallows erected, nothing but Pyres lit to make them perish; and the reason for so much cruelty was that they were <term>MANICHAEANS</term> <note>Followers of a dualistic religion that taught a cosmic struggle between Light and Darkness; in the Middle Ages, the term was frequently used as a label for any perceived heretic.</note>.

To properly judge the facts, it was necessary to know, on one hand, the Heresies of <term>Manichaeus</term> <note>The 3rd-century Persian prophet Mani, who founded Manichaeism.</note>; and on the other, the Errors of this new Sect, in order to make a comparison. This was what led me into the study and examination of <term>Manichaeism</term>: an undertaking of which I have repented more than once, when I saw the difficulty of truly knowing this Heresy. However, being unable to resolve to abandon a Design that I had begun to execute, I persisted in finishing it, and it is this which produced this *Critical ESSAY on the History and Dogmas of Manichaeus*.

Having learned through my own experience that one does things very poorly when one does not go back to the sources, I left all the Moderns, who

gave us Descriptions of the <term>Manichaean Heresy</term> <note>A dualistic religious movement founded by the prophet Mani, which taught a strict division between the spiritual world of light and the material world of darkness.</note>, or rather I took only one, who always seemed to me one of the most exact: I mean <term>Mr. de Tillemont</term> <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian famous for his exhaustive collections of historical documents, though often criticized for his traditionalist devotion to his sources.</note>, an excellent Author in terms of collections, but who would be even more so in all respects if he were less credulous, less a slave to his Prejudice, and if he had dared or wished to use all his discernment. Fundamentally, the Modern authors were quite useless to me, my design being not to pile up, without choice or examination, everything that the Ancients tell us about *Manichaeus*, and about his Errors, but to treat this matter as a <term>Critic</term> <note>A "critic" here refers to the then-emerging field of "Higher Criticism," which used linguistic and historical evidence to challenge the traditional dating or authorship of religious texts.</note>, which others had not done. Thus, without stopping at the Compilations of the Moderns, I went straight to the sources, and following the stream of Tradition back to its source, I soon arrived at the *ACTS of the Disputation of Archelaus, Bishop of Cascara, with Manichaeus*. This is the source from which all the Greeks have drawn.

As soon as I had read this Piece, which the late *Mr. Zaccagni* <note>Lorenzo Alessandro Zaccagni (1657–1712), a librarian at the Vatican who published the first complete version of the "Acts of Archelaus" in his *Collectanea Monumentorum Veterum* (1698).</note>, Librarian of the Vatican, was the first to publish in its entirety, I had a great suspicion that the Disputation of *Cascara* <note>Cascara, or Cascar, was a city in Mesopotamia. The "Acts of Archelaus" depicts a public debate between the local bishop and Mani; the author of this preface argues the event was a literary invention.</note> was nothing but a Fiction of some Greek author who, having acquired memoirs concerning the Life and Dogmas of *Manichaeus*, wished to write his History and refute his Errors. My examination changed my suspicions into certainty. The fabrication appeared evident to me, and I dare flatter myself that it will appear so to all Readers who have the taste and love for Truth, and in whom Prejudice cannot long hold out against Reason. For the others, it would be folly to try to persuade them. They see only what they want to see. They are not accessible

...to the Truth as soon as it clashes with their Prejudices, and the maxims of their Party. The more evident it is, the more it irritates them. They become angry with those who reveal it, and believe that, to overturn a new <term>Hypothesis</term> <note>In this context, a "hypothesis" refers to a new historical interpretation or critical theory regarding the origins of a text.</note>—however well established it may be—it is enough to cry out that there is an unbearable audacity and presumption in contesting today these <term>Acts</term> <note>Referring specifically to the *Acts of Archelaus*, a document purportedly recording a 3rd-century debate between a Christian bishop and the prophet Mani. The author is arguing that these "Acts" are actually a later fictional construction.</note>, which the <term>Church</term> has recognized as authentic for fifteen hundred years: which have had the general approval of all that was most holy and most enlightened in <term>Christian Antiquity</term> <note>The period of the early Church, roughly from the 1st through the 5th centuries AD.</note>, and which no modern <term>Critic</term> has doubted until now.

Regarding People of this character, I declare to them that it is not for them that I write: And, although there is no hope of persuading them, I am willing to answer them in advance that there is neither audacity nor presumption in examining the Witnesses and their testimonies before giving them credence: That a forged document <note>original: "Piéce supposée"</note> cannot become legitimate simply by growing old: That a Lie is not Truth simply for having been believed: That the approval of the Ancients cannot make authentic those *Acts* in which there are manifest Proofs that they are not: That any approval which is not the result of a mature Examination can have no weight: That the <term>Criticism</term> of the Ancients was generally quite superficial, as one sees by the false Pieces and fabulous Stories they accepted: That the Moderns, who have read the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>Archelaus was the legendary Bishop of Caschar (in Mesopotamia) who allegedly defeated Mani in a public dispute.</note> with attention, have indeed felt that they contain very suspicious Facts, as we [shall see]...

-># P R E F A C E.<-

...we shall see in its proper place: That *Photius* <note>Photius I of Constantinople (c. 810–893), a powerful Byzantine scholar and patriarch known for his "Bibliotheca," which summarizes hundreds of works from antiquity.</note> attributed them not to *Archelaus*—to whom they belong if they are authentic—but to a certain *Hegemonius*, who could only have written more than fifty years after the death of *Mani* <note>original: "Manichée". Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the Iranian prophet who founded Manichaeism.</note>, since *Eusebius*, who published his History around that time, made no mention of the *Dispute of Caschar*: That, in a word, the *Acts* of this *Dispute* are evidently a Fiction similar to that of that Impostor who took the name of *Clement of Rome* <note>Refers to the "Pseudo-Clementine" writings, a set of 4th-century works falsely attributed to an earlier Pope to give them authority.</note>, and who introduced *St. Peter* debating against *Simon Magus* <note>A religious figure mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, traditionally viewed as the first heretic and the father of Gnosticism.</note>: Or to that of a Christian Philosopher named *Maximus*, who likewise introduced *Origen* debating against a *Marcionite*, a *Valentinian*, a *Bardesanist*, and I know not what other Sectaries <note>These groups represent various "heretical" Christian movements from the 2nd and 3rd centuries.</note>. I am far from blaming skillful Writers who imagine <note>original: "supposent"</note> debates between Catholics and Heretics, provided they take care to give notice of the fiction. One can treat important matters usefully and agreeably by imagining Dialogues between Persons who hold contrary opinions, and placing the scene of the Dispute wherever one sees fit: *Plato* and *Cicero* did this so well, and *Methodius* <note>Methodius of Olympus (died c. 311 AD), an early Church Father who wrote theological works in the form of Platonic dialogues.</note> imitated them. The artifice is innocent: But one must not present these ingenious Fictions as real Events. Now, this is exactly what the Author of the *Acts of Archelaus* has done, who has thereby deceived <note>original: "en a imposé" — a phrase meaning to mislead or trick someone into believing something false.</note> all the Ancients and all the Moderns; and he would have deceived me like the others, had some passages not made me suspicious, and obliged me to examine this Work, and to melt it down, so to speak, in order to assure myself if it was of genuine quality <note>original: "de bon alloi" — a metallurgical metaphor meaning "of the right alloy," used here to describe the historical authenticity of the text.</note>.

-># P R E F A C E.<-

->IX<-

I believed I should begin this Preface with these Reflections. I come now to my Work. I have divided it into two Parts: the first Historical, and the second Dogmatic. I first present to the Reader, with short marginal notes, the History of *Mani* <note>original: "Manichée". Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the Iranian prophet who founded Manichaeism.</note>, and the origin of Manichaeism, as it is found in the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century anti-Manichaean work, long considered the primary source for Mani's life, though now viewed by many scholars as largely fictional.</note>. I then examine all the Facts therein. I distinguish what is false from what is true, or what might be so. I explain what needs clarification, and remain always either a Critic or a Commentator. But as this History of our Heresiarch <note>A term for the founder of a heretical sect or movement.</note> is very different from that which we find in Persian and Arabic Authors, I believed I should present each of them separately. Furthermore, I have tried to make them more pleasant and interesting by mixing in Episodes which are not too far-fetched, and which the principal subject could tolerate. Such is, for example, what I relate concerning the Religion of *Zoroaster* <note>The ancient Persian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism, which heavily influenced Mani's thought.</note>, the Revolutions of that Religion among the Persians, the Christians of *Turkestan* <note>original: "Turquestan". A historical region in Central Asia.</note>—where *Mani* retired to escape the pursuit of *Shapur* <note>original: "Sapor". ...that a certain **Tyrbo**, a Mesopotamian who had been a disciple of Mani, must have given to *Archelaus* <note>Archelaus was the fictional Bishop of Cascara in the *Acts of Archelaus*, the primary anti-Manichaean source used by early Church fathers.</note> concerning the heresies of his master. I do not even know if the beginning has been altered; for one can indeed accuse *Mani* of establishing two Gods by admitting two Princes and two eternal Empires. But it is not likely that a Manichaean, who knew his doctrine well, would have accused him of *serving two Gods*; or, if he did, that is enough to prove him a notorious liar.

*Tyrbo's* account serves as my text. I explain it, critique it, and correct it. I limit certain general maxims which are only true when applied to specific cases. I supply what was omitted. I distinguish between actual errors, or dogmas, and the consequences that were drawn from them. I attempt to discover the origin of so many absurd opinions and fictions. I reduce all Manichaean theology into a system: I first report its principles. One can well imagine that all this was not done without difficulty, but having undertaken it, I wished to carry it through.

The first principle of Manichaeism is Authority, which our Heresiarch <note>A founder of a heresy or leader of a heretical sect.</note> seized for himself, acting as an **Apostle** of Jesus Christ and a prophet immediately enlightened by *the Paraclete* <note>The "Paraclete" (from the Greek *paraklētos*, meaning advocate or helper) refers to the Holy Spirit. *Mani* <note>original: *Manichée*</note>, having denied the Inspiration and Authority of the Hebrew Prophets, took it upon himself to oppose them with other Prophets, whose books the Orientals <note>Eastern peoples, particularly those from Persia and Mesopotamia.</note> claimed to possess; this is what I call his third Principle. He supposed, therefore, that *Seth*, *Enoch*, and other Patriarchs, having been instructed by good Angels, had transmitted to all their descendants the truths they had learned from them. That these instructions had been preserved, either in books that still survived, or in the schools of the Oriental Philosophers, from whom all others had learned Wisdom. *Mani* further supposed that, since Divine Reason enlightens all minds that do not place obstacles before its light, all nations had their own Prophets: that the Christian Church, being composed of *Gentiles* <note>People of non-Jewish origin; in this context, the Greeks and Romans.</note>, ought to listen to its own Prophets, and not those of the Hebrews, who had not been sent for it. By this means, he transferred to unknown Prophets the authority of which he stripped the true Prophets; and he did this because he found in the former enough to confirm his false hypotheses and his fables. I examine these three Principles in the first Book of my second Part.

As this multitude of false Writings, which appeared in the second century, provided the Freethinkers <note>original: *Libertins*. In the 18th century, this term often referred to skeptics or "free spirits" who questioned religious orthodoxy and the historical claims of the Bible.</note> with a plausible pretext to deny, or to cast doubt upon, the Authenticity of the Books of the New Testament, I felt it my duty to show how ill-founded their claim is. It is not tinsel <note>original: *clinquant*. Cheap, flashy material used to imitate gold.</note> that one might mistake for gold: it is iron, and the basest of metals. Our sacred Books are distinguished, by their own light, from this jumble of obscure and fabulous Books. After all, these others do not date from Apostolic times, and far from our Skeptics being able to derive any advantage from them against the miraculous Facts of the Gospel—which is nonetheless their goal—they actually concur in establishing their certainty.

After having treated the Principles of Manichaeism, following the Plan I have set for myself, I begin in the III. Book to examine its Dogmas <note>The established beliefs or doctrines held by a religion.</note>. In it, I set forth the Doctrine of the Manichaeans concerning the Nature and Attributes of the Divinity.

-># PREFACE.<-

Their ideas on this matter are not entirely accurate. However, this flaw is not unique to them. *Mani* <note>original: *Manichée*. The 3rd-century Persian prophet and founder of Manichaeism.</note> believed the Divine Nature was extended and finite. This is an error; for once one assumes this Nature is extended, one cannot believe it to be infinite. After all, fairness requires us to excuse in him an error that is found among Saints and Martyrs; and since he did not limit the Divine Perfections, his error fundamentally does no harm to Religion.

*Mani* was a Trinitarian; but once again, on this point, his ideas were not entirely accurate. He recognized the Consubstantiality <note>The doctrine that the three persons of the Trinity—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—are of the same substance or essence.</note> of the Persons, but he believed these Persons to be as truly distinct as three men are. By this, he established three Gods. He nevertheless denied this consequence, which we must not attribute to him—no matter how logical it may be—because it would then have to be attributed to several of the most illustrious Fathers of the Church, who certainly thought as he did. This is a certain fact, acknowledged by the theologians who have best studied ancient Doctrine.

The Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus Christ was created by God and was not co-eternal with the Father.</note> perpetually reproached the Catholics <note>In this historical context, "Catholics" refers to the "universal" orthodox Church that followed the Nicaean Creed.</note> that their dogma of the generation of the Son of God introduced into Religion either the *Valentinian Probola* <note>original: *Probole Valentinienne*. In Gnostic thought, a "probola" is an "emission" or "projection" of a divine being from the primary Godhead.</note>—that is to say, an extension or diffusion of the Divine Nature—or the *Manichaean Division* of that same Nature. This leads me to treat the various Heresies that arose in the Church regarding the Divinity of the Lord, and which compelled *Constantine* to assemble the Council of Nicaea <note>The first ecumenical council of the Christian Church, held in 325 AD to resolve the Arian controversy and define the nature of Christ’s divinity.</note>. I treat in the following Books the antiquity of the *Intelligible World*, <note>original: "Monde Intelligible". In Platonic and Neoplatonic philosophy, this refers to the realm of pure thought and spiritual reality, as opposed to the sensible, physical world.</note> that is to say, the World of immortal *Spirits*: the Creation of the material World, and what gave occasion to it: the Nature and the origin of the Soul; its being sent into Matter: the formation of corporeal Man, his Attributes, his Sin, his Condemnation, his Redemption, and the Person of the Redeemer: the return of Souls to Heaven: the Errors of the Manichaeans <note>The Manichaeans were followers of the Persian prophet Mani (3rd century AD), who taught a dualistic struggle between a spiritual world of light and a material world of darkness.</note> on all these Articles: and finally their Morals and their Discipline. In all this, one will see quite bizarre Imaginations, but one will see at the same time that they had their sources in an ancient Philosophy, which reigned in the East.

It is now necessary to justify the Method that I have followed, and to anticipate, as much as possible, the judgments of certain Readers who have love and zeal for Religion, and whose sensitivity or temperament one might find that I do not sufficiently accommodate. 2. Since one cannot blame Impartiality in a Historian, it will be necessary, in order to condemn mine, to give it another name. I admit to the Indulgence, but I deny the excess. It is true that I have a great inclination to excuse **Human Errors**; but this is when they are neither voluntary nor malicious; when the Proofs are so balanced by Difficulties that the most attentive Mind hardly knows what to decide; when they do not touch the Foundations of the **Faith**; when they are not in manifest contradiction with the clear and formal Decisions of **Scripture**; and finally, when they do not in any way destroy the worship, obedience, and deep veneration belonging to the Divinity. This Indulgence for Human Errors is, in my view, an essential Duty of the Christian—one of the branches of **Charity**, and the only means of preventing Dissensions and **Schisms**.

### P R E F A C E.

...tations too ample and too abundant, it is a superfluity that has cost only me, and the Reader may well forgive me the expense. As for the passages themselves, I have rendered their substance in the Text without binding myself to translate them in a completely literal manner, because these sorts of translations usually possess neither grace nor clarity. Furthermore, I believe that the Reader can count on the testimonies I allege: I have extracted almost all of them from the Originals, and when I have not done so, I have taken care to give notice. I have scrupulously attached myself to citing them only in the sense intended by the Authors, whose sentiments <note>The word "sentiments" here refers to the authors' underlying opinions, beliefs, or intentions.</note> I have tried to know well. Books are full of citations that are accurate in their terms, but which are not always so in their meaning; when detached from the rest of the Discourse, they present ideas that were never those of the Authors.

I have promised a kind of Introduction to Manichaeism. I have already reported what I call the *Principles*: I must now finish and report the principal *Dogmas*. It was properly a Theological and Philosophical System, the Hypotheses of which are taken from the Theology and Philosophy of the Orientals <note>In this 18th-century context, "Orientals" likely refers to the Persians and other Near Eastern cultures whose dualistic religions, like Zoroastrianism, influenced the development of Manichaeism.</note>. Having no concept of a Substance that possesses neither place nor extension <note>In 18th-century philosophy, "extension" refers to the quality of occupying physical space; the author suggests Mani could not conceive of a God that was purely abstract and spaceless.</note>, he believed the Divinity to be a living and immaterial Light that resides from all eternity in the Supreme Heaven. It was always accompanied there by those pure and immortal Intelligences to which he gave the name of *Aeons* <term>Aeon: from the Greek *aion*, meaning an age or eternal cycle; here it refers to eternal beings emanating from God</term>, a name that signifies their immortality. A duration that is always equal, without increase or decrease, is the idea that the Ancients attached to the word *Aeon*. These Spirits are so many emanations of the Divinity. *Mani* <note>original: "Manichée"</note>, not believing that anything could be made from nothing, and being unable to bring forth Holiness and Immortality from the bosom of Matter—which is the source of vice and corruption—was obliged to suppose that the *Aeons* are formed from the celestial substance, or that they emanate from the Divine Essence. He preferred this latter opinion, which was also that of *Plato*. However, as God communicates His perfections only as much as He wishes, these spirits are always infinitely below Him and are not properly Gods.

The Supreme Heaven and the Intelligences that inhabit it compose the *Intelligible World*, which is eternal. The luminous substance from which Heaven was formed has the same eternity as God: it exists by itself, because nothing can be made from nothing. But Heaven and the *Aeons* have only a *Secondary Eternity*, because they have a cause, which is God. However, since this Cause is eternally active, they have existed from all eternity. This was again Platonic. *Plato* believed the world to be eternal with a *Secondary Eternity*, because

In a corner of the immense Space resided from all eternity a malignant Power, which *Mani* <note>original: "Manichée"</note> called **Matter** in the Philosophical style, the **Demon** in the vulgar style <note>The "vulgar style" refers to the common or everyday language of the people, as opposed to specialized philosophical or mystical terminology.</note>, and **Darkness** in the mystical style. One might say that this arrangement is an imitation of that of the celestial Spheres. Each of these Regions contained one of the Elements of Matter, along with Animals formed from them, which consequently could live there. Everywhere some Prince reigned, but they were all subject to the Great Prince, the sole Leader of the malignant Powers.

To remedy this disadvantage, Divine Providence first made use of the ministry of good angels, who taught the first Patriarchs the truths of salvation; these, in turn, transmitted this knowledge to their descendants. And to prevent this light from being entirely extinguished, God has never ceased to raise up Sages and Prophets in all times and among all nations, until it finally pleased Him to send His Son into the world. This celestial Minister perfectly taught souls their true origin, the causes of their captivity, and the means of their deliverance. After having performed an infinite number of miracles to confirm His doctrine, He showed them, in His *Mystical Crucifixion*, how they must unceasingly mortify the flesh and its passions. He further showed them through His *Mystical Resurrection*, and through His *Ascension* into Heaven, that death does not destroy Man; it only destroys his prison, and it restores to purified souls the freedom to return to their celestial homeland.

Because the flesh is composed of Matter—and even of that which is most vicious within Matter—it followed from this that the Son of God could only have taken its outward form, and not its reality. This led *Manichaeus* <note>The founder of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion that competed with early Christianity.</note> to deny the Incarnation. He consequently <term>Docetism: From the Greek *dokein* (to seem), this is the belief that Christ's body was not physical or human, but a phantasmal appearance, because matter was viewed as inherently corrupt.</term>

He likewise denied that the Lord had used necessary nourishment to preserve animal life; that He had a soul susceptible to innocent affections; that He had suffered, that He died, and rose from among the dead. He nevertheless agreed that all this was done in appearance, but he denied that it had actually happened <note>This theological position is known as Docetism, from the Greek *dokein* (to seem), which argues that Christ's body was phantasmal or celestial rather than physical.</note>. He disapproved of Marriage, as having been invented by Demons, in order to bind Souls with the Flesh, and to delay their return to Heaven. He strongly recommended all austerities that serve to mortify the Body, because the weaker it is, the less it resists the Spirit. *Mani* <note>Original: "Manichée." The 3rd-century Persian founder of Manichaeism.</note> disapproved, for the same reason, the use of wine and meat, under the pretext that all of this nourishes and strengthens the flesh too much, and inflames <term>Concupiscence</term> <note>A theological term for strong physical desire or lust, which was seen as a product of the "dark" or "material" side of human nature.</note>. He required that his *Elect*, or his *Perfect* ones, embrace voluntary Poverty, that they possess nothing of their own, and that they absolutely not involve themselves in any secular affairs.

I have used the word *disapprove* on purpose, rather than *condemn*. The <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A term used by traditional church historians to refer to the founder of a heresy.</note> felt well enough that Concupiscence takes too much power over the Will to be able to forbid marriage to all of his disciples. That is why he permitted it, or tolerated it in the Laity, as well as...

Since not everyone was strong enough to rise to <term>Evangelical Perfection</term> <note>In this context, "Evangelical Perfection" refers to the "Counsels of Perfection"—poverty, chastity, and obedience—which went beyond the basic moral requirements for all Christians.</note>, he showed condescension toward the Weak <note>In Manichaean circles, "the Weak" refers to the *Auditors* (Hearers), the lower tier of believers who were permitted to marry and eat meat, unlike the *Elect*.</note>. But for the *Perfect*, and particularly for the Clergy, he desired that they imitate the life of the Savior, who was never married and possessed nothing in this World. He permitted them only the most spiritualized pleasures, such as, for example, those of Music and Fragrances. His goal was to detach the Soul from the Senses and all earthly affections, because it cannot re-enter Heaven without a perfect purification.

Since it is not possible for all Souls to acquire perfect purity during the course of a single mortal life, *Mani* <note>Original: "Manichée."</note> admitted the <term>transmigration of Souls</term> <note>More commonly known as reincarnation or metempsychosis; the belief that the soul is reborn into new bodies to continue its spiritual evolution.</note>, a dogma very common among the Nations that have recognized Immortality. He therefore taught that they pass from one Body into another; but those that are not purified through a certain number of revolutions are delivered to the <term>Demons of the Air</term> <note>In Gnostic and Manichaean cosmology, the atmosphere was thought to be filled with "Archons" or spirits who tried to capture or purge souls as they ascended toward the light.</note> to be tormented and subdued by them. After this harsh penance, they are sent back into other Bodies, as if into a new School, until, having acquired a sufficient degree of purification, they cross the Region of Matter and pass into the Moon. When the Moon is full of them—which happens when its entire surface is illuminated—it discharges them into the arms of the Sun, which in turn returns them to that place which the Manichaeans called the *Column of Glory* <note>The *Column of Glory* (often identified with the Milky Way) was envisioned as a massive pillar of light made of purified souls returning to the Divine Realm.</note>. We shall see roughly

### P R E F A C E.

...near the origin of most of these Imaginations, of which *Mani* <note>original: "Manichée"</note> was by no means the Inventor.

The *Holy Spirit*, who is in the Air, continually assists Souls with his precious influences. The *Sun*, which is composed of a pure and purifying Fire, facilitates their ascension into Heaven, and detaches from them, as they rise, the material particles that weigh them down.

When all the Souls, and all the Parts of the Celestial Substance have been separated from Matter, then the consummation of the age <note>A term referring to the end of the world or the final era of time.</note> will arrive. The malevolent Fire will emerge from the Caves where the Creator has imprisoned it. The *Omophoros* <note>Derived from the Greek for "shoulder-bearer," this is the name of an angel in Manichaean cosmology who supports the weight of the world.</note>—that is, the Angel who supports the Earth in its position and its balance—will let it fall into the Flames, and will then throw this useless mass outside the bounds of the World, into that place which Scripture calls the *Outer Darkness*. It is there that the Demons will be banished forever. The most slothful Souls—that is to say, those that have not completed their purification when this Catastrophe occurs—will have as the penalty for their negligence the task of keeping the Demons confined in their Prisons, in order to prevent them from attempting anything further against the Kingdom of God.

This, in broad strokes, was the mythical System of *Mani*. I leave aside various details which are its dependencies, and which I shall report in their proper place. But I do not dare to flatter myself as having either understood everything or explained everything. Thus, I give this Work only as an ESSAY on a Theology which is very obscure, and which the Ancients, who report it and refute it, did not always correctly understand.

->In Berlin, January 30, 1734.<-

->*Origin of Manichaeism. System of the MAGI concerning the two Principles.*<-

Definition of the Principles. Two Principles according to some: God & Matter. A single Principle according to others: a single Substance, namely Extended Substance. 167
The System of the Magi is infinitely opposed to this latter view. ibid. <note>original: "ibid." — abbreviation of the Latin "ibidem," meaning "in the same place" or "on the same page."</note>

## CHAPTER I.

*The Manichaeans did not forge a* LETTER *from Jesus Christ. They are not the Authors of certain Additions to the* GOSPELS. *They are not the authors of the false Gospels of ST. THOMAS and ST. PHILIP.*

The artifice of this Author. 339, 340 <note>Jerome Xavier (1549–1617) was a Jesuit missionary to the Mughal court; his "Life of Christ" (Mirat al-quds) incorporated many non-biblical legends. Denis Pétau (Petavius) was a prominent 17th-century Jesuit scholar.</note>
Another imposture of the Jesuit *Villote*. 340 <note>Jacques Villotte (1656–1743), a Jesuit traveler and missionary in Armenia and Persia.</note>
IV. The Manichaeans accused of having corrupted the Scriptures, and of forging Books under the names of the Apostles. The Catholics have done both. 341

V. The Manichaeans are not the Authors of an Addition made to *St. Luke 6:5.* 342 <note>This refers to a famous variant in the Codex Bezae where Jesus sees a man working on the Sabbath and addresses him; the author argues this is not a Manichaean interpolation.</note>

# CHAPTER II.

### *Regarding* LEUCIUS *and some of the false Acts attributed to him. Regarding the* GOSPEL OF THE NATIVITY OF THE VIRGIN *and the* PROTEVANGELIUM.

I. The Manichaeans possessed some Apocrypha. The conjecture of Cave <note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English church historian.</note> is poorly founded. *Turibius* <note>Turibius of Astorga, a 5th-century bishop who campaigned against Priscillianism and Manichaeism.</note> accuses them of having composed or falsified them all. This falsification is attributed to a certain *Leucius*, who is said to have been a Manichaean. 348
His name was corrupted by the Ancients. It is the same as that of *Luke*. 349
II. He was not a Manichaean. 349
1. He was a Disciple of *St. John*, according to *St. Epiphanius*. 2. And according to the pseudo-Melito, a Disciple of the Apostles. 3. Testimony of *Pacian* <note>Pacian of Barcelona (c. 310–391), a bishop and writer.</note>, which justifies the antiquity and authority of this man. 4. Other proofs drawn from his *Gospel of St. Peter*. 5. And from his *Acts of the Apostles*, and particularly those of *St. John*. 6. Testimonies of *Grabe* and *Cave*. *Fabricius* believes Leucius to be a Manichaean; his reasons. Response. 350, 351
III. There was only one *Leucius*, who is the Heretic of that name. 352
IV. *Gospel of the Nativity of Mary* attributed to *Leucius*. 352
Imposture of an unknown Latin author. Subject matter of this Book. Intent of the Author. 353
He wished to destroy the opinion that the Virgin was the daughter of a Priest, a claim that the Manichaeans maintained. 354
V. Antiquity of this Opinion; it seems to be in the Testament of the Twelve Patriarchs. 354

<column-break/>

This piece is believed to be by an *Ebionite* <note>A member of an early Jewish Christian sect that emphasized Jewish law and often denied the divinity of Jesus.</note>, but it has been falsified. The opinion that the Virgin was the daughter of a Priest was not rejected by *Marcantonio de Dominis* <note>An Italian archbishop and scientist (1560–1624) who defected to the Church of England for a time.</note>. How it might be justified. It is contrary to *St. Paul*. 355
VI. False thoughts of the Fathers to unite the Empire and the Priesthood in the person of Jesus Christ: from *St. Augustine* and *Gregory of Nazianzus*. 355, 356
A piece supposedly from the time of *Justinian* written with the same view. False conjecture of *Richard Montagu* <note>An English bishop and controversialist (1577–1641).</note>, who attributes this piece to the Manichaeans. 356, 357
VII. *The Gospel of the Nativity* supposed to supplant another that appeared Heretical. 357
VIII. Regarding the *Protevangelium of St. James*, and its Author. *St. Epiphanius* appears to attribute it to the Ebionites. They are not the authors of it. 358
This book is more likely by *Leucius*. 359
IX. Views of this Impostor. First view: to condemn Marriage. 359
Why he invented a first marriage for *Joseph*. An imprecise word from *Tillemont* <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a rigorous ecclesiastical historian.</note>. 360
Constant variation in Tradition. 2. Second view of the Impostor: to confirm his Heresy regarding the Person of Jesus Christ. Fable invented to persuade that Jesus Christ did not have a real Human Body <note>This refers to Docetism, the belief that Christ's body was an illusion, a common theme in Gnostic and Manichaean thought.</note>. 361

### CHAPTER III.

*Regarding the GOSPELS of the INFANCY. Regarding those of NICODEMUS & of ST. PETER. Regarding an APOCALYPSE of ST. STEPHEN.*

**I.** Regarding the Gospels of the Infancy. 364
The first in Greek. The second in Arabic, Syriac, and Armenian. Conjecture of Mr. *La Croze* <note>Mathurin Veyssière de La Croze (1661–1739), a French scholar and librarian known for his work on oriental languages.</note>. He believes this book was composed by a Nestorian <note>A follower of Nestorius, whose doctrine emphasized the distinction between the divine and human natures of Christ.</note>. A custom specific to the Nestorians. Reflections on this conjecture. 365
*The Gospel of the Infancy* is the ancient Gospel of *St. Thomas*. 2. It is not by a Manichaean. 3. Its author is unknown. It gives Jesus Christ a cruel character. 4. The work itself is a wretched novel. 366
Example of a man changed into a mule. A similar fable in *Christian Armenia*. 5. The antiquity of these fables. Opposing judgments of *St. Epiphanius* and *St. Chrysostom*. 6. Origin of these fables. 367
They come from Christians of Jewish origin, and in particular from the *Marcosians* <note>A Gnostic sect led by Marcus in the 2nd century, known for their mystical interpretation of the alphabet and numbers.</note>. The fable of Jesus Christ learning to read. Explanation of this fable. Jewish subtleties regarding their alphabet. Declamation of *St. Jerome* on this occasion. 368, 369
8. *The History of the Infancy* of Jesus Christ is not today as the *Marcosians* had it. 369

<column-break/>

**II.** Regarding the Gospel of Nicodemus attributed to *Lenthius* and to *Carinus*. 370
These two names can only designate *Leucius Charinus* <note>A legendary figure to whom many apocryphal Acts were attributed; the text suggests the names Lenthius and Carinus are corruptions of his name.</note>. What part he may have had in this false Gospel. 371
Observations on two passages. When the Jews began to calumniate the birth of the Savior. 372
A reflection of *Origen* that is more subtle than solid. Baptism of the Dead whom Jesus Christ delivered from Hell and whom He resurrected. The antiquity of this imagination. 373
Ridiculous thoughts that the necessity of Baptism has given rise to. An amusing scene in Hell when Jesus Christ appeared there. A quarrel between the Prince of Tartarus <note>original: "Tartare" — referring to the classical underworld, used here as a synonym for Hell.</note> and the Demon, judged by the Lord. 374
**III.** Other Gospels attributed to *Leucius*. The first is only the *Gospel of the Infancy*. The second is the Gospel of *St. Peter*. It is by *Leucius*, which proves that he was not a Manichaean. *Tillemont* <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a prominent French ecclesiastical historian.</note> attributes it wrongly to the author of the *Recognitions*. *Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458), an influential theologian and church historian.</note> confused it with the Gospel according to the Hebrews. 375
The two marriages of *Joseph* were found therein. The doctrine within it was sound.

# CHAPTER IV.

### *Regarding the Heresy of <term>Leucius</term> [Leucius Charinus, a 2nd-century author of apocryphal texts], and his <term>Acts</term> [apocryphal accounts of the apostles’ deeds], or <term>Travels</term> of the Apostles: particularly those of ST. JOHN.*

I. Antiquity of the two Sects of the <term>Ebionites</term> [a Jewish-Christian group that emphasized Jesus's humanity and the Law of Moses] and the <term>Docetists</term> [a group that believed Jesus only appeared to have a physical body]. St. John combats them in his Gospel. 377
The Error of the Ebionites prevails among Christians of Jewish origin. That of the Docetists among Christians from among the Gentiles. <note>Gentiles refers to people of non-Jewish heritage.</note> 378
II. These two Sects multiply in Asia. Authors of the Docetist sect. ibid.
Origin of Docetism and the cause of its progress in Asia. It was the Heresy of the Learned and the Noble. 379
III. Reasons of the Docetists. 380
These are in part the same reasons that have since been used to defend the *Real Presence*. <note>The theological doctrine that the bread and wine used in the Eucharist are the literal body and blood of Christ.</note> This opinion provides the Docetists with invincible proofs. Docetism and the Real Presence prove one another reciprocally. 382
IV. Leucius writes false *Acts of the Apostles* to authorize his Errors. His Style. Exaggeration by *Tillemont*. <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), an influential French ecclesiastical historian.</note> 383
Dogmas of Leucius. 384

It is doubted whether he believed that the God of the Jews was evil. It is unknown how he gave to Jesus Christ the names of *Father* and *Son*. The Docetists did not confuse the Divine Persons. 385

<column-break/>

3. Fables of Leucius to persuade that Jesus Christ did not have a true Body. Opinion of Clement of Alexandria. The Body of Jesus Christ was true, but impassible. <note>Incapable of physical suffering or decay.</note> 386

5. Error of *Photius*. It was not another man, but a phantom that Jesus Christ delivered to the Jews. 387
6. Error of *Leucius* regarding Marriage. 388
7. Another Error of *Photius*. Neither Leucius nor his kind believed in a Resurrection. ibid.
8. God did not create the Demons. An opinion common to several ancient Heretics. ibid.
9. Leucius dogmatizes against Images. <note>Referring to the religious use of icons or statues.</note> ibid.
VI. History of St. John and Lycomedes cited by the Council of Constantinople. 388, 389
St. John disapproves of the action of a Christian who had his Portrait made. Reflection on this History. The Bishops of Nicaea agree that it is a Pagan Idolatry to crown Images. 389
VII. Hymn and Dance of Jesus Christ with his Apostles. Apocrypha of the Priscillianists. <note>A 4th-century ascetic movement in Spain led by Priscillian, often accused of magic and Gnosticism.</note> Reflections on this Dance of the Apostles. 390
Religious dances have been in use...

# D I S C O U R S E,

->Wherein it is demonstrated that the Apocryphal and Fabulous Books, far from undermining the certainty of the miraculous Facts contained in the Gospels, and consequently the certainty of the Christian Religion, actually serve to confirm them.<-

I. Reason why this Discourse is inserted here. 438
II. Objection of the Jew *Isaac Orobio de Castro* <note>A prominent Jewish physician and philosopher (c. 1617–1687) who famously engaged in theological debates with Christian scholars.</note> against the Gospels. *ibid.*
III. Remarks on this Objection. Manifest falsehood of the Jew, his Error. Apparent contradictions did not cause true Gospels to be excluded. 439
IV. Direct answer to the Objection. Five Propositions which entirely refute it. 440
V. First Proposition: Rules and Criteria by which the Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers," early influential Christian theologians and writers.</note> judged the authenticity or the fabrication of Books. 440, 441
1. First Rule. Written Doctrine must have been consistent with the preached Doctrine. It does not follow from this that Tradition is the Rule of Faith. 441
2. Second Rule. No Book was recognized at the beginning as authentic unless it had the constant and perpetual testimony of all the Churches. 442
3. Third Rule. Doubtful or forged books were judged by comparing them with authentic Books. 443
VI. Response to the invective of *Mr. Simon* <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and a pioneer of modern Biblical criticism.</note> against the Reformed <note>The "Reformed" refers to the French Protestants or Huguenots.</note> of France. 444
Two Questions: one of fact, and the other of faith. It is on the Question of faith, and not of fact, that the Reformed allege the testimony of the Holy Spirit. It is absurd to wish to decide the Question of faith by the testimony of the Church. 445

<column-break/>

Example of the Alcoran <note>original: "l'Alcoran," an older European spelling of the Quran.</note>. Explanation of the words of St. *Augustine*: *I would not believe the Gospel if I were not moved to do so by the authority of the Church.* <note>The famous quote: "Ego vero Evangelio non crederem, nisi me catholicae Ecclesiae commoveret auctoritas."</note> 446
The Fanaticism for which the Reformed are reproached by *Mr. Simon* is a Catholic Dogma. 447
VII. Second Proposition: Circumspection and religious care of the Fathers in the judgment of Books. Three Classes of Books: The true, the doubtful, and the false or forged. *ibid.*
VIII. Example of this Circumspection in the examination and judgment of the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation.</note>. 448
IX. Third Proposition: Origin and cause of the Apocrypha. 449
The Constitution of the Christian Church rendered them inevitable. Reflection of *Mr. Simon*. A passage of St. *Ignatius* poorly rendered. Paraphrased version of this Passage. 450, 451
Of which Heretics St. *Ignatius* wishes to speak, and what word of the Gospel they were contesting. 451
Testimony given to the Gospel of the Nazarenes <note>An early Jewish-Christian community.</note>. 452
X. Fourth Proposition: the number of Apocryphal Gospels is much smaller than is believed. A single Gospel appearing under several names. 453
The Fathers give the name of "Gospel" to Heretical Books, which were not properly Gospels. 454

The Ancients knew of no necessary link between Self-Existence <note>The quality of existing by one's own nature rather than being created</note> and Divine Perfections. Only *Dionysius of Alexandria* <note>A 3rd-century Bishop known for his theological writings on the Trinity</note> is known to have perceived this. Their error regarding the substantial Immensity of God does not destroy Religion. Axiom of *Servetus* <note>Michael Servetus (c. 1511–1553), a Spanish theologian and physician often cited in debates about the nature of the Trinity.</note>, who recognizes Substantial Immensity. Consequences drawn by the Libertines. *506*
Sentiment of *Philippe de Marnix* <note>A 16th-century Dutch statesman and theologian.</note>. God is only present everywhere through a presence of Power and Majesty. The theologians who hold this view nonetheless attribute Infinity to God. *507*

V. The Manichaeans give God a very vast Empire. *In the same place.* <note>original: "ibid."</note>

VI. The Land of Darkness, or the place of *Matter*. Some place it in the South. Its true situation in the lowest region of Space. *508*

VII. Description of God by *Manichaeus*. Explanation of the twelve members of *God*, which are spoken of in this description. It is believed that these are the same thing as the *Sephiroth* <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite reveals itself.</note> of the *Kabbalists*. *509, 510*

<column-break/>

VIII. Manichaeus recognizes divine Omnipotence, yet is accused of denying it. Why? Necessary conditions to base such an accusation. 1. Define the idea of *Omnipotence*. The ambiguity of this word. It gives cause to accuse the Orthodox of denying Omnipotence. 2. Determine what is possible. False accusations for failing to observe this rule. The error of the Manichaeans is not to have denied Omnipotence, but to have believed that Creation out of nothing <note>The concept of "creatio ex nihilo," which Manichaeans rejected in favor of the eternity of matter.</note> is among the things that are impossible. *510, 511, 512*

IX. Simplicity is essential to God. The Manichaeans recognized it. *512*

X. They likewise believed God to be *indivisible*. *513*

XI. *And impassible* <note>Incapable of suffering, pain, or being changed by external forces.</note>. Formal testimonies from *Fortunatus* and *Manichaeus*. Admission of St. *Augustine*, and of St. *Ephrem*. The Impassibility of God led them to deny the Incarnation <note>The Manichaeans argued that if God cannot suffer, He could not have truly become human in the person of Jesus.</note>. *513, 514*

XII. The Manichaeans recognize the Moral Perfections of the Divinity, such as *Goodness*. Observation on *Luke 18:19.* <note>The verse where Jesus asks, "Why do you call me good? No one is good except God alone."</note> They recognized *Mercy*, *Holiness*, and *Justice*. *515, 516*

<summary>This page outlines the Manichaean view of God's attributes, arguing that they maintained his omniscience and moral perfections while rejecting "creation from nothing" and the physical suffering of the deity.</summary>

## CHAPTER V.

*The Manichaeans confessed the* TRINITY, *and the* CONSUBSTANTIALITY *of the Divine Persons.*

**I.** The Manichaeans recognize the *Trinity* and *Consubstantiality* <note>The doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the same substance or essence.</note>. They are accused by *Socrates* <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439), a Christian church historian.</note> of denying the Personality of the Word <note>The Logos, or the Second Person of the Trinity.</note>, which does not appear just. Confession of *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean Bishop.</note>, Admission of *St. Augustine*. *Other* Testimonies of the same, of *Photius*, of *St. Epiphanius* regarding *Hierax*, of *Photius* regarding *Agapius*, and of *Facundus of Hermiane*. 517, 518
**II.** The Manichaeans were led to Consubstantiality by their own Principles. 518
**III.** Critique of *Victor of Vita* <note>A 5th-century bishop who wrote on the persecutions in Africa.</note>, who accuses the Manichaeans of having been Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who taught that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father.</note>. 519
**IV.** It is uncertain if the Manichaeans believed the Generation of the Word to be eternal. *In the same place.* <note>original: "ibid."</note>
A **great** number of the early Fathers placed the Generation of the Word immediately before the Creation of the World. Testimony of *Du Pin* confirmed by *Petau* and by the *Bishop of Avranches* <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721).</note>. Critique of *Petau’s* conjecture on the origin of this sentiment. Critique of the Remark by Mr. *Du Pin*. 520, 521, 522

<column-break/>

**V.** The Generation of the Word in time was the result of another Opinion, namely that the Generation of the Word is an act of the Father's will. This was the sentiment of the Eusebians <note>Followers of Eusebius of Nicomedia, often associated with the Arian controversy.</note>: their reasoning. Critique of this reasoning. 522, 523
**VI.** The Manichaeans believed Jesus Christ to be the *First-born* of the Father, and they have explained this term well. 523
**VII.** Clarification of a calumny by *Euthymius Zigabenus* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine monk and theologian.</note> against the Bogomils <note>A medieval dualist sect often compared to the Manichaeans.</note>. Origin and pretext of this calumny. 524
**VIII.** Examination of the System of *Valentinus* <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic teacher.</note> and *Manichaeus* on the Generation of the Son. Preliminary reflections. Christians are divided on the Question of how Jesus Christ is the Son of God. Why one enters into a Historical discussion on this. 1. Reason of equity. 2. Reason: This Discussion overturns the Sophism of *Variations* <note>A reference to Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet's argument that the changing doctrines of non-Catholics prove their error.</note> by the Bishop of Meaux. Confirmation of this proof. 525, 526

It also explores historical theological debates regarding whether the "Generation of the Word" was eternal or occurred just before Creation.</summary>

### CHAPTER VI.

*The Fathers could not dispense with explaining how Jesus Christ is the* **SON OF GOD**; *from this comes a prodigious variety of Sentiments. Reflections on the number of Bishops at the Council of Nicaea, and on the different Sects that were found there.*

I. IT was impossible for the Fathers not to examine *How Jesus Christ is the Son of God.*
<margin>Reasons.</margin>
1. It was necessary to enlighten the Faith. 2. To exclude Error. 3. To answer the Pagans. 4. To show them that this idea did not originate from them. 5. The Doctors believed themselves obliged to study the Mysteries in depth. Precept of Petau <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit theologian and scholar of the history of dogma.</note> on this subject, retracted by himself. 527, 528

II. Surprising variety of Opinions on the Question, *How Jesus Christ is the Son of God.* 529

III. Reflections on the number of Bishops at the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD), the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church.</note>. Variation of the most ancient Writers on this. St. Athanasius and Eusebius corrupted. Why the number of Bishops of the Council of Nicaea was fixed there. False mysteries found in this number by St. Hilary, by St. Ambrose, and by Dorotheos of Monemvasia <note>A 16th-century Greek writer who compiled historical and ecclesiastical chronicles.</note>. 529, 530, 531

IV. Eutychius counts 2048 Bishops at the Council of Nicaea. Reflections that may confirm this number. <term>Chorepiscopi</term> <note>From the Greek 'khorepiskopos,' these were "country bishops" or rural assistants to city bishops.</note> at the Council. Bishops of the Sectarians. The Priests were seated in the Councils. The Greeks counted only the Catholic Bishops. 531, 532

V. Sectarian Bishops who were present at the Council, besides the Arians.
1. Of the Mariamites, an imaginary Sect. These were Nazarenes who called the Holy Spirit the Mother of the Lord. 532

VI. Sabellians at the Council. 533

VII. Digression on Sabellianism <note>A 3rd-century heresy teaching that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are different modes or aspects of one God, rather than three distinct persons.</note>. Sentiment attributed to Praxeas and Noetus. God the Father was born, he suffered, he died. Reasons to doubt that this is the true sentiment. Extravagances attributed to Noetus. God the Father was born, he suffered, he died. Reasons to doubt that this is their true sentiment. Extravagances attributed to Noetus. The same accusation brought against the Sabellians, though it is obviously false. Testimony of St. Epiphanius. 533, 534, 535

VIII. The origin of Sabellianism was the fear of multiplying the Divinity <note>The fear of appearing polytheistic by recognizing three distinct persons in God.</note>. Testimonies of St. Epiphanius, Origen, Eusebius, and Tertullian. 535

IX. The idea of Sabellianism. There is only one Divine Person, of whom the Word and the Spirit are the Attributes and Properties. The union of the Word with Jesus is only an operation of the Word within Jesus. 537

X. From which it follows that the Sabellians were not <term>Patripassians</term> <note>Literally "Father-sufferers"; the belief that God the Father himself suffered on the cross.</note>, and could not be. The Monophysites <note>Those who believe Christ has only one nature (divine) rather than two (divine and human).</note> likewise accused of believing that the

### C H A P T E R VII.

They married him with *Sige* <note>original: "Sigé," the Greek word for Silence.</note>, or Silence. Explanation of this Enigma. The Father produces the Son.

### PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE,
->Wherein the Plan of this Work is presented.<-

<margin>THE AUTHOR'S DESIGN.</margin>
I WOULD NOT UNDERTAKE to provide a History of MANI <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), also known as Manichaeus, was the Persian prophet who founded Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that once rivaled Christianity.</note>, nor an idea of his Dogmas <note>technical vocabulary: established beliefs or doctrines of a religious sect.</note>, if my only intention were to report what the Ancients <note>Referring to early Church Fathers and historians such as Epiphanius or Augustine.</note> have said of them. A great many Modern authors have taken this trouble upon themselves. But no one, in my opinion, has succeeded better than Monsieur de TILLEMONT <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a renowned French ecclesiastical historian celebrated for his exhaustive and accurate compilations of historical documents.</note>. He has gathered nearly everything found in...

## PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE.

<margin>Tillemont: very accurate, but lacking in critical judgment.</margin> ...found in the ancient Ecclesiastical Authors regarding *Mani* and his errors, and has reported them with great order and accuracy. All I would have desired from such a skilled man is that he had made more use of his discernment. But, biased in favor of the Ecclesiastical Historians and the Church Fathers, he assumed with too much confidence that they were faithful and accurate; usually, he did nothing more than collect what they said and compose his Memoirs from it.

<margin>The excessive partiality of the Ancients concerning Heretics and Heresies.</margin> He could have easily perceived, however, that regarding Heretics and Heresies, the general spirit of Antiquity was constantly to admit, without examination, everything that Fame <note>original: "Renommée," here referring to public rumor or reputation personified</note> published to their disadvantage, however fabulous it might be: to inflate and exaggerate the absurdities of their opinions; to attribute to them views they never held; to rank among their articles of Faith all the consequences that might result from their Principles—in a word, to load the portraits they draw of the persons, doctrines, and morals of Heretics with an infinite number of foreign and monstrous features. Nevertheless, I excuse Monsieur de *Tillemont*. Born and raised in the Roman Catholic Church, which finds its only defense and resource in Tradition, he feared undermining a foundation that cannot be shaken without ruining the entire edifice it supports.

<margin>Always flawed, and fundamentally harmful.</margin> I confess that I have always felt an extreme aversion to this method of Antiquity. 1. First, it is contrary to natural <term>Equity (the principle of fairness and justice that transcends written law)</term>, to which all men are bound, which must be inviolable to the Christian, and even more so to the Bishop or the Minister of the Gospel. The Sophist and the Christian Teacher are characters that should be as opposite as Falsehood and Truth. 2. Secondly, this method does not only tarnish those who follow it; it dishonors the very Religion they profess. 3. In the third place, it inspires in the <term>Orthodox (those adhering to the established, "correct" doctrines of the Church)</term> who read the histories of Heretics—I will not say an aversion for their errors, which is just—but a hatred for their persons, which stifles all feelings of Compassion, Charity, and even Humanity in the hearts of these same Orthodox, converting them into cruel Persecutors. 4. Finally, far from this method bringing Heretics back to the communion of the Church, it distances them infinitely. How would they return to the bosom of a Society that slanders them, outrages them, hates them, persecutes them, and, to authorize these persecutions, attributes to them Errors they do not hold and Practices they abhor? I do not see that St. *Augustine* converted many Manichaeans or <term>Donatists (a rigorous Christian sect in North Africa that clashed with Augustine over church purity)</term>. He might have succeeded better had he taken a different approach.

### PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE.

->A 2<-
<meta>catchword: the</meta>

<margin>Reflections on the Article regarding the Manichaeans in Bayle's work.</margin>
The late Mr. **Bayle** has given us, in his Dictionary, an Article on *Mani* and the *Manichaeans*: but it seems to me that he would have done better either to omit it or to compose it differently. He ought to have treated this matter as a Critic; he should have taken the History of this <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>a founder or leader of a heretical sect</note>, his Dogmas, and the Ceremonies of his Sect, etc., from the first Authors who spoke of them, and used all his sagacity to disentangle the false from the true. Is this not what the title of his great Work announces to the Public, and what he has executed so very well on other subjects? But it is also what he often neglected, and, if I dare say so, what he seems to have neglected by design when he spoke of several Christian Sects. I do not believe that this was his intent, but one would almost say that he was quite pleased to find, within the body of Christians, the most senseless Fanaticism and the most foolish and impudent obscenities. I believe, therefore, that the late Mr. **Bayle** should have given us a History as exact as one can have of the Heresiarch *Mani*, and marked his opinions precisely for us, rather than amusing himself by pushing and embellishing, as he did, the arguments of the Manichaeans. A **Historical and Critical Dictionary** required him to do the former, and certainly excused him from the latter.

<margin>The Author’s Motives. Justification of his Design by St. Augustine himself.</margin>
My design is to attempt what I would have required from the late Mr. **Bayle**. Wishing to know the **Modern Manichaeans** <note>referring to medieval groups like the Albigensians or Paulicians, who were often labeled "Manichaeans" by their enemies</note>, with whom people have confused Sects much purer and more Christian than one might imagine, I was obliged to go back to the Ancients. And finding much exaggeration, contradictions, and false imputations in what we are told of *Mani*, of his Dogmas, and of his Morality, I have tried to examine him as a Critic. I felt pity for a Sect already too unfortunate for having strangely corrupted the Christian Faith, and for having been from its birth the object of the furies of an inhuman zeal. I justify the sect when it appears to me that they have been slandered; I excuse it when it appears to me excusable, and I do not believe that anyone should take it ill of me. If I am (1) in error, it is the most innocent error in the world. And St. *Augustine* himself, the Scourge of the Western Manichaeans, shall be my apology.

<margin>(a) Augustine, *On the Profit of Believing*, Chapter 4.</margin>

> ...the pleasures of Virtue; and not in the pleasures of the Senses. <margin>Judicious reflection of the Author of the *Republic of Letters* on the same subject. (a) *News of the Rep. of Let.* by Mr. Bernard. Sept. 1705. p. 317. <note>Jacques Bernard (1658–1718) was a theologian and journalist who continued Pierre Bayle's famous literary journal.</note></margin>
I entirely approve of this maxim of St. Augustine (1), coming fresh from **Manichaeism** <note>A major dualistic religion founded by the prophet Mani, which St. Augustine followed for nine years before converting to Christianity.</note>, and at a time when the wounds that this Heresy had inflicted on his Soul were scarcely closed. I will add to it the reflection with which the learned Author of the *News of the Republic of Letters* begins the Extract of the Book of **Mr. Réland** <note>Adriaan Reland (1676–1718), a pioneering Dutch scholar of Oriental languages and Islamic studies.</note> concerning the Religion of the Mohammedans (a). *There are people,* says this Author, *who cannot suffer that the Public be disabused of the unjust prejudices it may have against persons whom these people do not like, especially if those persons are in an opposing Party. What good is it, they say, to undertake the Apology of Heretics? Can one have too much hatred for their opinions? When they are believed to be a little more pernicious than they actually are, it will serve to further distance those who hold such a disadvantageous judgment. I have never been of this opinion. The love of Truth alone must lead us to render justice to everyone. Furthermore, this desire to charge Heretics with errors they did not hold can sometimes be very harmful. For if people, who are otherwise poorly informed, once come to discover that Heretics are being falsely accused on certain Articles, they will be tempted to believe that it is the same for the other Articles, and could easily allow themselves to be seduced.* This Reflection is equitable and judicious. What confidence can a Disciple have in a Master who lies, who imposes upon him? One does not think of it, but the Frauds, which one dares to call *pious* <note>original: "fraudes pieuses," referring to the historical practice of "pious frauds" where lies or forgeries were used to promote religious faith.</note>, are fit only to shake the certainty of the Christian Religion.

---

<columns>2</columns>

(1) The Book *On the Advantage of Believing* <note>original Latin: "De Utilitate credendi"</note> is from the year 391. It is addressed to *Honoratus*, a friend of St. Augustine, who was still involved in Manichaeism.

(2) ACTS *of the Disputation of Archelaus, Bishop of Mesopotamia, and Mani the Heresiarch.* <note>original Latin: "ACTA Disputationis Archelai, Episcopi Mesopotamiae, & Manetis Haeresiarchae"</note> It is under this title that this piece was published by Mr. *Zaccagni*, Librarian of the Vatican. See his MONUMENTS *of the Greek and Latin Church* <note>original Latin: "MONUMENTA Ecclesiae Graecae & Latinae"</note> printed in Rome in 1698. The work itself is entitled in the Text, *The True Treasure, or the Disputation held in Cascar, a City of Mesopotamia.* <note>original Latin: "THESAURUS Verus, sive Disputatio habita in CASCAR, Civitate Mesopotamiae"</note> The title of *True Treasure* is an allusion and an opposition to that of *Treasure of Life*, which Mani had given to one of his Books.

(3) That is to say, of a City of Mesopotamia.

<header>PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE.</header>
<sig>A 3</sig>

<margin>Antiquity does not authorize Fables.</margin>
We must not, therefore, impose upon Heretics, nor should we bear ill will toward those who, without undertaking their defense, content themselves with making them known as they truly were. This is the sole goal I have set for myself in this Work. Fables acquire much credit as they age, but they are no less Fables for it. And what harm is there in tearing away the mask of Truth from them, even if they have worn it for fourteen or fifteen hundred years? Is this not what a number of skillful Critics have done in our own century, who, without any scruple, have placed among the rank of Fables the history of the *Thundering Legion* <note>The "Thundering Legion" (Legio XII Fulminata) was a Roman legion; a popular Christian legend claimed a miraculous rainstorm saved them in 174 AD in response to the prayers of Christian soldiers.</note>, that of the *Statue* erected by the Romans in honor of *Simon the Magician* <note>Simon Magus, a figure from the New Testament; early Church Fathers claimed a statue in Rome inscribed "Simoni Deo Sancto" was dedicated to him, though modern scholars believe it was actually dedicated to the Sabine deity Semo Sancus.</note>, and many others of the same sort.

<margin>Origin of the History of Manes.</margin>
When I looked closely at the history of **Manes** <note>The prophet Mani (c. 216–274 AD), founder of Manichaeism.</note> and **Manichaeism**, it appeared to me to be of the same character as those I have just mentioned.

<margin>Acts of his Dispute with Archelaus. Syriac Original. Greek Translation.</margin>
We primarily derive this history from an ancient piece titled: (2) *ACTS of the Dispute between ARCHELAUS, Bishop of Mesopotamia (3), and the Heresiarch MANES.* It is believed that (4) the Original of these Acts was written in Syriac and translated into Greek by a certain **Hegemonius**. Some even imagine that this (5) Translation followed the Original very closely. But I am persuaded that this Work did not appear in Greek until after **Eusebius** <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the foundational historian of the early Christian church.</note> had composed and published his *Ecclesiastical History*; that is to say, in the span of time between the year (6) 326 or 330, and the year 348 or 350, when **Cyril of Jerusalem** was writing his *Catecheses* <note>The "Catechetical Lectures," a series of twenty-three instructions for Christian converts.</note>.

<margin>This Translation only appeared after the year 330 or 340.</margin>
The reason for this is that *Cyril* speaks at length, in his *VIth Catechesis*, both of the *Disputes of Archelaus* and of the History of *Manes*; whereas *Eusebius* says not a single word about them in his *Ecclesiastical History*. It even appears from his silence that he had not heard of *Archelaus*, and that he knew no particulars of the life of our **Heresiarch** <note>A term used for the founder of a heretical sect.</note>.

<margin>Only a Latin Version remains.</margin>
The Syriac Original, assuming it ever existed, and the Greek Translation are lost. All that remains to us is a Latin Version, made from the Greek, which is very ancient.

---

<columns>2</columns>

(4) The questions concerning this piece, its Author, and when and how it may have been composed—all of this will be examined when we treat the Authenticity of these Acts. For now, it is only a matter of reporting what is said of them.

(5) Mr. **Zaccagni** <note>Lorenzo Alessandro Zaccagni (1657–1712), a Vatican librarian who published ancient Greek and Latin manuscripts.</note>, as will be seen hereafter, believes that *Hegemonius* himself wrote at least the second Dispute of *Archelaus* in Syriac, and that he immediately translated the entire Work into Greek.

<column-break/>

(6) **Father Pagi** <note>Antoine Pagi (1624–1699), a French ecclesiastical historian known for his chronological critiques of Baronius.</note> claims that *Eusebius* published his *Ecclesiastical History* in 328. See his *Critique of Baronius* Year 328. § 18. 19. And **Mr. Cave** <note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English church historian.</note>, in *Eusebio Caesariensi*. Other skillful Moderns, such as **Daillé** <note>Jean Daillé (1594–1670), a prominent French Protestant theologian.</note> etc., judge that the *History* of *Eusebius* did not appear until 330. He died around the year 340.

<header># PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE.</header>

<margin>made toward the end of the 5th or in the 6th Century.</margin>
...the Greek translation of the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century work claiming to be a transcript of a debate between Bishop Archelaus and Mani; modern scholars agree it is likely a fictionalized polemic.</note> are either lost or hidden in some Library. We have only a Latin version remaining, and a rather barbaric one at that, the precise date of which is unknown. It is only judged to have been made before the 7th century; what is certain is that it is later than the time of St. **Augustine**, and even that of Pope **Leo I**, who died around the year 461, for no trace of it is seen in their works against the Manichaeans.

<margin>This is the sole source from which the Church Fathers drew the History of Mani.</margin>
It is from this Greek Translation, or from the Latin Version, that all the Church Fathers took what they tell us of the *History of Mani* and the *Origin of Manichaeism*. **Cyril of Jerusalem**, St. **Epiphanius**, **Socrates** <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian church historian.</note>, and the Greeks in general, have all drawn from this source, as Father (1) **Petau** and Mr. (2) de **Tillemont** <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian known for his scrupulous use of primary sources.</note> acknowledge. The Latins had no other source either. However, I dare to assert that this source is not at all pure. There are some truths, but few in number, and what little there is has been altered, confused, and mixed with manifest fables, as will be seen by the Examination I am about to make of them in this Work.

<margin>Plan of the 1st Part.</margin>
It is divided into two Parts. The first contains a CRITICAL EXAMINATION of the *History of Mani, and the Origin of Manichaeism*: but having found that this History was reported very differently by the Greeks and Latins on one hand, and on the other by the Syrians, Persians, and Arabs, I have divided it into two Books.

<margin>History of Mani, according to the Greeks and Latins.</margin>
In the first, I provide the History of **Mani** and Manichaeism according to the Greek and Latin Authors. This is the one that all our **Heresiologists** <term>heresiologists: writers, typically orthodox, who cataloged and refuted what they considered to be heretical sects</term> have copied. I examine it step by step, and I show that it is full of ignorance, lies, and absurdities. I then report the substance of the *Disputes of Archelaus against Mani*, and I show that everything in it is fabricated, right down to the setting, which the Author saw fit to place in **Kashkar**, in Roman Mesopotamia, where no city of that name can be found. In general, this entire piece, which is called the *Acts of the Dispute of Archelaus*, is nothing but a Romance fabricated by a Greek and published after the year 330—sixty years, or thereabouts, after the death of **Mani**.
