**origin** of his Heresy, according to the Syrians, the Persians, and the Arabs. This latter account has almost nothing in common with the first: one would say that these are the Histories of two entirely different men. However, the latter has the advantage of being much better proven, and of presenting to the Reader a face where one perceives natural traits—which, if they are not entirely those of the truth, at least approach it extremely closely. Furthermore, when I find the opportunity, I mix in here and there a few Episodes, which serve to vary a narration that is entirely intertwined with Criticism, and whose principal subject interests only those persons who apply themselves to the study of Ecclesiastical History and who see with pleasure the new discoveries that can be made there.

<margin>Concept of Part II.</margin>
That is the Plan for the *Historical Part* of this Work. The second part, which is *Dogmatic*, will be much more extensive. There, I shall report the Principles of our Heresiarch <note>A "Heresiarch" is the founder of a heretical sect or movement.</note>, his Opinions or his Errors, the Worship, the Morals, the religious Observances, and the Ecclesiastical Government of the Sect. I shall endeavor to discover the Origin of his Errors, which for the most part come from Eastern Philosophy. A (3) Modern Scholar seems to have noticed this, but he did not take the trouble to research it.

<margin>Necessity of Criticism in the Reading of Ecclesiastical History. (a) 1 Thess. 5:21.</margin>
I shall treat my subject critically, following the Rule of St. Paul: *(a) Prove all things; hold fast that which is good.* History in general, and Ecclesiastical History in particular, is very often nothing but a confused mixture of the false and the true, piled up by writers who were poorly informed, credulous, or passionate. This applies above all to the History of Heretics and Heresies. It is up to the attentive and judicious Reader to make the discernment, with the help of a Criticism that is neither too timid nor too rash. Without the help of this Art, one wanders through History like a Pilot upon the seas when he has neither compass nor sea chart. I only pray the Reader to remember that I am giving him only an *Essay on the History and the Dogmas of Mani*. Often one feels, one perceives well enough what is false, but it is not as easy to discover the true, because the monuments <note>In this context, "monuments" refers to primary source documents and historical records.</note> are missing, and those we have are full of confusion, inaccuracy, and—if one dared to say it—unreliability. Even when we have the good fortune to grasp the truth...

<margin>(3) In which (referring to the Dogmas of Mani) this seems to me worthy of singular notice: that many things, though usually attributed to the superstitions of the ancient Greeks and Latins, have an origin far older than is generally believed, and should be traced back to the Ancient Discipline of the Orientals. <note>Original Latin: "In quibus... illud mihi animadversione singulari dignum videtur, multa, e veterum Graecorum Latinorumque superstitione, antiquioris esse quam censentur Originis, & ad Priscam Orientalium Disciplinam referenda."</note> <term>Tollius</term> <note>Jacobus Tollius (1633–1696), a Dutch classicist and alchemist.</note>. *Notable Observations from an Italian Journey*, p. 128.</margin>

None, however, has carried impudence further than this *Scythianus*, for he has not only recognized two enemy Principles, both co-eternal, but he has admitted all the consequences that result from such an Error.

<margin>His History.</margin>

# THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. I.
<page-num>17</page-num>
<center>C</center>
<meta>catchword: conferred</meta>

<margin>Tyrbon & Sisinnius.</margin>
...as was recounted by *Archelaus* to the people of Diodoris. The Bishop cites two witnesses, both disciples of the <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>The leader or founder of a heretical sect, in this case, Mani.</note>, one named <term>TYRBON</term> and the other <term>SISINNIUS</term>. These are two very different men.

<margin>Tyrbon is highly suspect.</margin>
*Tyrbon* is an obscure man, a disciple of the lowest rank, and a weak and frivolous spirit if there ever was one. Discouraged by the difficulties he encountered while traveling from *Arabion* to *Cascar*, he resolved "no longer to return to his Master, and to have no further communion with him from that point forward" (5). He renounced Manichaeism and embraced the Faith, but his conversion bore two poor characteristics: first, it was too hasty; second, it was not freely given, since (6) *Marcellus* showered him with gifts, and *Archelaus* immediately raised him to the <term>Deaconate</term> <note>An ordained ministry in the Christian church, often a step toward the priesthood.</note>. *Tyrbon* chose the right side, but he chose it too soon, and he has more the look of a deserter from heresy than a true proselyte of the Faith. He should at least have waited until his Master, defeated in a public dispute, gave him just reasons to abandon him.

<margin>Sisinnius did not testify to what is attributed to him.</margin>
All of this makes *Tyrbon's* testimony highly suspect. That of *Sisinnius* would carry greater weight, but it is hindered by a difficulty that is not easy to resolve, and which persuades me that he is a witness invented by the author of the *Relation* to gain credibility with the common people; I believe *Sisinnius* never said what he is made to say. Here is the nature of that difficulty:

<margin>He succeeded Mani in the Pontificate of the Sect.</margin>

He intended for this college of twelve <term>MASTERS</term> to endure forever under a fixed President who would hold his place.

It is not known whether, before dying, the Heresiarch himself designated *Sisinnius* as his successor, or if the primacy was conferred—

<margin>
It is impossible that the sect would have chosen, as its Leader, a man who had just renounced and betrayed Manichaeus.
</margin>
...altered by his colleagues, but it is certain that he succeeded *Manichaeus*, and was, after his death, the Leader and Prince of the new <term>Heresy</term><note>A belief or opinion contrary to orthodox religious (especially Christian) doctrine.</note>. This is what our (1) Ecclesiastical Writers testify: from which it follows, first, that it is not at all true that *Sisinnius* embraced the *Orthodox Faith*, as (2) *Archelaus* says; and secondly, that it is not at all true that he recounted to him, and upheld in the presence of his Master, the scandalous History of all the Authors of the Sect. Who could be persuaded that *Manichaeus* would have, upon dying, placed his authority into the hands of an <term>Apostate</term><note>A person who abandons a religious or political belief or principle.</note>, who had just renounced his Doctrine and betrayed him? Or that his Disciples would have elevated this Apostate to the Seat of their Master? If *M. de Tillemont* <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian known for his meticulous use of primary sources.</note> had thought it through, I do not believe he would have dared to say

<margin>
(a) Tillem. as above. Article VI. & XI.
</margin>
with such confidence, (a) *that the History of Manichaeus comes originally from* SISINNIUS *his Disciple, who, having converted, reported the History of this Impostor to Archelaus, and maintained it in the presence of Manichaeus himself.*

What makes this objection invincible is that between the conversion of *Sisinnius* to the Catholic Faith and his elevation to the Manichaean Pontificate, only a few days, a month, or perhaps two at most, could have elapsed.

*Manes* <note>Another name for Mani.</note> goes to *Cascar*; *Sisinnius* accompanies him there: it is there that he abandons him, embraces the Catholic Faith, reveals to *Archelaus* all the shameful secrets of the Sect, and maintains them to the face of *Manichaeus* himself. The latter, forced to flee, is discovered, taken, led to the King, and delivered to the Executioner. *Sisinnius* succeeds him. After such great cowardice, after such a great scandal, while the blood of *Manichaeus* is still smoking, the Disciples of this <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>The founder of a heretical sect.</note> nonetheless choose him as their Leader and raise him to his chair. I would sooner believe that the Apostles would have chosen Judas as the successor of Jesus Christ, if that Traitor had lived, and that they would have proclaimed him his Vicar in the universal Church.

After these reflections on the Witnesses of *Archelaus*, let us examine his Narrative, and begin with the History of *Scythianus*.

### CHAPTER II.

### *Examination of the History of* SCYTHIANUS, *and of the Origin of Manichaeism.*

<margin>Various errors of Archelaus.</margin>
I. Archelaus relates (1) "that a certain SCYTHIANUS, who was a native of Scythia, and who lived in the time of the Apostles, was the Author and Leader of the Manichaean <term>Heresy</term><note>A belief or opinion contrary to established religious doctrine.</note>." This opening does not predispose one in favor of the Historian: *Scythianus* is not a Scythian by birth: he is an Arab. He did not live in the time of the Apostles: he is removed from them by two whole centuries. And finally, he is not the first who sought to introduce the opinion of <term>Two Principles</term><note>The dualistic belief that the universe is governed by two equal and opposing forces, one of Good (Light) and one of Evil (Darkness).</note> into the Christian Religion.

<margin>1st Error. Scythianus is Arab, not Scythian.</margin>
1. Firstly, *Scythianus* was not from *Scythia*: he was an Arab, from that region of Arabia which is named *Saracene*, and descended from the Peoples who inhabited it. This is testified to by (2) *Cyril of Jerusalem*, *St. Epiphanius*, *Photius*, and *Archelaus* himself.

The idea that the Greeks and the Western Peoples have chosen to form of the Arabs predisposes one at first against the Person of *Scythianus* and against his Philosophy. This Nation is regarded as a Barbarous Nation, and one would not be wrong if one understood by that only a People who inhabit Deserts: for that is, according to some Scholars, the true meaning of the word (3) BARBARIAN, which they claim draws its origin from two Syriac words meaning SON or INHABITANT OF THE DESERT. But if one understands by a *Barbarous People* a Nation that has neither Science, nor <term>Politeness</term><note>In this 18th-century context, "politeness" refers to social refinement, civilization, and advanced culture.</note>, nor Morals, one would do a great wrong to the Arabs by qualifying them in such a manner. The journey that the Queen of *Sheba* made to Jerusalem to hear *Solomon* shows that in the most ancient times the Arabs loved the Sciences: And, what seems to do little—

A Prejudice, which I shall call religious, has led most of our Theologians to believe that the Hebrew Language is a Divine Language, that it deserves preference over all others, under the pretext that it was that of *Adam* and *Eve*, and that God was, so to speak, its Inventor. this perfection of a People's Language is manifest proof of the superiority of their Genius. For it is from the vivacity, taste, and delicacy of the Mind, the extent of Knowledge, and the fertility of Imagination, that abundance, beauty, and the precision of expression are born.

<margin>The Arabs long preserved the true Religion.</margin>
As for the Religion of the Arabs, it was also preserved for a long time—and perhaps longer among them in its original purity—than among other Nations. The Israelites had corrupted theirs in Egypt, while it was still maintained in Arabia. It was in that Country that the illustrious and incorruptible *Job* allowed the lights of a pure Faith and eminent virtue to shine forth at once. It was in the same Country that *Jethro*, the Father-in-law of *Moses*, offered Sacrifices only to the true God. If this Religion was later defiled by Idolatry, it is a misfortune that has been only too general, and from which even the Hebrews did not protect themselves, notwithstanding the Revelations of so many Prophets, and although their Republic was, so to speak, founded upon the faith and the worship of a single God.

<margin>A poor parallel between Scythian and Mahomet.</margin>
Since *Scythian* <note>Scythianus, a legendary figure in Christian accounts who is said to have visited Egypt and India, bringing back the dualistic doctrines that would later influence Mani.</note> descended from the Arabs, and the famous Impostor *Mahomet* <note>The Prophet Muhammad, whom the author, writing from an 18th-century Christian perspective, labels an impostor.</note> had the same origin, Modern Authors have not failed to draw a parallel between them. They have even taken this opportunity to tarnish Arabia, as if Heresy were a product of the soil, or as if some evil Demon breathed Imposture and Error into the minds there. I well understand that such reflections may escape even good Geniuses, but they are both too lacking in substance and too dangerous to be adopted. For after all, was it not in Arabia that *Moses* formed himself for the great Ministry to which God had destined him from birth? Was it not while he wandered in the solitudes of Midian that God appeared to him, and gave him the glorious commission to deliver his People from both oppression and the Idolatry of the Egyptians? Let us avoid parallels that would provide Libertines <note>In this context, "Libertines" refers to freethinkers or skeptics who might use such comparisons to undermine the divine origin of all religions.</note> with pretexts to make their own, in turn, which would be very injurious to the true Religion.

<margin>Division of Arabia.</margin>
Geographers have long divided Arabia into three Parts, which they distinguish by the nature of their Soil, and which they name for that reason, *Arabia Felix* <note>Happy or Fertile Arabia.</note>, *Arabia Petrea* <note>Stony or Mountainous Arabia.</note>, and *Arabia Deserta* <note>Desert Arabia.</note>. The latter bordered Assyria; the second Egypt and Idumaea; and the first, which was<note>Catchword: was</note>

->### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. II.<-

<margin>India, where the Apostles preached, is Arabia Felix.</margin>was separated from the rest of the Continent by the two other parts, and extended to the Ocean, along the Red Sea and the Persian Gulf. It is called today the *Yemen*, or the *Yeman*. It was formerly known under the name of *India*, and it is likely there <margin>(a) *Tillemont, Ecclesiastical Memoirs, St. Bartholomew. Article I. Note II.*</margin> and not *(a)* in the East Indies, that Christianity was carried by one of the Apostles, or by their first Disciples.

<margin>Two *Saracenias*.</margin>When one consults the Geographers *(1)* on the situation of this region of Arabia, which they call *Saracenia*, one finds that they place it very differently. This could come from the fact that there were two *Saracenias*; one in *Mountainous Arabia*, near the *Red Sea*, and separated from Egypt both by that Sea and by Mountains that *(2)* *Ptolemy* calls *The Black Mountains*: The other in *Arabia Felix* <note>Arabia Felix, or "Happy Arabia," was the ancient name for the fertile southern region of the Arabian Peninsula, modern-day Yemen.</note>, but very close to *Arabia Deserta*, and consequently also to *Chaldea*. However, *Eusebius* (3) testifies "that the *Saracens* are a People who inhabit the heart of the Arabian solitudes, and who extend to the borders of Assyria. He adds that the Prophet *Isaiah* calls them *Arabs*, because their Country was neighboring that of the *Arabs*." But, as the ancient Geographers seem to speak of two *Saracenias*, whose positions I have marked, and as learned <margin>(b) *See Assemani, as cited above. Vol. III. Part II. p. 568.*</margin> Moderns *(b)* appear to be of their opinion, it is also the one I shall follow.

<margin>*Scythian* was from the *Saracenia* near *Chaldea*.</margin>I had first believed that *Scythian* <note>Scythianus, according to early Christian writers like Epiphanius, was a merchant who traveled to India and Egypt, developing the dualistic philosophy that Mani would later inherit.</note> was from *Mountainous Arabia*, or the sterile region; based on what *Archelaus* tells us, and after him St. *Epiphanius*, that his wife being Egyptian, persuaded him to prefer the pleasant stay in Egypt to that of the Arabian Deserts. But stronger reasons than the testimony of *Archelaus* have made me change my mind. As soon as one speaks of *Saracens*, not only to the common people but even to certain scholars, they conceive only of troops of thieves, who run about everywhere to carry out their banditry. It has even been imagined that *Saracen* and *Brigand* were synonymous terms. This nation is being wronged. Perhaps it abused its liberty, but it is known in general that it had its own police, its laws, its philosophers, that it was very much devoted (2) to commerce, and that *Saracen* means (3) *Oriental* <note>The author is refuting the popular 18th-century prejudice that "Saracen" derived from a word for "thief," arguing instead for a geographical meaning related to the East.</note>.

M. de Tillemont’s weak evasion.

D 2

...had been a follower of *Aristotle*. (5) He *imitated*, says Cyril, the *Doctrine* and the *Discipline* of *Aristotle*. I have two observations to make on this passage: the first against *Cyril* himself; the second against certain Modern authors who have misunderstood his expression.

<margin>Critique of Cyril of Jerusalem. Manichaean philosophy is very different from that of Aristotle.</margin>
Regarding *Cyril*, there is no proof that Manichaean philosophy drew its origin from that of *Aristotle*. For although this philosopher believed, like *Plato*, that Evil came from Matter and from its eternal and incorrigible imperfection, it is nonetheless not yet decided among scholars whether he did not also teach the eternity of the world; or rather, whether he recognized two truly distinct Substances—one thinking, free, and active, which is God; the other which was the subject of God’s action. <note>The author is debating whether Aristotle was a dualist—someone who believes in two separate co-eternal principles like God and Matter—or a monist who saw them as part of the same system.</note> For if there are skillful men who justify *Aristotle* against the charge of Atheism, there are others who accuse him of it, maintaining that he was a Spinozist. <note>original: "Spinofiste." A follower of Baruch Spinoza, a 17th-century philosopher often accused of pantheism, or identifying God with the physical universe.</note> One may specifically see this question treated by Mr. *(a)* *Wolff*.

<margin>*(a)* *Manichaeism before the Manichaeans*, section XXXV, p. 145 and following. It is the Sabaeans who are Aristotelians.</margin>
If *Cyril* had known that ancient Pagan Sect which the Arabs call the *SABAEANS*, I believe he would have confused them with that of *Mani*. <note>The Sabaeans of Harran were a group of pagans in the Islamic world known for preserving Greek philosophical and scientific traditions.</note> For it is true *(b)* that the former are entirely in agreement with the sentiments of *Aristotle* regarding the *Principles of all things*, the *Elements*, the nature of *Time*, and that of the *Heavens*—which they say are made of a *fifth Essence* <note>The "quintessence" or ether, a celestial substance distinct from the four earthly elements (earth, air, fire, water).</note> which, being exempt from any kind of mixture, is also incorruptible; as well as on *Meteors* and the *eternity of the World*. *Mani* held very different views on almost all these matters, and if he agreed in anything with the *Sabaeans*, it was on a sort of worship he rendered to the Sun and the Moon; but he did not hold the same opinion of them as this Pagan Sect.

<margin>*(b)* See Hottinger, *Oriental History*, Book I, 8, p. 283; and compare the *Specimen of Arabic History* by Pococke.</margin>
<margin>Critique of some Moderns: Meaning of the word Bios.</margin>
Regarding the Moderns, several have misunderstood *Cyril’s* expression, and instead of translating that *Scythianus imitated the Doctrine of Aristotle*, they translated that he *imitated his Life* or *Manners*. These clever men did not notice that the Greek word *Bios*, <term>βίος</term> <note>original: βίος (bios). While commonly meaning "biography" or "life," the author argues that in this context it refers to a system of thought or a school of study.</note>, does not signify in this context a *way of life*, but rather *Art* or *Discipline*, as a (6) German scholar very well observed in his remarks on the first book of *Photius* against the *Manichaeans*.

<margin>Critique of Cyril of Jerusalem. The philosophy of Mani is very different from that of Aristotle.</margin>

For although this Philosopher believed, like *Platon*, that Evil came from Matter and from its eternal and incorrigible imperfection, it is nonetheless not yet decided among the learned whether he taught the Eternity of the World; or rather, whether he recognized two truly distinct Substances—one thinking, free, and active, which is God; the other which was the subject of God's action. For if there are skilled men who justify *Aristotle* against charges of Atheism, there are others who accuse him of it, maintaining that he was a <term>Spinozist</term>. <note>A follower of Baruch Spinoza; in this 18th-century context, it refers to the belief that God and the material universe are the same substance, often equated with atheism.</note> One can see this question treated in particular by Mr. *(a)* Wolff.

<margin>*(a)* Manichaeism before the Manichaeans. §. XXXV. p. 145. & seq. It is the Sabians who are Aristotelians.</margin>
If *Cyril* had known that ancient Pagan sect which the Arabs call the *SABIANS*, I believe he would have confused them with the followers of *Mani*. <note>The Sabians were a religious group in Mesopotamia often associated with the preservation of Greek philosophy and Hermeticism.</note> For it is true *(b)* that the former are entirely in agreement with the sentiments of *Aristotle* regarding the *Principles of all things*, the *Elements*, the *nature of Time*, and that of the *Heavens*, which they say is of a fifth *Essence* <note>The "quintessence," a celestial element distinct from earth, air, fire, and water.</note> which, being exempt from any kind of mixture, is also incorruptible; as well as on *Meteors* and the *Eternity of the World*. *Mani* held very different sentiments on almost all these matters; and if he agreed in any way with the Sabians, it was on a kind of worship that he rendered to the Sun and the Moon, though he did not hold the same opinion as that Pagan sect regarding them.

<margin>*(b)* See Hottinger, *Oriental History*, Book I. 8. p. 283. & compare the *Specimen of Arabic History* by Pococke.</margin>
<margin>Critique of some Moderns: Significance of the word βίος.</margin>
Regarding the moderns, several have misunderstood *Cyril’s* expression; instead of translating it as *Scythianus imitated the Doctrine of Aristotle*, they translated it as *he imitated his Life and Morals*. These learned men did not notice that the Greek word *Bios* (βίος) does not signify in this context a "way of life," but rather "Art" or "Discipline," as a (6) German scholar very rightly observed in his remarks on the first book of *Photius* against the *Manichaeans*.

# HISTORY OF MANI ACCORDING TO
<meta>catchword: says</meta>

<margin>
Scythianus and Mani as contemporaries.
(a) See the *Library of the Fathers*, Vol. IV, Part II, col. 857.
Proof of this fact.
</margin>
Scythianus flourished approximately two centuries after the Apostles. Mr. de *Tillemont* placed him toward the middle of the second century, in which he perhaps followed (a) *Serapion of Thmuis* in Egypt, who places *Scythianus* after *Valentinus* and *Marcion*. But Father *Alexandre* <note>Referring to Noël Alexandre, a 17th-century Dominican theologian and church historian.</note>, who judged the time of this <term>heresiarch</term> <note>The founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note> more accurately, places him in (1) the 3rd century, without specifying precisely if it was at the beginning or toward the middle. The learned Dominican could have said that *Scythianus* flourished at the same time as *Mani*, as is clearly proven by a letter the latter wrote to him, of which *Photius* has preserved (2) a fragment. I am well aware that in the *Greek Library* of Mr. *Fabricius*, this fragment is attributed by some to *Valentinus* and by others to *Mani*. But it would have been easy to ensure the true author if one had taken the trouble to resort to the original—that is, the extract that *Photius* left us of the work of *Eulogius of Alexandria*. It is there that this Patriarch quotes in these very words (3), **Mani writing to Scythianus**.

<margin>
Weak evasion by Mr. de Tillemont.
</margin>
Thus, Mr. de *Tillemont* did not deny that the letter was by *Mani*; but to avoid the necessary consequence of this admission—which is that *Scythianus* and *Mani* were contemporaries—he chose to suppose, without any foundation in history, some other *Scythianus*, a Manichaean like the first but a hundred years later. This is the last resort of bias and stubbornness. Therefore, the learned Mr. *Fabricius* pays no regard to it and has very rightly concluded from the fragment in question that *Scythianus* and *Mani* lived at the same time, with the only difference being that the former was older and the latter younger.

<margin>
3. Archelaus's error regarding the origin of Manichaeism. It does not originate with the Greeks.
(b) *Ecclesiastical History*, Book I, 22.
</margin>

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO
<meta>catchword: toû-</meta>

Such then were the Masters of *Scythianus*, if we are to believe the Fathers: *Pythagoras*, according to *Archelaus* <note>The author of the *Acts of Archelaus*, an early anti-Manichaean polemic.</note>; *Empedocles*, according to *Socrates* <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian historian.</note>; *Aristotle* according to *Cyril* of Jerusalem. *St. Epiphanius* associates another with them, whom M. de *Tillemont* <note>Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a celebrated French ecclesiastical historian.</note> has not forgotten. As if three Pagan Philosophers were not enough to turn the head of the Arabian Philosopher, that clever Modern calls the evil Spirit to their aid, and assures us that the Demon came to help *Scythianus* to invent and form his System of the two Principles <note>Dualism: the belief in two co-eternal, opposing powers of Good and Evil.</note>. Since this passage is so carefully crafted, I believe the Reader will be pleased to see it here.

<margin>Tillemont's Reflection on the causes of the Heresy of Scythianus.</margin>
*Scythianus*, says M. de *Tillemont*, *finding himself in abundance, in idleness, and in delights, agitated by that mobility and restlessness which is a natural consequence of Voluptuousness; puffed up by the Vanity that his Mind and Science gave him, and driven by the unfortunate desire—which was then ruining so many others—to see himself at the head of a Party, set himself to dreaming in order to find something new. Indeed, reasoning on the Principles of Pythagoras and Empedocles, and* **BEING AIDED BY THE DEMON**, *he took it into his mind that, since the World was filled with contrary things, this opposition must come from two Roots, from two enemy Principles.*

<margin>Critique of this Reflection.</margin>
M. de *Tillemont* provides us in these words with an example of the false judgments into which a wise and judicious man allows himself to be led when he wishes to be a servile imitator of the Ancients. One senses all the trouble this Author has taken to trace this Portrait, and to gather all the disproportionate and ill-matched features from which *St. Epiphanius* had composed it. For after all, are Abundance and Delights suited to producing Systems on the Origin of Evil? Is it in dreaming upon this that the Voluptuous amuse themselves? Their generous Audacity has quite other objects. It seeks reasons to doubt the existence of a God, of a Providence; it tries not to discover the cause of Evil, but to annihilate it; to confound Vices and Virtues, to erase the idea of Sin in the Conscience, and to tear away the fear of Punishments. As for this restless, fickle Spirit, this love of Novelty, this Ambition to become *Head of a Party*, by what right have the Ancients accused *Scythianus* of them—a man they knew so little that they were ignorant even of the time in which he lived? Will we never recover from the malignant and rash habit of seeking

### CHAPTER III.

->Where one continues to examine the Origin of Manichaeism.<-

I. I resume the Narrative of *Archelaus* <note>The author refers to the *Acts of Archelaus*, an early 4th-century work that is the primary source for the legendary life of Mani and his supposed predecessors.</note>. What he says regarding the origin of *Scythianus's* <note>A legendary figure described as a predecessor of Mani; he is often depicted as a wealthy merchant who traveled to India and Egypt, bringing back dualistic teachings.</note> Manichaeism is not certain: it even appears quite likely that he is mistaken, and that it was not from Pythagoras that our Arabian Philosopher drew his Errors. What he adds—that *Scythianus* was the first who tried to introduce Manichaeism into the Christian Religion—is altogether false. It is also false that this man was the Inventor of the War that suddenly ignited between the two Principles <note><term>Two Principles</term>: The fundamental dualistic belief that the universe is a battlefield between two co-eternal, opposing forces of Good/Light and Evil/Darkness.</note>, and which was the occasion for the Creation of the World. All this was known in the East, where the Human Spirit had long before imagined all these ridiculous chimeras.

<margin>Slight Contradiction of M. de Tillemont for following the Ancients too closely.</margin>
I have just observed this, but let me be permitted to remark upon it again: the imitation of the Ancients spoils the judgment of M. de *Tillemont* <note>Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont, a 17th-century historian known for his meticulous but often uncritical compilation of primary sources.</note>, whom I would criticize less if I did not esteem him so infinitely. He has represented *Scythianus* to us as dreaming profoundly in order to invent something new: to create, by dint of Meditation, a *new System* on the origin of Evil. However, the same Author tells us, following *Archelaus* and *Socrates* <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century ecclesiastical historian.</note>, that *Scythianus* had taken his Heresy from Pythagoras and *Empedocles*, who had taught it to Greece more than six hundred years before he came into the world.

<margin>Whether Pythagoras was a Manichaean.</margin>
The question of whether Pythagoras was a Manichaean has become Problematic. It is indeed so in one respect, but in another, it certainly is not. It is merely a question of the degree of conformity between the two Systems. If one judges that of Pythagoras by the manner in which *Porphyry* and *Plutarch* represent it, one will easily confuse it with that of *Mani*. "(1) Pythagoras, says *Porphyry*, conceived of two opposing Powers: one GOOD, which he called *Unity*, *Light*, the *Right*, the *Equal*,

# HISTORY OF MANI ACCORDING TO
D 3
<meta>catchword: Life</meta>

> "...the Equal, the Stable, the Right. The other EVIL, which he named the <term>Binary</term> <note>The "Dyad" or "Binary" in Pythagorean thought represents duality, division, and the source of evil, as opposed to the "Monad" or unity.</note>, the *Darkness*, the *Left*, the *Unequal*, the *Unstable*, the *Agitated*, or that which is carried away on all sides." All this appears very Manichaean, both in the ideas and in the terms used. But *Pythagoras* had not invented these ideas, nor these expressions; he held them from the Chaldeans, who were his masters on this subject, as well as those of *Scythianus* and *Mani*.

<margin>He took his ideas and his expressions from the Chaldeans.</margin>
*Pythagoras* (1) being still very young, *Mnesarchus* his father, who recognized his natural dispositions for all the Sciences, took him to *Tyre*, and recommended him to certain *Chaldeans*, because he had an extreme passion for knowing their Philosophy. These Philosophers apparently had a school in *Tyre*. Later, *Pythagoras* went to *Babylon*, where he remained for twelve years, and often saw a Magus named *Zabratus* (2), who instructed him in nature and <margin>He had Zabratus as his teacher.</margin> THE PRINCIPLES OF ALL THINGS. It is from the same and from other (3) Magi that he learned the rules and maxims that he brought to Italy, regarding everything concerning Religion, Purifications, Morals, and the Abstinences that befit Wise men.

<margin>If this Zabratus is Zoroaster. It is proven that he might be. (a) Hyde, as cited above, Ch. XXIV. p. 309. Ch. XXXI. p. 379.</margin>

Life during his travels in Egypt, Judea, Arabia, and finally (8) in Chaldea, where he stayed twelve years in Babylon. He likely did not return until around the sixty-third <term>Olympiad</term> <note>A four-year period used by the ancient Greeks for dating, starting from the first Olympic Games in 776 BCE.</note> (9), at the time when *Polycrates* had just suppressed the liberty of Samos, his homeland, which prevented him from returning there and obliged him to go and establish his school in Italy. This is confirmed by *Eusebius*, who asserts (10) that *Pythagoras* did not begin to make a noise in the world until around the second year of the sixty-fifth Olympiad. Thus, the timing of this Philosopher is very well marked. As for that of *Zoroaster*, *Abulfarage* <note>Also known as Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286), a prominent scholar and historian of the Syriac Orthodox Church.</note> testifies that he flourished under *Cambyses*, who succeeded *Cyrus* in the fourth year of the sixty-second Olympiad; three or four years before the tyranny of *Polycrates*, and when *Pythagoras* could still have been in Babylon. *Zoroaster* did not rise all at once to the status of a Prophet, and undoubtedly had a great reputation among the <term>Magi</term> <note>The priestly caste of ancient Persia and practitioners of Zoroastrianism.</note> several years prior. Regardless, it appears from this chronological calculation, which is quite well proven, that it is very possible that the Greek philosopher and the Persian philosopher had frequent conversations together on *Nature* and on the *Principles of all things*, and consequently, that the *Zabratus* of *Porphyry* and the *Zaratas* of *Plutarch* are the same as the *Zardasht* or the *Zerdusth* of the Persians.

<margin>Pythagoras is only half Manichaean if he is Zoroastrian.</margin>
To resume now the question of the Manichaeism of *Pythagoras*, it is certain that if he adopted the system of *Zoroaster*, he was only Manichaean in part. For it is proven that this latter philosopher recognized only one single supreme Principle, who is God, and who produced two subaltern Principles, one the Author of Good, and the other of Evil. Now *Mani* was careful not to admit that God was the Creator of the Demon; this proposition was horrifying to him. But if one supposes that *Pythagoras* had <term>Dualist</term> <note>Philosophers who believe the universe is governed by two opposing forces, such as Good and Evil or Light and Darkness.</note> Magi for teachers, it is very possible that he adopted their sentiments; however, he

<margin>What the Manichaeism of Pythagoras was.</margin>

The former, through their activity and lightness, remained in the Region of the Moon; the others, by their weight and immobility, were in the lowest Region, where our Earth is placed: God made the sublunary <note>The earthly realm below the moon, considered by ancients to be the place of change and decay.</note> World by mixing them together. There is a kind of Manichaeism in this, but it is not that of the **Scythian** <note>Scythianus, a legendary figure described in early Christian writings as a traveler to India who brought dualistic teachings back to Egypt, pre-dating Mani.</note>.

<margin>Which Heretic first attempted to introduce it into Christianity.</margin>
II. Let us pass to the question of who was the first who tried to introduce this Error into Christianity. The Author of the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century work recording a legendary debate between Mani and a Christian bishop named Archelaus.</note> believes it is our **Scythian**, because he imagined that this man lived in the time of the Apostles: but as he was mistaken in the Principle, he was also mistaken in the consequence. Learned Moderns trace the origin of Manichaeism to the famous <margin>Some Moderns say it was Simon the Magician.</margin> **SIMON**, surnamed **the Magician**, whom I would almost call the HERO of the *Romance of Heresies*. Never was History more fabulous than his. And regarding his Errors, those who report them mix in so many extravagances and contradictions that one does not know what to settle upon.

It is said (1) then that **Simon** was the first who undertook to introduce pure Manichaeism into the Christian Faith. If that were true, it would be necessary that this man had at least made a profession of recognizing the Authority of Jesus Christ and his Divine mission, whereas instead he fought it with all his strength. He collected everything he could find in the Gospels of apparent contradictions, in order to show that Jesus Christ was not a Prophet at all. This impious man even dared to blaspheme the Lord, as seen by these horrible words that the Author of the *Recognitions* <note>The *Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions*, an early Christian "religious novel" that features Simon Magus as a primary antagonist to Saint Peter.</note> has him say while speaking to **St. Peter**: (2) *The MAGICIAN, who sent you, and who could not even save himself from the punishment of the Cross.* I do not know why such a man is placed in the rank of Heretics, unless one also places there the Jews and Pagans who rose up against Jesus Christ and against his Gospel.

Let us speak a little of this Philosopher, whom some say was born in the Province of Samaria: others, on the Island of Cyprus, and who was, if I am not mistaken, an Apostate from Judaism. He held Errors which

<margin>The Fable of *Simon’s* *Helen*.</margin>
Nothing is more curious in his History than the Fable of his *Helen*. The Ancients tell us that this Impostor found in *Tyre*, in a house of prostitution, a very beautiful woman named *Helen*, and took her with him: That he said this woman was the first fruit of his Understanding, the first of the *Aeons* <term>Aeons: In Gnostic thought, these are divine emanations or beings that bridge the gap between the supreme, unknowable God and the material world.</term> who had emanated from it; That it was through her that he had formed the Angels, who created the World: That the Angels, in love with her beauty, had waged war for the love of her; that some had held her prisoner to prevent her from returning to Heaven, from whence she had descended: That she had then been obliged to hide herself, and to pass from body to body: That she was the same *Helen* who had excited the Trojan War; That he, *Simon*, was the Good Shepherd, who had come to seek and save this *Lost Sheep*. The Ancients add that he made his Disciples worship his Statue under the name of *Jupiter*, and that of *Helen* under the name of *Minerva*. If I am asked who the Authors are that recount this fine Story, I answer that it is (a) *St. Irenaeus*, *St. Epiphanius*, *Cyril of Jerusalem*, *Theodoret*, but in particular *Tertullian* <note>These figures are known as the "Church Fathers," early Christian theologians whose writings shaped the doctrine and history of the Church; they were often highly critical of "heretics" like Simon.</note>, who embellished it with all the ornaments provided by a vivid and fertile Imagination.

<margin>(a) *Irenaeus, Book I. 20. Epiphanius, Heresies XXI. Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechesis VI. Theodoret, Heretical Fables Book I. I. Tertullian, On the Soul, Chapter XXXIV.*</margin>
<margin>This Fable explained.</margin>
I do not know if this Impostor *Simon*, who was a Platonic Philosopher—as can be recognized by several of his Dogmas—was imitating Plato, who sometimes took pleasure in wrapping his Doctrine in allegorical Fables; but, without speaking now of the name *Helen*, because I shall say something of it in the Second Part of this Work, I shall content myself with explaining all this Mythology. It pleased the Ancients first to suppose that *Simon* claimed to be the supreme God, of whom the Creator of the World was only the Minister. I leave to them the care of reconciling this supposition with the ideas that *Simon* had of the Divinity. He defined it (3) "as a pure Light, an immense Light, an intellectual Light, a unique Being, supremely perfect, infinitely more excellent than all other Beings, but who, retired in an inaccessible light, communicated only to the most perfect Intelligences, and acted outwardly only through the Ministry...

...ministry of his Angels. With what audacity, with what impudence, could a man, visible and living among other men, claim to be this Supreme God, whom he maintained had never been seen, neither by the Creator of the World, nor by Jesus Christ himself?

It is also said that he boasted of being the *Son of God*, and the author of the *Recognitions* <note>The *Pseudo-Clementine Recognitions*, an early Christian work of prose that often portrays Simon Magus as a primary antagonist of the Apostle Peter.</note> has the boldness to put these words into his mouth (1) *I am the Son of God, who exists eternally* <note>original Latin: "Ego fum Filius Dei stans in æternum."</note>. However, the same author introduces him elsewhere saying to *St. Peter*, (2) "Remember, you said that God has a Son, which is an insult to God; for how can God have a Son, if he does not experience passions similar to those of men?" The author of the *Homilies*, called the *Clementines*, also has *Simon* say, (3) "I know well those who are worthy for these truths to be revealed to them, BUT I AM NOT THE SON" <note>original Greek: "Οἶδα τοὺς ἀξίους καὶ υἱὸς οὐκ εἰμί."</note>. These are very formal disavowals; and all the less suspicious since I draw them from Christian authors who refuted the doctrine of *Simon*. It was necessary to make these observations before developing the Fable of *Helen*; because it is founded on the supposition that *Simon* called himself the Supreme God.

<margin>Helen is the Soul, emanated from the supreme God, captive of the evil Demons, etc.</margin>
The beautiful *Helen* is the *Soul*. *Simon*, who was a Platonist <note>A follower of the philosophy of Plato, which emphasizes the ideal world and the soul's liberation from the material world.</note>, made her come forth from the Understanding of God. She is a (4) particle of the infinite Spirit, of the infinite Light, or an Emanation of the Supreme God. It appears that, in explaining the Fables of the Pagan Poets, he said that *the Soul was Minerva*, whom these poets made emerge from the *Brain*, or the *Understanding of Jupiter*. This Soul had been surprised by the Angels, Creators of Bodies, who had bound her with Matter, and who by this means held her captive and prevented her from returning to Heaven. To delay her return, they made her pass from body to body. This is *metempsychosis* <term>Metempsychosis: The transmigration of the soul; the belief that after death, the soul enters a new body.</term>, a dogma of Pythagoras, of Plato, and of so many others; but a dogma that had passed among the Samaritans and the Jews. This Captive had excited a war among the Angels, because the bad Angels made every effort to retain her, and the good Angels on their side tried to deliver her. She was in the Human Body as if in a house of prostitution. It is through generation <note>Biological reproduction.</note> that men bind her with Matter. She is the *Lost Sheep*: It is regarding the Soul that the Valentinians <note>A prominent Gnostic group named after their teacher Valentinus.</note> explained the (a) Parable of the Lord concerning the *Stray Sheep*.

### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. III. ###

This was the *Simonian* imposture: *Simon* claimed to be sent on behalf of the supreme God to deliver the Soul from its Prison and from the Tyranny of the evil Angels. He rejected the Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ, whom he said was merely the *Son of the Creator of the World*, if we believe <margin>(b) *Homily* XVIII. § 4. P. 738.</margin> (b) the Author of the *Clementines* <note>The *Pseudo-Clementine Homilies*, a 4th-century Christian work that portrays Simon Magus as a villainous sorcerer.</note>—that is to say, his *Minister*, and not the minister of the supreme God.

If one asks me for Authorities to prove that such was the mystical sense of the Fable of *Helen*, I will content myself with answering (5) for now that Common Sense, on one hand, does not allow us to believe that a reasoning Philosopher could have said in a literal sense what the Church Fathers make him say; and on the other hand, that this explanation is consistent with the Gnostic System regarding the loss and deliverance of the Soul. Furthermore, I am content for the Reader who does not approve of my ideas to stick blindly to the Accounts of the Ancients. He may believe, if he wishes, all the Fables that an old Impostor—whom I suspect to be the famous (6) *Leucius* <note>Leucius Charinus, the supposed author of several apocryphal "Acts" of the Apostles characterized by Gnostic leanings.</note>—inserted into his Apocrypha concerning *Simon*, including the Disputes of this Impostor with St. *Peter*; his foolish and unfortunate undertaking to ascend to Heaven, supported by two Demons; his apotheosis <note>The elevation of a human to divine status.</note> performed by the Romans and the Statue they erected for him; and finally, the institution of the Saturday Fast, which was said to have been established in Rome by the order of St. *Peter* to be a perpetual Monument of the Prayers that the Church made that day to obtain from Heaven the Victory that the Apostle won the following day over his profane and reckless Rival.

*Simon* did not believe that the sovereign God was the Creator of the visible World. He claimed that it was one of the Principal Angels who, with a certain number of other Angels of whom he was the Chief, worked on this great Work—nevertheless, by the (7) command and under the orders of the supreme God. He did not refuse this Angel the title of *God*, which has led some to say that he believed in a plurality of Gods. But I dare to assert that this is not accurate. He himself protests that he...

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO #
<meta>catchword: That</meta>

...recognizes (1) only one single God, who is the most excellent of all Beings. He therefore maintained only that the supreme God is not the immediate Creator of the visible World, and based this, among other points, 1st. on this Platonic Maxim, (2) "that the eternal Being makes only eternal beings like himself, and that Corporeal and fragile Beings are the productions of subaltern Intelligences." <note>Simon uses the Platonic idea that the highest God is too pure to touch matter directly, necessitating lower "craftsman" spirits or angels to build the physical world.</note> He based this 2nd. on the imperfections of our Sublunary World, which does not correspond to the idea he formed of divine Perfections. Thereupon Simon sought the cause of Evil and the Wicked one <note>The "Wicked one" refers to the Devil or the Demiurge in this context.</note> who is its Author. He proposes to St. Peter all possible means by which the Wicked one can exist, in order to conclude from them that the Sovereign God is not his Creator, nor consequently the creator of a World where his Adversary has so much power.

<margin>Question on the Origin of the Demon.</margin>
"Either the Wicked one was made, (3) said *Simon*, or he was not. If he was made, he was made by the God who made all things, either as an Animal that he formed, or as an Emanation that came out of his Substance and which, being foreign to Nature, came to mingle with it. Or perhaps there was a Matter, animate or inanimate, from which the Wicked one was born of himself, or from which God formed him: Or finally, God drew him from Nothing, in which case he is no longer a real Being, but a simple (4) Relation. <note>In philosophy, a "relation" suggests something that has no independent existence but only exists in reference to something else, like a shadow.</note> But if the Wicked one was not made, he has therefore always existed; he is eternal." This is the complicated Dilemma that *Simon* proposes to St. Peter, who is quite embarrassed <note>In 18th-century French, "embarrassé" often means being at a loss for an answer or placed in a difficult logical position.</note> by the choice he must make. He tries to show that, whatever supposition one makes, the true God cannot be the cause of Evil, and says finally that Scripture did not judge it appropriate to explain itself on the Question of the origin of the Demon. (5) *I recognize with you*, he says to *Simon*, *that there is a Prince of Evil, about whose origin Scripture has dared to say neither what is true, nor what is false.*

# THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. Book I. CH. III. #
<meta>Catchword: Cease</meta>

<margin>Simon's view appears to be pure Manichaeism.</margin>
It is a pity that this *Clementine* <note>The *Pseudo-Clementines*, a 2nd or 3rd-century series of Christian philosophical novels attributed to Pope Clement I, which feature debates between St. Peter and Simon Magus.</note> is imperfect, the Manuscripts being defective: for one would have seen there both the true sentiment of the Author, who was not an unskilled man, and that of *Simon*. However, it seems that the latter [Simon] held the opinion of *Manichaeus*, namely that the Demon is a production of Matter. This is suggested by these words, which he finally says to his Adversary, (6) *But if Matter is equal to God, both in duration and in force, as it is the enemy of God, it produces from itself Powers which oppose his Wills.* That is pure Manichaeism <note>A major dualistic religion founded by the prophet Mani, teaching a struggle between a good, spiritual world of light and an evil, material world of darkness.</note>. However, I would not dare to assert (7) that this was the sentiment of *Simon*; because he only proposes it without affirming it, and the conversation ends at that point. But as this Impostor, far from having been a Christian, rose up against Jesus Christ and wished to found a new Sect opposed to the Christian Church, one cannot say, it seems to me, that he was the first who tried to introduce this Heresy into it. He is, moreover, so little known in the East that I do not believe *Manes* borrowed anything from him, nor that he should be regarded as one of his Precursors.

<margin>Basilides is the first who introduces it into the Church.</margin>
III. I will say the same of *Cerdon*, *Menander*, and *Saturninus*, who are said to have been Disciples and Followers of *Simon*, and whose sentiments I do not know perfectly. Therefore, if one must decide on the question of who was the first Author of Manichaeism among the Christians, I believe it was *Basilides*, who, according to (8) some died under Hadrian, and according to others, under Antoninus. The latter made a profession of recognizing Jesus Christ as the Son of God, since he wrote (9) a *Commentary on one of our Gospels*, or perhaps on all the Gospels. We are indebted to *Hegemonius* for having preserved a considerable fragment of it for us, in which one finds both the true origin of the Manichaean Heresy and the time at which it began to slip into the Church.

<margin>...to his wills. Homily XIX, at the end, p. 748. <note>original: "αὐτὸ τοῖς βουλήμασιν"</note></margin>
(7) A German Scholar, Father of the late Mr. *Thomasius*—who during his life brought honor to the University of *Halle*, where he was Professor of Law—a Scholar, I say, nevertheless affirms that such was the sentiment of Simon. <note>original: "E Gentilium certe, sed imprimis tamen è Principiis Magorum Zoroastris Schola, Magus ipse (SIMON) duos sibi adversantes Deos accepit, Bonum & Malum, ἀγαθὸν θεὸν, & ἀεὶσερὰν δύναμιν."</note> *Certainly from the Gentiles, but primarily from the principles of the school of the Magi of Zoroaster, the Magus himself (SIMON) accepted two opposing Gods for himself, the Good and the Evil, a good god and a dark power.* *Jacobus Thomasius, in Wolff, as cited above, 177.*

(8) See *Grabe, Spicilegium, Vol. II, pp. 36-37.* The diversity of opinions comes from the different reading found in the Manuscripts of St. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men [De Script. Eccl.]*. One reads in some *mortuus est* [he died]; in others *moratus est* [he stayed/remained].

See the learned Mr. *Fabricius, Apocryphal Code of the New Testament, Vol. I, p. 343.*

*Basilides* learns this in Persia.
</margin>

*Basilides* was from Alexandria, where he established a School in the first years of the second Century, in which he taught his Errors. He must be considered a philosopher-theologian who mixed his Philosophical opinions with Religion. People thought with more freedom then than today on an infinite number of things; and after having established the Dogmas of the Christian Religion, which were regarded as fundamental, a Scholar was permitted to philosophize on the rest. The more one tried to align Religion with established Principles, the more plausible one made it, and the more success one had. *Clement of Alexandria* and *Origen* were philosopher-theologians who had their Schools in Alexandria where Pagan philosophers had theirs. As for *Basilides*, he traveled to Persia. *Hegemonius*, who testifies to this, adds (1) that he went there to preach his Heresy. It is more natural to say that he learned it in that Country, since he himself asserts that it was the sentiment of the Barbarians. Philosophers traveled to learn the various opinions of Peoples and their Sages. *Bardesanes*, a learned Mesopotamian, had been to the Indies to learn about the Manners and Philosophy of the Brahmans <note>The priestly and scholarly caste of ancient India.</note>. He had written (2) an account of it,

explanation, which was seen by those in the retinue of the Emperor *Antoninus* <note>Likely referring to Caracalla, who visited the East in the early 3rd century.</note>, as he was returning from *Emesa* in *Syria*. We know of the travels made by *Apollonius* <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a Neo-Pythagorean philosopher and traveler.</note> for the same reason, and we are not ignorant of those of *Origen*, who was curious to hear all the Philosophers of his time and to know the opinions of all the Christian Sects. *Basilides* undoubtedly shared the same curiosity. He went to Persia, heard the Magi discourse on the origin of evil—a question that was then extremely debated—and adopted their System, which he subsequently brought to the Greeks. *Eusebius* asserts (3) that to authorize his Errors, he invented certain Prophets who never existed, such as a *Barcabbas*, a *Barcoph*, and others, to whom he gave Barbaric names. It is more natural and more likely to think that he found, among the Chaldeans or the Eastern Syrians, Books attributed to certain Prophets of their Nation who were unknown to the Jews and Christians. The names *Barcabbas* and *Barcoph* are clearly Syriac names. Such was then the *origin of Manichaeism*. It does not come (4) from the Greeks: it has its source in Barbarian Philosophy, in that of the Magi, and in that of the Brahmins. Thus *St. Ephrem*, who lived very close to the time of Mani, calls his heresy (5) **THE HERESY OF THE INDIES**, not to say that he received it from the Indians, but because it had reigned in the Indies from time immemorial; for it was common in Persia, and the learned *Abulpharage* <note>Also known as Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century scholar and prelate of the Syriac Orthodox Church.</note> testifies that *Mani* did nothing but refine (6) the ancient error of the Persians and attempt to confirm it with probable reasons.

<margin>Manichaeism comes from Persia and the Indies.</margin>
<margin>Testimonies of St. Ephrem and Abulpharage.</margin>

It is therefore not true that *Scythianus* <note>A legendary figure in early Christian polemics described as a predecessor to Mani who allegedly brought dualist books from Egypt or the East.</note> invented the System of the two Principles: but it is also not true that he imagined the war that broke out between them, and which forced God to create the World. The Author of the *Acts of Archelaus*, who says so (7), was not acquainted with the ancient Theology of the Magi. When we come to the Dogmas of *Mani*, we shall see that this Heresiarch <note>A founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note> did nothing but renew and reshape in his own way an ancient fiction of the Persian Philosophers who had preceded *Zoroaster*, a fiction that was still in vogue among the Sect of the *Maguseans* <note>A group of Diaspora Magi who lived in Asia Minor and preserved ancient Persian religious traditions.</note>.

### CHAPTER IV.

#### Continuation of the History of Scythianus: His Manners, Character, Marriage, Books, and Death.

**I.** From the errors of Scythianus, let us pass to the history of his life. I will not deal here with *Archelaus* <note>Referring to the 'Acts of Archelaus,' a primary but controversial source on Mani's life.</note>; it is with *St. Epiphanius* and *Cyril of Jerusalem* that I must engage, as I must correct their exaggerations, their inaccuracies, and, if I may be permitted to say so, their slanders.

<margin>Education of Scythianus, his Mind, his knowledge, his riches.
(a) Epiph. Heresy LXVI. p. 618.</margin>
Scythianus (a) left Saracenia <note>A region in Northern Arabia.</note> at an early age and was raised on the borders of Palestine, where he learned the Language and the Sciences of the Greeks. He particularly studied the books of *Aristotle*, and (1) it was by reading them that he acquired his style and Greek turns of phrase. Since he possessed (2) a fortunate *genius*, he made great progress in the Sciences. *Medicine, Philosophy, Mathematics, Astronomy*—it is said that he excelled in all. *Archelaus* and *St. Epiphanius* agree on this. I will only remark that the latter, who asserts in one place that *Scythianus* (3) was a prodigy in the vain sciences of the world, elsewhere (4) gives him a *crude and stupid mind*. This does not seem easy to reconcile; I believe, nonetheless, that *St. Epiphanius* meant to say that this man, who had so much talent for the Human Sciences, had none for the Divine Science of Religion.

<margin>He was an illustrious Merchant.
The Saracens were such.</margin>
To all these advantages, *Scythianus* had added very considerable wealth acquired through commerce. *Eusebius* informs us (5) that the peoples of Saracenia were great Merchants. This man sailed to the East Indies, from which he transported rich merchandise to Egypt via the Red Sea. Thus, he was one of those (6) illustrious Navigators who combine the fine Arts with trade,

Arts, and beautiful knowledge to the labors and utility of Commerce.

<margin>Is accused of Magic by St. Epiphanius.</margin>
A fine genius, vast knowledge, and great riches are advantages rarely found in a single man. What a pity that heresy should tarnish such brilliance! Had it only been heresy—which is essentially a weakness, an involuntary straying of the mind seduced by the appearance of Truth—one would pity him rather than hate him. But he was, says *St. Epiphanius*, a consummate Magician. He studied and penetrated all the secrets of Magic, and all the discoveries ever made in that diabolical art by the Egyptians and the Indians, nations infamous for their commerce with demons. It is true that *St. Epiphanius* did not see fit to name his authors; and if these are the same sources who taught him that *Scythianus* flourished in the time of the Apostles, they are either great liars or great ignoramuses. We shall speak of Manichaean Magic in the second part; it will suffice to note for now that neither the author of the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A primary polemical source against Manichaeism, likely dating to the 4th century.</note>, nor *Cyril of Jerusalem*—both older than *St. Epiphanius*—ever accused *Scythianus* of it. Their silence on the matter at least balances the testimony of an author as credulous and as violent as *St. Epiphanius*.

<margin>The silence of Archelaus and Cyril justifies him.</margin>
<margin>Slander by St. Epiphanius against the wife of Scythianus.</margin>
I almost added "as slanderous," and I do not think I should be blamed for it after the anecdote I am about to relate. *Archelaus* had simply said (7) that *Scythianus married a woman from the Upper Thebaid <note>A region in Upper Egypt known for early Christian monasticism.</note> who was a captive.* *Socrates* (8) repeated this after *Archelaus*. It is known that there were Arabs who constantly made raids to pillage and take slaves. *Scythianus* saw one of these slaves and found in her enough beauty, and perhaps enough virtue, to marry her. Nothing is more common among the Orientals. But this account seemed too simple and too fair to *St. Epiphanius*. In his view, *Scythianus* would have done nothing base or shameful by marrying a girl whose misfortune had reduced her to servitude. ...took her in a place of debauchery, where she was abandoned to *Public Lewdness*.

<margin>Contradiction of the Author.</margin>
Can an equitable reader—who, without being a partisan of Heresy, loves only Justice and Truth—read such passages without feeling indignation against the Author? *St. Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his fierce "Panarion" against heresies, often accused of being overly credulous of rumors.</note> does not yet tell us where he found these scandalous anecdotes which are known only to him, and which, if he had correctly placed the time of *Scythianus*, must have occurred more than three hundred years before he wrote against the Heresies. For my part, I strongly suspect that it is his violent zeal and his passion that revealed these slanders to him; for, after having put them forward as a certain fact, he is forced to hesitate. *Certainly*, he says (1), *Scythianus married this woman, <term>EITHER IN PROSTITUTION, OR IN CAPTIVITY</term>*. 

<margin>Pious fraud of Petau.</margin>
Father Petau <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit scholar and theologian.</note> must have noticed the contradiction of his Author, for he tried to hide it in his Version, where he placed—contrary to his Original—that *Scythianus* took this woman (2) <term>BOTH FROM PROSTITUTION AND FROM SERVITUDE</term>. The intention is not bad, but it is nonetheless (3) a fraud; and one must never deceive the Reader under any pretext whatsoever.

<margin>Scythianus was a Christian. Error, or rather exaggeration of Cyril.</margin>
Let us move on to Cyril of Jerusalem: He is a Preacher who throws himself into declamation and Hyperbole. If we are to believe him, *Scythianus* was a Philosopher of the Aristotelian Sect (4) who *had nothing in common with either Judaism or Christianity*. Regarding Judaism, that may be so: the Manichaeans did not regard *Moses* as an inspired Prophet, and although they admitted a part of his History, they placed no faith in the account he gave us of the Creation of the World. They loudly rejected all his Ceremonial Laws and denied that he had ever predicted the coming of the Son of God. But as for Christianity, *Scythianus* made profession of it, and there are evident proofs of this.

...sought to compensate themselves by becoming Leaders of a Sect. Now, I do not think that a Philosopher, a Pagan by profession, would have thought to aspire to the **Episcopal Dignity** <note>The office or rank of a bishop.</note>, nor that one can treat as an *Apostate*—a deserter of the Faith—a man who never embraced it. Let us remark in passing, that the Episcopate must have had great attractions, if it is true, as the Fathers say, that most Heretics threw themselves into their errors only out of despair at not being able to reach it. I suspect, however, that those who speak in this manner considered the Episcopate as it was in their own time, and not as it had been in the time of *Marcion* and *Valentinus* <note>Two of the most famous early Gnostic leaders of the 2nd century.</note>, for example. 2. (7) *The Son of eternal Light*, the **Heresiarch** <note>The founder of a heretical sect.</note> says to him, *manifested his own Essence upon the Mountain. There he showed that he does not have two Natures, but only one, whether in the visible World or in the invisible...* Manichaeus means to speak of the Transfiguration. He says that the Lord showed what he truly was when, stripping away that appearance of flesh—that veil under which he hid his Divinity—he appeared luminous and resplendent like the Sun: from which it follows that *Scythianus* made profession of Christianity, that he received our Gospels, and in particular the History of the Transfiguration of the Lord. If he had nothing in common with those Christians who believed Jesus Christ was a man, and a mere man, he had much in common with those who believed him to be God, emanated from the Substance of the Father.

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO

<page-num>46</page-num>

<margin>(a) D'Herbelot. cited above at the word BRAHMA.</margin>
Mr. D'Herbelot (a) says that they believe the first of the Intelligences emanated from **God**; the one by which he created the World is **Brahma**; a name which, in the Indian Language, means **Permeating All Things**. They also believe that this *Brahma* left them four Books, which they call **Beth**, or **Beid** <note>Reference to the Vedas, the primary scriptures of Hinduism.</note>, in which all their Sciences and all the Ceremonies of their Religion are contained. It is because of these four Books that he is usually represented with four heads. What Mr. *D'Herbelot* <note>Barthélemy d'Herbelot (1625–1695), a French orientalist whose "Bibliothèque orientale" was a standard reference.</note> says of the Books of the Indians is true; the rest is very doubtful, and I would prefer the opinion of Mr. *Hyde* <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703), an English orientalist who attempted to link various Eastern religions to biblical figures.</note>, who believes that the *Brahman* of the Indies is *Abraham*, from whom the *Brachmanes*, or *Brahmins*, take their name, and claim to hold their Religion and their Sciences.

<margin>It is not well-founded.</margin>
Be that as it may, Mr. *Assemani's* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani, a Maronite scholar known for his work on Syriac manuscripts.</note> conjecture is not only without proof, but contradicted by the *Account of Archelaus*, for he recognizes its authenticity. Certainly, the four Books of *Scythianus* were not those of the *Brahmins*, because his Religion and his Faith were very different from the Faith and Religion of those Philosophers.

<margin>Various opinions on the Author of these Books.
(b) Socrat. cited above. L. I. 22. Suidas under the word Manes. Cedren. Comp. Histor. p. 213. Tollius Insignia. Itin. Ital. p. 126. Zaccag. in Not. Act. p. 96.
(c) Cited above p. 93. Epiphan. cited above §. 2.
(d) Act. p. 98.</margin>
Since the (1) expressions of *Archelaus* are ambiguous, some have attributed these Books to *Scythianus*, others to *Terebinthus*. (b) *Socrates*, *Suidas*, *Cedrenus*, *Tollius*, and *Zaccagni* attribute them to *Terebinthus*; (c) *Cyril of Jerusalem*, *St. Epiphanius*, and (d) *Archelaus* in another place, attribute them to *Scythianus*.

The learned Mr. *Fabricius* (2) followed them. For my part, as I place almost no faith in the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A polemical work describing a fictional debate between Mani and a bishop named Archelaus; modern scholars consider it largely legendary.</note>, I would willingly take them away from both, to give them solely to *Manichaeus*. For what likelihood is there that this **Heresiarch** <note>The founder of a heretical sect.</note> would have been the plagiarist of *Scythianus*, who lived at the same time as he? That he would have translated his Books, interpolated them, and published them under his own name? Whatever the case, we can say nothing of the alleged Works of *Scythianus*, of which only the *Titles* remain; but we can say something of those that *Manichaeus* gave to the Public, without pious Antiquity having taken every possible precaution to destroy them.

It appears, by comparing *Titus of Bostra* <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his refutation of Manichaeism.</note> with *St. Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403), a Church Father known for his anti-heretical works.</note>, that the Book of *Mysteries* began with these words: *(5) GOD AND MATTER existed; Light and Darkness, Good and Evil. </margin>

Regarding the Subject Matter of this Book, it is true that *(b) Manichaeus* blasphemed the Old Testament therein, but that is not what this pernicious Work primarily revolved around. It is about the Doctrine of the two Principles <note>The core Manichaean belief in two co-eternal, opposing forces: Light/Good and Darkness/Evil.</note>, which *Mani* <note>The text uses "Manès," the French form of the name.</note> tried to prove by an *a posteriori* demonstration—I mean by the mixture of Good and Evil that is in the World. All his reasoning is based on this maxim: that if there were only a single Cause, most simple, most perfect, and most good, all effects would correspond to the nature and will of that Cause. Everything would bear the mark of its Simplicity, its Perfection, its Goodness; everything would be immortal, happy, and holy like It. One can surely judge what the Book *Of Mysteries* contained by the refutation made of it by *Titus of Bostra*, who appears to follow his Adversary step by step, although he does not deign at times to amuse himself by showing all the ridicule of his Philosophical imaginations.

Peter of Sicily (a) <note>A 9th-century Byzantine historian and diplomat who wrote a key history of the Paulicians and Manichaeans.</note> calls this book *κεφάλαιον* <note>Greek: *kephalaion*</note>, a word which signifies *the Abridgment, the Summary*, but also the *Principal* or *Essential* part of a thing. Could this not be that Epistle of Mani which was read in the assemblies of his sect, and which Saint Augustine calls the *Epistle of the Foundation*? It contained the *Principles* and the *Summary of his Doctrine*.

<margin>The GOSPEL. The error of Photius.</margin>
V. The third book was called the **Gospel**. *Photius* <note>Photius I (c. 810–893), Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar.</note> says (3) that it was the work of some abominable people who had composed a false history of fake acts of Jesus Christ. This passage is an example of Photius's rashness in pronouncing upon what he does not know and what he has not seen. Furthermore, he is contradicted by Peter of Sicily, who wrote at the same time as him and on the same subject. The latter assures us (4) that this *Gospel* contained *no actions of Jesus Christ* and *had nothing of a Gospel but the name alone*.

<margin>(b) Cyril, as cited above, §. 13.</margin>
His testimony is all the more significant because he did nothing but copy (b) *Cyril of Jerusalem* <note>Bishop of Jerusalem in the 4th century (c. 313–386).</note>, who was five hundred years older than him. I will speak later of the **Gospel of Mani**, which he qualified (5) as the **Gospel of Life**, and which was only a collection of his meditations or his alleged revelations. This book was written in Persian and was apparently not translated into Greek, for it seems to me that one sees no trace of it in the Greek and Latin Fathers. *Gospel* does not always mean a history of the life and actions of our Lord, but rather the *Preaching*, his *Doctrine*; the Gospel of Saint Paul is simply the doctrine preached by Saint Paul.

The title of *Treasure* <note>Latin: *Thesaurus*</note> is quite common among Eastern writers.

### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. IV. ###

-> G 2 <-
<meta>catchword: vice</meta>

> “...of a great Prodigy; but his Demons having abandoned him, &
> “ his conjurations being useless, he fell from the top of the House, &
> “ killed himself, without having been able to achieve anything.”

<margin>According to his Hypothesis, *Terebinthus* would have lived more than two hundred years.</margin> However indulgent one may be toward *St. Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403 AD) was a bishop known for his "Panarion," an encyclopedia of heresies. Modern scholars often find his accounts prone to exaggeration and chronological errors.</note>, it must be admitted that there is neither Judgment nor Good Faith in his account. As for Judgment, there is none. This is easily demonstrated. *Scythianus* goes to Jerusalem while the Temple still stands, while the Service is performed there, and while the Priests teach the Law. He therefore goes there, and dies there, before the year seventy of our Lord. *Terebinthus* (7), his sole Disciple, withdraws to the Province of Babylon immediately after the death of his Master: He dies there when *Manichaeus* <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism.</note> was seven years old. Since this Heresiarch was born in 240, *Terebinthus* must have died around the year 247. Let us grant him thirty years; when he left Jerusalem to go preach Heresy to the Chaldeans, he could hardly have been less than that. Let us calculate now, and we shall find that, according to *St. Epiphanius*, *Terebinthus* must have lived more than two hundred years: and even then, the Demon had to cast him down like his Master, from the top of a House to the ground.

<margin>The Narrative of *St. Epiphanius* is untenable.</margin> But let us change the Epoch: let us place *Scythianus’s* journey to Jerusalem, and his Disputes with the Priests and the Teachers of the Law, either in the interval between the ruin of Jerusalem by *Titus* <note>The Roman Emperor who destroyed the Second Temple in 70 AD.</note> and the construction of *Aelia* <note>Aelia Capitolina, the city built by Emperor Hadrian over the ruins of Jerusalem.</note> in the place of, or near, the ancient Jerusalem by *Hadrian*: that is to say, from the year 70 until around the year 119. Or let us place this journey and these Disputes after *Hadrian* had built *Aelia*. All this could be done, if the account of *St. Epiphanius* permitted it. But firstly, this is to depart from the time of the Apostles, of whom none survived the ruin of Jerusalem, except perhaps *St. John*, to whom the Lord seems to have predicted that he would see this terrible Event when he said to *St. Peter*, *(a)* <margin>(a) *John XXI. 22.*</margin> *If I want him to remain until I come, what is that to you?* The destruction of Jerusalem is represented as the effect of an advent of Our Lord.

I say in the second place, that neither since the destruction of Jerusalem by *Titus*, who passed the plow over its ruins, nor since the construction of *Aelia*, was there any Temple in Jerusalem, except the one that *Hadrian* had built there in honor of Jupiter: no more Service...

Fable of the death of *Scythianus*.
</margin>
What shall we say now of the Magic Spectacle, by which *Scythianus* wished to stun & confound his Adversaries, & gain the faith of all Jerusalem? And what can we say of it, except that it is a lie invented to blacken the memory of a Heretical Philosopher, & to make the first Preachers of Manichaeism be regarded as Ministers of Demons, & at the same time as Victims of their errors? If *St. Epiphanius* is the Author of it, he is very guilty; & if he reported it on the account of someone else, although he alleges no witness, he is a fickle man who deserves no credit. *Archelaus* <note>The author of the "Acts of Archelaus," a 4th-century anti-Manichaean work that serves as a primary source for later writers.</note>, who is at heart his Original source, does not accuse *Scythianus* of Magic at all, & speaks of his death as a natural death. *Cyril of Jerusalem*, who wrote thirty years before *St. Epiphanius*, & who ought at least to have known what had happened in the city of which he was Bishop, also makes no mention of the Magic of *Scythianus*, nor of the prodigy he had intended to perform, nor of his tragic end. He **died**, says *Cyril*, **of a disease**, with which the Lord struck him. *Photius* (a) & *Peter of Sicily* stick to the account of *Cyril of Jerusalem*, although they neglect nothing that might tarnish the Manichaean Sect. *Father Alexandre* (b) <note>Noël Alexandre (1639–1724), a French theologian and historian whose "Selecta historiae ecclesiasticae capita" was a major work of its time.</note>, & other Moderns, would have done better to imitate them, than to insert the false marvel of the death of *Scythianus* into their Relations.
