### CHAPTER V.

### Examination of the History of TEREBINTHE.

<margin>Terebinthe moves to Assyria. Petau’s inaccuracy.</margin>
I. Archelaüs <note>The protagonist of the "Acts of Archelaus," a foundational anti-Manichaean text written in the 4th century.</note> relates that **Terebinthe**, the sole disciple of *Scythianus*, having rendered the final honors to his Master, *withdrew into the Province of Babylon* (1). St. Epiphanius says, *into the Land of the Persians* (2). This is correct, though less precise; but Father *Pétau* <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), also known as Petavius, was a French Jesuit theologian and one of the most brilliant scholars of the 17th century.</note> should not have translated it as *into Persis*, a term which designates the specific province that gave its name to the Nation, or rather (a) which took its name from the *Persian* Nation itself. It is true that Cyril of Jerusalem also said (b) *into Persis*, but Father *Pétau* is a Translator, and not an Author. Furthermore, *Cyril* expressed himself poorly, the provinces of Persia and Babylon being very different.

<margin>(a) See Cellarius, *Notitiae Orbis Antiqui* Vol. II. p. 787. & seq.
(b) As above p. 93.</margin>

<margin>Takes the name of BUDDAS. False reasons for this change.</margin>
By changing his residence, *Terebinthe* also changed his name, and took that of **Buddas** <note>This "Buddas" is often interpreted by modern scholars as a corrupted historical memory of the Buddha, whose life story influenced the Manichaean tradition.</note>. The question is to know what the causes were for this double change, and one can well believe that the Church Fathers are not inclined to imagine innocent ones. Indeed, St. Epiphanius boldly says (c), "That having seized the gold and silver of his Master, he dared not return to his Widow." But *Cyril* of Jerusalem, who follows the *Acts of Archelaüs* more exactly, contents himself with saying (d) that being known in Judea on the footing of a Heretic, he was forced to take refuge among the Persians. This is how these two Authors differ and agree. They differ on the nature of the motive, and agree in assuming a bad one. According to one, he is a Thief, who flees and hides; according to the other, he is a proscribed Heretic. But fortunately for the reputation of the unfortunate *Terebinthe*, he is justified by the *Acts* themselves of *Archelaüs*, which testify (3), "That arriving in the Province of Babylon, he published that he was no longer called **Terebinthe**, but **Buddas**, and that this name had been imposed upon him." He is therefore not a fugitive Criminal, who changes his name to remain unknown, to escape punishment or ignominy, since he publicly declares that he is **Terebinthe**,

(d) Cyril, as above §. 13.</margin>

...but that henceforth he should be called **Buddas**, because that name had been given to him.

A little more attention and fairness on the part of the Ancient writers would have revealed the innocent reason why this man, who was called *Terebinthe* among the Greeks, was called *Buddas* among the Chaldeans <note>The "Chaldeans" here refers to speakers of Aramaic or Syriac, the languages of the Near East in late antiquity.</note>. I shall explain this shortly, after I have recounted the conjectures of several learned men on this subject.

<margin>Imprecise conjectures regarding this change. (a) Fabricius, as cited above. Vol. V. p. 281.</margin>
Mr. Fabricius (a) remarks, following *André Muller of Greiffenhagen*, that the Indians call their Philosophers by the name of *Buddas*. This perhaps stems from the fact that in ancient times there was a celebrated Philosopher in India, who is still venerated there as a Divinity because of his great Virtues, and who was called **Bouttas**. (1) *Clement of Alexandria* <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150 – c. 215), a Christian theologian who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note> speaks of him. Mr. *Hyde* <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703), an English orientalist and librarian at Oxford, author of a major work on Persian religion.</note> admits that he does not know if the one the Indians honor was some Holy Philosopher; but he believes that if they called him (2) **Bout** (the Arabs say **Budd**), it is because this word signifies an *Idol* in Persian. This conjecture is certainly not fortunate. It is much more likely that the name of the Pagan Philosopher passed to his Image, and that this same name, which originally signifies nothing but the *Image* or *Idol* of the Philosopher, became among the Persians, neighbors to the Indians, the general name for Idols.

Be that as it may, Mr. Fabricius seems to believe that *Terebinthe* had taken, or had been given, the name of *Buddas* because of his Learning. If this skilled man had thought it through, he would have easily perceived that *Terebinthe* and *Buddas* are essentially the same name, and that they differ only as *Christ* and *Messiah*, as *Peter* and *Cephas*, or as *Dorcas* and *Tabitha* <note>The author is pointing out that these are bilingual doublets: one in Greek and one in a Semitic language (Hebrew, Aramaic, or Chaldean) meaning the same thing.</note>.

<margin>Terebinthe and Buddas are the same name; the first Greek, the second Chaldean.</margin>
**Terebinthe** (Τερέβινθος) is a Greek word signifying a type of tree <note>Specifically the Turpentine tree (*Pistacia terebinthus*).</note>. Scholars are divided on the exact species: but they agree that the Chaldeans call the tree *Boutema* or *Butam*—

(1) There are some among the Indians who follow the precepts of Bouttas, whom they have honored as a god because of his extraordinary sanctity. <note>original: "Εἰσὶ δὲ τῶν Ἰνδῶν, οἱ τοῖς Βούττα πειθόμενοι παραγγέλμασι, ὃν, δι ὑπερβολὴν σεμνότητος, εἰς θεὸν τε τιμήκασι."</note> *Clem. Al. Stromata. Book I. p. 305.*

(2) *Buddas*, *Bouttas*, is the word **Boutt**, or **Budd**, with a Greek ending. I have seen in the Extract of an Account of the Island of Ceylon <note>Modern-day Sri Lanka.</note>, (*Europe Savante. August 1719. p. 220.*) that the Inhabitants of this Island call **Buda** that which they represent as the most excellent of all Beings. They represent him in the form of a man, but of a Gigantic stature, being more than 32 feet high. One may see in a fragment of *Porphyry’s Book, On the Styx*, (*In Lucas Holstenius, following the Life of Pythagoras, p. 283.*) the Description that *Bardesanes* <note>A Syriac Gnostic and poet (154–222 AD) known for his writings on Indian philosophy and astrology.</note> had made of a mysterious Statue he had seen in India, in a very deep Cave, which was ten to twelve cubits in height. This Statue did not represent the Divinity itself. The Brahmins <note>A member of the highest Hindu caste, that of the priesthood.</note> said it was the model that God had given to his Son when he commanded him to create the World.

(3) The Monastery of Bethma, that is, of the Terebinthe <note>original: "Cœnobium Bethma, id est, Terebint"</note>.

<margin>(a) Chap. XXXV. 4.</margin>
...the tree that the Greeks call the *Terebinth*. For example, it is said in Genesis (a) that *Jacob buried, under an Oak, near Shechem*, the foreign Gods that he had brought from Mesopotamia. The LXX <note>The Septuagint, the earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> translated this as *under a Terebinth*, and the Chaldean Paraphrase <note>A Targum, or ancient Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note> as *under a Boutema*. Mention is made in *Isaiah* (b) of two trees that our translators call the *Oak* and the *Holm Oak*. To express the Hebrew word that we have rendered as *Oak*, the LXX used *Terebinth*, and the Chaldean Paraphrase used *Boutema*. The Eastern Syrians have a monastery called (3) the *Monastery of Bethma, that is to say, of the Terebinth*.

<margin>(b) Chap. VI. 13.</margin>
Here then is the whole mystery of this change of name. The friend and companion of *Scythianus* was called *Terebinth* among the Greeks because he bore the name of a tree that the Greeks named in that way. Let us go to the Babylonians, who call this tree *Boutema* or *Boutam*; he takes this latter name—or, if one prefers, the Babylonians gave it to him—because it has the same meaning as *Terebinth* in Greece. I had guessed this little mystery and believed myself to be the first to do so, but I have since found that Mr. Hyde (4) had preceded me, as had the learned *Bochart* <note>Samuel Bochart (1599–1667), a renowned French Protestant scholar of biblical geography and zoology.</note> whom I am about to cite. The reader may see (5) at the bottom of the page my thoughts on this entire story.

<margin>How the Greeks changed *Butema* into *Buddas*.</margin>
I do not believe that any poor Grammarian would take it upon himself to contest what I am putting forward under the pretext that *Boutema* (or *Butema*) and *Buddas* seem to be very different names. In any case, I would refer him to a man who is an oracle on these matters, who would teach him (6) that the Greeks, having no words that end in M, remove this final letter when they naturalize a foreign word. Among other examples, he cites the name *Buddas*, which was formed from the Assyrian *Boutam*. This observation by Bochart will perhaps serve, in what follows, to let us know the true name of *Manichaeus*.

(5) My thought is that *Buddas* was one of the first disciples of *Manichaeus*, as is proven by the testimony of Cyril of Jerusalem; that he was *Assyrian*; that having come from Assyria to Egypt or Judea, he was called there *Terebinth*, and resumed his name of *Buddas* when he returned to his Master. *Bud* or *Buddas* was an Assyrian name. <meta>catchword: I</meta>

<margin>A new slander against Buddas refuted. He did not call himself the Son of a Virgin. (a) Acts p. 96.</margin>
II. I have just justified *Terebinthus* against the accusation of having changed his name to hide his shame and his crime. Let us now justify him against a much more criminal imposture. *Archelaus* <note>Archelaus was a 3rd-century bishop traditionally credited with the "Acts of Archelaus," an early anti-Manichaean polemic.</note> says, "that as soon as he arrived in the Province of Babylon, he spread the rumor that he was born of a Virgin, and that he had been raised in the Mountains by an Angel." This time, the lie is crude—not on the part of the Accused, who was not guilty of it; but on the part of the Accuser, whoever he may be. I would not speak in such a firm tone if I did not have a Demonstration ready at hand to support what I claim. This Demonstration is that it is contradictory for a Manichaean to have claimed to be the Son of a Virgin; because one of the Principles of <term>Manichaeism</term> <note>A dualistic religion founded by the prophet Mani, viewing the world as a struggle between light and darkness.</note> was that it is impossible for a woman to bring a Son into the World without the cooperation of a man. This is what I will prove by an irreproachable witness.

<margin>The Manichaeans denied the possibility of the fact.</margin>
It is well known that the Manichaeans denied the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The Christian doctrine that God became flesh in the person of Jesus Christ.</note>. They maintained that two Natures as disproportionate as that of the Word and that of Man could not be united together, nor compose a single Person. Furthermore, they attacked the History of the birth of the Lord and denied the Article of the Creed: *He was born of a Virgin*. This is what St. *Ephrem* <note>Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), a prominent Christian theologian and hymnwriter.</note> testifies in a Discourse entitled, THE PEARL. The Manichaeans (1) called the *Human Soul* in this way, that *Particle of Light* <note>In Manichaean belief, souls are sparks of divine light trapped in the "matter" of the human body.</note> which is in Man, where it is entangled with *Matter*. St. *Ephrem*, alluding to this Manichaean opinion, and having as his subject the Parable of the Gospel, *Matt. XIII. 45*, compares the Human Nature of Jesus Christ to *a pearl*, and carries this parallel quite far. It is in this Discourse that he speaks in these terms: (2) "The Manichaeans maintain that a man can only be born from the union of the two Sexes, adding that if Jesus Christ had been formed like Adam, he would indeed have the <term>hypostasis</term> <note>The underlying reality or substance of a person.</note> of a man, that is to say, a true Human Nature; but that if he was born of a Virgin, and without the cooperation of a man, he can only have taken the figure of a man." There is no middle ground: *Terebinthus*, being Manichaean, must either have claimed—

---

<margin>(1) <note>original: "Particulam Luminis quam, (Manichæi) dicunt MARGARITAM."</note> "The Particle of Light which (the Manichaeans) call the PEARL." This is in the *Indiculus* attributed to St. *Jerome*.</margin>
<margin>(2) <note>original: "Πρὸς Μάνην διαλέγομαι... Οἶδα τι λέγουσιν. Διὰ συμπλοκῆς σώματος φύσιν γεννηθεὶς, οὐ δύναται εἶναι ἄνθρωπος. Εἰ μὲν γέγονε ὡς Ἀδὰμ ἔιχε, φησὶν, ἀνθρώπου ὑπόστασιν: εἰ δὲ γενήθη ἐκ παρθένου, ἐκτὸς συνουσίας ἀνδρὸς, σχῆμα ἀνείληφε."</note> "I am debating Mani... I know what they say. A nature born through the union of bodies cannot be [just] a man. If he was like Adam, he says, he had a human substance; but if he was born of a virgin, without the intercourse of a man, he took on [only] an appearance." *Ephr. de Margarita, Op. Dare I say it, or rather repeat it, for this reflection presents itself incessantly to my Mind. The Ancients abuse the credulity of the Catholic Commoners with a bit too much license: The slightest pretext is enough for them to attribute the most foolish opinions and the boldest impostures to Sectarians. Let us reveal the origin of this one to the Reader.

<margin>Origin or pretext of the Slander.</margin>
I have just spoken of an ancient Philosopher of the Indies named *Buddas*. *Terebinthus* bears the same name. It takes nothing more than this to attribute to him the boast of that fabulous Privilege which the Indians gave to their Philosopher. (3) "It is," says *St. Jerome*, "an ancient Tradition of the <term>Gymnosophists</term> <note>The "naked philosophers," a term used by the Greeks to describe ancient Indian ascetics and yogis.</note>, that BUDDAS, the Author of their Philosophy, was born of a Virgin, who gave birth to him through her side." <note>original Latin: "Vetus est apud Gymnosophistas traditio, quod BUDDAS, auctor eorum philosophiae, natus sit de Virgine, quae eum ex latere edidit."</note>

<margin>The Fathers attributed to the Manichaean Buddas what the Indians said of their Buddas.</margin>
That is the origin of the bad tale told about our *Buddas*. If he had kept his Greek name, no one would have ever thought to reproach him with the ridiculous vanity of calling himself the Son of a Virgin. He owes this to his new name. I correct at the bottom of the page a mistake by *Tollius* (4), who confused the *Buddas* of the Gymnosophists with that of the Manichaeans; and I warn the curious Reader here in passing that among the extravagances the Ancients attribute to <term>Simon the Magician</term> <note>A figure from the New Testament (Acts 8) often portrayed in early Christian literature as the first heretic and a practitioner of magic.</note>, there is also that of wanting to pass for the Son of a Virgin.

<margin>Error of Tollius.</margin>
The Author of the *Recognitions* put these words into his mouth: (5) *Before my Mother Rachel had any commerce with my Father Antony, she conceived me while still a Virgin.* <note>original Latin: "Ante enim quam mater mea Rachel conveniret cum eo, adhuc Virgo concepit me."</note>

<margin>Simon the Magician accused of calling himself the Son of a Virgin.</margin>
There is no Heretic about whom more false or ridiculous tales have been made than this *Simon*. I will not stop to refute this one.

...of [the soul]; on the *Sphere*; on the two Luminaries <note>The sun and the moon, central symbols in Manichaean cosmology.</note>: on the place where the Souls of the dead go: on the manner in which they are transported there: how they return to animate other Bodies: and finally, on the war that the Powers had waged against *God*.

I do not know why St. *Epiphanius* <note>An early Church Father known for his "Panarion," a massive work refuting various heresies.</note> leaves his Author *Archelaus* here, and reduces all the Disputes of *Buddas* with the Prophet and the Priest of the *Persians*, to the single Question, *whether there are two Principles of all things* (1). "Buddas," he says, "disputed with them concerning the two Principles, and could not answer the arguments of these two Leaders of Idolatry, who convicted him of error."

<margin>It is not likely that it was on the two Principles, a sentiment common among the Persians.</margin>

We will see, in the second Part of this Work, what the sentiments of the *Manichaeans* were on these various Questions. I am only surprised that there were great disputes about this between *Buddas* and the <term>Magi</term> <note>The hereditary priestly class of ancient Persia, followers of Zoroastrianism.</note>, or the Persian Doctors. For even though *Zoroaster* and his Disciples recognized only a single supreme Principle, as I have shown, I believe nonetheless that one can assert that this System was not the general System of the *Persians*, nor the most common System. At least *Plutarch* did not believe it so. "The Persians teach (2)," he says, "that there are two Gods opposed, and rivals of one another; one, whom they call the *good God*, is the Author of Good, and the other, whom they name *the Demon*, is the Author of evils." *Agathias* has said since, "that the Persians were in the same error as the *Manichaeans*, in that they recognized two first Principles; one, which is good, and which produces all Good; the other, which is evil, and which produces all evils." It was therefore not natural that *Buddas* would have great Disputes with Persian Doctors on a Question upon which the Learned of the Nation were divided: And unless St. *Epiphanius* knew the System of *Zoroaster* better than all the Greeks did, he could not have believed that there was, among the Persians, a Sect wise enough to recognize only a single sovereign Principle. Thus *Archelaus* does not say that the Disputes revolved around the Question of the two Principles, but on *the war that the Powers had waged against God*. This war was, however, an ancient fiction of the *Magi*, invented to explain the mixture of Good and Evil. *Manes* had borrowed it from them.

<margin>Account of the death of Buddas. He was cast down by the Demon.</margin>
IV. "Buddas (4), being unable to gain any Disciple, retired," says *Archelaus*, "to the home of a widow: it was there that, having climbed, very early in the morning, onto the terrace of the House <note>In the ancient Near East, houses often had flat roofs used for prayer or staying cool.</note>, to invoke certain Names, which are known only to the seven Elect of the Sect, and to perform certain operations, God commanded a Spirit to cast him down; which was executed at once."

<margin>Examination of this Account.</margin>
It is rare that Writers, who report a History, do not add new circumstances to it. *Archelaus* said simply that *Buddas* wished to invoke certain names, which are known only to the Elect: *Cyril of Jerusalem* says (5), that he invoked the demons of the air, those demons that the Manichaeans still invoked in his time in their detestable (6) *Ischas* <note>A term used by Cyril to disparage the Manichaean version of the Eucharist; it literally refers to a dried fig.</note>. *Archelaus* admits that he does not know what operations or ceremonies Buddas intended to perform. *St. Epiphanius*, better informed, says (7), "that with the help of his Magic he wanted to perform some wonder, which would confound his Adversaries, and which would close their mouths." *Archelaus* says that God commanded a Spirit to cast him down. *St. Epiphanius* says that this Spirit was (8) an *Angel*. *Cedrenus*, on his part, insists that it was (9) an *impure Spirit*: And the Historian *Socrates*, as if he had seen this Tragedy, represents the Spirit (10) seizing the unfortunate *Terebinthus*, and throwing him down from the top of the house. But what is most admirable in this whole narrative is that, by the admission of the first Author, *Tyrbo*, who had told it to *Archelaus*, *Buddas* was alone (11), because he feared being seen and being caught in the act, so that unless by a Divine Revelation, no one could have known either what *Buddas* intended to do, nor what he did, nor how he fell from the top of the House and killed himself.

<margin>Falsehoods of this Account.</margin>
Let us strip ourselves a little of this hatred, so ancient and so inveterate against Heretics, and let us not give ourselves over, without reserve, to all the suspicions, or rather, to all the illusions, that it causes us. There is a way of viewing the account of *Archelaus* that is simple, natural, and innocent: why not consider it from this perspective? *Buddas* will be no less a Heretic: What interest do we have in making him wicked?

<margin>Buddas climbs onto the roof to pray.
(a) Early in the morning.
The Manichaeans were diligent in Prayer.</margin>
He climbs alone *(a)* early in the morning, at the break of day, onto the flat roof of the House. What is he going to do there? He goes there to pray to God. The Manichaeans were very diligent in prayer: it was with this that they began the day. Let us remark, on this occasion, a different reading found in the *Formula for the Reception of Manichaeans*. One reads, in the edition by *Cotelier*: *(1)* "I anathematize those... who always turn toward the side of the Sun in that infinite number of prayers they perform." But in the edition by *Tollius*, one reads *(2)* "in their profane prayers." I cannot decide which reading is the true one, but it is certain that the Manichaeans prayed a great deal.

<margin>Praying on the roof, a custom of Orientals.</margin>
I say that *Buddas* climbed alone at the break of day onto the flat roof of the House in order to pray there. Nothing is more natural than this thought. 1. Prayer requires solitude. This is the precept of our Lord. 2. The Manichaeans prayed to God with their faces turned toward the East, or toward the Sun. *(a)* <margin>(a) Prideaux, History of the Jews. Vol. I. p. 392.</margin> ZOROASTER had taught his followers that Fire was the true *Shekhinah* <note>original Hebrew: "Schekinah", referring to the dwelling or settled presence of God, used here to describe a physical manifestation of the divine.</note>, or the Symbol of the Divine presence; *(3)* that the Sun, being the most perfect fire, God had established His Throne there and resided there in a more glorious manner than elsewhere. He ordered them to worship God with their faces turned first toward the Sun, which they called *Mithra* <note>A Persian deity associated with the sun, justice, and covenants, adopted into various religious systems including Roman mystery cults.</note>. This was the ancient custom of the Sect of the Magi. The Manichaeans had preserved it. 3. In the third place, it was the custom of the Orientals to climb onto the roof of the house when they wished to pray, as is seen <margin>(b) Acts 10:9.</margin> by the example of *(b)* St. *Peter* when he was at *Joppa*. <margin>(c) Priceus on Acts 10:9.</margin> "When the Ancients wished to do something in secret," says *(c)* *Priceus* on this passage of the *Acts of the Apostles*, "they were accustomed to withdraw into the highest rooms of the House. It is said in the History of *Esther* that she had a tent set up on the flat roof of the Palace."

<margin>Archelaus's ignorance. The number of the Elect among the Manichaeans was not fixed.</margin>
*Archelaus* continues and says that *Buddas* invoked certain Names known only to the seven Elect of the Sect. If *Tyrbo* spoke to him in this way, *Tyrbo* is utterly ignorant. The number of the *Elect* <note>The "Elect" were the elite ascetic core of the Manichaean community, distinguished from the "Hearers" who were the lay followers.</note> was not fixed in the Manichaean Sect. It was the College of the *Masters* which could only be composed of twelve, not counting the *President*. It is also said that the number of Bishops was fixed at seventy-two: the Priests and Deacons...

<margin>They did not invoke them; still less the Demons.</margin>
I do not believe, and I see no evidence, that the Manichaeans invoked the Angels; they honored them; they praised them because of their virtues, and for the services they provide to the Saints.

But is Cyril <note>Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386 AD), a theologian whose works often criticized various heresies.</note> permitted to confuse Angels with Demons, and to accuse these Sectarians of invoking the *Demons of the Air*? They believed that Demons were confined within the space below the Moon: there the Empire of Matter ended. But far from invoking them, they detested them, and I wish for no other proof than what *Tyrbo* <note>A figure in anti-Manichaean literature, often depicted as a disciple of Mani who revealed his secrets.</note> relates, which is (1) "that *Mani* ordered his Elect to pray after eating, and to perfume their heads with an EXORCISED oil, while pronouncing certain mysterious names, the knowledge of which was reserved for the Elect alone." It pleased M. de Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian.</note> to say, (a) *With an ENCHANTED oil*; although it says, both in the Latin Version and in the Greek of St. *Epiphanius*, *an exorcised oil*. If Exorcism and Enchantment were the same thing, what would become of the infinite number of ceremonies in the Roman Church? That of exorcising oil before using it is proof that the Manichaeans were biased toward the ridiculous opinion—which has only too often prevailed in the Church—that Demons infest the Elements and Bodies, and that they must be driven out by Prayer and Exorcism. But it is also an invincible proof that they did not invoke Demons in their Mysteries.

(a) Ibid, p. 762.</margin>

<margin>The miraculous nature of the death of Buddas is a childish Fable.</margin>
V. I leave without examination the miraculous nature of the death of *Buddas* <note>Buddas, or Terebinthus, was described in anti-Manichaean polemics as a predecessor of Mani who died after falling from a roof.</note>. I believe the Sacred Writers when they say that an *Angel struck Herod*. But for other writers, the more they strive for the miraculous, the less faith I place in their accounts. However, even if I were the most credulous person in the world, I could not persuade myself that an Angel hurled a man from the top of a house and killed him, if I find that this man was alive fifty or sixty

In the second Dispute, which took place at *Diodoris*, he treats the Incarnation—one of the most secret and greatest Mysteries of Christianity—in the presence of the entire multitude.

(1) "He commanded his Elect, when they finished eating, to pray and put EXORCISED oil on their heads, invoking many names for the confirmation of this faith. ...sixty years later. Could the reader imagine that I mean to speak of this *Buddas* <note>In anti-Manichaean polemics, "Buddas" (or Terebinthus) was described as a predecessor of Mani who traveled to India and adopted the name Buddha; the author here disputes the dates assigned to him by earlier historians.</note> who was dead and buried when Mani was only seven years old, yet whom I find living not only after this Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> had published his heresy, but even after his execution? I will be asked for evidence; I believe there is as much of it in my proof as one can require in matters of historical fact.

<margin>He survived Scythianus and Mani.</margin>
I say first, that *Buddas* was still living when *Mani* was publishing his heresy. Here is the demonstration: 1. *Buddas* survived *Scythianus*. The *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century anti-Manichaean work, likely fictionalized, which served as a primary source for later writers like Cyril and Epiphanius.</note> testify to this: it was after the death of *Scythianus* that *Buddas* traveled to the Province of Babylon. 2. Now, *Scythianus* was still living when *Mani* published his heresy, at the time when he maintained that there is only the Divine Nature alone in Jesus Christ, hidden under the appearance of a man. This fact is proven by the Letter that (2) *Mani* wrote to *Scythianus*, of which *Eulogius*, Patriarch of Alexandria, who flourished around the year 580, has preserved a fragment for us, which is found in *Photius* <note>Photius (c. 810–893) was the Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who documented many now-lost works in his 'Bibliotheca'.</note>. Therefore, *Buddas* was living when *Mani* taught his heresy, and consequently, it is false that he died when the latter was only seven years old.

<margin>And was one of his disciples.</margin>
I say secondly, that *Buddas* was one of the disciples of *Mani*, and that he survived him, being far from having been his Master through the books he left behind, or having died more than sixty years before him. Indeed, *Cyril* of Jerusalem testifies (3) that the first three disciples of *Mani* were THOMAS, BUDDAS, and HERMAS. It is true that there is (*b*) *Adas*, instead of *Buddas*, in some (4) manuscripts of *Cyril*; but this is evidently a copyist's error. For (*a*) *Photius* and (6) *Peter of Sicily* <note>A 9th-century Byzantine historian who wrote an influential account of the Paulician and Manichaean sects.</note>, who took their history of Mani from *Cyril* of Jerusalem, read it as *Buddas*, which shows that it was read thus in the manuscripts of *Cyril* more than eight hundred years ago. This reading is confirmed by the (7) Formula of Reception of the *Manichaeans*, where *Buddas* is placed immediately after *Thomas*. All the authors I know of who—

<margin>Rash and ridiculous exception.</margin>
I foresee that people, to whom an excessive zeal for Antiquity leaves almost no freedom of thought or judgment, will have recourse to creating a second (1) *Buddas*. The first would have been the Predecessor of *Mani*; the second, his Disciple. If they had need of it, they would create many others; for such creations cost nothing. But these phantoms, which have no existence except in the imagination of those who forge them, vanish before a Mind that is not prejudiced. After all, it suffices that these two facts be proven: first, that *Scythianus* was alive when *Mani* declared himself a Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note>, even to the point of denying the Incarnation of the Lord; second, that *Buddas* survived *Scythianus*. This suffices, I say, to show that the History and the death of *Buddas* are Fables, that the *Account of Archelaus* <note>The 'Acta Archelai,' a 4th-century anti-Manichaean work that claims Mani was originally a slave named Corbicius.</note> is false, and that *Tyrbon* and *Sifunnius* <note>Characters presented in the 'Acta' as sources of information about Mani's life.</note> could not have told him what he recounts on their testimony.

This testimony from the *Chronicle of Edessa* seems to be confirmed by that of *Eutychius* <note>Eutychius of Alexandria (877–940), a Melkite Patriarch and historian.</note>, who says that *Manes* (a) appeared under *Gordian*. It is evidently of the time when his Heresy caused the most stir and brought upon him his punishment. Moreover, this Author commits a strange anachronism. For he places the death of *Bahram I* <note>The text uses "Varanes," the Latinized form of Bahram.</note>, Son of *Hormizd*, at (3) the 3rd year of *Gordian*, that is to say, around the year 241 or 242; this is evidently false. <margin>(d) Dynasties p. 83.</margin> *Bar Hebraeus* (d) <note>A 13th-century scholar and prelate, also known as Abulpharage.</note> places the first year of the reign of *Bahram I*, who reigned three years and three months, at the first year of *Probus*, who was hailed Emperor in 276. This Chronology does not agree with ours, but it does not stray far from it.

<margin>
There is no reason to reject the testimony of the Chronicle of Edessa on the birth of Mani.
(e) See Pagi, as above, Year 271, § 12.

I see no reason strong enough to reject the testimony of the *Chronicle of Edessa* regarding the time of the birth of *Mani*. It is true that, according to the Account of *Archelaus*, he was more than (4) sixty years old when *Shapur* <note>Sapor I, the Sassanid King of Kings.</note> had him put in prison. Now, as this Prince died in (e) the year 271, or in (f) 272, Mani could only have been thirty-two or thirty-three years old at that time. It is also true that one might be surprised that *Mani* became the Head of a Sect while still so young. But these reasons cannot outweigh the testimony of a Syrian or Mesopotamian Author, who appears well-informed of the facts that took place in the East. For, as for the *Acts of Archelaus*, they have very little authority. And as for reasons of plausibility, they cannot be opposed to such formal testimony. All that one could allege would be some error in the numbers, which could only be clarified by means of Manuscripts. But what confirms that there is no error is that in the Conference that *Mani* had with *Archelaus*, and which *Severus of Ashmunayn* <note>A 10th-century Coptic historian and bishop.</note> recounts in brief in his *History*—

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO

*History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria*; in this conference, I say, *Archelaus* having asked *Mani* (1) how old he was, he replied: THIRTY-FIVE YEARS. Now, there are indeed thirty-five years from the year 240 until the year 275 or 276, which is approximately the time when our writers place the era of the Manichaean Heresy and the Dispute of Cascar <note>The "Dispute of Cascar" refers to a legendary debate in the city of Kashkar, Mesopotamia, between Mani and the Christian bishop Archelaus; it is the central subject of the "Acts of Archelaus."</note>.

<margin>Mani was from the Province of Babylon or Chaldea. These provinces are often confused.</margin>
Almost all the Ancient writers say that Mani was (2) PERSIAN. This is certain if they meant by that he was a subject of the Kings of Persia. But if they meant to say he was from the Province of Fars, or Persia proper, it is doubtful. Saint *Ephrem* (3) testifies in Hymn XIV that he was *Babylonian*, that is to say, from the Province of Babylon, or from that of Chaldea, which is often <margin>(a) See Cellarius, *Ancient World Notes*, Vol. II, p. 755. (b) *Acts of Archelaus*, p. 63.</margin> (a) confused with that of Babylon. This seems confirmed by the *Acts of Archelaus*, where this Bishop reproaches Mani (b) for only knowing his *Chaldean* <note>original: "Caldaïque"; likely referring to the Syriac or Aramaic dialect used by Mani.</note>: which suggests he believed him to be *Chaldean*.

<margin>Suidas and Cedrenus make him of the race of the Brahmans.</margin>
*Suidas* and *Cedrenus*, who apparently copied *Suidas*, hold an opinion that seems bizarre regarding the origin of our Heresiarch. They say (4) that he was of the race of the *Brahmans* <note>original Greek: Βραχμὰν τὸ γένος (Brahman by race)</note>. I initially thought these two authors meant to say that *Mani* made a profession of the philosophy of the *Brahmans*, and that he believed, as they did, in two Principles—in which they would agree with Saint *Ephrem*, who testifies (5) that he had drawn his heresy from the Doctrine of the Indians. But I changed my mind when I read in *Suidas* (6) "That BRACHMAN was a King, who gave his name to the Country where he reigned; that this Country is an Island in the Ocean, inhabited by a very religious Nation called the BRACH- <margin>(c) Above, p. 533. Names of his Father and Mother.</margin> MANES." I refer the reader to what (b) *Cellarius* said of this after *Ptolemy*.

Tradition holds that the Father of Mani was called (7) PATECIUS.

His first name was CORBICIUS, according to the Latin *Acts*, but one reads (8) Cubricus in the Greek authors. Saint Augustine alone said (c) URBICUS, which is a (d) mistake, either by this Father himself or by his copyists. For my part, I suspect that Corbicius and Cubricus are equally mistakes, and that these words are a corruption of CARCUBIUS, which designated Mani by his Fatherland <note>Meaning "the man from Carcub."</note>. Neither Corbicius nor (9) Cubricus have an Oriental air; however, if these are names of our Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heretical movement.</note>, they must be Chaldean or Babylonian, since he was from that country.

<margin>
It is believed that these names are a corruption of Carcubius.
Carcub, a City in the Province of Ahvaz where Mani was a Priest.
</margin>
Here then is my conjecture on this matter. Mani was first a Priest (10) at Ahvaz or Elvaz, the capital of a small province that was part of Chaldea: now, in ancient times, Bishops and Priests were natives of the Cities, or the Territory of the Cities, in which they were Priests or Bishops, because people wanted to know their families, their education, and their morals. This has led me to judge that Mani was either from the City or the Province of Ahvaz. Now, as there was in this province a city called (11) Carcoub, or Carcub, I thought that the Heresiarch was nicknamed Carcubius, from his place of birth, and that it is from that name that the Greeks made those of Corbicius or Cubricus, in which they preserved all the radical letters <note>The "root" consonants or letters that form the basis of the word.</note>.

<margin>
Theodoret says his first name was Scythian: the occasion of this error.

(f) Suidas, as cited above.
(g) Cedrenus, as cited above.
</margin>
Theodoret (e) is the first, as far as I know, who said that he was called Scythian at the beginning. (f) Suidas and (g) Cedrenus followed him—

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEISM ACCORDING TO

followed. It even seems that *Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD), an influential theologian and Christian bishop of the 5th century.</note> knew of no other *Scythian* than *Mani*. However, since it is certain that they are two distinct men, I have endeavored to discover what might have caused *Theodoret's* error. It should be known—as I will relate in the following pages—that *Mani*, while being pursued by *Shapur* <note>original: "Sapor," referring to Shapur I, King of the Sassanid Empire.</note>, went to seek refuge in *Scythia* <note>An ancient region in Central Eurasia, often used broadly by ancient writers to describe lands to the north and east of the Black Sea.</note> and remained there until the death of that Prince. Now, the Greeks did not hear mention of his Heresy until after his return, during the reign of *Hormizdas* <note>Hormizd I, son of Shapur I.</note>, son of *Shapur*, and likely after *Bahram* <note>original: "Varanes," referring to Bahram I, who ordered Mani's execution.</note> had put him to death. For *Eusebius* recorded (1), in his Chronicle, the birth of the Manichaean Heresy in the second year of *Probus*, which is precisely the time of *Mani's* execution; this demonstrates that his Heresy was only known to the Greeks from that time onward. Furthermore, *Archelaus* <note>Supposed author of the *Acts of Archelaus*, an early anti-Manichaean polemic.</note> had heard nothing of it before *Tyrbon* came to inform him at *Cascar*. It is therefore apparently this journey to *Scythia*, and the stay *Mani* made there, which provided the occasion for *Theodoret’s* error. He must have found the epithet "Scythian" attached to the name of *Mani* somewhere, and this epithet—which merely designated his travels and his stay in *Scythia*—led this learned Bishop to believe it was one of his names. How many mistakes have the Ancients made in History based on even slighter foundations? The Reader can see at the bottom of the page what others have thought on this matter (2).

<margin>Mani's servitude. It has no appearance of truth. The Greeks are prone to slandering Heretics.</margin>

We have good proof of this in the person of the famous (3) *Xenajas*, better known to the Greeks by the name of *Philoxenus*. He was the author of a Syriac version of the New Testament, and one of the most illustrious and learned Bishops the Monophysites <note>A Christian sect holding that Christ had a single, divine-human nature.</note> ever had. *Theodore the Lector*, and after him the Second Council of Nicaea, had the impudence to reproach him,

Suppose, nevertheless, that he were a slave; he would have had that in common with a great number of excellent (5) Philosophers: with the famous *Zoroaster*, whom certain Arabic authors say was the (6) *Slave of Ezra*. <columns>2</columns>

Manichaeus would have replied to him that Providence had managed its measures quite poorly; for a great many Greeks were not at all struck by such a scarecrow: and fundamentally, they were right. These names, which appeared barbaric and contemptible to the Greeks, were beautiful and illustrious among the peoples where they were in use.

<margin>Origin of the names Manichaeus and Manes. St. Epiphanius derives it from Mana, a Chaldaic word meaning VASE.</margin>
Since Manichaeus was *Assyrian* or *Chaldean* <note>Chaldean refers to the Aramaic-speaking people of Mesopotamia.</note>, the etymology of his name has been sought in the Chaldaic language. *St. Epiphanius* (1) <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his fierce opposition to heresies.</note> derived it from <term>MAN</term> or <term>MANA</term>, which in that language means a *Vase*, an *Instrument*, or a *Garment*. It seems that *Archelaus* <note>The Bishop of Cascar, who allegedly engaged Mani in a public debate.</note> alludes to this meaning of the name *Manes* when he says to him in the Dispute of *Cascar* (2), *You are a* VASE, *an* INSTRUMENT *of the Antichrist. Furthermore, you are not an honorable instrument, but a filthy, unworthy instrument.* It also seems that *St. Ephrem* <note>Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), a prolific Syriac deacon and hymnographer.</note> had this idea in mind when he says (3), "that the Demon covered *Manes* with his own GARMENT, in order to use him as an INSTRUMENT, a MINISTER belonging to him, and to publish through his mouth his own Oracles."

<margin>An unjust reflection by M. de Tillemont. (a) Tillemont, as cited above, p. 770.</margin>
M. de Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a rigorous French ecclesiastical historian.</note> approves of this etymology and takes this occasion to make one of those hasty reflections that sometimes escape even the most judicious authors. He says (*a*) "that, to further erase the memory and the shame of his servitude, *Manes* left behind the name CUBRICUS and took that of *Manes*, which signifies *Vase* in Babylonian." I am quite persuaded that *Manes* is not a slave's name among the Easterners; far from it. However, it was such a name (4) among the Greeks, and *Manichaeus* could not have chosen better if he wished to perpetuate the memory of his servitude in this latter nation. We know of the word of *Zeno* <note>Zeno of Citium, the founder of Stoicism.</note>, who, being ill, said to his physician who advised him to eat a pigeon: "Treat me," he said, "as you would treat MANES"; that is to say, as you would treat my slave.

# THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. VI.

<margin>Error of Cyril of Jerusalem on the meaning of the word *Manes*.</margin>
I do not know on what testimony, nor on what foundation, Cyril of Jerusalem <note>Cyril of Jerusalem (c. 313–386 AD) was a prominent theologian and Bishop of Jerusalem known for his catechetical lectures.</note> took it upon himself to say that (5) *Manes* means *Discourse* in Persian, and that the Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heresy.</note> took this name because of the high opinion he had of his own Eloquence. Mr. Hyde (*a*) <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703) was a pioneering English orientalist and librarian at the Bodleian Library.</note> has remarked that *Manes*, or *Mani*, does not have this meaning in the Persian language; and, far from *Manichaeus* priding himself on eloquence, he himself protested in the letter he wrote to *Marcellus* (6) that Nature had not given him this talent.
<margin>(*a*) Hyde, as cited above, p. 280.</margin>

<margin>Of the learned Pearson on the same subject.</margin>
The learned *Pearson* <note>John Pearson (1613–1686), Bishop of Chester, was a highly influential English theologian and scholar.</note> derives *Manes* from (7) <term>Min</term>, which in the style of the Rabbis means *Heretic*. But this illustrious author did not remember that *Manichaeus* gave himself this name, as (*b*) the Ancients testify. Now, I do not believe he would have wanted to appear as a Heretic even in his own name. Furthermore, some Rabbis say that their word *Min* comes from *Manes*, rather than *Manes* coming from *Min*.
<margin>(*b*) See Augustine, *On Heresies*, Chapter 46; Cyril, as cited above, §. 14.</margin>

<margin>Inadvertence of a modern scholar.</margin>
It is by oversight that another (8) modern scholar attributes to Mr. *Hyde* the claim that *Mani* is a Persian word meaning Painter, and that the Persians called our Heresiarch such because he excelled in Painting. This skillful man did not pay enough attention to the words of his author, who does not say that *Mani* means *Painter*, but rather that (9) *Mani*, or *Manes*, was nicknamed **THE PAINTER** by the Persians.

<margin>Conjecture of Ussher: *Manes* comes from *Menahem*, which means *Comforter*.</margin>
IV. I would not dare to assert that the celebrated Archbishop *Ussher* <note>James Ussher (1581–1656), Archbishop of Armagh, was a prolific scholar famous for his biblical chronology.</note> hit the mark exactly; but his conjecture seemed to me so ingenious and likely that I have taken pleasure in developing and confirming it. (*a*) This learned Prelate, having remarked that (10) *Sulpicius Severus* calls **MANE** a King of Israel who is named **MENAHEM** in the (*b*) Second Book of Kings, and **MANAEM** in the Septuagint <note>The ancient Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, believed that the name *Manes* is none other than that of *Manaem*, which means *Paraclete* or *Comforter*.
<margin>(*a*) *Ussher*, Annals, Vol. I, Year 3032, p. 82.
(*b*) II Kings 15:14, 16. In the Septuagint, *Manaem* <note>original: "Μαναήμ"</note>.</margin>

Nothing is simpler or more natural than this origin. It is easy

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO...

It is easy to conceive that from *Manaem* they formed *Manem*. There are even examples of this; for the Orientals say sometimes (1) *Beth-Manaem*, and sometimes *Beth-Manem*, or simply *Manem*: this is the name of an Episcopal See. Now, since the Greeks do not admit endings in *M*, as I remarked above, they converted *Manem* into *Manès*, just as they changed *Buddam* into *Buddas*. There are, moreover, proofs that *Manès* must come from *Manem*, or *Manen*.

<margin>(a) On Heresies, Chapter 46.</margin>
First, St. *Augustine* <note>Aurelius Augustinus (354–430 AD), a foundational Christian theologian who was himself a Manichaean for nine years before converting to Christianity.</note> testifies that our Heresiarch was called (a) MANIN, that is to say *Manen* <note>original: Μάνην</note>, because the Latins often substitute an *i* for the long *e* of the Greeks. It is in this way that St. *Augustine* says *Adimante* for (2) *Adémante*. Secondly,

<margin>(b) Theodoret, in the work cited above, Chapter 26.</margin>
*Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), a prominent theologian of the School of Antioch and a bishop.</note> calls the Heresiarch (b) MANENS, and not *Manès*. He adds an *s* to *Manen* to give this name a Greek ending. Thirdly, *Suïdas* <note>The Suda is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> remarks that (3) *Manès* becomes *Manentos* <note>original: Μάνεντος</note> in the genitive case, which shows that the nominative is properly *Manens*.

<margin>Manichaeus also comes from Manahem, pronounced differently.</margin>
But if that is the origin of the name *Manès*, where shall we find that of MANICHAEUS? For it is thus that this Heresiarch is named, not only by his Disciples, but by many Greek and Latin Fathers. I respond that *Manichaeus* has the same origin as *Manès*: it also comes from the Chaldaic word *Manahem*, but pronounced slightly differently. Indeed, very learned men

<margin>(c) See the Bibles of Pagnin, Junius, and Tremellius.</margin>
in the Oriental Languages, such as (c) *Pagnin*, *Junius*, *Tremellius*, (4) *Pocock*, etc. <note>These were 16th and 17th-century scholars famous for their translations of the Bible and their expertise in Hebrew, Syriac, and Arabic.</note> write and pronounce MENACHEM, MANACHEM, giving to the Chaldaic letter <term>Heth</term> <note>original: ח</note> the sound of CH, whereas others give it only the sound of H. This, then, is the whole mystery of these two names, which have appeared so different that clever people believed they designated two people. It is the same name at heart, because they both have the same origin (5).

<margin>...nahem in order to pass for the Paraclete. This does not seem solid.</margin>
...promised to his Church. This conjecture is striking at first and may win the reader's approval; however, it does not seem solid to me. The world would not have been fooled by such a crude artifice. Besides, if one relies on the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century anti-Manichaean work, traditionally attributed to Bishop Hegemonius, which presents a fictionalized debate between Mani and Bishop Archelaus.</note>, *Cubricus* <note>According to Christian polemics, Cubricus was Mani's original slave name before he adopted the name Mani.</note> took the name *Manes* as soon as his benefactress died. Now, being only *twelve years old* at the time, it is unlikely that he had already formed the design of passing himself off as the Paraclete <note>From the Greek *paraklētos* ('advocate' or 'helper'). In the New Testament, Jesus promises the coming of a Paraclete; Mani claimed he was this promised divine figure.</note>. It would be much more reasonable to say that the widow who bought him named him *Manahem* upon freeing him.

<margin>The widow who bought him may have given him this name. Slave names were changed upon manumission.</margin>
For it was the custom to change the names of slaves, or at least to add some syllables to them, when they were given their freedom. As they became new men, they were also given new names. It would therefore be very probable that this woman, who freed and adopted *Cubricus*, gave him the name *Manahem*, because she regarded him as *her consolation*, being alone and elderly. *Photius* <note>Photius I (c. 810–893 AD), Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who wrote against the Manichaeans.</note> suggested this conjecture to me. *She bought (6), he says, a young boy to be her CONSOLATION in her widowhood.* But the servitude and sale of *Manes* are very uncertain and entirely unknown to the Easterners.

<margin>MANES was an honorable name, common to several Kings of the East.</margin>
VI. Perhaps we are looking for mystery where there is none. The Persians and the Arabs call our heresiarch MANI, and this name could well be a diminutive of *Manahem*. But what is certain is that it was a very honorable name, and assuming it meant something, as there is reason to believe, it can only be for advantageous qualities. Indeed, several (*a*) Kings of Edessa <note>Edessa (modern-day Şanlıurfa, Turkey) was a major center of early Syriac Christianity.</note> called themselves MANES, or MAANES, and Mr. *Asseman* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a famous Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican who specialized in Eastern Christian manuscripts.</note> has remarked (7) *that it is a common name among the Princes of Syria and Arabia.*

<margin>(*a*) See the Chronicle of Edessa, Assem. Orient. Library Vol. I. p. 418. 419. & follow.
(*b*) Pocock Spec. Hist. Arab. P. 49. 95.</margin>
The Arabs had an idol that they named (*b*) MANA, and among the names of their families one finds those of ABD-MANA and ABD-MANAHA, that is to say, *Servant of Mana*. Similarly, in the Ecclesiastical History of the East, one finds Patriarchs and Bishops named MAANA or MAANES. I refer the proof (8) of this to the bottom of the page.

It was this, if we are to believe *St. Augustine* (a), which obliged his Disciples to change the name of *Manes* to that of *Manichaeus*, or *Mannichaeus*. The Moderns have not failed to copy this passage from *St. Augustine*. Mr. de *Tillemont* (b) has done so like the others, and a German scholar has taken the opportunity to censure the celebrated (1) GOTTFRIED ARNOLD with too much bitterness. Arnold (2), he says, *falsely supposes that Manes called himself* MANICHAEUS, *even though it was not he who took this name, and it was only given to him by his Disciples*. Now, either the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century anti-Manichaean work that claims Mani was a former slave named Cubricus.</note> are false in the part that should be the least suspect, or the Heresiarch <note>A leader of a heretical sect.</note> called himself *Manichaeus*, and not *Manes*. For it is thus that he names himself at the head of (3) the Letter that he wrote to *Marcellus*, and it is thus that *Marcellus* names him at the head of his Response. When *Tyrbo*, his Disciple, speaks of him, he calls him *Manichaeus*.

<margin>Another frivolous observation copied by the Moderns.</margin>
*St. Augustine* says further (4), "that he had learned from some Manichaean or other, that, to better disguise the shocking nature of the name *Manes*, his Disciples had changed it to *Manichaeus*, or MANNICHAEUS, which, in the Greek Language, signifies a person *who pours Manna* <note>original: *qui répand de la Manne*; a play on the Greek *manna* (the divine food of the Israelites) and *cheein* (to pour).</note>." This is yet another passage that the Moderns do not fail to copy, although to tell the truth, it is not worth the trouble. I am willing to believe that some ignorant Manichaean told *St. Augustine* what he reports to us: I do not even doubt that this bad pun was enjoyed by the Latins, who did not understand the Greek Language. But the clever Manichaeans were careful not to put forward such a ridiculous etymology, which would have been hissed at by the Greeks; for it would have been necessary to say *Mannichoos*, and not *Manichaios*.

# THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. Book I. Ch. VII.

# CHAPTER VII.

->*Continuation of the History of <term>MANICHAEUS</term> <note>Also known as Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the prophet and founder of Manichaeism.</note> until his arrival at Cascar.*<-

I fear I have detained the Reader too long with the examination of the name *Manichaeus*. Most people do not care for such discussions, but they will hopefully have the kindness to permit them for the sake of a few others to whom they are not indifferent. Let us now resume the History of our <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>The founder of a heretical movement.</note>.

<margin>It is believed that Manichaeus lived in Seleucia. This is not certain. (a) Acts, p. 98. (b) See Strabo. Book X. p. m. 502. Book XVI. p. 605. Tillemont. Vol. VII. Part I. p. 168.</margin>
I. *Archelaus* <note>The purported author of the *Acts of Archelaus*, an early Christian polemic against Mani.</note> recounts, (a) “That finding himself master of the great wealth that his Benefactress had left him, he went to live in the middle of the City, very near the Palace of the King of Persia.” As the Author does not name this City, it is judged to be either (1) *Seleucia* or *Ctesiphon*, Cities situated on the banks of the *Tigris*, which were separated only by that River. As these had been the winter residence (b) of the Parthian Kings, they became so for the Persian Kings after the conquest. The Arabs have given them the name (2) *Modain*, which means *the Cities*.

<margin>Contradiction between St. Epiphanius and Archelaus. They can be reconciled.</margin>
St. *Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Bishop known for his "Panarion," a massive work attacking various heresies.</note> seems to be in contradiction with *Archelaus* here, for he asserts, (3) “that Manichaeus did not live in the Royal City, but in a City very far from there.” We can, however, reconcile these two Authors by saying that the young *Manichaeus* was raised in the Royal City, which was the center of Sciences and the great School of the <term>Magi</term> <note>The priestly class of the Persian Empire, associated with Zoroastrianism and secret knowledge.</note>; but that having reached a more advanced age, he went to establish himself in some provincial City. Indeed, he lived in *Huzitide* <note>Modern-day Khuzestan.</note>, which is a Province of Babylonian Iraq.

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO

<margin>Mani, highly learned in the Persian Sciences.</margin>
The Greeks tell us no details of his life from the age of twelve until the age of (1) sixty. This is not surprising: they knew very little of what happened outside the borders of the Roman Empire. They are content to say (2) "That *Mani* was one of the most learned men of his century in the Sciences of his Country, but that he studied above all else the four Books of <term>Scythianus</term> <note>A legendary figure in Christian anti-Manichaean polemic, claimed to be the ultimate source of Mani's dualist doctrines.</note>, and that (3), having reached the age I just mentioned, he translated and altered them, mixing in a great many fables of his own invention: He even removed the name of the Author and put his own in its place."

<margin>Archelaus’s manifest contradiction.</margin>
Our Historian did not remember in this spot that, in the Dispute he had just held with *Manichaeus*, he had reproached him to his face (4) *for knowing only the <term>Chaldean</term> language* <note>A term often used historically for Aramaic or the language of the Babylonian region.</note>; for to translate a Book, one must understand at least two Languages. Monsieur de *Tillemont*, who noticed this contradiction, tried to resolve it by saying, <margin>(a) Tillemont, as cited above, p. 769.</margin> *(a) that the Books of Scythianus were apparently written in Greek, but that <term>Terebinthus</term> <note>According to the polemical history, the disciple of Scythianus who allegedly bequeathed the books to Mani's benefactress.</note> could have translated them into Chaldean, because that was the only Language Manichaeus understood.* There is more zeal than prudence and sincerity in such a solution, *Archelaus* having said in his own words that *Mani took the Books of Scythianus*, TRANSLATED THEM, *interpolated them, and put his name on them.*

<margin>Mani’s first Disciples.</margin>
II. At first, he had only three Disciples, namely THOMAS, ADDAS, and HERMAS. *Cyril* puts *Buddas* in the place of *Addas*, as I have noted; and it is certain that the Authors who name the twelve Disciples of our <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A leader of a heretical sect; the author uses this term from a traditional Christian perspective.</note> give this second rank to *Buddas*. <margin>Their Mission.</margin> After instructing them in his Doctrine, he sent them to preach it in the Towns and Villages of the upper part of the Province where he resided. But, later forming larger designs, he dispatched *Thomas* to Egypt, *Addas* (5) to Scythia, and kept only *Hermas* by his side.

K 3

...tianity <note>continuing from the previous page: "Christianity"</note>, at least if we believe *Archelaus*, his Missionaries must have preached at that time (6) only Philosophical Heresies concerning the System of the two Principles and the Creation of the World, being unable to speak of either Jesus Christ or the Gospel, since they did not know them.

<margin>The mission of *Addas* in Scythia presents no difficulty.</margin>
I have nothing to say against the Mission of *Addas* in Scythia. It is even quite likely, provided that by *Scythia* one understands the Provinces neighboring Persia, beyond the *Oxus* River. For besides the fact that there were Christians in that country, *Mani* went there to seek asylum against the Persecution of *Shapur* <note>original: Sapor; Shapur I was the Sasanian King of Kings who initially protected Mani before later Persian rulers turned against him.</note>. Now it was very natural for him to retreat to a place where he already had friends and Disciples.

<margin>That of *Thomas* in Egypt is true.
(a) False conjecture of *Petau*.
(b) *As cited above §. 12.*
(c) *Notes on this passage.*
(d) *Compendium of Heretical Fables, Book I. 26.*</margin>
There is some difficulty regarding the Mission of *Thomas*. *Archelaus* says he was sent to Egypt, and *St. Epiphanius* (b) to *Judea*. Ultimately, they do not contradict each other <note>original: "ils ne se connoissoient point" - in this context, the author means the accounts are not mutually exclusive.</note>, as *Thomas* could have begun his preaching in Judea, which was on his route, and passed from there into Egypt. But Father *Petau* (c) believes there is an error in *St. Epiphanius*, and that one should read *the Indies* instead of *la Judée*. He bases this on the testimony of (d) *Theodoret*, without considering that the error could just as well be in *Theodoret* as in *St. Epiphanius*. For besides the authority (7) of skillful Moderns who judge it so, there are very good reasons to prefer the common reading in *St. Epiphanius*. I will not say that Manichaeism should not have been carried to the Indies, where it already was, since *St. Ephrem* calls it (8) *the Error of the Indies*, and it is because of this that *Suidas* believed *Mani* was of the race of the *Brahmins* <note>original: Brachmanes; referring to the priestly caste of India.</note>. Nor will I allege that *St. Epiphanius* says elsewhere (e) that *Thomas was sent to Syria*, because this Father seems to speak of two different Missions.

<margin>(e) *Epiphanius as cited above §. 34.*</margin>

This *Papus* is found under the name *Paapis* (f) in the Anathemas of the Greeks against the Manichaeans.

Whether *Thomas* the Manichaean is *Thomas* the Apostle of the Indies.
</margin>
Although the thought of Father Pétau <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit scholar and theologian</note> is not entirely correct, there are nevertheless critics who, based like him on the testimony of *Theodoret*, have conjectured that *Thomas*, Apostle of the Indies, could very well be the *Thomas* whom the Christians of India venerate as an Apostle of Jesus Christ and as the founder of their churches. M. de *Tillemont* <note>Sébastien le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian known for his scrupulous accuracy</note> does not distance himself from this thought.

The learned author of *Christianity of the Indies* reports (b) that the ancient monuments of *Malabar* make mention of a *Magus*; that is to say, a *Persian*, to whom they give the title of MANNACAVASSAR, a word which can only mean a MANICHAEAN. This *Magus*, according to them, passed into their country before they were submitted to the (1) CATHOLICOS, or Patriarch of *Persia*, and performed false miracles, and taught his doctrine with such success that he attracted many people to his party. Who could be sure that this heresiarch is not the THOMAS put to death at Mylapore, where his ashes are equally honored by the Indians and the Portuguese? Other scholars (2) dispute these conjectures without, however, asserting that the Thomas of India is the disciple of Mani.

<margin>

</margin>
It is certain that peoples have more than once venerated the relics of bandits, heretics, and infamous people, and that it has been published that these relics worked miracles. But it must also be admitted that if this kind of religious honor has been rendered to the ashes of some Manichaean, it is in spite of him and against the principles of his sect, which loudly condemned all worship of the dead and of images. But as the monuments of Malabar do not name the Manichaean who entered that country, it could just as well be *Addas* as *Thomas*. "The King's son having fallen ill," (a) says *Archelaus* <note>A 3rd-century bishop and the purported author of the 'Acts of Archelaus,' a primary—though hostile—source on Mani's life</note>, "*Mani* undertook to heal him; but the Prince died in his hands, or rather, he killed him. This having irritated the King, he had him put in prison and loaded with chains." *St. Epiphanius* contents himself with adding to this account that the Heresiarch gave the patient (4) some remedies which did not succeed. *Cyril* omits the remedies and says (5) that *Mani*, wanting to give himself the air of a Prophet and a Saint, promised to heal the Prince solely by the virtue of his prayers.

<margin>Critique of the account by Cyril of Jerusalem, Photius, Father Alexandre, and Tillemont.</margin>
One might allow this commentary to *Cyril of Jerusalem*, even though it gives the Heresiarch an air of imposture or fanaticism that the others do not. But who can excuse the impertinent reflection with which *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and influential scholar</note> wished to embellish this adventure? Disregarding even the appearance of probability, this learned man dared to say (6) "*MANI HAVING BECOME FAMOUS FOR HIS CRIMES*, his reputation reached the ears of the King, who, seeing his son ill and learning that he promised to heal him by his prayers, employed this presumptuous man." Since when, then, do Princes hope to obtain miraculous healings from Heaven through the intercession of the greatest villains? Finally, the Moderns <note>17th-century historians like Tillemont and Noël Alexandre</note>, supposing that the Heresiarch had close intelligence with Demons, by favor of which he performed great wonders, boldly assert (7) *that he only undertook to heal the Prince of Persia because of the confidence he had in his Magic*. But these learned Moderns should at least take care not to so manifesty contradict *Archelaus*, their source, who, to convince our Heresiarch of not being the *Paraclete* <note>The "Comforter" or Holy Spirit; Mani claimed to be the final messenger promised by Jesus</note>, reproaches him (8) for having never performed ANY SIGN nor ANY MIRACLE. He even pushes him vigorously on this point: the Paraclete promised by Jesus Christ must glorify the Lord by an infinity of miracles, and *Mani*, who was nearing the end of his course, had not yet performed the slightest wonder.

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO

<margin>Uncertainty of this History.</margin>
...vain Churchmen dare to treat History. I do not wish to deny, but neither would I dare to affirm, that *Sapor* <note>Shapur I, the second King of Kings of the Sassanid Empire</note>, seeing his son ill, entrusted his cure to *Mani*; that the latter undertook it, and that, the success not having met his expectations, he drew upon himself the King’s indignation. All that surprises me is that such a public and memorable cause for his disgrace escaped the Eastern writers. For *Bar Hebraeus* <note>A 13th-century polymath and bishop of the Syriac Orthodox Church, also known as Abulfaraj, who wrote extensively on history and philosophy</note> is the only one, as far as I know, who has mentioned it. Even then, he only speaks of it as an (1) *uncertain rumor*, which he would likely have been as ignorant of as the others, had he not read the Greek authors. However, if the fact is true—which I do not wish to contest—it must at least be agreed that *Mani* only undertook to treat the Prince at the request of the King, who had a high esteem for his knowledge and his virtue. What I put forward is confirmed, firstly, by the testimony of *Socrates* <note>Socrates Scholasticus, a 5th-century Christian church historian whose "Ecclesiastical History" is a major source for late antiquity</note>, who says in precise terms, "that the King of Persia, having heard very advantageous reports of *Mani*, sent for him (2) AS HE WOULD HAVE SENT FOR AN APOSTLE of Jesus Christ"; and secondly, by the testimony of all the Eastern writers, who assert that *Mani* first won (3) the confidence of *Sapor*, and persuaded him of his doctrine.

<margin>If it is true, the King only employs Mani out of esteem for him.</margin>

<margin>Firstly because of his apparent Holiness.</margin>
This Heresiarch <note>A term used by historical church writers to describe the founder of a heretical sect</note> combined in his character everything that could acquire for him the King's esteem. Firstly, he passed for a great Saint. Continence, abstinence, fasting, a seductive air of devotion—all these appearances of a sublime spirituality, which have so often won for hypocrites the veneration of the people, shone forth in his person. One must imagine him as austere, somber, pale, emaciated, diligent in prayer, trampling underfoot all that the world holds precious or agreeable, and making a profession of entire poverty. I do not paint him from my imagination. *St. Ephrem* <note>Ephrem the Syrian, a 4th-century deacon and prolific Syriac-language hymnwriter and theologian</note>, who lived in the East only a few years after him, tells us that he was a man weakened by fasting and mortifications. *The Demon (4), he says, had spread paleness over Mani's face, in order to seduce the simple-minded.* Regarding poverty, it is certain that *Mani* made a profession of it, since he subjected his Elect <note>The "Elect" were the elite tier of Manichaean believers who followed strict rules, including vegetarianism and celibacy</note> to it, who were forbidden to possess anything at all in the world. ### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. Book I. CH. VII.
<sig>L 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: chan-</meta>

There is no part in the *Account of Archelaus* more obviously false than this one. It must be examined because it would suffice on its own to show that this entire *Account* is nothing but a fable. <note>The *Acta Archelai* is a 4th-century polemical work that purports to be a record of a debate between Mani and a bishop named Archelaus; modern scholars consider it largely fictional.</note>

<margin>Manifest falsehood.</margin>
1. Thus, St. *Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403) was a prominent bishop and counter-heretical writer.</note> clearly perceived it, at least in part: For although he follows his Author quite closely, he abandons him here, and says positively that *Manès* (3) *had possessed the Books of the Christians before being put into prison, (4) and that these Books were the Law, the Prophets, the Gospels, and the Writings of the Apostles.*
<margin>Recognized by St. *Epiphanius*.</margin>

<margin>He was instructed in Christianity from his youth.</margin>
2. I would not wish to assert that *Manichaeus* was born a Christian, because I do not remember seeing any certain proof of it. If he (5) came from a family of Magi <note>Zoroastrian priests of ancient Persia.</note>, as *Sharistani* <note>Al-Shahrastani (1086–1153), a Persian historian of religions.</note> says, and if he was a Magus himself, he would only have been a Christian because he embraced the Christian Faith when he reached adolescence. What seems certain is that he was never involved in any heterodox sect. For the Manichaean *Felix* having told St. *Augustine* that *Manichaeus his Master (6) had not come out of any sect*, this Father replied nothing, and his silence on the matter seems to be an admission.

<margin>*Abulpharage* testifies that he was a Priest, and zealous for the Faith.</margin>
3. *Gregory Bar-Hebraeus*, better known by the name *Abulpharage*, (7) who was *Primate of the East* and the most skillful writer the *Monophysites* <note>A branch of Eastern Christianity that believes Christ has a single, divine-human nature.</note> ever had, testifies that *Manès (8) was at first a Priest at* EHVAZ, *that he taught and explained there* THE SACRED BOOKS: *that he disputed there against the Jews, against the Magi, and against the Pagans, but that he afterwards abandoned the Faith.* I do not know if we have other Oriental Authors who testify to the same thing, but here is what one of the most learned men in France regarding Oriental Languages says on this subject. *This Impostor—he is speaking of Manès—was a Priest among the Christians of the Province (9) of Ahovaz, which is a small Country extending from Arabia to the mouths of the Euphrates and the Tigris, and forms a part of the Chaldea of the Ancients. He often disputed with the Jews and the Magi.*
<margin>Testimony of *Dherbelot* on this.</margin>

<margin>The Books attributed to *Scythian*, and said to have been translated by *Manès*, contained a corrupted Christianity.</margin>
4. The author of this *Account* must have lost his head, or made no reflection on what he was saying, to advance at the same time that *Manichaeus* only knew the Books of the Christians after having been in prison for a long time, and that before being put into prison, *he studied the Books of Scythian, translated them, and interpolated them.* <note>Scythian (Scythianus) is a legendary figure in anti-Manichaean polemics, described as a precursor to Mani who traveled to India and Egypt.</note>

HISTORY OF MANI ACCORDING TO

<margin>...that he declared himself a Christian.</margin>...sent his disciples, with orders to boldly preach his errors *under the name of Jesus Christ*, he <note>Referring to the Persian King, likely Shapur I or Bahram I.</note> resolved to make him suffer the punishment he deserved.

Here we see openly the true crime of Mani, the one that was the cause of his punishment. It was not for having failed to cure the King's son; it was not for maintaining that there are two eternal Principles, nor for so many other philosophical questions that composed his system: it was because he declared himself a Christian, and had his doctrine preached under the name of Jesus Christ, of whom he claimed to be the Apostle. And to say more, it was because he dared to rise against the religion and the worship of the Magi <note>The Magi were the Zoroastrian priestly class of the Persian Empire; Mani's new religion was a direct threat to their state-sanctioned authority.</note>. This will be confirmed hereafter.

<margin>He is warned in a dream and flees to the Castle of Arabion.</margin>The King's resolution (1) was revealed to him in a dream, which the Manichaeans will attribute to an Angel of Light, and the Catholics to an Angel of Darkness. Then he wins over his guards and escapes to a castle named **Arabion** (2), which belonged to the Persians and was only three or four days' journey from *Cascar*. Between these two places there was a river called (3) *Stranga*, and which served as the boundary between the two Empires. Whatever research I have conducted, I have been unable to find in Mesopotamia either a river called *Stranga* or a castle named *Arabion*, which, to tell the truth, makes this whole history very suspicious. It will appear even more so when one learns that *Hormizdas*, successor to *Sapor*, and protector of *Mani*, gave him a castle to serve as a retreat, but situated far from Mesopotamia and the Roman frontiers.

(a) Note IV on the Manichaeans.

This History has so much the air of a Legend, that Monsieur de Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French priest and ecclesiastical historian renowned for his rigorous use of primary sources.</note> *(a)* could not hide that it was very suspicious to him. *Where can one find, he says, ten or twelve thousand Christians in a single City during the reign of Paganism? It is perhaps (b) in Osrhoene <note>A historical region in Upper Mesopotamia, often cited as one of the first kingdoms to adopt Christianity.</note>, which is said to have had Christian Princes from the beginning of Christianity.* But, besides the fact that one would have had great trouble finding them in *Edessa* itself, which was its Capital, these Soldiers were surely camping on the frontiers of the Persians, from which *Edessa* was quite distant. Monsieur de Tillemont is also very surprised to see among the Christians an *ordinary fast*, continued at least until midnight, since there was only the Easter Fast that lasted until that hour. *Is it easy to believe, he continues, that, in the time of Paganism, ten thousand Christians had the custom of leaving a City to go pray together in the Countryside for a whole day, and that in the year two hundred seventy-six, at the latest, this was already an ancient Tradition.*
