### HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO ###

The Author raises further objections against this History, despite his desire to accept it, and finds it finally quite inconceivable *that ten thousand people, instead of returning to the City in the evening, would remain in the Countryside to let themselves be overcome by sleep.*

<margin>It is a pure fable.</margin>
Mr. de **Tillemont** <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698) was a French priest and historian known for his exhaustive histories of the early Church.</note> is too indulgent toward Authors who have not respected the Truth. This Narration is nothing but a pure fable, and bears all its characteristics. If the Christian subjects of the Empire were then enjoying Peace, was it permissible for Roman Soldiers to massacre them, to take them prisoner, and to sell them in a Roman City? And if they were persecuted, was it permissible for these same Soldiers to desert the Militia under the pretext of embracing the Christian Faith? Is there any example of the early Christians having the custom of going to spend the day and night in the fields, with their small Children and their wives, to ask God to bless the fruits of the Earth?

<margin>**Tillemont** would like to blame the Translator; which is absurd.</margin>
Mr. de **Tillemont** cannot, therefore, resolve to admit so impertinent a fable. But if he rejects it, what becomes of the *Acts of Archelaus*? What becomes of the whole History of **Manichaeus**, and who will want to place faith in an Author so bold and so fabulous? To extricate himself from this embarrassment, the modern scholar takes the side of attributing this entire tale <margin>(a) Tillemont Note II on the Manichaeans.</margin> (a) to the Translator, although there is nothing in the Work that supports his conjecture, and this piece is entirely essential to the Romance <note>The author uses "Romance" here in the sense of a fictionalized or embellished narrative.</note>. For it was the generosity that **Marcellus** exercised toward this troop of captives that made him known to **Manichaeus**, and which was the occasion for the Letter he wrote to him, and the journey he made to *Cascar*. Without that, these two men would never have met. There is therefore no way to detach this piece from the rest of the History, nor consequently to attribute it to the Translator, unless one attributes the entire Work to him.

However, as fables usually have some foundation, I wanted to discover what might have given rise to this one. And I ingenuously confess that, misled by a truncated citation from Mr. **Hyde** <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703) was an English orientalist and librarian at the Bodleian who wrote extensively on ancient Persian religions.</note>, I almost believed I had guessed it: but I was soon disabused upon consulting the Original. I will not fail to propose my conjecture to the Reader, who perhaps will make some use of it: at least it will not bore him.

<margin>Conjecture on what may have served as a pretext for this Fable.</margin>
Believing, therefore, that the Fable in question must have at least some foundation in History, I had first supposed that if **Marcellus** was a real Personage, he could only be a Roman, not only very wealthy, but invested with great power in Mesopotamia, and apparently Governor of the Province.

<meta>catchword: Rest</meta>

I had proposed in the second place, that this unfortunate troop, upon which Roman soldiers fell in the night, and upon whom they committed a great slaughter, taking seven or eight thousand prisoners, could only have been a group of Persians.

Finally, I had proposed that if they were assembled for some religious devotion, it must have been for a Persian devotion, as Mr. de *Tillemont* <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698) was a French historian whose work on the early Church is still referenced today.</note> agrees that it is not a Christian practice to go spend the day and night in fasting and prayer in the countryside to implore God's blessing on the fruits of the Earth. These are my three suppositions.

<margin>*Marcel* is likely *Marcellinus*, Governor of Mesopotamia.</margin>
Regarding the first, I could put it forward as a certain proposition; *Marcel* was indeed Governor of Mesopotamia. It is true that this Governor was properly called *Marcellinus*, but if it is a mistake to confuse two names that are so similar, it is a most excusable one, and many examples of it could be found. *Zosimus* <note>Zosimus was a Greek historian based in Constantinople who wrote a history of the Roman Empire in the late 5th century.</note> informs us that under the reign of *Aurelian*, around the year 273—precisely at the time when one would have to place the tragic adventure of which we speak—Mesopotamia was governed by (1) *Marcellinus*, a Captain with an integrity proof against the most delicate temptation, and one to which the greatest men have so often made a kind of honor of surrendering. The *Palmyrenes* <note>People of the city-state of Palmyra, who established a short-lived empire under Queen Zenobia that challenged Rome.</note>, in despair over the treatment they, their city, and *Zenobia* their Queen had suffered at the hands of the Romans, made every effort to shake his loyalty. They proposed to join their forces to his, if he would seize Mesopotamia and all the Orient. But he constantly refused their offers, and after having tried in vain to dissuade them from revolt, he finally gave notice of it to the Emperor. Perhaps *Marcellinus* had an inclination toward Christianity.

<margin>Character of this Captain.</margin>
My second supposition seemed evidently true to me, for the reasons I have already alleged. However brutal one might suppose Roman soldiers to be, one cannot conceive that their leaders would be barbaric enough to slaughter an unarmed troop they surprised in the countryside, composed of women and children, all subjects of the Republic. One can conceive even less that they would have the power to reduce innocent and free people to slavery. But if they are Persians, the soldiers might believe they are a party of enemies who have come by night to invade the lands of the Empire, to kill some and take the rest prisoner. It is natural after that, once these poor captives made their innocence known to the Governor of the Province, that he would have them set free without ransom.

There remains the third supposition, namely, that it involves a Persian Devotion. This appears to be a pilgrimage, a Persian devotion, and an annual one: it takes place every year after the harvest to give thanks to God for having blessed the fruits of the Earth. Based on this, I had conjectured that these poor Persian pilgrims unfortunately passed near the Roman soldiers who were camping on the frontier, and who, taking offense at their march and their numbers, treated them as enemies.

<margin>Abuse he made of it.</margin>
The building was not poorly constructed, but the foundation was worthless. <margin>Reflections on this Letter. Judgment of Tillemont. (a) In the place cited above, p. 782.</margin>
Mr. de Tillemont finds, *(a) that there is nothing so sweet, nor so attractive as this Letter: that it is entirely composed in an Apostolic style, and full of the expressions of St. Paul.* Indeed, it does not appear to be the work of a neophyte <note>A person newly converted to a belief.</note> who has known the Sacred Books for only a very short time. Nor does one recognize in it that barbarian, ferocious, and impious man often depicted when the portrait of our Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heresy; here referring to Mani, the founder of Manichaeism.</note> is drawn for us. There is a sweetness in this Letter, an air of modesty that is perhaps more apparent than real. One also notices several expressions of St. Paul. (3) The Manichaeans held a great veneration for this Apostle, both because they believed they found in his writings their doctrine of the two Principles <note>The core Manichaean belief in the eternal struggle between Light/Good and Darkness/Evil.</note> and the natural corruption of Man, and because of all the Apostles, he is the one who worked hardest to deliver the Christian Church from Mosaic observances <note>Religious laws and customs from the Old Testament/Torah.</note>. The salutation at the beginning of this Letter is also an imitation of St. Paul. A very similar one is found in the famous letter called (4) THE EPISTLE OF THE FOUNDATION: *May the peace of the invisible God, and the knowledge of the Truth, be given to all our Holy and most dear Brothers, who believe the heavenly Commandments and who observe them. May the Right Hand of God protect them, and deliver them from all the Assaults of the Demon, and from the Snares of the World.*

<margin>Tillemont's error regarding the Virgins who accompany Mani. (b) In the place cited above, p. 785.</margin>
Mani writes to Marcellus on behalf (5) *of the Saints and Virgins who are with him*; that is to say, the Saints who made a profession of CONTINENCE <note>The religious practice of refraining from sexual relations.</note>. Mr. de Tillemont mistook these *Virgins* for girls. Mani, he says *(b), soon arrived with several young men and several young girls of his Sect.* I do not know if those disciples accompanying him were young men; but I am quite sure there were no young girls with them. *Mani* would have taken care not to associate with women or girls, lest he make himself highly suspect regarding what he considered the source and origin of all human corruption. These *Virgins* and these *Saints* are the same people. Thus, in one part of the Latin version, we find *(c) chosen Virgins* <note>original Latin: "Virgines electos". The use of the masculine ending "electos" indicates that the "Virgins" being described were male.</note>, which indicates they are men.

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEISM ACCORDING TO #

<margin>He treats the Orthodox Bishops as Teachers of the simple.</margin>
As for these *Masters*, or *Doctors* of the *simple* and the *ignorant*, these *Fools*, or *unwise*, they are the Catholic Doctors <note>In this context, "Catholic" refers to the "universal" or "orthodox" Christian Church as opposed to "heretical" sects.</note>. The ancient Sectarians, who emerged from the School of the Philosophers, did not claim to be guided by *Faith*—which they confused with *Credulity*—but by *Science* <note>The term here refers to 'Gnosis' or higher knowledge rather than modern physical science.</note>. *Credulity* is suited to the Craftsman and the Common People; whereas the rational Man, the Sage, believes nothing for which he lacks proof, and measures his persuasion by the degree of evidence and strength that his proofs possess. In this regard, the Gnostics <note>A diverse group of early Christian sects that emphasized personal spiritual knowledge (gnosis) over orthodox teachings and faith.</note> did not reason poorly. One would do them an injustice to believe that they understood *Faith* as the persuasion of truths that cannot be discovered by the Senses. They were not unaware that there are things accessible only to the pure Understanding.

<margin>The Heretics confuse credulity with Faith.</margin>
In what, then, did their Error consist? It was this: these Heretics were Philosophers who, having built certain Systems, accommodated Revelation to fit them. Revelation was the *Servant* of their *Reason*, and not the *Mistress*. *Mani* boasted in particular of possessing the perfect Science of all things; of having banished Mysteries, and of giving a just idea of all that must be. This is what the Manichaeans called the *knowledge (1) of the beginning, the middle, and the end of all things*. *St. Augustine* testifies that what had seduced him in his Youth (2) was the hope of knowing everything through demonstration, and of reaching God through the lights of Reason alone, without need for Faith. This is what the Manichaeans promised, and what they delivered quite poorly, as *St. Augustine* later perceived. But one sees on the other hand, through the words of this Father <note>Referring to St. Augustine, one of the "Church Fathers."</note>, that they were beginning in his time—or rather, they had already begun—(3) *to furiously assert the Authority of the Church*, or of the Bishops, and to impose a Yoke upon Reason and Faith that they neither can nor should bear. From this came the breaches through which the Enemy entered the Church and triumphed over it.

<margin>The Manichaeans boast of giving an account of everything.</margin>

### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. Book I. CH. VIII. ###

<margin>Proofs that Mani knew Greek.</margin>...that a Roman would understand Chaldaic or Syriac. Moreover, there are good reasons to believe that **Mani** <note>Also known as Manès, the 3rd-century Persian prophet and founder of Manichaeism.</note> knew the Greek language. One finds Greeks among his earliest disciples. **Sisinnius** and **Hierax** were Greeks, as can be recognized by their names. **Terebinthus** knew both Greek and Babylonian. The books of **Scythianus**, which **Mani** had translated and <margin>(a) *Cited above, pages 770, 771.* (b) *Against the Manichaeans, section 12, beginning.*</margin> interpolated, were written in Greek, as Monsieur de Tillemont *(a)* very rightly judged, and as *(b)* Photius positively testifies.

<margin>Explanation of a passage from this Letter.</margin>It even seems to me that I perceive in the Letter that the Heresiarch <note>A term for the founder of a heretical sect.</note> addressed to **Marcellus** an indication that it was written in Greek. It is found in these words *(4)*: *I do not have the phrases, the proper or natural expressions*. The ancient Latin interpreter and Father Petau believed that this meant *(5)*: *I am not naturally eloquent*. I pray the reader to compare my translation with that of these two interpreters; and, if mine is accurate, as I believe it is, **Mani** is telling **Marcellus** that he is not writing him a longer letter both *so as not to abuse his patience* and because he does not express himself well enough in Greek, which is a foreign language for him. *I do not have*, he says, *the phrases, the proper or natural expressions*. This excuse is reasonable if he is writing in Greek, as it is not his native tongue; but such an excuse would be quite unworthy of him if he were writing in Syriac or Chaldaic.

Here is another indication that **Mani** understood the Greek language. **Archelaus** says *(6)* that Mani sent his disciples to the places where the books of the Christians were transcribed. Saint Epiphanius adds that this was in **Jerusalem**. If **Mani** wanted to have the books of the New Testament in Syriac, they could be found everywhere in the East. Did the Churches of Mesopotamia, Assyria, and Persia not possess these books? No one would dare suggest such a thing. From this it follows that **Mani** wanted to have the books of the New Testament in Greek to compare them with the Syriac version used throughout the East. He wanted to see if this version agreed with the Greek original; for it is true that he practiced a form of criticism—I will not call it reasonable or judicious, but rather insolent and bold—upon these books, under the pretext that they had been corrupted by the **Galileans** <note>A derogatory term often used by critics and outsiders in antiquity to refer to Christians.</note>. If these reflections do not constitute a absolute demonstration, they provide at least a very strong proof that our Heresiarch understood the Greek language; from which I conclude that the Letter addressed to **Marcellus** was written in that language.

IV. *Marcellus* had no sooner received the letter than he shared it with *Archelaus*. Upon reading it, the Bishop flew into such a great rage, (1) *that he gnashed his teeth like a caged Lion, burning with the desire to have the Author of such a Letter in his power*. If the Reader wishes to know how St. *Epiphanius* <note>St. Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403) was a staunch opponent of heresy and a primary source for early Christian accounts of Manichaeism.</note> paraphrased this passage, I shall satisfy him. It must be admitted that St. *Epiphanius* had strange ideas of *Divine zeal*: And for my part, I confess that if I believed the description he provides, I would confuse this zeal with the fury of a wild beast.

<margin>Moderation of Marcellus. (a) Acts p. 9. Epiph. p. 625.</margin>
*Archelaus* and *Marcellus* being the two Heroes of this story, the Author divides between them the Virtues that suit their different characters. He grants to *Archelaus* Episcopal zeal; he is a roaring Lion. To *Marcellus*, he grants Lay moderation. He maintains his composure, attempts to appease the Bishop, and sends word to the Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> (a) that, not having fully understood what he meant to say, he begs him to come to *Kashkar* <note>An ancient city in Mesopotamia, near modern-day Iraq.</note> to explain his Sentiments. And as *Tyrbon* refused to carry this response, *Marcellus* sent it by one of his own Servants.

<margin>Mani suspects a trap; yet does not fail to go to Kashkar.</margin>
*Mani*, surprised not to see his Messenger return, suspected some evil design. He was a Persian; *Marcellus* and *Archelaus* were Romans: but furthermore, they were Catholics: and the hatred of the Catholics against the Heterodox <note>Those holding non-orthodox or "other" beliefs.</note> surpassed, perhaps, that of the Romans against the Persians. He feared, therefore, that they might hand him over to the King of Persia, and that they were detaining *Tyrbon* to hide the Trap being set for him. He was not much mistaken, as will be seen hereafter; nevertheless, he traveled to *Kashkar* accompanied (3) by twenty-two of his Disciples.

<meta>catchword: When</meta>

<margin>The Cloak, a garment of the Persians.</margin>
The Persians wore the Cloak. This is an outer garment, which they called (b) *Sudra* <note>A traditional Persian tunic or shirt, often ritual in nature</note>, and which reached down to the middle of the leg.

<margin>The color sky blue was honorable.
(b) Hyde, in the place cited above, p. 379.</margin>
People of the highest rank wore it in purple. Strabo uses a word (1), which literally means "flower-colored," but in common usage means a bright, dazzling, and perhaps variegated color. Sky blue was also an honorable color among the Assyrians, for we see in the History of *Esther* that (2) *Mordecai* appeared dressed in a Royal Robe, of hyacinth color and sky blue. It must even be a modest and fitting color for a religious man among the Persians, since (a) the robe of their *Dervishes* <note>Sufi Muslim ascetics, though the author uses the term here to describe ancient Persian religious figures</note> or their *Monks* is of that color.

<margin>(a) D'Herbelot, Oriental Library, at the word Dervish, p. 292.</margin>
Regardless, *Mani*, who had been at the Court of *Shapur* <note>King Shapur I, who reigned 240–270 AD</note>, where the Sciences granted considerable rank, could have been dressed as a man of quality without anyone finding fault with it. Mr. de Tillemont, who knows how Popes and Cardinals are dressed on ceremony days, should not have found Mani's clothing so un-Apostolic.

<margin>All bright colors were sacred among the Persians.
(b) Diogenes Laertius in the Introduction. Compare Aelian, Various History, Book XII. 32.</margin>
We imagine that a Philosopher, a grave man, must be dressed in brown or black: but our customs are arbitrary and prescribe nothing to other peoples. The *Magi* dressed (b) in white and carried a cane in their hand. The Persian Priests were dressed in (3) red, or fire-colored, because this color, and in general all brilliant colors, were sacred out of respect for the Fire <note>A reference to Zoroastrian veneration of fire as a symbol of divinity</note>.

<margin>The Pontifical Habits of the Eastern Patriarchs are of cheerful colors.</margin>
Regarding the Christians, their Bishops, their Metropolitans, and their Patriarchs chose the colors that pleased them, without any regard for the taste that reigns in the West. Red, green, blue, etc., have been used indifferently as the colors of their Pontifical garments. *Acacius* (4), who was consecrated Patriarch of Seleucia in 485, took the green Pallium <note>A circular band of fabric worn over the shoulders, signifying authority</note>: (5) *Babeus* and (6) *Ezekiel*, his successors, did the same; (7) *Machica* preferred violet, *Denha* rose-colored: others have worn white, red, blue, yellow, iron-gray, or lemon. In general, *Amnis* (8), a writer of the Nestorian Communion, testifies that the Patriarchs used fifteen kinds of colors in their sacred garments.

Two-colored hose. Remark on the Royal vest of Cyrus.

So far, Mani's equipment has nothing very strange about it. There are only these *two-colored hose*, which might offend our modern taste, but which perhaps did not offend that of the Persians. For I see in *Xenophon* (10) that the Tunic or Royal Vest of Cyrus was "half-parted," half-colored purple and half-white; and that this variety was a privilege, a mark of his Dignity.

(b) "*It is known*," he says, "*that Muhammad loved green, and that those who claim to descend from him affect the wearing of a green Turban to show they are of his race. It is believable that the Arabs took this custom from Mani, as they did a number of other things. For the Sect of the Manichaeans took root in Arabia, and reached its perfection in Persia and Mesopotamia. <margin>Mani has the appearance not of an Artisan, but of a Philosopher. An error of the Latin Translator of the Acts.</margin>
I have just reported an example of a poor translation from the Syriac. Here is one of a poor translation from the Greek. Our Latin Translator has *Archelaus* say that *Mani* had (1) *the face, or the look, of an* OLD PERSIAN ARTISAN, *and of a General of an army*. There was undoubtedly in the Greek *Technicos*, or *Technites* <note>original: "τεχνικός, ou τεχνίτης"</note>, which signify in this place a (2) Philosopher, a man learned in the fine Arts. It would be a strange disparity to compare the *look of an Artisan* to that of a *General*. But a grave and serious Philosopher may well resemble a General of an army, for whom a serious and grave demeanor is no less fitting than for a Philosopher.

<margin>Character of Archelaus. It appears that Epiphanius lends him his own.</margin>
When *Archelaus* had learned that *Mani* had arrived in *Cascar* <note>A city in Mesopotamia, modern-day Iraq, where the legendary debate between Bishop Archelaus and Mani supposedly took place.</note>, his zeal redoubled, and (3) *if he had had the power*, says St. Epiphanius, *he would have gone on the spot to fall upon this man, and kill him, as one kills a wolf or a leopard, so much did he fear that this wild Beast would devour some of his sheep*. Let us not, however, entirely believe St. Epiphanius, for I suspect it is the Bishop of Salamis <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403), a church father known for his fierce and often personal attacks on heretics.</note> whom he is describing, rather than the one from *Cascar*. Epiphanius—ardent, angry, and passionate—lends *Archelaus* his own hot-headedness, and borrows from himself the false Virtues he gives to his Hero.

<margin>The Acts represent him as more moderate.</margin>
Indeed, although *Archelaus* would have been very glad for *Mani* to perish, he took care, however, neither to kill him with his own hands, nor to have him killed by the People. For when he saw the irritated Rabble ready to throw themselves upon him (4), *he raised his voice like a trumpet, and cried out for moderation: Stop, my Brothers, he said, lest on the Day of Judgment, we be found guilty of having shed human blood*. He similarly repressed (a), on another occasion, the fury of the People, who wanted to fall upon *Mani*. ### CHAPTER IX.

->*The Debate of CASCAR.*<-

<margin>The first public Debate at Cascar.</margin>
I. Marcel gave a respectful welcome to *Manichaeaus* <note>Mani, the founder of Manichaeism.</note>, and resolved to hear them—both him and *Archelaus*—in a public Debate. As they both made profession of believing in Jesus Christ, and because neutral Judges were required, *Marcel* chose, from among the principal Citizens of *Cascar*, four persons most celebrated for their knowledge and their integrity, but all four of whom were Pagans.
<margin>The Judges are Pagans. Their professions and their names.</margin>
These Judges were: (1) *Manippus*, a learned Grammarian perfectly versed in Rhetoric and Literature; *Aegialeus*, a very skilled Physician; and *Claudius* and *Cleobulus*, brothers, both of whom were celebrated Rhetoricians.
<margin>(a) Epiphanius, as cited above, § 10.</margin>
St. *Epiphanius* (a) describes these Judges somewhat differently. According to him, *Manippus* was learned in the Philosophy of the Gentiles and taught it at *Cascar*; *Claudius* was a Grammarian, and *Cleobulus* a Rhetorician or *Sophist* <note>In this context, a professional teacher of philosophy or rhetoric.</note>. Their names show that they were all Greeks.

<margin>The Scene took place in Marcel's House.</margin>
The House of *Marcel* was opened to everyone, and, although it was very spacious, it was found to be filled with Spectators. The Judges sat upon a sort of platform; the two Antagonists placed themselves in the middle of the hall, and, when silence had been established, *Manichaeaus* spoke first.

### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. Book I. Ch. IX.

if there is any Gap in the Acts, it is certainly not at the beginning of the Conference. Everything there is full, everything is complete & well-followed. 2. It began with the Question of the two Principles, and not by that of the Old Testament, which was only debated after the former, so that it is impossible that *Mani* & *Archelaus* could have said, at the opening of the Dispute, what *Cyril* makes them say.

<margin>Mani opens the Dispute. The titles he gives himself of Apostle & Paraclete.</margin>
*Manichaeus* spoke first, and began with these words: (3) *I am a Disciple of Christ, and an Apostle of Jesus.* He distinguishes between *Christ* and *Jesus*, not that he believed they were two Persons, but it seems that he gave the title of *Christ* to the Son of God to mark his Person; and that of *Jesus* in relation to his Economy <note>The "Divine Economy" refers to God's management of the world and the plan for salvation, particularly through the incarnation.</note>. He is made to say, a few lines later, that he is (4) the *Paraclete* <note>original: "Paraclet"; from the Greek "Parakletos," meaning "Advocate" or "Comforter," a title for the Holy Spirit promised by Jesus in the Gospel of John.</note> promised by *Jesus*. This is one of the places that show this Dispute is feigned, *Mani* having never claimed to be the *Paraclete*, as will be seen in Part II of this Work. There is even a manifest contradiction in the titles of *Paraclete* and *Apostle*, or *Disciple* of *Jesus Christ*. These are incompatible qualities. Can the *Paraclete*, the Holy Spirit, be an *Apostle*, a *Disciple* of the Lord?

<margin>He raises himself above St. Paul. (a) 1 Cor. 13:10.</margin>
*Mani* continues, and bases the necessity of his Mission on these words of St. *Paul*. (a) *We know only in part: we prophesy only in part; but, when perfection has come, everything that is imperfect shall be abolished.* The Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> claims (5) that the *Perfection* predicted by St. *Paul* is the Doctrine that he announced. Regarding this passage, there is nothing suspicious. For the Manichaean *Felix* alleged these same words of St. *Paul* in the (6) Dispute he had with St. *Augustine*, and concluded from them that *Manichaeus* his Master had brought to the world the *Perfection* that St. *Paul* had not known.

<margin>Questions debated in the Dispute of Caschar. 1. That of the two Principles. 2. That of the Authority of the Old Testament.</margin>
II. After having tried to establish his Divine Mission in this manner, *Manichaeus* briefly sets out his views, first on the Question of the two Principles; and second, on that of the authority of the Old Testament. He maintains the affirmative regarding the first Question, and the negative regarding the second. *Archelaus* attacks these two Errors, and does so like a man who lacks neither wit nor knowledge. But, just as there are places where he is strong, there are also those where he is weak.

<meta>This page continues the examination of the debate between Archelaus and Mani, specifically focusing on the logical arguments against the idea that the soul is of the same substance as God and the refutation of the Manichaean dualist system.</meta>

### HISTORY OF MANI ACCORDING TO
<meta>catchword: It</meta>

<margin>of God. Archelaus’s Reasoning against this Error.</margin>
Divine Substance. *Archelaus*, who combats this Error, insists on a reason that was the great argument of St. *Augustine*. It is that if Souls are emanated from God, they are consubstantial <note>sharing the same fundamental essence or substance; of the same nature as God himself</note> with God; from which it follows, first, that they can neither sin nor be unhappy, unless one says that the Divine Substance can be subject to both Sin and misery, which is absurd. Second, that Souls must be immutable <note>incapable of change</note>, because the eternal substance cannot change. However, it is clear that Souls change, and pass from good to evil, and from evil to good. It is astonishing that *Mani* responds with nothing to these difficulties—he whom they represent to us as so clever, and to whom these points were certainly not new. He would have satisfied them poorly, I believe, but at the last he would have tried to satisfy them; his silence on this matter is a strong indication that the Author of this text makes him respond, or leaves him without an answer, as he sees fit.

<margin>Reasoning of the same against the two Principles.</margin>
*Archelaus* also proves that the *Spirit* and *Matter*, the Body and the Soul, which compose Man, being united together and having a reciprocal action, could not possibly come from two Principles <note>the Manichaean belief in two separate, eternal powers: one of Good/Light and one of Evil/Darkness</note> independent of one another. Because these two Principles are contrary, they could not have reached an agreement to form a single composite being. *Mani* again responds with nothing to this difficulty, although his System could have provided him with some solution, whether good or bad.

<margin>How he explains the origin of evil.</margin>
The Bishop, explaining why Sin exists in the World, sets down as a Principle that every intelligent Creature is necessarily free, because it is intelligent, and mutable <note>subject to change</note> because it is a Creature. He makes other arguments that I will not report, and sometimes uses Scripture quite appropriately; but it must also be admitted that he abuses it very often, and that it is not in the Authors of that time that one should seek the most certain and solid Explanations of the sacred Books.

<margin>Ingenious explanation of Matthew 12:32.</margin>
The explanation of the passage that has been cited for a long time to prove Purgatory is quite ingenious and natural. Jesus Christ said that *the Sin against the Holy Spirit will be forgiven neither in this Age, nor in the Age to come*. This means, according to *Archelaus*, that this Sin will be punished in this Age by temporal death, and in the Age to come by the pains of Eternity: Or to express myself as this Bishop does, (1) "that this Sin will be subject both to the curse of the Mosaic Law in this Age, and to that of Jesus Christ on the day of the last Judgment."

### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. Book I. Ch. IX.
O

<margin>Objection from Mani. J. Christ establishes two Principles, John VIII:44, when he says that the Devil has a Father, who is a liar.</margin>
It is far from certain that this same Bishop <note>Archelaus, the Bishop of Carchar, who supposedly debated Mani</note> extricates himself as successfully from a passage in *St. John*, which the Heresiarch <note>Mani, the founder of Manichaeism</note> was abusing to prove his Principle of evil. The latter insisted on these words of Our Lord: *“Because there is no truth in him (in the Devil), whenever he speaks a lie, he speaks from his own nature, for he is a liar as well as his father.”* It was in this way that Mani rendered the words of the Lord, and Archelaus did not contest the translation. Thereupon the Heresiarch asks him: <margin>(a) Acts p. 56.</margin> *(a) Who is the Father of the Devil? It is not God,* he continues, *for God is not a liar. Who is it then? There are only two ways to be someone’s Father: Generation or Creation. If God is the Father of the Devil by way of Generation, the Devil would be consubstantial <note>sharing the same essence or substance</note> with God. This conclusion is impious. And, if God is the Father of the Devil by way of Creation, then God is a liar, which is another impiety. It must be, therefore, that the Devil is the Son or Creature of some wicked Being who is not God. There is, therefore, another Principle besides God.*

<margin>Bad solution from Archelaus.</margin>
Archelaus speaks in this place with much confidence, but he is pitiable. He says (2), that the first Father of the Devil is the Serpent, into which he entered when he wished to tempt *Eve*; that the Serpent then found himself quite heavy and swollen, and that he gave birth to the Demon. He adds that *Cain*, *Pharaoh*, and *Judas* are likewise the Fathers of the Devil, and in general all those who obey his suggestions. One perceives clearly enough that this response leaves the victory to Mani. However, the latter is a simpleton who has no retort, and who remains stunned by an answer over which he should have triumphed.

<margin>Another bad solution from St. Epiphanius. (a) See Heresy XL. §. 5. & 6. This passage has been employed by all the Heretics who have recognized two Principles.</margin>
Furthermore, *St. Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his catalogs of heresies</note> did not fare any better with this objection. He replied *(a)* that the *Devil* of whom *Jesus Christ* speaks in the passage of *St. John* is *Judas*; that the Father of *Judas* is *Cain*; and finally that the Father of *Cain* is the Devil himself. This is the miserable resource of a man who succumbs under the weight of the difficulty. However, this shows that these Ancients did not believe that the pronoun <term>αὐτῷ</term> <note>autō; in Greek, this can mean "him" or "it"</note> could be understood as anything other than a person. For us, who understand it as a thing, this passage causes us no embarrassment. *Jesus Christ* said *that the Devil is a liar, and that he is the Father of Lies.*

<margin>Specifically the portrait drawn by Eusebius.</margin>
This passage is proof that *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and bishop known as the "Father of Church History"</note> drew a portrait of *Manichaeus* that bears very little resemblance to the truth when he said (2) *that this man was savage and intractable by nature, barbarian in his actions and in his speech.* There is certainly imposture in *Manichaeus*; perhaps it is merely fanaticism; but the Character he portrays is more beautiful than that of a Bishop who gnashes his teeth and roars like a Lion at the sight of a Heretic.

<margin>The Judges grant victory to Archelaus. This circumstance makes the entire History suspect.</margin>
IV. *The Judges pronounced in favor of Archelaus*; at least the Acts say so; and, if this is true, they set an Example of justice and generosity that one would have great difficulty finding among Christians. For, being Pagans, how could they condemn *Mani* <note>original: "Manès"</note> without condemning their own Religion? If this Heresiarch <note>A founder of a heretical sect</note> honors the *Sun*, as *Archelaus* reproaches him for doing, did the Pagans not do the same, especially in Mesopotamia? If he believes in **two Principles, God and Matter**, what does he believe there that all the Pagan Philosophers have not also believed? Is it not to this **Matter** that they attributed, as he did, the cause of imperfections and evils found in the World? *Manichaeus* rejects the Old Testament and the inspiration of the Prophets. Now, Pagans could not award the victory to *Archelaus*, who maintained the inspiration of these Prophets, without admitting that their own Gods were Demons; that their Images and Statues were Idols; and that they themselves were fools, Idolaters, and impious men. Certainly *Marcellus* <note>The Roman official who supposedly hosted the debate</note> could not have chosen better: and I know not if, in the rest of the Earth, he could have found four learned Pagans generous enough to do justice to the Orthodox Faith at the expense of their Philosophy, their Religion, and their Gods. It is true that such a fine disinterestedness gives some suspicion to the Reader, and I am willing to admit to him that I am not exempt from it myself. These Pagan Judges have very much the appearance of being Characters invented to embellish either the History or the Romance of the Dispute of *Caschar* <note>A legendary debate between Mani and Bishop Archelaus, often considered by modern scholars to be a fictionalized literary work rather than a historical transcript</note>.

# THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. IX.

<margin>The Conference of Caschar was not recorded by Notaries. Tillemont’s error regarding this. (a) As cited above p. 786.</margin>
Mr. de Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a rigorous French ecclesiastical historian</note> believed that it was written on the spot by secretaries who had been chosen for that purpose. *Marcellus*, (a) he says, *desired that everything taking place in the Conference be written down at the same time*. He bases this on the word *Excipi* <note>original Latin: "Excipi," meaning to take down or transcribe, often used for shorthand</note>, which appears in the Latin Version, and which would indeed confirm Mr. de Tillemont’s thought if everything else did not contradict it. The Author, whoever he may be, expresses himself in these terms: (3) *Marcellus, having desired that this Dispute be set down in writing (taken down and transcribed), I could not refuse it, hoping that the Reader will have enough indulgence to forgive me the defects of this Work, my intention being only to make known to those who desire it how things occurred*. These words, **I COULD NOT REFUSE IT**, <note>original: "contradicere non potui"</note> are evident proof that this does not concern secretaries; for with what face could Archelaus <note>The Bishop of Caschar and protagonist of the debate</note> have opposed having exact and faithful secretaries write down, on the spot, everything said in the Conference? Furthermore, would the Author, who informs us that *Pagan Judges* presided over the Dispute, have failed to tell us that it was written by secretaries, a circumstance that would serve immensely to confirm his account? As for the word (4) *Excipi*, upon which Mr. de Tillemont relies, he might have considered that it is a word from the Translator and not the Author, and that the word in the Original could have had other meanings.

<margin>Manifest alterations and falsifications in this Piece.</margin>
I. There are not only errors in our Acts; there are manifest additions and falsifications, and one knows not to whom they should be imputed. For example, Archelaus reproaches the Heresiarch <note>Mani, the leader of the Manichaean "heresy"</note> (5) "with knowing neither Greek, nor Latin, nor Egyptian, nor any other Language than Chaldean, *which*, he adds, *does not even deserve to be counted among the Languages*." One can boldly assert that Archelaus said nothing of the kind. What rudeness, or rather, what imprudence would he have shown in scorning in such a way the Language of a Country where *Archelaus* was Bishop, in which he himself preached the Gospel, and doing so before an entire People who knew no other? If the Author confuses Syriac with Chaldean, he speaks with great impertinence, for the Syriac Language was highly esteemed throughout the East. One recognizes a Greek in these words. <margin>Observation by *L. de Dieu* <note>Louis de Dieu (1590–1642), a Dutch Protestant theologian and expert in Oriental languages.</note> on the Syriac Version of *John 8:44*. It proves that *Manes* <note>Another name for Mani, the founder of Manichaeism.</note> quoted the Greek, or that it is a Greek who makes him speak.</margin>
2. I say that the words I have just reported could only have been uttered by a Greek: but I add that the Dispute itself is the work of a Greek, which I shall prove in an invincible manner by an observation of (1) *Louis de Dieu* on verse 44 of Chapter 8 of *St. John*.

I have remarked that *Manichaeus* insisted on this passage to show that God is not the Creator of the Demon. This objection is very specious <note>Meaning plausible-sounding but fallacious.</note> if one cites the passage in Greek; likewise, the Greek Fathers were greatly embarrassed to resolve it. But if one cites the same passage according to the Syriac Version, the objection no longer holds. The reason for this is that it is founded on an ambiguity that exists in the Greek, but which is not in the Syriac, where the word signifying *Lie* is feminine, and the pronoun, which in the Greek can be of the masculine or neuter gender, is feminine as well. One only needs to know how to read Syriac and understand its terms to judge that Jesus Christ said *that the Devil is a liar, and that he is the Father of Lies*. Let us put *falsehood* in place of *lies*; the Syriac reads literally, *the Devil is a liar, and the Father OF IT* <note>original: "D'ICELLE," referring back to the feminine noun for falsehood</note>, that is to say, of *Falsehood*. In the Greek, the ambiguity is complete, for one reads, *the Devil is a liar, and the Father OF HIM* <note>original Greek: "αὐτοῦ" (autou), which can mean "of him" or "of it."</note>, that is to say, either of the *Devil*, whose name immediately precedes, or of the *Lie*, a word that is further away.

This remark evidently proves one of two things. First, that it is a Greek who fabricated this Dispute and who proposed the objection that the Marcionites <note>Followers of Marcion, who believed the God of the Old Testament was separate from and inferior to the God of the New Testament.</note>, the Manichaeans, and other heretics who believed in the eternity of Matter were accustomed to making to the Orthodox, to show that God is not the *Father* or the Creator of the Demon, since the *Father* of the Demon is a liar according to Jesus Christ. Second, that if the Dispute is genuine, *Manichaeus* cited the Greek original of St. John and not the Syriac Version, and consequently,

# HISTORY OF MANI ACCORDING TO #

<meta>catchword: refut-</meta>

> “...that it is in our power to sin, or not to sin. *Archelaus* <note>A 3rd-century bishop, likely a fictional character in the "Acts of Archelaus," used as a mouthpiece for orthodox theology against Mani.</note> proves that Man is free, and master of his actions, because there is a *Judgment*; for, according to him, if there were no liberty, there would be neither Judgment, nor punishments, nor rewards. Such is the reasoning of *Archelaus*, reasoning which one finds in all the Church Fathers, and in *St. Augustine*, as in the others. But, in the middle of this reasoning, these words have been put in parentheses, which not only divide it and cut the thread, but which limit it, and at the core overturn it: *If we sin, it is our own work, but if we do not sin, it is a gift of God.* <note>original: "Si nous péchons, c'est notre ouvrage, mais si nous ne péchons pas, c'est un don de Dieu."</note> One recognizes this sentence, which was common among the Latins since the Century of *St. Augustine*.”

<margin>Tillemont was misled by this Addition.
(a) In the place cited above, p. 796. <note>original: "Ub. sup." for ubi supra.</note></margin>
This Addition deceived Mr. de *Tillemont* <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a renowned French ecclesiastical historian.</note> (a). He believed he found in it proof that *Archelaus* taught both the necessity of Grace and the Freedom of man. I have nothing to say regarding the Dogma itself, but I am surprised that this modern Scholar did not perceive that it is an Addition by the Latin Translator, who found the Proposition of *Archelaus* contrary to the System of his Church. What I say is evident. The Greeks, and especially the Greeks of the time of *Archelaus*, who were dealing with the Marcionites and the Manichaeans, gave to Man an entire Liberty—an equal power either to obey the Divine Law or to violate it. The Latins, such as *Tertullian* and *St. Irenaeus*, defended the same Principle in all its generality. *Archelaus* did so, and was obliged to do so. For if he had argued that Man has need of a supernatural Grace in order not to sin, *Mani* would have concluded from this—rightly or wrongly—that Nature is evil in itself, and the Question would then have been only whether this vitiosity comes from the very core of Nature itself, or if it is accidental. Anyone reading the Ancient authors cannot be too attentive in discovering the falsifications that have been made to them. Let us pass to the Conference of *Diodoris*.

The heresiarch <note>Mani, the founder of Manichaeism.</note> preached his Errors there, and the Priest, not feeling strong enough to resist him, gave notice to his Bishop and asked him for Instructions and help. This is what obliged *Archelaus* to first write him a long Letter (1), the address of which is conceived in these terms: <margin>Letter from Archelaus to Diodorus.</margin>

->TO THE PRIEST DIODORUS, MY MOST HONORABLE SON.<-

<margin>The address has two characteristics of being a forgery. 1. In the beginning, there was no Church without a Bishop.</margin> I find in this address two things that seem very suspicious to me, and which, if I am not mistaken, show that it is not from the time of *Archelaus*. The first is that it assumes a Church without a Bishop, governed by a simple Priest. Now, I do not believe one can find, around the middle of the 3rd Century, in either Cities or Towns, any Church that did not have its own Bishop. When the Church was small in number, the Bishop had only Deacons beneath him; but he was no less a Bishop: he held the title and performed all the functions. It was only much later that these Country Bishops, or *Chorepiscopi* <note>term: *Chorepiscopi* — from the Greek for "rural bishops," these were assistants to city bishops who oversaw smaller village congregations.</note>, were stripped of their authority and forced to descend into the *Order* of Priests. *Diodoris* was a *Fortress* (*Castellum*) or a Town, for they are the same thing. Now, there were then, and have been since, Bishops in *Towns*, as can be seen in the (2) Oriental Library of Mr. *Assemani* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a famous Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> and elsewhere.

<margin>2. Bishops at that time styled Priests as Brothers, and not as Sons. The title of Son was only given to Deacons.</margin> The second thing that makes this address suspicious to me is that, even assuming the Country Churches had only simple Priests, it is at least certain that the Bishops gave them the title of BROTHERS, and never that of SONS. This latter title was only given to Deacons, who were properly the Ministers of the Bishops in Divine Service. I do not believe that one finds in the first three Centuries any certain example of a Bishop who addressed a Priest as *Son* when writing to him.

He based himself (2) principally on these words of St. *Paul*: *Jesus Christ (a) took the FORM of a Servant, or, he made himself LIKE unto men: he appeared in the EXTERIOR, or, in the FIGURE such as a man.* And to confirm the explanation he gave to these words of the Apostle, he alleged what St. *Luke* (b) says: *The Holy Spirit descended upon Jesus, in a bodily form, LIKE THAT OF A DOVE.* As the Holy Spirit was not united to the body of a Dove, and only appeared under that form, *Manichaeus* also maintained that the Son of God only took the *form* and the *appearance* of a man because it suited his purpose not to be truly man, but to appear so.

<margin>*Archelaus* refuted it well.</margin>

Thus we see our <term>Saint Archelaus</term> <note>Archelaus is the legendary Bishop of Caschar (Carchar) in Mesopotamia, famous for his supposed public debate with Mani in the 3rd century.</note>, this illustrious Bishop who first fought against Mani and his Heresy, now associated with Heretics who are hardly better than <term>Mani</term>; at least if one judges them by the anathemas hurled against them and the punishments to which they were condemned. He is a Saint for the Unitarians <note>A term used here to describe non-Trinitarians who believe in the single personhood of God, often denying the full divinity of Jesus.</note>, but not for the Catholics. <margin>(a) Acts, p. 90.</margin>
He interrogates his Antagonist in these terms: (a) "Answer me this, Mani: If you say that the *Christ* was not born of *Mary*, but that he simply appeared to be a man, although he was not in effect, and this by means of the Power that was in him: tell me, upon whom did the Holy Spirit descend like a Dove? For (2) *if he were already Perfect, if he were already the Son of God, if he were the Power, the Spirit could not enter into him, just as one Kingdom cannot enter into another Kingdom.* <note>original Latin: "Si perfectus erat, si Filius erat, si Virtus erat, non poterat Spiritus ingredi, sicut nec regnum potest ingredi intra regnum."</note>

<margin>Critical observation on the Text.</margin>
It must be remarked first that there is an error, or a falsification, in these words: *If you say that the Christ was not born of Mary.* The word *Christ* was put for *Jesus*. For our Author (3) carefully distinguishes between *Jesus* and the *Christ*; one is the Son of Mary, the other the Son of God. And he was careful not to say that the *Christ* was born of Mary, since, according to him, he only descended upon *Jesus* after his Baptism. This observation will appear evident to anyone who wishes to read the Author with attention and without prejudice.

(They say Jesus is different from the Christ; and that Jesus was born of the Virgin, but the Christ descended upon him.)</note> Theodor. Heret. Fab. L. <margin>According to him, Jesus Christ is the Son of God only since his Baptism.</margin>
This, then, is what *Archelaus* means to say: if there were in *Jesus* only the Divine Nature under the simple appearance of a man, the Spirit could neither descend upon him nor enter into him, because that would be a Divine Power entering into a Divine Power, or a Spirit entering into a Spirit. From this it follows, in his view, that it was necessary for Jesus Christ to be a man so that the Spirit could enter into him. But, in making this argument, the Author teaches—and even establishes as a Principle—that this Jesus, born of Mary, only became the Son of God after he was baptized; and that previously he was neither perfect, nor the *Son*, nor the *Power*. This view effectively destroys the entire Doctrine of the <term>Incarnation</term> <note>The central Christian belief that God became flesh in the person of Jesus Christ from the moment of conception.</note>.

Subsequently, *Mani* presents this argument to *Archelaus*: (4) "If you say that he who *was born of Mary is simply a man*, and that he received the Spirit in Baptism, it follows that he became the Son of God through progress and growth, and that he is not so by Nature." *Archelaus* responds, but without in any way denying this consequence.

<margin>A strange reason for the Lord’s Baptism.</margin>
The <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A title given to the founder of a heretical movement, in this case, Mani, the founder of Manichaeism.</note> proposes another argument, to which his Adversary gives a strange reply. *Mani* denied the Baptism of Jesus Christ on the grounds that if he had been baptized, he must have been a sinner. (5) "Far be it!" responds *Archelaus*: "on the contrary, he was made sin for us, taking our sins upon himself. But, being born of a Woman, he was baptized in order to receive the purification of *this part of himself*, so that the body he had taken could carry the Spirit, which descended upon him in the form of a dove." The Bishop recognizes the perfect innocence of Jesus. He did not receive Baptism to be washed of his own sins; that is quite orthodox. However, when the Author adds that Jesus was baptized in order to *confer* upon that part of himself born of a woman a degree of holiness that would make it capable of sustaining the Spirit that descended into it, he wanders infinitely far from the Principles of the Catholic Faith. Did this *Part of Jesus*, this *Flesh*, which from the moment of its conception was personally united to the <term>Word</term> <note>The 'Word' (Logos) refers to the divine second person of the Trinity.</note>, need to rece—

<column-break/>

—ive [anything], since a celestial Intelligence cannot enter into another Intelligence.

(3) Jesus who is born of Mary. *Acts, p. 93.* Jesus who is born of Mary above all Saints. *Ibid.* <note>original: "Qui de Mariâ natus eſt Jeſus. Act. p. 93. Qui ex Mariâ natus eſt ſuper omnes Sanctos Jeſus. Ibid."</note>

(4) For if you say that he is only a man from Mary, and received the Spirit in Baptism, then he will appear to be the Son through progress, and not by nature. *Acts, p. 91.* <note>original: "Si enim hominem tantummodo ex Mariâ eſſe dicis, & in Baptiſmate Spiritum percepisſe, ergo per profectum Filius videbitur, & non per naturam. <margin>Arianism and Nestorianism of *Methodius*, contemporary of *Archelaus*.</margin> Such appear to have been the Sentiments of *Archelaus*, who was, as they say, Bishop of *Cascar* in the 3rd Century. Nevertheless, the Reader should not be surprised to find such opinions in the Fathers of that time. For example, this Author says in his own words, that the Word (1) is nothing but the <term>OLDEST OF THE AEONS</term> <note>Aeons: In early Christian and Gnostic thought, these were various levels of divine beings or emanations from God.</note>, (that is to say, of the immortal Intelligences) and <term>THE FIRST OF THE ARCHANGES</term>. I do not know if this opinion was preserved in the East, but it is still found in a Syrian Author of the 10th Century, named (3) *Moses Bar-Cepha*. <margin>Particular opinions of Archelaus.</margin>
*III. Archelaus* holds several other opinions that will seem quite singular today, now that many theological opinions have been fixed by Decisions, though in the beginning, one could think on them with liberty. According to him (5), only the Divine Substance is invisible. 
<margin>On the visibility of Angels.</margin>
All spiritual creatures—Angels and Archangels—are visible, and necessarily so. He also believes that the Devil (a) became wicked only after the creation of Man, an opinion which is presently as common as it is uncertain. 
<margin>On the time of the Devil's fall. (a) Act. p. 32.</margin>
But here is a very singular one. He wishes to prove that Darkness does not exist by itself, but is merely the effect of an opaque body that intercepts Light. 
<margin>On the origin of Darkness.</margin>
To this end, he supposes (6) "that before the creation of Heaven and Earth, and of all bodily creatures, a constant light illuminated all space, because there was no thick body to prevent it from spreading everywhere." I do not know how he reconciled this opinion with the history in Genesis.

<margin>On those who cast the golden calf.</margin>
He thinks on the subject of the *Golden Calf* in a manner that suggests he was acquainted with the sentiments of the Jews. For he maintains that it was not the Israelites who cast the Golden Calf, but Egyptian proselytes <note>Proselytes: Converts to Judaism from other nations—in this case, Egyptians who followed the Israelites out of Egypt.</note> who had followed them. Some Rabbis have said this to excuse their nation.

Mr. *Assemani* <note>Giuseppe Luigi Assemani, the Maronite scholar mentioned on the previous page.</note> challenges the authenticity of these Acts, and does not hesitate to say (4) that *Hegemonius* <note>Hegemonius (4th century) is the traditionally attributed author of the "Acts of Archelaus," the primary source for the dispute between the Bishop and Mani.</note>, who lived some time after Archelaus, removed certain things from them and added others. The second is that *Severus*, Bishop of *Asmonine* <note>Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (10th century), a Coptic Bishop and historian known for his History of the Patriarchs.</note>, whose account I will report shortly, asserts that *Mani* was thirty-five years old when he entered into conference with *Archelaus*.

Of all the opinions held regarding the time of these Disputes, none is better founded than that which places them in the year 277. I do not declare myself on the question of whether they are true or fabricated; I will say later what I think of them, and what may have given occasion to invent them. But if they are admitted, they must belong to that year. What persuades me of this is: 1. That *St. Epiphanius* himself (*b*), in the *Manichaean Heresy*, placed *Mani's* journey to Mesopotamia under the Empire of *Probus*, who succeeded *Tacitus* in the year 277—and consequently fifteen to sixteen years later than he had done in his *Treatise on Weights and Measures*. 2. I see no reason to contest the testimony of the Author of the *Acts of Archelaus*, whoever he may be, when he reproaches *Manichaeas* <note>The Latinized form of Mani.</note> that, if he were the Paraclete <note>The "Paraclete" refers to the Holy Spirit or "Comforter" promised by Jesus in the Gospel of John; Mani claimed to be this promised figure.</note> promised by Jesus Christ, he would not have waited (5) until the Empire of *Probus* to manifest himself to the world. 3. This is the only Epoch that can be reconciled with the history of *Manichaeas* by the Syrians, the Persians, and the Arabs, who must be better informed than the Greeks about the life and death of a Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heretical sect.</note> who appeared in the East. 4. Finally, there is no likelihood that the founder of a heresy which had such a run in the world, and which had already been preached by two or three different missions in Egypt, Scythia, Syria, and Judea, died at the age of twenty-one or twenty-two.

<margin>Two Epochs of the Manichaean Heresy.</margin>
Since I am on this subject, I will examine two questions that must be clearly distinguished: the first is the Epoch of <term>Manichaeism</term> <note>A dualistic religion founded by the prophet Mani, teaching a struggle between a good world of light and an evil world of darkness.</note> itself; the second is that of its eruption into the Roman Empire, or rather the time when this heresy began to be known and to cause a stir there.

<margin>Its birth in Persia should be placed around the year 267.</margin>
Regarding the first, I believe that St. Epiphanius places it too early when he sets it (1) in the year 261. Here is the proof. **Mani** was born in 240. This is attested by the *Chronicle of Edessa*. He was a Priest at *Ahvaz*; *Abulpharage* <note>original: "Abulpharage"; refers to Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286), a prominent Bishop and historian of the Syriac Orthodox Church.</note> bears witness to this. He could not have received the Order of Priesthood until around the age of twenty-four, and approximately in the year 264. The same *Abulpharage* asserts that at the beginning he was very zealous for the Faith, and that he defended it against the <term>Magi</term> <note>Zoroastrian priests of the Persian Empire.</note>, against the Jews, and against the Pagans. He must therefore have remained in the communion of the Church for at least two or three years, until about the year 267 or 268. Furthermore, the learned <term>Monophysite</term> <note>A member of a Christian sect believing that Christ has only one nature; here referring again to Abulpharage.</note> whom I just cited places the birth of the Manichaean heresy under *Aurelian*, who was made Emperor in 270 according to Father *Pagi*; according to others, in 269. But it should be noted that *Abulpharage* moves the Empire of *Aurelian* forward by a few years, which leads me to judge that **Mani** began to reveal his heresy around the year 268, and that he then retired to *Sapor* <note>Shapur I, the Great King of the Sassanid Persian Empire.</note>, whose favor he won. His disgrace having occurred a few years later, he fled to *Scythia*, where he must have stayed until after the death of *Sapor*, as we shall see in the following.

<margin>Its appearance in the Empire in the year 276 or 277.</margin>
As for the time when his heresy began to be known in the Roman Empire, there is too much agreement among our authors to deny that it was the first or second year of *Probus*. For besides the fact that this Epoch is confirmed by all the testimonies I have just cited, it is also confirmed by (2) *Eusebius* in the most detailed and precise manner. And what the reader should observe well is that since *Eusebius* had not seen the *Acts of Archelaus*, it cannot be said that he borrowed the date from them. The same Epoch is confirmed by *Cyril of Jerusalem*, who testifies

---

<columns>2</columns>

(1) One of the most skillful and moderate critics of our time (I mean Father *Pagi*) reports, on the year 282, § 4, what *Photius* says after St. *Epiphanius*: namely, that *Manichaeus* came to *Cascar* in the 9th year of *Valerian* and *Gallienus*. And as he does not correct this date, one would think he approves of it. However, the same author shows elsewhere (*An.* 277. § 6.) that the Manichaean heresy only began in the second year of *Probus*. I do not wish to accuse him of contradiction; but I warn the reader of this diversity, so that one is not mistaken.

<margin>(c) See Pagi, cited above. Year 144, § 2.</margin>I interpret all these passages not as the time of the birth of Manichaeism, which had begun in Persia about ten years earlier, but as the time when this heresy began to make a stir in the Empire. This explanation is entirely natural and is the unique (4) means of reconciling the Eastern writers with the Greeks and the Latins. Mr. *Cave*, who had only consulted the latter, placed the origin of Manichaeism (5) in the year 277 and the death of the <term>heresiarch</term> <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> at the end of the 3rd century. What surprised me in his opinion is not so much that it is contrary to the accounts of all antiquity—which place the death of *Mani* at the latest in the year 278—but that it cannot be reconciled with the *Acts of Archelaus*, whose authenticity he maintains and which he believes were written (a) in Syriac by *Archelaus* himself in the year 278. For it is clear, as Mr. *Asseman* remarked above, that the death of *Mani* followed very shortly after the disputes in Mesopotamia, which were the occasion for it.

<margin>It is by this distinction that one must reconcile the Easterners with the Greeks and Latins.</margin>

### CHAPTER XI.

->*Retreat and punishment of* MANICHAEUS.<-

<margin>Archelaus wishes to have Mani delivered to the Persians and to have him put to death.</margin>
I. ARCHELAÜS, <note>Archelaus is the legendary Bishop of Caschar (Kaskar) in Mesopotamia, known primarily through the *Acts of Archelaus*, an anti-Manichaean polemical work.</note> having won a second victory over his Adversary at Diodoris, and having forced him to abandon the field of battle to him, told the Multitude the History of the Heresiarch <note>term: Heresiarch; the founder of a heretical sect.</note> which I have related, and finished it with these words: (1) *"Having been informed of these things, I find myself under the necessity of informing you of them, because the King of Persia is even now searching for Mani everywhere."* <note>original Latin: "Hæc ego cum cognoviſſem, neceſſarium me etiam vobis indicare, quia requiritur ipſe a Rege Perſarum uſque in hodiernum diem."</note>

If the Bishop had been content to reveal to the People the Errors of *Mani*, and to show them their source, he would have done the duty of a Pastor. But why tell them that this miserable man caused the death of the Son of the King of Persia; that, this Prince having had him put in prison, he corrupted his Guards, escaped, etc.; and that finally the King is searching for him everywhere to punish him? It is not difficult to guess the intention of the Bishop of *Caschar*. He wants to engage the People of Diodoris and the surrounding areas to seize the Heresiarch and make of him a sacrifice to the Persians, from whom they were separated only by the River *Stranga*, which served as the limit for the two <margin>(a) Ibid. p. 100.</margin> Empires. This is also what the People understood very well. *(a) For, having heard the Discourse of the Bishop, they wanted to take Mani to deliver him to the neighboring Barbarians.* <note>The "Barbarians" here refers to the Sassanid Persians, seen as the external enemy of the Roman/Byzantine world.</note> But he fled in haste and reached the Castle of *Arabion*.

<margin>St. Epiphanius has disguised this passage.</margin>
St. Epiphanius <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his fierce opposition to heresy in the *Panarion*.</note> must have felt clearly that such a proceeding dishonored the Episcopal character; for, leaving the Relation of Archelaus at this point, he substituted another entirely different one, <margin>(b) Epiph. ibid. §. 11.</margin> and which is certainly of his own invention. He relates then *(b)*, "that the People being transported with zeal, and wanting to stone Manichaeus, <margin>(c) Ibid. p. 793.</margin> Archelaus opposed it, and made him escape." M. de Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a prominent ecclesiastical historian.</note> *(c)* recognizes that this fact is not in the Relation, from which it follows that St. Epiphanius has supposed it. <margin>Mani is captured and brought to the King. His punishment.</margin>
This did not fail to happen. The King was soon informed of the place where *Mani* had retreated. He had him seized and led to his Capital; and commanded *that he be flayed*. The terms of the Account (2) do not necessarily mean that he was flayed alive. *Abulpharage* <note>Abulpharage, also known as Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286), was a prominent scholar and bishop of the Syriac Orthodox Church.</note> even says (3) that it was only after his death. His flesh was given to birds of prey. His skin was prepared, and after having filled it with air, *like a bellows*, it was hung at the gate of the City. I have several Observations to make on this History.

<margin>Critique of St. Epiphanius.
(a) *As cited above, question 12.*</margin>
I first observe that, according to his custom, *St. Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403) was a bishop known for his fierce opposition to heresies.</note> has adorned it with several new circumstances. He says first that *Mani* (a) *was flayed with the point of a reed*. This is of no consequence, but it is found neither in the Acts nor in any ancient Author, as far as I know.

<margin>Mani's skin was filled with air, and not with straw.
(b) *Abulpharage, as cited above.*</margin>
He then says that *his skin was filled with straw*. I do indeed find the same thing in *Abulpharage*, who nevertheless speaks neither of his *flaying* nor of this circumstance except as a rumor, (b) IT IS SAID <note>original Latin: *FERTUR*</note>. It is very likely that he copied *St. Epiphanius* in this place, for he understood the Greek Language very well. Be that as it may, *Photius* <note>Photius I (c. 810–893) was the Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar.</note>, who had seen the Greek of the *Account of Archelaus*, testifies that the skin of the Heresiarch (4) *was filled with air, or wind, like a bellows*. Indeed, it was *with air*, and not *with straw*, that they filled the skins of the unfortunate souls who were flayed.

<margin>Likewise that of the Emperor Valerian.</margin>
When the Emperor *Valerian* was dead, *Sapor* <note>Sapor I (Shapur) was the Sasanian King of Persia who famously captured the Roman Emperor Valerian in 260 AD.</note> commanded that he be flayed, that his skin be prepared to preserve it, and that it be filled with air. It was a monument that the Persians took pleasure in showing to Roman Ambassadors. Moreover, if we are to believe the Greek Legends, the Apostle (5) *St. Bartholomew* suffered the same fate as *Manichaeus*, as did a certain (6) *Studite* Monk.

ments. One of the precepts of their Religion was to keep them pure. *Agathias* (b) <margin>(b) Agathias, History of Justinian, Book II, 12.</margin> relates that *Simplicius* and those other Pagan Philosophers, whom the rigorous Laws of the Emperors forced to seek asylum among the Barbarians, stopped in a field to refresh themselves while returning from Persia to their homeland. There, they perceived a dead body thrown upon the ground without burial, **in the fashion of the country**. I indicate (3) in the margin the Authors who attest to this custom of the ancient Persians and some of their neighboring Peoples. If what *Strabo* reports were true, it would have been an honor granted to *Manichaeus* to give *his flesh to the Birds*; for he says (4) that the Persians gave only the bodies of the Magi to birds to eat, while they buried the others.

I know not, nonetheless, if the testimony of *Strabo* is accurate regarding burial. For I find in Oriental Writers that Peter, Prefect of the Praetorian Cohorts, who negotiated the Peace between *Justinian* and *Khosrow*, obtained from the latter (5) "that the Christians would have the liberty (6) to bury their dead according to the Custom of the Greeks." Now, it is not likely that the Persians would have forbidden Christians the use of Burial if they practiced it themselves. I learn elsewhere that King *Zamaspes*, conversing with the Nestorian Patriarch *Babeus*, said to him (7): "Since human bodies decay and return to dust, why do you make such a case of them? Why do you honor the Bones of the dead and not burn them after the example of the Magi?" This shows that the Persians burned the Bones of the Bodies after the Birds, or other beasts, had eaten the flesh.

<margin>Regarding the superstitious [honor] that Westerners pay to the Relics of Saints. For the discussion concerns all the Dead in general, "YOUR DEAD" <note>original: "MORTUORUM VESTRORUM"</note>, and the honors of burial, and not a religious cult. One can read in Mr. *Assemani* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768) was a famous Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> the Extract from the Book of *George of Arbela* concerning Funerals and the Commemoration of the Dead (cited above, p. 538), and one will see that it concerns the honors that Christians generally rendered to all their Dead. See the Question, *Why do we pay great honor to the Deceased?* <note>original: "Quare Defunctis magnum deferimus honorem?"</note> As for the Relics of Saints, if one wishes to know what sort of honor the Orientals pay them, it may be learned by the response they made to *Rashid*, Caliph of Baghdad. His Physician having reported to him that Christians adored the Bones of the dead, this Prince, indignant at such a profane superstition, ordered that all their Temples be demolished; this was partially executed. But finally, they represented to him that they were careful not to serve or adore the Bones of the dead; that they rendered only to the bodies of Martyrs and the Righteous the same honor that the Muslims themselves did not refuse to the Tombs of the Prophets. "Christians are by no means accustomed to worship or adore the bones of the dead: but they honor the bodies of martyrs and the righteous in exactly the same way as they are accustomed to honor the tombs and bodies of the Prophets." <note>original: "Christianos mortuorum ossa colere, aut adorare neutiquam consuevisse: sed martyrum & justorum corpora ea prorsus ratione, qua Prophetarum sepulchra eorumque corpora honorare solent."</note> This took place under the Nestorian Patriarch *Timothy*, who was elected in 778. *Assemani, Oriental Library, Vol. III, Part I, p. 158.*</margin>

<margin>The error of Archelaus. He places under a single King a tragedy that begins under the grandfather and ends under the grandson.</margin>
II. It is an inaccuracy, which makes the report of *Archelaus* <note>The *Acts of Archelaus* is a 4th-century Christian polemic against Mani, presented as a debate between Mani and a Bishop named Archelaus. However, as one can provide a plausible reason for this omission, I will not dwell on it. One might say that a historian recounting an event that just happened under a living and still-reigning Prince can dispense with naming that Prince, because he assumes everyone knows him. But here is an instance of ignorance, an error that cannot be excused. It is having placed under a single reign the entire course of an affair that began under the grandfather, or the great-grandfather, and was only completed under the *grandson*, or (2) the *great-grandson*. The first act of the tragedy occurs under (3) *Sapor I*. The scene changes its face under his son *Hormizdas*. This reign is as favorable to *Manes* as the previous one had been contrary to him. The beginnings of *Varane I*, grandson of *Sapor*, are still favorable to the Heresiarch <note>A leader of a heretical movement.</note>, and the catastrophe only arrives toward the end of his reign—and even, as the most skilled moderns believe, it was not until the reign of *Varane II*. However, according to the report of *Archelaus*, it is the same King who has the Heresiarch imprisoned, who keeps him in prison for several years, who has him captured after his escape, and who finally puts him to death.

<margin>The Execution of Manichaeus in the month of March 277.</margin>
It was in the month (1) of March, and near the feast of Easter, in the year 277, that our Heresiarch <note>A leader of a heretical movement.</note> ended his career and his Deception. For it was at that time that his followers celebrated the anniversary of the death of their Patriarch, as St. *Augustine* informs us. This Feast was called **Bema** by the Greeks, a word that the Latins retained. Now *Bema*, which means a *Step*, also signifies a **Chair**, a **Pulpit**, or a **Rostrum** <note>original: "Chaire," "Tribune"</note> from which a preacher speaks to the People, or rather, where a Master is seated when he teaches. It was therefore the Feast of the *Chair of Mani*, the Feast of the Teacher. I shall say more about this in the *Second Part* of this Work, when I treat the Worship of the Manichaeans. The matter at hand is to determine what judgment should be passed on the **Acts of Archelaus**.

<margin>His conjectures do not seem well-founded.</margin>...in a language more generally known than the Syriac Language, so that all the Faithful might be instructed by them. These are the conjectures of this learned Roman scholar <note>Lorenzo Alessandro Zaccagni (1657–1712), a Vatican librarian who published a famous edition of these "Acts."</note>. But they are supported by suspicions rather than by proofs; and they are countered by an insurmountable difficulty: that is, if the *Disputes of Archelaus* had been written or translated into Greek as early as the year 277 or 278, the Greek Authors we have from that time until *Cyril of Jerusalem* <note>Cyril (c. 313–386 AD) was one of the first Greek fathers to mention Mani in detail.</note> would have known them and spoken of them.

<margin>Hegemonius is the true Author of the Disputes of Archelaus.</margin>One must not attempt to reconcile *Heraclean* with *St. Jerome*. The Author and the Translator of the same Work are entirely different characters. However, it is natural to prefer the testimony of *Heraclean* <note>Heraclean of Chalcedon (5th century), who wrote a massive refutation of Manichaeism.</note>, who made a study of Manichaeism, who wrote <margin>(a) See Photius, Codex 85.</margin> (a) *twenty books against this Heresy*, and who, being Bishop of Chalcedon, was better acquainted than *St. Jerome* with what happened in the Eastern Church. The question would only be to know if *Hégémonius* had some Syriac Memoirs which provided him with the materials for his history. <margin>That he had no Syriac Memoirs.</margin> Mr. *Zaccagni* does not doubt it and offers fairly plausible <note>original: "spécieuses," which in this context means "fair-seeming" or "credible" rather than "misleading."</note> reasons. I myself was inclined to believe it when I considered the opinions that the Author attributes to *Archelaus* regarding *Christ* and the *Incarnation*. They have an air of antiquity and seem not to suit a man who lived and wrote after the Council of Nicaea, around the year 330. Moreover, the description of the clothing and appearance of *Mani* <note>original: "Manichée." The text later describes Mani's exotic Persian attire: trousers, a multi-colored cloak, and a heavy staff.</note> appears to have something original about it, so different from Greek ways that one cannot suspect a Greek of having imagined it. All this concludes in favor of some Syriac Memoirs; and I would decide for this sentiment if I were not stopped by a difficulty that seems impossible to resolve: that is, whatever research I have done, I have found no Syrian Author who made mention of either *Archelaus* or his Disputes with *Mani*. So that I am forced to conclude, either <margin>But was instructed, or deceived by some Mesopotamian, a deserter from the sect of Mani.</margin> that *Hegemonius* invented and supposed this whole history; or that he held it from some *Mesopotamian*, apparently from *Tyrbo* <note>A disciple of Mani's predecessor, who supposedly defected and provided information to the Christians.</note>, who had seen *Mani*, had been of his Sect, and who told him a tale which he then embellished with many circumstances of his own invention. At heart, this sentiment, which appears extreme at first, differs from that of some modern Scholars only in degree. For they agree—some that this Piece is not by *Archelaus*, others that *Hegemonius* added to it and removed from it what he judged appropriate. This is the sentiment upon which I have settled, until I have new light on this matter.
