### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. XII.
<margin>2. Question: Whether the Dispute of Cascar is real.</margin>
III. Let us now examine a second Question: namely, *Is the Dispute of Cascar real, or imagined?* I say the *Dispute of Cascar*. For I do not wish to assert that *Manichaeus* <note>The Latin name for Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism.</note> had conferences regarding his errors with an Orthodox Bishop, nor do I wish to deny it. I do not wish to assert it because we have very ancient examples of Authors who imagined Disputes, not only between Orthodox Bishops and Heretics, but even between Apostles and Heresiarchs <note>The leader or founder of a heretical movement.</note>.

<margin>Example of imagined Disputes between St. Peter and Simon Magus.</margin>
Did not the Impostor who fabricated the *Recognitions* <note>An ancient Christian adventure story, once wrongly attributed to Clement of Rome, which details the travels of St. Peter.</note> under the name of *St. Clement* have the boldness to introduce *St. Peter* disputing against *Simon Magus*? Did he not lend this Apostle his own thoughts? Did he not note the circumstances of the days and places, naming the Persons and the witnesses? In a word, did he not adorn his Fable with all the characteristics of History?

<margin>(a) Literary History. Under Clement of Rome.</margin>
If the conjecture of Mr. (a) *Cave* <note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English church historian.</note> is correct, this Romance came to us from *Syria* or *Mesopotamia*, and its Author was the famous *Bardesanes* <note>A 2nd-century Syrian Gnostic philosopher and poet.</note>, who was very well-versed in the Greek Language. It would not be impossible, then, that a *Syrian* had imagined a Dispute between a Catholic Bishop and *Manes* in order to have the opportunity to refute the principal errors of this Heresiarch. There is even a certain arrangement in these Disputes that appears suspicious. In the first, they treat only the cause of evil and the authority of the Old Testament. These are the questions debated before Pagan Judges. And as the question of the Incarnation is more mysterious, the Author relegates it to another Dispute—one that is public, to be sure, but which has as its witnesses and Judges only the Christian People. However, as it is not impossible, and even quite probable, that *Manichaeus* had some dispute against an Orthodox Bishop, I do not wish to absolutely deny this fact: and that is not the issue at hand. The issue is a public dispute which takes place 1st. in a city of *Mesopotamia*; 2nd. in a city subject to the Romans; 3rd. in a city named *Cascar*, or *Carcar* (1). For the Scene of the Dispute of *Archelaus* unites these three characteristics: If, therefore, we find no City where they meet, what can one conclude, except that this Dispute is imagined, since the Author places the scene in a place that does not exist?

---

<margin>(1) This is how this City is named in the Acts of Archelaus *In Civitate CARCHAR p. 1.* <note>original: "In the City of CARCHAR"</note> except in Ch. III where it is called *Charra*: but *Epiphanius, Heresies LXVI. §. 5. 10. On Weights and Measures §. 20. Socrates, Ecclesiastical History, Book I. 22. Peter of Sicily, History of Manichaeism p. 36. # HISTORY OF MANICHAEISM ACCORDING TO THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS.

<margin>
I. Proof that it is fictitious. Zaccagni sets the Scene at Carrhae.
(a) Preface p. 7.
</margin>
4. The late Mr. *Zaccagni*, who was certainly a learned man and a good critic, seeking a city that could fit all these characteristics, decided on (a) **Carrhae**, (1) a place famous for the defeat of the Roman general *Crassus*, and which is said to have been the ancient home of (2) *Charan* <note>A biblical site often identified with Harran in modern-day Turkey.</note>. This city was a (3) Roman Colony.

<margin>
His reasons.
</margin>
Mr. *Zaccagni's* reasons are 1. that, in one place of the Latin version, the city is named *Charra*. 2. That one finds in History no Roman city situated in Mesopotamia that is called *Cascar* or *Carcar*. 3. But since one might believe that the city in question is that of *Carcha*, because this name is very close to *Carcar*, this Author responds that there are two cities named *Carcha*: one in *Arabia Felix* <note>original: "Arabie heureuse," meaning "Happy Arabia," the ancient name for the southern Arabian Peninsula.</note>, which the *Anonymous of Ravenna* mentions in his Geography; the other, beyond the *Tigris*, outside of Mesopotamia, and under Persian rule. Now, since the city of which *Archelaus* was Bishop was situated in Mesopotamia and subject to the Romans, it can be neither one nor the other. From this, Mr. *Zaccagni* concludes that this city is *Carrhae*. His opinion has since been refuted by (a) Mr. *Asseman*, a learned <term>Maronite</term> <note>A member of an Eastern Catholic church in Lebanon.</note> and Secretary to the Pope for Syriac and Arabic letters. I will make use of his remarks and add several others.

Firstly, *Cascar* is not *Carrhae*. # THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. Book I. Ch. XII.

<columns>2</columns>

*Xaboras* according to *Ptolemy*, *Aboras* according to *Zosimus*. No historian, neither Greek nor Roman, makes mention of this *Stranga* <note>A river or boundary mentioned in the Acts of Archelaus that does not appear in other historical records of the region.</note>, which ought to be very well known, since it served as the boundary between the Romans and the *Persians*. Nor can one find this *Arabion Castle*, where *Mani* <note>The founder of Manichaeism, often referred to as Manichæus or Manichée.</note> had retired, and which would have been the primary Persian stronghold on the side of *Carrhae*, if *Carrhae* and *Cascar* were the same city. However, the continuous wars that the Romans had to sustain, sometimes against the *Parthians* and sometimes against the *Persians*, gave historians the opportunity to describe Mesopotamia very accurately, as it was usually the theater of war.

<margin>Carrhae was a city too idolatrous to have been the scene of the dispute.</margin>
In the third place, if what we are told in the *Acts of Archelaus* is true, *Carrhae* could not be the scene of his dispute with *Mani*. We are told that this Bishop pleaded the cause of the Catholic Faith there and won it before Pagan judges, and in the presence of a people who, struck by his reasoning, would have stoned the heresiarch <note>A leader of a heretical sect.</note> if they had been allowed to do so. We are also told that *Archelaus*, indignant toward *Mani*, reproached him for being nothing more than a priest of *Mithra* <note>An ancient Persian deity associated with the sun, whose mystery cult was popular in the Roman Empire.</note>—that is to say, of the Sun—and for serving only this false divinity. This reproach might have been applauded in a Christian city and under Christian Emperors; but it could only have incited the whole people of *Carrhae* against the Bishop, a city (5) which was full of *Pagans* and *Idols*, and where there was a famous (a) Temple dedicated to the *Moon*, or to the God *Lunus*. It is for this reason that the Emperor *Julian* the Apostate, marching on his fatal Persian expedition and wanting to avoid *Edessa* because there were many Christians there, (6) went straight to *Carrhae* to offer sacrifices to his gods and consult them. This city was so Pagan at that time, and so devoted to idolatry, (7) that the inhabitants stoned the unfortunate man who brought the news of *Julian's* death there and buried him under a pile of stones. How would they have treated, nearly a hundred years earlier and under Pagan Emperors, a Bishop who had the audacity to publicly blaspheme the God *Mithra*, or the Sun, which was one of their principal deities?

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS.

<margin>No Bishop at Carrhae in the time of Mani.</margin>
I have a reason more powerful still to maintain that *Carrhae* <note>The ancient city of Harran in Upper Mesopotamia, famous in Roman history for the defeat of Crassus.</note> could not be the theater for the Dispute of *Archelaus*; it is that, in all likelihood, there was no Bishop at *Carrhae* during the time of *Mani*. I had even suspected that there were none during the time of *Julian* <note>Julian the Apostate, Roman Emperor from 361 to 363 AD, who attempted to revive Roman paganism.</note>: and what led me to believe this is what one reads in a
<margin>(b) In Assemani, book cited above, p. 57.</margin>
(b) *Life of St. Ephrem*, that *Jovian*, who accompanied the Emperor to *Persia*, detached himself to go to *Edessa* to perform his devotions in the Temple of the Mother of God, and before her Image. This *Image*, and this *Prayer before the Image of the Virgin*, are inventions (1) of the 6th or 7th Century. But as for the journey of *Jovian* to *Edessa*, it may be true; and if it is, it suggests that there was no Christian Church at *Carrhae* in the year 363, since this Roman leader, seeing the approach (2) of the solemnity of Easter and finding himself on the eve of a very perilous expedition, went to perform his devotions at *Edessa*. I have seen since then that I was mistaken, and that all that should be concluded from this fact is that the Church of *Carrhae* must have been very small: for one finds, in the lists of the Bishops of the East, (3) one *Eusebius*, Bishop of *Carrhae*, who had been a Monk; a *Bitus*, who was also Bishop of the same city; and a *Protogenes*, who had been a Monk, and who succeeded *Bitus* under the Empire of *Valens*. But if this *Eusebius*, who had been a Monk, was the first Bishop of *Carrhae*, the city had none in the time of *Mani*. We know that *St. Anthony* instituted Monasticism <note>The religious practice of living as a monk, characterized by renouncing worldly pursuits to devote oneself to spiritual work.</note> in Egypt at the age of fifty-five, around the year 305 of our Lord. It is said that *Hilarion*, his disciple, brought it soon after to
<margin>(a) Sozomen, Book VI. 33.</margin>
Syria: and (a) *Aones* to Mesopotamia, assisted by two of his companions, namely, *Gaddanas* and *Azizus*. This *Aones* is an imaginary name. The true name of this Monk is *Eugene*: but as the Syrians nicknamed him out of respect *Avun*, or *Abun*, that is to say *Father*, the Greeks, who imagined that this was his proper name, converted it into *Aones*. If, therefore, there was no Bishop at *Carrhae* before the Monks, there was none during the time of *Mani*. I may be mistaken on the facts, and I shall be delighted to receive instructions on this matter from the Learned, who know the Ecclesiastical History of the East better than I.

HISTORY OF MANI ACCORDING TO

is (1) in *Assyria* very close to *Seleucia* and *Ctesiphon*. Because of this, the Syrians call it *Beth-Seleucia*, which is as if to say (2) the *Borough of Seleucia*. It is the city that the Jewish Geographer <note>Benjamin of Tudela, a 12th-century traveler who documented Jewish communities.</note> calls (3) *Alcorcha*; adding that the Jews have twenty-eight synagogues, as many in this city as in that of *Baghdad*. It is also named *Mahuza*, and is beyond the *Tigris*.

<margin>(a) Assemani, as cited above, Vol. III. Part II. p. 732. 733.</margin>
There is a second (a) *Carca*, which is in *Chaldea*, and quite near *Baghdad*; and a third, on the borders of *Syria* and *Arabia*, which is the one mentioned by the historians of the Crusades. There is therefore no way to substitute *Carca* for *Cascar*, since the latter was in *Mesopotamia*, and all the *Carcas* of the East are in other provinces.

<margin>Christians in Cascar from the beginning.</margin>
V. Let us come to the point. What compelled Mr. Zaccagni to say that *Cascar* is *Carrhae* is that he found no city in Mesopotamia named *Cascar* that was subject to the Romans. Mr. *Assemani* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a famous Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> refutes the first part of this reasoning, maintaining (4) that there was, (5) at the edge of *Mesopotamia*, a city called *Cascar*, in which there have been Christians from time immemorial. The Syrians claim (6) that *Mares*, a disciple of *Addai* or *Thaddeus*, after having preached the Gospel and founded a church at *Seleucia*, founded another at *Cascar* and ordained a bishop there: that because of the antiquity of this foundation, the Bishop of *Cascar* holds the first rank after the *Catholicos*, or the Patriarch of *Seleucia*. It is true that this Syrian tradition may be doubtful. But it is not at all doubtful that in the time of *Mani*, and even before him, there was a city named *Cascar* in which there was a church and a bishop.

<margin>But the question is to know if it belonged to the Romans.</margin>
VI. As for the second part of Mr. Zaccagni's reasoning—namely, whether *Cascar* was subject to the Romans in the time of *Mani*—Mr. *Assemani* does not touch upon it; however, as this fact is decisive in the *Question of the Authenticity of the Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century account of a debate between Bishop Archelaus and Mani, the historical accuracy of which is debated because of these geographical discrepancies.</note>, I shall examine it.

---

<columns>2</columns>

(1) <note>original Latin: "Carcha, Urbs apud Seleuciam..."</note> *Carcha, a city near Seleucia and Ctesiphon, in Assyria, which they call by the full name Carcha or Beth-Seleucia. Assemani, as cited above, Vol. III, Part I, p. 173.*

(2) *Beth* means *House*, but it is taken here in the sense I give it <note>specifically meaning a "place" or "borough".</note>.

(3) <note>original Latin: "MAHUZA, quæ alias Carcha dicitur..."</note> *MAHUZA, which is otherwise called Carcha, near Ctesiphon, on the other side of the river; the same which is ALCORCHA to Benjamin of Tudela, about which he [says] in Bochart's "Phaleg": There are twenty-eight synagogues of the Jews, as many in Baghdad as in Alcorcha, which is across the Tigris. Assemani, as cited above, Vol. III, Part II, p. 624.*

(4) <note>original Latin: "Cascar, vel Cascar, indeclinabiliter..."</note> *Cascar, or Cascar, indeclinable, in singular or plural number, Cascara and Carchara, which city is situated on the borders of Mesopotamia. The older Syrians prefer Cascar; the more recent, Gargar, or Cascar, or Carcha. Assemani, as cited above, p. 555.*

(5) Mr. *Assemani*, as skillful as he is, here follows his own prejudice; for we shall see hereafter that he places *Cascar* outside of Mesopotamia, between *Kufa* and *Basra*.

<margin>When this custom changed and why?</margin>
...Achadabues and *Kam-Jesu* <note>These are traditional figures in the early history of the Church of the East; Kam-Jesu is often associated with the early spread of Christianity in the Sasanian Empire.</note> to Antioch, and asked the Patriarch to consecrate whichever of the two he found most worthy to be his Coadjutor and Successor. The Governor of Antioch, who regarded these men as Persian spies, had *Kam-Jesu* crucified. *Achadabues* (1) had the good fortune to escape to Jerusalem, where the Patriarch ordained him and sent him back to the East. It is from this time that the *Western Syrians*—that is, those of the Patriarchate of Antioch—permitted the Easterners to consecrate their own Primate whenever the See became vacant. In consequence of this permission, (2) *Sciaglupha, who was from the City of Cascar, was the first to be established by the Easterners*. He died at Seleucia in the fourth year of Sapor I, which corresponds to the year 244 or 245 of Our Lord. From this I conclude that *Cascar* belonged to the Persians. For I do not think that, in such circumstances...

<column-break/>

...which they claim was written to them by the Fathers of the West, in which the latter give the Primate of Seleucia the title and honors of a Patriarch, and create him the fifth Patriarch, subjecting all the East to his jurisdiction. This letter can be seen in *Assemani, as cited above, p. 54.* <note>Joseph Simon Assemani (1687–1768) was a Lebanese Maronite scholar whose work *Bibliotheca Orientalis* is a primary source for Syriac Christianity.</note> According to the Patriarch *Timothy*, it was written in the year 108 of Our Lord; according to *Barhebraeus*, in the year 140; and according to *Amrus*, around the year 220. It is evidently a forged letter; likewise, our learned Author made no scruple of demonstrating its falsity. This shows, in passing, that the ambition of Bishops and Churches has been the same everywhere, and that they have used the same artifice: namely, that of supposing and fabricating false titles.

I do not know if it is with the same bad faith, or through ignorance, that modern Nestorians who have reunited with the Roman Church—abusing this expression, *the Western Fathers*—have said that the Primates of Seleucia originally held their mission from the Bishops of Rome, from whom they used to receive ordination. They claim that in consideration of the dangers and difficulties of a long journey, the Popes had granted the Bishops of the East the privilege of consecrating their own Primates. I believe that the first Nestorians to spread this fable were schismatics who, having elected *Sulacha* as their Patriarch, turned to Rome to maintain him and wrote on this subject to *Julius III* in the year 1552. (See *Assemani Vol. III, Part II, p. 371.*) Mr. *Assemani* informs us that in the Pontifical of the Chaldeans, or Nestorians, it is written that their Catholicos, or their Patriarchs, are ordained *Permissu Sanctissimorum Patrum Occidentalium* <note>original: "By the permission of the most holy Western Fathers."</note>. The Latinized Syrians have claimed that these *Western Fathers* are the Popes. *Putant Romanum Pontificem, Latinamque Ecclesiam per ea verba designari* <note>original: "They think the Roman Pontiff and the Latin Church are designated by these words." (Assemani, as cited above, Vol. III, p. 59).</note> Although Mr. *Assemani* is in the service of the Pope and, as far as one can judge by his work, a very good Catholic, he could not help but correct this error, or this flattery. He stated that the Holy Fathers of the West are the *Patriarchs of Antioch*, who are to the west of the Syrians of Mesopotamia and all other Easterners. *Quæ nempe verba*, he says, *de Antiocheno Præsule haud dubiè intelligenda sunt* <note>original: "Which words are undoubtedly to be understood as referring to the Prelate of Antioch."</note>. One sees with pleasure in the work of this learned man various marks of his sincerity. This succeeds better and brings more honor to the Roman Church than the artificial and passionate zeal of certain writers who make use of anything, provided it can serve to enhance the authority of the See of Rome. The Eastern Syrians say that *Jerusalem is in the West*. Everything on this side of the Euphrates is Western to them and in their language.

It is almost unnecessary to dwell on this further. Whatever the precise location of *Cascar* <note>Cascar, or Kashkar, was an ancient city in Mesopotamia, located near the modern city of Kut in Iraq; it was a significant center of the Church of the East</note>, it was near Seleucia and belonged to the Persians. Among the Bishops whom *Sapor II* <note>Shapur II, the Sasanian King of Kings who reigned from 309 to 379 CE and was known for his long and often harsh treatment of Christians</note> put to death during the long persecution he waged against the Christians, there is mention of (6) *Abdas*, Bishop of CASCAR, and *Hebed-Jesu*, another Bishop of the Province of the CASCARIANS.

It happens to this learned author, as it happens only too often to many other writers in the course of a long work: they are not consistent in their accounts. They take them from different authors and report them exactly as they find them, without considering that they contradict each other. In the first part of his third volume, Mr. *Assemani* places, as we see, the election of *Sciaglupha* around the year 224, since he held the See of Seleucia for twenty years and died in 244. In the second part of this same volume, he says that *Sciaglupha* was elected and consecrated by the Eastern Bishops after the death of *Achadabues*, because the war that *Lucius Verus* <note>Roman Emperor who co-ruled with Marcus Aurelius</note> waged against *Vologeses*, King of the Parthians, prevented him from going to be ordained in Antioch, as was the custom of his predecessors. *On the occasion of that war, Sciaglupha was elected after the death of Achadabues; following the example of his elders, he was unable to proceed to Antioch for the sake of ordination, but was instead initiated at Seleucia by the Eastern Bishops.* <note>original Latin: "Ejus belli occasione electus, post Achadabuae obitum, Sciaclupha, Majorum exemplo, Antiochiam ordinationis causâ pergere nequivit, sed Seleucia ab Orientalibus Episcopis initiatus est."</note> Vol. III, Part II, p. 42. <margin>From which it follows that the Acts of Archelaus are not authentic.</margin> All these facts clearly show that *Cascar* was a Persian city, and that the Bishop of *Cascar* was a subject of the Persians, since he was the primary suffragan <note>A suffragan is a bishop who is subordinate to a higher-ranking archbishop or primate.</note> to the Primate of *Seleucia*. <margin>Frivolous response that might be made to these objections.</margin> VIII. One would defend the authenticity of these Acts very poorly by claiming that *Cascar*, which usually belonged to the Persians, had been taken by the Romans when *Odenathus*, leader of the *Palmyrenes*, defeated the Persians and penetrated as far as (1) *Seleucia* and *Ctesiphon*, which he seized. But this invasion had no lasting result. The Persians soon re-entered their provinces; whereas, according to the Acts, *Cascar* is a city long subjected to the Romans, where there were schools, Greek grammarians, and rhetoricians, and where a very wealthy citizen resided whose name indicates he was Roman. It must also be remembered that the Disputes of *Cascar* date to the beginning of the reign of (2) *Probus* <note>Roman Emperor from 276 to 282 CE.</note>, and that the invasion of *Odenathus* is older by fifteen or sixteen years.

### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. XII.

...to have had a public dispute with a Bishop who was a subject of the Romans.

These are the reflections I had made before having seen the second part of the third volume of the *Oriental Library* by Mr. *Assemani* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768) was a Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican who published the *Bibliotheca Orientalis*, a massive catalog of Syriac and Arabic manuscripts.</note>, in which he treats the Nestorian Sect at length. It was there that I found evident proof that *Cascar* was a Persian city, situated not in *Mesopotamia*, but in (5) *Chaldea*, and in the heart of the *Province of Babylon*. Here then is what our learned *Maronite* <note>A member of the Maronite Church, an Eastern Catholic Church from Lebanon.</note> says, following the famous geographer *Abulfeda* <note>Abulfeda (1273–1331) was a Kurdish prince and geographer whose works remained authoritative for centuries.</note>. (6) *Al-Hajjaj <note>Al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, a famous governor of the Umayyad Caliphate.</note> laid the foundations of Wasit between Kufa and Basra, IN THE TERRITORY OF CASCAR, in the year 84 of the Hijra, and completed it in the year 86. Basra*, (7) or *Bassora, is a famous city of the Babylonian Iraq, situated to the west of the Tigris, near the Persian Gulf. Kufa* (8) *is in the same province, seated on the Euphrates, at the borders of Desert Arabia. Wasit*, (9) an Arabic word which means *in the middle*, was built between these two cities, at an equal distance from one and the other, in the Territory of *Cascar*: *Cascar* was therefore in this Province that the Arabs call *Erak*, or *Babylonian Iraq*: it was in *Chaldea*, between *Kufa* and *Basra*, and consequently very far from *Mesopotamia*, where the author of the Acts of *Archelaus* placed it, and where it had to be placed so that it might be a Roman city.

After such a demonstration of the true situation of *Cascar*, can one be surprised enough that Mr. *Assemani*, who informed us of it, did not notice the falsity of the Acts of *Archelaus*? These Acts claim that *Cascar* was (10) a city of *Mesopotamia*, which belonged to the Romans, distant from the Persian frontiers by two or three days' journey—that is to say, twenty to twenty-five French leagues. However, the truth is, according to Mr. *Assemani* himself, that it was in the heart of *Chaldea*, and under the power of the Persians. This does not prevent the learned Maronite from saying, in the same place where he describes its situation, (11) that *Archelaus*

### CHAPTER XIII.

->*In which we continue to show that the Dispute of* CASCAR *is fictional.*<-

<margin>Proof that the Dispute is fictional. It must have caused a great stir, and yet no one in the East mentions it for 70 years.</margin>
I have just shown that the setting of the dispute is misplaced: It cannot have been at *Cascar*, a city situated in the heart of Chaldea, or Assyria, and dependent on the Persians. Let us now show that the dispute itself is fictional. The author of the Acts of *Archelaus* assures us that it took place in a Roman city, which was episcopal <note>A city that serves as the seat of a Bishop.</note>, and in which the Christian religion was flourishing. Never was an act more solemn. It takes place in the hall of an illustrious Roman, who was likely *Marcellus*, Governor of Mesopotamia. His name *Marcellus*, his wealth, and his authority confirm this thought. Four Pagan judges presided there: they were the elite of the most learned in the city. *Mani* appears there in person with his principal disciples. He has as his antagonist *Archelaus*, one of the most learned Bishops of the East. All the Christian people, and even the Pagans, are witnesses to this memorable action, and confirm, by

Now, he did not suppress the *Disputes of Archelaus* for reasons of prudence or interest. He did not do it out of contempt for an Event that is rightly regarded as one of the most memorable in Ecclesiastical History. It would therefore have to be said that he was unaware of it. <margin>Silence of other Greek Writers until Cyril.</margin> To the silence of *Eusebius*, one must add that of all the Greek Writers until *Cyril* of Jerusalem, although they often had occasion to speak of *Mani* & his Heresy, & indeed did speak of it.

I have no other Oriental literature than that which I borrow from the skillful men who have studied the Languages & the Ecclesiastical History of the East. I have consulted them, not doubting that I would find there the Disputes & the Victory of *Archelaus*. But all my research has been in vain.

<margin>Silence of St. Ephrem, who lived in Mesopotamia & followed Mani closely. (a) *Assemani, cited above. Vol. I. p. 24.*</margin> *St. Ephrem* <note>Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373 AD), a prominent Syriac Christian deacon, hymnographer, and theologian.</note> was from *Nisibis*, in Mesopotamia. He was a Deacon there, after having been a Monk. Following the example of *Bardaisan* <note>Original: "Bardésanes." A Syrian Gnostic and poet (154–222 AD) known for his hymns.</note>, who had been an excellent Syrian Poet, he composed many Hymns to teach the Youth, from their childhood, the Dogmas of the Faith, the Duties of Morality, the noble actions of the Saints; the Errors and the lies of the Heretics. He speaks of *Mani* <note>Original: "Manès"</note> in several of his (b) Hymns: he inveighs against him & against his Heresy. He also speaks of him in his other Works. But, in all that I have read of him, I have not been able to perceive any trace of the Disputes of *Kashkar* <note>Original: "Cascar," an ancient city in Mesopotamia near modern-day Al-Kut, Iraq.</note> & of *Diodoris*, nor of the Victory that *Archelaus* won over *Mani*. <margin>Silence of *Eutychius* of Alexandria.</margin>
I had previously consulted the Annals of *Eutychius*, Patriarch of Alexandria <note>Eutychius (877–940 AD) was a Melkite Patriarch and one of the first Christian Egyptian writers to use Arabic.</note>. <margin>Silence of *D'Herbelot* in his *Oriental Library*.</margin>
We have the ample and rich *Oriental Library* of *Mr. D'Herbelot* <note>Barthélemy d'Herbelot (1625–1695), a pioneering French orientalist whose "Bibliothèque orientale" was the standard Western reference for Islamic and Middle Eastern history for decades.</note>. But there again, there is no mention of this flight of *Manichaeus* into Mesopotamia, nor of his Conferences with *Archelaus*.

<margin>Silence of *Hyde* in his History of *Manichaeus*.</margin>
When one compares what *Mr. Hyde* <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703), an English orientalist and professor at Oxford who wrote a major work on the religion of the ancient Persians.</note> relates concerning this Heresiarch <note>term: Heresiarch (original: *Hérésiarque*). A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> with what *Mr. D'Herbelot* says, one recognizes that they have drawn from the same sources. They agree, and the only difference between their accounts is that one adds details that the other omitted. Why must they also agree in saying nothing of our *Archelaus*, nor of his Disputes with our Heresiarch?

<margin>Silence of *Assemani* in his *Oriental Library*.</margin>
*Mr. Assemani* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican, famous for compiling the "Bibliotheca Orientalis."</note> follows these Scholars. I have seen, I have looked through, I have even read the first four Volumes of his rich *Oriental Library*. This skillful man points out a mistake made by *Mr. Zaccagni*, who mistook the City of *Cascar* for that of *Carrhae*. This gives him occasion to speak of the Disputes of *Archelaus*: but this learned Syrian cites no Writer of his Nation who reported this memorable Event.

<margin>Silence of *Ebed-Jesus* in his Catalog of Syrian Writers.</margin>
We have an ample Catalog of the Ecclesiastical Writers of the East, composed by *Ebed-Jesus* <note>Ebed-Jesus (Abdisho bar Berika, died 1318), a Metropolitan of the Church of the East and a prolific writer in Syriac.</note>, Metropolitan of (2) *Sobe* and *Armenia*, published by *Abraham Echellensis*, and since by *Mr. Assemani* with learned Notes. This writer begins with the Sacred Authors and continues century by century until his time—that is, until the year 1318, which was that of his death. He speaks of (a) *Titus of Bostra*, of (b) *Diodorus of Tarsus*, and of other Fathers who wrote against *Manes*: but he says nothing of *Archelaus*, nor of his Disputes. This Bishop, who filled all the West with the sound of his name and his deeds, is unknown in his own Homeland. I find only, in the list of Arabic Manuscripts that *Mr. Assemani* brought from the Levant, (c) *A Life of St. Archelaus*; but I know neither who the Author is, nor from what time it dates, nor what it contains, nor which (3) *Archelaus* it treats, for the learned Maronite reported only its title.

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO
<meta>catchword: prophets</meta>

<margin>Abbé Renaudot, censured by Assemani.</margin>Although I insist on the silence of the Orientals, I do not intend to claim that there is no one who has mentioned the Disputes of our *Archelaus*. Such an assertion would be too rash, and I would well deserve the reproach that the Roman Scholar <note>referring to Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a celebrated Maronite orientalist and librarian at the Vatican</note> makes, in more than one place, against Abbé Renaudot <note>Eusèbe Renaudot (1646–1720), a French theologian and orientalist known for his studies of Eastern liturgies</note>, who possessed great knowledge of Oriental Literature, but who spoiled it by his presumption and by the shocking haughtiness with which he dared to treat great men, whom he should have regarded only with respect. *It was his habit, says Mr. Assemani (1), to assert with extreme boldness that a thing did not exist, as soon as he had not read or observed it.* All I wish to say is that the Scholars I have consulted do not speak of any Oriental Author who bore witness to the Disputes of *Archelaus*, even though they had the occasion to do so, and naturally should have done so.

<margin>Account of the Dispute of Archelaus by Severus of Ashmunein.
(a) See Cave Hist. Lit. Vol. II. p. 320.</margin>II. It is true, however, that Mr. Renaudot cites an Egyptian Author named *Severus*, who was Bishop of *Ashmunein* <note>Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (10th century), a Coptic Bishop of Hermopolis (Ashmunein) and historian</note>, and who flourished around (a) the year nine hundred and seventy-eight. This author gives us a History of the Conference of *Archelaus* with Manichaeus: but far from confirming our own, he provides us with clear evidence that it is filled with fables.

> "Mani (2)," says the Egyptian Bishop, "had been instructed by a Magus. A very rich woman left him great wealth, and among other things, Magic Books. He boasted of being the PARACLETE <note>from the Greek 'parakletos', meaning 'advocate' or 'helper', a title Mani used to claim he was the successor to Jesus</note> promised in the Scriptures, and seduced many people through his illusions and his wealth. He was refuted by Archelaus, Bishop of a certain City in Syria."

<margin>Simpler and more natural than that of the *Acts* in certain respects.</margin>Mr. *Renaudot* adds that it has since been known that this City is *Cascar* <note>Kashkar, an ancient city in Mesopotamia near modern-day Wasit, Iraq</note>, but it seems to me he should have also added that it was known that *Cascar* was in *Mesopotamia* and not in *Syria*. "There was in this City," *the Author continues*, "a very opulent man named Marcellus, more illustrious for his charity than for his wealth, who distinguished his liberality by ransoming a great number of Christians who had been taken prisoner by the Persians (3), and by building for them Hospices and Churches." This account is beyond comparison simpler and more natural than that of *Hegemonius* <note>The purported author of the 'Acts of Archelaus'</note>. One finds there no mention of the servitude of *Mani*: one sees in which School he took his Principles. He had for Masters the Ma- <unclear>gi</unclear>,

<margin>The Letter from *Manes* to *Marcellus* is very poorly reported.</margin>
The Reader may compare this Letter with the one for which I have given him the Translation, and which is perhaps the only genuine monument existing in the Acts of *Archelaus*. At least it has nothing that makes it suspect of forgery or alteration. One sees there the style and the Dogmas of *Manichaeus*, whereas one sees neither the one nor the other in this one. First, he did not give himself the title of PARACLETE <note>from the Greek 'parakletos', meaning 'advocate' or 'comforter', a title Mani used to claim he was the promised Holy Spirit</note> in his Letters, but of *Disciple*, of *Apostle* of J. Christ. Thirdly, it is not possible that *Manichaeus* would have ever accused the Prophets of having

make two very different men. They have nothing in common but the Episcopate: speeches, sentiments, situation, character—nothing agrees. 4. In the fourth place, *Severus* says nothing of those four Pagan Judges whose names and professions the author of the *Acts* notes for us, who intervene from time to time in the dispute, and who finally adjudge the victory to the Orthodox, at the expense of both their philosophy and their religion. 5. *Severus* speaks only of a single dispute; *Manes*, who had retired to the home of a country priest, flees to Persia as soon as he hears the name of *Archelaus*. It is therefore not true, according to *Severus*, that this priest wrote the letter to his Bishop that is in the *Acts*: It is not true that this Bishop sent him the response found there: It is not true that he hurried in haste to the aid of his priest and his sheep, nor that he had a second dispute with the heretic in the presence of the people of *Diodoris* and the surrounding areas. 6. In *Severus*, *Manes* does not come into *Mesopotamia* as a criminal who flees and hides, and whom *Shapur* <note>original: "Sapor," the King of Persia.</note> has hunted; for he returns to Persia, where he teaches his heresy with more liberty than he could have done among the Romans. Finally, that long harangue that *Archelaus* gives to the peasants of *Diodoris*, in which he tells them the history of *Manes*, is a fiction of the Greek author, since the Bishop did not even come into their village, where his presence was useless after the flight of the heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect.</note>.

<margin>Conclusion. The Acts of Archelaus are a romance composed by a Greek.</margin>
III. All the reflections I have just made have convinced me that the disputes of *Archelaus* with *Manes* <note>original: "Manichée"</note> are fundamentally nothing but a romance, composed by a Greek with the aim of refuting *Manichaeism*, and giving the Orthodox faith the advantage of having triumphed over it by confounding the head of the heresy, who defended it in person. I say that it is a romance composed by a Greek because if he had only translated or amplified Syriac memoirs—which appears to be the opinion of Mr. *Assemani* and even Mr. *Zaccagni*—it is inconceivable that these memoirs would have escaped the Syrian authors and that no trace of them could be found in their works. It is true, nonetheless, that the description of *Manes*, of his clothing and his air, has something original about it that does not seem to have been invented by a Greek. This is what leads me to judge that *Hegemonius*, who wrote this entire history, had conversed with some—

### THE GREEKS AND THE LATINS. BOOK I. CH. XIII. ###
### Vol. I. V ###
<meta>catchword: A</meta>

...some Mesopotamian, who might well have been named **Tyrbon**, who had seen *Mani*, who had been one of his disciples, and who had subsequently abjured his errors. For it is certain that in the time of *Hegemonius* there were people who had seen our heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect, in this case, Mani.</note>, since there were still some in the time of (1) *Cyril* of Jerusalem, who is somewhat more modern. *Papas*, (2) who was Primate of *Seleucia* when *Manes* published his errors there and expiated them by his execution, died only in 326 according to some, and according to others in 335, ten years after the Council of Nicaea.

<margin>Published around the year 330 or a little later.</margin>
I have only to examine the time in which these Acts were written: regarding which I will say, without needlessly reporting opinions that the reader can see in the learned Preface of Mr. *Zaccagni*, that it was between the years 330 and 340. The proof is in the Acts themselves, and if Mr. *Cave* had taken notice, (3) he would not have said that one cannot find the time *when Hegemonius lived*. This time is marked very distinctly in the words that the author puts into the mouth of *Archelaus*, when, to convince *Manes* of not being the Paraclete <note>A term from the Gospel of John referring to the Holy Spirit or "Comforter," whom Mani claimed to be.</note>, he has him make this argument: (4) “By calling yourself the Paraclete, you perhaps do not realize that you make Jesus Christ a liar; because, having promised to send him soon after his resurrection, he would nonetheless only have sent him **more than three hundred years later**.” These three hundred years fall in the year 333 or 334 of our Lord. Mr. *Zaccagni* (5) believes that this slipped from *Archelaus* in the heat of the dispute, because from the death of Jesus Christ until the Conference of *Cascar*, there are only two hundred and forty-nine years. For my part, I judge it otherwise. Nothing is more common to deceivers who make someone speak than to not remember everything suitable for the character they borrow, and to substitute their own without thinking about it. *Hegemonius*, who actually lived more than three hundred years after the resurrection of our Lord, thought only for a moment of the time in which he was writing, and not that in which *Archelaus* was supposed to have spoken. For even supposing that, in the heat of the dispute, this Bishop had let slip such a gross error against chronology, was he still in that heat when, in cold blood, he put into writing what he had said to the heresiarch?

->A<-

---

The HISTORY of *Manichaeus* is so different in the writings of the Greeks from that of the Eastern writers, that just as there have been scholars who believed that *Manes* and *Manichaeus* were two different men, one might imagine, with just as much foundation, that the *Manes* of the Easterners and that of the Greeks are two different <term>heresiarchs</term> <note>The founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note> who shared some similarities in their opinions, but almost none in their history. This is not to say that one should rely entirely on the accuracy and faithfulness of the Syrians, the Persians, and the Arabs. They are all biased against *Manichaeus*. The followers of *Zoroaster* <note>The ancient Persian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism, the state religion of the Sasanian Empire.</note> hated him no less than the Orthodox did. However, since we are dealing with facts that occurred in their own country, it is properly to the Easterners that it belongs to instruct us. Moreover, their account appears much more natural than that of the Greeks, which, as I have shown, is filled with manifest errors and blatant fables.

<margin>False Reflection of Abbé *Renaudot*.</margin>
I am therefore not of the opinion of Abbé *Renaudot* <note>Eusèbe Renaudot (1646–1720) was a French theologian and renowned Orientalist known for his work on liturgy and history.</note>, who, after having reported what he read in the Easterners regarding the History and Dogmas of *Manichaeus*, pronounces a judgment that I believe is more founded on self-love—on a National Partiality—than on equity, experience, and reason. "When one compares," he says (1), "the certain monuments of the Ancients with the imperfect accounts of the Easterners, one perceives immediately that if the latter have anything true, it is solely what they borrow from the Greeks and Latins. For they draw from their own stock nothing but ridiculous and impertinent fables." I leave it to the scholars who have read the best Syrian and Arabic authors to examine the judgment of this Abbé, and to avenge the entire East for his contempt. I content myself with saying in general that, in matters of fact, it is more natural to rely on the testimony of historians who are on the spot, than on foreign writers who do not even know the language of those countries. I add that if one were to draw a parallel between the Greeks and Latins and the Easterners, I do not know among which one would find more fabulous stories and more poor reasoning.

<margin>Birth of *Manichaeus* in the year 240. (a) Above, Book I, Ch. VI, p. 65.</margin>
II. I had occasion to remark *(a)* that the Chronicle of *Edessa* <note>A significant historical record from the city of Edessa (modern Şanlıurfa, Turkey), a major center of early Syriac Christianity.</note> places the birth of *Manichaeus* in the year two hundred and forty of Our Lord, but without naming the place where he came into the world. His name *Corbicius*, which I do not find at all in the Easterners, made me conjecture that he might have been born in CARCUB, a city of *Huzitide* <note>Also known as Khuzistan, a province in modern-day southwestern Iran.</note>, a province where there were many Christians from the beginning. I did not believe that one should contest the testimony of the Chronicle of *Edessa*, since I have seen no author who contradicted it; Mr. *Asseman* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican who cataloged many Eastern manuscripts.</note> admits it without difficulty: and it is evidently confirmed by the account of *Severus of Asmonine* <note>Severus ibn al-Muqaffa (10th century), a Coptic bishop and historian known for the "History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria."</note>, who must have found in some Egyptian, Syrian, or Arabic author that *Manes* was only thirty-five years old when he had a conference with *Archelaus*.

Such a skilled mathematician and good geographer was not capable of falling into a common error that persisted for a very long time among Christians, and with extreme obstinacy: the belief that the Earth is flat and that there are no <term>Antipodes</term> <note>The concept of people living on the opposite side of the globe, which was often rejected by early medieval theologians who believed the Earth was flat.</note>. He understood very well that the Earth must be of a spherical figure, just like (3) the Heavens which surround it on all sides. This is one of the heresies for which his sect was reproached, as seen in (4) *Cosmas*, surnamed *Indicopleustes* <note>A 6th-century Greek merchant and monk who wrote the *Christian Topography*, arguing for a flat earth based on Biblical literalism.</note>, and as we shall see ourselves in Part II, where we will examine his dogmas. Finally, he was learned in Astronomy and Astrology. He had even written on these sciences, but as nothing remains of him but the title of his work, we cannot further inform the reader of his ability. Ridiculous opinions regarding meteors and lunar eclipses are indeed attributed to him, which I shall have occasion to discuss in Part II. To all these sciences must be added *Medicine*, which the Persians in general took care to study, and to which the <term>Magi</term> <note>The priestly class of ancient Persia, known for their knowledge of stars and natural philosophy.</note> in particular were very attached; and the fine art of Painting, in which he excelled. To boast of his skill, the Easterners say (b), *that he could draw a line twenty ells <note>original: "vint aunes"; an old unit of measurement roughly equal to 45 inches.</note> in length without the help of any ruler.*

But, as clever as he is, it happens to him, as to many others, to be the dupe of a certain anti-heretical zeal, from which even the most moderate Authors have much trouble preserving themselves. It is for the same reason that *Abulpharage* had the weakness to write, <margin>(a) *Dynasties* under Marcus Aurelius, p. 79.</margin> (a) that the celebrated *Bardesanes* <note>A 2nd-century Syrian philosopher and Gnostic teacher.</note> was not content with calling the Sun the FATHER OF LIFE and the Moon the MOTHER OF LIFE—expressions that one could tolerate. He further added the ridiculous fiction that at the waning of the Moon, this *Mother of Life* "left her clothes: went to find the Sun her Husband: and that then these two Planets "lay together, and produced children, who continued the Human Race." <margin>Example of ridiculous accusations.</margin> I have seen, with a sort of astonishment, but yet with pleasure because of the insights I drew from it, that the same extravagance was blamed, more than a thousand years later, on those alleged Manichaeans to whom were given the ridiculous names of *Patarins*, *Popelicains*, *Cathars*, or *Cazares* <note>Various medieval dualist sects that the Catholic Church often grouped together or accused of being secret Manichaeans.</note>, as I shall have occasion to remark in their History. But, to return to *Abulpharage*, either he allowed himself to be deceived by some Syrian Author who accused Manichaeus of calling himself the *Messiah*, or—what seems more likely to me—*Pocock* <note>Edward Pococke (1604–1691), an English scholar who translated Bar Hebraeus's work from Arabic and Syriac into Latin.</note>, who translated the History of *Abulpharage*, gave us, without thinking, a false idea of what his Author meant to say. *Christ* and the *Messiah* are for all the same Person; but in those ancient Doctors who preceded the Council of Nicaea, *Christ* is sometimes only the Holy Spirit, or the Divinity which descended upon Jesus at his Baptism. That is undoubtedly what the Syrian Author meant to say, and what the Interpreter did not understand. <margin>Mani, excommunicated, attaches himself to Shapur.</margin>
<margin>(b) Work cited above, p. 4.</margin>
IV. *Mani* <note>original: "Manichée"</note> having manifested his Errors, he was banished from the Communion of the Catholic Church; it was apparently then that he went to dwell in the Royal City <note>likely Ctesiphon, the capital of the Sassanid Empire</note>, and began to be known by *Shapur I* <note>original: "Sapor I"</note>, who reigned in Persia. *Alexander of Lycopolis* <note>A philosopher from Egypt who wrote one of the earliest critiques of Manichaeism around 300 AD.</note> (b) testifies that he *accompanied him in his Armies*; and I have judged that this was in the capacity of a Physician. He soon gained the favor and confidence of this Prince, so well known in History for the Victories he won over the Romans, and for the ravages he committed in the Eastern Provinces of the Empire.

<margin>Character of this Prince.</margin>
*Ardashir* <note>original: "Ardezhir"</note>, surnamed *Babakan* <note>original: "Babecan"</note> after the name of one of his ancestors (he is the one the Greeks call *Artaxares*, or *Artaxerxes*), being Persian by origin, restored to his Nation the Empire which had been taken from it by the Greeks, and which from the Greeks had passed to the Parthians. This Revolution is placed in the year (3) 226. *Eutychius*, Patriarch of Alexandria, says that this Conqueror reigned fourteen years and six months, (4) *with all possible justice*. He left as his Successor *Shapur* <note>original: "Schabour" or "Sapor"</note>, a Prince formed to strengthen an Authority which, being only recently born, needed to be sustained by prudence, by valor, and by justice. The Romans complain exceedingly of his cruelties, but the Easterners praise him more than they blame him.

<margin>Digression on the ancient Religion of the Persians.</margin>
The Religion of the Persians had followed the fate of their Nation; lowered when that Nation was subjected, it rose again when the same Nation returned to the Throne. *Shapur* was very zealous for this ancient Religion of his Predecessors, which, in the manner it is described to us, is the purest that Human Reason has ever imagined. Let us make known to Readers who do not have the leisure or the convenience to consult the Authors who have treated it, what was the Religion of the Persians, of their Priests, of their Philosophers, and that of *Zoroaster* in particular, because all of this is linked with Manichaeism.

when he remarked that (c) *Mog* is an ancient name for the Sacrificers of the Persians, the origin of which is unknown; and *Pococke* observes that the idea attached to this term is nothing other than that of a *Fire-Worshiper*, or a *Priest who performs the Service before the Fire*.

<margin>The Magi did not worship Fire.</margin>
One must not imagine that the Persians, nor their Priests, worshipped the earthly Fire before which they performed Divine Service—they who did not even worship *Mithra*, who is the pure Fire, the celestial Fire, or the *Sun*. They rendered sovereign Worship only to the Supreme God, who is the Creator and the Sovereign Arbiter of the World. When these remnants of the ancient Persians, who retreated to India after the Arab conquest <note>referring to the Parsi community</note>, were asked what worship they render to the Sun (1); they replied that they do not worship the Stars, nor the Sun, nor the Moon, nor any of the Planets; that they only turn their faces toward the Sun when they pray.

<margin>Zoroaster as Reformer of Magism.</margin>
The Ancients and the Moderns do not agree on the question of whether the Religion of the Magi was already established among the Persians when <term>ZOROASTRE</term> came into the world, or if <term>SABIANISM</term> <note>original: "Sabaïsme," a religion centered on the worship of celestial bodies</note> and Idolatry reigned among these People. <margin>Idea of his Religion & his Theology.</margin>
The Religion of *Zoroaster* consisted of these three capital Articles: in the purity of Faith, in the sincerity and honesty of words, and in the justice and holiness of actions. It recognized only one single God and forbade the worship of any other than Him. This is seen in these words from the *Sad-Der*: <margin>(a) According to Hyde, cited above, p. 442.</margin> (a) *Know before all things, that your Lord is* UNIQUE; *that he is* HOLY, *that he has no equal: that he is the Lord of Power & of Glory.* This fundamental Article is confirmed by the testimonies of Arabic Authors, who assure us that *Zoroaster* taught (1) only one single God, without companion, without Associate, without equal. It is this same God who exists by himself, and who, before all Ages, formed the World of pure and blessed Spirits. These are the same as the *Aeons* <note>In Gnosticism and Manichaeism, divine emanations or beings that bridge the gap between God and the material world</note> of the Manichaeans, or the <margin>Creation of the World of Spirits. Of the World of the Stars.</margin> *Intelligences* of Plato, the *Anges* of the Jews and Christians. Three thousand years after this first Work, (2) God sent HIS WILL, in the form of a brilliant Light; it appeared in the figure of a Man. It was accompanied by seventy of the most honorable of his Angels, and it was then that it formed the Sun, the Moon, the Stars, and Men. These are certainly nothing but Human Souls, with the luminous, subtle, transparent body that they never leave, and which is like their Envelope and their vehicle. For as for the material and corruptible body, they were only clothed in it when they descended into this sublunary World, which was not yet created. We shall see elsewhere that *Manichaeus* kept several of these ideas.

<margin>Of the Sublunary World.</margin>

Above this, all is happy and immortal: but before <margin>Cult of Zoroaster.</margin> speaking of the origin of Evil, let us finish the Description of the Religion of *Zoroaster*. THE SYRIENS, THE PERSIANS, etc. BOOK II. CH. I.
X 3

it was the same in its worship. No Images or Statues were in the Temples, which were consecrated only to the Divinity. The unique Symbol of his presence held there was a continual fire. When one worshipped him, one turned toward the East, because it is from that side that Light comes, and that the Stars begin to appear. No Religious Worship was rendered to the Angels. They were considered only as Ministers of the Supreme Being, each having their own task, their department in the Government of the World; performing the office of Mediators between an invisible and inaccessible God, and between sinful and mortal men. Regarding what the Pagans named the *visible Gods*, the Sun and the Stars, they were regarded only as Images of the Divinity: but animated Images, which having been formed by the Divinity itself, also deserved a sort of veneration. For the rest, the Persians addressed prayers and asked for graces only from God alone. A Paradise, a Hell which they call *Gehenna* <note>A term of Hebrew origin (Gehinnom) used here to describe the Zoroastrian concept of a place of punishment</note>, the Immortality of Souls, and the Resurrection of Bodies were the constant Dogmas of their Faith. They claimed to hold this faith from *Abraham*, who had taught it and defended it against the Idolaters who were rising and multiplying in Assyria.

<margin>This Religion is altered in the Empire of the Greeks and the Parthians. Council of the Magi to reform it. (a) Hyde, as cited above. Cap. XXI.</margin>
This Religion, of which *Zoroaster* had been the Restorer or the Institutor, having suffered great alterations during the course of eight hundred years—during which it ceased to be the dominant faith under the rule of the Greeks and then the Parthians—it stood in need of a new reformation. This is what obliged *Artaxerxes* <note>Refers to Ardashir I (r. 224–242 AD), founder of the Sassanid Empire, who established Zoroastrianism as the state religion</note> (a) to assemble a Council composed of the Principal Magi <note>The priestly caste of ancient Persia</note> of his Empire. It is also said that this Prince wished to consult them regarding doubts he had concerning the state of the Dead, Paradise, and Hell. To strengthen him in the ancient Faith on all these Articles, a Mage celebrated for his holiness, named *Erdaviraph* <note>Likely Arda Viraf, the protagonist of a Middle Persian religious text who journeys through the afterlife</note>, fell into an Ecstasy which lasted seven days and seven nights, during which his Soul, transported into Heaven, saw what passes in that unknown World. Having returned from this rapture, he gave an account to the King of his Revelations; he attested to the fundamental truths upon which the Faith of this Prince had been shaken, and confirmed his testimony with several Wonders. It is thus that the Religion of *Zoroaster* was re-established in all its luster and resumed its ancient credit. There remained only a certain number of Unbelievers, whose number is estimated at eighty thousand.

<meta>This page continues the history of the Persian religion and its interactions with early Manichaeism. The previous page discussed the Zoroastrian restoration under the Sassanids; here, the focus shifts to the reign of Sapor I, the trial by fire, and the arrival of Manichaeus at court.</meta>

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO #

<margin>Unbelievers converted by the ordeal of fire. The antiquity of this Ordeal.</margin>
Sapor having succeeded (1) his father *Artaxerxes* in the year 241, and wishing to bring the Unbelievers back to the Faith of their Ancestors, ordered the Magi to seek means to convince them. Thereupon one of their Pontiffs, or Archbishops (for a Hierarchy was established among them), named *Adurabâd Mahrasphand*, offered to undergo the ordeal of fire. This ordeal is quite ancient, since it was in use before the time of *Sophocles*, who lived, as did *Euripides*, more than four hundred and sixty years before our Lord. The Reader may see the verses (2) of *Sophocles* at the bottom of the page. The Magus therefore proposed that eighteen pounds of molten copper, straight from the forge and glowing hot, be poured upon his naked body, on the condition that if he were not harmed by it, the Unbelievers would submit to such a great Miracle. It is said that the ordeal was performed with such success that they were all converted.

<margin>Manes goes to the Court of Sapor and there finds minds still wavering on the Resurrection, which he denies.</margin>
Manichaeus having been born only toward the end of the reign of *Artaxerxes*, I cannot place him among the number of those Unbelievers who were the remnants of those whom that Prince could not bring back to the Faith of their Fathers. Moreover, he was at first a Christian and passed for Orthodox, since he was a Priest. It was therefore not on his account that the Miracle performed by the Magus *Adurabâd Mahrasphand* took place; but this species of Heresy, which attacks either the immortality of the Soul or the resurrection of the dead, has no Stronghold, nor any asylum where it defends itself with more boldness and obstinacy, than the Courts of Princes, in which proud and hot-headed men impatiently suffer the fear of a future life to restrain their Passions and the abuse of their power. Thus, when Manichaeus came to the Court of *Sapor*, he undoubtedly found many Minds still wavering on the Questions that had been debated since the time of *Artaxerxes*, which revolved around the state of the Dead. I do not believe it is giving too much rash flight to one's conjectures to say that one of these Questions was that of the Resurrection—a Dogma affirmed by the Magi, but absolutely denied by *Manichaeus*.

<margin>He persuades the Prince of his Error.</margin>
This man, who was learned and whose manners were austere, soon gained the esteem of *Sapor* and so well insinuated himself into his mind (3) that he persuaded him at least of his Heresy regarding the Resurrection. I am much mistaken if it was not in that regard that he took this Prince by surprise. For besides the fact that Reason admits this Dogma only with reluctance and through a great submission of Faith, we shall see in the following that it was the principal Head of accusation for which he was put to death.

### CHAPTER II.

#### Origin of MANICHAEISM. The system of the MAGI regarding the Two Principles.

<margin>Definition of Principles.</margin>
I. THERE are two general opinions on the subject of PRINCIPES <note>In this context, "Principles" refers to the fundamental, uncreated sources or origins of all reality—the primary building blocks of the universe.</note>. By Principles, I mean eternal Beings who exist by necessity, and who have no external Cause for either their existence or their manner of existing; but who are, on the contrary, the Causes of all that exists.

<margin>Two Principles, according to some. God and Matter.</margin>
The first opinion is that of those Philosophers who recognized two eternal Beings in the World, one *active* and the other *passive*: the Agent, and the Subject upon which he exerts his action. In a word, *God* and *Matter*. Both are indeed eternal substances, but essentially different, because one has properties and perfections that the other neither has nor can have; and all the beauty, ornament, arrangement, and symmetry in physical bodies comes from the Wisdom and Will of the Spirit, which gave movement to Matter, or at least directed it.

<margin>Only one Principle, according to others; a single Substance, namely extended substance.</margin>
But others have imagined that there is only one Substance in the Universe, which unites within itself all possible Perfections. They believe that by virtue of the Movement it holds from the same Necessity from which it holds its existence, it ceaselessly gives to itself, and receives, that infinity of different modifications which form the various Bodies of which the World is composed.

I do not believe that before the Christians there was any other System than these two; no one having ever conceived that it was possible to make something from nothing <term>ex nihilo<gloss>The theological concept of "creation out of nothing," which the author argues was unfamiliar to ancient pagan philosophers.</gloss></term>. This is a Question I shall examine when I treat the System of *Manichaeus*.

<margin>The System of the Magi is infinitely contrary to the latter.</margin>
That of the Persian Philosophers had the advantage of being infinitely removed from the System I proposed second, which is known today under the name of SPINOSISM, because the famous SPINOZA <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677) was a philosopher who proposed that God and the universe are one and the same substance, a view often labeled as pantheism.</note> brought it back into fashion, although it is very ancient. It is found, in fact, both in the Greek Philosophers and in the Jewish Philosophers called *Cabbalists* <note>Followers of the Kabbalah, a school of Jewish mysticism.</note>, from whom...

HISTORY OF MANICHAEISM ACCORDING TO
<meta>catchword: and</meta>

<margin>They conceived of Matter as a Being that possesses movement and perception, and from which the Evil Powers have emerged.</margin>...it is believed that *Spinoza* <note>Baruch Spinoza (1632–1677), a Dutch philosopher often associated with the idea that God and Nature are the same substance; the author here suggests Spinoza’s ideas might have ancient roots in Persian thought.</note> drew from it. On the other hand, the system of the Magi added something to the first one I described. For while recognizing two eternal Beings, like all other Philosophers of the same class, and consequently an eternal Matter as well as God, they nevertheless did not believe that this Matter was in itself a dead, formless mass, destitute of movement, feeling, and perception. In a word, they believed it to be animated, and possessing the power to produce from itself an infinity of Beings clothed in the imperfections of the Cause that produced them. It even seems that they recognized, in the Region of Matter, a *Chief*, a *Prince*, who held in his Empire a power nearly equal to that which God held in His own. These two Empires were eternally separate. In one, pure Good; in the other, pure Evil. The first was called LIGHT; the second, DARKNESS. But when it pleased God to create the sublunary <note>The "sublunary" world refers to the Earth and its atmosphere—the realm beneath the moon's orbit, traditionally considered in ancient cosmology to be the place of change, decay, and the mixing of elements.</note> World, as He created it in the Region of Matter, then Good and Evil, Light and Darkness were mixed, these two Principles entering equally into the composition of this lower World, as is recognized by the effects we see.

<margin>They did not believe Evil to be an effect of the Freedom of a changeable Spirit.</margin>According to this system, Evil is a Substance, or an eternal Property of an eternal substance; and Good is likewise a Substance, or an eternal Property of an opposite substance. Evil is not an "accident" <note>In historical philosophy, an "accident" is a property that can change or be lost without the substance itself being destroyed. The author is arguing that for the Magi, evil wasn't a "wrong choice" (an accident), but part of the very "stuff" of the universe.</note> resulting from the variations of an intelligent and free Being who, placed between what is permitted and what is forbidden, between Virtue and Vice, with the power to choose, can distance himself from or approach either to infinity. Moral Evil and Physical Evil come from the same source.

All the Magi in general agreed that there are two Principles, one of the Good and the other of the Evil. I have seen no proof that these Philosophers ever regarded Evil as the effect of the free determination of a thinking Being, who, being created, cannot be immutable: For that which does not have the necessary cause of its existence within its own nature cannot have the necessary cause of its manner of existing and thinking either.

<margin>The System of the Magi was well represented by the Greeks.</margin>The Greeks did not poorly represent the System of the Magi when they said (1) that these Philosophers recognized two contrary Powers, one the Cause of good things, the other the Cause of evils:

...and that they gave to the first the name of *God*, and to the second that of *Demon*. "The Persians," *says Agathias (2)*, "fall into the same error as the *Manichaeans*, in that they recognize, like them, two Principles: one, which is good, and which produces all good things; the other, which is evil, and which produces all evils. They have bestowed upon these two Divinities two barbarian names, drawn from their own Language. They call ORMIZDAS the God who is the source of good; and ARIMANE, the God who is the source of Evil." Everything is accurate in this account, except for the attribute and name of *God*, which the Magi <note>The Magi were the priestly caste of ancient Persia, associated with Zoroastrianism and the study of stars and elements.</note> did not give to the evil Principle, because they were too wise to serve it. They thus protected themselves from the horrible Superstition of a great number of Peoples, who offered sacrifices to evil *Demons* in order to prevent the harms they might have done to them.

<margin>Ormizdas, name of the good Principle. Origin of this name.</margin>
II. I have not noticed—and perhaps it is my own fault—that Mr. Hyde <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703) was a pioneering English orientalist and Professor at Oxford, known for his work on ancient Persian religion.</note> has given us the true meaning of the Persian name, *Ormizdas*, or rather *Hormizdas*. He did well to note somewhere that this name is attributed to the Planet *Jupiter*, and that when it designates the Divinity, it is accompanied by some Epithet that characterizes it and determines its meaning. For example, the Persians say <margin>(a) Hyde, in the work cited above, p. 161.</margin> (a), HORMIZDA CHODA, which is to say, *O sovereign God*. An (3) able Englishman <note>James Windet, a 17th-century physician and scholar.</note> believes that *Oromazdes* being composed of two words, one of which signifies Light and the other *to preserve*, designates the SOURCE OF LIGHT, the RESERVOIR, so to speak, OF LIGHT. Another Scholar, who sought the origin of this name in the Chaldean Language <note>Chaldean refers to the ancient Semitic language of Mesopotamia, often associated with early astronomy and magic in this period.</note>, believes that it means (4) A GLOWING, RESPLENDENT FIRE; and it is true that nothing is more common among the Chaldeans than to call the Divinity A FIRE, a *pure Fire*, an *intellectual Fire*.

There is a likelihood that these skilled Moderns are mistaken by seeking, in the Chaldean Language, the etymology and meaning of a name that comes from the ancient Language of the Persians. This is what a Scholar, who perfectly possesses Armenian, as well as other Oriental Languages, has shown in a Remark that he communicated to me, and which the Reader will find in its entirety...

<margin>This idea of *Zoroaster's* System is more beautiful than it is real.</margin>
Nothing is more beautiful, nothing more Orthodox, than this System. I only fear that it is a bit too advanced for those times: to make *Evil* consist in a simple privation of *Good* is a metaphysical refinement which, if I am not mistaken, is more modern than the Prophet of the Persians. Thus, there are authors who do not make him as orthodox as Mr. Prideaux <note>Humphrey Prideaux (1648–1724), an English theologian and author of "The Old and New Testament Connected."</note> represents him.
<margin>(a) *As cited above* P. 931.</margin>
*The Tarik Montekheb testifies*, says (a) Mr. D'Herbelot <note>Barthélemy d'Herbelot (1625–1695), a French Orientalist whose "Bibliothèque orientale" was a standard reference.</note>, *that Zoroaster, Author of the Sect of the Megiousch, or Magi, is also the first who taught the Doctrine of the two Principles of all things, and that the surname of Megiousch given to him is a name corrupted by the Arabs from the Persian word Meikhoulch, which signifies* SOUR-SWEET, *because of the two Principles, good and evil, that he established.* The learned Author whom I cite, and who possessed a vast knowledge of Oriental Literature, testifies everywhere that *Zoroaster* recognized two Principles.

<margin>The Persians do not believe in two Gods. (b) *In Hyde.* P. 163.</margin>

*Zarvam*, this Critic derives with much likelihood from the Arabic word *(a) ZARAHON*, which means, *the Author of all things* <note>original Latin: *Omnium Sator*</note>; this is the Father of all things, who, according to *Zoroaster*, produced two Intelligences, two subordinate Principles, one of which is the Cause of Good, and the other the Cause of Evil.

<margin>Conformity between the System of Zoroaster and that of Lactantius.</margin>
This System of the Persian Prophet has a great conformity with the one that *Lactantius* <note>Lactantius (c. 250 – c. 325) was an early Christian author who served as an advisor to Constantine I.</note> expressed in these terms: "God, wanting to form this World, which was to be composed of completely contrary things, began by forming two sources of these same things, which are in opposition, in a continual war; namely two Spirits, one good, the other evil; of which the first is like the right hand of God, and the second like his left. These two Spirits are the Son of God and Satan."

All that has just been said shows that *Zoroaster* was orthodox on the article of a single Creator Principle. Having perhaps learned from the Jews that one and the same God created *light and darkness, peace and war, prosperity and adversity, life and death*, he banished from the system of the Magi these two co-eternal prin-

<margin>Zoroaster believed Darkness was a very real Being, and not a Privation.</margin>
ciples, both active, thinking, and Formative, which were recognized by the *Dualists*, a belief which led to them being accused of believing in two Gods. But when Mr. Prideaux <note>Humphrey Prideaux (1648–1724), an English theologian and orientalist.</note> asserts that *Zoroaster* made evil consist in a pure *Privation of Good*, he surely attributes to him ideas that he never had. He believed that Darkness was a real Being, since it enters, like Light, into the composition of the Beings of this sublunary World. Now, Nothingness and Privation compose nothing. They must remain mixed with Light, *until the Light has conquered them*. Are Nothingness and Privation enemies that can be fought? When Light has won the Victory, Darkness will not be annihilated; it will not vanish as a shadow vanishes as soon as the Body disappears; they *will return to their Principle, and re-enter forever into their own World*. They existed, therefore, before being mixed with Light;

<margin>Idea of the System of Zoroaster.</margin>
I would very much like to develop now the true System of *Zoroaster*; but the Extracts that Mr. Hyde <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703) was an influential English orientalist and professor at Oxford who wrote a major history of the religion of the ancient Persians.</note> has given us from his Arabic Authors are so obscure, and so entangled with ideas that appear contrary, that I almost dare not flatter myself with having caught their thought. I perceive some quite distinct lights, but the rest is an enigma that must be solved.

<margin>He recognized only one Creating Principle.</margin>
I. I see first, then, that *Zoroaster* recognized only a single God, the immediate Creator of the World of Spirits, but the mediate Creator—both of the World of Stars and Planets and of the lower World, which is our terrestrial Globe—which he formed through the intervention of a Power that *Zoroaster* calls HIS WILL. This idea very much approaches the Christian idea.

<margin>Attributed Eternity only to God, not to the exclusion of Matter.</margin>
II. This Philosopher attributed Eternity only to God: but this can only be to the exclusion of SATAN, or AHREMAN <note>Also known as Ahriman, the personification of evil and darkness in Zoroastrianism, often contrasted with Ahura Mazda, the god of light.</note>, who was created, and not to the exclusion of Matter, from which he was created. For no ancient Philosopher ever conceived that it was possible to make something out of nothing <note>original Latin: *ex nihilo*. The author notes that ancient thinkers generally believed matter was eternal and that creation was the act of shaping that matter.</note>.

<margin>Satan created.</margin>
III. When Mr. Hyde says that, *according to Zoroaster, (2) God created the Light and the Darkness, and that he is the sole Author of them*, it is necessary to understand by *Darkness*, not *Matter* itself, but *Satan*, whom *God created from Matter*. Without this, how could he add *(3), that one must not attribute the existence of Darkness to God? (4) The contradiction would be manifest*. One must therefore conceive of Matter existing from all eternity in the depths of space, where the Earth is now located. It was in these depths that Matter resided: It was precipitated and held there by its weight.

<margin>The World formed from the mixture of Light with Darkness by the Good-pleasure of God.</margin>
IV. Among the Questions debated in the Schools of the Magi <note>The Magi were the priests and learned class of ancient Persia, from whose name we derive the word "magic."</note>, there were two main ones, upon which revolved their gran-

<column-break/>

<margin>p. 55. The Distinction that I establish removes the contradiction. One must not attribute the existence of Darkness—that is to say, of Matter—to God: Darkness is uncreated. But one must attribute the existence of Satan to God, because He created him. Zoroaster recognized only a single eternal, thinking, Creator Principle. He did not believe that Satan was eternal, nor that he possessed the Empire of Darkness from all eternity, as God possessed that of Light. He did not believe that Matter had, of itself, the force to produce evil Powers. This is what I see in Mr. Hyde’s Authors, and I do not believe one is well-founded in rejecting their testimony on this article. I have reported that of Theodore of Mopsuestia <note>Theodore of Mopsuestia (c. 350–428 AD) was a prominent Christian theologian and Bishop of Mopsuestia.</note>, who was Greek, who was very skillful, and who confirmed the testimony of the Arabs.</margin>
