### HISTORY OF MANICHAEISM ACCORDING TO...

great Disputes (1). The first: *What was the cause of the mixture of Light with Darkness?* Did God create this mixture? Or did it happen by itself? Did He will it? Did He permit it? Was this permission free or forced? All the answers carried their own disadvantages, and seemed to wound one of the Divine Perfections. The second Question revolved around *the causes of the deliverance of Light.* The Magi <note>Ancient Persian priests or followers of Zoroastrianism, known for their study of the stars and dualistic theology.</note> sought by what means it would finally be separated from Darkness and freed from such a fatal association. The authors cited by Mr. Hyde <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703), an English orientalist and author of "De Religione Veterum Persarum."</note> explain to us in a word the sentiment of *Zoroaster* on the first of these Questions. He said that God mixed Light with Darkness **BY HIS GOOD PLEASURE** (a) (**ACCORDING TO HIS WILL** <note>original: "PRO ARBITRIO"</note>). <margin>(a) Ibid.</margin> By this, *Zoroaster* maintained the Divine Majesty. God is not forced. The Portions of Light that are in our World are not captives that the Powers of Darkness took from Him by force, or that they stole from Him clandestinely. God willed to create the lower World: He did it **ACCORDING TO HIS GOOD PLEASURE**.

<margin>How God is not the Author of the Evil of which this mixture was the occasion.</margin> V. This sentiment of *Zoroaster* opened a wide breach for Objections, which entered in crowds into his System to attack the Goodness, Holiness, and Divine Justice, which seem to equally disavow a mixture that offends them all. For if God made it, and if He made it freely, then He is the Author of the Evil that results from it. Without this mixture, there would be no Evil, or, if there were, it would be relegated to its own World, where it would torment only itself. The authors cited by Mr. *Hyde* indicate the answers that *Zoroaster* made to this Difficulty. But whether this stems from the authors themselves or from their Translator, they are so obscure that it is quite difficult to give a distinct and consistent idea of them. Here, nevertheless, is what I understand of them.

1. Firstly, God did not properly give existence to Darkness: He only made use of it to form a World in the composition of which it necessarily enters, since it is a part of it.

2. Secondly, if Evil resulted from the mixture of Light with Darkness, God should not be blamed for it, because He did not properly will that Evil should exist: it was not—

Just as he who creates a Body does not intend to create a Shadow; although the Shadow is a necessary consequence of the existence of the Body, placed in a certain position relative to the Light, it is the same with Evil. It did not enter into the Plan of God creating the World.

3. *In the third place, Mr. Hyde tells us that God saw that Darkness existed in some manner, but that it did not really exist.* This means, if I am not mistaken, that matter existed, but it was only a dead and confused mass, without order or action. This is existence *in some manner*. It acquired real existence when, by mixing it with Light, it received modification, arrangement, and action. Light animated it (2). Finally, *Zoroaster* <note>An ancient Persian prophet whose teachings founded Zoroastrianism, centered on the struggle between light and dark.</note> said that Darkness was a consequence of Light, because one Opposite entails the existence of its Opposite; one cannot be without the other being. The Reader may see (3) at the bottom of the page the words of Mr. Hyde, and compare them with the explanation I have just given.

<margin>Advantage of the System of Zoroaster.</margin>
There would be many Reflections to make on this System, which is certainly not shielded from difficulties. But is there any system that is? *Zoroaster* is still very estimable for having maintained the sovereign Authority of God, and for having excluded another co-eternal, thinking, active Principle, which is *Matter*, or the Prince of Matter. If after that he did not sufficiently satisfy all the difficulties that could be opposed to him, it is quite right to excuse in him what we want people to excuse in all. God created the sublunary World <note>In ancient cosmology, the "sublunary" region refers to the Earth and everything below the moon, which was believed to be subject to change, decay, and the mixture of elements.</note>. It is a good thing, since He made it. He could only make it by mixing Light with Darkness, because these are the two general Elements that compose this World. The Evil that resulted from it was not in His intention. It is a consequence of the Creation of the World, which God should not have renounced because of this inconvenience.

<margin>Different Sects among the Magi.</margin>
Although the System of *Zoroaster* was the most reasonable, the others nonetheless always had their Followers. The Magi <note>Followers of Zoroaster, often described as priests or wise men specialized in astrology and theology.</note> were divided into different Sects, but they were too wise and too moderate to anathematize one another, or to persecute each other with fire and blood. Opinions of this Sect.

IV. Among these different Sects, there was one that the Arabs call the **MAGUSEANS**. *Magusean* signifies in our Greek Authors only a follower of the Magi <note>The Magi were the priestly caste of ancient Persia, associated with Zoroastrianism and occult wisdom.</note>. It is in this sense that this term is used by (1) St. Epiphanius, by Bardesanes, by St. Basil, and by others. But the Arabs seem to call *Maguseans* a Heretical Sect that had degenerated from the belief of *Zoroaster*. *Manes*, says Sharistani <note>Al-Shahrastani (1086–1153), a prominent Persian historian of religions.</note> (a), *was originally a* **MAGUSEAN**, *and approved of the Popular Sects. He recognized that the World was made, and that it is composed of two coeternal Principles, one of which is Light, and the other Darkness. That these two Principles have an eternity antecedent to all Beings, and that neither the one, (2) nor the other will ever end. He also denied that any thing could exist unless it had an eternal Principle.* This means, firstly, that he did not believe there was any Power that could draw Being out of nothingness; and secondly, that nothing is contingent: that everything is the effect of a Cause, which must either exist by itself or be the effect of another Cause that exists by itself, because nothing comes from nothing.

<margin>(b) According to Hyde, p. 295.</margin>
In another place, the same Sharistani describes *Magusaism* in these terms: (b) *The Maguseans, he says, believed in a Duality that was peculiar to them. They established two eternal Conductors, or Governors, who create Good and Evil, Vice and Virtue, the Useful and the Pernicious. One is called Light; the other, Darkness. One is* **YEZDAN** <note>A Persian term for God or the principle of Good.</note>, *or God; the other,* **ABREMAN** <note>Also known as Ahriman, the personification of the evil spirit in Middle Persian.</note>, *or the Devil.*

<margin>General idea of his Heresy.</margin>
Such was the true origin of the Error of *Manichaeus* regarding the subject of the two Principles. As for his Heresy in general, it was properly a (4) Philosophical System, the foundations of which he had found in the Philosophy of the Magi, and which he accommodated as best he could with the Revelation of *Jesus Christ*. In this, he did nothing other than what many Greeks had done before him, and what the Greeks and Latins have almost never ceased to do after him. One has seen, in every age, Philosophers filled with the ideas of *Plato*, or of *Aristotle*, who, under slight pretexts, [mixed them] with Christian Truths and established them as articles of Faith. Furthermore, the artifice of *Manichaeus* was, first, to keep the Oriental opinions in order to make his Religion palatable to the Persians. And second, to reconcile, if possible, these same opinions with the Christian Religion in order to win over the Christians. But as he found obstacles in the Books of the Evangelists and the Apostles, he first supposed that these Books had not been written by the disciples of the Lord, and that if they had been, "Galileans"—that is to say, Christians steeped in Judaic superstitions—had falsified them. He supposed in the second place, that *Jesus Christ* having promised to send to his Church an extraordinary Minister, enlightened by the Li—

...that the most skillful Manichaeans maintained that the Principle of Evil would be destroyed by the fire of the Last Judgment: that then Matter would be reduced to ashes and cast out of the World.

I. I hope that, far from boring the Reader, I shall provide some refreshment if, before continuing the History of Manichaeus, I recount the origin of the Christian Religion in Persia and the state in which it was found when the Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heresy.</note> undertook to corrupt it—by merging, so to speak, Magianism <term>Magianism: the ancient dualistic religion of Persia, centered on the teachings of Zoroaster and the class of priests known as the Magi.</term> and Christianity together, and by mixing the base metals of Oriental opinions with the pure gold of the Faith.

<margin>The Christian Religion brought into Persia from the first Century. (a) Eccl. Hist. Book II. 2.</margin>
Sozomen (a) believed that the Gospel was not announced to the Persians until toward the end of the 3rd Century, by Preachers who were sent to them from *Edessa* and *Armenia*. But the contrary has been quite well proven without resorting to doubtful, not to say entirely false, Traditions.

<margin>St. Thomas preaches to the Parthians.</margin>
It is claimed that St. Thomas went to preach the Gospel in *Edessa* in Mesopotamia, and from there into the Country of the Parthians. The Eastern Syrians (this is how those who live beyond the Euphrates call themselves) assert that St. Thomas was their Apostle, and make him the Head and the Root of the Succession of all their Bishops. And for the Syrians, one may consult the *Oriental Library* of Mr. *Asseman* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note>. <margin>This Babylon is that of Assyria.</margin>
It is true (3) that various Interpreters, both ancient and modern, have believed—some, that *this Babylon was Rome*; others, that *it was Babylon in Egypt*; but, whatever deference I have for their discernment and for their authority, their reasons do not seem strong enough to me to substitute a very little-known Babylon for the one that had carried that name for so many centuries, or to persuade me that *St. Peter* affected to hide the name of *Rome* under that of *Babylon*. The reasons invented for this are too far-fetched to be true. It is a fancy of *Papias* <note>Papias of Hierapolis (c. 60–130 AD), an early Christian author whose works survive only in fragments cited by others.</note>, which the Ancients adopted too easily, and which St. *Jerome* would have rejected with contempt (4) if, in the bad mood he was in against Rome, he had not been pleased to confound it with Babylon. Nevertheless, a very famous Protestant Bishop (c), who acknowledged that Babylon is not *Rome*, maintains that it also cannot be *Babylon in Assyria*: first, because the latter was nothing more than a heap of ruins, a city completely depopulated when *St. Peter* wrote his First Epistle; and second, because a great massacre of Jews had taken place there and in the province around the fortieth year of our Lord, so that very few or none at all could have remained there.

I noted above that from the beginning there were many Christians in the Province of **Elam**, which is often confused with that of **Persia**, in **Susiana**, in **Chuziana**, and in **Huzitide** <note>These regional names refer to areas in modern-day Khuzestan, Iran.</note>, of which **Ahvaz** was the Metropolis.

<margin>Christians were not persecuted there, or very little, during the first three centuries.</margin>
The Christians were quite tranquil in **Persia** during the first three centuries, before the Roman Emperors had embraced the Faith: there was no persecution then, or very little. Whether out of indifference or natural equity, the Kings of the East treated the Christians with humanity. But when the Emperors declared themselves for Christianity, and this Religion—born in the lands of the [Roman] Empire—became the Dominant Religion, then the Christians appeared suspicious to the Persians, who began to distrust their loyalty and to regard them as secret enemies of their State. One perceives this cause of the Persecutions in the conduct of **Perozes** <note>Peroz I, King of Kings of the Sassanid Empire (reigned 457–484 AD).</note>.

<margin>Why they were persecuted later.</margin>
**Nestorianism** <note>A theological doctrine emphasizing the disunion of the divine and human natures of Jesus.</note> having arisen around the year four hundred and thirty-one, and **Monophysitism** <note>The doctrine that Christ has only one nature, the divine.</note> about twenty years later, **Perozes**, who learned that **Zeno** <note>Byzantine Emperor Zeno (reigned 474–491 AD).</note> favored this latter Sect and persecuted the former, violently pursued the **Monophysites** and protected the **Nestorians**. Subsequently, the more these two Sects were persecuted by the Romans, the more they were either protected or tolerated by the Persians, because the latter could no longer suspect them of being in intelligence with their enemies.

The Hatred or Jealousy of neighboring Nations exerted their influence on the Religions born within their midst. **Manichaeism** was initially odious to the Romans because it drew its origin from the Persians, their irreconcilable enemies. **Diocletian**, having learned at **Alexandria** where he was, that this Heresy was making great progress in Proconsular Africa, issued a bloody Law (4) against it, based first on the fact that it was born among the Persians—always enemies of the Roman People—and secondly, because it was to be feared that the Manichaeans, coming into the lands of the Empire, would bring their execrable and inces-

<margin>Doubt regarding the incests attributed to the Persians.</margin>
An idea occurred to me at this point, which I shall share with the Reader. It is a doubt regarding the incests with which the Persians have been so often reproached; this doubt was suggested to me by the regulations concerning the degrees in which marriage may be permitted, which were made by **Timothy**, Patriarch of the Nestorians of Persia and of the entire Sect. <note>Timothy I (c. 727–823), an influential Patriarch of the Church of the East under the Abbasid Caliphate.</note> Article XIX is conceived in these terms: (1) *“The Father and the Son shall not marry two Sisters, because the Pagans and the Magi are accustomed to doing so.”* <note>original: "le Pere & le Fils n'épouferont point les deux Sœurs, parceque les Payens & les Mages ont accoûtumé de le faire."</note> It is also forbidden, in Article XXV, for a Paternal or Maternal Uncle to marry the wife of his Brother’s son, or the wife of his Sister’s son, for the reason (2) *“that this is another custom of the Magi.”* <note>Magi: The priestly caste of the Zoroastrian religion in ancient Persia.</note> The Patriarch spoke, in the preceding Articles, of incestuous marriages in the first and second degrees, but he did not say, in forbidding them, that they were practiced among the Magi. Does this silence not give reason to think that, in fact, they were not practiced, at least in that time?

<margin>Papa was Patriarch of Seleucia when Mani published his Heresy.</margin>
The Churches of Persia were at peace when **Manichaeus** <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism.</note> attempted to corrupt their Faith. The timing was favorable enough for him to make pernicious progress, if one considers the character of the man who should have opposed him with the most vigor and success, as he found himself at the head of all the Clergy of the East. I speak of **Papa**, son of **Aggai**, <note>Papa bar Aggai (died c. 327), the first historically documented Bishop of Seleucia-Ctesiphon.</note> who was then Primate of **Seleucia**, and who held that See for a very long time. The most honorable thing attributed to him (3) is having regulated the rank of the Metropolitans according to the time of the foundation of their Sees. Otherwise, he was a Prelate of insufferable pride and boundless ambition, treating with the ultimate indignity not only the Priests and his Deacons, but even the Bishops, his brothers. Here is what the Syrians tell us of him:

<margin>Mani publishes his Heresy.</margin>
It was while such a Prelate held the first See of the East that *Mani* <note>The founder of Manichaeism (c. 216–274 AD), known for synthesizing Christian, Buddhist, and Zoroastrian elements.</note> began to publish his Heresy. I have marked the time as the year two hundred and sixty-seven, in which I followed *Abulpharage* <note>Bar Hebraeus, a prominent 13th-century Syrian scholar and bishop.</note>, who testifies that it appeared under *Aurelian*. As for the manner in which the Heresiarch <note>The leader or founder of a heretical movement.</note> claimed to have received his Vocation, I find in the extract that *Hottinger* <note>Johann Heinrich Hottinger (1620–1667), a Swiss philologist and theologian.</note> gave us from an Arabic manuscript (1), that it was during sleep. This man could well boast of having Divine Dreams, since, according to the report of *Archelaus* <note>A 3th-century bishop whose disputations with Mani are a primary, though polemical, source.</note>, he was warned in a dream of the plan that *Sapor* <note>Shapur I, King of the Sassanid Empire.</note> had formed against his life. However, I would rather believe that he based it on an *Ecstasy* <note>A state of mystical trance or vision.</note>. The *Magi* <note>Zoroastrian priests of ancient Persia.</note> assumed such things occurred, as seen by the example of *Erdaviraph* <note>Ardaviraf, a Zoroastrian priest said to have visited the heavens and hells in a trance.</note>, which I have already reported (a), and perhaps these Philosophers held among their secrets the method for procuring such *Ecstasies*. Father *Ange de Saint-Joseph*, a Carmelite and Missionary in the Levant, recounts (2), "that a trustworthy person, having taken a pill of " the Persian Opiate, was forced, for several hours, to laugh " and to say several foolish things despite themselves. They saw passing be- " fore their eyes small phantoms and very grotesque Goblins, and " felt several extraordinary effects, without any bad " consequence." This example shows what certain compositions can do to the Imagination and the Senses. Whatever the case may be, *Mani* might well have intended to imitate *St. Paul*, whom he regarded as the first of the Apostles, as much for his zeal in delivering the Church from Judaism as for the proofs he believed he found in his Writings in favor of the corruption inherent in Nature. All this could have inspired him with the desire to imagine an *Ecstasy* similar to that of *St. Paul*, and the hope of persuading the world of it. He therefore boasted of having received his Apostleship directly from Heaven; and alleged, to establish it, not Miracles—for I have nowhere seen that he boasted of having performed any—but primarily the perfection and fullness of his knowledge, and secondly the promise that *Jesus Christ* had made to the Church to send the *Paraclete* <note>From the Greek 'Parakletos,' meaning Advocate or Comforter; Mani claimed to be the promised Holy Spirit.</note>.

### THE SYRIANS, THE PERSIANS, etc. BOOK II. CH. III. ###

<margin>Sapor, when Mani sets himself up as an Apostle of Jesus Christ and seeks to reform Magism.</margin>
This fanatic initially gained the confidence of *Sapor* <note>Shapur I, the second Sassanid King of Kings of Persia, who reigned from 240 to 270 AD.</note>, but it is very likely that he did not reveal the full mystery of his doctrine to him at first. He was content to show him only the side that most resembled Magism <note>The ancient Persian religion of the Magi, centered on the struggle between light and darkness.</note>, presenting what was new, plausible, and philosophical. Having been excommunicated by the Christians and leaving their society, the King of Persia viewed him only as a great philosopher. But as soon as he wished to give this same doctrine the appearance and name of the doctrine of Jesus Christ; when, setting himself up as an Apostle of the Lord, he sought to reform the worship and opinions of the Magi and introduce a new religion, then *Sapor* abandoned him and resolved to put him to death. "*Mani*," says Mr. *D'Herbelot* (a) <note>Barthélemy d'Herbelot (1625–1695), a French orientalist and author of the *Bibliothèque Orientale*.</note>, "after having made himself ad-

<margin>(a) Orient. Biblioth. p. 549.</margin>
"mired for some time, began to assemble people under the name of Disciples, WHO OPPOSED THE ZOROASTRIAN WORSHIP AND CEREMONIES, which the Persians practiced at that time. This novelty, having excited troubles, *Sapor* wanted to put him to death."

<margin>This cause of his disgrace is seen in the Acts of Archelaus.</margin>
This narrative is clearly confirmed by the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A controversial early Christian text detailing a supposed debate between Bishop Archelaus and Mani; it is often biased but provides key historical details.</note>, despite all the care the author took to disguise it, in order to deprive *Mani* <note>Original: "Manichée"</note> of the glory of having died, in a sense, for Christianity. Although this writer affects to attribute Mani's disgrace entirely to the death of the King's son, he nevertheless admits (3) "that this Prince only resolved on his execution after he had sent his disciples everywhere, with orders to preach his errors boldly UNDER THE NAME OF JESUS CHRIST." One sees clearly in these words the true crime of *Mani*. It is his doctrine preached *under the name of the Son of God*, whose Apostle he claimed to be. It was his desire to reform the belief and worship of the Magi according to the plan and ideas he believed he found in the Gospel. Then he met the fate of most of those who undertake to change established religions. *Sapor*, says (b) a historian of the Persians, *either of his own accord, or at the solicitation of the Magi, resolved to put him to death*.

<margin>(b) Khwandamir. Cited in Hyde, page 282.</margin>

It is situated to the East of the Caspian Sea and borders (5) *Sogdiana*, which was the last of the provinces the Persians formerly possessed.

### THE SYRIANS, THE PERSIANS, etc. Book II. Ch. III. ###

"Superstitions, which have blinded the Indians, the Chinese, and neighboring peoples for several centuries, do not take their origin from the doctrine of *Manichaeus*, nor from the remnants of the sect of *Zoroaster*." <note>Manichaeus (Mani) was a 3rd-century Persian prophet who founded Manichaeism, a dualistic religion. The *Literati*, or the learned class, are at the opposite extreme of Manichaeism. **(4) They attribute to the power of Matter all the effects that we attribute to Spiritual Nature, the existence and possibility of which they reject.** They recognize only one Principle, and this Principle is Matter. The truth is, **(5)** that there have been a great number of Manichaeans in *Turkestan* and in *Cathay* <note>Cathay is an archaic name for Northern China, popularized by Marco Polo.</note>; and that there are still some there today. But the fundamental error of the "Two Principles" <note>The belief that the universe is governed by two equal, opposing forces: Good/Light and Evil/Darkness.</note> and that of Metempsychosis <note>The transmigration of souls, or reincarnation.</note> were established, received, and, so to speak, canonized there so many centuries before *Manichaeus* that one would be quite hard-pressed to mark their true origin.

In the former, *Mani* only becomes acquainted with Christianity toward the end of his life; here, he knows it from his youth, and knows it so well that he becomes a Priest; he teaches it and defends it against the Infidels. There, he took his two Principles <note>The dualistic concept of Light vs. Darkness.</note> from the Books of *Scythianus*, and *Scythianus* from the Philosophy of *Pythagoras*. Here, he found them in the ancient Theology of his own Country, from which *Pythagoras* himself had drawn all that he thought on the subject. There, *Mani* incurs the disgrace of *Sapor* <note>Shapur I, the Sasanian King of Persia.</note> for having been unable to heal his Son; here, his fall is attributed to an entirely different cause. *Sapor* only becomes angry with him because he wants to found a new Sect under the name of *Jesus*, and because he disapproves of the Worship and Faith of the Persians. There, this King holds him in Prison for a long time; here, he prevents the Prince's plan to arrest him by fleeing. There, finally, he takes refuge on the frontiers of Roman Mesopotamia; here, it is at the opposite extremity of the Persian Empire—in Turkestan. However, it is precisely at this extremity that we will find the only point where they might agree.

<margin>Digression on the state of Christianity in Turkestan. The Scene of the Dispute would be better placed there than in Mesopotamia.</margin>
IV. The Acts of *Archelaus* state that the fugitive *Manichaeus* retired to Mesopotamia and came to that Roman City named CASCAR, where he had a Dispute with the Bishop of the place. We have been unable to find any City in Mesopotamia bearing that name, and indeed, none exists. *Cascar* <note>Referring to Kaskar, an ancient city near Wasit in modern-day Iraq.</note> is in *Babylonian Iraq*, in the heart of the Persian Empire, where the Romans did not penetrate—or, if they did, they did not stay. From this, I concluded that the Dispute of *Cascar* is fabricated. But my Conclusion was perhaps more general than the Premises. I have well proven that the Dispute did not take place in Mesopotamia; but if we place it in *Turkestan*, it might be sustained. It is there that the Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical movement.</note> retired, according to the Orientals; it is there that one finds a CASCAR <note>Likely referring to Kashgar, a major city in modern-day Xinjiang, China.</note> which is not subject to the Persians, and where he could plead his Cause in total safety. It is there that there are Christians and Bishops who could not fail to rise up against a Heretic who destroys the principal Articles of the Christian Faith. It is there that *Syriac* is spoken; this language is the Sacred Language of the Christians, the language of the Learned. I had not thought of it: we must restore this Dispute, which I have so heavily attacked; we need only move it...

...to place them well. *Hegemonius* <note>The supposed author of the "Acts of Archelaus."</note> did nothing more than transport the theater of events to the lands of the Empire; whereas it should have been placed in *Turkestan*: this single change restores the entire structure that I have taken such pains to break down. Knowing nothing of the <term>Cascar</term> <note>Kashgar, an ancient oasis city in modern-day Xinjiang, China.</note> of *Turkestan*, he went looking for one in Roman Mesopotamia, where none exists.

<margin>Reason why Mani retired to Turkestan.</margin>
*Mani* took refuge in the *Transoxiana* <note>The region "beyond the Oxus river," historically a crossroads of Central Asian civilizations.</note> Provinces, and it must be admitted that he could not have chosen his retreat better. There, he was safe from the pursuits of *Sapor*, and among a People who were not, like the Romans, the irreconcilable enemies of the Persians. Furthermore, he was already known there, and his Doctrine had made some progress. <term>MANES</term>, says Abulpharage <note>Also known as Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286), a prominent Bishop and historian of the Syriac Orthodox Church.</note>, *had sent some of his Disciples to India and China, where they had sown the Doctrine of the Dualists*. I have already remarked that *China*, in this context, refers to the Land of the Turks; the place from which that Nation draws its origin. The Acts of *Archelaus* testify that *Mani* had sent *Addas* into *Scythia*, that is to say, into the Provinces of *Scythia* which were neighboring Persia, in *Turkestan*.

(1) Around the year 1514 of the Era of the Greeks <note>Also known as the Seleucid Era; this calendar was widely used by Eastern Christians.</note>, that is to say, around the year 1203 of Our Lord, the Chief of all the Turkic Tribes was a Prince named UNG-KHAN. He descended from the *Cerrit* <note>The Keraites, a powerful Turco-Mongol tribe of the 12th century who had converted to Nestorian Christianity.</note> Tribe, and was consequently a Christian, as his name of JOHN <note>This Prince was known in the West as Prester John (Prestre Jean), a legendary Christian priest-king of the East.</note> makes sufficiently clear. He always kept near him an Officer of merit and experience named (2) TAMUJIN, who had raised him and served him very well. But envious men having led the King to believe that he was a Traitor who wished to destroy him, this Prince resolved to seize him at night in his tent. *Tamujin*, warned of the conspiracy by two of the King’s servants, left his tent that evening, and accompanied by his friends and servants, went to set an ambush. He suddenly fell upon *Ung-Khan* and his troop, and defeated them entirely. Various battles occurred between them afterward, in which he always held the advantage. In the meantime, one of the Princes of the *Mongols*, or *Tartars*, played the Prophet: he went through the Mountains and Deserts barefoot during the winter; upon his return, he published that God had spoken to him and ordered him to tell the Nation that He had given the whole Country to *Tamujin* and his posterity, and that He Himself had named him JINGIZ-KHAN <note>Genghis Khan, the founder of the Mongol Empire.</note>. This Prophet was listened to and believed, and *Tamujin* thus became King of the Mongols. I realize well that I am straying from my subject, led away by a reflection that struck me: it is that two great Empires, that of the Arabs and that of the Mongols, were founded upon the impostures of two false Prophets. I return now to the one whose history I am writing.

Consequence of the proven facts.
</margin>
*Mani* thus retired into *Turkestan*; *Cascar* <note>Kashgar, an important oasis city in modern-day Xinjiang, China.</note> is in *Turkestan*; it is the capital of a small Kingdom. Their establishment in that Country is so ancient that one cannot mark its beginning.

That the Antagonists would speak Syriac there, and that the Dispute having turned to the advantage of the Orthodox, the Bishop would have written the Account of it in that Language? Let us prove this last point; it is the only one that might appear doubtful. Was Syriac spoken in *Turkestan*?

<margin>
The Syriac Language is the Sacred Language of the Easterners.
</margin>
I admit that Syriac was not the Language of the People; but it was the Language of the Bishops, of the Priests—the Sacred Language. Indeed, the Christian Religion was carried into the Eastern Regions of the Syrians by Chaldeans and Armenians who made use (3) of the Syriac Language, which was highly esteemed throughout the East. The Chinese Monument (4) <note>This refers to the Nestorian Stele, or the Xi’an Stele, discovered in 1625, which records the arrival of Christianity in China in the 7th century.</note>, which was discovered in 1625 in the Province of *Shaanxi*, contains Syriac Characters. And regarding the Chinese Inscription, *Mr. Assemani* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a renowned Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> has remarked that the Latin Translator wrongly stated in the title that the *Seventy Preachers* who had gone to announce the Gospel to the Chinese had been sent from Palestine, whereas he should have put *Assyria* or *Chaldea*. The Christians of India, who are called those of *St. Thomas*, have their Liturgy (*a*) in Syriac. The Nestorians conduct their service in this Language, whether in India, in Tartary, or in China. They read the Gospel and the Epistle in Syriac, but they then explain it to the People in the vulgar Tongue. Thus, all difficulties disappear. The Dispute of *Mani* becomes real as soon as one places it in *Turkestan*. The great Objection of the silence of *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History," whose lack of mention of this specific dispute was used by critics to doubt its authenticity.</note> in his Ecclesiastical History vanishes entirely. The Reader will perhaps ask me if I am speaking seriously; my answer is ready: and I am convinced he has already guessed it. My sole design was to compose, in my turn, an Ecclesiastical Romance, but with this difference, that it is better founded in History than that of *Hegemonius*, that probability is better observed within it, and that if it were fourteen or fifteen hundred years old, I would at least share the votes of the Critics. I flatter myself, moreover, that the Reader will not be displeased with me for having taken him on a little excursion into *Turkestan*, where *Manichaeaus* has led us. We have seen there objects more pleasant and more real than most of those I have been obliged to entertain him with.

Bb 3

This is the work that is called—and which he perhaps called himself—his **GOSPEL**. That is to say, his **DOCTRINE**, his *Preaching*. Thus, this Book did not contain a false History of Jesus Christ, as *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople known for his vast library and summaries of lost ancient books.</note> imagined it did.

<margin>No fragment of it remains.</margin>I do not know if any portion of this work remains to us. I have found none in the ancient Greek or Latin Authors I have read; and what has led me to believe that none exist is that the learned Moderns, who speak to us of the Books of Manichaeus and who do not neglect to report the fragments they have been able to discover, provide us with none. I believe, nonetheless, that some might be found in the Orient, either in the Christian Authors who refuted *Manes*, or in the Persian and Arabic Authors. Furthermore, I confess once again that (3) I regret the loss of a Book which was the Masterpiece of a fine Genius, and of one of the most learned men of his time in Oriental Philosophy. I do not doubt that, among facts worthy of our Curiosity, many Visions and poor reasonings would be found. But if all the Books containing such things were burned, good God! what conflagrations, and what a loss fundamentally for the Republic of Letters! <note>The "Republic of Letters" (République des Lettres) was the long-distance intellectual community of scholars and philosophers in the 17th and 18th centuries.</note> For example, what a shame it would be if one took it into their head to bury in the dust or the flames (4) the History of a Modern Saint, which a Prelate, who possesses much wit and eloquence, published recently! It is true that there are Frenchmen who regard this Work as one of the greatest insults that could be offered to the Judgment and Discernment of their Nation and their Age. However, they must agree that this Book has its beauties, and that unless one lacks all taste, one cannot see without pleasure an infinity of trifles, encased with much art in the gold of the most beautiful words and the most well-chosen expressions.

# HISTORY OF MANICHAEUS ACCORDING TO #

<margin>How the Persians distinguish this Gospel from that of Jesus Christ.
(a) Hyde, as cited above, p. 282.</margin>
Persian authors inform us, *(a)* that when they speak of the Gospel of Our Lord, they add certain words to distinguish it, such as **Christ**, **Christian**, **Cross**, **Syrian**, or **Girdle**; but when they join the words **Painting** or **Painter**, **Roses**, **Tulips**, or **Variety of Colors** to the word **Gospel**, one must understand it as the **Gospel** of Manichaeus, or the **book adorned** with *paintings* in which he had written his *revelations* and his *dogmas*.

<margin>Use of the Girdle among the Persians and the Christians of the East.</margin>
It is easy to understand why the Persians distinguish the Gospel of Our Lord by the words *Cross*, *Christian*, or *Syrian*. *Jesus is the Christ*; He was *crucified*; He was born in *Syria* (of which Palestine was considered a part). However, it is not as immediately clear why they distinguish this Gospel by the word **Girdle**. This point, which deserves to be clarified, will not detain us long and will not displease the Reader.

<margin>The Persians gave confirmation by the Girdle.</margin>
*The Persians gave the Girdle to young people* when they had reached the age of reason. It was, so to speak, the Sacrament of their Confirmation. They then renewed and ratified the commitments into which their birth had placed them: to faithfully observe the Laws of their Creator. We read in the Book *Sad-Der* <note>The *Sad Dar* is a Zoroastrian text, likely the version translated by Thomas Hyde.</note>, which contains a summary of the moral precepts of Zoroaster *(a)*, that *God commanded the taking of the Girdle* because *it is the sign of obedience due to the Creator*. The Persians attribute to this *Girdle* the same virtue that Roman Catholics attribute to their *Sign of the Cross* and their *Holy Water*. It drives away Demons and delivers a man from their power. All superstitious religions are marked by the same die; everywhere one finds the marvelous embedded in ceremonies.

<margin>(a) In Hyde, as cited above, p. 441. See also Ch. XXX, p. 370, 371.</margin>

<margin>Eastern Christians wear the Girdle as a religious duty.</margin>
I do not know if the Christians of the Levant wished to conform in part to the custom of the dominant Religion, or if they effectively believed it was a precept of Our Lord, but it is certain that they believed themselves obliged to wear the *Girdle*. "All Christians of the Levant (1)," says a modern scholar <note>Referring to Giuseppe Simone Assemani, a famous Maronite scholar and librarian of the Vatican.</note>, "the Syrians,

But *Kasan* <note>Ghazan Khan (reigned 1295–1304), a ruler of the Mongol Ilkhanate.</note>, who began to reign in 1295, having as his General a certain *Neuruzus* <note>Nowruz, a powerful Mongol emir.</note> who was a Muslim and a great enemy of the Christians, the latter (2) forbade them, under heavy penalties, from appearing in public without the Girdle. The Persecutor soon suffered the penalty of his unjust hatred. *Kasan*, who had made good use of him (b), got rid of him two years later when he no longer had need of him. This was because he feared that a Muslim of the Arab race might one day do to take the crown from him what he had done to acquire or preserve it for him.

### THE SYRIANS, THE PERSIANS, & BOOK II. CH. IV. ###
<meta>Cc</meta>

Diamonds, worth *one hundred thousand Dinars*; the King refusing to take them, the Minister informed him, *that there was a hundred percent to be gained*. Neither a hundred, nor a thousand in profit, means anything to me, he replied. *For if I meddle in the business of trade, who is it that will perform the trade of King? And what will become of the Merchants?* Avarice, pernicious everywhere, is especially so in Princes. It is excused in those who, being only Elective, act more as usufructuaries <note>A person who has the right to enjoy the profits or benefits of property belonging to another.</note> than as the Owners of a State. But it is inexcusable in Hereditary Monarchs.

<margin>He has a Castle built for the safety of the Heresiarch <note>The founder of a heresy or leader of a heretical sect, here referring to Mani.</note>.</margin>
The Protection of the King was nevertheless not sufficient to put Mani entirely in safety. As the object of hatred from all Religions, the Christians & the Magi <note>Zoroastrian priests of the Persian Empire.</note> pursued him as a Heretic and an Apostate; the Jews & the Pagans, as the sworn Enemy of their Sects. This is what obliged the King (5) *to have a fortified place built for him specifically, between Baghdad and Susiana, to serve as a retreat against those who pursued him because of his Doctrine. The Castle was called* DESKAREH, *a name which has remained since that time for all Castles in general.* This Place was apparently situated on some rock in a solitary location, for the Author remarks that *Dascarah* is also often used by Arabian Historians for a *Hermitage*.

<margin>It is likely the Castle that Archelaus calls *Arabion*.</margin>
This detail has confirmed me in the thought I hold that the History of Mani by *Archelaus* <note>Archelaus, a 3rd-century bishop, famously debated Mani in a likely fictionalized account.</note> is nothing but a mixture of false and true, in which the false dominates and the true is altered. This Author recounts that *Manes*, condemned by *Sapor* <note>Shapur I, the father of Hormizd I.</note>, retired to a Castle named *Arabion*. This is likely the Castle that Hormizdas had built for him to keep him safe. But the Author, who did not know the location of this Place, or who could not accommodate it for the construction of his Romance, transported it into Mesopotamia, on the frontiers of the Romans; whereas it was in the heart of the Persian Monarchy, between *Baghdad* which is in the Province of Babylon, and *Susiana*, (6) which is to the East of that Province. If the geography of the places allowed it, I would suspect that *Arabion* was put for (7) *Hebraeum* <note>original: "Hæbræum"</note>, which is the name of a Castle built on the Tigris, in the Province of Nineveh, at the foot of which there was later a Monastery.

<margin>Hormizdas reigns at most only two years.</margin>
Unfortunately for the Heresiarch, the Reign of *Hormizdas* was very short.

It was fatal for Mani; and whether he defended himself poorly, or the influence of his Adversaries outweighed his own, he was condemned as a Heretic.

accompanied by a certain number of his Disciples. The Judges of the Debate <note>The author uses the term "Dispute," referring to a formal, public theological contest common in late antiquity.</note> were Pagans, for they were undoubtedly the King, his Ministers, and his Councilors. The Heresiarch <note>A term for the founder of a heretical sect; here referring to Mani.</note> is condemned and perishes. The Debate may have even taken place at *Kashkar* <note>An ancient city in Mesopotamia, then part of the Sassanid Empire.</note>, if one wishes: there is no longer any inconsistency, since this City was subject to the Kings of Persia and was close enough to their residence. After this, everything is explained. The silence of Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the 4th-century "Father of Church History."</note> is no longer surprising. He was not informed of a Debate between *Mani* and the Magi <note>The Zoroastrian priestly caste of the Persian Empire.</note>, which took place deep within Persia and does not belong to the History of the Church. For the same reason, the Eastern Christians do not speak of it. Better informed than the Greeks regarding what happened in their own lands, they do not grant an Orthodox Bishop the honor of a Victory in which he had no part.

If it were now necessary to show by examples how very ancient Authors have abused certain Events and turned them to the honor of the Church and the confusion of Heretics—even though neither the Church nor the Heretics were ever involved—it would be easy to produce such examples. An educated and critical Reader has no need of them. He grasps the truth as soon as it presents itself, without such help. However, I am willing to report a single one, to dispel the scruples of those minds too biased in favor of the good faith of Antiquity.

<margin>Example of a completely similar fraud. An Event is attributed to Simon and St. Peter in which they had no part.</margin>
Everyone may have heard of the tragic end of SIMON the Magician <note>Also known as Simon Magus, mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles.</note>, that supposed Rival of St. Peter, who, to deceive the faith of the Romans and triumph over the Apostle who pursued him everywhere, invited the People of Rome to the Theater to witness a Wonder he was to perform. This wonder was *(4) to fly through the air*. He indeed did so: but at the prayer of St. Peter, the Magician fell, *(5) and broke his hip and the extremities of his feet, or the soles of his feet*. Few people today put faith in such an absurd fable, which is reported very differently by the Ancients. However, not everything is invented. These bold and fabulous Authors have merely attributed to the rashness and imposture of *Simon*, and to the prayer of *St. Peter*, an Event that Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus, a Roman historian.</note> reports in the *Life of Nero*. Among the spectacles that this Prince gave to the Romans, there was that of an *(6) Icarus*, who attempted to fly, but who succeeded badly,

IV. The heresy that caused *Mani* to perish is not that of the Two Principles <note>The core Manichaean belief in a cosmic struggle between the forces of Light/Good and Darkness/Evil.</note>. The Persians and the Arabs testify that it was SADDUCEEISM. Mr. Hyde <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703), an English orientalist and author of "De Religione Veterum Persarum."</note> assures us that the word (a) <term>Zendik</term> <note>A term used in Sassanid and Islamic periods to label heretics; it likely derived from those who provided unauthorized interpretations (Zend) of the Avesta.</note>, by which he is characterized, means SADDUCEE, and (b) Hottinger confirms it. In truth, this term has a more general meaning and is used for (1) *the Impious*. But it may well properly designate a *Sadducee* and have acquired through usage the general meaning of an *Impious* person, a man without religion.

<margin>
For having denied, not the existence of Spirits, but the Resurrection.
</margin>
The *Sadduceeism* of *Mani* certainly did not consist in denying the existence of spirits, their immortality, or the punishments and rewards that follow death. He was so far from this that *Sharistani* <note>Al-Shahrastani (1086–1153), a Persian scholar and historian of religions.</note> includes among his dogmas *that, not only thought, but* (2) *the sensory faculties of sight and hearing are never lost*. It must therefore be for having denied the Resurrection of the Body. Indeed, the Magi believed in the Resurrection, as testified by (3) Diogenes Laertius. It was one of the Articles of the religion of (c) *Zoroaster*.

He suspects that the authors who attributed this sentiment to them mistook what the Magi say about the *Vehicle of the Soul*, and the *Shadow*, the *Simulacrum*, which accompanies this *Vehicle*—or, as an ingenious (e) author of our time calls it, *the subtle chariot of the soul* <note>Referring to the "astral body" or an intermediate substance between the physical and the spiritual.</note>—for a human body. ### THE SYRIANS, THE PERSIANS, &c. BOOK II. CH. IV.
Cc 3
<meta>catchword: natu-</meta>

<margin>They held the same idea as the Jews.</margin>
If I am asked what idea the Persians had of the Resurrection, I will answer that they apparently held the same idea as the Jews. Bodies exactly like those of the present, with the same organs and the same animal functions (I do not know if they excepted any)—to drink, to eat, to have wives, and to lead a peaceful and delightful life on an Earth purified by Fire; such was the hope of the Persians, as it was that (5) of the Jews, who never spoke so clearly of the Resurrection until after they had been captives among the Assyrians. Furthermore, it is only since that time that one sees among them the opposing Sects of the *Pharisees* and the *Sadducees*. <note>The author suggests that Jewish theology on the afterlife was heavily influenced by Persian Zoroastrianism during the Babylonian Exile.</note>

<margin>The execution of Mani.</margin>
V. *Mani*, having been condemned as a Sadducee <note>In this context, "Sadducee" or "Zendik" refers to a heretic or one who denies the orthodox interpretation of the afterlife and resurrection.</note> and as an impious man, King *Bahram* ordered that he be put to death. However, historians do not seem to agree on the nature of his punishment. *Khwandamir* (6) testifies, according to Mr. *Hyde*, that he was crucified at the City gate. <margin>According to some, he was crucified.</margin> If this is so, it is likely that he was condemned to the same punishment as Our Savior because he accepted the Prophecy of Jesus Christ and claimed to be an Apostle, an Envoy sent by Him to reform both Christianity and Magism <note>The religion of the Magi, or Zoroastrianism.</note> simultaneously. The Abbé *Renaudot* cites *Khwandamir* and has him say (7), "that <margin>According to others, he was flayed.</margin> Mani was flayed alive, and that his skin was filled with hay and hung from a gibbet to serve as an example to others." He also cites the author of an Abridgment of Persian History, titled *Majmal al-Tawarikh*. *Bar Hebraeus* also speaks of the flaying of the Heresiarch, but the manner in which he expresses himself (8), in the translation by *Pococke*, suggests that it was done only after his death.

I do not know if there is any evidence that flaying was a customary punishment among the Persians. I see only that, being unable to preserve bodies because of corruption, and yet wishing to keep the likeness of the Persons, they would have the skin removed, prepared, and filled with air or straw; this is how *Shapur* treated *Valerian*. <note>Valerian was a Roman Emperor captured by the Persian King Shapur I in 260 AD.</note> He kept him for nine years and treated him with enough humanity, for I do not believe one should trust what the Greeks say: that every time he mounted his horse, he used the back of this unfortunate Prince as a stirrup. Whatever the case may be, *Valerian* having died a natu-

"... but in characters unknown to all the world, which shows a very great antiquity. A number of bas-reliefs represent Divinities, Sacrifices, Funeral Processions, and processions of people in wide jackets, with long hair and mitre-like caps." It was only later, and I know not under which King, that the Seat of the Empire was transferred to *Seleucia*; but it was apparently not during the first eight or nine reigns.

<margin>Sapor built this city in imitation of Constantinople.</margin>
*Sapor*, who was the second of the Kings of the last race <note>The Sassanid dynasty.</note>, wrought furious havoc in Mesopotamia and Syria in the year two hundred and fifty-seven. He continued this in the following years and took *Valerian* prisoner in two hundred and fifty-nine. There was no city in the East richer or more superb than *Antioche*, which had been the residence of the Kings of Syria, and subsequently that of the Roman Governors and the Prefects of the East. *Sapor* took this City and carried away its rich spoils into the Province (4) of *Elam*, which is often confused with *Persia*, but is different from it. *Elymais* is its capital, and is only six <term>parasangs</term> <note>A Persian measure of distance; six parasangs is roughly 21 to 24 miles.</note> away from *Susa*, which makes twenty-four thousand paces. It was there that he wished to erect lasting trophies of his victories, to employ the treasures he had amassed in his campaigns, and to place the rich ornaments he had taken from *Antioch* (5). He built a city there (6) on the model of that of Constantinople, and kept *Valerian* his prisoner there. It was named *Ghond-Schabur*, or, as our writers call it, *Gandi-Sapor* or *Gendi-Sapor*. One finds it in ancient Syrian authors under the names of *Lapeth*, *Beth-Lapeth*, and *Elymais*. It is said that *Papas*, who then held the See of *Seleucia*, established it as a Metropolis, and gave its Bishop the first rank among all the Metropolitans of the East. Mr. *Assemani*, who testifies to this following his historians, nonetheless assures us that the institution of Metropolitans is not so ancient in *Persia* (7). According to him, they only began after the Bishop of *Seleucia* had established himself as Patriarch, and consequently wished to have Metropolitans under him. Previously, he was the only one to whom this title applied, all the others being...

It is thus that *Gandi-Sapor* was the Metropolis of the Persian Empire and that of the Manichaean Heresy—at least if the Sect had consecrated the City where its Leader was martyred. But, to tell the truth, whatever errors it had, it at least protected itself from the unreasonable opinion that the ashes of the dead grant holiness, majesty, or authority to the Cities where they rest. I do not know of the Manichaeans ever having had a *Pilgrimage*.

> "It is said," (1) (it is the famous *Bar Hebraeus* <note>Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286) was a prominent bishop and scholar of the Syriac Orthodox Church known for his extensive historical and theological writings.</note> speaking,) "that un-
> "til the time of the CATHOLICOS *Timothy*, the Bishops of the

> "Seleucia." This *Timothy* <note>Timothy I (778–823), one of the most influential patriarchs of the Church of the East.</note> held the See from the year 778 until the year 820. It was he who, having found the means to give the Persians a Metropolitan of his choice named *Simeon* (2), forbade him from eating meat and FROM MARRYING, and *ordered him to wear only garments of white wool*. There is no reason to suppose that the liberty to marry was unique to the Bishops of Persia in the third Century, since all the Bishops of the East still possessed it, not only at the time of the Council of Nicaea, but even at the time of the Council of Constantinople, as is seen by (3) the *Poems* of Gregory of Nazianzus, which were published by *Tollius*.

<margin>Papas does an injustice to the Manichaeans.</margin>
4. *Papas* did not do justice to the Manichaeans when he accused them of believing in TWO GODS. There is a great deal of difference between *two Gods* and *two Principles*. The Magi <note>Followers of Zoroastrianism, the state religion of the Persian Empire.</note> admitted the latter, as did the Manichaeans, but not the former. Regarding the *Earth*, *Abulpharage* <note>Another name for Bar Hebraeus (Gregory Abu'l-Faraj).</note> testifies that they spoke of it with too great a contempt, and that this was one of the things that the famous *Avicenna* <note>Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), the influential Persian philosopher and physician.</note> had most condemned in their system. As for *Metempsychosis* <note>The transmigration of souls or reincarnation.</note>, it was a common opinion throughout the East, and almost throughout the entire world, such that I cannot believe the King of Persia could regard it as either an Error or a dangerous Error. Finally, one can assert that although the Manichaeans did not praise Marriage, they nevertheless only forbade it to their Clergy <note>In Manichaeism, only the 'Elect' (the clergy) were required to be celibate; the 'Hearers' (laypeople) were permitted to marry.</note>, as *Faustus* maintains against St. *Augustine*, and as we shall have occasion to show in the second Part; so that if *Amrus* and *Mares* have told the truth, the Catholics and the Manichaeans did not differ at all on this article regarding practice.

[...Ma]nichaeans of the abominations that have been attributed to them. It must even be that they were not accused of such things at that time; since neither the Prelate <note>Referring to Bishop Papas bar Aggai.</note>, nor those who put words in his mouth, say anything about it, and furthermore, the Edict which condemned them to death was based only on their aversion to Marriage.

<margin>Authors who wrote against Manichaeism.</margin>
It is surprising that throughout the entire course of this History we have not seen any Bishop of the Eastern Churches combat the Manichaean Heresy. It is said, nonetheless, that there were several who did so. "A great number of Doctors (4)," says *Amrus* <note>Amrus, or Amr ibn Matta, was a 14th-century scholar from the Church of the East who compiled histories of the patriarchs.</note>, "wrote at the time of *Papas* against the *Simonians*, against the *Marcionites*, and against the *Manichaeans*." But their works, written in Persian or Syriac, have not come to the knowledge of the Greeks. I do not know what has been preserved of them in the East.

THAT IS what I have been able to discover thus far regarding the History of *Mani* and the Origin of *Manichaeism*. I shall now give the reader an account of his Principles, his Doctrines, his Morality, his Worship, and his Ecclesiastical Government, as far as the few remaining Monuments <note>In this context, 'monuments' refers to surviving historical records and primary source documents.</note> will allow.

#### *The difficulty of providing a just & complete idea of the Manichaean System. A critique of the ancient Authors who spoke of it.*

<margin>Difficulty of providing a just idea of the Doctrine of Mani.</margin>
It is very difficult, if not impossible, to provide today a just and complete idea of the Philosophical and Theological System of Mani <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the Persian prophet who founded Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that once rivaled Christianity.</note>.

<margin>I. All the Books of the Sect have been suppressed or burned.</margin>
I. To know with certainty the Opinions of Heretics <note>The term "heretic" was used by the established Church to describe those whose beliefs deviated from official dogma.</note>, one would need to see them in their own Confessions of Faith, and in the Books where

where they set them forth themselves, dispassionately and with precision. Now, we currently possess no Books by *Mani*, nor by his early disciples; barely a few fragments have been preserved in the works of authors who refuted them and who, following the method of polemicists <note>The term "polemicists" refers to writers who engage in aggressive arguments to undermine opposing religious or philosophical views.</note>, usually seized upon what seemed the least reasonable and most susceptible to a negative interpretation. Furthermore, one cannot judge an author's thought well by pieces detached from what precedes and what follows. What idea would one have of Protestant Doctrine on *Liberty*, on *Justification*, or on *good Works*, if one judged them by the detached propositions that were presented to the Council of Trent? <note>The Council of Trent (1545–1563) was the Roman Catholic Church's formal response to the Protestant Reformation.</note> Regarding the Books themselves, Antiquity made it a religious duty to burn them. I do not know if it was *(a) Leo I* <note>Pope Leo I, also known as Leo the Great (reigned 440–461 AD).</note> who set the example, but he was well imitated by his successors. *Gelasius* *(b)* had burned in front of the Church of Saint *Mary* all the Manichaean Books he could discover. *Symmachus* did the same shortly after: *(1) He had burned, says Anastasius, all their images, and all their Books before the door of the Constantinian Basilica.* I do not know what these *images* <note>original: "Simulacres". While this often refers to statues, the author questions this because Manichaeans were generally aniconic (avoiding religious images).</note> could have been, for certainly the Manichaeans had none. *St. Epiphanius*, who recognizes *(c)* that the *Magi* <note>Followers of Zoroastrianism, a Persian religion that influenced Mani.</note> detested *images*, adds that they *worshipped the Idols of Fire, the Moon, and the Sun.* If these are those of the Manichaeans, it was not possible to burn them. Whatever the case, *(d) Hormisdas* followed the example of his predecessors, and one sees in *(2) St. Augustine* that as soon as books by our Heretics were found, the Magistrates seized them, doubtless to throw them into the fire.

<margin>
Reflection on the Practice of burning Books.
</margin>

It is not easy to correctly characterize the zeal of these ancient Bishops, who were the first to move the Christian Emperors to condemn the Books of Heretics to the fire, and *(3)* to decree the death penalty against those who would read them, or keep them in their houses. I am willing to believe the motive was good, but it must be admitted that the example was very dangerous, and that the Christians themselves would have condemned it as the most unjust violence.

<margin>
The early Christians strongly blamed it.
</margin>

(4) "It is the **Demons**," he says, "who suggested such a Law, to hold **the Human Race** in their chains, and to prevent it from **knowing the Truth**." <note>original: "Ἐνεργείαν τῶν Φαυλῶν Δαιμόνων." — Justin Martyr, *Apology II*, p. 64.</note> Nevertheless, one cannot deny that the Romans had their reasons. These Books, as favorable as they were to the Christian Religion, deserved to be suppressed, because at heart they had been forged by Impostors, and because the one bearing the name of *Hystaspes* (5) predicted the ruin of the Empire. In what State does one allow free course to Books which announce to the People that the Fates have resolved upon their destruction, and that one can no longer defend them without resisting the Decrees of the Divinity? When, later, the Pagan Emperors ordered the sacred Books of the Christians to be seized everywhere and burned, the latter cried out against such unjust and barbaric Orders. They could not, however, complain of them except by assuming that one must refute Books containing Lies and Errors rather than throwing them into the fire; for any other Principle would have been worthless before Infidel Princes.

I do not wish, however, to either blame or praise a custom authorized by so many Laws. There are indeed Books that are worthy of the fire; such as those which corrupt morals, or which sap the foundations of Religion and at the same time those of Society. For the others, it seems to me that one could have been satisfied with keeping them hidden from the People, without suppressing them entirely, just as one takes care to hide poisons from those who are not prudent enough to use them usefully. Regarding the Books of the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Mani, who taught a dualistic religion seeing the world as a struggle between light and dark.</note>, if they were such as they are represented to us, I dare say that it was a great mistake to burn them. What could one do more advantageous to the Faith than to expose to the contempt of the entire Earth writings full of Fables, whether ridiculous or obscene? As soon as one had read therein, (6) "that picking a fruit, clearing a field, harvesting, grinding wheat, baking bread, are so many crimes and homicides, and that those who commit them will in their turn be torn by the plowshare, harvested, ground, and thrown into a burning oven," what contempt would one not have had for such Books, for their Authors, and for the Sect which established such extravagances as Articles of Faith?

# PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE

<margin>II. Fragments that remain to us of Mani.
1. Of the Epistle of the Foundation.</margin>
II. In Africa, there was a Latin version of a letter by *Mani* <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the Persian prophet who founded Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion.</note>, which is titled the <term>EPISTLE OF THE FOUNDATION</term> <note>original: "Epitre du Fondement"</note>. This title announces an explanation of the principal articles of Manichaeism—a summary of this impertinent system. The original was in either Greek or Syriac. *St. Augustine* undertook its refutation and used an excellent method. This was to quote the entire text of his adversary before responding to it; however, I do not know why this learned Bishop stopped at the point where *Mani* begins to explain his system of the two Principles <note>The "Two Principles" refers to the core Manichaean belief in a cosmic struggle between the co-eternal realms of Light (Good) and Darkness (Evil).</note> and the origin of all things. <margin>(a) Retractations, Book II, Ch. 2.</margin> (a) He informs us, in truth, that he had made remarks to serve as notes for when he would have the leisure to refute the entire Letter; but this leisure never came, although he lived for more than (1) thirty years afterward. I suspect that reasons of prudence stayed the pen of *St. Augustine*, and that he had already put on paper everything he had to say of any strength against Manichaeism. Whatever the case may be, I cannot help but regret the loss of a piece of such importance, even if it were only a translation, and even a rather barbaric one, as all those of that time were. We would at least have the satisfaction of knowing the sentiments of *Mani* from *Mani* himself, if it is true, as *M. de Tillemont* <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a renowned French ecclesiastical historian.</note> believed with much <margin>(b) Tillemont, St. Augustine, Vol. XIII, Art. 112.</margin>reason, (b) that this Letter contained all the *Articles of his Belief*.

<margin>2. Of a Letter to Menoch.</margin>
The disputes of *St. Augustine* against the Pelagians <note>Followers of Pelagius, who emphasized human free will over the Augustinian doctrine of original sin and divine grace.</note> were the reason that some fragments of another letter by *Mani* have been preserved, addressed to *Menoch*, one of his spiritual daughters. *Julian* <note>Julian of Eclanum, a leader of the Pelagians and a fierce intellectual rival of Augustine.</note>, claiming to prove that *St. Augustine* had not entirely abjured Manichaeism, discovered this letter in Constantinople and inserted several excerpts into one of his books against the Father of the Church. *St. Augustine* transcribed them, along with *Julian's* reflections, in his response titled <term>UNFINISHED WORK</term> <note>original: "OPUS IMPERFECTUM"; Augustine's final, incomplete rebuttal to Julian of Eclanum.</note>, so called because he did not complete it. One sees there, in general terms, the sentiments of the Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> regarding the corruption of Nature and the reciprocal love it inspires in the two sexes—a love that *Mani* believed was evil in itself and derived its origin from what he called *Matter* <note>In the Manichaean worldview, physical matter was seen as inherently evil and a prison for the divine sparks of light.</note>.

<margin>3. Letter to Marcellus.
(c) Matthew 7:17.</margin>
In the first part of this work, I provided the translation of a letter he wrote to *Marcellus*, which generally contains two articles of his belief: one, that there are two Principles, which Jesus Christ designated by (c) the good and the bad tree; the other, that the Son of God took on only the appearances of human nature <note>This is the doctrine of Docetism, the belief that Christ's body was not physical but purely spiritual or an illusion.</note>.

likelihood that *St. Augustine* believed it was more appropriate to suppress this piece than to make it known to the entire Church.

# ON THE SECOND PART.
Ee 3

<margin>Fragments of other Letters.</margin>
The late Mr. Grabe <note>John Ernest Grabe (1666–1711) was a Prussian-born Anglican theologian and scholar of early Christian texts.</note> gathered from all sides the fragments he could discover, whether from the Church Fathers or from heretics, to compose the work he named his *Spicilegium* <note>original: "Spicilége," Latin for "gleanings." A collection of early Christian fragments not found in the works of the major Fathers.</note>. It is a pity that his death, which occurred in 1711, prevented him from continuing such a useful labor. Not only did he benefit from the manuscripts in England, but the correspondences he maintained abroad provided him with curious pieces. Father Lequien <note>Michel Le Quien (1661–1733), a French Dominican historian.</note> had sent him some fragments from several Letters of **Mani**. These have fortunately fallen into the hands of the learned and industrious Mr. **Fabricius**, who has inserted them into the fifth volume of his *Greek Library* <note>original: "Bibliothéque Grecque" (*Bibliotheca Graeca*), a massive bibliography of Greek literature.</note>. Although all these fragments revolve around the unity of Nature in Jesus Christ, I have nonetheless found Principles within them that have served me in understanding the true sentiments of our <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>The founder of a heresy; here referring to Mani.</note> regarding the Nature and Attributes of the Divinity. This is all that I have been able to discover until now of the works of **Mani**. I shall not speak of a word that **Photius** attributes to him, which I shall examine in the *History of the Paulicians*.

<margin>III. The Account of Mani's Dogmas in the *Acts of Archelaus* is full of confusion and inaccuracy.</margin>
III. We have in the *Acts of Archelaus* <note>A 4th-century anti-Manichaean work attributed to Hegemonius, presented as a debate between Bishop Archelaus and Mani.</note> an account of his dogmas, the author of which is a man named **Turbo**. I have said in the first part what I think of this piece. I will only add that this **Turbo**, who was only in the rank of the <term>Hearers</term> <note>The "Hearers" (Auditores) were the lower lay rank of Manichaeans, who were not permitted to know the "mysteries" reserved for the "Elect."</note>, admitted himself that he did not know the Mysteries of the Sect. Indeed, there is so much confusion in his account that one can clearly see it is an ignorant man speaking. Let us apply to him what **Origen** said regarding **Celsus**, who boasted of knowing the Christian Religion very well: (a) "In Egypt," says **Origen**, "the
<margin>(a) Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book I, p. 11.</margin>
"philosophers have a sublime and hidden science regarding the Nature of
"God, which they show to the People only under the cloak of fa-
"bles and allegories. **Celsus** (here we must say **Turbo**) resembles
"a man who, having traveled in that country and having
"never conversed with anyone but the coarse Rabble, would believe he understood the
"Religion of the Egyptians. All the Eastern Nations—the
"Persians, the Indians, the Syrians—hide secret Mysteries
"beneath religious Fables: The wise man of all Nations
"penetrates their meaning, while the Rabble sees only the external Sym-
"bol and the bark." **Turbo**, whoever he may be, was but a man of the common Rabble who did not understand the Mysteries of Manichaean Theology, and who also reported them very poorly. Furthermore, he is (2) a Liar, who deceives his master from the very beginning of his Account.

<margin>IV. St. Epiphanius appears to have seen the Book of Mysteries, without</margin>
IV. St. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his *Panarion*, a refutation of eighty different heresies.</note> appears to have seen a Book by **Mani** entitled OF THE MYSTERIES: but all he tells us of it is that he is refuting it.

(a) As cited above <note>original: "Ub. sup." (*Ubi supra*)</note>, No. 13. & 14.

...that this Book was divided into 22 Sections, according to the number of Letters in the Syriac Alphabet, and that it began with these words: *(a) GOD and MATTER, Light and Darkness, Good and Evil existed. They were so opposed that they had no communication with one another.* Behold, continues **St. Epiphanius** <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403), a bishop known for his fierce opposition to heresies.</note>, *what is the beginning of this Impostor’s work, after which he explains his pernicious Dogma: This Book is long-winded, and contains only things as evil and as ridiculous as that: Furthermore, it is difficult, obscure, and filled with contradictions.* Regarding the contradictions, I am unaware of them, and I have not noticed that **Titus of Bostra** <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian who wrote a significant refutation of Manichaeism.</note> found any there. Being *long-winded* is a fault from which **St. Epiphanius** himself is not exempt; and as for the *obscurity*, it may stem from several causes. **Plato’s** *Timaeus* is considered obscure, even though **Plato** possessed all the graces of Discourse: but this is attributed to the Subject Matter he treats. The obscurity of the Book of **Mani** <note>The founder of Manichaeism (216–274 AD).</note> could have come from that, without counting that the Syriac Phrasing and the figures of that Language were quite barbaric to the Greeks. I confess that I am very distrustful of the Critique of **St. Epiphanius**, who, not understanding (1) Syriac, never read the *Treasure of Mani*. What persuades me of this is that he seems to have mistaken the Language for Persian written in Syriac characters, although it was truly Syriac, and apparently the *Dialect of the Palmyrenes*, which this Father calls (2) *very deep*, that is to say, *the most difficult*; it was also the most elegant and the most esteemed in the Orient.

<margin>
V. Titus of Bostra, a good Author, refuted the Book of MYSTERIES.
</margin>
V. What was an obstacle for **St. Epiphanius** was not one for **Titus of Bostra** in Phoenicia. This Bishop had indeed read the Book of *Mysteries*, since he reports its Errors quite distinctly and refutes them with solidity. He is learned, judicious, and does not evaporate into insults against his Adversary. He accuses him neither of Magic, nor of invoking *Demons*, nor of using abominable Ceremonies in these Mysteries. He represents him as a Philosopher who, persuaded that the World does not correspond to the idea we have of Divine Perfections, became convinced that there is another Principle besides God. I have made useful use of this Author, who is incomparably more exact and more moderate than **St. Epiphanius**. However, he seems not to have known the sentiment of **Mani**...

One had to be well-versed in Oriental Theology to understand them.

VI. One rightly regrets the Work that *Diodore of Tarsus* <margin>VI. *Diodore of Tarsus* wrote 25 Books against the Manichaeans. The Greeks let them perish.</margin> composed to refute a Book by *Addus*, a Disciple of *Mani*, titled **Modium**. *Diodore* was very learned and very judicious, a good Interpreter of Scripture, and lived close to the times and places where Manichaeism was most flourishing. We would likely find in his book a distinct idea of this Heresy, but the Greeks have let it perish: It is said, however, that the <term>Nestorians<note>A branch of Eastern Christianity that followed the teachings of Nestorius; they were known for preserving many Syriac texts.</note></term> possess a Translation of it in Syriac.

We have similarly lost, and no doubt through the envy of the Greeks, <margin>They did the same with the Works of *George of Laodicea*.</margin> two Works against the Manichaeans, which must have been excellent, if one judges by the ability of the Authors. The first is by *George*, Bishop of *Laodicea*, whom *St. Athanasius* decries as the most wicked of all men, because he was one of the primary supporters of <term>Arianism<note>The theological belief that Jesus was a created being, subordinate to God the Father; George’s adherence to this view made his other works targets for destruction by the orthodox Greek church.</note></term>, but to whom *Theodoret* bears witness of having been one of the greatest Philosophers of his time. It is from a philosopher, rather than a theologian, that I would wish to have the refutation of Manichaeism, because this System drew its origin primarily from Oriental Philosophy, which *Pythagoras* brought to the Greeks, and to which *Plato* later gave more grace and a new form.

The second Book of which I wish to speak is by *Eusebius of Emesa*, to <margin>And those of *Eusebius of Emesa*.</margin> whom *Theodoret* gave the nickname *Phoenix*, although he had favored Arianism as well as *George of Laodicea*. This Bishop, being born in *Edessa*, in *Mesopotamia*, understood Syriac, which was the common language of that Province, and could read the Books of *Mani* in the original. He lived, moreover, in a time when the memory of his life and actions was still quite recent...

### PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE

<margin>VII. Judgment of the work of Faustus; character of this author.</margin>
VII. What we have that is most authentic and complete regarding the system of <term>Manes<note>The Latinized name of Mani, the founder of the Manichaean religion.</note></term> is the work of an African Bishop of his sect, named FAUSTUS, whose text *St. Augustine* recorded before refuting it. The heretic shines there with much wit and the elegance of his style—which is quite beautiful for his time and for the land where he was raised—and by the ingenious turn he gives to his difficulties and his proofs. He is lively, clear, and concise, and possesses little or nothing of the <term>African roughness<note>A contemporary stylistic critique suggesting that North African writers of the period often had a harsh or unrefined Latin prose.</note></term>. He attacks with considerable force and defends himself with prudence and skill. One could not better gloss over the flaws of the Manichaean dogmas. When I read the *Exposition of Catholic Doctrine* by the Bishop of Meaux <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a famous French Catholic orator; the author suggests that the heretic Faustus shares Bossuet’s persuasive elegance.</note>, it seems to me that *Faustus* was his model. Furthermore, he does not insult his opponent, which is so fitting and yet so rare for a controversialist. *St. Augustine* is, without comparison, more learned; *Faustus* was not very much so. Moreover, this Father [Augustine] triumphs over him because he defends a better cause, but he certainly does not triumph in terms of the graces of discourse. He is diffuse and often quite obscure; he constantly returns to the same objections and vents too much in invectives. This critique will not please the admirers of *St. Augustine*, but it is just.

<margin>He treated only a small number of questions.</margin>
It is, therefore, in this work of *Faustus* that one should find Manichaeism in its purest form. But, besides the fact that the African sect was one of the crudest and most heretical, *Faustus* treated only a small number of questions. He turns all his strength against the authority of the <term>Old Testament<note>original: "V. Testament" (Vieux Testament)</note></term>. He believes the New [Testament] has been altered; he strives to show that the Catholics could not combat his sect's opinions on marriage, or on the use of and abstinence from meats, without contradicting their own principles and their own practice.
