...doctrine that Jesus Christ preached, and in doing what he commands. Furthermore, he does not explain the system of *Manes* <note>The author uses the name of the founder, Mani, interchangeably with the Latinized Manes or Manichaeus.</note> regarding the two Principles, the mixture of *Light* with *Darkness*, the Creation of the World, etc. And what deserves to be well observed is that his work being an Apology for Manichaeism, in which he responds to the objections made against his sect, he justifies it neither for the childish fables nor for the profane ceremonies with which almost all our authors accuse it. This silence seems to me a strong presumption that these were only popular rumors, despised by serious persons. Otherwise, would *Faustus* have failed to respond to them, since that is what made the Manichaeans the loathing of the human race?

<margin>VIII. Judgment of various writings against the Manichaeans. Of Didymus, of Serapion.</margin>
VIII. We will not draw great insight from the small works of *Didymus* of Alexandria <note>Didymus the Blind (c. 313–398), a learned theologian in Alexandria who led the Catechetical School.</note> and of (1) *Serapion* of Thmuis in Egypt, because they only combat the capital error of the two Principles, and try to show that Evil is a consequence of the abuse that Man has made of his Liberty.

<margin>Of Cyril of Jerusalem.</margin>
The sixth Catechesis of *Cyril* of Jerusalem contains only a declamation against the Manichaeans, in which he does nothing but copy, extend, and exaggerate some parts of the *Report of Archelaus* <note>Referring to the *Acta Archelai*, a 4th-century fictionalized account of a debate between Mani and a Christian bishop named Archelaus, which became a primary (though often inaccurate) source for later anti-Manichaean writers.</note>. He even obviously falsified it, as I showed in the first part. Moreover, he has the honor of having first spread the rumor of the horrible ceremonies with which it was said our heretics profaned the sacred meal of the Lord’s Supper. Instructed in the impure rites of a certain festival of the Athenians, he applied them to the Manichaean Eucharist.

<margin>Of Philastrius.</margin>
I say nothing of *Philastrius*, Bishop of *Brescia*, a contemporary of St. *Ambrose*. No reliance can be placed on the testimony of this author, who forges imaginary heresies, and who treats those that did exist in such an impertinent and unfaithful manner that a modern scholar calls it (2) *Philastrizing*.

<margin>Of St. Epiphanius.</margin>
St. *Epiphanius* drew from the *Acts of Archelaus* everything he told us of the doctrine of the Manichaeans. He had no other source, although some scholars have imagined that he had read the *Book of Mysteries* <note>One of the seven canonical works written by Mani himself, now largely lost.</note>, which certainly is not true, as I have remarked. Little fruit will be drawn from the long, and if I may be allowed to add, the tedious treatise that he composed against our heretics, in which he often fights phantoms rather than real errors.

# PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE

<margin>On Leo I: His methods and character.</margin>
These wretched people, having been driven out by the Vandals <note>A Germanic tribe that established a kingdom in North Africa in the 5th century.</note> from Proconsular Africa—where they had multiplied almost from the very birth of their sect—many fled to Rome, hoping to hide there and find help among their brothers. *Leo I* <note>Pope Leo the Great (reigned 440–461), known for strengthening the authority of the Roman papacy.</note>, being informed of this, went to great lengths to purge his Church of such a pernicious leaven. However, he went about it in a manner more suited to irritating them and driving them to despair than to converting them. He claimed to have convicted them of abominable ceremonies, and gave notice of this to all the bishops of Italy. This proceeding produced two bad effects. The first was to inspire in the common people an extreme horror for the Manichaeans, and to incite magistrates to punish them according to the full rigor of the law. The second was to inspire in the Manichaeans themselves an extreme horror for the Catholic Church, whose bishops were their calumniators and persecutors. For, whatever one may say, they were not guilty of the crimes imputed to them. As for the letters and sermons of *Leo*, they do not contain a description of their doctrine. They consist of almost nothing but invectives against the *Priscillianists* <note>Followers of Priscillian, a Spanish bishop who was the first person in the history of Christianity to be executed for heresy.</note> and against the *Manichaeans*; this Pope perpetually affected to confuse these two sects in order to involve them in the same penalties. *Leo’s* zeal has something estimable about it, but I would wish him more moderation; above all, I would not wish him to have been one of the first bishops to have (1) approved the execution of heretics. However, upon reflection, I have found the cause of this in his character. Ambitious men think less of winning minds through gentleness and persuasion than of taming them by force.

<margin>On Theodoret: His character.</margin>
*Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393 – c. 458), an influential theologian and historian of the Greek Church.</note> is, in my view, one of the most estimable of the ancient Fathers. He is learned: he reasons well, especially in his dialogues against the Greek heresies of his time, and he is a good literal interpreter of Scripture. I could not help but admire his prudence and moderation when I considered that he ended his *Ecclesiastical History* at the point where the quarrels of *Nestorianism* <note>A Christological doctrine that was condemned at the Council of Ephesus in 431; it emphasized the distinction between the divine and human natures of Jesus.</note> began, in which he was so deeply involved. But I fear that his zeal against heretics may have deceived him almost as much as his admiration for the heroes of the *Ascetic Life* <note>A lifestyle characterized by abstinence from worldly pleasures, often associated with early Christian monasticism.</note>, with which he was enchanted. Great men have emerged from monasteries, but they acquired there a tint of superstition which fa- <note>The word is cut off by the page break; the catchword indicates it completes as "efface," meaning to fade or wear away.</note>

### ->ON THE SECOND PART.<-
### Ff 2
<meta>catchword: so</meta>

...were difficult to erase. If the *History of the Heresies* written by *Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–458 AD) was a deeply influential theologian and bishop in Syria, though his works were often caught in the crossfire of early Church politics.</note> is no more exact or faithful than his *Religious History*, he had more than one reason to title it **On the Fables of the Heretics**. It seems that the flaw of this learned man was one of extreme credulity. Regarding Manichaeism <note>A major dualistic religion founded by the prophet Mani, teaching a struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note>, he describes the system of the Creation of the World and what occasioned it reasonably well. He does not charge the Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical movement; here referring to Mani.</note> with having believed that the Soul is a part of the Divine Substance that found itself caught in the nets of Matter—where it is bound, captive, defiled by all the vices of Human Corruption, and subjected to all the miseries of the world. This is what *St. Augustine* <note>Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a foundational Western theologian who was himself a Manichaean for nine years before converting to Christianity.</note> repeats continually. *Theodoret* contents himself with saying that, according to *Manichaeaus*, God did nothing more than cast a particle of Light to the Powers of Darkness, as one throws a hook hidden under bait to the fish one wishes to catch. Now, all that is Light is not the Divine Essence, as *St. Augustine* believed. In this regard, *Theodoret's* account is quite accurate. But after this, he recounts certain fables regarding the production of *Adam*, which are either mysterious or too extravagant to have been believed by philosophers. What he adds concerning the "abominable ceremonies" of the Manichaeans is, in my view, pure calumny; and the power that these "Mysteries" supposedly gave to Demons over the people who participated in them is nothing but a folk tale. I am willing to believe that these heretics were difficult to convert, but I will not easily believe that the difficulty arose because the Demons who initiated them held their souls enchained by charms. In short, the credulous *Theodoret* falls too blindly into the ridiculous stories being told in his time regarding this Sect.

> „ the change in the Works he wrote against him, and to 
> „ pursue an *Hannibal* and a *Mithridates* under the name of *Manichaean*. 
<note>original: "poursuivre un Annibal & un Mithridate sous le nom de Manichée." Hannibal and Mithridates were legendary military enemies of Rome; the Manichaean Secundinus implies Augustine is fighting an imaginary or misplaced enemy.</note>

<margin>Either this Father <note>Referring to Saint Augustine as a "Church Father," the influential early Christian theologians whose writings established orthodoxy.</note> was ignorant of it, or he misrepresented it.</margin>

This Paradox will be subject to great contradictions. Firstly, it comes from the Heretics, which makes it very suspect: And secondly, it clashes with the most dazzling and authorized prejudice in the world. What! *St. Augustine*, the most skillful, the most ingenious of the Latin Fathers, the Oracle of the Western Church, was a Manichaean for nine years, and did not know Manichaeism? Can anything more rash or absurd be put forward? However, there are only two paths to take: The first, to say with the Manichaeans that *St. Augustine* did not well understand their System: The second, which will pass for almost a Heresy among certain people, is that *St. Augustine* disguised it. I value as much as any other the excellent qualities of this Father: I admire his happy genius and his knowledge: I honor his memory: I recognize all the merit of his pious labors: But the Rules of good Logic, and Experience, have taught me not to walk blindly in his footsteps. The Ancients never aspired to the Infallibility that Posterity gives them. They were men like us, and if we are more so than they in certain things, there are others where they were more so than us. I do not wish, however, to maintain that *St. Augustine* disguised the Manichaean System in order to triumph over it. That would be to accuse him of bad faith: but it is certain that he employed Sophisms <note>Fallacious arguments, especially those used deliberately to deceive or outmaneuver an opponent in debate.</note> against them: that he often misrepresented their Belief, and that he gave credit to fables which were disadvantageous to them: that he established as Dogmas of the Sect certain consequences which they disavowed; that he gave a bad meaning to words that were evidently innocent, and that he took advantage of certain passages which had been falsified. Let us allege some proofs of this, in order to stop, or at least suspend, the judgments of a biased Reader.

<margin>Example and Proof of these facts.</margin>
The Manichaeans, not believing that the Son of God had a real body, did not believe either that he had been truly crucified, nor that he had died. They did not deny that the Jews had taken him, that they had attached him to the Cross as much as that depended on them, and that he had appeared to die, but they denied that he had died in fact. This is what made *Mani* say that the Devil, who incited the Jews against Jesus Christ and who led them to crucify him, was crucified himself, because the

->## PRELIMINARY DISCOURSE ##<-

The Manichaeans were only human. The truth is that this folly is a consequence that the Orthodox <note>The "Orthodox" refers to the mainstream, established Church of the time, as opposed to the Manichaean "heretics."</note> drew from their principles, and not one of their own dogmas.

<margin>A horrible opinion falsely attributed to the Manichaeans by St. Augustine.</margin>
These are absurdities; here are the horrors. Let us explain ourselves as decently as we can. Among the profane opinions that St. *Augustine* attributes to the Manichaeans is this one: that certain Virtues, or celestial Powers dwelling in the Sun, transform themselves—sometimes into beautiful girls, sometimes into handsome boys—to excite the impure lust of the Powers of Darkness who see them. These dark powers struggle to seize them and, in their fury, let escape parts of the Divinity <note>In Manichaean cosmology, divine light was trapped within dark matter; the "Powers of Darkness" are the demonic entities that hold this light captive.</note>. It is by this artifice that God delivers these captive parts. St. *Augustine* repeats this filthy imagination in almost all of his <margin>(a) *On the Nature of the Good*, Ch. XLIV; *Against Faustus*, Book XX, 6; *Against Felix*, Book II, 7; *On the Faith*, Ch. XIV.</margin> (a) works against the Manichaeans. Then he exclaims: (1) *Who can suffer such things? Who can believe, I do not say that this is true, but that it could have been put forward by anyone? Great God! who can hear it without shuddering? Who can be blind enough to put faith in such things?*

St. *Augustine* is right. Nothing is more hideous than these profane extravagances. But I have a question to ask him. I ask how he could have remained in a sect where such abominations were taught? How could he have defended this sect against the Catholics? Let no one answer me that, being in the class of the *Auditors* <term>The "Auditors" (Auditores) were the lower rank of Manichaean followers who lived normal lives while supporting the "Elect."</term> and not that of the *Elect* <term>The "Elect" (Electi) were the Manichaean elite who practiced strict asceticism, including celibacy and vegetarianism.</term>, he was unaware of these blasphemies. For he tells us himself that they were found in the VIIth Book of the *Treasure of Mani*, a book that was in the hands of all his followers. (2) **These wretches**, he adds, **read these things, say them, hear them, and believe them.** St. *Augustine* was therefore not ignorant of them when he was a Manichaean. From this it follows either that this Father [of the Church] was, from the age of 19 until 28, a man without reason, without conscience, and without discernment—capable of hearing, reading, and believing the most insulting blasphemies against the Divinity—or that these blasphemies were not understood or believed among the Manichaeans at all, and that they were not read in the Book of the *Treasure*, as indeed they were not there. I will show hereafter that this passage of Mani has been horribly falsified.

### ON THE SECOND PART. ###

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>Public disputes of this Father with Felix and Fortunatus.</margin>
We have records of two public disputes held by St. *Augustine* against two Manichaean priests, one named *Felix* and the other *Fortunatus*. *Felix* was an uneducated man who did not understand his own words, as *Erasmus* <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the famous Renaissance scholar and editor of Augustine's works.</note> rightly observed. *Fortunatus* was more capable; thus, one finds in his responses some clarifications regarding the doctrine of his sect. One sees there in particular that the *Parts of Light*—which are mixed with the Darkness—could not be *Parts of the Divinity*, since *Fortunatus* maintains that the Divine Nature is *inviolable* and *inaccessible* to *Matter*, which can neither seize nor touch it. I also observed in these disputes that St. *Augustine*, who was a skilled *rhetorician* <note>A professional teacher of public speaking and argumentation.</note>, always adroitly seized the offensive, reducing his opponent to a defensive position.

<margin>He skillfully seizes the advantage of attacking.</margin>
*Fortunatus* was willing at the beginning to take the role of the attacker, but St. *Augustine* did not yield this advantage to him for long and reclaimed it immediately. In such intellectual combats, to hold the "windward side" is to blow smoke upon the enemy that chokes and blinds them. When *Fortunatus*—who claimed that the Soul could come from neither Nothingness nor Matter—pressed St. *Augustine* to explain its true origin, that clever man felt clearly that it is easier to raise difficulties than to resolve them. He knew there are questions upon which, whatever side one takes, the finest minds are forced to bend under the weight of objections.

<margin>X. The Formulas of abjuration prescribed for the Manichaeans do not contain their doctrine.</margin>
X. These reflections tend to show that one is mistaken if they imagine they can find a fair idea of Manichaeism in St. *Augustine*. But one is no less mistaken if they hope to find it in the *Formulas of abjuration* <note>Oaths of renunciation that converts were forced to sign to prove they had abandoned their "heresy."</note> that the Greeks and Latins prescribed for these "heretics." These documents have always included far less of what the Manichaeans actually believed than what they were accused of believing. Subsequently, their own confessions—which should have been authentic testimony of their creed—were falsified or dictated by the Inquisitors, who made them say whatever they wished.

<margin>Greek Formulas.</margin>
We have the Greek Formula published by (3) *Cotelier*, and later by *Tollius*. It is anything but accurate, and if one judges it by (4) the one the Greeks made the *Armenians* sign, one cannot have too poor an opinion of it.

„ flourished.” This testimony from *Theophanes* <note>Theophanes the Confessor (c. 758–818), a Byzantine monk and chronicler.</note> could only be partially true, since the Arabs were no less opposed to the *Manichaeans* than were the *Catholics*. If the *Caliphs* granted asylum to the *Paulicians* <note>A medieval Christian sect from Armenia and the Byzantine Empire, often accused of dualism similar to Manichaeism.</note>, whom the Greeks had driven to despair through their barbarities, it is not because they favored *Manichaeism*—with which I do not believe the *Paulicians* were infected—but rather for reasons of politics and humanity. Certainly, it is not against them that *Damascene* <note>Saint John of Damascus (c. 675–749), an influential theologian who lived under the Umayyad Caliphate.</note> wrote. For, besides the fact that one sees no sign of it in his Dialogue, it is clear that he had in view only the ancient Manichaeans who still existed in the East, since he took everything he said regarding their errors from the *Relation of Tyrbo* <note>Tyrbo was a character in an early anti-Manichaean work called the "Acts of Archelaus," which served as a primary source for many later writers.</note>.

Whatever esteem I may have for *Damascene*, I will nonetheless judge his work with the same freedom as I would judge that of a modern theologian. This author combats the <term>two Principles</term> <note>The core Manichaean belief that the universe is ruled by two opposing eternal powers: Good (Light) and Evil (Darkness).</note>, but he thought more of multiplying and piling up his arguments than of choosing them well and giving them clarity. It is thus, for example, that he claims to demonstrate that there is only one Principle, by the reason that Unity is the principle of all numbers, and that the <term>binary</term> <note>The number two, representing duality.</note> issues from it as from its cause. It is its *production* (3). This is not at all accurate. The binary is merely a composite of two Unities, each having its own separate existence, and one of which is not at all the production of the other.

The Manichaeans said that the Powers of Darkness, having perceived the Light, found it so beautiful that they wanted to seize it. To show the absurdity of this supposition, the Orthodox person asks the Manichaean: <margin>(c) Ibid. p. 440.</margin> *(c) whether Darkness is not blind?* And the latter having replied *that it is*, the Orthodox person concludes from this *that it could not therefore have seen the Light*. This reasoning is based on a pure equivocation. Although the Manichaeans gave the name *Darkness* to the malevolent Powers, they nevertheless granted them life and perception, and denied them only what is called <term>Mens</term> <note>Latin for "Mind" or "Intellect," referring here to the higher rational soul as opposed to mere sensory perception.</note>, or the *Spirit*.

As for the system of these heretics, it is in no way explained in *Damascene’s* Dialogue, which only applies itself to showing the absurdity of the hypothesis of the two Principles. He even attributes to our heretics errors that they did not hold. He says,

Was it, then, imitating the example of God, and practicing what he wished to teach us, to *massacre* and *have the Manichaeans burned*?

It is therefore not from the Dialogue of **Damascene** that one will learn the System of **Manichaeus**. He says nothing of it that has not already been said by **Tyrbo** <note>A figure in the "Acts of Archelaus," a 4th-century anti-Manichaean text that served as a source for many later writers.</note>, from whom he copies several passages. But he provides us with a very evident proof, in my opinion, that our Heretics were not guilty of the abominable Mysteries attributed to them. If they had been even suspected of them, is it believable that an Author who refutes them, and who was furiously incensed against them, would have made no mention of it, and would not even have insinuated that there was anything to reproach in their morals?

<margin>XI. **Constantine** seems to distrust the Bishops: He gives a layman the commission to instruct him on Heresies.</margin>
XI. Since ecclesiastical writers were generally of such obvious partiality, it would be neither prudent nor fair to trust their accounts. I do not know if experience had taught this to **Constantine the Great**, but I could not read, without reflecting upon it, that this Prince—wishing to know the true sentiments of the Sectarians—gave the commission to investigate and instruct him to a secular person, instead of giving it to the Bishops. It is **Ammianus Marcellinus** <note>Ammianus Marcellinus (c. 330–397 AD) was a Roman soldier and historian whose work is valued for its relative objectivity.</note> who informs us of this particular detail. (3) "**CONSTANTINE**," he says, "wishing to know exactly the opinions of the Sects, and having no one suited to give him accurate enlightenment on the matter, was recommended **STRATEGIUS** as a man very capable of it. The Emperor entrusted him with this task and was so satisfied with his report that he wished him to be called **MUSONIANUS** from then on." This officer, who eventually rose to the dignity of Praetorian Prefect of the East, possessed great knowledge and eloquence; and, what was even more necessary to fulfill his commission well, (4) he possessed much *moderation* and *gentleness*. At least **Libanius** <note>Libanius (c. 314–393 AD) was one of the last great teachers of Greek rhetoric and a prominent pagan intellectual.</note> praised him for it. I wish that we still possessed the report he made to **Constantine**, for I confess that I would place more faith in it than in those of the Church Fathers.

<margin>XII. **Simplicius** writes against the Manichaeans. A judgment of his refutation.</margin>
XII. The Christians were not the only ones who fought against Manichaeism <note>Manichaeism was a major dualistic religion founded by the prophet Mani, teaching a struggle between a good world of light and an evil world of darkness.</note>. There were also pagan philosophers who involved themselves. **Simplicius** <note>Simplicius of Cilicia (c. 490–560 AD) was one of the last great Neoplatonist philosophers of antiquity.</note> refuted it in his (5) Commentary on the *Enchiridion of Epictetus*, but he did not do so with enough moderation or fairness. For example, he reproaches the Manichaeans for teaching (6) "that the Evil Principle is not only equal in dignity and power to the Principle of Good, but that it is stronger than it; and that Man is not free, and that it is not in his power not to sin." I dare say that these two accusations are false, as I shall demonstrate in the proper place.

<margin>XIII. **Alexander of Lycopolis** does so as well.</margin>
XIII. Since Manichaeism had taken deep root in Egypt, there was in the city of Lycopolis in the Thebaid a philosopher named (7) **Alexander**, who undertook to refute it. I have several observations to make regarding the era of this author, his religion, his character, and his method.

---

<column-break/>

(5) See his Commentary, Chapter XXXIV, p. 163 and following. **Simplicius** lived under **Justinian**. **Vossius** says, following **Suidas**, that he was from Phrygia (*On the Sects of Philosophers*, Chapter XVII, § 18). But **Agathias** testifies that he was from Cilicia (*History of Justinian*, Book II, 2, p. 65). See the *Greek Library* of **Fabricius**, Volume VIII, p. 660.

(6) "They established a distinct principle of evil, equal in honor and power to the Good, or rather, even stronger." <note>original: "Ἀρχὴν ὑπεστήσαντο ἰδίαν τοῦ κακοῦ ἰσότιμον αὐτῇ καὶ ἰσοσθενῆ τῷ Ἀγαθῷ, μᾶλλον δὲ ἰσχυρότεραν."</note> Simplicius, cited above, p. 168.

(7) His work is titled, "Against the opinions of the Manichaeans." <note>original: "Πρὸς τὰς Μανιχαίων δόξας."</note> Father **Combefis** published it in Greek in the *Newest Supplement to the Library of the Fathers, Part II*.

<margin>
On the time in which he lived.
(a) *Literary History* <note>original: "Hist. Lit."</note> Vol. II, Dissertation I, p. 4.
</margin>
1. Regarding the era in which **Alexander** <note>Alexander of Lycopolis (fl. c. 300 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher and author of a treatise against the Manichaeans.</note> flourished, it is quite difficult to determine it precisely. Doctor **Cave** (a) <note>William Cave (1637–1713), an English divine and ecclesiastical historian.</note> reports that **Sambucus** <note>Johannes Sambucus (1531–1584), a Hungarian scholar and collector of manuscripts.</note> had marked on the manuscript—which Father **Combefis** <note>François Combefis (1605–1679), a French Dominican scholar and patrologist.</note> had printed—that he lived under the empire of **Heraclius**, around the year 640. The learned Englishman rejects this opinion and places **Alexander** in the 4th century, before **Cyril of Jerusalem** and St. **Epiphanius**, for the reason that he did not cite these two authors. However, since this reason is based on the false assumption that **Alexander** was a Christian, it falls apart as soon as the contrary is proven. All that seems certain is that he lived at a time when Pagan philosophers were beginning to adopt some hypotheses of Christian philosophy. We know that **Hierocles** <note>Hierocles of Alexandria (5th century AD), a Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> and other Platonists recognized that Matter is not eternal, and even claimed that **Plato** had believed in its creation, although we have evident proof to the contrary. The Egyptian philosopher <note>Referring to Alexander of Lycopolis.</note> does not declare himself so positively on this question, but he finds no absurdity in saying that God brought the Matter of the world out of nothingness; an opinion that Pagan philosophers did not begin to appreciate until after the Christians had demonstrated the absurdities resulting from the eternity of matter.

<margin>
2. Regarding his Religion.
(a) As above, p. 2.
</margin>
2. As for the religion of **Alexander**, Father **Combefis** imagined that he made a profession of Christianity and compared him, in his (a) Preface, to St. **Augustine**, who, after having been infected by Manichaeism, returned to the bosom of the *Church* and fought the errors he had once defended. **Photius** <note>Photius I of Constantinople (c. 810–893), an influential patriarch and scholar.</note> went even further: he took him for a (1) Bishop of *Lycos*, or *Lycopolis*, and Doctor (2) **Cave** followed them. I excuse Mr. **Cave**, but I do not know how to excuse Father **Combefis**, who published the Greek text of **Alexander**. It is surprising that this learned man did not perceive that he was a Pagan philosopher. 1. He never cites Scripture in his dispute against the Manichaeans, which a Christian would not have failed to do, since after all, they recognized the authority of the books of the New Testament. 2. He speaks <margin>(b) Al. Lycop. as above, p. 16.</margin> OF THE (b) SOULS OF THE NYMPHS; this is not in the Christian style. 3. says, that (3) from ALL THE GODS the Manichaeans honor only the SUN AND THE MOON. 5. Finally, he clearly places himself among the Pagans. After having remarked that our Heretics tried to confirm their Errors by History, or the Fable of *Bacchus*, by the Enterprise of the Giants, etc., he adds (4) *The most learned among them, those who have some Greek literature,* ALLEGE OUR OWN CEREMONIES AND OUR OWN MYSTERES TO US. It seems that what deceived Father Combéfis <note>François Combefis (1605–1679), a Dominican scholar who edited many patristic texts.</note> is that *Alexander* is a moderate Pagan, who judges the Christian Religion fairly. He calls it (5) A SIMPLE PHILOSOPHY, meaning that it is fit to form the *simple-minded* in Virtue, who must be led by Authority, because they are not capable of knowing the excellence of Virtue, nor of feeling the force of the Demonstrations that prove it. *Ammianus Marcellinus* (6) <note>A 4th-century Roman historian known for his relatively objective view of Christianity despite being a Pagan.</note> thought like *Alexander* on the subject of the Christian Religion, and explained himself in nearly the same terms.

<margin>3. His Character.</margin>
3. The character of *Alexander* is very beautiful and very estimable. He remains composed everywhere and never insults his Adversaries. He does not go looking, among the different Manichaean Sects, for the one whose System was the most poorly devised or most disfigured by foolish fictions. He attacks Manichaeism at its Stronghold, and chooses, to combat it, the Sect (7) which was considered the most reasonable and the most refined. I cannot see without regret that a Philosopher makes war on Philosophers in a more generous and magnanimous manner than the Orthodox are accustomed to do against Heretics.

<margin>4. His Method.</margin>
4. *Alexander's* Method is very good. He first reports a summary of the System of the Manichaeans and then refutes it step by step. But, besides the fact that he limited himself to what he calls *their* (8) *Principal Dogmas*, he did not develop them sufficiently, apparently because he was writing for People who were already informed of them. He is, moreover, obscure; (9) his style smells much of the Egyptian Soil <note>This refers to the "Alexandrian" style of writing, which was often criticized by later scholars as being overly complex or obscure.</note>. The matter is not very well known, and errors have slipped into the Manuscript that are difficult to correct. I have noticed therein that he attributes to the Manichaeans neither profane Mysteries nor shameful ceremonies.

->### ON THE SECOND PART.###<-

...and the Dogmas of *Manichaeus* <note>The Latinized name for Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the Persian prophet who founded Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that once rivaled Christianity.</note>. But I will frankly admit that I did not think I should waste time reading many of them. I know of only one who has written on this matter with a critical eye, all the others having been content to copy the Ancient authors I have mentioned and to follow them without examination. By reading the Moderns, one does nothing but adopt prejudices, and that is what I have tried to protect myself from. I esteem them greatly, but I have no need of them when I can go myself to the sources from which they drew.

<margin>Only *Arnold* is known to have written about Heresies with a critical perspective.</margin>
The Critical Author I wish to speak of is the late Mr. *Gottfried Arnold*, born in 1666 and died in 1714 at *Perleberg*, in the states of the King of Prussia, where he was a Pastor and Inspector of the Lutheran Churches of that small province. As early as the year 1699, he published in German an IMPARTIAL HISTORY of the *Church* and of *Heretics* <note>Arnold’s *Unpartheyische Kirchen- und Ketzer-Historie* was revolutionary for its time, as it often sided with the "heretics" against the established church institutions.</note> which caused a great stir. Some (4) Scholars have spoken well of it, but in general, the (5) Lutheran Theologians rose up against this Work and against the Author. One of their principal grievances is that *Arnold* did not hide the faults of his own Communion, nor those of several Figures who are elevated there to the heavens. I do not intend to judge the quarrel between these Scholars and the partisans of *Arnold*. I cannot even state my sentiment regarding his History because I do not understand the German Language well enough. I will content myself with remarking, in general: 1. That his design deserves praise. It is certain that the History of the Church, and especially that of the Heretics, has been horribly corrupted, and it is very worthy of a Man who loves Truth to work at correcting it. Can People who have dared to reshape Religion and reform its abuses find it wrong that others undertake to reform its History? 2. If *Arnold* made mistakes in his own work, that is no reason to decry it as people do. There is no Work of this nature in which there are not more or fewer errors. It is good to point them out, but to conclude from this defect that the Work is worthless is to draw a very false consequence from a true Principle.

For Modern History, he had memoirs and assistance to guide him and was not forced to proceed by the light of his own conjectures. Regarding his own sentiments, I shall say nothing. It appears to me only that he was quite infatuated with <term>Mystical Theology</term> <note>A branch of theology focusing on the soul's direct union with God through subjective experience rather than dogma or ritual.</note>; that he indulged in the (1) visions of certain Moderns; that he was too indulgent toward very real <term>Heresies</term> <note>Beliefs or opinions contrary to orthodox religious doctrine.</note>; and that by dint of wishing to distance himself from contentious theologians—who make Religion consist of subtle and very indifferent opinions—he seems not to have valued highly enough the Truths that Scripture teaches distinctly. Otherwise, one must do him justice. A learned man, extremely industrious, and an enemy of lies, he made every effort to discover the Truth and to disentangle it from the infinite Fables under which it is, as it were, buried. He also had the courage to publish it, whatever it might cost his fortune and his peace of mind.

<margin>Reflections on the Report of Turbo.</margin>
Such is the Report that Turbo <note>Called Tyrbon in the original French; modern scholars usually identify him as Turbo, the disciple of Manichaeus in the 'Acts of Archelaus.'</note> gave to *Archelaus* and *Marcellus* regarding the Manichaean system. General reflections must now be made on this document.

<margin>The Greek and Latin versions are corrupted.</margin>
1. The Latin version has been greatly corrupted by scribes, and the Greek of *St. Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century bishop and writer who recorded many early Christian "heresies."</note> is likewise not exempt from errors. This apparently results from the fact that the Greek and Latin scribes understood nothing of the Manichaean system. There are even (8) some passages where the Greek of *St. Epiphanius* and the Latin version share almost no common ground.

<margin>This Report was not delivered orally. It is a Memoir prepared by some Manichaean.</margin>
2. As I believe I have demonstrated that the Conference of *Cascar* <note>A famous, though likely legendary, public debate between Bishop Archelaus and Manichaeus.</note> is a fabrication, it follows quite naturally that the Report of *Turbo* is as well. The system of Manichaeus is very obscure: the *Aeons* <note>Divine emanations or eternal beings that bridge the gap between the infinite God and the material world.</note> are designated there by terms that reveal neither their nature nor their functions. *Marcellus* and *Archelaus* understood nothing of a theology that must have seemed so strange and new to them. Yet they ask no questions of *Turbo* on the matter; they seek no clarification. This confirms my belief that this account was not given orally, as is claimed. It is likely a memoir drawn up by some Manichaean and provided to the author of the Acts.

*mass*, <note>original: "ὁ βῶλος" (ho bolos)</note> is surely what will remain of the Earth after it has been burned. The *Young Aeon* is some Intelligence tasked with binding criminal souls to this mass to punish them for their sins and their unbelief. The Latin version says, *They send back the soul* (other reading: *the soul is sent back*) *which is placed in the middle of the new age.* <note>original Latin: "Iterum dimittunt animam (Al. dimittitur anima) quæ objicitur inter medium novi sæculi."</note> This version is so different from the Greek of *St. Epiphanius* that the translator must have had a Greek copy that differed from that father's. Nevertheless, this translation aligns well enough with an opinion attributed to Manichaeus: that criminal souls will be placed between the Light and the Darkness to keep the Darkness within its boundaries and prevent it from invading the Kingdom of Light.

Acts of Archelaus. Perhaps it is a Mesopotamian, named *Turbo*, who gave it, or sent it, to *Hegemonius* <note>Hegemonius is the name traditionally attributed to the author of the 'Acts of Archelaus,' though his historical identity remains obscure.</note>.

<margin>It is unfaithful, or it has been altered.</margin>
3. Whoever the author of this Memoir may be, it contains evident proofs of his ignorance, or of his unfaithfulness. For example, he accuses Manichaeus **of serving and honoring two Gods, one good and the other evil.** This is a notorious calumny, as will be shown at the beginning of the second *Book*, or else it is an addition that was made later. For I have good reasons to suspect that this piece was altered even before *St. Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 315–403), a fierce hunter of heresies whose works are a primary source for lost Manichaean texts.</note>, because one should not presume that, in such a short account, the author would have so manifesty contradicted himself on the origin of the Soul.

<margin>Contradiction on the origin of the Soul.</margin>
He says at the beginning that the Soul was part of the armor of the *First Man*, which was composed of *Air*, *Wind*, *Light*, *Water*, and *Fire*—that is to say, *the five celestial elements*. What the powers of Darkness took from this armor is the *Light*, and this Light is the *Soul*. *The Mother of Life* emanates from the *Father*: *the First Man* emanates from the *Mother of Life*. But the *Armor of the First Man* does not emanate from them, and consequently does not come from *God*, neither mediately nor immediately. It is a celestial substance, in truth, but it is not the substance of the Father. Thus, when the author enumerates the Divine Emanations, the Soul is not included. However, he is made to say, (1) that **the Soul is a proper part of the Divinity, and that every soul, even that of animals, is a portion of the Substance of the Father.** Certainly, either these last words are an addition, or the author has evidently contradicted himself, which does not seem likely.

<margin>A mixture of false and true.</margin>
4. There is some truth in this account, but there is also much that is false, and if the Doctrine of Manichaeus had been such as it is represented, far from making great progress as it did, it would have been the contempt of all the Earth. Who could be persuaded that Agriculture, the most necessary and innocent of all the Arts, is a crime deserving eternal punishment: or that the same applies to *grinding wheat*, *baking bread*, or *building a house*? Who could be persuaded that *one wounds the Air when moving the hand, and that one wounds the Earth when walking*? Such extravagances would have revolted everyone against Manichaeus. Thus, one can be assured that the description of Manichaeism by *Turbo* is filled with fables that have been stuffed in, among

<margin>The Author converts particular Precepts into general Precepts.</margin>
5. The Author makes a manifest error when he reports the Maxims of *Manichaeus*. He converts particular precepts, which concerned only the *Elect*, into general Precepts. It was to the *Elect* <note>The 'Elect' (Electi) were the ascetic elite of the Manichaean community who lived under strict rules, including celibacy and vegetarianism.</note> that it was forbidden to *harvest*, *build houses for themselves*, and *amass wealth*, their profession closely resembling that of our Mendicant Monks. Some Authors have made the same error in reporting the Precepts of *Pythagoras*.

<margin>One must not take everything Manichaeus said literally.</margin>
6. I have little doubt that there are also Parables in *Tyrbon's* account that must not be taken literally. *Manichaeus* had this in common with the Orientals and the Egyptians: he shrouded his Doctrine in emblems, the meaning of which was only well known to the Masters of the Sect.

<margin>The Author's silence regarding Marriage.</margin>
7. It is surprising that the Author says nothing of *Manichaeus's* sentiment on Marriage. This was, however, one of his major Heresies <note>Manichaeism generally viewed procreation as a way of further trapping the divine light in matter, thus discouraging marriage among the Elect.</note>.

<margin>Silence of the same author regarding the abominable Mysteries of the Manichaeans.</margin>
8. Finally—and this is my last Reflection—this Author maintains a profound silence regarding the abominable Mysteries attributed to *Manichaeus* and his Sect, which clearly shows that they are false. It is inconceivable that a deserter from Manichaeism would have concealed these horrible secrets, nor that *Hegemonius*, who composed the Acts of the Dispute of *Archelaus*, would have suppressed them. I should not be countered with the objection that *Tyrbon*, being only a Catechumen, was not initiated into the Mysteries of his Sect and consequently knew nothing of what occurred there in secret. *Tyrbon* was, in truth, only a *Hearer* <term>Hearer: The lower rank of Manichaean followers (Auditores), who lived in the world and supported the Elect</term>, but the Hearers were not *Catechumens* as many have imagined. They differed from the *Elect* as laypeople differ from Priests and Monks. Otherwise, they attended Worship like the others. The *Elect* had Rules that were peculiar to them, but it does not appear that they had a Worship unique to themselves. All that *Tyrbon* says is that they invoked certain Names which were unknown to the *Hearers*, which is of no consequence regarding secret Mysteries and Ceremonies, and even less so regarding abominable ceremonies.

These are the general Reflections that I thought necessary to make on this piece before examining in detail the Principles, Dogmas, Morality, and Discipline of the Manichaeans.

HISTORY OF DOGMAS

# CHAPTER II.

### Principles of Manichaeism. Examination of the first Principle. MANICHAEUS did not call himself JESUS CHRIST, nor the HOLY SPIRIT. What Authority he attributed to himself.

<margin>Principles of Manichaeism.</margin>
TO understand the Manichaean System as much as is currently possible, one must first explain its PRINCIPLES. I call Principles those certain Propositions or Maxims which serve as the foundations of Manichaeism, and which were, in some sense, peculiar to this Heresy <note>In this context, "heresy" refers to a set of beliefs that diverged from the established orthodox Christian doctrines of the time.</note>.

<margin>I. Principle; Manichaeus claimed to be the Apostle of Jesus Christ.</margin>
I. MANICHAEUS was not content to present himself to the World as a great Philosopher, and to the Church as a Christian Teacher. Had he taken only one of these two roles, he would have been subject either to Holy Scripture, which is the common Rule of Christians, or to Reason and Experience, which are the Rules of Philosophers. He would have been obliged to prove his Dogmas either by the testimony of the Sacred Books or by evident reasoning. But, being unable to do either, he assumed a Divine Mission; he seized the character and authority of the APOSTLE OF JESUS CHRIST, but an Apostle superior in Enlightenment to the first Apostles, and extraordinarily instructed by the Holy Spirit, in order to reveal Truths to the World that had been unknown before his Ministry, and to reform all established Religions. This is his first Principle.

<margin>II. Principle. He rejects the Old Testament and claims to correct the New.</margin>
The second principle, which can be seen as a consequence of the first, is that although he received most of the Writings of the New Testament, it was nonetheless only insofar as they agreed with his alleged Revelations and his false Knowledge. Otherwise, he denounced our Gospels as false, asserting that they were not the work of the Disciples of Jesus Christ, or that they had been corrupted. As for the Old Testament, he regarded it as a compilation of Books composed by the Hebrews and for the Hebrews alone, filled with Ordinances that were not worthy of Divinity, and with Judaic fables and superstitions.

<margin>III. Principle. He admits the Books of Philosophers and prefers the Wisdom of the Orientals to that of the Hebrews.</margin>
The third Principle of Manichaeus is that all the Peoples of the World—and among these Peoples, the Orientals—had their Sages, their Philosophers, and their Prophets who, by virtue of the Enlightenment that Divine Reason communicates to all who listen to it, had discovered Truths that the Jews ignored: That

these Sages and these Prophets being the Fathers of the Gentiles, of whom the Christian Church is composed, it is more natural and more reasonable to consult them than the Prophets of the Jews: That the few *Moral* Truths, which were still found in the Judaic Religion, did not come originally from these Prophets, but from the first Fathers of the Human Race, who had lived and died in the East; who had been instructed by good Angels, and who had transmitted them to their descendants.

<margin>IV. Principle. He opposes Apocrypha to the Books received by the Church.</margin>
Finally, the fourth Principle of *Manichaeus* is that the Sacred Books received by the Orthodox, being neither faithful nor authentic, had to be corrected by other Books, which the Catholics had only rejected because they did not agree with their Errors. From this came various Apocrypha <note>Ancient religious texts that were not included in the official canon of the Bible.</note>, which the Manichaeans opposed to the Canonical Books, and which they claimed contained the Doctrine of the Apostles.

In general, the fundamental Maxim of the Manichaeans is that one must not recognize as true any fact, nor any Dogma, under whatever name it is announced, and in whatever Book it is contained, unless it agrees with the Doctrine of *Manichaeus*, who is (a) *the spiritual Man, who judges all things, and can be judged by no one* <note>original Latin: "spiritualis homo, qui judicat omnia, et a nemine judicatur."</note>. The reason for this is that, being enlightened and directed immediately by the *Paraclete* <note>A title for the Holy Spirit as "Advocate" or "Helper," promised by Christ to guide the Church into all truth.</note>, promised and sent by Jesus Christ, he knew and manifested all Truths, and corrected all Errors.

<margin>(a) 1 Cor. 2:15.</margin>

<margin>Subject matter and plan of this Book I and of Book II.</margin>
Such are the Principles of the Manichaeans, which I am going to examine. I will investigate first, what idea the Heresiarch <note>A term for the founder of a religious movement considered heretical by the mainstream church.</note> wanted to give the World of his Person and his Ministry: secondly, what he, or at least his Followers, thought of the Old and the New Testament, and their primary Objections, whether against *Moses* and the Prophets, or against the Apostolic Writers. I will examine in the third place which Pagan Books the Manichaeans might have used, and what authority they gave to these Books: In the fourth place, which are the Apocrypha they are accused of having forged or corrupted, and by the authority of which they claimed to justify some of their opinions and their Observances. I will end this fourth Article with an enumeration of the Books of *Manichaeus* and of his first Disciples, the memory of whom has come down to us. This is the Subject Matter of Books I and II, after which I will treat his particular Dogmas.

<margin>I. EXAMINATION of the Principle of Manichaeus.</margin>
I. I begin with the first Principle of *Manichaeus*; I mean, by the idea he wanted to give the World of his Person and his Ministry. It cannot be denied that he was either a great *Imposter* or a great *Fanatic*. Those who say that he withdrew

### HISTORY OF DOGMAS

<margin>He was an Imposter, or a Fanatic. Perhaps both, but not as the Ancients described him.</margin>...in a Cave, where he composed his *Gospel*, and then boasted of having brought it down from Heaven, make him out to be an Imposter. But those who tell us that he received his Mission in a *Dream*, or in an *Ecstasy*, seem rather to make him a Fanatic—at least if it is true that the *Dream* or the Ecstasy were not feigned. I do not wish to decide this Question, especially since it is not impossible to unite these two characters. A man who begins with *Imposture* may well end with *Fanaticism*, and persuade himself that he is effectively what he intended to be. However, it is a far cry from our Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> having carried Imposture or Fanaticism to the extreme that the Ancients have claimed. I am sorry to find so little truth and accuracy in their accounts; but I would fail in both myself if I did not uncover their error.

<margin>The falsehood of Photius, Peter of Sicily, and the Greek Formula.</margin> Photius and Peter of Sicily, Authors of the 9th Century, have claimed (1) that <term>Scythianus</term> <note>A legendary figure often cited as a precursor to Mani.</note> *called himself God the Father*; <term>Terebinthus</term> (or <term>Buddas</term>) <note>Alleged disciples of Scythianus.</note> *the Son of God*, and <term>Manes</term>, *the Holy Spirit*. The Greeks did not fail to insert such an impertinent calumny into the (*a*) *Formula of Abjuration* <note>A formal oath of renunciation required of those leaving a heresy to join the Orthodox Church.</note>, which they prescribed for the Manichaeans; even the learned Mr. (*b*) Cave had the weakness to copy it. It is so coarse and so visible an error that I will not stop to refute it, all the more so since, not having been found in any ancient Author, it is supported only by the testimony of the medieval Greeks I have just cited. Such a claim would not have escaped their predecessors if it had any foundation.

<margin>(*a*) From Cotelerius, Apostolic Fathers, Vol. I, p. 539.
(*b*) In Addenda, Vol. II, p. 470.</margin>

<margin>Another falsehood from the same Formula.</margin> I believe I must treat with the same contempt another lie which the Greeks forced the Manichaeans to abjure, as if it had been an Article of their Faith. (*c*) This is the claim that *Zarades (or Zoroaster), Buddas, Christ, Manichaeus, and the Sun* (2) *are one and the same Person*. This is certainly a frightful calumny. It is refuted by the incontestable dogmas of the Manichaeans, who recognized <term>Jesus Christ</term> as the only Son of God: who, far from deifying Zoroaster, had reformed his Religion: and who did not doubt that *Buddas* and *Manichaeus* had been men, and that the Sun was a Creature, composed of the assembly of Parts of Light that had preserved their purity. We shall see this in the following sections.

<margin>(*c*) Ibid. From Cotelerius, p. 537.
From Tollius, Distinguished Italian Travels, p. 135.</margin>

<header>ON MANICHAEUS. Book I. Ch. II.</header>

<margin>II. Puerile reasoning of Archelaus, intended to show that Manichaeus usurped Divinity.</margin>
II. From the Greeks of the Middle Ages, let us return to the Ancients, and begin with *Archelaus* <note>A legendary 3rd-century Bishop of Cascar in Mesopotamia, known primarily through the "Acts of Archelaus," a polemical account of a debate with Mani.</note>. This famous Bishop of *Cascar*, wishing to convict *Manichaeus* of usurping Divinity, told the Judges who presided over the first Dispute they had together (3): "No other Heretic has had the audacity to boast of being <term>God</term>, or the <term>Christ</term>, or the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>From the Greek 'parakletos,' meaning 'comforter' or 'advocate,' used in the New Testament to refer to the Holy Spirit.</note>. This is a pride peculiar to this man, who discourses now of the Ages (that is to say, the <term>Aeons</term> <note>In Gnostic systems, these are divine emanations or powers that make up the spiritual world.</note>), now of the Sun, and of the manner in which they were made, as if he were greater than they. For whoever explains how a Being was formed shows by that very fact that he is greater and older than the Being of which he speaks." By this account, *Moses* must have intended to show that he was greater and older than the World, because he recounts its Creation.

<margin>According to Eusebius, Theodoret, and Suidas, he called himself the Christ and the Holy Spirit.</margin>
Although *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339), a historian often called the "Father of Church History."</note> had seen no Work by *Manichaeus*, he accuses him (4) "of having tried to counterfeit the *Christ*, and to pass for the *Christ*." The same Author adds (5) "that he sometimes called himself the <term>Paraclete</term>, and the very Person of the Holy Spirit." *Theodoret* confirms the testimony of *Eusebius* (6): "This scoundrel," he says, "had the audacity to glory in being both the *Christ* and the Holy Spirit." This was faithfully copied by (a) *Suidas* <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist.</note>. However, as the *Christ* and the *Holy Spirit* are two very distinct Persons in the Manichaean System, one must absolutely choose: for one cannot accuse the Heresiarch of wanting to pass for both. The truth is that in the style of some ancient Ecclesiastical Doctors, who lived before the Council of Nicaea but are not accused of Heresy, the *Christ* and the *Holy Spirit* are the same Person. And it is this which caused the Error of *Eusebius*, *Theodoret*, *Suidas*, and even *Abulpharagius* <note>Bar Hebraeus (1226–1286), a prominent bishop of the Syriac Orthodox Church.</note>, who said (7) that *Manes named himself the Messiah*.

<margin>(a) Suidas, under the entry "Manes."</margin>

<margin>Frivolous pretext of Eusebius.</margin>
When I examined on what pretext *Eusebius* could have accused *Manes* of having tried to counterfeit the *Christ*, I found no other than this (8): that following the example of *Jesus Christ*, he chose for himself twelve Disciples, of whom he was the Master and Head. But if such innocent imitations were enough to bring such an accusation, would it not also be necessary to bring it against *St. Mark*, who is claimed to have been the first Bishop of Alexandria, and say that this Evangelist affected to counterfeit the *Christ*? For it is asserted (b) that he created twelve Priests for himself.

<margin>(b) Selden, *On the Origins of the Church of Alexandria*.</margin>

<margin>III. According to Cyril and Leo I, Manichaeus only called himself the Holy Spirit.</margin>
III. *Cyril of Jerusalem* <note>A 4th-century bishop and Doctor of the Church known for his catechetical lectures.</note> seems a bit better founded when he accuses *Manès* (1) of having blasphemed, *by calling himself the Holy Spirit*. At the least, the accusation is more plausible, and *Leo I* <note>Pope Leo the Great (r. 440–461), known for his influence on Church doctrine and for meeting Attila the Hun.</note> would have done well to copy him, rather than to extend and paraphrase his words with an inexcusable liberty (2). "The Manichaeans," he says, "ADORE Manichaeus their Master, under the name of the Holy Spirit. They believe," (3) he says elsewhere, "that the Holy Spirit appeared in Manichaeus their Master, such that HE WAS NOTHING OTHER THAN THE HOLY SPIRIT HIMSELF, who, by the Ministry of a Tongue and a corporeal voice, led his Disciples into the Truth." If all this were true, our <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>The founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note> would have carried pride and blasphemy to the highest degree. But, if *Leo* is no more faithful in his account than he is just in his reasoning, we shall be well excused from placing faith in it.

<margin>Impertinent word of Leo.</margin>
For, to refute in a word the proud pretensions of *Manichaeus*, the Bishop of Rome alleges to his People (4) *that he came from that part of the World which cannot receive the Spirit of Truth*. Thus the Holy Spirit is quite limited, and the Peoples of the East quite disgraced. I would not have believed that a Bishop to whom one gives the pompous title of GREAT could have said such an impertinent thing in a Sermon that has been passed down to Posterity. Had he then forgotten that the first among the Gentiles who came to adore the Messiah were the MAGI, <term>Persian</term> <note>Followers of Zoroastrianism or similar Eastern traditions; the author links them to Mani's Persian origins.</note> Philosophers (5) and, so to speak, the Ancestors of *Manichaeus*? Had he forgotten what he himself said in another place: that the Magi only knew by the appearance of the Star that Christ was born in Judea (5) *by a Divine inspiration*?

<margin>IV. Violent efforts of St. Augustine to convict Manichaeus of having called himself the Holy Spirit.</margin>
IV. I have pity for *St. Augustine* when I see the embarrassment into which his zeal against *Manichaeus* throws him. He would like to find some way to convict him of having called himself the Holy Spirit, or at least of having boasted (6) *that the Holy Spirit was united to him, just as we say that God*

He observes, then, <margin>(a) *Against the Fundamental Letter, Chapter VI.*</margin> (a) that the <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>The original leader of a heretical movement.</note> everywhere calls himself **Apostle of Jesus Christ**, and never **Apostle of the Paraclete** <note>original: "Paraclet." The Phrase used by *Manichaeus* has nothing suspicious or embarrassing about it. As for this *Assumption* <note>The idea of a human nature being taken up by a divine one.</note>, it is absurd to attribute it to a man who stubbornly maintained that the Divine Nature and the Flesh could never be united.

<margin>V. *Affectation of the Ancients in accusing Heretics of usurping Divinity.*</margin> V. Before defining what opinion the Manichaeans held of their Master, I wish to give the Reader the satisfaction of seeing with what affectation, and under what pretexts, the Ancients accused Heretics of having attributed to themselves the Divine Nature and Perfections. It is not fraud, I agree: but it is a blind Prejudice, inspired by hatred and by a poorly regulated zeal. Let us begin with *Simon*, the Father and the most odious of all Heretics.

<margin>(a) Irenaeus, as cited above.</margin>

The clever Jesuit <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a prominent French Jesuit theologian known for his work on the history of dogmas.</note> finds no contradiction even in another testimony from St. *Irenaeus*, where this Father asserts that *Simon* boasted of being himself alone the three Divine Persons, *(a) the Father in Samaria, the Son in Judea, and the Holy Spirit among the Gentiles.* If that were true, this famous <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A leader of a heretical movement.</note> would have paved the way for the <term>Sabellians</term> <note>Followers of Sabellius (3rd century), who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but merely three modes or "masks" of a single God.</note>. But I would very much like Father *Petau*, who sometimes has such a flexible and conciliatory mind, to have taken the trouble to reconcile the testimony of St. *Irenaeus* with that of the *Author of the Recognitions*, and those Homilies called *Clementines* <note>The "Pseudo-Clementine" writings are a 4th-century religious romance and collection of discourses falsely attributed to Pope Clement I.</note>; for my part, I cannot reconcile the ideas that *Simon* had of the Divinity—if we believe the Pseudo-*Clement*—with the foolish impieties that the Bishop of *Lyon* <note>St. Irenaeus served as the Bishop of Lugdunum (modern-day Lyon).</note> attributes to him.

<margin>Capital error of Simon. His ideas of God the Father. (b) See Recognitions, Book II, No. 38, p. 512. Clementine Homilies III, No. 2, p. 534.</margin>
*Simon* had taken into his mind an opinion of which he was not the inventor, and which was embraced by several ancient heretics, namely *(b)*, that it is not God the Father who created the world, but Intelligences who acted with his consent and under his orders. In this, he diverged from Christian theology only in that he attributed to Angels what it attributes to the Son of God. His sentiment will appear less absurd if one supposes, as he did, that Matter is eternal. Since, in this supposition, it is only a matter of arranging a Matter that already exists, the Creation of the World does not surpass the idea one has of the power of Angels. *Simon* further maintained that it was not God the Father who gave the Law and who manifested himself to *Moses* and the Patriarchs. One of his reasons was that (1) THE SUPREME GOD, whom he qualifies as the GOD OF GODS, (2) *who is* UNIQUE, *who is* INCOMPREHENSIBLE, (3) WHO GAVE THE BEGINNING TO ALL THINGS, and to WHOM CONSEQUENTLY THEY ARE NECESSARILY SUBJECT, *as the* PRINCE OF ALL THINGS, *as the one who has an eminent superiority over all things*; that this Supreme God, I say, does not communicate himself. He is (4) UNKNOWN, because he is withdrawn into an (5) INEFFABLE and INCORPOREAL *Light* which emanates from him, and with which he fills the sublime dwelling place where he resides. *Simon* defines this *Supreme God* as an (7) IMMENSITY OF LIGHT.

These are certainly the ideas that *Simon* held regarding God the Father. The Author of the *Recognitions* <note>The "Recognitions" of Clement is an early Christian philosophical novel that portrays Simon Magus as a primary antagonist to St. Peter.</note> had read his books, and there is no reason to dispute his testimony. Now, how could a man who holds such ideas of the supreme God boast of being that very God? I do not wish to emphasize the sacrilege and the impiety of such a claim; I will assume that *Simon* had no fear of God. Nor do I wish to emphasize the absurdity of this claim: it could only arise in the mind of a madman, not a philosopher. I only wish to compare it with his own Principles. He maintains that the supreme God does not communicate at all: that he is withdrawn into an *ineffable Light* <note>original: *Lumière ineffable*</note> that emanates from him. That it is not this God who has sometimes appeared to men; that he acts externally only through his Ministers. This is the general System of the ancient Gnostics <note>Gnostics were early Christian-era groups who believed in a distant, supreme God and that the material world was created by a lesser, often ignorant deity.</note> who maintained, like *Simon*, that the Supreme God did not create the World. And yet they would have us believe that *Simon* called himself that God? We must, once and for all, shake off the yoke of a foolish credulity: let us respect the Church Fathers, but let us not allow ourselves to be led by them like little Children.

Moreover, if **Montanus** <note>Montanus was a 2nd-century prophet and founder of Montanism, a movement emphasizing new prophecy and strict asceticism.</note> had called himself **God the Father and the Holy Spirit**, how could the **Montanists** be Orthodox on the Article of the Trinity? Now, if the Leader of the Montanists has been so indignantly slandered, what has not been done regarding other Sects and their Leaders?

<margin>VII. The same accusation brought against Paul of Samosata. (f) Ecclesiastical Library, Vol. I. p. 214.</margin>
VII. One knows **Paul of Samosata** and his Heresy. Those who deposed him reproached him for being too proud; and I know not whether it is to excuse his faults, or to indirectly rebuke those of the Prelates of our own century, that the **Abbot du Pin** <note>Louis Ellies du Pin (1657–1719) was a French ecclesiastical historian known for his critical approach.</note> said (f), that the Bishops of the Council of Antioch accused him of all the vices common to the Bishops of great Sees: But at least they did not accuse him of having called himself the **Christ**. This is, however, what St. **Epiphanius** did a hundred years after his condemnation. (7) **He gave himself the title of Christ**, says this Father. This is a flagrant slander. For, besides the fact that this accusation is altogether incredible, it is not found at all in the Letter that the Council of Antioch wrote to all the Churches, which can be seen in (g) **Eusebius**.

<margin>IX. Against a certain Peter, Head of the Bogomiles.</margin>
IX. Let us move on to a slightly more modern Heretic, but whose era I cannot precisely mark. It is said that he was the Head of a supposed species of Manichaeans <note>Followers of Mani, a Persian prophet who taught a dualistic worldview of light versus darkness.</note>, who were called **Bogomiles**, and of whom I shall write the History after that of the Paulicians <note>A dualistic Christian sect that flourished between the 7th and 9th centuries.</note>. This man, named **Peter**, is also accused (2) **of having called himself Christ** <note>original Greek: "Τῷ Χριστῷ ἑαυτὸν ἀποκαλέσαντι."</note>, by *Euthymius Zigabenus* <note>A 12th-century Byzantine monk and theologian known for his encyclopedia of heresies.</note>, a famous Greek Monk, who treated Heresies much like St. *Epiphanius*, and with the same "impartiality." The Reader shall judge by the fable I am about to relate.

<margin>Ridiculous fable of Euthymius concerning this Peter.</margin>
*Euthymius* relates that *Peter*, seeing himself condemned to be stoned, warned his Disciples that he would rise again on the third day. These followers, full of hope to soon recover their Master, remained for three days and three nights near the Heap of Stones under which he was buried. But what was their astonishment and fear when, the three days having expired, (3) *they saw a Demon come out in the shape of a Wolf* <note>original Greek: "Ὡς λύκος, ἐν αὐτῷ Δαίμων ἐφάνη, τῆς σωρᾶ τῶν λιθῶν ἐξερχόμενος."</note>. From this comes the fact that the Greeks call this Peter **Lycopetros**, that is to say, **Peter the Wolf**, and his Disciples, **Lycopetrians**.

This is the fine piece that the learned (4) *Lambecius* <note>Peter Lambeck (1628–1680), a German historian and librarian to the Emperor.</note> communicated as a precious fragment to the late Mr. *Cotelier* <note>Jean-Baptiste Cotelier (1629–1686), a French scholar who specialized in early Christian literature.</note>, to enrich his Remarks on the Monuments of the Greek Church. For my part, if I had to illustrate this fable, I would add the one I found in *Philostratus* <note>Flavius Philostratus (c. 170–247 AD), author of the "Life of Apollonius of Tyana."</note>, for I am much mistaken if it is not the original that *Euthymius*, or other Monks before him, have imitated.

...seemed so barbaric, they hesitated to execute it: but finally, someone having begun to throw stones at this miserable man, his eyes were suddenly seen to spark and become all flaming. The Ephesians then recognized that they were stoning a Demon. Indeed, *Apollonius* <note>Apollonius of Tyana was a 1st-century Greek philosopher and reputed miracle-worker often compared to Jesus in antiquity.</note> having commanded that they remove the stones covering this monster, they found only *a large mastiff, black as a blackberry, as large as the greatest lions, spewing from its mouth a foul and stinking foam*, as rabid dogs are accustomed to do. <margin>X. *Manichaeus benefits from the promise of the Paraclete.*</margin>
X. All these examples confirm what I intended to prove: that, under the slightest pretext, the Ancients accused Heretics of usurping Divinity. They accused *Manichaeus* <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion.</note> of this, like the others, though he was quite innocent of it: *this is what must be proven*.

Persian historians assert that (5) *Zoroaster* <note>The ancient Iranian prophet and founder of Zoroastrianism.</note> discovered, by favor of his science in Astrology, that the time had come when a Prophet of the same order as *Moses* should arise, who would acquire a great reputation in the world and great authority through the extent of his Light and through the use of fire in Divine Service. This testimony from *Chondemir* <note>Ghiyas ad-Din Khwandamir, a 15th-16th century Persian historian.</note> seems to suppose that the Impostor had knowledge of the Oracle where *Moses* predicted the coming of a prophet like himself, and that he took it into his head to pass for that Prophet. I do not know if this account is entirely accurate, but it is certain that *Manichaeus* wished to benefit in his turn from the promise that Jesus Christ made to his Apostles to send them the Paraclete <note>From the Greek 'parakletos,' meaning 'advocate' or 'comforter,' usually identified by Christians as the Holy Spirit.</note>. Persian and Arabic writers agree on this with the Christians, and the Manichaeans maintain that their Master received the Spirit promised by Jesus Christ. *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a 4th-century Manichaean bishop famous for his debates with Saint Augustine.</note> said to Saint *Augustine*: (6) "The Paraclete, who was promised to us in the New Testament, teaches us what we must receive from this Book, and what we must reject from it." Now, it is through *Manichaeus* that his followers claimed to have this knowledge. Thus, when Saint *Augustine* wanted to show *Felix* <note>Another Manichaean leader with whom Augustine held a public debate.</note> that the Paraclete had come a few days after the Ascension of the Lord, the Heretic replied to him, (b) "that the Spirit communicated to the Apostles was not..."

<margin>Never titles himself anything but APOSTLE OF JESUS CHRIST.</margin>
This Proof, which is, in my view, a clear Demonstration, is confirmed by the repeated declarations of the Heresiarch <note>A "Heresiarch" is the founder or leader of a heretical sect or movement.</note>. If he had claimed to be the *Paraclete* <note>The "Paraclete" is the "Comforter" or Holy Spirit promised by Jesus in the Gospel of John.</note>, or the *Holy Spirit*, he would have titled himself as such in his Letters. Why would he have hidden from his Disciples what he wanted the whole world to believe? However, he never takes any title other than that of APOSTLE OF JESUS CHRIST. *St. Augustine (5)* testifies in his own words that he began ALL his letters with these words: MANICHAEUS, APOSTLE OF JESUS CHRIST. Indeed, it is in this manner that he titles himself in his famous *(6)* Epistle of the Foundation; in *(c)* the one he wrote to *Menoch*, his spiritual Daughter; in *(d)* the one he wrote to *Marcellus* when he wished to go to *Cascar*, and which I reported in the first Part. His *Devotees*, his *Perfects* <note>The "Perfects" or "Elect" were the elite tier of the Manichaean community who followed the strictest ascetic rules.</note>, gave him no other title than that. *Victor of Vite* recounts *(7)* that among the Manichaeans of Africa, whom *Hunneric* <note>Hunneric was a King of the Vandals who persecuted various Christian sects in the 5th century.</note> punished with the ultimate penalty, there was found one of their Monks named CLEMENTIANUS, who had written on his thigh, MANICHAEUS, DISCIPLE OF JESUS CHRIST. This was, therefore, the only quality the Heresiarch had claimed for himself: the only praise his followers gave him.

One reads in all the Modern authors that *Manichaeus* said he was the Holy Spirit; while we have incontestable proofs to the contrary, proofs attested to by his own Accusers. Holy *Spirit*? Is *Jesus Christ* the LORD of the *Holy Spirit*, who is a Divine Person just as much as He is? Who is of the same Divinity as He? Is *Jesus Christ* the SAVIOR of the *Holy Spirit*? Was this Divine *Spirit* ever subject to Sin & condemnation? <note>The author is using rhetorical questions to demonstrate the theological absurdity (from an orthodox perspective) of Mani being the Holy Spirit if Christ is Mani's Savior.</note>

<margin>XI. His Disciples only believed him to be a great Saint, & a Prophet inspired by the Paraclete. Testimonies of St. Augustine.</margin>

XI. What then was the Sentiment of the Manichaeans regarding the *Person* & the Ministry of their Patriarch? I answer, that regarding his Person, they believed him to be a *Man* & a *mere Man*, but a very great *Saint*: Thus they usually titled him, OUR BLESSED FATHER, just as Monks title the Founders of their Orders. And regarding his Ministry, they believed him an Apostle of *Jesus Christ*, superior in his Enlightenments to the first Apostles, because the Holy *Spirit* had revealed Truths to him that the Lord had not judged appropriate to entrust to His Disciples. In a word, they believed him a Prophet enlightened immediately by the Holy *Spirit*, who resided in him, & spoke through his mouth. And St. *Augustine* himself, having quite recently left Manichaeism & writing to his friend *Honoratus*, who was still a Manichaean, did not dare say more than this. (1) *You know*, he says to him, *that the Manichaeans, wishing to place* AMONG THE NUMBER OF THE APOSTLES *Manichaeus their Master, say that the* HOLY SPIRIT HAS COME TO US THROUGH HIM. They did not, therefore, wish to make him a GOD, whom they would *worship*, as Pope *Leo I* says. They only wished to make him an APOSTLE. Nor did they pretend that he was the Holy *Spirit*: but only, *that the Holy Spirit came to us through him*. Elsewhere, St. *Augustine* questioning our Heretics, & asking them how they knew that the Son of God was not born of a Virgin, he puts this response in their mouths, (2) *it is through the* HOLY SPIRIT, WHO WAS IN MANICHAEUS.

<margin>Concerning a Formula of abjuration from the 6th Century.</margin>

We have a *Formula of abjuration* <note>A formal statement of renunciation of heresy required by the Church for those returning to orthodoxy.</note>, which the Latins had read & signed in the 6th Century by all those suspected of Manichaeism. They were obliged to anathematize <note>To "anathematize" is to formally denounce or curse a doctrine or person as excommunicated.</note>, not, *whoever believes that Manichaeus is the Paraclete* <note>The "Paraclete" is the Comforter or Holy Spirit promised by Jesus in the Gospel of John.</note>, but (3) *whoever believes that the Spirit Paraclete* HAS COME INTO MANICHAEUS. And subsequently, (4) *Anathema to whoever believes that Manes or Manichaeus* POSSESSED THE HOLY SPIRIT: And again, (5) *Anathema, to whoever believes that the Spirit Paraclete* HAS COME THROUGH HIM. The truth is, therefore, that Manichaeus was struck by the same Fanaticism <note>In this 18th-century context, "fanaticism" refers to the claim of receiving private, direct divine revelations.</note>

<margin>XII. *St. Augustine doubts whether Manichaeus called himself the Paraclete or the Minister of the Paraclete. Reflection on this doubt.*</margin>

XII. After such formal and precise declarations, I do not understand how *St. Augustine* could have been in such uncertainty regarding the idea the Manichaeans had of the Person of their Master. He asserts in his Books against *Faustus*, (7) "that the promise of *Jesus Christ* provided the Manichaeans with a pretext to say, EITHER THAT MANICHAEUS WAS THE PARACLETE, OR THAT THE PARACLETE WAS IN MANICHAEUS." These two propositions are as different as these: *the Paraclete was in St. Peter*, or, *St. Peter was the Paraclete*: and what amounts to the same thing, *St. Peter was the Holy Spirit*, or, *the Holy Spirit was in St. Peter*. Now, how is it that *St. Augustine*, after nine years of Manichaeism, could be in doubt whether our heretics believed their Master to be a Divine Person, or a man divinely inspired? Can one imagine that this Father was ignorant of what their true belief was on an article that was the basis of their heresy? Will a clever man be a Christian for nine years without knowing what Christians think of the Person of *Jesus Christ*? Whether they believe him a simple Man, who is the Son of God only through the miraculous gifts that the Holy Spirit conferred upon him: or whether they believe him a Divine Person who has clothed himself in Human Nature. I cannot extract myself from such an embarrassing question except by a solution that gives me pain. It is that in changing "Parties" <note>In this context, "Parties" refers to religious sects or theological camps.</note>, men change their ideas. They no longer see the same things with the same eye. One would say that it is with their mind as it is with our eyes. Their mind no longer discerns the errors of the Party they have left as they move further away from it. As long as *St. Augustine* was a Manichaean, he regarded Manichaeus only as an *Apostle of Jesus Christ*, extraordinarily enlightened by the lights of the Holy Spirit. Could he have had any other idea, he who, at that time, could not persuade himself that *Jesus Christ* was anything other than a simple Man? Could he then place Manichaeus—who only took the title of His disciple—above *Jesus Christ*? But what this Father would have regarded as a lie when he was a Manichaean, to him [now...]
