### CHAPTER III.

#### Second Principle of the Manichaeans: THEY REJECT THE OLD TESTAMENT. Their Pretexts.

<margin>I. The Manichaeans reject the Old Testament.</margin>
**I. M**ANI, having seized the title and authority of an Apostle of Jesus Christ—but an Apostle superior in his Enlightenment to the first Apostles, and one to whom the Holy Spirit had revealed truths unknown to them—no longer felt bound by any rule. He raised himself above the Holy Scriptures and began by rejecting the Old Testament. I do not know precisely what he thought of this ancient Revelation, but some of his followers had the audacity to speak of it with contempt, and even to treat the God of the Hebrews with (1) the most profane insolence.

<margin>Some more, some less.</margin>
As the Manichaeans were divided into different sects, they were not unanimous regarding the Old Testament. *Hierax*, for example, who is counted among the leaders of these heretics, <margin>(b) Epiphanius, Heresies LXVII. p. 710.</margin> (b) honored the memory of *Abraham* and the Patriarchs <note>The "Patriarchs" refer to the biblical fathers of the Hebrew people, such as Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.</note> of the Hebrews, whereas the Manichaeans of Africa unleashed a torrent of insults against these holy men. Furthermore, this African sect challenged the authenticity (2) of the first three chapters of *Genesis*, without troubling themselves (3) as to whether *Moses* was the author of that book or not. But *Hierax*, being wiser and more moderate, explained the History of Creation by Moses, <margin>(c) Epiphanius, ibid. p. 712.</margin> (c) while mixing into it, according to St. Epiphanius, a great many fables and empty allegories <note>Hierax was a 3rd-century scholar who, like many in that era, looked for hidden spiritual meanings (allegories) rather than literal history in the Bible.</note>. I do not know which specific type of Manichaeans *Leontius of Byzantium* intended to speak of, but he asserts (4) that they rejected only some books of the Old Testament, and in particular that of *Exodus*, under the pretext that it did not befit a good God to lead the Israelites out of Egypt only to inflict so many evils upon them in the desert. As far as I can judge, our heretics believed that the books of the Old Testament were a mixture of fables and truths.

(1) <note>original: "Sane Judæo si credat, ADONEUS debet videri defunctus, Gentili vero Idolum."</note> "Truly, if the Jew believes, ADONAI must appear dead; to the Gentile, indeed, an Idol." Faustus, quoted in Augustine, Book XV. 1. Instead of saying, like St. Paul, that we are dead to the Law and that it is dead to us, Faustus dares to say that ADONAI is dead for the Christian. *Adonai* is one of the names the Hebrews give to the true God, which is translated as "Lord."</margin>

They acknowledged that **Adam** had been the first man, and that he sinned. They placed **Seth**, **Enoch**, **Noah**, **Shem**, and other Patriarchs in the rank of the Righteous: But regarding the Doctrines, the Worship, and the Morality taught in these Sacred Books, they disapproved of them, and here are, in general, the Pretexts with which they colored their Unbelief.

<margin>II. Their Objections against this Sacred Book.</margin>
II. First, that the ideas of the Divinity found therein are not pure, and that some are even false and insulting to God. 2. Second, that its Morality is not perfect enough, and does not correspond to the Holiness of God. 3. Third, that these Books contain no promise of Eternal Life, and that the temporal promises, with which they are filled, are only fit to nourish the carnal inclinations of men. 4. Fourth, that the Mosaic Worship, and its religious ceremonies, are altogether unworthy of the Divinity. 5. Fifth, that the Histories of the Creation and the Temptation of Man are false and absurd. 6. Sixth, that it is not true that the Prophets of the Hebrews predicted the advent, the Preaching, the crucifixion, the resurrection, etc., of the Savior.

These are, in general, the Objections that the Manichaeans made against the Old Testament. They added that this Revelation, and 그at of the Son of God, were too contrary to draw their origin from the same Spirit. I did not believe I should hide these difficulties, since St. **Augustine** did not do so, and because, at heart, it is easy to resolve them. However, so that the least instructed Reader is not obliged to ruminate on them, I will make some reflections on each in passing.

<margin>III. First Pretext of the Manichaeans. Moses and the Prophets did not have just ideas of the Divinity.</margin>
III. *First Pretext*. The Manichaeans did not claim that the Divinity was exempt from every kind of *affections*. They gave Him (1) *desires* and *inclinations*, because they believed them inseparable from every intelligent Being. But conceiving Goodness as the first and most essential Property of God, they required that all these Desires tend toward the Good, toward the Happiness of all Beings that God formed, and that the Divinity never do them harm. <margin>The good God cannot do evil.</margin> *I say, the Beings that God formed; for as for Matter, and the Demons, they did not find it strange that God should punish them.*

### OF MANICHAEISM. Book I. Ch. III. ###

<columns>
<margin>The Opinion of the Philosophers.</margin>
It was a principle recognized by excellent Philosophers (2), that what is good can never do evil, nor can what is bad do good: "That it is as impossible for the Just to do evil to anyone at all, as it is impossible for what is hot to cool. Now, God is by His nature the most just of all beings; otherwise He would not be God." Prejudiced in favor of this principle, which is true in itself but which our Heretics <note>The "Heretics" referred to here are the Manichaeans, viewed from the perspective of the orthodox author.</note> pushed too far or understood poorly, they regarded as so many blasphemies these words of Moses or of the Prophets (a): <margin>(a) See the *Philocalia*, <note>original: "Philocalie"</note> Ch. I. p. 6, 7. *Acts of the Disputation of Archelaus*, p. 25. Faustus in Augustine, Book XV, beginning; Book XXII, 4, and elsewhere.</margin> *The anger of the Eternal was kindled like a fire, etc. The Eternal is a jealous God, who punishes the iniquity of the fathers upon the children, etc. He repented of having anointed Saul as King. There is no evil in the City that the Lord has not done.* An evil spirit, sent from God, choked Saul, etc. They judged similarly regarding the order that Moses gave to the Israelites to carry away the vessels and precious garments of the Egyptians, and to massacre the peoples of Canaan without sparing age or sex. They concluded from this that the God of the Hebrews was not the true God, or that their Prophets were not true prophets, or finally that their books had been corrupted by the Jews.

<margin>Some Christians justify Moses by saying he did not write the Law.</margin>
There were some Christians who held nothing of Manichaeism and who, wishing to defend Moses and the true God against the objections of the Heretics, took the side of saying (b) that this Legislator <note>Referring to Moses.</note> had not written the Law at all; that he had only taught it orally to the Elders of the People; that it was only written down later, and that having been lost, those who had redacted it in writing had mixed into it a quantity of false things. They claimed that our Lord had hinted at this corruption of the Law when he said to the Sadducees (3): *You err, because you do not know WHAT IS TRUE in the Scriptures.* This was how the author who took the name of Clement of Rome <note>Referring to the *Pseudo-Clementine* writings, an early Christian romance and theological work.</note> read it. From this, he concluded that there is Falsehood mixed with the Truth in the Old Testament. One should not be surprised, then, if among the early Heretics there were so many who wished to receive this Revelation only with several restrictions. They claimed to be following the orders of Jesus Christ in doing so (4).

<margin>(b) See the *Clementines*, Homily II, § 31, p. 633; Homily III, § 42, p. 643; Ibid. p. 645.</margin>

...considered, that the language of these holy men is a popular language, and that it had to be so. Metaphysical ideas of Divinity are not suited to preachers who wish to instruct and correct a common people. Secondly, when the Prophets attribute human passions to God, they ultimately attribute only their legitimate effects to Him. **Anger** is nothing more than the just punishment of sin; **jealousy** is but a just aversion to idolatry, which the Scripture very elegantly calls adultery, and so forth. In the third place, the sovereignty of the Master of the Universe alone would suffice to justify the severe orders that God gave to the Israelites regarding the Canaanites, whose crimes had reached their peak. The Manichaeans <note>Manichaeism was a major dualistic religion that saw the world as a struggle between a good realm of light and an evil realm of darkness; they often rejected the Old Testament as the work of the evil principle.</note> themselves did not dare to deny that God is the (1) just avenger of crimes. **Goodness itself** punishes for the sake of example, to correct obstinate sinners, and to protect a nation whose morals are honest from the **contagion** of corrupt nations. Finally, when these heretics were pressed by the Orthodox and could not provide a reason for Divine actions, (2) they knew well how to retreat into the submission that the creature owes to the Creator, and to impose silence on the murmurs of man with these words of St. Paul: <margin>(a) Rom. IX. 20.</margin> (a) *Will the thing formed say to him who formed it, "Why have you made me this way?"* <note>original Latin: "nunquid dixit figmentum &c."</note>

<margin>IV. Second Pretext. The Morality of the Old Testament.</margin>
IV. The second **pretext** of the Manichaeans. Photius <note>Photius (c. 810–893) was a Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar who documented many "heretical" beliefs.</note> accuses them (3) of attributing to the evil principle—to **Satan**—ALL THE DEEDS AND ALL THE WORDS CONTAINED IN THE OLD TESTAMENT. This is not true, and to speak plainly, it is a pure calumny. Here are their true sentiments:

That the moral (4) precepts contained in the Law, such as *You shall not kill*, etc., had not been revealed first to Moses, since they were as (5) ancient as the world itself. They believed that the Angels of Light had instructed the Patriarchs in them, and that the Patriarchs had transmitted them to all their descendants; that this was the eternal, invariable law, the **Law of Truth**. They held that Moses had merely taken advantage of it and inserted it into his (6) <term>Diptychium Lapideum (Stone Diptych): A dismissive term used by the Manichaean Faustus to describe the two Tablets of the Law (the Ten Commandments).</term> Furthermore, they claimed he had corrupted and disfigured this Divine Law by mixing into it, on the one...

Our Heretics <note>The Manichaeans.</note> then censured, with a bold and profane liberty, various Mosaic Laws: For example, the one that permitted Divorce, the one that commanded a Brother to marry the Widow of his Brother if he died without leaving children, etc. They claimed that laws of this nature directly offended the Moral Perfections of the Divinity. They declaimed (8) against the most illustrious Patriarchs, whose flaws they highlighted with the most insolent malice. Finally, they did not even spare (9) the God of the Hebrews, and said, to excuse their blasphemies, (10) that they were not attacking the true God, but rather Impostors who had corrupted his Laws and abused his sacred Name to authorize their false Religions.

<margin>Response to their Objections.</margin>
Although this Objection against the Old Testament contains several impieties, let us nevertheless judge it equitably and with moderation. 1. One must agree that Moral Precepts were older than Moses. But does it follow from this that God had not given him the **Decalogue**, in which they are contained? Is it not entirely worthy of a sovereignly wise and sovereignly holy Being, who founds a new Republic, to renew at the same time Laws that were poorly observed, to mark them with his Seal, and to arm them with his Authority? 2. One is quite willing to agree with the Manichaeans that the Commandment of the Sabbath was new, and that it had not been observed by the Predecessors of the Hebrews. But could they deny in turn that its institution was very wise and very just? It was, on one hand, the Feast and the Memorial of the Creation of the World, and on the other, a Preservative to protect the Israelites against the Idolatry of the Gentiles. 3. It is a very problematic Question, <margin>(a) This refers to the Sermon of Jesus Christ. *Matt.* V. 21. and following.</margin> (a) whether Jesus Christ only developed the sense of the Moral Law, or if he gave it an extent and a perfection that it did not have. <margin>Reasons of the Manichaeans against these promises.</margin>

<margin>Reflection on this Objection.</margin>
Here is, without a doubt, a Sect very detached from the world, and whose affections are highly *spiritualized*. I am willing to suppose that all this discourse is sincere, although there is perhaps more ostentation and hypocrisy than reality. However, it is easy to defend the Old Testament and the true God against these frivolous objections, 
<margin>(a) Book I. Chap. III. p. 46. and following.</margin>
to which *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an English theologian. His work *De Legibus Hebraeorum* (On the Laws of the Hebrews) was foundational in the study of comparative religion, suggesting that God adapted Jewish rituals from existing pagan customs to slowly lead the Israelites away from idolatry.</note> has made a very solid response in his (a) excellent Work *on the ceremonial Laws of the Hebrews*. The Heretics dare to make a crime against God out of the condescension He had for a carnal People, who found themselves surrounded by Idolatrous Nations to whom their false Gods made similar promises. He wished to prevent, through this condescension, the defection of this People. This is the response of *Spencer*. It has the advantage of solidity. It satisfies a reasonable Mind; whereas the Church Fathers, who throw themselves into Allegory and Mysticism, only touch upon the difficulty and can only satisfy Minds that are happily biased in favor of the Faith. Furthermore, it is true, as *Spencer* recognized, that the Books of *Moses* contain no *clear* promise of Eternal Life. It is also true that this life was not the reward for observing the Mosaic Covenant, as St. Paul showed. But it is no less true that the ancient Fathers hoped for an immortal Life, as the Divine Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews teaches in Chapter XI and shows in particular by the example of *Enoch*, who was transported into Heaven. However, the Reader must be warned that the Manichaeans did not believe (1) that *Enoch* or *Elijah* had been transported alive into the abode of bliss. I add that, if we believe *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve was a 4th-century Manichaean Bishop. He is primarily known through the writings of Saint Augustine, who wrote a massive refutation against him.</note>, (2) the Catholics maintained in his time that *Moses* had the same privilege, which is not at all founded in Scripture.

Their Error on this subject had, if I am not mistaken, the same origin as their Error regarding the promises of the Law.

# ABOUT MANICHAEISM. BOOK I. CH. III.
->Mm 3<-

<margin>The judgment of the Pagan Theologians was in agreement with theirs.</margin>
...well that St. Paul says, (3) THE GOD WHO IS ABOVE ALL THINGS <note>original: "LE DIEU QUI EST AU DESSUS DE TOUTES CHOSES"</note> cannot, nor should not, be honored by bloody sacrifices. As he is perfectly (4) "incorporeal and immaterial," everything that is Matter, everything that is sensible <note>Meaning anything that can be perceived by the five senses.</note> is impure in his eyes. One must not even offer him perfumes, nor praise him in hymns. The only Worship that suits him is that of a Soul purified of vicious Passions, which honors him in silence, through contemplation alone, and by the admiration of his Virtues.

Regarding the (5) *Intelligible Gods* <term>Intelligible Gods: In the Neoplatonic tradition, these are divine beings or "good Angels" that exist in the realm of the intellect, above the material world.</term>, that is to say the good Angels, who are the *children of the supreme God*, one may honor them with hymns, but these hymns must be dictated by (6) *Reason* and *Wisdom*. The Philosophers did not approve of those foolish praises that the Poets gave to the Gods, by which a virtuous man would have felt offended.

<margin>Only Demons require Sacrifices. Testimony of Porphyry.</margin>
This is all that these ancient Theologians <note>Referring to Neoplatonists like Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD), who argued that the supreme deity requires no material offerings.</note> believed should be offered to the true God, and to good Spirits, the pure Intelligences. But as for bloody Sacrifices, they were persuaded (7) that it was only the Demons who demanded them; because, being material and clothed in subtle Bodies, they nourished themselves on the vapor of the blood of the Victims and the smoke exhaled by their flesh burned on the altars. From this, these Theologians concluded (8) that a religious and prudent man would take great care not to offer such Sacrifices, because they would only serve to win him the favor of Demons. This is why his entire study will be to purify his Soul, because it is the only victim that is pleasing to the true God.

VII. Such were the general Objections that the Manichaeans raised against Mosaical Worship and Laws. <margin>Explanation of verse 23 of Chapter XXI of Deuteronomy.</margin>
3. Regarding the Ordinance of Chapter XXI of Deuteronomy, Verse 23: in attacking it, the Heretics showed only the vain subtlety of the most malicious Sophists. Moses commands that criminals put to death by justice, whose bodies were hung on gibbets, be removed and buried the same day, because *whoever hangs on wood is an object of Curse before God, or from God*. The sense is that God hates crime, and that the body of the criminal, dead though it is, must be removed from before His eyes, because it is an object of horror to Him. This is figurative: we well know that a body hidden under the earth is no less present to God than when exposed to the light of the Sun. ### CHAPTER IV.

#### *THE OLD TESTAMENT poorly defended by most of the Fathers. What the Manichaeans thought of the salvation of JOHN THE BAPTIST and of the JEWS.*

<margin>I. The Fathers did not always defend the Old Testament well.</margin>
I. I have just reported the principal Objections of the Manichaeans against the Old Testament. The Fathers tried to respond to them, but, if I dare say so, they did not always succeed well. Constrained by false Principles, they sometimes denied what should have been admitted, and admitted what should have been denied: And then, unable to extricate themselves from difficulties except by twisting the Scriptures and by resorting to wretched Allegories, they betrayed, so to speak, the Cause they wished to defend. Let us give some examples of this.

<margin>They applied to Jesus Christ Oracles that do not suit him.
(a) *Deut.* XXVIII. 6.</margin>
*Moses says that the Israelites (a) shall see their life hanging, and that they shall not believe.* <note>The author refers to Deuteronomy 28:66, which in many early Christian interpretations was read as a prophecy of Christ hanging on the cross.</note> The Catholics insisted (1) upon these words, claiming that they contained a clear and precise prediction of the crucifixion of the Savior, and of the Unbelief of the Jews. Some even had the boldness to add these words, (2) ON THE WOOD <note>original: "AU BOIS" / "IN LIGNO"</note>, and to make Moses say; *They shall see their life hanging* ON THE WOOD, although these words were neither in the Hebrew, nor in the LXX <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note>, as Faustus <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean bishop and contemporary of Augustine.</note> rightly reproaches St. Augustine. Although it is evident that it concerns neither Jesus Christ nor his death in the Oracle of Moses, this Father nonetheless persists in maintaining (b),

<margin>(b) *Ibid.* Book XVI. 22.</margin>
> „ that one cannot deny that this Oracle can be explained as 
> „ Jesus Christ, without denying at the same time that the Lord is *the* 
> „ *life of the World*; that the Jews saw him hanging on the Cross, and 
> „ that they remained unfaithful.

<header>HISTORY OF DOGMAS</header>
<meta>catchword: Therefore</meta>

to apply the words to an Event of the New Testament. In such cases, it is permitted to pay no attention to what follows, nor to the Author's goal, nor to the thought he wished to express. The reason is that these types of applications are fundamentally nothing more than allusions—ingenious accommodations—and not Proofs. They adorn a Proposition, but do not confirm it. But when it is a matter of showing that a Prophet predicted an Event, it is not enough to be able to accommodate the Prophet’s terms to that Event. It must further appear that his intention was to predict it, and that the meaning given to his terms is the one he had in mind; or at least that it is the meaning which the Spirit animating him intended to announce. It is true that the sacred Writers of the New Testament do not always seem to have subjected themselves to this Rule of Criticism <note>The author uses "Critique" in the sense of biblical exegesis and historical analysis.</note>. But it must also be agreed that in those cases, the explanations they give to the Oracles of the Old Testament drew all their force and evidence from the Divine Authority with which these Interpreters were clothed. They are divinely inspired Interpreters, whose Doctrine was attested by the Gifts and Miracles of the Holy Spirit.

<margin>III. They evade Objections through frivolous Allegories.</margin>
III. The Laws of *Moses* are certainly very wise, and the more one examines their motives, the more one esteems the prudence of the Legislator. He had commanded that a Brother should marry the Widow of his Brother when the latter died without leaving children, and that whoever refused to submit to this Law should be covered in disgrace <note>This refers to the "Levirate Law" found in Deuteronomy 25:5-10, intended to preserve a man's lineage.</note>. This gives *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean bishop and contemporary of Augustine.</note> the occasion to say to *St. Augustine*, (a) "If such Laws are good, why do you not observe them? And if they are bad, why do you not condemn their Author?" Nothing would be weaker than this Objection if it were not supported by false Principles. But when one has supposed that second Marriages are at most tolerated—just as God tolerated Divorce—and that the Marriage of a Brother with his Brother's Widow has something incestuous about it, what means remains to justify a Legislator who not only tolerates, but commands both? One must therefore seek safety in Allegory. (1) The dead Brother is Jesus Christ; the Widow is his Church; the living Brother is the Preacher of the Gospel, who must provide children for the dead Jesus Christ. If one wished to press *St. Augustine* on this point, how many absurdities would spring from such a poor explanation?

<margin>Or by bad solutions.</margin>
We have seen the fury with which *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent 4th-century Manichaean bishop known for his critiques of the Old Testament.</note> treated *Moses*, because of the Law, which declares a **Curse from God, or before God, against anyone who hangs on a tree**. <note>A reference to Deuteronomy 21:23, which was a point of contention because Jesus was crucified ("hung on a tree").</note> He accuses the Prophet of having cursed the Son of God. What does *St. Augustine* reply? He answers, (2) that this Curse strikes not *Jesus Christ*, but the "old man," <note>A theological term for the sinful human nature that Christians believe was symbolically killed with Christ’s crucifixion.</note> whom *Jesus Christ* crucified, and Death, which he hung upon the tree.

<margin>Other bad allegories.</margin>
The Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious sect that viewed the material world as evil and often rejected the God of the Old Testament as being too "fleshy" or carnal.</note> found that the happiness promised to the Just man in *Psalm CXXVIII* is quite carnal: *Blessed is the man who fears the Lord and walks in His ways: his wife shall be like a fertile vine; he shall see around his table a great number of children like young olive trees.* This objection—so vain in itself and so weak against a theologian who has sound ideas about Marriage and who knows that the preference given by *Jesus Christ* and the Apostles to Celibacy is based not on the nature of these two states but on varying circumstances—this objection, I say, so embarrasses *St. Augustine* that he can only answer by saying that this *Wife* is the Church; that her *Husband* is *Jesus Christ*; and that the Prophet predicted the fertility of the Christian Church in this Psalm. These ingenious discoveries lack only an explanation of how what the same Prophet said of the Just man also applies to *Jesus Christ*: *He shall live by the labor of his hands.* Were not the Lord’s hands pierced with nails?

These same heretics attacked the History of the Creation; but as skillful as this Father <note>A term for early influential Christian teachers and bishops.</note> may be, he does not defend it; he surrenders it to his adversary. If he is to be believed, *the greenery of the fields designates Souls*, and when *Moses* says, <margin>(b) *Genesis II. 5.* (c) *On Genesis against the Manichaeans, Book II. 3. Retractions, Book I. 10.*</margin> (b) **that there was as yet no greenery on the earth**, it means, (c) that *Souls* had not yet conceived earthly affections. The Manichaeans objected: how could a wise and good God create plants that are either poisonous or fruitless? He gets out of it by saying that they were only created after the sin of Man—that is to say, he resolves a minor difficulty with a greater one.

...others superstitious, or unreasonable to those who do not know their true motives, were only introduced to serve as a Preservative against Idolatry. I do not know if *Theodore of Mopsuestia* and *Diodore of Tarsus*, two of the most learned Bishops of Antiquity, discovered this purpose of the Mosaic Laws; but (1) they both banished from their Commentaries on the Old Testament all that jumble of Allegories, attaching themselves solely to explaining the literal sense well. <margin>VII. It is dangerous to criticize what the sacred Authors say. Examples.</margin>
VII. Without employing the secular Arm against them, without burning their Books, without resorting to arbitrary Allegories—which are very often full of contradictions—our skillful Moderns would have defended *Moses* and the Prophets, and shown to these proud Heretics <margin>(b) I. Corinthians I:23.</margin> *(b) that the Foolishness of God is wiser than the Wisdom of men*. ->### ON MANICHAEUS. BOOK I. CHAPTER IV.<-
Oo
<meta>catchword: A</meta>

*Tooth, etc.* <note>Referring to the "eye for an eye, tooth for a tooth" law of retaliation from Exodus 21:24, which Manichaeans used to argue that the Old Testament God was vengeful.</note> But these Heretics did not consider that *Moses* and *Jesus Christ* are very different Legislators. They are both indeed Divine Legislators: but *Moses* is a Political Legislator, as well as a Religious one. He establishes a Religion, but he founds at the same time a Republic <note>In this context, "Republic" refers to the civil state or commonwealth of the Israelites.</note>, which cannot subsist without penal Laws. It must even be considered that *Moses* governed a People composed of Persons who all believed themselves equal, who were not at all accustomed to obeying the Leaders of their Nation, and were always ready to murmur and to rise up against them. From this come the examples of rigor that one sees in the Books of *Moses* and against which the Manichaeans exclaimed. But *Jesus Christ* is not a Political Legislator: he does not found a Republic or a Monarchy: he gives Precepts to individuals; he wishes, so to speak, to form true Philosophers, and to raise men to the most sublime virtues. The Christian Magistrate pardons injuries as a Christian, and punishes them as a Magistrate. In the former, he follows the precepts of *Jesus Christ*; in the latter, he conforms to those of *Moses*. These two characters are not at all incompatible.

<margin>IX. The Manichaeans did not condemn *John the Baptist*. *Didymus of Alexandria* and *Photius* corrected.</margin>
IX. Before leaving the Article of the Old Testament, I must say what the Manichaeans thought of *John the Baptist*, and of the salvation of the Jewish Patriarchs.

*Didymus of Alexandria* <note>A 4th-century blind theologian from Alexandria who was a major opponent of Manichaeism.</note> accuses the Manichaeans of having condemned *John the Baptist*, (2) as a man *who belonged to the Law*, and *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and influential scholar.</note> adds, (3) that *they blasphemed the Precursor* <note>A traditional title for John the Baptist, as he "ran before" Jesus to announce his coming.</note>. He has this Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical movement.</note> say, (4) "that *John the Baptist* had preached the Kingdom of Heaven, and that he had wished to show by the manner of his execution (he was beheaded) that everything which had preceded him, namely the Law of *Moses*, was henceforth abolished, and that one must keep only the Doctrine that was announced after him." This Mystical explanation of the execution of St. *John* is worth as much as most of the Allegories of the Church Fathers, and shows that he was Orthodox on the Article of the Precursor. He might well have justly blamed the <margin>(c) *See Matthew 11:2 and following, and what Faustus says. <margin>III. The Apocalypse, the Epistle of St. Jude, the Second of St. Peter, and the Second and Third of St. John were not received by the Manichaeans because they were not received by the Eastern Syrians. 1. The Apocalypse.</margin>
III. It does not appear that the Manichaeans had among their sacred Books either the Second Epistle of *St. Peter*, nor that of *St. Jude*, nor the Second and Third of *St. John*, nor the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note> of that Apostle. The reason is that all these Books were not recognized by the Eastern Churches at the time of the birth of Manichaeism, and they were not even so recognized for several centuries afterward.

"Regarding the *Apocalypse*, Mr. *Asseman* (1) testifies that neither *Ebedjesu*, Metropolitan of (2) *Sobe* and *Armenia*, nor *Gregory Barhebraeus*, nor *James of Edessa*, explained it, either because they did not recognize it as a Canonical Book, or because it is not found in the ancient Syriac Version of the New Testament, which the Syrians call the *Simple* <note>The Peshitta, the standard Syriac translation of the Bible</note>." The Author judges that this second reason is the most likely, but fundamentally it confirms the first. For, if the Syrians had recognized the authenticity of the *Apocalypse*, why would they not have translated it into their language, just as they did the other Books of the <margin>(a) Ibid. p. 15.</margin> New Testament? Thus, the same Author agrees (a) later on that the Eastern Churches of the Syrian Rite did not admit the *Apocalypse* into their Canon; *Barhebraeus* (3) rejected it absolutely, as a work either of *Cerinthus* <note>An early Gnostic teacher often accused by ancients of forging Revelation</note> or of some author who bore the name of *John*. A certain proof that the Eastern Syrians did not recognize the *Apocalypse* as a Divine Book is that (4) the two sects of the Nestorians and the Monophysites, otherwise so opposed, have no lesson in their Rituals taken from that Book. It is also not found in the Syriac manuscripts of the New Testament. It was not in the one that (5) *Moses Mardenus*, Deputy of Patriarch *Ignatius*, communicated to *Johann Albrecht von Widmanstetter*, and which was printed in Vienna in 1555.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on why the Manichaean canon excluded certain New Testament books. It specifically addresses the "minor" Catholic Epistles and the Book of Revelation, arguing that because the early Syriac churches (which influenced the regions where Manichaeism began) did not recognize these books, the Manichaeans did not either. # OF MANICHAEISM. BOOK I. CH. V.

<margin>2. The 4 Epistles. (b) Loc. cit. p. 9.</margin>
As for the Canonical Epistles, *Mr. Assemani (b)* <note>Joseph Simon Assemani (1687–1768), a Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note> acknowledges, following *Pococke* & *Fabricius*, whom he cites, that the Syrians receive only three of them: namely, that of *St. James*, the 1st of *St. Peter*, and the 1st of *St. John*. Likewise, *Abdisho* <note>Ebedjesu, a 14th-century East Syriac writer and bishop</note> did not include in his Catalog the four other Epistles, nor the *Apocalypse* <note>The Book of Revelation</note>. But *Abraham Ecchellensis* <note>A Maronite scholar who translated Syriac texts into Latin in the 17th century</note>, who had published this Catalog before *Mr. Assemani*, did not hesitate to add (6) the Epistle of *St. Jude* to it, and to place, after the entry for the Epistles of *St. Paul*: THE REVELATION of *St. John* was written in Greek on the Island of Patmos. This is a remarkable example of the bad faith of this Maronite. In the style of *Mr. Simon*, this is called "reforming the writings of the Ancients based on the word of the Moderns," but in the style of *Mr. Arnauld*, this is called "falsifying the writings of the Ancients," and I believe he is right.

<margin>Dishonesty of Abraham Ecchellensis.</margin>

<margin>Testimony of Cosmas, which confirms that of Assemani.</margin>
What *Mr. Assemani* says regarding the opinion of the Syrians touching the Canonical Epistles is confirmed by *Cosmas*, surnamed INDICOPLEUSTES <note>A 6th-century Greek traveler and monk whose name means "India-Voyager"</note>, because of his navigation to the Indies. This Author, who was Egyptian and flourished in the 6th Century, asserts (7) that the Syrians have only the 1st Epistle of *St. John*, the 1st of *St. Peter*, and that of *St. James*; and that regarding the four others, they are not even found in their Churches.

<margin>IV. Reflection on the Chinese Monument found in 1625. It is evidently a forgery.</margin>
IV. Manichaeism having thus been born in the East at a time when Christians had only that ancient common version of the New Testament, which is called <term>SIMPLE</term> <note>The Peshitta, the standard Syriac translation of the Bible, which originally excluded the minor Catholic Epistles and Revelation</note>, there is no likelihood that the Sect received either the *Apocalypse* or any of these latter Epistles. And this is, to say it in passing, an invincible proof of the forgery of the Chinese Monument <note>The Nestorian Stele, an 8th-century stone block documenting the arrival of Christianity in China</note> that the Jesuits claim to have found underground in 1625 near the City of *Xi'an-fu*, Metropolis of the Province of *Shaanxi*. The inscription read on this Monument states, among other things (8), that Jesus Christ, ascending to Heaven toward the hour of noon, LEFT TWENTY-SEVEN BOOKS, which contain his Doctrine. ->HISTORY OF DOGMAS<-

This false Principle having been assumed, our Heretics <note>The Manichaeans.</note> said that (1) "if Jesus Christ, who was predicted in the Old Testament, correctly made a separation of the Doctrine contained in that Book: if he excised the greater part of it, and preserved in his Religion only very little of it; likewise the PARACLETE <note>The "Comforter" or Holy Spirit, whom the Manichaeans believed was manifested in their leader, Mani.</note>, who was promised to us in the New Testament, has taught us what we must reject, Jesus Christ having said, *he will lead you into all truth*."

<margin>Rules of their Criticism: just but misapplied.
1. Two contradictory Propositions cannot be true.</margin>
I will not stop to refute a reasoning founded upon hypotheses that are evidently false. It is better to examine the Rules of Criticism used by the Manichaeans. For since it would be very absurd, and very suspect of imposture, for a man to proceed to reform Books authorized by the entire Christian Church without alleging any reason other than a pretended Inspiration, our Heretics tried to justify their Criticism, and for that purpose set down two general Rules. The first, "that two Propositions, or two contradictory Precepts, cannot both be true; and the Books of the New Testament containing such Precepts and Propositions, it was necessarily required that one or the other had been added by unfaithful men, and consequently must be excised." The Rule is excellent, but the application of it was worthless, as the Gospels do not contain such contradictions. One can find some apparent contrarieties there; some circumstances difficult to reconcile with others; but besides the fact that this concerns History and not Dogmas, at heart, their reconciliation is not impossible. However, our Heretics took advantage of this vain (2) pretext to excise from the Scriptures everything they could not reconcile with their Errors.

<margin>2nd Rule. Everything that offends Divine Perfections cannot be true.
(a) *As above, Book XXXII. 7.*</margin>
Their second Rule was, "that everything which appears to detract from the Greatness and Majesty of God, even if it be in the Scriptures, cannot be true." It is under this pretext that they rejected several facts clearly reported in the Gospels. "We do not receive from the New Testament," (a) says Faustus <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean bishop whose arguments were recorded and refuted by St. Augustine.</note>, "ONLY THAT WHICH IS HONORABLE TO THE SON OF MAJESTY";

Ipse vos inducet in omnem veritatem. Faust. ub. sup. L. XXXII. 6."</note> "If JESUS, promised through the Old Testament, now judges and sifts, and teaches that few of its parts are to be accepted, and very many rejected; and for us the PARACLETE, promised from the New Testament, likewise teaches what we ought to accept from the same, and what to reject, concerning whom Jesus further said... He himself will lead you into all truth." Faustus, as above, Book XXXII. 6.

<margin>Historical facts denied under this pretext.</margin>

We leave aside all the rest: not only what the Disciples put forward while they were still in ignorance, but also what the Writers of the Gospels imprudently inserted into the Scriptures and transmitted to Posterity. Thus, we do not believe what they tell us, (3) that the Son of God was shamefully born of a woman; that he was circumcised in the Jewish manner; (4) that he offered sacrifices in the Pagan manner; that he indignantly humbled himself so far as to receive Baptism; that he was led around everywhere in the Desert and miserably tempted by the Devil. We reject all of that, as well as what was taken from the Old Testament and falsely inserted into the New. But we believe all the rest, and especially the *mystical Crucifixion* of the Lord, through which he reveals to us the wounds of our Soul; his Parables, his Precepts, and in general all his (5) *Divine Discourses*, and in particular the passages where he clearly teaches that there are <term>two Natures</term> <note>The fundamental Manichaean doctrine of Dualism: the eternal struggle between the Kingdom of Light (God/the soul) and the Kingdom of Darkness (Matter/the body).</note>.

<margin>The Manichaeans receive all the Divine Discourses of the Lord.</margin>
Thus, what the Manichaeans removed from the Gospels was reduced principally to certain historical facts and to the passages from the Old Testament cited therein. They admitted the Instructions and the Commandments of the Lord, as St. *Augustine* testifies following *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean bishop and contemporary of Augustine.</note>. However, when someone opposed them with a word from the Son of God that appeared contrary to their System, they would first begin by explaining it in a sense favorable to them; but as a last resort, they would turn, says St. *Augustine*, (b) to that <term>Diabolical Privilege</term> <note>A phrase Augustine used to describe the Manichaean claim that any inconvenient text must have been "stuffed" or forged into the Bible by later editors.</note> which they had seized for themselves, and *would say that this word had been stuffed into the Gospel.*

<margin>(b) *Against Faustus*, Book XXII, 15.</margin>

<margin>They overturned 1. The Christian Religion.</margin>

<margin>2nd. Manichaeism.</margin>
But this supposition destroys Manichaeism no less: for the Apostleship of Mani being supported by the promise of the <term>Paraclete</term> <note>From the Greek 'parakletos', meaning 'advocate' or 'comforter'. You begin by accusing your witnesses of falsehood, and then you allege their testimony."

-># ON MANICHAEISM. Book I. Ch. V. <-

"...given the name OF THE GOSPEL, although it is a completely different Book." I have two Remarks to make on this passage.

<margin>The first fact is false.</margin>
1. It is not true that the Manichaeans did not possess the Gospels, nor that they did not read them. The contrary is evident from the little that remains of their Works, and by this response, which *St. Augustine* puts in the mouth of *Faustus* (4): THE FAITHFUL MUST READ THE GOSPELS, so as not to forget what they have believed. Furthermore, there is no accuracy in *saying* that our Heretics did not have *the Gospel in their own Language*. Was there then a specific Manichaean Language? A language proper to the Sect, in which it performed Divine Service and read the sacred Books? This custom of reading Scripture and performing service only in a certain <note>i.e., a "sacred" language like Latin or Sanskrit, rather than the common tongue.</note> language is much more modern than Manichaeism. Our Heretics spoke Greek in Greece, Syriac in Syria, Chaldean in Chaldea, and so on. They had many Books in Syriac, and if that is what *Titus of Bostra* <note>A 4th-century bishop known for writing against the Manichaeans.</note> calls *their language*, how could he say that they *did not have the Gospels in their language*, since the Syriac Version, which is called SIMPLE <note>The "Peshitta," the standard Syriac translation of the Bible.</note>, was made long before *Mani* came into the World. The Author perhaps wishes to speak of the *Persian Language*, because *Mani* was Persian. But who told him that the Persians did not have *the Gospel in their language*? (5) *St. Chrysostom* and *Theodoret* testify to the contrary. It is, moreover, certain that in the first Centuries, wherever the Christian Religion was established, versions of the New Testament in the common tongue were soon (6) available.

<margin>2. Examination of the second fact. The Gospel of the Manichaeans is either the DIATESSARON of Tatian.</margin>
2. Regarding *the Gospel* that *Titus of Bostra* claims was composed by the Manichaeans, it is, if I am not mistaken, either the DIATESSARON <note>A "Gospel Harmony" created by merging the four Gospels into a single continuous narrative.</note> of *Tatian*, or THE GOSPEL *according to the Syrians*. *Tatian*, a Philosopher as well as *Justin Martyr* his Master, and otherwise very learned, gathered into a single body the Accounts of the four Evangelists; he was the first to invent these *Harmonies*, or *Concords*, which appeared in the following years to be of great utility. *Concerning the Books of the Manichaeans, and primarily, the Books of the Philosophers, or the Prophets of the Gentiles. Their idea regarding Prophecy. The Religion of* ZOROASTER.

<margin>II. First TYPE. Books of the Philosophers. Principle of the Manichaeans for admitting the Books of the Philosophers. The Divine Word enlightens all these men.</margin>II. *Mani* <note>The French text uses "Manichée." Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the Persian prophet and founder of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that once rivaled Christianity.</note>, having examined the Books of the Hebrews in his own way, did not believe them to be inspired at all. He considered them at most as Books written by the Sages of that Nation, and for that Nation only, and was careful not to persuade himself that Religion and Wisdom were a deposit that God had entrusted only to them. According to him, the Legislator of the Hebrews <note>A reference to Moses.</note> did nothing but mix Pagan Ceremonies and some Histories—some true, others fabulous—with the Truths and Laws that the good Angels had taught the first Patriarchs. But these Truths and these Laws were not unknown to other Nations, who held them from the same source, and who have had their Sages and their Prophets as well as the Jews. *Mani* based this on the idea that Divine Wisdom never ceases to spread its Light in every direction and into all Spirits, in proportion to how much they are purified from the love of goods and sensible pleasures. There are only the clouds of earthly affections that prevent the rays of this spiritual Sun from penetrating into all Souls.

<header>OF MANI. BOOK I. CH. VI.</header>
->Qq 2<-

<margin>Opinion of the Fathers confirmed by Justin Martyr.</margin>
Several of the Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers" were influential Christian theologians and writers in the early centuries of the Church.</note> thought much like the Philosophers regarding this universal illumination; however, they possessed more accurate ideas of the Divinity. They considered the *Spirit*—human Reason—as a Ray, or a Light, which issues from the **WORD** <note>original: "VERBE"; referring to the *Logos*, the Divine Reason or the second person of the Trinity.</note>, or Divine Reason, and which (b) *generally enlightens all men*. This is what led *Justin Martyr* (1) to say *that Christ was known in part by Socrates, because Christ is the* **WORD**, *AND THAT THE WORD IS IN ALL MEN.* And elsewhere, (2) *We have said previously, that since Christ is the* **WORD**, *all of the* **HUMAN RACE PARTICIPATES IN HIM**. *For all those who live according to Reason are Christians. Such among the Greeks were Socrates, Heraclitus, etc.* *Justin* conceived that all Lights come from God, who is their source, but that they come through the **WORD**, who emanates from the Father and who immediately enlightens Spirits, provided they do not allow themselves to be blinded by carnal Passions.

<margin>(b) John 1:9.</margin>

<margin>Reflection of St. Augustine. Passions are the only obstacle to the Lights of the Holy Spirit.</margin>
St. *Augustine* (c) examining (3) why Socrates abandoned the study of natural truths to apply himself entirely to that of morals, gives two reasons for it. The first is that this Philosopher, repelled by the obscurity that shrouds Nature and the uncertainty of our discoveries, turned all the strengths of his fortunate Genius toward Moral Truths, to which the Spirit agreeably acquiesces because of their evidence and certainty. The second (4), "is that Socrates recognized that the causes of all things can only be perceived by a purified Spirit; it was therefore necessary to begin by purifying it of earthly Passions, unburdening it, so to speak, of their weight, so that having recovered all its natural vigor it could rise to the contemplation of God—to that incorporeal and immutable Light in which the Causes of created Natures subsist and live." *St. Augustine* attributes nothing false to *Socrates* on this occasion. This beautiful maxim—that to arrive at the knowledge of Divine Truths, one must above all else sanctify the heart—was common among the most ancient Philosophers. When *Pythagoras* wished to learn the Philosophy of the Chaldeans (5), *Zabratus* <note>Often identified in ancient texts with Zoroaster.</note> his Master began by purifying him of the stains of his past Life and teaching him the Holiness that befits Sages and men

<margin>(c) City of God, Book 8, Ch. 3.</margin>

<margin>Maxim of Zabratus, or of Zoroaster, on this matter.</margin>

---

<columns>2</columns>

of thorough instruction, he has only to read what Plato and Xenophon say on this matter in Chapter IX of the 1st Book of the *Evangelical Preparation* by *Eusebius*.

(4) "So that the mind, unburdened from the weighing down of lusts, might raise itself by its natural vigor toward eternal things, and might behold with purity of understanding the nature of that incorporeal and unchangeable Light where the causes of all created natures live in stability." <note>original Latin: "Ut, deprimentibus libidinibus exoneratus animus, naturali vigore in æterna se attolleret..."</note> Augustine, ibid.

<margin>III. Conclusion of this Principle: the Nations have had their Sages and their Prophets.</margin>
IV. From this Principle—that Divine Reason enlightens all Minds that place no obstacle before its Lights—the Ancients concluded, first, that (1) all Nations have had *Righteous* people, who were pleasing to God. And secondly, that they have had Sages and Prophets to whom God revealed himself. This is what *Clement of Alexandria* <note>Titus Flavius Clemens (c. 150–215 AD) was a Christian theologian who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria and sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Christian doctrine.</note> stated in these terms: (2) "Just as God, wishing to save the Jews, gave them Prophets, he likewise raised up the most excellent men from among the Greeks, those who were most fit to receive his graces. He separated them from common men, so they might be the Prophets of the Greeks and instruct them in their own language." This ancient Author confirms his claim with a passage from an Apocryphal Book entitled the *PREACHING of Peter*, a Book that is still found (a) in the East, where it is read by the Nestorians <note>A branch of Eastern Christianity following the teachings of Nestorius.</note> as a sacred Book. It is there that the Author has St. *Paul* say (3): "Take the Books of the Greeks: See therein how the Sibyl <note>The Sibyls were female oracles in Ancient Greece who were believed to possess prophetic powers; early Christians often cited "Sibylline Oracles" that they believed predicted Christ.</note> teaches of a single God, and how she predicts future things. Take also the Book of *Hystaspes* <note>Hystaspes was an ancient Persian king; a lost book of prophecies was attributed to him in late antiquity and used by Christian apologists.</note>, read it, and you will see the Son of God described in an even clearer and more precise manner." Although the *Preaching of Peter* is an Apocryphal Book, and those of the Sibyl and *Hystaspes* are considered forged, one nonetheless sees in them the sentiments held by ancient Christians regarding the Prophets of Paganism.

These points are incontestable if decided by the authority of the *Fathers*, and by the method they followed in the *Exhortations* they addressed to the Gentiles. VI. *Mani* <note>The founder of Manichaeism (c. 216–274 AD), a major dualistic religion that rivaled Christianity.</note>, being born in Chaldea, received from his childhood a Prejudice that not only favored the opinion I have just mentioned, but which naturally led him to give preference to the Philosophers and Prophets of his own Nation over the Philosophers and Prophets of the Hebrews. It was a very general sentiment that <term>WISDOM</term> <note>The author defines this as the science of Divine and natural truths.</note>, that is to say, the *knowledge of Divine Truths and natural Truths*, had the same origin as the Human Race; that it was born in the East, where the first Patriarchs taught it to their Descendants, and from where it passed (1) to the Egyptians, who communicated it to the Greeks. Scripture itself confirms the claim held by the Orientals <note>In this context, "Orientals" refers to the peoples of the ancient Near East, such as the Chaldeans, Persians, and Babylonians.</note> to be esteemed the most Learned of all Peoples, when, to exalt the *Wisdom of Solomon*, it says (c) *that he surpassed in this regard the* <term>ORIENTALS</term> *and the* <term>EGYPTIANS</term>, *and that he was even wiser than* <term>GETHA THE ORIENTAL</term> <note>A reference to 1 Kings 4:30-31. "Getha" likely refers to Ethan the Ezrahite mentioned in the biblical text.</note>.

<margin>
(c) I Kings IV. 30. 31.
</margin>

---

(1) See on this the learned Dissertation of Mr. Brucker, titled *The Agreement of the numbers of Pythagoras with the Ideas of Plato* <note>Original Latin: "Convenientia numerorum Pythagoræ cum Ideis Platonis"</note>. It is in the VII Volume of the curious Collection of Mr. Schelhorn, entitled *Literary Amenities* <note>Original Latin: "Amoenitates Litterariæ"</note>.

(2) It is a Question among the Learned whether the Egyptians were the masters of the Chaldeans, or if the Chaldeans were the masters of the Egyptians. I prefer the latter opinion. On which I refer the Reader to the Dissertation of the learned Christian Kortholt, *On the Origin, Progress, etc. of Barbarian Philosophy* <note>Original Latin: "De Origine, Progressu &c. Philosophiæ Barbaricæ"</note>. page 15. and following.

(3) One learns well in History that Orpheus was initiated into the Mysteries of the Egyptians. Diodorus Siculus says so. Book I.

23. # OF MANICHAEUS. BOOK I. CH. VI.

Rr

TEL. If one goes back to the Origin of this Philosophy of the Greeks, which is considered the wisest and most religious, one will see that it came from the Chaldeans. **Pythagoras** learned it from **Zoroaster**, and **Plato** traveled expressly to Italy to be instructed in it by the Disciples of **Pythagoras**. He kept all its Principles and did nothing more than (2) substitute his *Ideas* for the abstract and mysterious *Numbers* of the *Pythagoreans*. At its heart, it is the same System; they differ from one another only in these expressions. I am well aware that the Church Fathers believed, and have said, that *Orpheus*, *Pythagoras*, and *Plato* had borrowed from the Hebrews the Truths with which they enriched their Works. But is this sentiment not founded rather on bias than on a just examination of the facts? Be that as it may, since the Chaldeans are regarded as having invented the Sciences, or as having received them from the first Patriarchs, their Ancestors, it is not surprising if **Mani** preferred the Theology and Philosophy of his own Country to that of the Hebrews.

<margin>VII. Zoroaster honored with the gift of Prophecy according to the Christians and the Arabs.</margin>

VII. Among the Great Men who had come out of that Country, no one had acquired a greater Reputation than **ZOROASTER**. *Eusebius* cited a Passage from him which contains a Description of the Divinity that *Monsieur Du Pin* found so beautiful that he believed he should (3) take it away from the Prophet of the Persians to give it to some unknown Christian Author. I am surprised by this Criticism, since the Passage begins with these words: (4) *NOW GOD HAS THE HEAD OF A HAWK*. It is true that this *Hawk's* head is (d) Symbolic, but such a Symbol would never have been employed by a Christian. Besides, *Zoroaster* knew the true God very well: For, beyond the fact that one need only consult Reason and study Nature for that, there are proofs that he was well-instructed in the Religion of the Jews. The general Tradition of the Eastern Christians is that he was a Disciple of either (5) *Elijah* or *Jeremiah*—

<margin>VIII. Observation on Zoroaster.</margin>
VIII. Before reporting the Prophecies of *Zoroaster*, let me be permitted to add to what I have said of him in Part I, some particulars concerning his history, his works, his magic, and his religion.

<margin>1. His Homeland.
(a) Hyde, cited above. Ch. XXXIV. p. 314.
(b) Ibid. p. 311.</margin>
Some (a) have said that he was Jewish by birth and a native of *Palestine*. But it is better to believe the Persians and the Arabs, who say he was born in that part of the land of the Medes which is called today (1) ADERBIJAN <note>Now known as Azerbaijan.</note>. *Abulfeda* (b) adds that he saw the light of day in *Urmi* <note>Modern Urmia.</note>, a city situated in the *Gordian* Mountains, and the most western of the province. Indeed, the (2) names of his ancestors show that he was Persian, and not Phoenician. However, it is certain that he borrowed many things from the religion of the Jews, and that one still finds in his books many passages which appear to be taken (3) from the Psalms of *David*, whether he had read them in the original or had learned them from *Ezra*.

<margin>2. His Revelations.
The Gnostics boasted of possessing them.</margin>
*Porphyry* (4) testifies that the *Gnostics* <note>Early mystical sects that emphasized "gnosis" or secret knowledge.</note> boasted of having his *Revelations*, or his *Apocalypse*: And as the name of Gnostics was given to several sects, (5) *Clement of Alexandria* informs us that these were the followers of *Prodicus*. *Porphyry* asserts that these Revelations were forgeries, and claims to have proved it. Nevertheless, it would not be impossible for the Gnostics to have had the books of *Zoroaster*, which still survive among the remnants of the ancient Persians. The doctrine of the Gnostics was a composite of the philosophy of *Plato*, Oriental philosophy, and Christian doctrine.

<margin>This Book is not what is called the ORACLES of Zoroaster.</margin>
Skilled modern scholars have confused the Revelations of *Zoroaster* with a Greek poem, whose fragments, scattered in various authors, have been collected and published under the name of his (6) ORACLES. But (7) others maintain with reason that it is not the same work. For, besides the fact that the Persian philosopher wrote in neither—

<margin>3. ON THE ZENDAVESTA of Zoroaster. (d) Hyde, Ch. XXV. Explanation of this Title. It is the Bible of the Persians.</margin>
All the works of the famous *Zoroaster* are comprised under the name ZENDAVESTA, a compound word which signifies (d) *an instrument for lighting a fire*, literally THE FIRE-LIGHTER. The Persians call *Zenda* two small reeds which they rub against one another until they draw fire from them, which is called ESTA in their language. It appears likely that they gave this title to the collection of their Sacred Books because of the fire they maintain continually in their Temples, and because they perform divine service before the fire. The Author from whom I take these remarks teaches us that the collection of the Books of *Zoroaster*, which number XXI or XXII, contains first the *Zend*, which is like the Text, or the *Mishna* <note>The first major written collection of Jewish oral traditions.</note> of the Rabbis. It is there that he explains his Dogmas, his Philosophy, his Religion, and his Worship; and there is no doubt that this is properly the Book that has been called his REVELATIONS. All the others are like the *Gemara* <note>The component of the Talmud comprising rabbinical analysis of and commentary on the Mishna.</note>, serving to explain or confirm the first. The PIE, or the SUPPORT of the Zend. Furthermore, D'Herbelot <note>Barthélemy d'Herbelot de Molainville (1625–1695) was a French orientalist whose *Bibliothèque Orientale* was a major reference work.</note> testifies in his *Bibliothèque Orientale* that ZEND signifies LIVING. If this is so, Mani <note>Manichée (Mani) was the 3rd-century founder of Manichaeism, which combined elements of Christianity, Gnosticism, and Zoroastrianism.</note> would have imitated *Zoroaster* when he gave the title (1) OF THE LIVING GOSPEL to the Book of his Revelations. *Zoroaster*, having composed the Work containing his Doctrine during his retreat, went to find (2) *Hystaspes*, and spoke to him in this manner: (3) *I am a PROPHET, whom the MOST HIGH GOD sends to you, and I have brought you this Book from Paradise*. It is said that at the request of this Prince, he confirmed his Religion through wonders, and that *Hystaspes* having embraced it, it became dominant among the Persians, where his Book is regarded as a Divine Law. It is written in the ancient Language and in the ancient script of that Nation. There is no Fire-Temple <note>The original term used is "Pyrée," from the Greek "pyr" (fire).</note>—that is to say, a Temple in which the sacred fire is kept—nor any Oratory, where they do not have a Copy of it. The Priests are obliged to know it by heart, and one of the fundamental Articles of their Religion is to add nothing to it and to take nothing away from it.

<margin>IX. An idea of the Doctrine of Zoroaster.</margin>
IX. No doubt the Reader would be very pleased to know what the ancient Books of such a famous Impostor <note>In the 17th and 18th centuries, scholars often used the term "impostor" for founders of non-Christian religions, even when expressing a level of respect for their moral teachings.</note> contained, whose intentions were fundamentally not evil, since he banished idols, led the People away from Idolatry to the Worship of a single God, and applied himself to regulating their morals. Imposture is always vicious; but I would very much like to know which is more tolerable: that which assumes a Divine Calling in order to tear down Idols and abolish the plurality of Gods, or that which has assumed an infinity of false miracles in order to re-establish Idols in some manner, and to bring back the Worship of Angels and Heroes into the Christian Church. One would therefore wish to know what the Doctrine of *Zoroaster* was, but the ingratitude of our Century prevents us from being able to satisfy such a reasonable curiosity. People who spare nothing to satisfy their luxury and their pleasures refused the late Mr. Hyde <note>Thomas Hyde (1636–1703) was an English orientalist and librarian who wrote extensively on Persian religion but struggled to find funding for a full translation of the Avesta.</note> the necessary assistance to work on a Translation of the Works of *Zoroaster* and to give it to the Public. This is why we know almost nothing of what they contain.

*World*, that is to say, of our material world, in which spiritual substances are mixed or united with Bodies: That he distinguished two things within it, one which he called *Power*, and the other *Act*; which means, it seems to me, *Causes and their effects*. With regard to his Religion, it was reduced (4) to SERVING A SINGLE GOD, to RENOUNCING THE DEVIL, (5) <note>Note 5 is missing from the margin but implied in the text.</note> to RECOGNIZING BENEFITS, and to FLEEING EVERY SORT OF VICE AND IMPURITY. In general, it had three Parts. (6) The first treated OF FAITH, or the Truths that one must believe: The second, of HONESTY and SINCERITY in Speech: The third, of the RULES that one must follow in ACTIONS. Such a Work must have appeared not only new, but admirable to the Persians, if it is true, as (*b*) Abulfeda <note>Ismael Abulfeda (1273–1331) was a Kurdish historian and geographer.</note> testifies, that before *Zoroaster* they had no Book of Morality.

An able (7) Modern author has remarked that one must not confuse the Philosophy of the Chaldeans with that of the Magi. The Chaldeans were Idolaters, and it is from them that this Sect descends, which still exists in the East, and which are called *Sabaeans*: But the Magi had no Idols. This is why *Xerxes* destroyed the Temples of the Greeks, because he found Images and Statues everywhere there. However, although these two Philosophies were different in some respects, they had much affinity. I believe, moreover, that what the Greeks tell us of the Philosophy of the *Chaldeans* properly belongs to the Modern Chaldeans. I call these Philosophers such from the time they were subjected to the Persians, and the Religion of the latter became dominant. This being supposed, I will not distinguish between these two Philosophies, whose Morality I am about to represent.

### HISTORY OF DOGMES ###

To reach happiness and the sovereign Good, the sage must work unceasingly to weaken and tame the Body and the Passions of the Body, which make up the Animal Part of Man; and to strengthen that which is Divine within him, namely, *Reason* or the *Spirit*. The Magi, or the Chaldeans, had for a Symbol this mysterious phrase: (1) *We shall consume the dross of Matter by the Divine Fire.* <note>The original Greek phrase is "Τὴν σκύβαλον πυρὶ θείῳ ἀνυπανύσομεν." The dross or "manure" refers to the physical impurities of the material world.</note> It is through this operation that they claimed mortal Man could rise to the likeness of the Celestial Powers and contract with them a close friendship and a kind of union.

<margin>The four Cardinal Virtues, which constitute the Sage. (a) See Plato, in *Alcibiades* p. m. 32.</margin>
The Virtues essential to the Honest Man were, according to these Philosophers, WISDOM—that is to say, the knowledge and Worship of the Divinity—JUSTICE, TEMPERANCE, and VALOR or STRENGTH. It was in these Virtues that skillful (a) Preceptors tried to train Princes, who must be Models as well as Masters of the People. An Apology <note>A formal defense or explanation of a doctrine.</note> of *Zoroaster* has been preserved for us which relates to this subject. (2) "The Chaldeans say that (3) the Soul has wings, and that when it has lost its feathers, it falls into Bodies; but that it returns to its first dwelling when the wings have grown back. This led the Disciples of *Zoroaster* to ask him by what means one could make the wings of the Soul grow. *One must*, he told them, *water them with the waters of Life*. But *where can one take these Waters*, the Disciples replied? He answered them with this Parable. *The Paradise of God is watered by four Rivers, from which you can draw these salutary waters. The first descends from the North, and its Name designates that which is UPRIGHT, JUST, HONEST. The name of the second, which comes from the West, marks EXPIATIONS. The name of the third, which flows from the East, means LIGHT. And as for the name of the fourth, which flows from the south, we explain it by PIETY*." One can see clearly that these ideas are taken from Moses. Apparently *Zoroaster* understood in a mystical sense what the Prophet <note>Moses, traditionally the author of Genesis.</note> had said of Paradise, or the Garden of Eden, and of the four Rivers that watered it.

### ON MANICHAEISM. BOOK I. CH. VI. ###

<margin>Specific precepts divided into three Classes.</margin>
A (4) French Traveler, who took care to inform himself of the Precepts of this Lawgiver, included them in his narrative, and certainly there are some very beautiful ones. They are divided into three Classes, the first of which concerns the Laity. Their Duties are: 1.
<margin>1st Class: Duties of the Laity.</margin>
" *To adhere to Chastity, Honesty, Equity, and to flee pleasures, Pomposity, the Spirit of vengeance, and Theft.*
" 2. *To love Fear—a Precept which seems to contain this Scriptural Maxim: The Fear of God is the summary, the abridgment, the first foundation, or the Principle of Wisdom.* <note>The author refers to a common biblical theme found in Proverbs 9:10 and Psalm 111:10.</note> 3. *To consult Prudence in all Actions, in order to avoid those which are vicious, and to do only what is honest.* 4. *To begin the day by thinking of God, and by performing Acts of love for God, this sovereign being being the true object of our knowledge and our affections.* 5. *To pray to God with the face turned towards the Sun during the day, and towards the Moon during the night, because these two Planets are (5) the witnesses of the Divine Light against the Demons, who delight in Darkness.* " This practice was observed by the Manichaeans, who held it from *Zoroaster* <note>Zoroaster (or Zarathustra) was the ancient Iranian prophet whose teachings founded Zoroastrianism, which heavily influenced the later Manichaean faith.</note>.

<margin>2nd Class. Duties of the Priests.</margin>
The second Class comprises the Duties of the Priests: These are: 1. To change nothing in the Worship or the Prayers. 2. To desire no one's property. 3. To avoid Lying. 4. To keep impure thoughts away from their Minds. 5. To know the *Zendavesta* <term>Zendavesta: The primary collection of sacred texts of Zoroastrianism.</term> by heart. 6. To preserve themselves from pollutions. 7. To forget injuries. 8. To teach the People the Prayers and Ceremonies of the Sacrifices. 9. To preside over Marriages. 10. To frequent the Temples. 11. And finally to be firmly persuaded that there is no other Divine Law than theirs, and to change nothing therein under pain of eternal fire.

<margin>3rd Class: Duties of the High Priests.</margin>
The third Class concerns the High Priests or the *Arch-Magi*, whose Holiness must increase in proportion to their Dignity. Here are their specific Duties. The 1st: to wash themselves if they happen to touch an impure thing or person; The 2nd: to live by the work of their hands, to plant, to sow, to harv- <meta>The original French text cuts off mid-word "moisson-" (moissonner); the catchword "ner" completes "to harvest."</meta>

<margin>Observations on some of these Precepts.</margin> Let us make some observations on these *Precepts*. The sixth orders the Arch-Priests *to be clean in their eating*. This Precept is explained by another, which is entirely parallel, and which is found in the *Golden Poem* attributed to Pythagoras because it contains his Philosophy. (1) *Accustom yourself to have a diet that is clean and simple.* <note>The author quotes the Greek "Ἐιθίζε δὲ διαίταν ἔχειν καθάριον, ἄπυκτον," emphasizing moderation and purity.</note>

This same Precept enjoins the *Arch-Priests* to abstain from *their wives when they must perform divine service*. If these *Arch-Priests* are *Magi*, Clement of Alexandria must have been mistaken when he said of the latter (2) that they lived in entire continence <note>original Greek: "Ἀφροδισίων ἀπέχουσι" — they abstain from sexual pleasures.</note>. At the very least, it is certain that this Father [of the Church] is not in agreement with himself, since he says in the *Book* I cite, and ten pages earlier, (3) that *the Magi married their mothers and their daughters* <note>original Greek: "Μίγνυν οἱ Μάγοι μήτρασι καὶ θυγάτρασι."</note>. How can that be true if they kept perpetual continence? Furthermore, these incests of the Magi are very suspect to me. I said something of this in the first Part. Nothing can resolve me to admit them except a certain policy, of which one sees an example in the Kings of Peru. These Princes, not wishing to mix their Blood—or the Blood of the Gods—with that of Men or their subjects, married their own Sisters.

### OF MANICHAEUS. BOOK I. CH. VI. ###

<columns>
The 11th Precept orders the *Arch-Priests* to obtain *Manifestations of the Divine Glory*. This accords very well with what Diogenes Laertius <note>A 3rd-century biographer of Greek philosophers.</note> testifies. (4) *The Magi assert that the Gods appear to them.*

<margin>X. Zoroaster’s Magic.</margin>
X. The popular idea of *Zoroaster*, and even that held by the Church Fathers, is that this Philosopher was a consummate Magician, that he excelled in the Art of evoking Demons and of using their Ministry: that he learned secrets from them to perform Prodigies and impose them upon Men. Nothing is more false than this imagination. The Magic of *Zoroaster* consisted in the knowledge and Worship of the Divinity. This is how *Plato* (5) defined it. I correct at the bottom of the page the Translation by *Marsilio Ficino* <note>A celebrated 15th-century Italian scholar who translated Plato into Latin.</note>, which is quite literal but which certainly gives a false idea.

<margin>What Zoroaster's Enchantments were.</margin>
*Zoroaster* and the Magi used *enchantments*. At the hearing of this word, one imagines profane ceremonies or invocations of evil Demons. This is pure prejudice. The *Persian* Philosopher had no less aversion for malignant Spirits than Jews and Christians have always had, and he was careful not to invoke them when it came to charming <note>In this context, "charming" means to soothe, subdue, or gain control over wild impulses.</note> vicious Passions and deadening them. It is not in such things that Demons cooperate. There is in *Plato* an ingenious Fable on this subject. A Man having a headache because he had overindulged in debauchery, he was told that the leaf of a certain Plant had the virtue of curing his ill. (6) 

<margin>Plato’s ingenious Fable.</margin>
> "That is true," says *Plato*, "but one must add ENCHANTMENTS: without that, the leaf will be useless. Enchantments (7)," he continues, "are the remedies of the Soul; but they consist in good reasons, which persuade the Mind, and which effect Temperance. Now, by procuring this virtue, one procures the health of the head and of the whole Body."

The Enchantments of the Magi were of the same nature: Hymns in praise of the Divinity; Prayers by which one implored its assistance; Discourses on the excellence of Virtue and on the deformity and fatal consequences of Vices; the art of uniting as much as possible the forces of a Divine Spirit with those of Reason. It is in this that the *Enchantments of Zoroaster* (8) consisted. In order that a Discourse might

"to be able to persuade Temperance, and to bring it about in those who listen, one must unite a Divine Virtue, which acts on the Spirit, with the reasons and motives provided by Philosophy. Now, it is Discourses of this sort that *Plato* calls <term>MAGIC ENCHANTMENTS</term> <note>Plato uses this term in the *Charmides* to describe how words can heal the soul, just as medicine heals the body.</note>". This explanation by *Marsilio Ficino* seems very reasonable to me.

<margin>The Magi had some superstitious Ceremonies.</margin>
I do not pretend, however, that *Zoroaster* (1) and the Magi did not have some superstitious Ceremonies, which they regarded as a Worship pleasing to the Divinity, or as a means of winning the favor and affection of the celestial Powers for Men. It is
<margin>(a) Suidas, under "Julian the Philosopher."</margin>
said, for example, that (a) *Julian* the Philosopher—the father of the one surnamed the <term>THEURGIST</term> <note>A "theurgist" was a practitioner of Neoplatonic magic aimed at achieving union with the divine through rituals.</note>—had composed a Book concerning the <term>Kyphi</term>. This is a Perfume (2) which the Chaldeans and Egyptians used in their initiations, and of which *Plutarch* has given us a description at the end of his Treatise on *Isis* and *Osiris*. Some superstitious people imagined that this Perfume was an excellent preservative against the Power of Demons, and that it conferred a supernatural virtue upon the Soul. This is not Magic: it is superstition; and does not superstition creep into almost all Religions? Have not the Christians themselves had the weakness to attribute a kind of Divine virtue to Ceremonies and to certain
<margin>(b) La Croze, Christianity of the Indies, p. 437.</margin>
compositions? A modern scholar (b) has said, with much likelihood, that the *Myron* <note>A Greek term for consecrated oil or ointment.</note> of the Greeks, or the *Chrism* of the Latins, is but an imitation of the <term>Kyphi</term> of the Chaldeans and Egyptians. Ceremonies become odious and criminal when one invokes Demons through them, or when they form part of their worship. But it will never be proven, by certain testimony, that neither *Zoroaster* nor the Magi invoked evil Spirits, for whom they had no less horror than we do.

<margin>A kind of Baptism of fire practiced by the Magi.</margin>
Among their Ceremonies, there was one that might be named in Christian terms a *Baptism of fire*. It shared nothing with that barbaric custom, formerly practiced among the inhabitants of Palestine, who burned their children in honor of *Moloch*. The Persians (3) were content to have theirs pass through the flames, without them suffering any harm. By virtue of this expiation, if these Children, having reached the age of reason,

### CHAPTER VII.

->*Concerning the* PROPHECIES *attributed by Christians to* ZOROASTER.<-

What an advantage it was for our Heresiarch <note>A leader or founder of a heretical sect.</note> to be able to allege to the Persians an Oracle of their great Prophet in his favor, at the same time that he alleged to the Christians the Oracle of Jesus Christ, who had predicted and promised the Paraclete <note>The "Comforter" or Holy Spirit; Manichaeus claimed to be the fulfillment of this promise.</note>? By this means, he presented himself to the world equipped with double credentials: one from Zoroaster, venerated in the Persian Empire, and the other from the very Son of God.

They further possess a letter titled the EPISTLE of the wise *Hermes*, which passes for a kind of inspired Scripture among the Sects of the Levant. It is true that these sorts of books, which Christians used in the beginning during their disputes against the Gentiles, contain a theology that is Orthodox only in appearance. Everything in them is full of Platonic ideas: but it was for that very reason that they suited the Manichaeans better.

<header>ON MANICHAEISM. BOOK I. CH. VII.</header>
