...Manichaeans did not believe the Devil was eternal, but rather a production of *Matter*. After this, Pherecydes also treated (6) the War of the Gods. *Marsilio Ficino* <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar who was instrumental in translating Plato and other Greek works into Latin.</note> noted (7) "that Plato had learned from the Egyptians that *Jupiter* cast the impure demons into the Underworld; and from Pherecydes, that several demons had revolted against *Jupiter*, and that Ophioneus <note>A serpent-like giant in Greek mythology who led the rebellion against Cronus or Zeus.</note> was the leader of their armies." All these are Manichaean imaginings. These reflections tend to show the sources and antiquity of this heresy. Although the error was great and real, nevertheless the nations descended from *Ham*, such as the Persians, the Arabs, the Phoenicians, and the Egyptians, could not help but have veneration for him and for the oracles attributed to his name.

<margin>V. Explanation of Pherecydes' Emblem.</margin>
V. I do not doubt that the reader has the curiosity to know what mystery Pherecydes had hidden under the emblem of a **WINGED OAK**, covered with a **VEIL** or a **CLOAK OF VARIOUS COLORS**. Some scholars have tried to discover it. I will report their conjectures and add my own.

<margin>The thought of Sandius rejected.</margin>
Pherecydes, nicknamed the SYRIAN <note>Though his name implies Syria, he was actually from the island of Syros in the Aegean Sea.</note>, because he was from the island of *Syros* in the *Ionian* Sea, was (8) the first Greek philosopher to write on *Nature and the Gods*, and who taught the Greeks (9) the *immortality of the Soul*. I have already said that he drew his ideas from the ancient Book of *Ham*, and that this book contained the theology of the *Phoenicians*. The passage from *Eusebius* that I just cited confirms this. But as the ancients did not want to communicate their knowledge to everyone, he followed the method of the Egyptians and the Orientals. He wrapped all his dogmas in riddles. (10) *Sandius* <note>Christoph Sand, a 17th-century historian of Arianism and philosophy.</note> tried to explain that of the *Winged Oak* in his treatise *On the Origin of the Soul*. This being supposed, he conjectures that the *Wings of the Oak* are the *Wings of the Soul*, a concept that Plato employed after Pythagoras, and which, as has been seen, drew its origin from Zoroaster <note>The founding prophet of ancient Persian religion, often associated by early modern scholars with the origin of dualistic philosophy.</note> or the Chaldeans. Never did the Ancients, and much less *Pherecydes* and those like him, believe that Men were born from Oaks. The passages alleged by *Sandius* do not prove it. He has taken a proverbial expression for a literal one. The Reader may see the proof of this at the bottom of the page (1).

Another (a) modern Scholar <note>Referring to Johann Albert Fabricius, a prolific German classical scholar and bibliographer.</note> has conjectured that since the Oak is a tree that subsists for a long time, it is the image of *Nature*. He suggests that the Epithet *winged* is given to it by *Pherecydes* because of its branches, which it extends far and wide, and that the Cloak of various colors covering it signifies that infinite variety of Plants and Animals that Nature produces—that admirable embroidery which embellishes the surface of the Earth and which incessantly diversifies itself. This Explanation seems confirmed by the fiction of the Egyptians, who represented Nature under the figure of a Woman covered with a veil, with these words: (2) *I am all that has been, all that is, and all that will be, and never has any mortal been able to lift the veil that hides me.* <note>This is the famous inscription of the goddess Isis at Sais, often interpreted as an allegory for the mysteries of Nature.</note> Everything goes well in this Explanation, except for the wings of the Oak, which he insists must be taken for its branches. One only gives wings to something to express its movement. Poets, like *Hesiod* for example, call the *oars* and *sails* of a Ship its *wings*, but that is because sails and oars serve to make it move. It is not the same for the branches of a Tree: they remain immobile. As for the Variegated Cloak, it suits *Nature* or *Matter* very well, which reminds me of an Apologue of the Gentiles of India (b). The late Mr. Grabe *(c)* had a thought which at first dazzled me. He believed there was an error in the text of *Clement of Alexandria*, and that instead of reading *Drys*, which means *Oak*, one should read *Dryops*, which is a kind of bird mentioned in *(d) Aristophanes*. But since the epithet *winged* would be quite redundant if taken in its literal sense—as there is no bird that does not have wings—I have taken it in a figurative sense, meaning *(3) quick, rapid, light*. As for the *Cloak of various colors*, it would suit a *bird* with varied plumage very well. Mr. Grabe's correction does not explain the emblem, but it gives it a very natural air, and that is what first struck me; it might even have seduced me, if *Maximus of Tyre*, whom I have cited, had not taught me that the emblem of *Pherecydes* was a *Tree* and not a *Bird*. (4) *Consider*, he says, *these fictions of the Syrian; Jupiter, the Earth (or Matter), and Love, which is in both; the birth of Ophion, the combat of the Gods*, THE TREE AND THE VEIL. It is therefore certain that the symbol of Pherecydes was a *Tree*, or an *Oak*, and that nothing should be changed in the reading of Clement of Alexandria. But the question remains to explain the symbol: I believe this to be very difficult, and what I am about to say on the matter is only a conjecture that I venture, but which will perhaps provide someone else with the opportunity to guess the truth.

<margin>The Author's Conjecture.</margin>
I suspect that the *Oak* is the emblem of Divinity. We know the custom of the Ancients to perform Divine Service in the Woods, and the veneration that the Druids <note>Ancient Celtic priests who held the oak tree in high religious esteem.</note> had for Oaks. *The wings of the Oak* represent the figure of *Time*, whose continual and rapid course they represent. Pherecydes placed *(e)* *Time*, or *Saturn*, among the rank of Principles, and associated him in this regard with *Zeus*, or *Zas*, that is to say, with God. Although the Poets have rendered this name of Zeus odious, it is nevertheless in itself very proper for expressing Divinity; the idea it gives is not only that of a *living Being*, but of a *Being* who has life by himself, and who

(1) The *Pythagoreans* <note>Followers of the philosopher Pythagoras, known for their mystical approach to mathematics and cosmology.</note>, says *Hierocles*, were accustomed to venerating the Creator and Father of the Universe under the name of **Zeus**. *For it is quite reasonable to designate the one who gave* **Being and Life** *to all that possesses them, by a name that expresses his powerful operation.* <note>The author is playing on the etymological connection in Greek between "Zeus" and the verb "to live" (*zen*).</note> As for *Saturn*, or *Time*, the Phoenicians represented him with wings, some extended, because he always flies; others folded, because his movement is imperceptible, and as *Philo of Byblos* expresses it, (2) *because he rests without ceasing to fly, and he flies without ceasing to rest.* The *Embroidered Cloak*, or cloak of various colors, with which the Oak is covered, is effectively Nature, the Earth, and the Seas, which act as the garment under which the Divinity hides and reveals itself all at once. (3) *Jupiter*, says *Pherecydes* in another passage reported by *Clement of Alexandria*, **Jupiter makes a large and beautiful cloak**, *upon which he embroiders* **the Earth, Ogenus**, *and the houses of Ogenus.* We know that *Ogenus* is the ancient name for the Ocean. (4) *Clement* remarks that the idea of *Pherecydes* is an imitation of *Homer* describing the Shield of Achilles. That may be: but it seems to me that this last passage can serve to explain the enigma of the first. For whom does *Jupiter* make this vast and beautiful cloak embroidered with diverse colors, if not for himself?

If he had intended to produce false Scriptures, he would have released them under names venerated by the whole Church, rather than under "barbarous" or obscure names; for this is the usual method of impostors. I would rather believe, then, that these alleged Prophets were among the apocryphal writings of the Jews, which still held some authority even though they were not included in the Canon of the Scriptures <note>The "Canon" refers to the official list of books recognized as genuine Holy Scripture.</note>. <margin>Response to an objection from Mr. Fabricius regarding the latter's book.</margin>
I have stated, following Mr. *Asseman* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a famous Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian at the Vatican.</note>, that the Syrians boast of possessing a *Book of Seth*: however, the learned Mr. *Fabricius* <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a German scholar known for collecting "pseudepigrapha" or books falsely attributed to biblical figures.</note> asserts (1) that they reject this book, and bases this on a letter from *Stephen Peter*, Patriarch of the *Maronites* <note>The Maronites are an Eastern Catholic Church in full communion with the Pope, primarily located in Lebanon.</note>, who takes, as is customary, the grand title of (2) *Patriarch of Antioch*, although his diocese is limited to the Monastery of *Qannubin* and a few villages of Mount *Lebanon* and its surroundings. This *Stephen* informs *Huntington* (3) *that the Book of Seth is certainly among the forbidden books among the Syrians*. I do not doubt the truth of this testimony. I only believe that it must be restricted to the *Maronites* alone, upon whom *Father de St. Joseph* bestowed this praise: (4) *That they are THE FLOWER OF CATHOLICITY throughout the Levant, and that they SWEAR BY THE HEAD OF THE POPE*. But as for the other Eastern communions that have not been "Romanized," they still receive the *Book of Seth*, along with many others of the same kind, the list of which can be seen in Mr. *Asseman*, in the passage I cited. As for the Manichaeans <note>Followers of Mani, who believed in a dualistic struggle between Light and Darkness.</note>, there is no reason to doubt that they possessed this apocryphal work; but before proving it, let us relate the history that the Syrians give us concerning the Patriarch *Seth*.

<margin>Tradition of the Easterners regarding the subject of this Patriarch.</margin>
It is a (5) constant tradition among the Easterners, which passed from them to (6) the Greeks, "that the Angels carried away *Seth* and instructed him in future events, particularly regarding (7) the birth of the Savior which was to happen around the year 5500 of the World <note>A common chronological calculation in early Christianity, placing the arrival of Christ 5,500 years after the Creation.</note>: That they taught him the art of writing and astronomy: That they gave him, on behalf of God, laws concerning Religion and Justice: That he communicated all this knowledge to his children, and inspired in them such a love for Virtue, and such an ardor to recover the blessed life which *Adam* and *Eve* had enjoyed in Paradise, that, being unable to re-enter that abode of Felicity, they retired to Mount *Hermon*. It was there that they lived in a perfect—

Christ deserved their esteem and veneration because of his eminent virtues and excellent precepts; but (1) they refused to place faith in the Gospels under the pretext that he had not written them himself, and that his disciples, instead of representing him as a man of high wisdom—which he was—had made him into a God. This Father <note>The term "Father" refers to a "Church Father," the influential early Christian theologians.</note> responds (2) that although *Pythagoras* and *Socrates* (he could have added *Apollonius* and *Epictetus*) had left no written monuments of their doctrine, posterity nonetheless recognized that it had been faithfully reported by their disciples. St. Augustine's response is plausible, but regardless of what *Mr. Simon* <margin>(a) Critical History of the New Testament Vol. I. p. 24. 25.</margin> (a) <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and father of modern biblical criticism.</note> says, it is by no means sufficient. The disparity is too great and too visible. It is of no importance to one's salvation to know with certainty what the doctrine of *Socrates* or *Pythagoras* was; no one is obliged to believe it under pain of being deprived of eternal life. It is not the same with the Gospel: faith in the truths it contains and the observance of its precepts are the conditions of salvation. If the witnesses who certify to us that this is the doctrine of J. Christ had not been directed by an infallible Spirit, and if their preaching had not been confirmed by their miracles, we would be forced, despite ourselves, to drift in uncertainty, and faith would be quite shaky.

I simply leave it to the Reader to judge if it requires less audacity to copy and print such a lie, without any correction, than to invent it. I almost suspected that the Author wanted to apply to *Abgar* the History of *Lazarus*, which is in Chapter XI. of St. John.

<margin>IV. The Manichaeans accused of having corrupted the Scriptures, and attributed Books to the Apostles.</margin>
IV. Pope Leo I accuses the Manichaeans (5) “of having violated the sanctity of the Scriptures by sacrilegious subtractions or additions; and of having composed, under the name of the Apostles, a quantity of false Books, in which they made Jesus Christ speak.” Leo has said it; that is enough: All those who write after him copy him, without bothering to see if Leo told the truth. The Manichaeans maintained that the Books of the New Testament had been altered, but they did not alter them themselves; and we shall see in what follows that they are not the Authors of the false Gospels, nor of the other Apocryphal Acts, which are lightly attributed to them. What I advance will perhaps seem new, but it is no less certain.

<margin>The Catholics have done both.</margin>
For a long time, the Catholics have been in possession of accusing Heretics of an outrage of which they are guilty themselves. If Providence had not watched over the preservation of the sacred Books, these sources of Truth would not have flowed entirely pure down to us. Things were added in some places, and in others, what seemed to offend popular prejudices or received sentiments was removed. For example, some People find that it is unworthy of the Savior to shed tears. They remove from *St. Luke* these words, *(e) Jesus wept*, and (6) *those who remove them are the Ortho-*

Nothing seems bolder than the undertaking of those Orthodox believers who, unable to reconcile the Genealogies of Jesus Christ, took it upon themselves to put into (b) St. Luke the one reported by St. Matthew, making some changes to hide their fraud. Furthermore, it would be in vain for freethinkers <note>original: "Libertins"; here referring to skeptics or critics of religious authority.</note> to try to take advantage of these alterations. For if they prove the temerity of some misguided zealots, the restoration of these passages is an authentic testimony to the good faith of the Christian Church. It took no part in the fraud and corrected it as soon as it was perceived.

<margin>VI. They do not do this based on another addition made to St. Mark 16:14.</margin>
VI. St. *Jerome*, in his second *Dialogue against the Pelagians* <note>The Pelagians were followers of Pelagius, who argued that human nature was not inherently corrupt and that humans could choose good without special divine aid—a view Jerome fiercely opposed.</note>, cites a passage for them that was found in some copies of St. Mark, but especially in Greek copies, immediately after verse 14 of Chapter 16. In it, the Lord’s disciples are made to speak in these terms: *(1) This age is <term>THE SUBSTANCE</term> of iniquity and unbelief; it is this which, by means of impure spirits, prevents one from understanding the true Power of God: therefore, Lord, manifest your justice now.* As this passage was not found in all copies, St. *Jerome* adds, still addressing the Pelagians, *If you reject this testimony, at least you must not reject this one: (2) the whole world is under the power of the evil one.* Since this expression—*the age is <term>THE SUBSTANCE</term> of iniquity*—relates to the error of the Manichaeans <note>Manichaeism taught a radical dualism where the physical world was made of evil matter or "substance."</note>, a <margin>(a) J. Croius. Observations on the New Testament, Ch. XIV. In Fabricius, as cited above, p. 325.</margin> (a) clever modern scholar believed it was taken from one of their false Gospels—from that of *Thomas*, for example, or that of Philip. This conjecture would give a very poor idea of St. *Jerome's* judgment. For, if he had cited against the Pelagians a passage suspected of being shoved into St. *Mark* either by Mani or his disciples, he would have prepared a fine victory for his adversaries, who never ceased to reproach the Orthodox by claiming that their views on human corruption were pure Manichaeism. The truth is that these words, *the present age is the very <term>THE SUBSTANCE</term> of iniquity*, are merely a very beautiful and vivid expression that aptly represents the extreme corruption of the world.

### CHAPTER II.

->*Of* **Leucius** *and some of the false Acts attributed to him. Of the* **Gospel** *of the Nativity of the Virgin and the* **Proto-Gospel**.<-

<margin>I. The Manichaeans possessed certain Apocrypha.</margin>
I. It appears from the Formula of abjuration, which the Greeks prescribed for the Manichaeans <note>A dualistic religious movement founded by the Persian prophet Mani in the 3rd century AD.</note>, that they possessed some Apocrypha, which they were made to renounce in these terms: (1) **I anathematize the Book of Apocrypha.** <note>original: "Τὴν βίβλον τῶν Ἀποκρύφων"</note>
<margin>Cave's ill-founded conjecture.</margin>
Doctor *Cave* (2) imagined that this anathema referred to the Ritual of the Sect, that is to say, that secret Book in which their abominable Mysteries were described, and in particular those of their **Bema** <note>The Bema was the most important Manichaean festival, commemorating the death of Mani; it involved a throne or "bema" representing the teacher's authority.</note>. But it is sheer prejudice that has caused the invention of such an unnatural explanation. No one, as far as I know, has even heard of this Ritual of the Manichaeans; and regarding their *Bema*, that is, the anniversary Feast of the death of Manichaeous, *St. Augustine*, who had attended this solemnity and who described it, was unable to reproach them for any ceremony, whether obscene or idolatrous. It is therefore a matter of a *Book*, or a *Collection of Apocrypha*, which were used by his Sect.

<margin>Turibius accuses them of having composed or falsified them all.</margin>
If we were in the mood to rely on the testimony of *Turibius*, Bishop of *Astorga* <note>A 5th-century bishop in Spain known for his opposition to heresy.</note> in the 5th Century, we would believe (3) **that there is no Apocryphal work that was not composed or corrupted by Mani or by his Disciples.** We shall see in what follows that this accusation is not only false, but absurd. However, it is necessary above all else to discover who is the personage said to have been the great author of the fabrication or the falsification of so many books.
<margin>This imposture is attributed to a certain **Leucius**, who is said to have been a Manichaean.</margin>
This is a certain **Leucius**, who is named by the Ancients as **Lucius, Leicius, Leuticius, Leontius, Lentitius**,

<margin>(4) His name corrupted by the Ancients.</margin>
<margin>(a) In the Decree, [cited] above. (b) Tillemont, [cited] above.</margin>
...TIUS, LENTIUS, and finally SELEUCUS: For *Baronius* <note>Cesare Baronio (1538–1607), an influential Italian cardinal and ecclesiastical historian.</note> and other scholars do not doubt that *Seleucus* and *Leucius* are basically the same person. The Ancients were quite accustomed to disfiguring names. *Gelasius* <note>Pope Gelasius I, associated with the "Gelasian Decree" which lists canonical and apocryphal books.</note> (a) calls him *Lenticius*, (b) and gives him the eulogy of DISCIPLE OF THE DEVIL, *which is so well deserved*, says M. de Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French priest and historian known for his meticulous accuracy.</note>, *by the authors of false and forged works, and all lovers of lies*. This reflection is very just, but it applies to people whom M. de Tillemont would have been forced to respect. Since the time of the Apostles, every century has had these forgers, whose writings and memory are still defended today because people profit from their fraud.

<margin>(5) It is the same name as that of LUKE.</margin>
It is said, then, that LEUCIUS, or LUKE—for that is his (5) true name—was a Manichaean, and that it was he who wrote or falsified almost all the ancient Apocrypha; this necessarily engages me in a discussion of a great number of these pieces. The matter is quite curious, and I shall try to treat it in a way that does not bore the reader. I am not even sorry to have the opportunity to point out the difference between the true writings of the Apostles and those which have been falsely attributed to them. Nothing is better suited to demonstrate the weakness of the objections raised by "Libertines" <note>In this 18th-century context, "Libertines" refers to free-thinkers or skeptics who questioned the authenticity of the Bible.</note>, both ancient and modern, who try to confuse the productions of a flighty, fanatical, or impostor spirit with those of Wisdom and Truth itself. Furthermore, one will find in these Apocrypha the origin of many fabulous stories which make up the legends of the Holy Virgin and the Apostles. While the authors and their books are condemned and proscribed, their stories are canonized and included in Lectionaries, Church Offices, and sermons.

<margin>II. He was not a Manichaean.</margin>
II. Since most ancients and moderns assert that *Leucius* was a Manichaean, it is something of a paradox to maintain the contrary. However, unless one understands by "Manichaean" a heretic who held errors similar to those of Manichaeous, it is certain that Leucius was not a Manichaean, having lived—

—[as noted] in his Remarks on *Leo I.* Vol. II. p. 824. In truth, this Spanish Bishop is somewhat flattered there. The phrase *it is manifest* <note>original Latin: "manifestum est"</note> in the passage I have just cited is evident proof of the lightness with which the Ancients put forward facts that were entirely false.

<margin>1. He was a Disciple of St. John, according to St. Epiphanius.</margin>
1. St. Epiphanius testifies, "that (1) *Leucius was one of those Disciples of St. John, who, after the death of the Apostle, defended the Divinity of the Lord against the Ebionites.* <note>The Ebionites were an early Jewish-Christian sect who maintained that Jesus was a human prophet and not divine. Epiphanius of Salamis (c. 310–403) was a staunch defender of orthodoxy known for his "Panarion" or "Medicine Chest" of heresies.</note> This fits very well with our Leucius, whose Heresy was directly opposed to that of Ebion, as we shall see in the following.

<margin>2. And according to the false Melito, Disciple of the Apostles.</margin>
2. We have, in the second volume of the *Library of the Fathers*, a Narrative of the PASSING of the Blessed Virgin, that is to say, of her death. The Imposter, who took the name of *Melito*, Bishop of Sardis, addresses his History to the Faithful of Laodicea, and informs them, (2) *that he remembers having often spoken to them in his Letters of a certain* LEUCIUS, WITH WHOM HE CONVERSED IN THE COMPANY OF THE APOSTLES. <note>Melito of Sardis was a real 2nd-century bishop, but many later works were falsely attributed to him. This "Passing of Mary" (Transitus Mariae) text is an early apocryphal story about the death and assumption of the Virgin Mary.</note> It is true that this Piece was only made in the 5th Century; but, besides that the Latin Author drew the substance of his Romance from some fabulous Greeks, *Leucius* must have passed for a Disciple of the Apostles, since the Author, wishing to give himself the same antiquity, associates himself with this Heretic, whose Errors he otherwise condemns.

<margin>3. Testimony of Pacian, which justifies the antiquity and authority of this man.</margin>
3. *Pacian*, Bishop of Barcelona in the fourth Century, testifies, in one of his Letters, that (3) *the most noble of the Phrygians, that is to say, the Montanists, falsely boasted of having been animated and illuminated by Leucius.* <note>Montanism, originating in Phrygia, was a movement that emphasized new prophetic revelations. Pacian (c. 310–391) is a key source for early Spanish church history.</note> Effectively, he had the same Errors as the Montanists on the subject of marriage, as one sees by his false Acts of the Apostles. Now if it is true that these Sectarians boasted of having been animated and enlightened by Leucius, it must first be that he had acquired a great authority in Asia, which would well suit a man who had seen and heard the Apostles: And secondly, that he lived at least at the birth of Montanism, which arose around the year (4) 156 of our Lord.

<margin>4. Other proofs drawn from his Gospel of St. Peter. (a) Eccl. Hist. L. VII. 12.</margin>
4. *Eusebius* informs us that (a) *Serapion*, who was Bishop of Antioch towards the end of the (5) 2nd Century, found in the Churches of Asia a *Gospel of St. Peter*, which contained the Heresies of the Docetists. <note>Docetism was the belief that Jesus only *seemed* to have a physical body and only *seemed* to suffer on the cross. Eusebius is the "Father of Church History," writing in the 4th century.</note> Now this false Gospel being a Work of Leucius, as we shall see in the following, this Heretic must have lived in the beginning of that Century.

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>He sought to destroy the opinion that the Virgin was the daughter of a Priest, a view held by the Manicheans.</margin>
Faustus had argued, in his Book against St. *Augustine*, (1) "that even if the Lord were a man, he would not be the 'Son of David' if he were not the 'Son of Mary,' because this Holy Woman descended from the Tribe of *Levi*, being the daughter of a Priest named *Joachim*." Faustus even adds that "this is a constant and notorious fact." This was undoubtedly found, along with other Errors, in the Book of *Seleucus* <note>Seleucus is a variant of the name Leucius Charinus, the reputed author of many apocryphal texts used by Manicheans.</note>, who had written the History of the Virgin. St. *Augustine* replies, (2) that, since the fact in question is not attested by a Canonical Writer, he is not obliged to believe it: that only the Apocrypha testify that Mary’s Father was named *Joachim*.

<margin>V. Antiquity of this Opinion.
(a) Luke I. 5.</margin>

<meta>catchword: Prin-</meta>

However vain this thought might be, it had something too dazzling not to be adopted by the Fathers. <margin>From St. Augustine.</margin> Baronius <note>Cesare Baronius (1538–1607) was an influential Italian cardinal and historian best known for his *Annales Ecclesiastici*.</note>, searching for the reasons for the differences found between the two Genealogies of Jesus Christ, said, following St. Augustine, (1) that the Evangelists, wishing to represent a different personage in Our Lord—namely, *St. Matthew that of King, and St. Luke that of Priest*—St. Matthew began his Genealogy with Solomon and continued it through the Kings of the Jews; and St. Luke, by Nathan, son of David, and by the adoptions of Our Lord: so that by this means the Mystery of both anointings, of the Priesthood and the Royalty, might be joined in the Person of Our Lord, who instituted the <term>Royal Priesthood</term> <note>A concept referring to the combined spiritual and temporal authority of Christ.</note>.

It is not St. Augustine alone who thought this way. <margin>From Gregory of Nazianzus.</margin> Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note> had said before him, "(2) that Jesus Christ drew the blood of Kings from Solomon; and from Nathan, that of the High Priests." # HISTORY OF DOGMAS #

Du Pin (1) <note>Louis Ellies du Pin (1657–1719), a celebrated French ecclesiastical historian.</note> has remarked that the Narrative of Gregory of Nyssa <note>A 4th-century Church Father known for his philosophical theology.</note>, who cited an ancient Book of the *Nativity of the Virgin*, is simpler and less burdened with incidents than the one we possess today. <margin>VIII. Regarding the Protevangelium of St. James, and its Author.</margin>
VIII. <margin>VIII. On the Protevangelium of St. James, etc. by the Author.</margin>
VIII. This is what I am focusing on, because it is precisely what is important to know, and what has been neglected by those who discuss it.

<margin>St. Epiphanius appears to attribute it to the Ebionites.</margin>
*St. Epiphanius* <note>A 4th-century bishop of Salamis and a fierce hunter of heresies; his most famous work is the Panarion.</note> accuses the *Ebionites* (3), "of having forged books under the names of *St. James*, *St. Matthew*, and several other Apostles." And as the *Protevangelium* is the only known work bearing the name of *St. James* that is old enough <margin>They are not the Authors.</margin> to be attributed to the *Ebionites*, it is believed that *St. Epiphanius* intended to speak of this apocryphal piece. I cannot say what his thought was, but I can certainly assure you that unless this book has been entirely changed, it could not be the work of an *Ebionite* <note>A Jewish Christian sect that emphasized the humanity of Jesus and the continued validity of Jewish law.</note>.

Here is the substance of that fable.

The midwife, who had been sent for to assist the Virgin in <margin>Fable invented to persuade that Jesus Christ did not have a true Human Body.</margin> her childbirth, having only arrived after she had been delivered, did not hesitate to touch her. # HISTORY OF DOGMAS #

<margin>The belief regarding the childbirth comes from this Heresy.</margin> ...by these words of Clement of Alexandria <term>Clement of Alexandria: A 2nd-century Christian theologian who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</term>: (1) "MANY have held this opinion, and STILL DO, that *Mary* gave birth to a Son without her delivery having produced any change in her Person. FOR SOME say that a Midwife, having examined her after her delivery, found in her all the marks of Virginity." *Clement* does not cite the *Protévangile*; but as this Book existed in his time, there can be no doubt that this fable was taken from it.

<margin>An Oracle of Ezekiel fabricated to confirm it.</margin> However, the deception did not stop there. They felt they should make the Prophets speak, and it was asserted that the marvelous delivery of *Mary* had been predicted by *Ezekiel* in these terms: (2) A YOUNG COW HAS GIVEN BIRTH, AND HAS NOT GIVEN BIRTH. The Orthodox agreed with the Heretics that the Prophecy was real: that the young cow represented the Virgin; but they did not agree on the meaning of these words, *She has given birth, and has not given birth*. The Heretics said, *she has given birth* because she brought a son into the world: but *she has not given birth*, either because she remained a Virgin during and after the delivery, or because the son she brought into the world was not formed from her blood. This is what we learn from *Tertullian* <term>Tertullian: A prolific early Christian author from Carthage, known for his rigorous defense of the faith against heresy.</term>, refuting the *Heresy of the Valentinians* <term>Valentinians: A prominent Gnostic sect that believed Christ’s body was spiritual rather than physical matter.</term> and other Heretics on the subject of the Body of Jesus Christ. "We recognize therefore," says this ancient Doctor, "that the conception and the delivery of the Virgin *Mary* was <margin>(a) Luke 2:34.</margin> (a) this *sign* which was to be the subject of contradiction. It is also of this delivery that our Academicians say, *She has given birth, and has not given birth*." These Academicians are the Valentinians, whom *Tertullian* labels in this way because they had drawn their Theology from *Plato*. It was they who maintained that, since the Body of Jesus Christ was a spiritual Body, it had emerged from the Virgin’s womb without making any opening, because a spiritual Body penetrates another Body and does not divide it. *Tertullian* refutes this sentiment, showing that the delivery...

St. Jerome writes to (a) Paula, and explains the Hebrew alphabet to her just as Eusebius did. Apparently, they both drew from the same source. After having satisfied Paula's curiosity, he exclaims, enraptured with admiration: "What is there, I pray you, more sacred than these mysteries? What delights comparable to these? What honey sweeter than to know and taste the wisdom of God, to enter into His secrets, to penetrate the thoughts of the Creator, etc. Let us not envy the Great ones of the Earth their treasures and their pleasures. Let them drink the most exquisite liquors from gold vessels enriched with precious stones, etc. For us, our riches and our delights are to meditate day and night on the Law of God, etc." I am shortening the passage extremely, so as not to bore the reader; but I confess that this part astonishes me. Does St. Jerome indeed admire such vain mysteries? Can he take such false tinsel for gold? Or does he use what he calls *Dispensations*? <note>original: "Dispensations"; St. Jerome often used the "economical" or "dispensational" method of writing, where a writer says what is necessary for the audience rather than their absolute private opinion.</note> One would wrong his judgment; the other would not do honor to his sincerity. Let the reader decide: for my part, I do not dare to pronounce. And all I can say is that St. Jerome imprudently praised the most vain Judaic traditions and the daydreams of the **Marcosians**. Will one be surprised after this if these Sectarians, wanting to represent Jesus Christ as a great Teacher upon leaving the cradle, made him say what St. Jerome so much admired?

<margin>An amusing Scene in Hell, when J. Christ appeared there.</margin>
Let us finish the Article on the *Gospel of Nicodemus* with a little tale, which is one of the prettiest and most agreeable of the whole Romance. I believe it to be a fiction by *Leucius* <note>Leucius Charinus was the purported author of several 2nd and 3rd-century apocryphal "Acts."</note>. It is a quarrel between <term>Satan</term> and the <term>Prince of Tartarus</term> <note>In this apocryphal tradition, the "Prince of Tartarus" (or Hades) is a personification of the Underworld itself, distinct from the devil (Satan).</note>. ### CHAPTER IV.

#### *On the Heresy of <term>LEUCIUS</term> <note>original: Leuce; referring to Leucius Charinus, a 2nd-century author of apocryphal texts often associated with Gnosticism and Manichaeism.</note>, & of his <term>ACTS</term> or <term>TRAVELS</term> of the Apostles: particularly those of ST. JOHN.*

Before speaking of the Works which are incontestably by <term>Leucius</term>, it is necessary to make known to the Reader the pernicious Sect of which this Impostor was one of the principal supports, and whose Heresies he sought to advance by putting forward false <term>Acts</term> of the Apostles.

<margin>I. Ancient origin of the two Sectes of the <term>Ebionites</term>, & the <term>Docetics</term>.</margin>
I. After the Sect of the (1) simple *Judaizers*—that is to say, those Christians who, having come out of the Synagogue, maintained the necessity of keeping the Ceremonies of the Law—there are none more ancient than the opposing Sects of the <term>EBIONITES</term> <note>A Jewish-Christian movement that regarded Jesus as the Messiah but rejected his divinity and the virgin birth, insisting on the observation of Jewish law.</note> & the <term>DOCETICS</term> <note>original: Docétes; from the Greek "dokein" meaning "to seem." They believed Jesus' physical body and sufferings were only an illusion.</note>. They both arose as early as the first Century, under the eyes and despite the opposition of some of the Apostles. St. *Jerome* <note>A prominent Latin Father of the Church (c. 347–420 AD), best known for the Vulgate translation of the Bible.</note> testifies (2) "that St. *John* wrote his Gospel at the request of the Bishops of Asia, with the view of combating the Errors of *Cerinthus* <note>A Gnostic heretic who was a contemporary of St. John.</note>, and in particular the rising Dogma of the <term>Ebionites</term>, who maintained that Jesus Christ did not exist before being born of *Mary*."

<margin>St. *John* combats them in his Gospel.</margin>
The same Author assures us (3) "that the Blood of Jesus Christ was still smoking in Judea when they began to teach that his Body had been nothing but a Phantom." The testimony of this Father appears confirmed by the first Chapter of St. *John*, where the Apostle establishes first, against the <term>Ebionite</term>, <margin>(a) *John I. 1.*</margin> (a) that the *Word is God*, and that it is through Him that God created the World: And, against the <term>Docetic</term>, <margin>(b) *Ib. v. 14.*</margin> (b) *the Word was made flesh*. It is because of the antiquity of these two Heresies that *Theodoret* <note>Theodoret of Cyrus (c. 393–457 AD), a bishop and influential theologian.</note>, who follows chronological order in his books concerning the Fables of the Heretics, employs the first to refute the various types of <term>Docetics</term>: And the second to combat the different Sects of <term>Unitarians</term> <note>In this historical context, "Unitarians" refers to those who denied the Trinity, specifically the Ebionites or Monarchians.</note>, or <term>Ebionites</term>, who had appeared up until the 5th Century.

# HISTORY OF DOGMAS
<meta>catchword: of the</meta>

<margin>The error of the Ebionites prevails among Christians who came out of Judaism. That of the Docetics among Christians from among the Gentiles.</margin>
The *Ebionites* thus denied the Divinity of Jesus Christ; the *Docetics* <note>From the Greek 'dokein,' meaning 'to seem' or 'to appear.'</note> denied his Humanity. According to the former, the Lord is but a simple man, who became the Son of God at his Baptism through the full communication of the gifts of the Holy Spirit. According to the latter, J. Christ is not a man at all: He had only the appearances of one: He is pure God, and only clothed himself in a human form to carry out his ministry on Earth, and to appear to suffer, die, and rise again, although he was impassible <note>Incapable of feeling pain or suffering.</note> and immortal. *Docetism* prevailed principally among the Gentiles who had embraced the Christian Faith. They had no difficulty in recognizing the Divinity of the Lord. But being unable, or unwilling, to understand how a Divine Person could unite with a Human Nature, and believing moreover that the Body is formed of a matter which is evil in itself, they imagined that the Lord had taken only the appearances of flesh, without having the reality of it. Regarding (1) *Ebionism*, it was mainly in vogue among Christians who came out of Judaism: who, raised in the Faith of the Unity of God, misused it to deny the Divinity of the Son, under the pretext that the plurality of Divine Persons is incompatible with Unity. Thus it was that the error of the Gentile prepared him for the Faith, and that the Truth, on the contrary, was an obstacle to the Truth in the mind of the Jew.

<margin>II. These two Sects multiply in Asia.</margin>
II. The Gospel having made great progress (2) in Asia, where most of the Apostles stayed, it was also there that these two Sects took deep root. This is why, as has been very well observed, they are the only ones that (3) St. Ignatius, Bishop of Antioch, fought against in the Letters he wrote before his Martyrdom, around the year 107 of Our Lord. I will speak at present only of the *Docetics*. If we believe Theodoret, (4) *Simon* <note>Simon Magus, often cited by early church fathers as the first heretic.</note> was the first Master of this Sect. *Cerdon* followed him: *Marcion* came next; I place <term>Leucius</term> <note>original: Leuce; also known as Leucius Charinus.</note> after *Marcion*, and before *Julius Cassianus* <note>original: Jules Cassien</note>, whom *Clement of Alexandria* calls (5) the Leader and Prince

<margin>Authors of the Docetic sect.</margin>

<margin>That Docetic and Phantasiastic <note>A term for heretics who believed Christ's body was a "phantasm" or optical illusion.</note> Heretics erupted in the times of the Apostles. In the notes to the Epistle of Ignatius to the Romans, page 24. <note>original Latin: "DOCETAS & PHANTASIASTAS Haereticos, temporibus Apostolorum inficiaretur erupisse. In Not. ad Ep. Ign. ad Rom. pag. 24."</note></margin>

(2) One sees, for example, in the Letter of Pliny to Trajan concerning the Christians, that Bithynia was full of them, and that the Temples of the Idols were almost deserted.

(3) I wish neither to defend nor to combat the authenticity of the *Letters* of St. Ignatius. ### ON MANICHAEISM. BOOK II. CH. IV.

...of *Docetism* <note>The belief that Jesus Christ did not have a physical body, but only the appearance of one.</note>, although it appeared later than the others. What is said of *Simon* <note>Simon Magus, a figure often called the "father of heresies" by early church writers.</note> is very uncertain; but what is quite sure is that <margin>(a) 1 John 4:1, 2, 3.</margin> (a) *the false Teachers, who denied that J. Christ had come in the flesh*, were teaching their dogmas in Asia as early as the time of *St. John*, and that the Holy Apostle had the sorrow of seeing that <margin>(b) Ibid. v. 5.</margin> (b) THE WORLD LISTENED TO THEM. This word of the Apostle struck me, and prompted me to research the origin of *Docetism*, and the cause of its progress. Here is what I have thought on the matter.

<margin>Origin of Docetism, and the cause of its progress in Asia.</margin> Minds raised in the School of (6) *Plato*, whose Philosophy was highly esteemed in Asia, believed that from the SUPREME GOD there emanated a PERFECT INTELLIGENCE who is a SECOND GOD, and whom they called MIND, <term>Nous: Greek for mind or intellect</term> or WORD, <term>Logos: Greek for "word" or "reason," often used to describe Christ's divine nature</term>. Persuaded by this Principle, they had no difficulty in conceiving that this SPIRIT desired to reveal himself to men, and to teach them the means of salvation. But they could not believe that such a sublime Intelligence would have united itself with a portion of matter, and much less that it would have put on Human Nature with all its infirmities. That could only be suited to the Soul, which is a spiritual but mixed Substance; composed, according to the Platonists, of a celestial Substance and of the most spiritualized parts of Matter. Such was, if I am not mistaken, the origin of the Error of the *Docetics*. It was invented, received, and applauded by Philosophical minds who rose above the simplicity of the faithful common people: And as positions and Authority naturally belong to Persons who are worthy of them <margin>It was the Heresy of the Learned and the Noble.</margin> by their knowledge and capacity, this Heresy was primarily in vogue among the Learned and the Nobles of the Christians in Asia. This is seen in the Letter of *St. Ignatius* to the *Smyrnaeans*, where he speaks of the *Docetics* in these terms: (7) "Let no one deceive himself. The celestial Powers, the glorious Angels, the Princes, whether visible or invisible, will not go unpunished if they do not believe in the Blood of J. Christ. (8) Let one pay close attention to what I say."

---

<columns>2</columns>

<unclear>...and of Marcion</unclear>, etc. <note>original: "καὶ Μαρκίωνος"</note> Theodoret in the Preface to Dialogue I.
(5) <term>The leader of the Docetic sect</term> <note>original Greek: "Ὁ τῆς Δοκήσεως ἐξάρχων"</note>. Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata*, Book III, p. 465.
(6) In Book III, we will provide the idea of the Platonic Trinity.
(7) <term>Let no one be misled: both the heavenly beings, and the glory of the Angels, and the rulers, visible and invisible, if they do not believe in the blood of Christ, for them also there is judgment. Let him who is able to receive it, receive it; let place puff up no one.</term> <note>original Greek: "Μηδεὶς πλανάσθω: Καὶ τὰ ἐπουρανία, καὶ ἡ δόξα τῶν Ἀγγέλων, καὶ οἱ ἄρχοντες, ὁρατοί, τε καὶ ἀόρατοι, ἐὰν μὴ πιστεύσωσιν εἰς τὸ αἷμα Χριστοῦ, κἀκείνοις κρίσις ἐστίν. Ὁ χωρῶν χωρείτω, τόπος μηδένα φυσιοίτω."</note> Ignatius, Epistle to the Smyrnaeans, No. 6, p. 36.
(8) *Let one pay close attention*. This is, in my opinion, the sense of these words, <term>He who can receive it, let him receive it</term> <note>original: "ὁ χωρῶν χωρείτω," often translated in Latin as "Qui capit capiat."</note>. Let us notice in passing that the Author of this Epistle, whoever he may be, teaches that Faith in J. Christ crucified is a condition for the salvation of Angels. <margin>III. Reasoning of the Docetics.</margin>
III. Although the System of these Heretics was evidently
contrary to all Scripture, and to the Preaching of the Apostles attested to by all the Churches, it nevertheless managed to introduce itself and to
find a great number of Supporters. It must even be admitted
that it possessed something dazzling.

1. It had the advantage of abolishing the *scandal and the folly of the Cross* <note>A reference to 1 Corinthians 1:23; the idea that a Divine Being could suffer a shameful death was a major intellectual barrier for many in the ancient world.</note>,
and of making the Christian Religion more plausible. J. Christ had
delivered to his Executioners only a Phantom, which resembled him, while, always impassible <note>Incapable of suffering or feeling pain.</note> and immortal, he watched with contempt their blind and powerless fury.

2. This System appeared more Philosophical, more in line with the
light of Reason, than that of the Orthodox. That a Spirit
should take for some time the form of a Man, Reason conceives of as quite possible. These apparent Transformations have nothing that
surpasses the idea one has of the power of Celestial Intelligences. The
Jews believed in them, relying on the experience of their Fathers; and the
Pagans, on their religious Fables. It is not the same for the
Incarnation, which makes of the Divine Nature and the Human
Nature only a single Person. It is a Mystery that Faith
adores, but that Reason does not understand. I add that, misunderstood (4) by the ancient Heretics, and perhaps poorly explained

3. Although the *Docetics* <note>From the Greek 'dokein', meaning 'to seem'. They did not fail to allege that the *Word*, or the Son of God, according to the explanation of the <gloss>(5) Fathers, appeared to <margin>(a) *Gen.* XVIII. 1. 2. 9. 33. 4. The *Docetics* further relied on various places in the Gospels, and in the Epistles of St. *Paul*, which appeared to them to favor their Error. They said that a Human Body is always visible, always palpable, and that it has a weight proportioned to the quantity of matter of which it is composed: that it can neither penetrate other Bodies, nor be penetrated by them; yet, they added, the Body of J. Christ has none of these Properties. It was *visible* only by dispensation <note>In this theological context, 'dispensation' refers to a divine arrangement or a temporary suspension of natural laws for a specific purpose.</note>, and not by its nature, since it became *invisible* whenever the Lord willed it. It was thus that he passed <margin>(b) *Luke* IV. 30.</margin> (b) without being perceived, through the midst of a multitude who had formed the design <gloss>(7)</gloss> of casting him headlong from the summit of a mountain. It was also thus that he <margin>(c) *Luke* XXIV. 31.</margin> (c) suddenly disappeared from the eyes of the two Disciples who recognized him at *Emmaüs*. This same Body of J. Christ had no weight, since he <margin>(d) *Mark* VI. 48. 49.</margin> (d) walked upon the surface of the water without sinking. It had no solidity, since it penetrated other bodies, as was seen when his Disciples being assembled and <margin>(e) *John* XX. 26.</margin> (e) the doors of the house being closed, he entered and appeared suddenly in their midst.

<margin>These are in part the same arguments that have since been used to defend the Real Presence.</margin>
Such were, in general, the arguments of the Docetics <note>The Docetics were an early Christian sect who believed that Jesus' physical body and his suffering were only appearances, not reality.</note>. I find no difficulty in reporting them, following the example of the Ancients, who did not hide them, and of a learned (1) modern theologian who presents them in his *Observations on the Letter of St. Polycarp to the Philippians*. As for Manichaeus <note>Also known as Mani, the 3rd-century founder of Manichaeism, who incorporated Docetic ideas into his dualistic religion.</note>, he alleged several other passages from the New Testament, which we shall examine when I set forth his system. Let us only remark here that all these ancient heretics defended their error using the same scriptural testimonies and the same reasons that have been used in subsequent centuries to defend the <term>Real Presence<note>The doctrine, primarily in Roman Catholic and Orthodox theology, that the bread and wine of the Eucharist become the actual, physical body and blood of Christ.</note></term> of the Body of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist. These two opinions have this in common: they strip the Body of the Lord of all the properties of a body. If they differ, it is because in the system of the *Docetics*, anything that does not have the properties of a human body is not a human body. Whereas, in the system of the Real Presence, a human body does not cease to be a true human body even though it possesses none of the properties of a body—neither visibility, nor extension, nor weight, nor impenetrability. I leave it to the reader to judge which of these two principles is the more reasonable.

<margin>This opinion provided the Docetics with invincible proofs.</margin>
There is another observation that I cannot resolve to omit. It is that if it had been believed, in the time of the *Docetics*, that the Body of our Lord—the same Body born of the Virgin and crucified—is entirely present in the Bread of the Eucharist and in every particle of that Bread, it would not have been possible to defend the Orthodox Faith against their objections. They would have said to the Catholics: "Anything that exists without any property of the human body cannot be a human body. Now, you agree that the Body of Jesus Christ exists without any property of the human body; therefore, you agree that the Body of Jesus Christ is not a human body at all."

<margin>Docetism and the Real Presence prove one another reciprocally.</margin>
The *Docetics* further maintained that Jesus Christ appeared to have a human body even though he did not actually have one. It was a "dispensation," a miracle on the part of the Lord. Now, by what right, and under what pretext, could people who believed in the real presence of the Body of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist have rejected a miracle that was perpetually repeated in the Church, and of which the proof and example were at every moment before the eyes of the Faithful? For what absurdity was there in saying that Jesus Christ, during the—

Just as he has all the appearances of Bread and Wine, without being either one or the other, he likewise had all the appearances of a true Body, even though he was a purely spiritual Substance, and there was nothing material in him. These are two miracles that follow one another and prove each other reciprocally. Jesus Christ is truly and really in the Eucharist, stripped of all the appearances of the Body. Is it then more incredible and more absurd to clothe himself in them, when he judges it necessary, than to strip himself of them when he finds it appropriate? It is always the same Jesus exercising his Power and his Goodness, whether he appears as what he is not, or does not appear as what he is. <margin>Remarks on the Extract from Photius and on the Dogmas of Leucius.
There is doubt whether he believed the God of the Jews was evil.</margin>
1. I could not say exactly what he thought of the God of the Jews, but, if he was a *Marcionite* <note>Followers of Marcion, who taught that the God of the Old Testament was a "Just" but inferior creator, distinct from the "Good" God of the New Testament.</note>, as some (4) scholars have judged, he did not believe that this God was *evil*; the *Marcionites* attributed to Him the quality of being *Just*. It is added in the Greek Acts of the Council of Nicaea that *Leucius* carried his blasphemy so far as to say (5) that the God of the Jews, *the one who gave them the Law, is the Serpent*. But as these words, which are currently found in the Greek, are not in the old Latin version, there is great reason to suspect they were added by the Greeks out of hatred for the *Iconoclasts*. It is unlikely that the author of that version would have omitted them if they had been in his copy.

<margin>Fables of Leucius to persuade that Jesus Christ did not have a real Body. (a) 2nd Council of Nicaea, col. 858.</margin>
3. It is beyond doubt that *Leucius* denied the Incarnation. This impostor has *St. John* say (a), "That having touched *Jesus Christ*, he had sometimes (1) found him with a material and solid body, but that at other times he had found him completely *incorporeal* and *immaterial*, such that he was like a pure nothingness: That having observed the Lord when he walked upon the Earth, he had never been able to discover any trace of his footsteps: That when he was invited to the home of some Pharisee, he was given his portion of bread, like the others; but that instead of eating it, he distributed it to his Disciples, who were sufficiently nourished by the virtue he gave to this bread by blessing it."

<margin>Opinion of Clement of Alexandria. The Body of Jesus Christ was real, but impassible.</margin>
These are fables, but they do not surprise me. We know that very learned but very ancient Ecclesiastical Authors held similar ideas about the Body of Our Lord, even though they did not doubt that he had a real human body. "It would be truly RIDICULOUS to imagine," (2) says *Clement of Alexandria*, "that the Savior's body required for its preservation the food and care necessary for the maintenance of other bodies. For example, HE ATE, not to nourish his Body, which a holy Virtue preserved in its entirety, but to prevent those who conversed with him from thinking that he had only the shadow and appearance of a Body. For otherwise he was absolutely impassible <note>Incapable of suffering or feeling pain.</note>, exempt from every feeling, whether of pleasure or of pain." This reflection is somber, but it is only too true: the Mystery of the Incarnation has been the occasion for an infinity of bizarre opinions; and what we cannot deplore enough, for lamentable Schisms and cruel persecutions, which ultimately brought about the ruin of the Christian Church in the East.

5. I believe that *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar.</note> was mistaken when he reported the opinion of *Leucius* on the crucifixion of the Lord. This heretic did not say that he substituted another person in his place; that is the sentiment attributed to *Basilides* <note>An early Gnostic teacher who claimed Simon of Cyrene was crucified in Christ's place.</note>. (6) *A form entirely similar to his own was attached to this Cross.* Above it I saw the Lord, but without any figure. It was nothing but a simple Voice, different indeed from that with which he was accustomed to speak to us: a voice sweet, pleasant, and truly of God. J O H N, he said to me, *I have something to tell you, of which you must preserve a firm memory. I shall speak through your mouth, and I shall call this Cross of light sometimes* <term>INTELLIGENCE</term> <note>original: "Νῶς" (Nous), meaning Mind or Divine Intellect.</note>, *sometimes* THE WORD" <note>original: "Verbe" or "Logos".</note>, etc. All this shows, if I am not mistaken, that the opinion of *Leucius* was that Jesus Christ had delivered to the Jews to be crucified not some other man—which would have seemed violent and unjust—but a Phantom, to which he had lent his likeness, and which they took for him. <margin>Leuce's Error regarding Marriage.</margin>
6. I do not doubt that *Leuce* <note>Leucius Charinus, a 2nd-century author of apocryphal acts.</note> was heterodox on the subject of Marriage. Never was a heresy more contagious than that one; but it had its degrees, and it is not possible to know precisely how far *Leuce* carried his own. We have seen above that the most noble of the *Montanists* <note>A prophetic Christian movement that emphasized rigorous asceticism.</note> took pride in his support.

<margin>Another Error of Photius. Neither Leuce nor his peers believed in the Resurrection.</margin>
7. Here is a point on which *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar who critiqued Leuce's writings.</note> was certainly mistaken. He accuses *Leuce* of teaching the Resurrection of certain species of Animals, as well as that of Men. The word RESURRECTION misled him, for the *Marcionites* (1) <note>original Greek: "Ψυχῆς δὲ ΑΝΑΣΤΑΣΙΝ εἶναι λέγει (Marcion) καὶ ζωὴν, καὶ σωτηρίαν μόνην." — Epiphanius, *Against Heresies*, p. 364. Translation: "He [Marcion] says there is only a RESURRECTION of the Soul, and life, and salvation."</note> used this term to mean the deliverance of Souls. They considered souls as dead as long as they remain in the Body, because they are there subjected to bodily Passions. The death of the Body was their RESURRECTION and their Life. This was a concept held by ancient Philosophers: and this passage could confirm that *Leuce* was a *Marcionite* <note>Followers of Marcion, who rejected the Old Testament and believed the material world was evil.</note>, or at least held the views of *Marcion*, as Mr. *Grabe* <note>John Ernest Grabe, a scholar of early Christian texts.</note> has conjectured. All the Heretics who denied that *Jesus Christ* had a true Body consequently denied the *Resurrection of the Body*. It was a logical result of their hypothesis. One should not object to my argument by saying that our heretic also taught the *Resurrection of certain Animals*: he must have believed in it just as he believed in that of Men, for it is a dogma of *Marcion* that (2) <note>original Greek: "Ὅτι μία ψυχὴ ἐστὶ, ἐν ζώοις, καὶ ἐν ἀνθρώποις." — Epiphanius, ibid. Translation: "That there is one [kind of] soul, both in animals and in humans."</note> Human Souls and those of Beasts are of the same substance. (a) *Justin Martyr* <note>An early Christian apologist and philosopher.</note> had held the same sentiment before embracing the Faith.

<margin>(a) In Dialogue, p. m. 171.</margin>

<margin>God did not create the Demons. An opinion common to several ancient Heretics.</margin>
8. "*Leuce* did not believe," *says Photius*, "that God is the Creator of Demons." This is apparently one of the errors that caused him to be labeled a *Manichaean* <note>Followers of Mani who believed in a dualistic struggle between Light and Darkness.</note>. One must not imagine, however, that he believed the *Demon* [the Devil] was eternal. Doubtless he believed him to be born from the disordered movement of Matter, just as ancient Philosophers believed that Animals were born from the decay of the Earth. This was the view of the *Manichaeans*, which is also attributed to the (3) *Priscillianists* <note>Followers of a 4th-century ascetic movement in Spain. Footnote (3) original Latin: "Nec Natura ejus (Diaboli) opificium Dei sit, sed eum ex chao & tenebris emersisse." — Leo I, Letter 15. Translation: "Neither is his [the Devil's] nature the handiwork of God, but rather he emerged from chaos and darkness."</note>.

<margin>Leuce dogmatizes against Images.</margin>
9. Finally, *Photius* testifies (4) that in the *Acts of St. John*, *Leuce* dogmatized against *Images*, just as the *Iconoclasts* <note>"Image-breakers" who opposed the use of religious icons.</note> did in later times. This is true, and it is what we are going to clarify through the fragment of the *Acts of St. John* that the Second Council of Nicaea has preserved for us.

...[Constan]tine <note>Constantine V (reigned 741–775), a Byzantine Emperor who led the movement against the use of religious images.</note>, whom the Icon-worshipers <note>original: *Iconolatres*; those who venerated religious images.</note> have unworthily nicknamed *Copronymus* <note>original: *Copronyme*; a derogatory name meaning "dung-named," reflecting the intense hostility between him and the image-venerating party.</note>, had condemned Images and cited, among others, a passage from the *History of St. John* by *Leucius* <note>original: *Leuce*; Leucius Charinus, the 2nd-century author of several apocryphal "Acts" of the apostles.</note>, the substance of which follows:

<margin>(a) Second Council of Nicaea, Act V. Greek column 357. Latin Version column 798. St. John disapproves of the action of a Christian who had his portrait painted.</margin>
(a) A Christian named *Lycomedes* had commissioned a painting of this Apostle. Upon seeing a portrait in his disciple's house and not knowing it was his own, St. John said to Lycomedes: *“What does this image mean, and which of your Gods is it? I see clearly that you have not entirely cast off the customs of the Pagans.”* Lycomedes replied: *“I recognize only one God, and He is the one who restored life to my wife and me. But if, after that God, one can call those men who are our benefactors 'GODS', then you are the God whom this image represents. It is you whom I* CROWN; *it is you whom* I LOVE, *and whom* I HONOR *as the faithful Guide who led me to the source of all good.”* *“You are joking,* MY SON,” said St. John; *“you will not make me believe that this is my portrait.”* Then, Lycomedes having brought a mirror, and St. John having recognized his own face: “THE LORD JESUS CHRIST LIVES,” he said, *“it is true that this image resembles me.”* (5) BUT YOU HAVE DONE A VERY BAD THING.

<margin>Reflection on this story.</margin>
The Bishops of the Council of Nicaea were outraged, as one might imagine, both against the Author of this account and against those who had dared to use it. Indeed, the *witness* was worthless: he is an author full of heresies and an obvious imposter. But as for the story itself, it contains nothing that contradicts the Apostolic Spirit, nor the practice and faith of the ancient Church. If it is not true, it is very plausible, and nothing makes it suspicious except its author. The same cannot be said for an infinite number of authorities and testimonies cited by the Bishops of Nicaea; the facts they present are clearly false, the books containing them are forged, and the authors who wrote them are perhaps the boldest and most shameless liars who have ever existed. What I say may seem sharp, but it is only too true, and one must not hold back when dealing with people of such bad faith. Regarding the Fathers of Constantinople, it was perhaps imprudent to cite the testimony of *Leucius*, but we also do not know with what limitations they did so.

<margin>The Bishops of Nicaea agree that it is Pagan Idolatry to crown images.</margin>
Although the Bishops of Nicaea rejected the story of *Lycomedes* as coming from a Heretical author, they nevertheless acknowledged that St. John would have been right to condemn a *crowned image*. To have images of the Saints and to venerate them is, according to them,

### OF MANICHAEISM BOOK II. CH. IV. ###
<meta>catchword: death</meta>

...would not have completely offended the proprieties of the time and place where *Leuce* <note>Leucius Charinus, the purported 2nd-century author of various apocryphal "Acts" of the Apostles.</note> was writing. He is a liar, but there is no reason to suppose that he is a fool. Let us only seek what might have been the occasion and origin of such a fiction.

<margin>Religious Dances have been in use among sensible Sects.</margin>
What rendered the Dances of the Pagans criminal in their Festivals and in their Sacrifices was, on one hand, that they were part of the Cult of Idols; and, on the other, that they were impure and lascivious. For otherwise, when modesty presided over them, and they were but testimonies of the gratitude and joy that men felt for the blessings of God, they were regarded as sacred Exercises. Such were the Dances of the *Therapeutae* <note>A Jewish ascetic sect in Egypt, similar to the Essenes, known for their communal devotion.</note> of Egypt, which *Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher.</note> describes and justifies in his Treatise *On the Contemplative Life*. Here is what he says of them, according to the Translation by *Morel*, which I shall copy, although it has a somewhat antique air.

<margin>Among the Therapeutae of Egypt.</margin>
<margin>(a) Translation of Philo. p. 846. See the Greek, *On the Contemplative Life* p. m. 902.</margin>
> (a) „ After supper the *Therapeutae* celebrate the holy Vigil,

Christ being in the middle, and his Disciples holding hands and forming a Circle around him—it is, in my opinion, a manifest imitation of the sacred Dances of the *Corybantes* <note>The Corybantes were the armed and music-making priests who worshipped the goddess Cybele with ecstatic dancing.</note>. There was in Greece, in the Islands of the Aegean Sea, in Asia, and in Phoenicia, a Pagan Ceremony that *Leuce* <note>Leucius Charinus, the 2nd-century purported author of several apocryphal Acts.</note>, who was Asian, had in view. They honored Gods there called (1) CABIRI <note>The Cabiri were a group of enigmatic chthonic deities, often depicted as "the Great Gods" in mystery cults.</note>, that is to say, THE STRONG ONES. It is a name that Scripture gives to the Angels. When someone was initiated into their Mysteries, they were crowned with an olive branch, given a purple Girdle, placed on a kind of Throne: AND ALL THE INITIATES, HOLDING HANDS, FORMED A CIRCLE AROUND HIM, AND DANCED WHILE SINGING HYMNS in honor of their Gods. This Ceremony was called (2) ENTHRONIZATION. Pagan Initiations figured a kind of association of Men with the Gods. They entered, so to speak, into their family, and into their most intimate favor. One cannot say that the Apostles initiate J. Christ into the Mysteries of the Divinity, but as he is going to re-enter his Glory, and retake possession of his Throne, it is very likely that *Leuce*, who knew the Pagan Ceremony I have just described, wished to adopt it, and represent the Apostles—who were then the *Initiates* into the Mysteries of the Savior—celebrating his *Enthronization* by Dances and by Hymns.

### CHAPTER V.

#### Continuation of the ACTS, or TRAVELS of the Apostles by LEUCIUS. On the Acts of St. PETER, St. ANDREW, and St. THOMAS.

<margin>I. The Fables of Leucius have made their way into Apostolic History.</margin>
I. ONE can judge the History of the Apostles that *Leucius* <note>original: "Leuce." Leucius Charinus was a 2nd-century author of apocryphal texts often associated with Gnosticism and Manichaeism.</note> had composed by the fragments I have just reported, which confirm well enough the judgment of *Photius* <note>Photius (c. 810–893 AD) was a Patriarch of Constantinople and a prolific scholar whose "Bibliotheca" preserves summaries of many lost ancient books.</note>. This judgment was that it contained (1) a myriad of childish, unbelievable, ill-conceived, false, and altogether impertinent things. Nevertheless, these crude fables did not fail to enter into Apostolic History, as Superstition eagerly embraced what had been invented by Imposture. I have already shown this in the preceding chapters, and I shall give new proofs of it in this one. Who would have believed that the impostor *Leucius*—the Manichaean *Leucius*, as he is called—could have infected the entire Apostolic Tradition with his fables?

<margin>The false Melito copies him, and the Moderns copy Melito.</margin>
*Francesco Maria Fiorentini* <note>original: "François Marie Florentinius." A 17th-century Italian physician and historian known for his work on martyrologies.</note>, a modern author very often cited by *Mr. de Tillemont* <note>Sébastien le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a French ecclesiastical historian noted for his meticulous accuracy.</note>, published with commentary an ancient Martyrology falsely attributed to *St. Jerome*, and joined to it a History of the *Passion of St. John* written by a certain *Mellitus*, or *Melito*, who calls himself Bishop of Laodicea. This other impostor asserts that (2) *Leucius* wrote the *Acts of St. John, St. Andrew, and St. Thomas*, in which he recounts fairly faithfully a part of the *Miracles* that the Lord performed through their ministry, although regarding *Doctrine*, he was in the error of the Two Principles <note>The "Two Principles" refers to the Manichaean belief in a dualistic struggle between a good god of light and an evil god of darkness.</note>, etc. The author gives the same testimony to *Leucius* in a book titled (3) ON THE PASSING, or, on the Death of the Virgin, which shows that he copied the fables that *Leucius* had invented, with the sole precaution of cutting out the grossest heresies. I say the "grossest," for he adopts the more subtle ones. What he did has been imitated by countless others. Almost all of Apostolic History has been drawn from such a poisoned source, and these

<margin>III. Origin of the battles of St. Peter in Rome against Simon the Magician.</margin>
III. This is all that I can find regarding the *Acts of St. Peter* in the Authors who have taken the trouble to collect fragments of them. I will dwell only on the one that Origen has preserved for us, because it led me to the source of a long fable which, since the fourth Century, has been received in the West as an Apostolic Tradition. The reason for this is that it serves to confirm the opinion of the stay and Martyrdom of St. Peter in Rome. I have often wished to know who might be its Author, and it seems to me that I have found him. It is apparently *Leuce* <note>Leucius Charinus, a 2nd-century author of several apocryphal "Acts" of the Apostles, often criticized for his unorthodox or "Manichaean" leanings.</note>, the liar *Leuce*, who invented the long fable of the battles of *St. Peter* in Rome against *Simon the Magician*, and all the rest of this ridiculous Romance, which another Impostor of the 4th Century—who took, or to whom was given the name (7) of *Hegesippus*—inserted into a false *History of the Ruin of Jerusalem* <note>This refers to "Pseudo-Hegesippus," a Latin adaptation of Josephus's "Jewish War" attributed to an anonymous 4th-century author, often confused with the earlier 2nd-century chronicler Hegesippus.</note>. This passage seems to me worthy of the Reader's curiosity, and I cannot believe they would hold it against me for pausing here.

<margin>Summary of this fable taken from the pseudo-*Hegesippus*. (a) *On the Ruin of Jerusalem Book III. 2.*</margin>
The pseudo-*Hegesippus* thus recounts there (a) the journey of St. Peter to Rome to pursue *Simon*: the Disputes they had together; the miracles of St. Peter; the wonders of Simon; the Undertaking of the Impostor, who, supported by his Demons, wanted to ascend to Heaven in the presence of the Roman People; and finally his tragic death, when, his Demons having abandoned him at the prayer of St. Peter, he fell, and was crushed or mortally wounded by his fall. The Author adds that *Nero*, irritated by the death of the Magician, wanted to take revenge on the Apostle: that the Faithful in Rome, seeing the peril to which he was exposed, entreated him to leave the City; that he yielded to their prayers, but having arrived at the gate, he met Jesus Christ there, adored him, and said to him, **LORD, where are you going?** (8) <note>original: "DOMINE, quo vadis?" This is the origin of the famous "Quo Vadis" legend.</note> *I am coming to Rome*, Jesus Christ answered him, *to be crucified a second time*. St. Peter well understood what that meant. He retraced his steps, was captured, and was crucified.

To these old Traditions, new ones have been added. In Rome, on the Appian Way, one is shown the place where the Apo-

It is not a matter of demonstrating the falsity of this Romance (1). Never did a fable show itself more clearly for what it is. However, it is defended by learned Moderns, and among others by Monsieur de Tillemont <note>Louis-Sébastien Le Nain de Tillemont (1637–1698), a priest and historian known for his immense erudition but also his traditionalist devotion.</note>, who tells us frankly, *(a) that he would rather be mistaken with Arnobius, Cyril of Jerusalem, the Legates of Pope Liberius, etc., than accuse a great number of the most illustrious and grave Masters of the Latin and Greek Church of indiscreet credulity.* Let us leave Monsieur de Tillemont to his scruples. Let us not even examine whether they arise more from a "carnal prudence" <note>A 17th-century term for worldly or political caution as opposed to spiritual or intellectual honesty.</note> than from a just veneration for Antiquity; let us stop only at this single consideration: *Arnobius, Cyril of Jerusalem, the Legates of Liberius, etc.* are the Masters of Monsieur de Tillemont. But these Authors had their own *Masters*, for the oldest, who is *Arnobius* <note>Arnobius of Sicca (died c. 330 AD), an Early Christian apologist.</note>, lived nearly two hundred and fifty years after the event. Now, it is these *Masters*, or this *Master*, whom I seek; and, if I have not found him, I am not far off. It is the Impostor Leuce <note>Leucius Charinus, the reputed author of several 2nd-century apocryphal Acts, often associated with Gnostic or Manichaean circles.</note>. To him must be left the glory of the invention. The others did nothing but expand and embellish it. The Reader will wish to know what gave rise to this thought. I am going to tell him.

<margin>This fable comes from the *Acts of Peter* by Leuce. Reasons which persuade us of this.</margin>
The words attributed to Our Lord, **"I am coming to Rome to be crucified a second time,"** are taken from the *Acts of St. Peter*. Origen testifies to this. The *Acts of St. Peter* are by *Leuce*. Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople and scholar who documented many now-lost ancient texts.</note> affirms it. These words are a dependency of the entire fabulous History of St. Peter, of which they form a part. The battles of St. Peter against *Simon* <note>Simon Magus, the sorcerer mentioned in Acts 8, who in legend became Peter's great rival in Rome.</note> are linked with his victory: his victory with his flight, because his victory irritated *Nero*: his flight is linked with the appearance of Jesus Christ, whom he meets at the gate of Rome, and with the words the Lord says to him: and these words are linked with the Martyrdom of St. Peter, of which they were the cause. All these Events are chained together. The first is the cause of the second; the second of the third, and so on with the others. From this I draw this consequence, which is at least very likely: that the entire fable comes from the same source. Since the words of Jesus Christ are taken from the *Acts of St. Peter*, of which Leuce was the Author, it must be that all the rest of the history has the same origin, save for the removal of the ornaments that later Authors
