<margin>Response to some Objections.</margin>
It seems to me that only two objections can be raised against me. The first is that the pseudo-*Hegesippus* <note>An early Christian chronicler; "pseudo" indicates works falsely attributed to him.</note>, *Arnobius*, *Cyril of Jerusalem*, etc., took only the flight of this Apostle and the word the Lord spoke to him from the *Acts of St. Peter*, and that regarding the rest, they drew it from authentic writings. But what proof is there for this assertion? It is one and the same History, of which all the parts are linked together. Everything in it indicates the same origin; everything is marked with the same stamp of the fabulous.

<margin>Grabe supposes two Books under the name of *Acts of St. Peter*. The futility of this supposition.</margin>
The second Objection is that there were two Books under the name of the *Acts of St. Peter*. This is indeed the resource of the late Mr. *Grabe* <note>John Ernest Grabe (1666–1711), a German-born Anglican theologian and scholar of early Christian texts.</note>, who had the same fault as Mr. de *Tillemont*: a blind and servile deference to Antiquity. But where did he find two kinds of *Acts of St. Peter*; some legitimate, the others forged; some the work of an Orthodox author, the others the work of a Heretic? *Origen* speaks of the *Acts of St. Peter*: did he distinguish between two kinds? *Eusebius*, *St. Jerome*, *Innocent I*, *Gelasius* speak of them. Did any of them distinguish between two kinds? I ask the same question regarding all the ancient Authors who mentioned these *Acts*, and there is no answer to give me, except that there are *Acts of St. Peter* (2), which were cited by the Orthodox, from which one concludes that there must have been legitimate ones: a miserable reason, and one against which a thousand Objections could be made. It is true, some Fathers cited these *Acts*, but how did they cite them? *Origen*, who alleges them, shows well enough that he does not hold them in high regard: (3) **IF ANYONE,** he says, **WISHES TO RECEIVE THIS WORD; IF IT GIVES HIM PLEASURE.** <note>original Latin/Greek: "Si quelcun veut bien recevoir cette parole; si cela lui fait plaisir." Origen is signaling his skepticism by leaving the choice to the reader.</note> *Clement of Alexandria* alleges them—or at least it is conjectured so—but he speaks of them as *Acts* without authority. He uses these words: (4) **SOME SAY.** Furthermore, did this Doctor not cite (b) the *Acts of St. John* by *Leucius* <note>Leucius Charinus, the reputed author of several apocryphal Acts of the Apostles, often associated with Gnostic or Manichaean circles.</note> under the name of *Traditions*, and that in a place that is manifestly heretical? The Ancients were not scrupulous in the matter of citations. They chose from false pieces whatever was honorable to the Christian Religion, or whatever suited their own sentiments. The most prudent among them provided the information without guaranteeing it. In a word, let someone prove to me that there were two Books under the name of *Acts of St. Peter* which were of different characters and by different Authors, or let my conclusion stand: which is that the entire fable...

<margin>IV. Concerning the *Acts of St. Andrew*. Two editions of this forged work.</margin>
IV. Let us move on to the *Acts of St. Andrew*, which are also a work by the impostor *Leucius*. Today there are (2) two pieces to which this name is given; or rather, there are (3) two editions of the same piece, of which the oldest is universally rejected, and the other is defended by modern Catholics; the ancient version is still found in Greek in the Oxford Library.
<margin>(b) Sandius, Nucleus Historiae Ecclesiasticae, page 11.</margin>
*Sandius* (b), who had read it, testifies "that it is the same thing as the book titled <term>The Passion of St. Andrew</term>, *written by the priests of Achaia*, and that furthermore it is nothing but a tissue of ridiculous fables, in which he found nothing that smells of Manichaeism, except in the articles upon which the Manichaeans agreed with the Montanists." <note>The Montanists were an early Christian movement known for their emphasis on prophecy and asceticism; the author suggests the "Acts" only overlap with Manichaeism on these shared points.</note> This testimony confirms what I have said: that the new *Acts of St. Andrew* are merely the old ones revised. Mr. de *Tillemont* suspects this as well. *It is much to be feared* (c), *he says, that this is a work composed in later centuries, either based on what tradition had preserved of the death of St. Andrew,* <margin>(c) Notes on St. Andrew, Tome I, pages 1062, 1063.</margin> **or even based on the Acts of Leucius, from which they have taken only what seemed best.** *Philastrius*, who had seen only the ancient Acts, believed he had found Manichaeism there because dogs and other animals were made to speak, "with the intention," *he says*, "of persuading the world that the souls of men and those of beasts are of the same species." <margin>(c) Philastrius, as cited above.</margin> This kind Bishop apparently did not consider that, since *Moses* had made a serpent and a female donkey speak, one could attribute the same intention to him.

Such is the pretty tale that was read in the *Travels of St. Thomas*; but, although the Manichaeans <note>A major dualistic religion that viewed the world as a struggle between light and darkness.</note> received this Apocrypha, there is no appearance that they were the authors of it. They would never have attributed to *St. Thomas* an action similar to that which they condemned in *St. Peter*, and which was directly opposed to the (f) Precept of Jesus Christ, which they prided themselves on observing. I also doubt very much that they would have introduced the heroine of their romance singing Hebrew Psalms. They condemned (g) the Book of Psalms because of the frequent imprecations <note>Cursing or calling down evil upon enemies.</note> that *David* makes there against his enemies and against idolaters, which seemed to them too opposed to the patience and mercy of the Lord.

The second, that the *Indies* spoken of in these travels are the East Indies.

# HISTORY OF DOGMES
<meta>catchword: of.</meta>

[...] such. Now, I will prove in an evident manner that it is *Persia*, and that neither *Leucius* <note>original Latin: "Leuce"; likely referring to Leucius Charinus, the purported author of apocryphal apostolic acts.</note>, nor any ancient author before the end of the 4th century, even thought of sending him to the *Coromandel* coast, or to that of *Malabar*; it is more modern writers who, deceived by the ambiguity of the name, imagined that the Apostle had preached in the *East Indies*.

<margin>2. Which Indias St. Thomas preached in. Three Indias. The first seems to be Arabia Felix.</margin>
One reads, in the fabulous *Abdias* <note>A legendary figure said to be the first Bishop of Babylon and author of a history of the Apostles, now considered apocryphal.</note>, "that the Ancients make mention of *three Indias*. (1) The first situated toward Ethiopia: the second, near the *Medes*, and the third at the extremity of the Continent." This is perhaps the most reasonable thing the author has said. There are two Indias of which it can be said that they are *toward Ethiopia*. One is in (2) Africa, and borders Egypt: the other is *Yemen* <note>original: "Hyémen"</note>, which is separated from it only by the Gulf that the Ancients name indifferently (3) *the Indian Gulf*, and *the Ethiopic Gulf*. The *Indians* to whom *St. Bartholomew* preached are the Arabs of *Yemen*, who are named by *Philostorgius* (4) the INNER INDIANS, or THE NEAREST, and by *Sophronius* (5) the FORTUNATE INDIANS, or *Blessed* <note>A reference to Arabia Felix, or "Happy Arabia."</note>.

<margin>The second is Persia. This is where Thomas went to preach.</margin>
The *India* which is *near the Country of the Medes* is evidently *Persia*, and the neighboring provinces which were subjected to the Parthians <note>An ancient Iranian empire.</note>, and later to the Persians. Now, it is in that country—in the Empire of the Parthians or the Persians—that (6) Ecclesiastical Historians testify that *St. Thomas* went to preach the Gospel. Thus, the Metropolitan of Persia has boasted for several centuries of being the Successor of *St. Thomas*. The author of the Travels of this Apostle, and the author of the *History of Abdias*, agree perfectly well with our other writers. It is not to the *East Indies* that they send *St. Thomas*: it is to *Persia*, as I have recognized by a word to which I do not know if anyone else has noticed.

<margin>Proofs of this fact.</margin>

"Under the name of India among the ancients come very extensive regions. For example: Libya, Egypt, Parthia, Ethiopia, Arabia, and Palestine, as observed by Turnebus, XXI. 9. They recount (a), "that the Apostle, unable to resolve to follow the Divine Vocation, which called him into such distant Regions, the Lord caused a Merchant to be found in Jerusalem, who had been sent from India (7) by **King Gundaphore**." It is this little word that began to put me on the right track. **King Gundaphore** is an imaginary King, but the **King of Gundaphore** is a very real King. He is the King of Persia. The name of the Royal City was given to the King. This *Gundaphore* is evidently **Gundishapur** <note>original: "Gundschavur"</note>, which is ordinarily called **Gondisapor**, of which I spoke at length in the First Part of this Work, because it was the Theater of the execution of Manichaeus. *This City became the Residence of the Persian Kings since Artaxares* <note>Referring to Ardashir I, founder of the Sassanid Empire.</note> *seized the Empire, or at least under the reign of* **Shapur**, *or* **Sapor I**, *who gave it his name.* The Greeks, who converted *Shapur* into *Sapor*, and by corruption into *Sephorus*, and into *Siphorus*, as we shall see, have similarly converted *Gundishapur* into *Gundaphore*.

<margin>Response to an Objection.</margin>
If one were to object to a Proof which has such a great air of evidence, that the Royal City was not called *Gundishapur* when *St. Thomas* went to Persia, nor even when *Leucius* <note>Leucius Charinus, the supposed author of several apocryphal Acts of the Apostles.</note> wrote his *Acts*, I would respond that nothing is more common in Narrations than to substitute new names of Cities for their ancient names, and that the Pieces of *Leucius*, and other similar ones, have been touched and retouched several times. I even have much reason to conjecture that what we have today in Greek and Latin was translated from Syriac. One finds expressions there that are neither Greek nor Latin, and it is certainly from the ignorance of a Translator, or the negligence of a Copyist, that this *King Gundaphore* came to us, meaning the King of *Gundishapur*, or of *Gondisapor*.

### CHAPTER VI.

*Reflections on THE APOSTOLIC HISTORY OF ABDIAS. That the Manichaeans did not baptize in oil. Various Anointings used in Baptism. Concerning the ACTS OF PAUL AND THECLA received by the Manichaeans.*

<margin>I. ON THE HISTORY of Abdias.</margin>
I have run through the various Apocrypha <note>Non-canonical texts whose authenticity or divine inspiration is rejected by the Church.</note> which are said to have been composed or falsified by the Manichaeans. I will now treat the *Apostolic History of Abdias*, because the Author made use of the Memoirs of *Leucius* <note>Leucius Charinus, the purported author of several apocryphal "Acts" of the Apostles.</note>, and because it is believed that one finds there proofs that the Manichaeans baptized in oil, which is quite false.

I. WOLFGANG LAZIUS, Physician and Historiographer to the Emperor *Ferdinand I*, a learned and industrious man, published the *History of Abdias* in 1551 based on two Manuscripts, one of which appeared to be seven hundred years old. This clever man allowed himself to be caught off guard by a (1) Piece which has been rejected by all good Critics and proscribed by *Paul IV*. *Melanchthon* <note>Philipp Melanchthon (1497–1560), a key leader of the Protestant Reformation.</note>, who had seen it in Manuscript, was not fooled by it. He sent it to *George*, Prince...

<column-break/>

...the Author's thought. The ancient Christians did not believe that the Sun illuminated the lower Hemisphere: This is what they called the *Region of darkness*. India, according to them, marked the end of the illuminated surface of the Earth.

(7) This Objection is that, according to the false *Abdias* and the *Greek Acts*, the Indies where *St. Thomas* went to preach were so far from Palestine that it usually took three years to make the voyage by sea. This only proves the ignorance of the Author, or his affectation in decorating his fable with miraculous circumstances, for *St. Thomas* arrived there in three months. Furthermore, even if it were a question of the East Indies, it did not take three years to get there, from whatever port one embarked, whether from Egypt or Arabia.

<margin>Jude and Thomas are the same person.</margin>
3. *Adée* <note>Addai</note>, or *Thaddeus*, is, in the works of our historians, a disciple of St. *Thomas*, and not of St. *Jude*; this seems to present a difficulty, but in fact does not. For it is a very ancient tradition that St. *Jude* and St. *Thomas* are the same person. *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), the "Father of Church History."</note> says positively that (3) *Jude* was also called *Thomas*, which is confirmed by the (4) fragment of the *Travels of St. Thomas*, which Mr. *Simon* <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a pioneer of modern biblical criticism.</note> inserted in his *New Observations on the New Testament*, and by other writers whom I cite at the bottom of the page.

<margin>The Apostolic History is the work of a Latin.</margin>
4. As for the author of the *Apostolic History*, it is certainly neither *Abdias*, nor *Addai*, nor *Craton* the disciple of the Apostles: it is also not true that the original was in *Hebrew*, as is claimed in the Preface. Furthermore, it is not true that a certain *Eutropius* translated it from Hebrew into Greek, nor that *Julius Africanus*, a Greek author, translated it into Latin. There are manifest proofs within the work itself that it was composed by a Latin speaker, as (g) Mr. *Fabricius* <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a renowned scholar of apocryphal literature.</note> has shown. <margin>(g) See his Notes p. 389.</margin> However, the author copied and interpolated ancient memoirs, most of which were originally in Greek, and some in Syriac, such as the *History of Simon and Jude*. One finds in his narrative a great number (5) of Greek turns of phrase, and in some places several Hebraisms. He borrowed heavily from the *Acts of St. Andrew*, *St. John*, and *St. Thomas*, (6) written in Greek by *Leucius* <note>Leucius Charinus, the reputed author of several non-canonical Acts of the Apostles, often associated with Gnostic or Manichaean circles.</note>. One can recognize that he drew from ancient sources by the customs mentioned, which belong to the earliest antiquity. And one recognizes likewise, by newer customs, that he interpolated these ancient memoirs, or that he copied from modern ones.

<margin>It was only composed in the 6th century, or at the end of the 5th at the earliest.</margin>
5. Regarding the era of the author, one cannot place him earlier than toward the end of the 5th century, but there is much appearance that he lived in the 6th, and perhaps even later. I say that one can-

### ON MANICHAEISM. BOOK II. CHAPTER VI. ###

<meta>catchword: Vol. I.</meta>

<margin>Origin of what is called the Sanctification of Water. It comes from Heretics.</margin>
I. This *Sanctification of Water* is an ancient Ceremony, but, in my opinion, very superstitious, being founded on two gross errors. The first is that evil Spirits infest the Elements, and that they must be driven out by Exorcism. The second is that the Holy Spirit, called upon by Prayer, descends into the exorcised water and penetrates it with a divine and sanctifying virtue. One finds nothing like this in the earliest Christian and Orthodox Authors; however, one finds these two Errors, and the Sanctification of Water which they cause, among the Valentinians <note>The Valentinians were followers of Valentinus, a 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who developed a complex system of spiritual eons.</note>. These Heretics taught (5) that *Water, being exorcised and thereby made fit for Baptism, no longer admits what is evil (that is to say, the malignant Powers, which have been driven out by Exorcism). On the contrary, it receives Sanctification, that is to say, the Holy Spirit, and the power to sanctify*. I would wish, for the honor of the Orthodox, that this Practice were found in certain and incontestable Acts older than the *Eastern Doctrine of Theodotus* <note>Theodotus was a Gnostic teacher; his works are known primarily through excerpts preserved by Clement of Alexandria.</note>, so that there would be no reason to judge that it draws its origin from Heretics.

<margin>Response to Objections.</margin>
One might object to me that the Author of the *Apostolic History*, in condemning Baptism in oil, would have removed that Practice as a superstition peculiar to the Manichaeans, and substituted Baptism in water in its place. I respond that if it had been in the Greek Acts that he copies, he would never have said that *it is a Book rejected by* SOME, BECAUSE OF ITS PROLIXITY <note>original: "prolixité" — meaning wordiness or excessive length.</note>. He would have said that this Book is rejected by the entire Church because of its Heresies.

<margin>Initiation through Anointing, through Baptism, and through the Eucharist.</margin>
One might object to me in the second place these words of the King of the Indies: *I have heard it said that this Magician initiates through oil, through bread, and through a magic water*, which means, according to the learned Mr. *Fabricius* <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a German classical scholar and bibliographer.</note>, through *Baptism in oil, and through the Eucharist distributed with bread and water*. It seems much more natural to me to say that the *Oil* designates the *anointing* <note>term: "onction" — the ritual act of applying oil to a person, common in both initiation and healing.</note> of Proselytes, which I am about to discuss; that the *Bread* designates the Eucharist, and the *Water* designates Baptism. It is called a *magic Water* because of the exorcism and the words by which it was consecrated.

<margin>Simon incorrectly rendered the word σφραγὶς <note>seal</note> as Confirmation. (b) New Observ. p. 8.</margin>
Finally, one might object to me a word from Mr. Simon, who says, in the extract he gave us from the *Acts of St. Thomas*, (b) that the King *fasting, in* SPRINGS, *which are held adjacent to the sea, of* EVERLASTING WATER *he gave me baptism*. <note>original Latin: "jejunium, in FONTIBUS, qui contigui habentur mari, PERENNIS AQUÆ mihi baptismum dedit." — Source: Pseudo-Clement, Recognitions, Book VI. 15.</note> And in the Clementines, Homily IX. No. 19. p. 684. *in an ever-flowing river, and spring, then even in the sea having washed themselves* etc. <note>original Greek: "ἀενάῳ ποτάμῳ, καὶ πηγῇ, ἔπειτα κἂν θαλάσσῃ ἀπολουσάμενοι" — The author is citing early Christian texts to show that water baptism, even in natural sources, was the standard tradition.</note> See also *Summary of the Deeds of Peter*. p. 769. and elsewhere.

(4) *He, however, went to the spring which was nearby, and sanctified it, and baptized the woman with many others.* <note>original Latin: "Ille autem abiit ad fontem, qui erat proximus, & sanctificavit illum, & baptizavit mulierem cum multis aliis." — Abdias, p. 701.</note>

(5) *So also the water, even that which is exorcised, not only keeps out the worse, but also acquires sanctification.* <note>original Greek: "Οὕτω καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ, καὶ τὸ ἐξορκιζόμενον, οὐ μόνον χωρεῖ τὸ χεῖρον, ἀλλὰ καὶ ἁγιασμὸν προσλαμβάνει." — Found in the Excerpts of Theodotus, p. 83.</note>

Abdias, p. 700. This allows us to judge the time in which he wrote. (On the Resurrection of the Flesh).

### ON MANICHAEISM. BOOK II. CH. VI. ###
Ggg 2

<margin>V. Observations on this Anointing and on the prayers.
(b) As cited above, p. 9.</margin>
V. I do not know why Mr. Simon finds all these (b) *prayers ridiculous, adding that the Books of the Gnostics and the Manichaeans were filled with these Formulas of invocation.* For my part, I judge them with more indulgence, or rather with more equity. Let us make some Observations on this passage, which contains nothing heterodox, nothing but what conforms to very ancient practices.

<margin>1. This Anointing is not a Baptism.</margin>
1. I remark therefore first, that the Anointing of the Proselytes <note>A proselyte is a person who has recently converted from one religion or belief to another.</note>, mentioned in the *Acts of St. Thomas*, could not be Baptism. The reason is that the Apostle did not immerse them in the oil: *he only poured it over their head.* Now, one did not baptize by sprinkling <note>original: "aspersion"</note> when the *Acts of St. Thomas* were written. This custom only began in the West toward the end of the (6) 6th century, and was never received in the East, where these Acts were composed.

<margin>2. Anointing in Baptism began among the Heretics and likely comes from them.</margin>
2. Anointing was introduced into Baptism early enough. But it was not yet in use in the Catholic Church in the time (7) of *Justin Martyr*, for he makes no mention of it in his Description of Baptism. One only sees that it was practiced in the time of *Tertullian*.

It is dangerous to offend Prejudices, but I do it so often that I hardly trouble myself about it anymore. I have remarked that the Exorcism of Baptismal Water drew its origin from the Heretics: I have a great suspicion that the Anointing used in Baptism comes from the same source. Here is the proof. The Valentinians <note>A major Gnostic movement founded by Valentinus in the 2nd century.</note> practiced it, as seen in the *Extracts from the Doctrine of Theodote*. (8) *The bread and the oil, he says, are sanctified by the power of the Name, that is to say, by the invocation of the Trinity. And although these things appear to be the same as when they were taken*

<column-break/>

<margin>Chapter VIII.) to say, marking it with the Sign of the Cross. But the Greeks did not then use the word "to seal" <note>original: "σφραγίζειν" (sphragizein)</note> in the same sense.</margin>
(2) *Then also the King, rising from the bath.* <note>original Latin: "Tum quoque Rex ascendens de lavacro."</note> Abdias, as cited above.

(3) It is a very ancient custom that Proselytes prepared to receive Baptism by fasting. Justin Martyr, describing the manner of receiving Proselytes, expresses himself in these terms: *They are taught to pray and ask God, while fasting, for the forgiveness of their past sins.* <note>original Greek: "Εὔχεσθαί τε, καὶ αἰτεῖν νηστεύοντας παρὰ τοῦ Θεοῦ, τῶν προημαρτημένων ἄφεσιν διδάσκονται"</note> Justin Martyr, *Apology* II. p. 73. See what is ordered in the *Apostolic Constitutions* Book VII. 22. But the time of this fast was not fixed.

(4) *The Apostle, taking the oil and pouring it over their heads, and anointing and chrismating them, began to say: Come, Holy Spirit of Christ, etc.* <note>original Greek: "Λαβὼν δὲ ὁ Ἀπόστολος τὸ ἔλαιον, καὶ καταχέας κατὰ τῆς κεφαλῆς αὐτῶν, καὶ ἀλείψας καὶ χρίσας αὐτὰς ἤρξατο λέγειν, ἐλθὲ τὸ ἅγιον πνεῦμα τοῦ Χριστοῦ &c."</note> Cited by Simon, as cited above, pp. 8 & 9.

(5) This Seal is not the Anointing: it is Baptism, which was administered after the Anointing, and of which it was a preliminary ceremony.

(6) *That sprinkling, or the pouring of water, was substituted for immersion, which was formerly used in Baptism, especially in the Western Church, more than a thousand years ago, namely in the time of Gregory I, etc.* <note>original Latin: "Mersioni, in Baptismo antiquitus usurpari solita, aspersionem, seu profusionem aquæ, in Occidentali præsertim Ecclesia, plus quàm mille abhinc annis, Gregorii videlicet Primi ætate, substitutam esse. &c."</note> Beveridge, *Annotations on the Apostolic Canons.*

(7) See Daillé, *On the religious cults of the Latins.* Book I. Chapter XI.

(8) *Both the bread and the oil are sanctified by the power of the name; not being the same, in appearance, as when they were taken, but by power they have been transformed into spiritual power. So also the water.* <note>original Greek: "Καὶ ὁ ἄρτος, καὶ τὸ ἔλαιον ἁγιάζεται τῇ δυνάμει τοῦ ὀνόματος· οὐ τὰ αὐτὰ ὄντα, κατὰ τὸ φαινόμενον, οἷα ἐλήφθη, ἀλλὰ δυνάμει εἰς δύναμιν πνευματικὴν μεταβέβληται. Οὕτως καὶ τὸ ὕδωρ."</note> From Clement of Alexandria, p. 800. col. 2.

<margin>Why the Holy Spirit is called the **Mother of Graces**.</margin>
As soon as one knows that the word (8) for *Spirit* <note>original: "Esprit" / Syriac: "Rucha"</note> is feminine in that Language, one will no longer be surprised to hear the Holy Spirit called the **Mother of Graces** and the **Revealer of Mysteries**. I do not believe that *Leucius* <note>Leucius Charinus, the reputed author of several apocryphal Acts of the Apostles</note> wrote in Syriac: He was Greek; but his Acts must have been translated from Greek into Syriac, and then from Syriac back into Greek, which was not done without additions or changes. For my part, I have judged that these Prayers might well come from the *Marcosians* <note>A Gnostic sect founded by Marcus in the 2nd century AD, known for elaborate rituals and numerology.</note>, who were a Judaizing Sect and who used many invocations in their sacred Ceremonies. St. Epiphanius testifies that the Judaizing Sects (9) made the Holy Spirit a *Woman*. This is a "bad word" <note>clumsy or poorly chosen phrase</note> from this Father <note>Referring to the Early Church Father Epiphanius of Salamis</note>, which must be forgiven him, and which he might not have said if he had considered that *Spirit* was feminine in the Language of these Sectarians.

...knowledge of the Theology of these ancient Sectarians, to say positively what they understood by *Mother of the seven Houses*. Perhaps this means *Creatress*, or *Creator*. And in that case the meaning is, *Come, CREATOR OF THE SEVEN HOUSES, so that we may reach the rest, which is in the EIGHTH*.

<margin>(a) See Epiphanius, Heresies XXXIV. No. 7. p. 241.</margin>
The *seven Houses* are the (a) seven Heavens of the Planets, and the *eighth*, which is above them all, is the supreme Heaven, the abode of rest and of blessed Souls. One must not believe that I am attributing ideas to the Heretics that they did not possess. *St. Irenaeus* informs us, and after him *St. Epiphanius*, that the number (b) EIGHT was very sacred and very mysterious among the *Marcosians* <note>The Marcosians were a 2nd-century Gnostic sect founded by Marcus, known for their elaborate numerology and rituals.</note>; they found it in various places in the Old Testament, and said of (1) THE celestial OGDOAD <note>original: "Τῆς ἄνω ὀγδοάδος τὸ ἀπέραντον, καὶ αἰώνιον, καὶ ἀόριστον, καὶ ἄχρονον." / "The infinity, eternity, boundlessness, and timelessness of the Ogdoad above."</note> *that it is infinite, eternal, without any limits, of either time or place*.

<margin>(b) Ibid. page 251.</margin>
<margin>The eighth House is the supreme Heaven.</margin>
This is the description of the supreme Heaven, which is the dwelling place of the Divinity. One also reads in the *Oriental Doctrine* these remarkable words, which confirm what I have just said. (2) *He whom his Mother brings into the world passes at once into the world and into death. But he whom Jesus Christ regenerates passes into Life and into THE OGDOAD* <note>original: "Ὅτι γεννᾷ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτὸ εἰς θάνατον ἄγεται καὶ εἰς κόσμον: Ὅτι δὲ ἀναγεννᾷ χρίστος, εἰς ζωὴν μετατίθεται, εἰς ὀγδοάδα."</note>. Let us express the Prayer of our Heretics in terms that are less foreign to us. Let us ask the Holy Spirit, "that he might deign to lead our Souls through the lower Heavens into the supreme Heaven, where an eternal rest reigns"; we would say nothing other than what the Heretics said, and they will be as wise as we are, or we shall be as foolish and as ridiculous as they.

<margin>9. Why the Marcosians sometimes baptized with oil and water mixed. (c) New Observations p. 9.</margin>

Nothing certain can be said on this matter, as these ancient *Gnostics* held quite similar views on several Articles of faith. Let us only remark that *St. Epiphanius* accuses the *Marcosians* of neglecting...

<margin>VII. The Manichaeans adopt all these apocryphal works because they favored their error concerning Marriage.</margin>
VII. Such were the Apocrypha said to have been forged or corrupted by the <term>Manichaeans<note>Followers of Mani, a dualistic religion that taught a struggle between a good world of light and an evil world of darkness; they practiced extreme asceticism.</note></term>. I believe the accusation to be false; at the very least, one must admit it is unproven. However, as these false Acts favored their views on the merit of Virginity and the imperfection—or even corruption—of the state of Marriage, it is not surprising that they took advantage of them. Do we not still see today the audacity to maintain the authenticity of a great many false pieces, whose only merit is to support modern superstitions? When one has become convinced that an opinion is true, one is easily deceived by imposters who lend it divine authority. Now, there were many of these imposters who, in accordance with what <margin>(a) 1 Timothy 4:5.</margin> St. *Paul* had said of them, rose up against Marriage and exalted <margin>How contagious this Error was. Its source. Its consequences.</margin> the merit of Virginity to the heavens. A Spirit of Error—and perhaps the most pernicious of all Fanaticisms if one weighs its consequences—seized a great number of Christians from the very beginning. They imagined that Evangelical Perfection called them to renounce Marriage: that of all the virtues, none is more sublime, more angelic, or more divine than that of overcoming natural Desires. Most took these for vicious Desires which, according to some, had their origin in a Nature evil in itself, and according to others, in a Nature corrupted in Adam. *Marcion* and his ilk, who held the former view, relied on the authority <margin>(b) Clement of Alexandria, *Stromata* (Miscellanies), Book III, p. 431 and following.</margin> of *Pythagoras* and *Plato*, philosophers much praised by the Christians. And as a false hypothesis leads to a multitude of false consequences, those who condemned Marriage were the same who maintained that Jesus Christ was man only in appearance. Such, among others, was *Julius Cassianus*, whom <term>Clement of Alexandria<note>A Christian theologian and philosopher (c. 150–215 AD) who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note></term> calls (1) the *Leader of Docetism* <note>original: "Τῆς δοκήσεως ἐξάρχων" (*Tēs dokēseōs exarchōn*). ### C H A P T E R VII.

*Of the Books of <term>MANICHAEUS<note>Also known as Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the Persian prophet and founder of Manichaeism, which taught a dualistic struggle between Light and Darkness.</note></term> & of the principal Authors of his Sect.*

I have only to speak now of the Books which were specific to the Manichaeans, and about which I have little to say, because the Ancients had all those they could discover burned, and because, the Sect being <margin>(1) extinct in the West for several Centuries, its Books perished with it. Perhaps some have been preserved in the East, but they are unknown to us.</margin>

<margin>I. Books of the Manichaeans written in various Languages. In Persian.</margin>
I. Our Heretics had a great number of Books written in the Persian Language. *(2) You command me, says St. Augustine, to believe in your Persian Books, you who forbid me to believe in the Hebrew Books.* The Heresy having been born in Persia, <term>Manichaeus</term> and his first Disciples composed various Books in that Language: And although it was not understood in the West, the Manichaeans nevertheless preserved the Originals with great care, as precious monuments of the labors and the Faith of their Fathers. For the same reason, Christians who did not know Hebrew nevertheless kept the Originals of the Old Testament with respect.

<margin>In Syriac.</margin>
The Sect also had a great number of Books in Syriac. For, besides the fact that <term>Manichaeus</term> had himself written in this Language, his Heresy was established, from the beginning, in the Provinces of Mesopotamia & Syria, which were the closest to the Persian Empire. I also have no doubt that the Manichaeans had many Books in Greek, when I consider <margin>In Greek.</margin> how much they multiplied in the Provinces of the Empire, where the Greek Language was the vulgar tongue, and in Egypt, where it had become very common, and where Manichaeism made great progress. <margin>In Latin.</margin>
I do not know if there were many works in Latin, but St. *Augustine* seems to have seen only a Work by *Adimantus* <note>Adimantus was a prominent disciple of Mani who wrote a work contrasting the Old and New Testaments.</note> against the Law, and the *Epistle of the Foundation*, which our Heretics read in their Assemblies. He indeed alleges two or three passages from the *Treasure of the Manichaeans*, but he had not taken them from the Original. Be that as it may, St. *Augustine* hardly knew the Books of the Sect, either because, being only a <term>Hearer<note>A 'Hearer' (auditor) was a lay member of the Manichaean community, as opposed to the 'Elect' (electi) who followed the strictest rules of the faith.</note></term>, the *Elect* did not share them with him: or because, being young, and having many other goals than becoming Archbishop of the Manichaeans of Africa, he neglected this reading. Full of wit, and (1) ambition, and devoted to the study of Roman Literature, which alone could acquire him a reputation and a brilliant fortune, he was not in the mood to read obscure Writings or barbarous Versions translated from Persian or Syriac to know the Mysteries of Manichaean Theology in depth. Such a thankless Science did not lead him to his goal. I can therefore say only very little about most of the Books of the Manichaeans, of which almost only the titles remain.

<margin>3. His Book THE CHAPTERS.</margin>
3. A third Book by Manichaeus is that which bore the title, THE CHAPTERS (<note>original Greek: *Κεφαλαιων* / Kephalaion</note>), or rather, THE PRINCIPAL AND FUNDAMENTAL ARTICLES of his Heresy. I stated in Part I what I thought of this Work, of which I have seen no fragment.

<margin>4. A Book ON FAITH attributed to Manichaeus, but without foundation. (c) *Literary History p. 200.*</margin>
4. It seems that Manichaeus had written a Book titled ON FAITH. Dr. (c) Cave <note>William Cave (1637–1713) was an English divine and ecclesiastical historian.</note> believed so, based on certain (4) words of St. Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop of Salamis known for his "Panarion," a massive work refuting various heresies.</note>, which are ambiguous. However, as no other Author has spoken of this Work, I judge that this Father did not intend to designate the title, but the subject matter. I am even persuaded that he is referring to the Book OF MYSTERIES; and as this piece is better known than the others, I will give an idea of what it contained.

<margin>5. His Book OF MYSTERIES. What it contained.</margin>
5. The <term>Heresiarch<note>The founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note></term> (5) therein established his *two Principles*, explained the creation of the World, the formation of Man, how Souls found themselves mixed or united with Matter, and how they may be delivered from this fatal Union. He exaggerated the alleged disorders that reign in the (6) sublunary and material World. But, instead of concluding from this, as others do, that God is not its Creator, he concluded only that a Work which, according to him, was so irregular, could not be the effect of a completely free Design, formed by the Wisdom of God, and executed by His Omnipotence, independent of the cooperation of any other secondary Cause. He claimed, therefore, that Creation was occasioned by some Enterprise of Matter. By this, he gave a reason for the novelty of our World, and tried to explain its various Phenomena, but especially those that seem to agree least with the Wisdom, Holiness, and Goodness of God. He attributed to the Power of Darkness the formation of fleshly Bodies, that of insects, harmful animals, poisonous plants, etc. In this same Work, he attacked Moses and the Prophets, whose Inspiration and Authority he rejected. He even attacked the Authenticity of the Books of the New Testament, maintaining that they had not been safe from the assaults of the Princes of...

...of the Darkness, who through their Emissaries had corrupted the purity of the Doctrine of J. Christ. This is generally what the *Book of Mysteries* contained, as seen by the refutation that *Titus of Bostra* <note>A 4th-century bishop and theologian known for his work against the Manichaeans.</note> wrote of it. *Tollius* (a) <note>Jacobus Tollius (1633–1696), a Dutch classicist and alchemist.</note> rightly judged that this Book was written in *Palmyrene Syriac*. It is true that Mr. (b) *Cave* <note>William Cave, an English church historian mentioned on the previous page.</note> does not agree, claiming that *St. Epiphanius* did not state it positively. But, whether *St. Epiphanius* said it or not, *Titus of Bostra* (1) testifies to it positively, and he must be believed. This Bishop, who resided in Phoenicia, apparently understood Syriac.

<margin>
The Creation of our World occasioned by events. Origen's sentiment on this.
</margin>
The sentiment of *Manichaeus* on the *Creation of the Material World*, which he believed to have been occasioned by an assault of Matter, is quite absurd at its core, but it is perhaps not as much as one might imagine. Excellent Philosophers of our time have introduced, into their systems, the "occasional causes" of Divine operations: And *Origen*, who was such a great genius, has them intervene everywhere, but in particular in the Creation of the World, and in the arrangement of the successive Worlds that this Christian Philosopher had imagined, to reconcile the account of *Moses* with the general ideas of the Pagan Philosophers. The free choices of intelligent Beings were, according to him, the occasional causes of the varieties of the Worlds that God had created and destroyed during the immense duration of the Ages. It must be admitted that these ideas could only arise in a great and beautiful genius, flourishing at a time when the Spirit was not yet constrained by dogmatic decisions that hold it in chains. *Origen* believed that any system which provides no reason for events other than the Good-pleasure of God is a system for the ignorant, and not for philosophical minds.

### ON MANICHAEUS. BOOK II. CH. VII.
Hhh 3
<meta>catchword: trolo-</meta>

<margin>6. Treatise of the Giants, another Book of Manichaeus.</margin>
6. Among the Books of Manichaeus, there is also included a work titled (2) **TREATISE** *on the Enterprise of the Giants*. I do not know if he had mixed into it some of the fables found in a Book bearing the name of (3) *Enoch*, which is believed to have been composed by some Hellenistic Jew before the time of the Apostles. This is likely the one cited by (c) St. Jude under the title of the *Prophecy of Enoch*. It reports the origin of the *Giants*, who are said to descend from the (4) impure commerce of the lowest order of Angels with the *Daughters of Men*. This could very well have been in the Book of Manichaeus as well, though it was not his main object. Be that as it may, having found in Pagan Fables that Giants (5) with dragon feet <note>original: "aux pieds de Dragon"</note> attempted to dethrone Jupiter, he claimed that this poetic fiction was based on an ancient truth—namely, the war that the Powers of Darkness waged against God. This is attested by *Simplicius* and *Alexander of Lycopolis*. Furthermore, I do not know if the *Apocryphal History of the Giants*, which bore the name of *Enoch*, is not the Book mentioned by George Syncellus <note>A 9th-century Byzantine chronicler and cleric.</note> around the year of the World 2585. He recounts that (6) *Cainan*, the great-grandson of *Noah*, while walking in the countryside, found the *Writing of the Giants* and hid it in his house. Manichaeus may have drawn from these corrupt sources.

<margin>(c) Jude v. 14.</margin>

<margin>7. On Astronomy and Astrology by the same.</margin>
7. He had also written on *Astronomy* and *Astrology*. St. Epiphanius mentions (7) *Astrology*, but this Father <note>A term for early Christian theologians known as the Church Fathers.</note> conflated these two sciences, as is seen when, speaking of *Hierax*, he is in doubt whether this learned Egyptian had also studied (8) *Magic* and *Astronomy*. *Astrology* is related to *Magic*, but *Astronomy* is not. In any case, Manès <note>Another name for Mani, the founder of Manichaeism.</note> was an *Astronomer* as well as an *Astrologer*: St. Epiphanius testifies that his disciples (d) took pride in understanding *Astronomy* very well. One can be a skilled *Astronomer* without being an *Astrologer*.

<margin>(d) Epiphanius p. 629.</margin>

...God had given charge of terrestrial things, and who inhabited the lowest region of the Heaven. This is the idea given in the false Book of Enoch. But it is not the idea one ought to have.

(4) This foolish imagination, which was adopted by the Fathers, is supported by the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Old Testament.</note> version of *Genesis 6:2*. There were, however, some who tried to give a mystical explanation to this passage of Genesis. They imagined that the love of the *Angels* for *Women* was nothing other than the inclination that Souls conceived for Bodies. See *Origen on John p. 132*. *Philo* believed that the Angels who reside in the air are simply Human Souls. These are the Angels of the lowest order.

(5) Dragon-footed. <note>original Greek: Δρακοντόποδες; Latin: *Anguipedes*. Ancient mythological descriptions of giants having snakes or dragons for legs.</note> See the *Recognitions Book I, p. 493*, and the Note by *Cotelier*.

<margin>His Epistle OF THE FOUNDATION.</margin>

LXVII.) calls him *Hierax*. <note>original Greek: "Ἱερακῖται, οὗτοι ἀπὸ Ἱέρακος" — "The Hieracites, these are [named] after Hierax."</note> He is placed by Photius, by Peter of Sicily, and by the *Formula of Abjuration* among the first Disciples of Mani. The Chronology is not contrary to this. Mani died in 277 or 278. St. Epiphanius, who wrote his Books *On Heresies* one hundred years later in 375, testifies that *Hieracas* had died several years earlier, after having lived more than ninety years. *Epiphanius p. 712.*

(7) In Leonto <note>original Greek: "Ἐν τῇ Λεοντῷ"</note>. Ibid. This City was named in this way because Lions were kept and venerated there. *Cellarius, Africa p. 29.*

(9) He accepts Isaiah and Jeremiah, and likewise considers them prophets. <note>original Greek: "Ἡσαΐαν καὶ Ἱερεμίαν δέχεται, ὁμοίως καὶ προφήτας ἡγεῖται." Ibid.</note>

# HISTORY OF DOGMAS
<meta>catchword: to make</meta>

...of the Flesh: 2nd, that he did not believe that J. Christ had a true human Body: 3rd, And that he admitted three Principles of all things, GOD, MATTER, and EVIL. <note>Hierax combined Christian teachings with Neoplatonic and Manichaean dualism, leading to his classification as a heretic.</note>
Let us remark in passing that one of the first Disciples of *Mani*, having distinguished himself throughout Egypt by his holiness and by his austerities, this alone suffices to justify the Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect.</note> and his Sect against the profanations and abominable Mysteries attributed to them.

<margin>III. Of Aphthonius. He was Bishop of the Manichaeans of Alexandria. Defeated by Aëtius.</margin>
III. I find nothing regarding *Aphthonius* except what *Philostorgius* <note>A 4th-century Church historian known for his Arian sympathies.</note> has recounted of him. This man flourished under the Empire of *Constantius* and made his residence in Alexandria (1), where he was the Patriarch of the Manichaeans and had acquired a great reputation for Knowledge and Eloquence. *Aëtius*, who was then in *Antioch*, drawn by the rumor that *Aphthonius* was creating in Egypt and by the zeal to stop the fatal progress of Heresy in that Province, hurried there and entered into a dispute with this formidable Adversary. The action was long and public. *Aëtius* defended Truth against Error with such force and advantage that *Aphthonius*, reduced to silence and covered in confusion, being unable either to console himself for his defeat or resolve to renounce his Errors, fell ill from spite and died seven days later. I am surprised to find such a memorable fact only in *Philostorgius*. Could it be because *Aëtius*, having been the teacher of *Eunomius*, and consequently the Head of the most dangerous of the Arian Factions <note>The Anomoeans, who believed the Son was "unlike" the Father.</note>, the Orthodox Historians did not judge it appropriate to mention his Victory? He was an Arian: that *is certain*; but was it necessary because of that to nickname him (2) *the Atheist*? I can say nothing of *Heraclides*, the third *Commentator of Mani*, as this man is entirely unknown to me.

<margin>IV. Collection of Prayers for the use of the Manichaeans.</margin>
IV. The Manichaeans had a (3) *Book of Prayers*. One might believe that it was the Liturgy of the Sect, if one were certain that Liturgies were in use in the time of *Mani*. Perhaps it was only a Form of Prayer, adapted to the various circumstances of life and for the use of individuals. The Greeks treat them (4) as *Spells* and *enchantments*, but this is pure calumny. *St. Augustine*, who had attended the service of the Manichaeans...

...chaeans, witnesses that their Worship was pure, and that all he had found to fault in their Prayers was that they pronounced them with their faces turned toward the Sun. <note>Manichaeans often faced the sun or moon during prayer, seeing them as symbols or "ships" of divine light, a practice frequently misunderstood by their critics as sun-worship.</note>

V. The Disciples of *Manichaeus* wrote various Works to establish and defend their Errors. *Adas* composed one, to which he gave the title of *(5)* MODIUM <term>Modium: Latin for a "bushel" or dry measure. The title likely refers to the "bushel" mentioned in the Gospels that should not hide a light.</term>. This Book was refuted by *(a)* *Diodore*, Bishop of *Tarsus*, one of the most learned men of Antiquity, but whose Writings the Greeks have allowed to perish because he is considered to have laid the foundations of Nestorianism <term>Nestorianism: A 5th-century theological doctrine that emphasizes the distinction between the divine and human natures of Jesus.</term>. *(b)* *Ebed-jesu* witnesses that the Nestorians possess in Syriac the twenty-five Books that he composed against the Manichaeans. I believe that *Adas* was Mesopotamian, or Syrian, and that his name is the same as that of *Addai* or *Thaddeus*, common among the Syrians: The Greeks turned it into *(c)* *Adantus*, which perhaps caused the error of *St. Augustine*, who confused *Adas* with *(6)* *Adimantus*.

<margin>(b) Cave, Hist. Literaria Vol. I. p. 218.</margin>
<margin>(c) Peter of Sicily, as cited above p. 30.</margin>
<margin>VI. Of Adimantus: he was the Apostle of Manichaeism in Africa.</margin>
VI. Let us speak of the latter. It was he, if I am not mistaken, who carried the Heresy into Proconsular Africa, where it had made great progress as early as the year 290 of Our Lord, twelve or thirteen years after the execution of the Heresiarch <note>Heresiarch: The founder or leader of a heretical sect, here referring to Mani (Manichaeus).</note>. I do not find, in truth, any Author who witnesses that *Adimantus* preached Manichaeism in Africa. But it seems to me that it can be inferred from the love and veneration that the Manichaeans of that Province had for his memory. *(7) After MANICHAEUS, our blessed Father, says Faustus, it is only ADIMANTUS who deserves all our admiration.* This preference, which the Manichaeans of Africa gave to *Adimantus* over all the Disciples of their Master, suggests, it seems to me, that he had been their Apostle. He was the Saint, the Patron of the Sect in that Country. It is certain, moreover, that Manichaeus *(8)* had sent him to various climates to preach his Errors there.

I was confirmed in this conjecture when I read in the *(9)* Anathemas, which those who abjured Manichaeism in the West were made to pronounce, these words so honorable to *Adimantus*. *(10)* "*I anathematize whoever believes that the promise of the Paraclete was not fulfilled on the day of Pentecost, but...*" <note>The Paraclete refers to the Holy Spirit or "Comforter." Manichaeans believed Mani himself was the fulfillment of this promise.</note>

<margin>VIII. THEOSOPHY of a certain *Aristocritus*.</margin>
VIII. The Greek Formula of abjuration of Manichaeism <note>A formal renunciation of heresy required of those returning to the orthodox Church.</note> mentions a certain ARISTOCRITUS, and a Work which he had composed under the name of THEOSOPHY, or the *Wisdom of God*. His goal was to show that, at their core, all Religions—Pagan, Jewish, and Christian—agreed in Principle and in Dogmas, and differed only in some Ceremonies.
<margin>Goal of this Work. To confound the Christian Religion with Paganism and Judaism.</margin>
(4) Everywhere a supreme God, and subordinate Gods, here under the name of *Gods*, there under that of *Angels*. <meta>This page continues the critique of Faustus of Mileve’s accusations against the Church, specifically focusing on his claim that Christians had adopted Pagan customs, before moving into a discussion of the lost library of the Manichaeans and St. Augustine's lack of direct engagement with their texts.</meta>

> "...[the] view is properly nothing but your Assemblies." Faustus supports this accusation by pointing to the Cult of the Dead, which was beginning to be introduced into the Church: to the Feasts of the Martyrs, and the vigils held near their tombs. Up to this point, the Heretic is not entirely wrong; but he is very much so when he adds that Christians [agree with Pagans], that is to say, on the unity of Principle <note>original: "sur l’unité de Principe." Faustus argued that both Christians and Pagans shared the same fundamental concept of a single divine source or "Monarchy."</note>. Faustus is certainly mistaken in this regard, and justifies what *St. Augustine* said: that he had more babble than knowledge. The Pagans generally recognized two Principles, one *active*, which is *God*, and the other *passive*, which is *Matter*. There were even several among them who did not doubt that Matter essentially possessed movement, action, and a kind of brute Soul, which is the origin of the vicious Passions and the evils that reign in the World. Now, that is pure Manichaeism. Furthermore, I say nothing of the Books of Faustus because I have spoken of them in the Preliminary Discourse.

<margin>IX. Manichaean Books in great number.</margin>
IX. I do not believe that any of these Books remain to us in the West, nor in general any Work of the ancient Manichaeans, although there were many in the time of *St. Augustine*. He informs us that these Heretics (2) "had A GREAT NUMBER OF VOLUMES, AND LARGE VOLUMES, which they preserved with great care, and adorned with very beautiful and very rich bindings." But, as I have already said, *St. Augustine* knew only their exteriors. What leads me to believe this is that he never cites them in his Disputes. If he had carefully read the Books of this Sect, he would have cited them to justify the Heresies of which he accuses them; he would have sought arguments against them there; he would have set their Authors in opposition to one another; he would have highlighted the absurdities he would have discovered there. In short, it is not possible that he would not have drawn great advantages from the Books of the Manichaeans against the Manichaeans themselves. Now, since he did not do so, it is, in my view, certain proof that he had never read them. It is also not possible that he would not have found answers to his Objections there, which would have compelled him to refute them.

<margin>St. Augustine had not read them at all.</margin>
I have drawn the same conclusion from several places in the Disputes of *St. Augustine* against *Faustus*. "You will PERHAPS allege to me," *he says to him*, "some Book of Mani, where it is said that Jesus Christ was not born of a Virgin." And again: "you will PERHAPS allege to me some other Book, which bears the name of a..."

<margin>(2) *Your books are so many, so large, so precious.* Aug. against Faust. Book XIII. 14. And thereafter, *Burn all those parchments, and the elegant bindings, fashioned from exquisite skins.*</margin>

# ON MANICHAEISM BOOK II. CH. VII.

> "...of an Apostle, where it is said that Jesus Christ was not born of Mary."

These *perhapses* <note>The author is highlighting St. Augustine's use of tentative language, which suggests he was speaking from hearsay rather than direct reading.</note> suggest that St. Augustine had read neither the Books of Mani <note>original: "Manichée"</note> nor the apocryphal writings of the Manichaeans. The principal reason for this is apparently that they were written in Persian, Syriac, and Greek—languages that this Father <note>A "Church Father," referring to the influential early Christian theologians whose writings established early doctrine.</note> did not understand. I do not know if the Manichaeans of Africa had any priest or bishop who was proficient in these foreign languages; however, they did not cease to preserve the books themselves, because they regarded some as the Scriptures of their sect and others as the works of their [spiritual] fathers.

<margin>I. Reason why this Discourse is inserted here.</margin>
I. If I were writing only for the learned, I would not interrupt the course of this Treatise to examine and refute an objection that Skeptics <note>original: "Incrédules"</note> never cease to raise against the authenticity and certainty of the Books of the New Testament. But writing in a language known throughout Europe, and this work being read by persons who do not have the leisure to study religious matters in depth, I felt it my duty to prevent the scandal <note>In this context, "scandal" refers to a stumbling block or something that causes a loss of faith.</note> that might be caused by this multitude of Apocrypha <note>Non-canonical books that were not included in the final version of the Bible.</note> of which we have spoken. It is, moreover, necessary to curb the triumph of the Enemies of the Faith, and to show that, at heart, all these Apocrypha confirm the truths against which they rise up. This is what <margin>(a) See above p. 370. Rem. 4.</margin> *(a)* I promised to do; and what I shall now endeavor to execute. Let us bring onto the stage only one Jew, who lacked neither wit nor knowledge. He is permitted to raise difficulties against a Religion that he believes rose upon the ruins of his own: And besides, his Unbelief is more excusable, and less scandalous, than that of those defectors <note>The author is likely referring to "libertines" or deists within the Christian community who critiqued the church from the inside.</note> who remain hidden within the Christian Church only to profit from its protection, while they exert all their efforts to shake its foundations.

<margin>IV. Direct response to the Objection. Five Propositions that refute it entirely.</margin> IV. To satisfy now the objection of the Jew and of other Unbelievers, it must be shown: I. What the origin of the Apocryphal Books was, and how it was naturally impossible that none should exist. IV. Now, this is precisely what the Unbelievers deny.

### APOCRYPHAL BOOKS

*...forgery of the Books which bore the names of the Apostles, or of Apostolic men.* <note>The term "Apostolic men" refers to the immediate disciples of the Apostles, such as Luke or Mark, who were not part of the original Twelve but lived during that era.</note>

<margin>Rules and criteria by which the Fathers judged the authenticity or the forgery of the Books.</margin>
<margin>First Rule.</margin>
<margin>Written Doctrine must have been consistent with Preached Doctrine.</margin>

I. First Rule. (2) The Fathers compared the Doctrine contained in the Acts <note>In this context, "Acts" refers generally to recorded deeds or writings presented as authoritative.</note> presented to them with that which had been announced by the Apostles in all the Churches, and which had been preserved there without alteration, since it was uniform everywhere. The Apostles had preached everywhere that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, the Messiah; that he was crucified, that he died, that he rose from the dead, and ascended into Heaven: That he taught the Faith and the Worship of a single God; promised to those who would believe in him and keep his Commandments the remission of their sins and Eternal Life; and confirmed his Doctrine by a great number of public Miracles, and in particular by his resurrection. These are the primary Articles of the Christian Religion, those which were received from the beginning and everywhere. Thus, all the Books that contained a contrary or different Doctrine bore an evident mark of forgery, for this reason—so natural and so certain—that the Preacher and the Writer could not be the same person if the Books produced under the name of the Writer contain a doctrine opposed to that which was announced by the Preachers in every place where they preached; and announced not only by him, but by the other Preachers of the Gospel sent, like him, by Jesus Christ.

<margin>It does not follow from this that Tradition is the Rule of Faith.</margin>
One should not conclude from this that (3) Tradition is the Rule of Faith, and that we must now judge Scripture by Tradition, rather than Tradition by Scripture. For there is a great difference between a Tradition that is quite fresh and recent, established at the birth of Christianity—which is uniform in all the Churches where the Apostles preached and attested by those who heard it—and Traditions far removed from the source, which are not certified by the universal Church or by witnesses who heard them from the mouths of the Apostles or their first Disciples. These latter traditions, consequently, lack the necessary confirmation to make them authentic. The former cannot reasonably be contested; the others may be.

***

<margin>Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book III, chapter 25, page 98. This is how Polycarp <note>Polycarp (69–155 AD) was a bishop of Smyrna and a direct disciple of the Apostle John.</note> wrote to the Philippians: "Therefore, leaving behind the vanity and the false teachings of the many, let us return to the word delivered to us from the beginning." <note>original Greek: "Διὸ ἀπολιπόντες τὴν ματαιότητα καὶ τὰς ψευδοδιδασκαλίας τῶν πολλῶν, ἐπὶ τὸν ἐξ ἀρχῆς ἡμῖν παραδοθέντα λόγον ἐπιστρέψωμεν."</note></margin>

(3) "Here I attribute nothing to the Church and Tradition above Scripture; I only make the Church a guide to the true Scripture: It is rather a certain condition, without which Canonical Books cannot be discerned from non-Canonical." <note>original Latin: "Hic ego Ecclesiæ, & Traditioni nihil trado supra Scripturam, Ducem solum facio Ecclesiam ad veram Scripturam: Est potius conditio quædam, sine qua Libri Canonici discerni non possunt à non Canonicis."</note> Marcantonio de Dominis, *On the Ecclesiastical Republic*, Book VII, Chapter I, 19. <note>Marcantonio de Dominis (1560–1624) was an Archbishop who famously clashed with the Papacy and moved toward Protestant ideas regarding the supremacy of Scripture.</note>

# DISCOURSE ON THE [APOCRYPHA]

...to being <note>Completing the sentence from the previous page: "a doctrine opposed to being [authentic/true]"</note>, and they very often do so with justice. One must not rush into one extreme to avoid the other. The abuse that one makes of a Principle does not render the Principle false or bad. **Tradition**—that is to say, the testimony of the Church, when it is well verified that it is her testimony—is a solid proof of the certainty of facts, and even of the certainty of Doctrine. *St. Luke* had not been an eyewitness to the History of *Jesus Christ*: he had not heard the Lord's Divine instructions from his own mouth. He knew nothing of them except by the testimony of those who had seen and heard *Jesus Christ*. The sacred Author of the Epistle to the Hebrews—whether he speaks of himself, or, by a common figure of speech, places himself among those to whom he writes—knew the Doctrine of salvation only through the testimony of those who had learned it from the mouth of the Lord. *Heb. II. 3.* The sacred deposit of the Gospel, entrusted by the Apostles to faithful persons, was at first kept inviolably in the Churches. This was not difficult in the beginning, because the number of the Articles of Faith had not been multiplied to the point it was later, due to the curious Questions that restless minds brought to light.

The only inconvenience that could result from this first Rule is that if some Impostor takes the name of an Apostle, or of an Apostolic man <note>A term for early Christian figures who were disciples of the original Apostles but not part of the Twelve.</note>, and writes under this borrowed name a Book in which he perfectly imitates their Doctrine, one might believe that the Book is indeed authentic. But the assumption of such an Act cannot be dangerous: it does no prejudice to the Faith. However, the Fathers avoided it by the precautions they took, as is seen by the following Rule.

<margin>
2. Second Rule.
No Book was recognized as authentic at the beginning unless it had the constant and perpetual testimony of all the Churches.

# APOCRYPHAL BOOKS
### Kkk 2
<meta>catchword: of the</meta>

...Predecessors, which were the Books they had received from the Apostles, or from <term>Apostolic men</term> <note>Early Christian figures who were disciples or immediate followers of the original Apostles.</note>, because they were cited there under their names, and in the terms found in their works. From this, they concluded, 1. that these Books were authentic. For ultimately, a testimony rendered by all the Churches—which is found, so to speak, at their very foundation, and which is perpetuated with them through the various Successions of its Bishops and Doctors—constitutes a certain Demonstration of the truth of a fact. As soon as it is not a matter of Religion, or where one does not have a secret or manifest interest in refusing to believe it, even the most difficult minds, and those most biased toward <term>Pyrrhonism</term> <note>An ancient school of skepticism that advocated for the suspension of judgment on all matters.</note>, will yield to such testimony and use it when they wish to decide a question of fact. From the same principle, the Fathers concluded in the second place, (3) that all the Books produced under the name of the Apostles, or Apostolic men, but which did not have the constant and perpetual testimony of all the Churches, were either forgeries or uncertain. It is for this reason (4) that even if a Book contained nothing <term>heterodox</term> <note>Teachings that differ from the established or "orthodox" standards of the Church.</note>, and even if its reading could be edifying, it was not admitted by the ancient Fathers among the number of <term>Canonical Books</term> <note>The list of books officially recognized as divinely inspired and authoritative scripture.</note>, because its authenticity was not sealed by the testimony of the universal Church, and because it did not appear that it had been recognized, from the beginning, as the legitimate Work of the Apostle, or the Apostolic man, whose name it bore.

<margin>Third Rule. Doubtful or suspected books were judged by comparing them with authentic Books.</margin>**Third Rule.** The Fathers, having Books that certainly came from the Apostles or Apostolic men, used them as a sure Rule for judging others. This is the constant Maxim of all critics. When it comes to judging suspect Acts, they are compared with authentic Acts. We have Books that are incontestably by ***St. Augustine***. They serve as a Rule for us to judge those that have been falsely attributed to that ancient Doctor. When, therefore, Books were produced under the name of the Apostles or Apostolic men, the Ancients considered, first: (5) whether one recognized in them the character and <term>Apostolic Doctrine</term> <note>The specific theological content and tone expected of the original Apostles.</note>. <meta>This page continues the discussion of the criteria used by the Early Church Fathers to determine the authenticity of biblical texts, specifically addressing the initial hesitation over certain Epistles and transitioning into a defense of Protestant theology against the criticisms of Richard Simon.</meta>

# DISCOURSE ON THE <note>This header is incomplete in the original, likely concluding as "Discourse on the Apostolic Writings" on the following page.</note>
<meta>catchword: who</meta>

...of the Apostolic Writings; but when one or the other was missing, they excluded them from the Canon. The Epistle of St. *James*: that of St. *Jude*: the second of St. *Peter*: the second and third of St. *John*, contain nothing that contradicts Apostolic Doctrine. In this regard, they deserve to be admitted into the Canon. But as their authenticity appeared doubtful because they lacked the universal and perpetual testimony of all the Churches, the Ancients placed them in the class of uncertain Books. They could be received without peril because they contained nothing contrary to the Faith, but in the first centuries, no one dared to place them in the rank of <term>Canonical Books</term> <note>Books officially recognized by the Church as divinely inspired and forming the authoritative rule of faith.</note> because their authenticity did not appear sufficiently well-justified.

<margin>VI. Response to Simon’s invective against the French Reformed.</margin>
VI. Such were the Rules that the Fathers followed to distinguish the Canonical Books from the <term>Apocryphal Books</term> <note>From the Greek for "hidden"; books of doubtful authorship or authority not included in the official biblical canon.</note>—rules dictated by Reason, which it will follow of its own accord when, free from prejudice and all self-interest, it sincerely seeks the Truth. However, the Protestants are accused of renouncing such a just and ancient method to rashly follow the internal suggestions of I know not what *particular Spirit*. This is what <term>Mr. Simon</term> <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and influential biblical critic who often challenged Protestant views on scripture.</note> did not disdain to do, following a host of controversial Authors. He reports with considerable confusion, as is his custom, the method the Fathers used to discern the sacred Books, after which he throws himself upon the French Reformed: *These proofs*, <margin>(a) Simon, Critical History of the New Testament, Vol. I. p. 11.</margin> (a) *he says, strongly establish the truth of the Books of the New Testament without having recourse to I know not what particular Spirit, which is an invention of recent times. One cannot imagine anything more opposed to Common Sense than these words from the Confession of Faith of those who formerly took the name of the Reformed Churches of France: We recognize these Books (speaking of all Scripture) as being Canonical, not so much by the common accord and consent of the Church, as by the testimony and internal persuasion of the Holy Spirit. # APOCRYPHAL BOOKS.
### K kk 3

<margin>Two Questions: One of fact, and the other of faith.</margin>
There are two Questions concerning the Books of the New Testament. The first is a Question of fact. It asks whether they truly belong to the Apostles, or to the <term>Apostolic men</term> <note>Followers and contemporaries of the original twelve Apostles, such as Mark or Luke, whose writings were granted similar authority.</note> whose names they bear. The second is a Question of faith: It asks whether these Books are Divine, or otherwise **Canonical**; that is, whether they form the sure and infallible Rule of our belief and our actions. The first Question was debated between the Church Fathers and the Heretics; the second Question was debated between the Fathers and the Unbelievers.

<margin>It is on the Question of faith, and not of fact, that the Reformed claim the testimony of the Holy Spirit.</margin>
Thus, when the <term>Reformed</term> <note>Protestant Christians, particularly those in the French tradition following John Calvin.</note> have said that they recognize the Books of the New Testament as **Canonical**, *not so much by the common accord and consent of the Church, as by the testimony and internal persuasion of the Holy Spirit*, they had the second Question in view, and not the first. They state, in their Confession of Faith, that they are persuaded of the Canonicity of the Books of the New Testament—that is, of their Divine authority—*not so much by the testimony of the Church, which they do not reject, but by the grace of the Holy Spirit*, who gives to Faith that evidence and certainty that one could not acquire by the strength of Human Reason alone (1). If <term>Mr. Simon</term> <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and critical scholar who challenged Protestant views on the history of the biblical text.</note> does not approve of this Proposition, he falls into <term>Pelagianism</term> <note>A theological position, declared heretical, that emphasizes human free will over the necessity of divine grace.</note>, which the Reformed have taken such great care to avoid. But regarding the first Question, namely that of the Authenticity of the Books of the New Testament, the Reformed have never said that they were informed of it by a private Revelation of the Holy Spirit; and had they said so, they would have been mistaken. Thus, when Mr. Simon maintains that a Christian can only know through the testimony of the Church that the Books of the New Testament are the work of the Apostles or Apostolic men, he says nothing to which the Reformed do not subscribe. But if he claims that the Christian’s persuasion regarding the Canonicity, or the Divinity of these Books, is founded solely on the testimony of the Church, he puts forward a Proposition that the Reformed do not believe, and which will appear utterly absurd to any man who reasons. I shall prove this by an example (2).

<margin>It is absurd to want to decide the Question of faith by the testimony of the Church.</margin>
Let us put the *Alcoran* <note>The Quran.</note> in the place of the *Gospel*, and the *Muslims* in the place of the *Church*. Let us then pose two Questions: The first...

(1) ...who strengthens and who inwardly enlightens our Mind. <note>original: "qui fortifie & qui éclaire intérieurement notre Esprit."</note> Augustine, *Against the Fundamental Epistle*, Chapter XIV.

(2) I shall confirm what I say by the testimony of a very learned Theologian of the past century. I wish to speak of Mr. <term>Antoine de Dominis</term> <note>An Italian archbishop and scholar (1560–1624) who moved between Catholicism and Anglicanism.</note>, Archbishop of Spalatro. *On the Ecclesiastical Republic*, Book VII, Chapter I, §. 17. He speaks of the manner in which one can convince an Unbeliever: <note>original: "ALIUD erit hunc Infidelem assentiri, Librum esse Joannis: ALIUD fidem adhibere iis, quæ in eo libro scripta sunt. Et ita ALIA est ei danda probatio, quâ constet ei esse Librum Joannis: ALIA vero, quâ ostendatur vera esse, quæcunque scripsit Joannes."</note> "It is **ONE THING** for this Unbeliever to agree that the Book is John's: it is **ANOTHER** to give faith to those things which are written in that book. And so, **ONE** proof must be given to him by which it may be established as the Book of John: but **ANOTHER** by which it may be shown that whatever John wrote is true."

<margin>Example of the Koran.</margin>
firstly, if the <term>Koran</term> <note>original: "Alcoran"</note> is by *Muhammad*: the second if the Koran is a Divine Book. The first, which is a Question of fact, is decided by the unanimous testimony of the Muslims. *Muhammad* is the Author of the Koran, whether he composed it alone, or was aided by some Apostate from Judaism or Christianity. But can the second Question be decided by the testimony of the Muslims? They would be both Judges and Parties. This example applies itself to our subject. If we are asked why we believe that the Books of the New Testament belong to the Authors whose names they bear, we answer that it is by the constant and universal testimony of the Church. But if we are asked why we believe these Books are Divine, and as the Confession of Faith expresses it, that they are **Canonical**, we no longer answer that it is by the testimony of the Church; because, at its core, this answer would be as absurd as that of a Muslim who, when asked why he believes the Koran is a Divine Book, would answer that it is because the <term>Mufti</term> <note>A Muslim legal expert or jurist empowered to give rulings on religious matters.</note> and the other Doctors of his Sect say so.

<margin>Explanation of the words of St. Augustine: *I would not believe in the Gospel etc.*</margin>
*St. Augustine* said, *(1) I would not believe in the Gospel if I were not moved by the authority of the Church.* <note>original Latin: "Ego vero Evangelio non crederem, nisi me commoveret Ecclesiæ auctoritas." This famous statement from Augustine's "Against the Fundamental Epistle of Manichaeus" was a central point of debate; Catholics cited it to prove the Church's authority over Scripture, while Protestants argued Augustine was referring to the Church's role in historical testimony.</note> This is a word boldly ventured by *St. Augustine* in the heat of Dispute, and in which one would find many faults if it were examined rigorously. However, the respect held for this Father has led to the invention of various explanations, all tending to make this statement reasonable. It can only be so, nonetheless, by 1. firstly removing *Authority* to put *Testimony* in its place. It is *Testimony*, and not *Authority*, that justifies facts; and the certainty of testimony does not depend on the *Authority* of the Persons, but on the proofs one has of their sincerity and their knowledge. However, as one sometimes says *authority* for *testimony*, *St. Augustine's* expression will be just if taken in that sense. 2. It is necessary, in the second place, to distinguish between the *authenticity* of the Gospels and the *truth* of the facts and Doctrine they contain. No one can have any other proof of the authenticity of the Gospels than the testimony of the Church, but this testimony cannot prove their Divinity, because then the Church would be a witness in its own cause, which would be absurd. 3. I do not doubt that *St. Augustine’s* word should be understood as referring to the *authenticity* of the Gospels, and not to the truth of the facts and Doctrine they contain. For it was not a matter of—

Hoc ei probato, ac proinde, præstito per eum assensu, Librum esse Joannis, tum postea SPIRITU SANCTO OPERANTE CREDIT IIS, QUÆ IN EVANGELIO JOANNIS scripta sunt &c."</note>

<margin>The Fanaticism for which M. Simon reproaches the Reformers is a Catholic Dogma.</margin>
Furthermore, the Fanaticism, or the "Private Spirit," for which <term>M. Simon</term><note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest and pioneering biblical critic who often argued against Protestant views of individual interpretation.</note> reproaches the <term>Reformers</term><note>Protestants who followed the principles of the Reformation.</note>, is truly a Catholic Dogma. <term>Father Combefis</term><note>François Combefis (1605–1679), a learned Dominican scholar and editor of early church texts.</note> teaches that, once the Church has declared a Book **Canonical**, it is no longer permitted for anyone to doubt its Canonicity. The reason for this is that the Church discerns Canonical Books from Apocryphal Books (2) by the light of the **Holy Spirit**, who resided in the Apostles, and who resides in their Successors. This opinion differs from that attributed to the Reformers only in that the learned Dominican grants the "Spirit of Discernment" only to the Bishops, who are said to be the Successors of the Apostles. Whereas, according to the Reformers, this grace belongs in general to all the true Faithful. It would be a Privilege of Faith, and not of the Office. Now, I would very much like to know which of the two opinions is better founded in Scripture. For my part, I know of no place where it is said that the Spirit of Discernment is an Episcopal Privilege. Moreover, if one appeals to experience, one will find that entire Councils have been very poor critics, and that they have based their decisions on testimonies drawn from false and forged books.

VII. Second Proposition. *The Fathers proceeded to the examination of authentic Books, not only with great wisdom and circumspection, but with a timid and scrupulous piety.*
