1. Firstly, there are the **authentic, incontestable** scriptures <note>original: ὁμολογούμενοι (*homologoumenoi*)</note>. These are those that the universal Church has recognized, without any particular Church ever calling their authenticity into doubt. 2. Secondly, there are the **doubtful** scriptures <note>original: ἀντιλεγόμενοι (*antilegomenoi*)</note>. These are those whose authors were not certain, and which did not have the constant and perpetual testimony of all the Churches. In this class were the five Epistles I mentioned; the Epistle to the Hebrews, and the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note> of St. *John*, the Epistle of St. *Barnabas*, etc. 3. Finally, there are the books that are **entirely**

<margin>(a) Ecclesiastical History, Book III, 31.</margin>
**false**, (a) <note>original: παντελῶς νόθοι (*pantelōs nothoi*)</note> that is to say, (1) that their content is worthless, and their authorship is forged. These are those which are ordinarily called *Apocryphal*, a term whose meaning sometimes varies. For it signifies (2) at times books of a doubtful authority, which have been excluded from the <term>Canon</term><note>The official list of books accepted as genuine and inspired scripture.</note>, even though they contain nothing bad; and at other times, books that are false and corrupted. It is in this latter sense that the author of the *Synopsis*, which is found among the works of St. *Athanasius*, says of certain writings (3) that they were more worthy of being placed among the Apocrypha than of being read. This clearly shows with what circumspection and religious care the Fathers proceeded in admitting certain books into the Canon and excluding others.

<margin>VIII. Example of this circumspection in the examination and judgment of the Apocalypse.</margin>
VIII. We have a fine example of this in the conduct of **Dionysius of Alexandria** in the 3rd Century, when it came to examining whether the Apocalypse, which bears the name of St. *John*, should be received as a Canonical Book. *Nepos*, a learned Bishop and a good man, had become infatuated with the opinion of a coming of Jesus Christ upon the Earth, where He would reign with the Saints, who would enjoy every possible, yet innocent, delight <note>This belief is known as Millenarianism or Chiliasm, the idea of a literal thousand-year earthly reign of Christ.</note>. He based this on the Apocalypse, the excellence of which he and his followers praised infinitely; and as other theologians wanted to explain St. *John’s* descriptions in a mystical sense, he wrote against the **Allegorists**. *Dionysius* assembled the most skilled clergy in Egypt and deliberated with them for three days, both on the opinion of *Nepos* and on the authenticity of the Apocalypse: they consulted all the Ancients; they examined and weighed all their testimonies. What prudence on one side, and modesty on the other, in *Dionysius’s* proceeding! He agrees (b) that some of his predecessors had not (4) only rejected it, but refuted it, claiming that it contained neither good sense nor reasoning.

That its title was false, since far from being a Revelation, which manifests hidden things, it was nothing but darkness and ignorance, and that finally this Book was the work of the <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>A leader of a heretical sect or a founder of a heresy.</note> *Cerinthus*, who had published his daydreams under the name of *St. John*. *Dionysius* expresses himself in even stronger terms in *Eusebius*. <margin>IX. Third Proposition. Origin and cause of the Apocrypha.</margin>
IX. Third Proposition. *What was the Origin of the Apocryphal Books, and how it was naturally impossible that there were none.*

The Life of our Lord was so beautiful, his character so sublime and so Divine, his Doctrine so excellent, and the Miracles by which he had confirmed it so striking and so numerous, that it was not possible that several writers would not undertake to compose memoirs of it. This produced several Histories of Our Lord, some more or less exact than others. It is unfortunate that we have lost them now, because we could consult them and judge for ourselves the character of the Authors and their composition. *St. Luke*, who speaks of the Accounts, or the Gospels, which had preceded his own, suggests indeed that they were defective, but he does not condemn them as fabulous or bad books. In the following period, several Histories of the Apostles, of their travels, and of their preaching were also composed; what zealous persons learned from others, who seemed to them worthy of trust, they turned into Accounts; but having (5) neither the instructions nor the grace of the Holy Spirit, which were necessary, these Accounts were more like essays than exact and true histories. <meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins of apocryphal (non-canonical) books. It argues that the decentralized nature of the early Christian Church, unlike the Jewish state, allowed for the proliferation of forged texts by various sects, and addresses historical criticisms of the Apostolic records by figures like Richard Simon and St. Ignatius.</meta>

### DISCOURSE ON THE

<columns>

mixing their Philosophy with Christian Doctrine, they also wrote Histories of Jesus Christ and his Apostles in order to introduce their own Systems.

<margin>The Constitution of the Christian Church made them inevitable.</margin>
The Constitution of the Christian Church made this inconvenience inevitable. If this Ecclesiastical Republic had been formed like that of the Jews—if it had possessed, from its origin, its own Government, its Magistrates, and a sovereign authority; and if it had been united under a single Head and confined within a specific Province—perhaps we would not have seen this multitude of false Acts. One would have been able to discover the Authors; they would have been punished, forced to recant, or required to prove what they advanced in their Writings with reliable testimony. But the Church being dispersed across the whole Earth, among Peoples who spoke different Languages; under Princes who, far from curbing the license of Impostors, actually had an interest in encouraging it, and who desired nothing more than to see the Church torn apart by Schisms and enemy Sects, it was not possible for there not to be Factions, Heretics, and consequently false Acts. Since all Sects claimed to be supported by the authority of the Son of God, and the authentic Writings of the Church convicted them of error and innovation, they had no other resource left but to accuse these Writings of falsification—as the <term>Manichaeans</term> <note>A major religious movement founded by the Iranian prophet Mani, which taught a dualistic struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note> did—or to produce false ones, as many other Heretics did.

<margin>Reflection of Mr. Simon. A passage from St. Ignatius poorly rendered.</margin>
Mr. *Simon* <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest often considered the father of modern biblical criticism.</note> made a reflection that relates to this. We know what his hypothesis was regarding certain public Writers, tasked by the Hebrew Republic with recording Events and collecting the Acts concerning their State. This is a supposition that has been contested, as sufficient proof for it has not been found. Since the Christian Church did not comprise a particular State, and its Members were dispersed everywhere, it could not have had Writers of this order: *This gave occasion*, (a) says Mr. Simon, *from the earliest times of Christianity, for some Heretics to doubt the truth of the Apostolic Books, which appeared to them to have no public testimony.* St. Ignatius complains

### APOCRYPHAL BOOKS.
Lll 2
<meta>catchword: cetes</meta>

...complains in one of his Letters that he heard some say they could not believe the Gospel unless they found it written in the Archives. This holy Martyr <note>St. Ignatius of Antioch (died c. 107 AD), an early Christian bishop and student of the Apostle John.</note> replies to them that it was indeed written there: that the death and resurrection of Jesus Christ, along with faith in Him, served as his true Archives. Let us explain this passage from St. Ignatius and restore to this Father the precision of his reasoning, which Mr. Simon <note>Richard Simon (1638–1712), a French priest often called the "father of biblical criticism."</note> seems to have stripped from him through an imperfect and confused translation.

<margin>Paraphrased Version of this Passage.</margin>
> "I exhort you (1)," says St. Ignatius in his Epistle to the Philadelphians, "to do nothing out of contention, but to submit yourselves to the Doctrine of Jesus Christ; for I have heard some say, 'If I do not find it in the Archives (or, in the ancient Copies), I will not believe that it is in the Gospel.' And when I replied to them, 'It is written there,' they answered me, 'Yes, but that is because it was placed there beforehand.' As for me, my Archives (my ancient Copies) are Jesus Christ. My authentic Archives (my Copies) are His Cross, His Death, His Resurrection, and the Faith He preached."

This is how I translate the passage of St. Ignatius. The version is somewhat paraphrased, but I do not believe the Reader will find the paraphrase too bold; furthermore, it is necessary to make the Author's thought understood, as it is not entirely expressed in the original.

<margin>Which Heretics St. Ignatius refers to, and which word of the Gospel they contested.</margin>
The question now is to know which Heretics St. Ignatius is targeting, and which word of the Gospel they claimed was not in the ancient Copies. One can learn both in the following Epistle addressed to the Smyrnaeans. There, one sees that these Heretics were the *Docetists* <note>From the Greek word *dokein* (to seem). They were early heretics who believed that Jesus was a pure spirit and only "seemed" to have a physical body.</note>, who were then the most prominent group in Asia. After having refuted them at some length, the Saint exhorts the Faithful (b) "to listen with docility to the Oracles of the Prophets, (2) particularly the Gospel, where the Passion of the Lord is clearly explained, and His Resurrection perfectly demonstrated. As for me," he says, "I know that even after His Resurrection He had a true body of flesh, and I believe it. For, when He presented Himself to Peter (3) and to those who were with him, He said to them, (4) *Take me, touch me, and recognize that I am not*

<columns>
<margin>(a) Luke 24:39.</margin>
" *I am not an incorporeal Spirit* ". These words, which were found in the Hebrew Gospel of the Nazarenes <note>An early Jewish-Christian gospel, now lost, that was similar to the Gospel of Matthew.</note>, are entirely parallel to those our Lord speaks in St. Luke, (a) *A Spirit has neither flesh nor bones, as you see I have.* This is, if I am not mistaken, the saying that St. Ignatius cited to the Docetes <note>The Docetes were early heretics who believed that Jesus Christ's body was an illusion and that he only "seemed" to suffer and die.</note>. "They replied that they would not believe this saying was in the Gospel unless they found it in the ancient Copies, or in the Originals. St. Ignatius retorted: 'It is written in all our Copies.' 'That is true,' the Heretics replied, 'but it is (1) *because it was placed there beforehand*' <note>original Greek: ὅτι πρόκειται; original Latin: quia præjacet. The heretics were suggesting the text had been tampered with or "pre-set" to favor the Church's position.</note>." This response having no other foundation than a *spirit of contention and stubbornness*, the Saint does not stop to refute it. He contents himself with saying, "For me, I do not wish to consult other Archives, other Originals, than the Cross of Jesus Christ, his death, his Resurrection, and the Faith which he announced to us, (2) <note>original Greek: καὶ ἡ πίσις, ἡ δι' αὐτῦ — "and the faith, which is through him."</note>" This response is worthy of a Martyr full of faith and piety. But it is no less worthy of a just mind. What clearly shows that the Gospel was not falsified in the place in question is the Cross, the Death, and the Resurrection of Jesus Christ. The reason for this is that an *incorporeal Spirit* cannot be crucified, cannot die, and cannot rise again: and all the Gospel bears witness that this crucifixion, this death, and this Resurrection were real, and not merely apparent.

<margin>Witness rendered to the Gospel of the Nazarenes.</margin>
I have only one more Remark to make. It is that this citation by St. Ignatius bears witness to the authenticity of the Hebrew Gospel of the Nazarenes. For otherwise, he would not have cited it in a Dispute against Heretics. The same Remark confirms what Papias <note>An early Christian author and Bishop of Hierapolis, known for his accounts of the origins of the Gospels.</note> says in (b) *Eusebius*, that St. Matthew had written his Gospel in Hebrew, and that several Versions had been made of it. The words cited by St. Ignatius were found in the Translation used in Asia, and in the Original held by the Nazarenes: but they are not found in our Gospel according to St. Matthew. Is this not what caused the Docetes to say they would not believe these words were in the Gospel unless they saw them in the Originals? Perhaps the Do-

<margin>X. Fourth Proposition. The number of Apocryphal Gospels is much smaller than is believed.</margin>
X. **Fourth Proposition.** *The ancient apocryphal works were of different kinds, and their number is much smaller than one imagines.* This Proposition has two parts; let us begin with the proof of the second.

I do not know what misguided zeal led to the multiplication of the number of false Gospels, as well as that of Heresies, but it is certain that there were many fewer than is said. Even the learned Mr. *Fabricius* <note>Johann Albert Fabricius (1668–1736), a German scholar famous for compiling and analyzing ancient "apocryphal" texts—writings not included in the official Bible.</note>, who made an extensive catalog of them and counted up to (3) fifty, nevertheless agrees that there are several which differ only by their title. Indeed, we speak of a Gospel of *Cerinthus*, and of another of *Carpocrates* <note>Two early Gnostic teachers who were often accused of altering Christian texts.</note>: it was (4) the Hebrew Gospel of St. *Matthew*, which is said to have been frequently altered.

<margin>One and the same Gospel under several names.</margin>
We speak of a *Gospel of the Twelve, of the Gospels according to the Hebrews, according to the Nazarenes, according to the Syrians, and according to the Ebionites.* At heart, all of this was nothing more than the Gospel of the Hebrews attributed to St. *Matthew*, although there were some (5) differences in the copies. We speak of a *Gospel according to St. Barnabas*. This is again (6) the Gospel of *St. Matthew*, which is said to have been found on the island of Cyprus under the Empire of *Zeno*, with the body of *St. Barnabas*, and lying upon his chest.

<margin>(a) See Grabe Spicil. Vol. I. p. 128.</margin>
We speak of a Gospel according to *St. Bartholomew*, (a) which is also nothing but the Gospel according to *St. Matthew*.

<margin>(b) Jerome in Catalog regarding Peter. Tertullian against Marcion Book IV. 5.</margin>
We speak of two Gospels of *St. Peter*, of which one is none other than that (b) of *St. Mark*, which, according to the report of some ancients, was dictated by *St. Peter* and written by *St. Mark*, his disciple and interpreter. The other was not written until toward the middle of the 2nd century, as we shall see shortly.

<margin>(c) 1 Timothy 2:9.</margin>
We speak of a *Gospel of St. Paul*. This is either an imagination of some ancients based on the fact that *St. Paul* speaks (c) of *his Gospel* <note>The author likely refers to Paul's phrase "my Gospel" found in Romans 2:16 or 2 Timothy 2:8, though the margin cites 1 Timothy 2:9.</note>—that is to say, of the doctrine he preached—or it must be understood as referring to his Epistles, which some Fathers (d) have called the Gospel of *St. Paul*.

### DISCOURSE ON THE [APOCRYPHAL BOOKS]

<margin>
(a) *Gelasius in the Decretals, Dist. XV. Ch. 3.* <note>original: "Gelas. in Decret. Dist. XV. Cap. 3." Refers to the Decretum Gratiani, a collection of canon law.</note>

The Church Fathers give the name of "Gospel" to the Books of Heretics which were not, strictly speaking, Gospels.

(b) *See Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History, Book IV. 7. Clement of Alexandria, Stromata, Book IV. p. 506. Acts of the Disputation of Archelaus, at the end.* <note>Sources referencing early Christian history and the refutation of various sects.</note>

(c) *Epiphanius, Panarion (Against Heresies), XXVI. 2.*
</margin>

There is talk of a *Gospel of St. Andrew*, which never existed, and which has been confused with the *Acts* or the *Travels* of that Apostle. There is talk of a *Gospel of the Encratites* <note>A radical ascetic sect that forbade marriage and meat.</note>. This is actually the *Harmony* that *Tatian* had composed from the four Gospels, which he had condensed into a single work <note>Known as the Diatessaron, this was a popular "all-in-one" version of the life of Jesus in the early Church.</note>. We hear of (a) false *Gospels of Hesychius* and of *Lucian*, even though these two learned men had done nothing more than compare the Greek copies of the Gospels and correct them based on the best manuscripts. They had worked in the same way to correct the copies of the Septuagint version <note>The Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>. There is talk of the Gospels of *Marcion* and *Apelles*, which were merely the Gospel according to *St. Luke*, which they are accused of having falsified in a few places. We hear of a *Gospel of (1) Basilides*; this was a (b) *Commentary* on the Gospels, or at most a copy of these sacred Books that did not entirely conform to the one used by the Catholics. We hear of a *Gospel of Valentinus*, (2) or of the *Valentinians*. This was not a *History of Jesus Christ*, but the system of their doctrine, to which they had given the title *Gospel of Truth*. It was the same with (c) the *Gospel of Perfection*, composed by the *Gnostics*, which contained the "false science" of those people. The same applies again to the *Gospel of Simon* and the *Simonians* <note>Followers of Simon Magus, often considered the first heretic.</note>, mentioned by the author of the Preface at the head of the Arabic Collection of the Canons of the Council of Nicaea. This author testifies that (3) "the Simonians had forged a Gospel for themselves which they had divided into four volumes, and which they named the *Book of the Four Corners of the World*, or *of the Four Hinges*, *of the Four Pivots*, upon which the machinery of the universe turns." I do not know in which class to place a (4) *Gospel of Judas*, which *St. Epiphanius* attributes to a sect he calls the *Cainites*; but it is clear from what he reports that it was nothing like a false History of Jesus Christ, but rather concerned certain mysteries that these people claimed had been revealed to Judas. The same judgment must be made of a *Gospel of Philip*, which (d) *St. Epiphanius* attributes to the *Gnostics*. The fragment he extracted from it shows that it was a collection of doctrine which they claimed had been announced by St. Philip.

(d) *Against Heresies, XXVI. §. 13. p. 95.*
</margin>

# APOCRYPHAL BOOKS

<margin>Other Apocrypha that have been improperly distinguished.</margin>
In the same way, other Apocryphal writings bearing the names of the Apostles have been wrongly multiplied. There is a *Doctrine of Peter* <note>original: "$\Delta\iota\delta\alpha\chi\eta$" (Didache)</note>; a *Preaching of Peter* <note>original: "$\kappa\eta\rho\upsilon\gamma\mu\alpha$" (Kerygma)</note>; and a *Judgment of Peter* <note>original: "$\kappa\rho\acute{\iota}\mu\alpha$" (Krima)</note>. All of these are apparently (a) one and the same Book. Mention is made of an *Apocalypse of Cerinthus* <note>Cerinthus was an early Gnostic teacher; some early critics suggested he was the true author of the canonical Book of Revelation to discredit it.</note>, attributed to St. *John*, and some imagine there are two *Apocalypses*, both attributed to this Apostle. This is based on a passage from *Caius*, a Priest of Rome, cited by (b) *Eusebius*. But we can be certain that *Caius* is speaking of the Apocalypse of St. *John*, which he believed was written by *Cerinthus*, as the late Mr. Grabe (c) observed. Let us therefore prune a large portion of the Apocrypha, but particularly the Gospels, which were the most significant. As for those that remain, they must be divided into two Classes: some that are ancient and have no fault other than being imprecise; others that are more modern, fabricated specifically to support Heresies.

<margin>(a) Grabe, Spicilegium Vol. I. p. 56.</margin>
<margin>(b) Ecclesiastical History, Book III. 28.</margin>
<margin>(c) As cited above, p. 312.</margin>

### XI. Two Classes of Apocrypha, differing 1. by time, and 2. by subject matter.

<margin>XI. Two Classes of Apocrypha, differing 1. for time, & 2. for matter.</margin>
XI. At the head of the first Class, we must place two *Gospels*, or Histories of the Doctrine and Actions of Our Lord, both of which date from the earliest Antiquity. The oldest of all, in my opinion, is the *Gospel according to the Hebrews*, which the Nazarenes <note>An early Jewish-Christian sect that followed Mosaic law.</note> claimed was (5) the original version of St. *Matthew*. It began with these words: (6) *it happened, that in the time of Herod, King of Judea, John came to baptize with the Baptism of repentance in the River Jordan.*

<margin>I. Class. The Gospel according to the Hebrews. It is from the time of the Apostles, & contained no Heresy.</margin>
Thus, one did not find in it the Genealogy of Our Lord, the History of his miraculous conception, that of the Magi, nor that of the Massacre of the children of Bethlehem, and his retreat into Egypt. This Gospel began, like that of St. *Mark*, with the Baptism of *John*, the Baptism of Our Lord, the Preaching of the Forerunner <note>John the Baptist.</note>, and subsequently the preaching of Jesus Christ. But otherwise, it appears from the Fragments that have been preserved for us that it contained no Heresy, and that except for a few circumstances, the History of Our Lord was faithfully reported therein.

<margin>The History of the adulterous woman was read there.</margin>
It is in this Gospel that one read the History of the woman caught in adultery, which is recounted in Chapter VIII of St. *John*. And as it was not in several copies of the latter—

# DISCOURSE ON THE...

...last Gospel <note>Refers to the Gospel of John, traditionally considered the last of the four canonical gospels to be written.</note>, some have conjectured (1) that it was taken from the *Gospel of the Nazarenes*, and inserted into *St. John*. If this is true, it is a testimony that the Ancients paid to the Gospel of the Nazarenes; and if this Story was originally in *St. John*, it is another proof of the truth of their Gospel.

<margin>The Gospel according to the Egyptians is of the same antiquity, and contained no Heresy.
(a) Preface to Luke.
(b) Stromata, Book III, p. 445, 452, 453.
(c) It is cited in this Epistle. 9. XII. p. m. 181.
(d) Chap. I. 1.
(e) See the Note by Cotelier. Apostolic Fathers, as cited above, p. 181.</margin>
The one named *according to the Egyptians* is of the same antiquity. *Origen* (a) made mention of it. *Clement of Alexandria* (b) had already cited it in several places. And if the second Epistle of *Clement of Rome* is truly by him, this Gospel would have a (c) testimony older than that of these two Doctors. We also have, in the Library of the Fathers, a Commentary on *St. Luke* attributed to *Titus of Bostra* (2), in which this Bishop seems to place the Gospel according to the Egyptians among those that *St. Luke* (d) indicated, and consequently as being prior to his own. As the Encratites <note>The Encratites were an ascetic Christian sect that practiced "self-control" by forbidding marriage and the consumption of meat and wine.</note> cited it to defend their Error regarding Marriage, the Fathers did not absolutely reject its testimonies. They tried (e) to explain them in an orthodox sense; which shows that this Book held a kind of authority, and that it was not even suspected of having been forged by Heretics. When I considered that it was received by the Christians (3) of Egypt, I could not help but think that it had been written by the *Essenes* <note>The Essenes were a Jewish sect known for communal living and strict asceticism; the author suggests they were the source of this early Christian text.</note> who had believed in Jesus Christ. The Religion of these people held much in common with the Christian Religion. *The Gospel of the Egyptians* was full (f) of Mysticism, Parables, enigmas, and allegories. This is attributed to the Spirit of the Nation; for my part, I would rather attribute it to the Spirit of the *Essenes*. Within it were found sentences that appeared to favor Encratism. Now, the Essenes lived in continence and abstinence. It is therefore very likely that persons from this Jewish Sect—the only one that Jesus Christ never censured—attached themselves to the Son of God and followed him; and that having retired to Egypt after his death, they composed there a History of his Life and Doctrine, which appeared in Egypt and was called, for that reason, *the Gospel according to the Egyptians*.

<margin>(f) Epiphanius, Heresies LXII. 2.</margin>
<margin>It is conjectured that it was written by the Essenes.</margin>

<margin>Other Apocrypha, which were not bad, nor forged by Heretics.</margin>
Although these ancient Acts were not sufficiently exact, they were nonetheless not bad, no more than some other Books which have not been preserved, and which were written not by Impostors or by writers of fables, but by Persons who were not sufficiently well-instructed, and who were neither Apostles nor Disciples authorized by the Apostles. ### APOCRYPHAL BOOKS.
Mmm

<margin>
*The Preaching, or Doctrine of Peter.*
(a) See the fragments collected by *Grabe, Spicilegium.* <note>Referencing J.E. Grabe’s *Spicilegium SS. Patrum*, a collection of early Christian fragments.</note>
*Apocalypse of Peter.*

These were writings that appeared before the birth of the great Heresies. They were not placed in the rank of Canonical Books, not because they were dangerous, but because their authenticity was not well established. Such was the *Doctrine*, or the *Preaching of St. Peter* (a), cited very often by the early Fathers, and apparently composed in the first century by certain disciples of St. Peter who are unknown to us, after the death of that Apostle. It is not quite the same for the *Apocalypse of St. Peter*, cited by Clement of Alexandria. This book was composed by an impostor who was of much the same character as those who forged the Sibylline Oracles, the Poimandres of *Trismegistus*, etc. <note>The "Poimandres" is a foundational text of Hermeticism, traditionally attributed to the mythical Hermes Trismegistus.</note> This author, apparently wishing to convert the Jews by making them believe that the Apostle had predicted the total ruin of Jerusalem, gave such a detailed and specific description of it that one clearly feels, when reading today what (b) *Lactantius* reports of it, that it is an historian hiding under the name of St. Peter and imitating a Prophet. However, as this book was not bad, it was read (c) every year at Easter time in the churches of Palestine, even though it was well known that it was not by St. Peter.

<margin>
(b) *Lactantius, Divine Institutes, Book IV. 21.* <note>original: "Lactant. Inst. L. IV. 21."</note> See also *Grabe, Spicilegium, Vol. I. p. 69. & p. 72. & following*, where one will find some fragments of this Apocalypse.
(c) *Sozomen, Ecclesiastical History, Book VII. 19.* <note>original: "Sozom. H. E. L. VII. 19."</note>

<margin>
Second Class of Apocrypha. The time when they appeared.

The second class of Apocrypha includes all those that appeared in the second century, after the death of the Apostles and their (4) first disciples. Then, as the spirit of falsehood no longer kept any bounds, one saw the rise of that multitude of Heretics who, according to the report of Clement of Alexandria, began to raise their heads under the reign of the Emperor *Hadrian*, and continued until that of *Antoninus Pius*. It was then that imposture gave birth to a quantity of false writings, some under the name of the Apostles, others under the name of their first disciples. These historians wrote, each in their own manner, the travels, adventures, and preachings of their supposed masters. This is the era of the pernicious writings that were rejected with indignation by the Fathers, and in which the doctrine of Jesus Christ was visibly altered.

<margin>
Their age and their obscurity show their fabrication. <note>The author uses "supposition" here to mean the act of forging or substituting a false work for a genuine one.</note>
</margin>
Great noise is made today about this multitude of Apocrypha, because most of them no longer exist, and because, distant as we are from the time of their fabrication, we are not in a position to show by whom, how, and for what purpose each was composed. One believes oneself entitled to confuse authentic—

<meta>This page continues the classification of early Christian writings, specifically contrasting the "authentic" texts accepted by the Church with the "fabulous" or forged works that appeared much later. It uses the Gospel of Peter as a primary case study for how these forgeries were identified and rejected by early Church leaders like Serapion of Antioch.</meta>

->DISCOURSE ON THE<-

authentic, sealed by the perpetual testimony of the universal Church, with fabulous ones, written a hundred years, more or less, after the others, and which bore evident marks of falsehood. These miserable pieces, born in obscurity, excited only the contempt and indignation of the critics, and were in circulation only among a few sectarians, or at most among some ignorant and superstitious people who were easily deceived. This is apparent from the example of the false (1) *Gospel of St. Peter*, which the name of that Apostle should have made more famous than most of the other Acts of the same nature, and which was nevertheless unknown even in Asia where it was born, to almost all the Churches and all the Bishops toward the end of the second century—which clearly shows that it had only seen the light of day toward the middle of that century.

<margin>Example in the false Gospel of St. Peter which was unknown to the Orthodox around the year 190. (a) Eusebius, *Church History*, Book VII, 12. <note>original: "Euseb. H.E. L. VII. 12." Note: Modern editions usually cite this account in Book VI, Chapter 12 of Eusebius's history.</note></margin>
*Serapion* (a), Bishop of Antioch, flourished around the year 190 of our Lord. Having gone to *Rhossus*, a city in Cilicia, he found the entire Church there divided over this Gospel, some stubbornly insisting on reading and defending it, and others wishing to banish it as an Apocryphal Book. Serapion had never heard of it. A Bishop, who occupied the primary See of the East, was entirely unaware that there was a *Gospel of St. Peter*, and consequently did not know what it contained. Since he believed the reading of it to be innocent, he permitted it in order to restore peace. But having been warned afterward that there was heresy in *Rhossus*, and that it was being taught through this false Gospel, he wished to read and examine it. Finding it nowhere in the Catholic Churches, (2) it was necessary to seek it among the *Docetes* <note>The Docetes were a group of early heretics who believed that Jesus Christ only "seemed" or appeared to be human and to suffer, rather than having a physical body.</note>, who read it assiduously, and to borrow it from them. It was, therefore, an obscure book, an evidently new book, unknown until then to the Christian Church, and which was only in the hands of a manifestly Heretical sect. Such were these false Acts, which the Unbelievers <note>Likely referring to Enlightenment-era skeptics or deists who used apocryphal texts to challenge the authority of the New Testament.</note> would today like to use to undermine the authenticity of those that have been received and venerated from the beginning by the universal Church as Apostolic Writings. It was impossible to be mistaken or to misidentify them at the time they appeared, unless Interest and Prejudice conspired with Imposture.

<margin>XII. Fifth Proposition: The Apocrypha confirm the Divine Authority of Jesus Christ, teaching, like the other Books, that he is the Son of God, and certifying his miracles.</margin>
### XII. Fifth Proposition. *All these Apocryphal works, of whatever order they may be, even the worst and most corrupt, far from ruining the Divine Authority of Jesus Christ and the Christian Religion, concur with the authentic Books in confirming it.*

<meta>This page continues the argument from the previous discussion regarding the reliability of the canonical Gospels. ### APOCRYPHAL BOOKS.
Mmm 2
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

The proof of this Proposition is that all these Books bear witness to these two capital Truths; the first, that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, whatever sense one gives to these terms: The second, that he proved his Mission by public miracles, by striking miracles. Now this is precisely what the <term>Skeptics<note>original: "Incrédules." Refers to those who reject the supernatural or revealed religion.</note></term> deny. They will readily grant us the Precepts of Jesus Christ, which they find, at least in part, in the Books of the Philosophers: They will likewise grant us the sacred Discourses of the Lord, in which a profound Wisdom reigns. I do not believe they contest either the beauty or the grandeur of his character, nor the sublime nature of his morals. It is therefore only his Miracles, his Resurrection, and his Ascension into Heaven that revolt their Minds. We maintain the truth of these facts because they are attested by irreproachable Witnesses, who can be suspected neither of imposture nor of illusion, and whose Accounts we have in the Gospels. To strip these Accounts of their authority, people cite to us a quantity of <term>Apocryphal Books<note>Literally "hidden" books; early Christian writings not included in the official Bible, often considered legendary or heretical by the early Church.</note></term> that were written in the first Centuries. The objection would have some force if these false Acts contradicted the true ones on the point contested by the Skeptics. Thus, when historians attest to a fact, and others from the same time, or the time following, deny it or make no mention of it, the silence or the negation of the latter balances the affirmation of the others. But if the Writers agree to attest the fact in question, the variations found in their Books on other Articles serve only to confirm this fact, upon which they are unanimous. Now all the Apocrypha agree with the authentic Books on the Miracles and on the Resurrection of the Lord, and it is here, it seems to me, that the Objection of the Skeptics is destroyed.

<margin>1. Testimony of the Judaizing Church and its Gospel.</margin>

They differed on the article of his Conception and his miraculous Birth. They had their Hebrew Gospel, which could differ in some things. St. Jerome translated that of the Nazarenes into Latin; and if we believe some (3) Moderns, his Translation still exists in Cambridge, in

<margin>2. On the Christians of Egypt and their Gospel.</margin>
2. The <term>Gospel according to the Egyptians<note>An early Christian text used primarily in Egypt during the 2nd century, often associated with ascetic traditions.</note></term> is of the same antiquity as the Gospel of the Nazarenes and was, in the beginning, the Rule of Faith for the Christians of Egypt. The <term>Encratites<note>A sect of early Christians who practiced extreme asceticism, including the rejection of marriage and the consumption of meat and wine.</note></term> used it; Julius Cassian, one of their leaders, relied on the authority of this piece. The <term>Sabellians<note>Followers of Sabellius, who taught that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit were not distinct persons but three modes of a single God.</note></term> believed they found there some foundation for their Error. The <term>Valentinians<note>A major Gnostic movement founded by Valentinus, which emphasized secret knowledge (gnosis) for salvation.</note></term> cited it, and we have seen that it was quoted by the Author of the second Epistle of St. Clement. The Church Fathers did not reject the testimonies of this Gospel as they surely would have done if it did not agree with the authentic Scriptures regarding the Divine Mission of Jesus Christ, attested by his Miracles and particularly by his Resurrection. Nay, neither the Encratites nor the Sabellians would have dared to cite it without betraying their own cause if it had not conformed to the Gospels on the most fundamental Articles of Religion.

<margin>3. On the false Gospels that remain to us.</margin>
3. We have the Gospel of the Nativity of Mary; the Proto-Gospel of St. James; the two Gospels of the Infancy, and that of Nicodemus. I do not know if any other of the same nature remains to us. But these writings, as fabulous as they are, bear witness to the true Gospels; the authors having drawn from them everything that suited their purpose, and having done only what poets are accustomed to do, who take a subject from History and adorn it with episodes and marvelous incidents provided by their imagination or held from rumor and from writers without authority.

as the Messiah, or the King promised to the Jewish Nation, but who believed him to be only a mere man. The second, the <term>Docetes<note>From the Greek 'dokein', meaning 'to seem'. They believed Christ's physical body was an illusion or a phantom rather than real flesh.</note></term>, of whom I have spoken. These, unable to conceive that the Divine Word could be personally united to Human Nature, imagined that he had only put on its form or outward appearance. Both these sects were found in Asia as early as the time of St. Ignatius, and it is they whom he combated in his Epistles. Both are accused of having forged or corrupted books. It is believed that the *Homilies* called the *Clementines* are the work of an <term>Ebionite<note>A group of Jewish Christians who maintained Jewish law and viewed Jesus as a human prophet rather than a divine being.</note></term> from the 2nd century. It is a well-written romance, composed by a Christian philosopher who wished to peddle his theology under the name of St. Peter or St. Clement. I have cited fragments from <term>Leucius<note>Leucius Charinus, the legendary author of various apocryphal Acts; his writings often emphasized Docetic themes where Christ appears in different forms.</note></term>, who was a Docete, and from other heretics of the same sect that have been preserved for us by the Church Fathers. But if one looks through all that remains of these opposing sects, one finds throughout that Jesus Christ is the Son of God; with the sole difference being that, according to the Docetes, he is so by sharing the same nature: *he is begotten of the Father*; whereas, according to the Ebionites, he is so only by an adoption based on his incomparable virtues and the presence of the Holy Spirit within him. One finds everywhere Jesus Christ confirming his doctrine with public miracles. The Ebionite (2) and those like him never doubted that the Lord had died and rose from the dead; whereas the Docete merely converted into appearances what the Ebionite believed had actually occurred. Both agreed on the fact. The Ebionite read in (a) his Gospel that Jesus Christ had said to St. Peter, *and to those who were with him, that is to say, both to him and to the other disciples: "Take me, and recognize that I am not an incorporeal spirit."* The Docete, on the contrary, read in some books or other, (3) "that St. John the Evangelist, wishing to touch the Lord, his hand sank into the apparent body of the Son of God and passed through it without the flesh offering any resistance." These two accounts, so contrary in one respect, nevertheless agree on the essential point: namely, that Jesus Christ presented himself alive to his disciples after his death—whether real according to some, or apparent according to others—that they recognized him, and that he conversed with them.

<margin>XIII. In what way the Apocryphal Gospels differed from the true ones.</margin> XIII. If one investigates in what ways the Apocryphal Gospels of the 1st Century differed from the true ones, one will see that it all consisted of a few specific details of the Life of Our Lord, which were either removed or added: in a few words, or in certain Sentences attributed to Jesus Christ but omitted by our Evangelists. Such is, for example, that saying of the Savior, <margin>(b) Acts 20:35.</margin> *(b)* *it is more blessed to give than to receive*. *Euthalius* <note>A 5th-century deacon known for dividing the text of the Pauline Epistles and Acts into verses.</note> reports that this was found in the Book entitled: (1) *The Teaching of the Apostles* <note>Also known as the *Didache*, a late 1st-century manual of Christian ethics and church order.</note>. subject: (1) It flees, so to speak, before those who seek it, and when they think they are approaching it, it sinks into an obscurity where it is impossible to follow. From this arises such a diversity of sentiments among the most skillful Philosophers regarding the Divine Nature: even the Christians themselves were not in agreement on this, as Revelation is more intent on instructing us in the Perfections of God than in His Essence, because it is these Perfections that serve to regulate our obedience and our worship.

<margin>II. Manichaeus believed the Nature of God to be a most pure Light.</margin>
II. Manichaeus, being both a Theologian and a Philosopher, undertook—following the example of many others—to define the Nature of God. He said "that it is (2) an eternal, intelligent, and most pure <term>Light</term> <note>Mani’s theology was deeply dualistic, seeing Light as the literal substance of the divine realm, in eternal conflict with the substance of Darkness.</note>, which is not mixed with any darkness, and which consequently is not susceptible to any alteration."

<margin>The Valentinians likewise.</margin>
This was also the opinion of the *Valentinians* <note>The Valentinians were a major Gnostic movement in the early Christian era, named after their founder Valentinus.</note>, who (3) defined "the Nature of the eternal Father of all things as incorruptible, a Light that exists by itself, which admits nothing foreign, no mixture, and no composition."

<margin>This idea is very general. It is found among the Magi. A saying of Zoroaster.</margin>
Men, being unable to conceive of anything more beautiful, more pure, nor more incorruptible than Light, easily imagined that the most excellent Nature is nothing other than a most perfect Light. This idea is found among all the Nations that have been regarded as the most learned. *Porphyry* (4) reports that *Pythagoras* had learned from *Zoroaster* that, on the side of the Body, God resembles Light, and on the side of the Soul, He resembles Truth. *Plutarch* reports the saying of *Zoroaster* (5) slightly differently. "*Pythagoras*," he says, "had learned from *Zoroaster* that of all sensible things, that which most resembles <term>Oromaze</term> <note>The Greek rendering of Ahura Mazda, the supreme god of Zoroastrianism.</note> is Light, as <term>Arimanius</term> <note>The Greek rendering of Ahriman, the destructive spirit or personification of evil in Zoroastrianism.</note> on the contrary resembles Darkness and Ignorance." *Arimanius* is the Demon, and *Oromaze* is God, or the Son of God. In Epiphanius, *Heresies*, XXXIII, p. 222. ...it is a Light more pure, more perfect, and more resplendent than that which illuminates the World. Thus, God is perpetually called (6) *Light, Radiance, Splendor, Fire*, in those Greek verses known as the Oracles of Zoroaster <note>The Chaldean Oracles, once attributed to Zoroaster, are a collection of 2nd-century philosophical poems combining Platonic and Middle Eastern thought.</note>, and which, although they are not truly by that Persian Philosopher, nevertheless contain a very ancient doctrine, likely that of the Magi and the Chaldeans.

<margin>Among the Philosophers of the Indies.</margin>
A Christian Author, whom some scholars believe to be *Origen* <note>While the text cites Origen, this work is now identified as the *Philosophumena* (Refutation of All Heresies) by Hippolytus of Rome.</note>, reports that according to the *Brahmins*, “(7) God is a Light,” but a Light that is not of the same nature as that of the “Sun and the Fire that we see. It is a <term>Word</term> <note>original: *logos*</note>; not an articulated Word, but a Word of Knowledge, by means of which the Sages perceive hidden Mysteries.” This idea of the Divinity seems quite spiritual, but what follows is less so, and I suspect there is some error or omission in the original. “The Brahmins say,” the Author continues, “(8) that this WORD *which they call God is* CORPOREAL, that it wraps itself in a Body, much like a man covers himself in the skin of a sheep; but that when it has stripped off this Body that surrounds it, it appears to the eyes.” There is a palpable absurdity here. Does a perfectly spiritual Being, such as <term>Reason</term> <note>original: *Raison*, likely referring to the *Logos* or divine intellect.</note>, become *visible to the eyes* when it has stripped off the Body it animates and in which it *wraps itself*? This leads me to believe that these Indian Philosophers meant to say that the Divinity is clothed in a luminous Body, which is not perceived at present because it is hidden under another—be it the Heavens or the World—but that it will show itself one day, when it has stripped off this foreign body, which is to it like the *Sheep’s skin* with which a man covers himself.

<margin>Among the Cabbalists or the Jewish Philosophers.</margin>
The Cabbalists, or the Jewish Philosophers, held the same idea of the Divinity as the Manicheans and the Orientals. They conceived of it (1) as a *most pure, yet extended Light*: This was also the sentiment of several Greek Philosophers. <note>The Cabbala is a school of thought in Jewish mysticism; "extended" here suggests the light fills all space.</note>
<margin>Among the Greeks.</margin>
Porphyry says, (2) "that the Divine Essence is of a lumi-
" nous Nature, and that it dwells in the midst of an ethereal and most
" pure fire: Democritus, (3) that it is an Understanding of the Nature
" of Fire: (4) Empedocles and (5) Heraclitus, *that God is an Intelligent
" Fire*." <note>Porphyry was a Neoplatonist; Democritus, Empedocles, and Heraclitus were Pre-Socratic philosophers who sought the fundamental substance of the universe.</note>

<margin>III. Scripture and the Fathers support it.</margin>
III. Holy Scripture does not combat this opinion; on the contrary, it seems to favor it. In the appearances of the Divinity one always sees (6) a *Fire*, or a great Light: And what the sacred Authors call the *Glory of God*, is very often nothing but the *splendor*, the *radiance*, which seemed to emanate from His Person. 
<margin>Passages from Gregory of Nazianzus.</margin>
It would be useless to report the proofs of this. Regarding the Fathers, the most learned and Orthodox constantly say, (7) "that *God is a Light, and a most sublime Light*: That
" all the brightness we see, however brilliant it
" may be, is but a small outflowing, a ray of this

" *Light*: (a) That the Son is a *Light*, who has no
" beginning: (8) That God is an *inaccessible Light*, which

" *Virtues*, which surround the Divinity, are Lights of a
" second Order, RAYS OF THE FIRST LIGHT: That God, who created the Sun to light the World, created no Light for the World of Spirits (10),

This is confirmed by a very certain proof of fact; for the Holy *Virgin*, who, according to the Hymns of the Church, was raised to Heaven in Body and in Soul, contemplates with **her bodily eyes**, **both God** **and the Essence of God**, because her eyes have been strengthened by a Divine Virtue. *...was a* LIGHT *too brilliant to be able to endure the sight of it. These are the words of this Father.*

<margin>VI. Consequences. 1. That the Fathers did not believe God to be absolutely incorporeal.</margin>
VI. Here are established facts; let us draw the consequences from them: 1. Firstly, when the Fathers said that God is an *incorporeal Light*, they advanced nothing that *Manichaeus* <note>Manichaeus, or Mani (c. 216–274 AD), was the founder of Manichaeism, a religion that viewed the universe as a struggle between light and darkness. He often described the divine in terms of literal light.</note> did not also say as well as they. But the *Incorporeal* of the Fathers did not exclude *visibility*, nor consequently all forms of corporality. There would be a manifest contradiction in saying that bodily eyes could perceive a purely intelligible Being, which has absolutely no extension, and of which the eye, therefore, could not receive any image.

<margin>2. That their sentiment is the same as that of Manichaeus and the Valentinians.</margin>
2. Secondly, the Fathers recognized that the Divine Nature is invisible to carnal eyes, unless God strengthens them in a supernatural manner, and raises them to a perfection they do not currently have. This is precisely what *Manichaeus* thought, and what the *Valentinians* <note>The Valentinians were a major Gnostic movement in the 2nd century, following the teachings of Valentinus, who explored the relationship between the divine "Fullness" and the material world.</note> had thought before him. Both believed that the Son of God revealed his Divinity on the Mountain: but they added that the Lord *fortified* the eyes of his Disciples so that they could contemplate it. <margin>(a) In *Excerpts from Theodotus*, §. V.</margin> (a) "The Disciples," said the *Valentinians*, "did not see the Light of the Savior with carnal eyes, because there is no affinity, no proportion between Divine Light and the flesh. (1) But the will of the Savior strengthened the flesh, so that it could contemplate it."

<margin>Everything that is visible is Body.</margin>
If one opposes these reflections with passages from the Fathers in which they say that the Divine Nature is invisible, without figure and without size, all that can be concluded is that they contradicted themselves—which happens only too often to those who reason upon the Nature of God. There are Bodies that their distance, or their smallness, render invisible, but there is nothing visible that is not a *Body*, and the *Valentinians* were right to <margin>Nothing visible could emanate from a pure Spirit.</margin> say, (2) *that everything that is visible is corporeal and shaped*. It must also be that the Council of Constantinople <note>The Council of Constantinople (1341) dealt with the Hesychast controversy, siding with Gregory Palamas against Barlaam of Calabria.</note>, which decided, in accordance with the opinion of *Palamas* <note>Gregory Palamas (1296–1357) was a monk and theologian who defended the practice of Hesychasm, distinguishing between God’s unknowable essence and His manifest "energies," such as the Uncreated Light seen by the Apostles.</note>, and on the authority of a great number of Fathers, that there emanates from the Divine Essence an *uncreated Light*, which is like *its garment*, and which appeared in Jesus Christ in his Transfiguration—it must be, I say, either that this Council believed that the Divinity is a luminous Body, or that it established two contradictory opinions; for it is absolutely impossible for a visible, and consequently corporeal, Light to emanate from a pure Spirit.

### ON MANICHAEUS. Book III. Ch. I.

<margin>VII. Manichaeus’s concept of the incorporeal does not exclude the Body when understood in a philosophical sense.</margin>
VII. As for *Manichaeus* <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism.</note>, he reasoned consistently. Although he defined Divinity as a most pure and simple Light, he nevertheless believed it to be *extended*, and consequently *corporeal*, if one takes this term in the sense used by the Philosophers <note>In ancient philosophy, "corporeal" often simply meant anything that occupies space or has dimensions, rather than necessarily being made of heavy, "fleshly" matter.</note>. This is evident from the reasoning he is made to give in the *Dispute* he had with *Archelaus*: <margin>(b) Acts of the Dispute, p. 66.</margin> (b) “If we suppose,” he says, “that there is but one single Nature, namely God: that this Nature fills all things, and that there is no place that is not full of the Divinity, what place will remain in which to put the Creature? Where will the Gehenna <note>A term for a place of fiery suffering or hell.</note> of Fire be? Where will the outer Darkness be? Shall we put them in God? That is absurd, for He would then be tormented Himself.” *Manichaeus* adds this comparison: “The World is a Vessel. If the Divine Substance fills this entire Vessel, how would it be possible to put anything more into it, unless one removed a part of what fills it? But where will one put what has been removed, if there is no place outside the Vessel?” I confess that this reasoning is partly suspicious to me, because I see in it a hypothesis contrary to Manichaean Theology. The Heresiarch <note>The "leader of a heresy"; here referring to Mani.</note> never believed that the Divinity could suffer, even though it is found in places of suffering, as Matter has no power to act upon it. It is only true that he denied the substantial Immensity <note>In this context, "immensity" refers to the theological concept of God being present everywhere without being spread out like a physical substance.</note> of the Divinity, and that he believed the Divine Nature to be extended and corporeal. This was also the idea that *St. Augustine* held during his time as a Manichaean. He believed the divine was spread out either within the World or outside the World in infinite Spaces, (3) because he could not conceive of a Substance that had neither place nor extension.

<margin>VIII. The Christian Doctors were not unanimous at the beginning regarding the Nature of God.</margin>
VIII. To properly judge the Error of *Manichaeus* regarding the Nature of God, one must transport oneself to the time in which he lived. If one does not place oneself in this point of view when examining the opinions of the Ancients, one cannot judge them in an equitable manner. One adopts a spirit of rigor toward some that must immediately be cast off for others—variations from which I try to preserve myself as much as possible.

Those who have some knowledge of the History of Dogmas know that the Christians, who were always unanimous regarding the Unity of God, were not at all so regarding his Nature. The Scripture (4) not explaining itself clearly on this subject, the Doctors followed <margin>They followed the opinions of their Teachers.</margin> the sentiment that seemed most probable to them: that of their Teachers,

This is certainly not clearly designated in our Preaching [teachings]."* <note>original: "Deus, quomodo intelligi debeat, inquirendum. An secundum habitum aliquem deformatus? An alterius Naturæ quam corpora sunt? Quod utique in Prædicatione nostra manifeste non designatur."</note> *Origen, in the Preface to the Book on Principles. See also Petau, Theological Dogmas, Vol. I. Book II. 1.*

Finally, another believed that it is a Substance which has nothing in common with the Elements of which our World is composed—(2) a fifth Nature, similar to that which *Aristotle* had imagined. <note>Also known as the "quintessence," a celestial element distinct from earth, air, fire, and water.</note> In general, the idea of an absolutely incorporeal Substance was not the common idea of Christians at the beginning. ### CHAPTER II.

*The Idea of a corporeal God holds ST. AUGUSTINE in Manichaeism. How he freed himself from it. Details on the opinions of this Father before his Conversion. What we should reasonably judge concerning the Manichaean Error.*

<margin>I. Difficulty of ridding oneself of the idea of a corporeal God. (a) Gassendi in Book X of Diogenes Laërtius p. 1272.</margin>
I. A skillful *(a)* modern Philosopher <note>Pierre Gassendi (1592–1655), a French priest and scientist who revived the philosophy of Epicurus within a Christian framework.</note>, wishing to excuse Epicurus, who gave the Divinity a human form—*not a body, but as if a body; not blood, but as if blood* <note>original: "non un corps, mais comme un corps, non du sang, mais comme du sang" / Latin: "non corpus sed quasi corpus, non sanguinem sed quasi sanguinem"</note>—made very reasonable reflections on this subject. He first remarked that (1) Tertullian believed God to be corporeal only because he was persuaded that everything that is not a Body is pure nothingness. He adds (2) "that we ourselves, when we wish to form some idea of the Divinity, can only conceive of Him as a very pure, very luminous Air, spread everywhere and without limits." Indeed, it is so difficult to uproot this idea from the Mind that St. *Augustine*, who was certainly one of the greatest and finest geniuses of Christian Antiquity, could not rid himself of it. He admits in his *Confessions* (3) *that this was the great cause, and almost the only cause, that held him invincibly in Manichaeism*. The Reader will be surprised to learn from his own mouth what drew him out of it. It is a small piece of his History that is not the least curious, and it is, moreover, linked with Manichaeism.

<margin>It holds St. Augustine in Manichaeism.</margin>

III. I cannot let this passage pass without making a few observations. 1st. We see here a proof of what I have always suspected: that *St. Augustine* was only half a Manichaean. It was not the heresy of the Manichaeans to believe Jesus Christ was a simple man. On the contrary, they believed him to be pure God, having only the appearance of a man. <note>The author refers to Docetism, the belief that Christ's body was an illusion.</note> 2nd. I do not know if *Constantine* the Great is the author of the discourse he delivered in the *Assembly of the Saints*, but he judges quite differently than *St. Augustine* regarding Platonic theology on this article. (3) *Plato*, says this Prince, *did very well when he taught a* FIRST GOD, *who is above all things: that to this first* GOD HE SUBMITTED A SECOND, *and that he distinguished* TWO ESSENCES DIFFERENT IN NUMBER. <margin>IV. Other Observations. 1. St. *Augustine* cured himself of Manichaeism through Platonic Books, even though Platonism and Manichaeism share great similarities.</margin>
IV. St. *Augustine* praises the goodness of the Lord, who used the books of the Platonists to deliver him from the snares of Manichaeism. This holy man is right: God enlightened him through a philosophy that was otherwise fit only to blind him. Indeed (5) did *Plato* not believe in two coeternal Principles, God and Matter? Did he not believe that Matter is the cause of evils: That pure Intelligences are Divine Emanations just as the Word is: That the Human Soul is only a mixture of *pure Spirit* (*Mens* <note>original Latin: "Mens" — Mind or Intellect.</note>) and the Substance that he calls *composed* <note>original Greek: "$\mu\acute{\epsilon}\rho\iota\sigma\tau o\varsigma$" (meristos) — partitioned or divisible.</note>, divisible—that is to say, of Matter, from which God took the most spiritual parts to form the Soul? Did he not believe that the Soul passes from Body to Body until it has acquired the necessary purification to return to its place of origin? All of this is pure Manichaeism. *Plato* had taken it from *Pythagoras*, and from the Pythagoreans whose books he bought at a high price: and *Pythagoras* had taken it from the *Magi* <note>term: "Magi" — Ancient Persian priests and philosophers; the author suggests a direct lineage from Persian dualism to Greek philosophy and then to Mani.</note>, who were the Masters and Predecessors of *Mani*. What would have been for others a scent of death was for him a scent of life. He acted like those prudent animals that leave poisonous plants and eat only those that are healthy. ### ON MANICHAEUS. Book III. Ch. II.
Ppp
<meta>catchword: in</meta>

> "...me as having given me Being, and I was beneath it, as having been created by it. He who knows the **Truth** knows also this Light, and he who knows this Light knows also Eternity; and it is Love <note>The original French uses "Charité," which in this theological context refers to *Caritas* or divine love.</note> that makes it known." St. *Augustine* then explains this *spiritual Light*, and says that it is nothing other than **Truth**. Then he adds, *Is **Truth** nothing, simply because it is not spread through finite or infinite spaces?*

<margin>Critical reflection on this idea of St. *Augustine*.</margin>
I have read these words, but I confess they have not enlightened me at all regarding the Nature of God. I conceive of two kinds of *Truths*: one is a modification of the Mind, the other is a Property of Substances. The first consists of a correct idea of things, in the conformity of our knowledge with their Nature, their properties, their effects, etc. But such a *Truth* is not a Substance: it is only a Perfection of Minds.

<margin>Truth is not a Substance.</margin>
<margin>Three kinds of Truth.</margin>
The second *Truth* is a Property of Substances, and especially of the Divine Substance, which, existing by itself, has no imperfection, no mutability, and no nothingness. (1) *Truth* belongs to God just as *Love* does, but neither one nor the other properly constitutes the Divine Essence. There are also those *Truths* which are the Principles of our knowledge, and which are called eternal because they appear founded upon the immutable Will of God, and because they are, so to speak, real Images of his eternal knowledge. But one cannot say of any of these Truths that it is the Essence of God. They may be Properties of the Divine Understanding and of the Divine Substance, but not the Substance itself. After all, even if this Substance were an *eternal Light, most pure, most simple, but extended* <note><term>Extended</term>: A philosophical term meaning "occupying space." The author is debating whether God has a physical-like presence in space or is purely conceptual.</note>, it would be no less *Truth* itself. *Manichaeus*, who believed the Divinity to be an extended Substance, preserved for Him the Attribute of (2) *Truth* as a property that is inseparable from Him.

<margin>*Manichaeus* recognized that *Truth* is a property of God.</margin>
<margin>(a) *Clarke*, On the Existence and Attributes of God. p. 217. Extension does not take away His Truth.</margin>
One of the most skillful Metaphysicians of our century <note>Likely referring to Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an English philosopher and cleric.</note> certainly does not intend to strip God of His *Truth*. *(a) However, he conceives of extension as a Property of the Substance that exists by itself. And although he adds that Extension is not suited to Thought, it is for the reason that Thought is not a Being. For otherwise, Extension remains necessary for the existence of every Being, whether it thinks or does not think.*

All that I can say on this is that the way in which *Plato* explains the formation of the Soul suggests that the *Indivisible* Substance is not absolutely without extension. This mixture of two Substances, made with certain proportions, and from which results a compound of the two and a reciprocal action of one upon the other, (7) cannot be conceived if one is extended and the other absolutely without extension.

VIII. All that may suit me is to weigh, on the scales of Equity and Religion, the Question of whether it is a dangerous Heresy to conceive of the Divine Nature as an extended Light. Here is what may cause one to doubt it.

<margin>Reasons for doubt. Silence of Scripture. The notion of the word Spirit includes the idea of Body.</margin>
1. Holy Scripture has not defined the contrary, as (2) Origen has remarked. 2. The term (3) *Incorporeal* is not even found in the Bible: This is another observation by Origen. 3. The passages of Scripture which testify that God is Spirit, far from proving that the Divine Essence is absolutely incorporeal, would prove the contrary. This is so true that the Christian Doctors, who believed God to be corporeal, alleged in favor of their opinion these words of the Lord (4), *God is Spirit*. The idea that we now attach at present to the word *Spirit* is not that which this word represents in the Greek Language, nor that held by the Ecclesiastical Authors who spoke that Language. (5) *Can you*, said Gregory of Nazianzus, *conceive of a Spirit, without conceiving of movement and diffusion?* <note>Gregory of Nazianzus was a 4th-century Archbishop and theologian. Here he suggests that the Greek concept of "Spirit" (Pneuma) traditionally implied something that moves or spreads through space, like air.</note> These are properties that belong only to the Body. Origen says likewise (6), *that every Spirit, according to the proper and simple notion of this term, is a Body*: This is confirmed by (7) Chalcidius. The Ancients never believed that Incorporeality was a property of the Spirit, since they were persuaded (8), that Spirits were corporeal. The idea of the *Spirit*, among the Ancients, is nothing other

<column-break/>

(1) *The soul is a substance without magnitude, immaterial, incorruptible, possessing life of itself, and having being.* <note>original Greek: "Ἡ ψυχὴ οὐσία ἀμεγέθης, ἄϋλος, ἄφθαρτος, ἐν ζωῇ παρ' ἑαυτῆς ἐχοῦσα τὸ ζῆν, κεκτημένη τὸ εἶναι."</note> *Porphyr. Sent. No. XIII. p. m. 225.* These Sentences or Maxims are for the most part extracted from *Plotinus*. <note>Plotinus was the founder of Neoplatonism; his student Porphyry edited his works.</note>

(2) *Which certainly in our Preaching is not clearly designated.* <note>original Latin: "Quod utique in Prædicatione nostra manifeste non designatur."</note> *In Proëm. ad Lib. De Princ.* *Preaching* here refers to the Gospel, or Scripture in general.

(3) *The designation "incorporeal" is unusual and unknown among our Writers.* <note>original Latin: "Appellatio ἀσωμάτου apud nostros Scriptores est inusitata & incognita."</note> *Ibid.*

(4) *John IV. 24. I am very much persuaded that God is a pure Intelligence; but the more I reflect on this subject, the more I find myself disposed to treat the contrary opinion with indulgence. For firstly, <margin>(a) Bayle, as cited above. No idea of spiritual Substances.</margin> (a) *the most skillful Cartesians agree that we have no idea of spiritual Substance. "...which quieted them." <note>This completes the thought from the previous page regarding ideas that settled the minds of certain thinkers.</note> *St. Augustine* was a great Genius, but it must be admitted that he aspired to the impossible. Spiritual Natures are inaccessible, not only to the Imagination, because they have neither shape nor size, but to Reason itself. We have proofs of their existence, but their Essence remains unknown. However, let us suppose that these Substances, which escape the penetration of the most subtle Philosophers of our time, had revealed themselves to *St. Augustine*; did he find himself, after that, at ease and quite tranquil? Did he not see new abysses opening before his eyes, whose darkness his Spirit could not penetrate? How can one reconcile such contradictory ideas (1) as those of being everywhere and being nowhere: of being entirely in each part of Space, and being in no space: of being entirely in parts that are at an infinite distance from one another, and yet being perfectly unique? Can one truly conceive that a Substance, which is entirely in each point of the immensity of Space, is not also as infinite in number as are the points of Space in which it is entirely present?

*Manichaeus* <note>The Latinized name for Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the prophet and founder of Manichaeism.</note> commanded his Disciples to honor several Gods. An ancient Egyptian Author, who wrote against Heresies, was content to say that the (4) *Manichaeans hold that there are two Substances*: But the Latin Translator judged it appropriate to put in his Version (5) *two Gods*. Finally, St. *Augustine*, whose testimony carries such great weight regarding Manichaeism, does not merely put forward this latter claim, but he attempts to prove it. As the accusation is a capital one, and since I wish to do neither wrong nor favor to our Heretics, I shall present to the Reader everything that St. *Augustine* said to maintain it, and what *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean bishop known through Augustine's polemic against him.</note> replied to him. It is a sort of Dialogue between St. *Augustine* and him.

<margin>II. Response of *Faustus* to the first accusation.</margin>
II. (6) ST. AUGUSTINE. "Do you believe that there are two Gods, or that there is only one? FAUSTUS. There is absolutely only one. ST. AUGUSTINE. From where does it come, then, that you assert there are two? FAUSTUS. (7) Never, when we set forth our Belief, have we even been heard to utter the words *two Gods*. But tell me, I pray you, upon what do you base your suspicions? AUG. It is upon the fact that you teach there are TWO PRINCIPES, one of Good, and the other of Evil. FAUSTUS. It is true that we confess two <term>PRINCIPLES<note>In this context, "Principles" (from the Latin 'principia') refers to the fundamental, eternal origins or sources of all reality.</note></term>, but there is only one that we call GOD. We name the other <term>HYLE<note>original Greek: ὕλη. A philosophical term usually meaning 'matter' or 'raw substance.' Here, it refers to the source of evil and darkness.</note></term>, or Matter, or, as one commonly speaks, the DEMON. Now, if you claim that this is establishing two Gods, you would also claim that a Physician, who treats *Health* and *Sickness*, establishes *two healths*: or that a Philosopher, who discourses on *Good* and *Evil*, on *Abundance* and *Poverty*, maintains that there are *two Goods*, and *two Abundances*." *Faustus* then expands on showing that White and Black, the *Antidote* and the *Poison*, are no more opposed than *God* and *Matter*, and that just as there would be an extreme absurdity in designating them by the same names, there would be no less in giving the—

# ON MANICHAEISM. BOOK III. CHAPTER III.
<sig>Qqq 2</sig>

<margin>III. The first question is easy to decide. The Manichaeans never believed in two Gods.</margin>
III. Regarding the first question, it is easy to decide. Neither *Faustus*, nor his sect, ever believed in more than a **single God**. "**Clearly one**," <note>original Latin: "Plane unus"</note> says *Faustus*, and it ill becomes Catholic writers to have said the opposite so many times. For, besides the fact that the Manichaeans explain themselves clearly on this article, they defined, as we do, the Divine Nature as an *infinitely perfect Being, infinitely happy, the sole cause of all Good*. 

<margin>Matter was, according to them, the sovereign Evil and the sovereign Imperfection.</margin>
They defined Matter, on the contrary, as *sovereign Imperfection, sovereign Evil*, so to speak, *and the cause of all evils*. They could not, therefore, confuse or unite under the common idea of Divinity two substances, one of which has all possible perfections and the other all the opposite imperfections.

What constitutes the <term>Divine Essence</term> <note>The fundamental nature or "being" of God as understood in philosophical theology.</note> is the assembly of natural perfections and moral perfections. They are equally essential to God. Now, if one excepts self-existence, Life—though an irrational life—Sensation, and Action, Mani gave to Matter none of the natural perfections of Divinity and refused it all the moral perfections, without which there is no God. *Marcion* <note>A 2nd-century teacher whose "Marcionite" church was a major rival to early proto-orthodox Christianity; he taught that the God of the Old Testament was a lower, vengeful creator, separate from the Good God of the New Testament.</note> was reproached for believing in two Gods, one whom he called **Good**, and the other **Just**. St. *Irenaeus* responds with reason that he strips them both of Divinity by taking from each a perfection without which they cannot be Gods. (4) "*The Just God*," says St. *Irenaeus*, "*cannot be God if he lacks Goodness; nor the Good God if he lacks Justice*." <note>original: "Le Dieu Juste... ne peut être Dieu s'il n'a la Bonté; ni le Dieu Bon, s'il n'a la Justice"</note> To take from God any moral perfection is, according to St. *Irenaeus*, to strip him of Divinity itself. From which it follows that the Manichaeans could not believe that Matter was God—they, who not only deprived it of all moral perfections, but who regarded it as the subject and source of all vices.

<margin>St. Augustine did not respond at all to Faustus's solution.</margin>
St. *Augustine* objects to us "that he had often enough heard the Manichaeans speak of two Gods in their disputes." That is true, but that is not what needed to be proven. It needed to be proven that they were speaking then **according to their belief**, and not according to **the opinion of idolaters**, and in conforming to the usage of their age. Now St. *Augustine* does not even touch upon such a decisive distinction, without which one could accuse the Prophets and the Apostles of having believed and taught several...

(4) For this one, who is Judicial [the Just God], if he is not good, is not God, because he is not God to whom goodness is lacking: And that one again who is Good, if he is not also Judicial, will suffer the same as this one, that his being God is taken away from him. ...many Gods. When St. Paul said (a) that there are many Gods and many Lords, did he then intend to say that there is another *God* other than the Father, and another *Lord* other than the Son of God? When he said of the Voluptuous (b) *that their Belly is their God*, did he wish to accuse them of believing that *their Belly is the God*, or one of the Gods of the Universe? Would one wish to accuse *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155 – c. 240 AD) known for his prolific Latin theological writings.</note> of having believed in two Gods because he said (1) *that the corruption of Nature is another Nature, which has its* **God** *and its* **Father**, *namely, the Author of this corruption*? Faustus is well-founded in citing the example of St. Paul, who indeed gives to the *Demon* the title of *God of this Age* <note>Referring to 2 Corinthians 4:4, often translated as "the god of this world."</note>, and St. Augustine is not [well-founded] in introducing into the Apostle's words a transposition of terms so unnatural, or rather so forced, that the most moderate (2) Critics speak of it only with contempt. What likelihood is there that the Manichaeans would give to Matter the name of *God*, since the Magi <note>Priests of the ancient Persian religion of Zoroastrianism, which famously divided the world into Light/Good and Darkness/Evil.</note> themselves did not do so, and called it the *Demon*, as *Plutarch* testifies.

<margin>IV. Examination of the 2nd Question: Whether the Manichaeans actually introduced two Gods.</margin>
IV. It is not so easy to decide the second Question, namely, whether by establishing two co-eternal Principles, one does not actually introduce two Gods. The reason for this is that self-existence <note>Often called "aseity" in theology: the property by which a being exists of itself, independent of any cause.</note> is a Perfection which appears so linked with all the others that any Being that exists by itself must have all possible Perfections, without any imperfection; that is to say, it is God. At the very least, modern Metaphysics places this Proposition among the certain Truths.

<margin>The Ancients knew no necessary link between self-existence and Divine Perfections.</margin>
However, it must be admitted that this was not evident enough to persuade all the ancient Philosophers, who believed Matter to be eternal and yet believed in only one God. I do not even know if most Christian Doctors felt the connection that the Moderns find between self-existence and Divine Perfections. But of all the ancient Fathers, I recall only Dionysius of Alexandria <note>The 3rd-century Bishop of Alexandria, a student of Origen.</note> who seems to have noticed it.

<margin>Only *Dionysius* of Alexandria is known to have noticed it.</margin>
Wishing to prove that Matter cannot be eternal, he made this argument: (3) "If God is not a Being existing by himself, and if self-existence is, so to speak, his Essence, certainly Matter does not exist by itself, for Matter and God cannot be the same thing." This reasoning appears founded upon

### OF MANICHAEUS BOOK III. CH. III.
