...because self-existence <note>The quality of existing by one's own nature, without being created by another; often called "aseity" in theology.</note> is not only an Attribute, but an incommunicable Property of the Divinity.

<margin>St. Augustine does not appear to have seen this.</margin>
Even assuming that Dionysius of Alexandria <note>A 3rd-century Bishop and theologian known for his defense of the Trinity against various heresies.</note> recognized this metaphysical truth, it remains certain that the Philosophers were ignorant of it, and that it escaped the insight of the most subtle of all the Church Fathers. I am speaking of St. **Augustine**. He admits (4), that if **Faustus** <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean teacher and Augustine's contemporary opponent.</note> conceived of Matter as an eternal Substance, but purely passive, no one could accuse him of making it a second Divinity. One must not, therefore, impute to **Manichaeus** a consequence that neither he, nor the excellent minds of Antiquity, ever perceived; and *(e)* *it seems to me that all one can say of those Philosophers who established two self-existing Principles, is that they only imperfectly recognized a Divinity.*

<margin>(e) Cudworth, Select Library, Vol. III. p. 18.</margin>

<margin>V. St. Augustine's Argument.</margin>
V. This judgment of the learned Mr. **Cudworth** <note>Ralph Cudworth (1617–1688), a prominent English philosopher and leader of the Cambridge Platonists.</note> being equitable, the reader might perhaps have no difficulty in agreeing with it, if **Manichaeus** had been content with establishing two eternal Principles. But (5) by attributing to Matter self-existence, and to "some unknown being other than God" the power to convert it into Elements, to clothe it in forms and qualities it did not possess, and to compose Bodies and Animals from it, one is right to say that he introduces a second God, by introducing a Being who does what was done only by the true God.

<margin>To give the Demon the power to form Animals is to make him a God.</margin>

<margin>Remarks on this Argument.</margin>
Although this argument by St. **Augustine** is strong, the most excellent Philosophers had admitted principles that weakened it extremely, and which provided the Manichaeans with answers suitable to maintain their illusion. 1. **St. Augustine was mistaken when he said that the Manichaeans attributed to "some unknown being other than God" the power to convert Matter into Elements.** This was not their hypothesis. They believed Matter was not only eternal, but eternally distinguished into **Fire**, **Water**, **Earth**, and **Air**, the same necessity that gave it Existence having given it the various modifications of its parts. 2. Far from the formation of Bodies being considered by ancient Philosophers as an operation belonging to the Divinity, they believed it to be entirely unworthy of Him, because Bodies are the seat of vicious passions, diseases, and death. It is for this reason that (6) **Plato** represents, in his...

<margin>1. According to the Manichaeans, the Elements are eternal.</margin>

<margin>2. The formation of Bodies is not the work of the Divinity.</margin>

<margin>The opinion of Plato and Philo.</margin>

<margin>The human body, being the seat of passions and death, cannot have been formed by the true God.</margin>
> (1) "It was," says *Philo*, "fitting and proper for God the

*Philo* took all of this from *Plato*: *Plato* took it from *Pythagoras*, and *Pythagoras* from Oriental Philosophy, from which *Manichaeus* <note>The 3rd-century prophet and founder of Manichaeism, a religion that viewed the universe as a dualistic struggle between a good realm of spirit and an evil realm of matter.</note> drew his own. But the latter did not adapt the system of *Plato* and *Philo*, because they justify the supreme God quite poorly. Is he any less the author of Bodies—and of the soul's dependence on their needs and movements—simply because he did not make them himself, and was content to order his Angels to form them? It is for this reason that *Manichaeus* attributed the "incorporation" of souls to the Evil Principle.

<margin>3. The Fathers recognize that spiritual Intelligences have the power to form organized bodies.</margin>
3. Let us continue to examine the instance of *St. Augustine*. He maintains that God alone has the power to form *Bodies* and *Animals*. However, this great man believed that the Angels who appeared to the Patriarchs formed human bodies for themselves, of which they were the Soul...

<margin>*Living beings, whom you might both support as living and winged, and receive joined to your bosom.* <note>original Latin: "Animantes, quos & vivos alatis, & conjunctos sinu recipiatis."</note> This is the translation from *Cicero* <note>The Roman statesman Cicero translated parts of Plato's Timaeus into Latin.</note>. See the *Timaeus*, edition by *Fabricius*, page 250. The Greek of Plato seems to say something more: "For the rest, you... fashion living creatures and give them birth" <note>original Ancient Greek: "τὸ δ' λοιπὸν ὑμεῖς... Ἀπεργάζεσθε ζῶα, καὶ γεννᾶτε."</note>. *You then work upon the living and produce them.*
(1) *Philo, On the Creation of the World.* Morel Vol. I. p. 29. *Philo* treats the same subject in *On the Confusion of Tongues*, p. 271. God does nothing that is not perfectly good and happy.</margin>
Everything that is a subject or occasion for evil was produced by the subordinate Powers, whom *Philo* calls subordinates <note>original Ancient Greek: "ὑπάρχοι", referring to under-governors or lieutenants</note>. The reason for this is "so that the successes of the soul may be attributed to him (God) alone, but sins to others" <note>original Ancient Greek: "ἵνα οἱ μὲν τῆς Νῆς κατορθώσεις ἐπ' αὐτὸν (Θεὸν) ἀναφέρωνται μόνον; ἐπ' ἄλλους δὲ αἱ ἁμαρτίαι."</note>. The Body is therefore the work of subordinate Powers, because it is through the Body and the Senses that Man became guilty and unhappy. The Reader may see what *Father Petau* <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit theologian who codified the history of dogmas.</note> has said on this matter, *Theological Dogmas*, Vol. III, Book II, Ch. 7, § 6.

### ON MANICHAEUS. Book III, Ch. III.

...the Soul for some time. He believed, as did most of the Church Fathers (2), that the Magicians of Egypt, assisted by Demons, produced *Serpents* and *Frogs*: The Manichaeans did not say that the Demon created the World; they believed him only to be the Author (3) of harmful Animals—those species of Animals that ancient Theologians (4) imagined were only created after the Fall <note>Original: "le Péché" (Sin). In this context, it refers to the theological idea that predatory or venomous animals did not exist before the Fall of Man.</note>, and specifically to punish the Sinner.

<margin>4. Only Creation from nothing is unique to God. Admission by Clarke and St. Augustine.</margin>
4. Finally, very skilled Theologians do not deny to "Intelligences" <note>In historical theology, "Intelligences" refers to spiritual beings such as angels or demons.</note> any power except that of making something from nothing. This is what the celebrated Mr. *Clarke* (5) says: "With the exception of the Power to create a thing from nothing, which appears to us entirely incommunicable, there is hardly any particular effect in the World, however great and miraculous it may appear, of which one can say with certainty that it surpasses the power of all created Beings." Mr. *Clarke* is right, and *St. Augustine* (6) himself, in a moment of calm reflection outside of active Dispute, appears to be of the same sentiment. As soon as it is only a matter of arranging a portion of Matter and giving it the form of an organized Body, I do not believe that any Philosopher would deny this power to these Intelligences.

<margin>Judgment on the Error of Manichaeus. His false hypothesis.</margin>
Let us now judge the sentiment of Manichaeus. His capital Error, and the origin of all his Errors, is to have supposed that Movement, Life, and Feeling existed within an eternal Matter. He believed Matter was animated, but *by an irrational Soul*, as *St. Augustine* put it. Once he admitted this false hypothesis, one does not need to be God to form organized and animated Bodies from such Matter: one merely gives order and arrangement to that which had none, and puts to use the Materials that Nature provides. If *Manichaeus* had supposed a Power that could give Life and Feeling to dead and insensible Matter, he would effectively have attributed to it an operation that belongs only to God. That would truly be making something from nothing; and indeed, it is making from nothing the greatest and most excellent thing in the World. But, as I have said, he gave to the Power of Darkness only the Power of forming Bodies

<margin>VI. Second accusation, which is very false. Manichaeus never served more than one God. What was done by people who believed in two Principles has been wrongly attributed to him.</margin>
VI. I will not dwell on justifying him against the charge of the impiety of having served several Gods and of having commanded his Disciples to do so. The Ancients who claimed this are inexcusable. It is true that those peoples who recognized two Principles <note>In this context, "Principles" refers to the fundamental dualistic forces of Good and Evil.</note> honored both of them. *Plutarch* even testifies that (1) *Zoroaster* had ordered that one should offer (2) pleasing Victims <note>In historical theology, "Victims" refers to animals sacrificed in a religious rite.</note>, sacrifices of thanksgiving, to *Oromaze* <note>Oromaze, or Ormuzd, is the supreme deity and spirit of light in Zoroastrianism.</note>; and to *Arimanius* <note>Arimanius, or Ahriman, is the spirit of darkness and evil.</note>, on the contrary, gloomy Victims of a hideous form. The Pagans did indeed sacrifice white Victims, gentle and tame Animals, to the celestial Divinities: and to the infernal and malevolent Gods, black Victims and wild Animals. One certainly sees nothing of the kind in the Mosaic Worship. Since God dispenses Good and Evil as a Sovereign—but as a Sovereign who is just, merciful, and wise—it is to Him alone that *Moses* commanded that either expiatory Victims or sacrifices of thanksgiving be offered. The Demon <note>The author uses "the Demon" to refer to the Devil or a malevolent spiritual power.</note> is merely the Executor of the punishments or vengeances of the Almighty. However, among the Ceremonies of the solemn Feast of Propitiations <note>The Day of Atonement or Yom Kippur.</note>, there was one which, although established with entirely opposite intentions, could have provided the Slanderers of *Moses* with a pretext to accuse him of having honored two Gods, one Good and the other Evil. The Law *(a)* states expressly that one shall choose *two goats* completely alike; that they shall be presented before the Lord at the door of the Tabernacle: that *Aaron* shall cast lots to know which of the two shall be sacrificed to the True God, and which shall be sent to *Azazel* in the wilderness. *Azazel* is certainly the Demon, as *Spencer* <note>John Spencer (1630–1693) was an English theologian known for his pioneering work on the origins of Hebrew rituals.</note> has proven. Here, then, is a Victim sent to the Demon; and a Victim entirely similar to the one sacrificed to the Lord: it is not even permitted for the Priest to choose the one he thinks deserves preference; the lot must decide it. *Spencer* makes laudable efforts to show that the Ordinance of the Law was made with the view of disabusing the people of the false opinion then prevailing that there are two Gods, or two Principles. <margin>VII. No ancient Heretic believed in several Gods.</margin>
VII. From this specific Case I pass to a general Thesis, and I maintain now that no ancient Heretic ever believed in several Gods. The Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers," the influential early Christian bishops and writers who established orthodoxy.</note> who said the contrary were mistaken. To demonstrate this fact, one need only define the true God, and take the definition of *Tertullian* <note>An early Christian author from Carthage (c. 155–220 AD) known as the "father of Latin theology."</note>, which is that of common sense and Reason. The true God, the only God, is, according to us, the infinitely perfect Being, or what amounts to the same thing, (3) THE SUPREMELY GREAT BEING. If there were Heretics who believed in two *supremely Great* beings, then there would have been Heretics who believed in two Gods. But no Heretic believed in two *supremely Great* beings. Therefore, no Heretic believed in two Gods.

<margin>Marcion's View.</margin>
Marcion saw two Principles: *God* and *Matter*. He believed that God is infinitely Good; that Matter is evil, and the Cause of Evil. He held that God is not the Creator of the sublunary <note>In the ancient and medieval worldview, "sublunary" refers to the region of the universe below the moon, specifically the Earth, which was subject to change and decay.</note> world, because one does not recognize His Perfections within it. Is it at the prayer of the *Demon*, that God *sent his Son into the World*, to deliver the World from the Worship & Tyranny of *Demons*? It is true that, according to *Pamphilus* <note>Pamphilus of Caesarea (d. 309 AD), a scholar and martyr who defended the works of Origen.</note>, *Apelles* gave the Creator the name of God: but the question would be to know if he speaks the Language of *Apelles*, or that of the Church, which attributes the Creation of the World to God alone. A "made" God, a God who works for the glory of another God, & who prays him to save the World, shows clearly enough that he recognizes him as his Sovereign.

<margin>VIII. Ptolemy's System. It clarifies that of Apelles.</margin>
VIII. The System of *Ptolemy* <note>A prominent teacher of the Valentinian school of Gnosticism in the 2nd century.</note> can serve us to clarify that of *Apelles*; although they were not of the same Sect, their Theology is similar. *Ptolemy* recognized (5) "only one Prin-
" ciple, namely the *Father*, who holds his existence from himself, who
" has no Cause, nor Principle, who is the Cause & the Prin-
" ciple of all things, & on whom all things depend. It is
" thus that he speaks of God the Father. He adds, (6) that this unique
" Principle produced two Natures; one, whose Property
" is *Justice*: the other, which is (7) the *Adversary*, the *Au-
" thor of Corruption & of Death, & to use his expression, the
" CORRUPTOR GOD". God the Father is Goodness, Perfection itself: the Demon is Wickedness, & Imperfection. *Ptolemy* conceived between these two extremes, so to speak, a *middle Nature* <note>term: Nature Moyenne (Middle Nature). In Gnostic thought, the Demiurge or Creator occupies a middle ground between the perfect spiritual realm and the corrupt material realm.</note>, which has neither the Divine Perfections, nor the Imperfections of the Demon: And it is there this *God*, if one wishes to call him so, who created the World, & gave the Law.

<margin>Testimony of Hippolytus, which confirms that no Heretic believed in two Gods.</margin>
Let us remove the term *God*, which shocks us, & which obscures the Question. Let us put in its place the definition of Divinity; & one will be forced to agree, that, no Heretic having recognized two *supremely Great Beings*, no Heretic recognized *two Gods*. Their true Error was, that this *lower & corporeal World*, in which Vices & Virtues, Good & Evil, are always mixed, cannot be the work of an Almighty God,

<margin>
I. Mani was not an Anthropomorphite. Errors of L. Danaeus on the origin of this error.

I. MANI <note>Also known as Manichaeus (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism, a dualistic religion that competed with Christianity.</note>, believing God to be an extended and corporeal Light, could not avoid attributing some external form to him. The *Valentinians*, who shared the same sentiment, did not specify what this form was, contenting themselves with saying that it is worthy of the most excellent and most perfect of all natures. I do not know if our Heresiarch <note term="Heresiarch">The founder or leader of a heretical movement.</note> was bolder than the *Valentinians*, but I cannot subscribe to the opinion of a modern author who imagined that he clothed the Divine Nature in a human figure. (1) *Anthropomorphism*, <note term="Anthropomorphism">The attribution of human characteristics or form to God.</note> says this author, *was a product of the Manichaean heresy and of monastic stupidity*. There are two errors in this observation. The first is to attribute to monks the origin of an error older than the institution of monasticism. The second is to impute it to the Manichaeans, who condemned it and used it as a pretext to reject the Old Testament and to insult the simplicity of the Catholics.

<margin>
1. It does not come from the Monks: it is older than their Institution.
</margin>
The Error of the *Anthropomorphites* <note term="Anthropomorphites">From the Greek "anthropos" (human) and "morphe" (form); those who believe God has a physical body or human shape.</note> is so ancient that it would be very difficult to mark its epoch. It is true that (2) *St. Epiphanius* seems to make its author a famous Monk of Mesopotamia, named *Audius*, who flourished toward the middle of the 4th Century, and who became celebrated for having censured, with Evangelical liberty, the Luxury, Avarice, and Incontinence of the Bishops and Priests of his time. But although this Monk was an *Anthropomorphite*, his Error is nevertheless much older than he, as is seen in (3) *Origen*, and in the Author of the *Homilies* that bear the name of *St. Clement*. As this latter was an *Ebionite* <note term="Ebionite">A group of early Jewish Christians who adhered to Jewish law and often held a literal, physical view of God as described in the Hebrew Bible.</note>, I have suspected that it came from the Jews, who had embraced the Faith and who took literally the Passages of the Old Testament where God is represented with corporeal Organs. However, the simplicity of these ancient Christians did not go so far as to clothe the Divinity with a (4) *fleshly Body*. They gave him only a subtle Body, thin, similar to Light, organized like the Human Body—not by necessity, but for ornament, and because it is the most excellent of all forms. It even seems that this opinion was quite common in the East, for the Author I cite speaks of the opposite opinion as a particular sentiment, (5) belonging to some who wandered from the *Truth*. It even seems that he regards it as a Heretical sentiment, because it was that of the famous Heresiarch *Simon* <note term="Simon Magus">A sorcerer mentioned in the Acts of the Apostles, traditionally considered the first heretic who claimed divine status.</note>, against whom he disputes, and who maintained that God *is infinite*, and *that he has no external figure*. What likelihood is there, after that, that this man boasted of being God the Father, the supreme God? I have therefore conjectured that Anthropomorphism was at first very common in the Christian Church, not only among the simple Faithful, but among the Bishops, and among those of the first Order, such as *Melito*, Bishop of Sardis, who wrote in favor of this Dogma. However, it was combated shortly after: in the West by (a) *Novatian*, and in the East by *Origen*; but it did not cease to maintain itself in the Church. The *Monks*, who soon became all-powerful, took up its defense: and almost all the Solitaries of *Nitria* <note>Nitria was one of the earliest and most important Christian monastic centers in Egypt.</note>

This same Error must have been very common in Proconsular Africa <note>A Roman province in North Africa, roughly modern-day Tunisia.</note> during the time of *St. Augustine*; for he testifies in his *Confessions* that it was one of the greatest obstacles preventing him from returning to the Communion of the Church *(a)*. This leads one to judge that it is not entirely without foundation that the Manichaeans, insulting the simplicity of the Catholics, asked them (3) "Whether the Divine Essence is therefore limited by a Human Figure? [Di]vine <note>Completing the word from the previous page.</note> [Nature] from an organized Body, they did not believe it to be immense <note term="immense">In this theological context, "immense" refers to being unmeasured or omnipresent—existing everywhere without spatial limits.</note>. When they were asked (6), "Whether the true God, the Sovereign God, "is infinite; they replied, that this Question is decided by <margin>Their reasons.</margin> "that of the two contrary Substances, one good, and the other "evil. If there is no evil Substance, they said, "God is infinite: But if there is such a Substance, He cannot "be so. Now, the evil Substance exists: Therefore God is not in- "finite. This is what *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent Manichaean Bishop whom Saint Augustine famously debated.</note> replies to *St. Augustine*.

This Error was a necessary consequence of the idea they <margin>This is a result of their Principles. If the Divine Nature is extended and corporeal, it cannot be immense.</margin> held regarding the Divine Nature. God being an extended Substance, and two extended Substances being unable to occupy the same place at the same time, there would have been only God in the Universe if He had been everywhere (7). "If God is a Body, says *Gregory of Nazianzus* <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers" of the Church.</note>, "one must either "annihilate all Bodies, or suppose that one Body is within another "and penetrates it, which is altogether impossible." *St. Augustine* reasoned in the same way. (8) "Whatever the nature of "Bodies may be supposed to be, whether earthly or celestial, "airy or thick, a part "is always less than the whole, and it is absolutely impos- "sible that two Parts should be at once in a place that has only "the extent of a single one." These two Fathers claim to show <margin>Reasonings of St. Augustine and Gregory of Nazianzus incompatible with the Presence of the Body of J. Christ in the Eucharist.</margin> that the Divine Nature cannot be corporeal; and the reasonings they use on this occasion are—to mention it in passing—incompatible with the opinion of the Real Presence of the Body of Jesus Christ in the Eucharist. For, whatever Spirituality one might grant to this Body after its Resurrection, it could not be greater than that which would be attributed to the Divinity, if one supposed that it were a Body. This Body would surely be the most subtle of all Bodies. Nevertheless, *St. Gregory of Nazianzus* and *St. Augustine* maintained that if the Divinity were a Body, its Parts could not penetrate one another, nor enter into each other. Impenetrability <note term="Impenetrability">The philosophical and physical principle that two solid objects cannot occupy the same space at the same time.</note> would be a Property of its Essence, because it is a property of all Bodies.

The Manichaeans, being unable to admit the Substantial Immensity of God for the reasons I have stated, nevertheless <margin>Our Heretics give God all the Infinity possible according to their Principles.</margin> spoke of it as Holy Scripture does. It is thus that, to show—

However, it was only at the age (2) of thirty that, while in Milan, he learned from the mouth of *St. Ambrose* (b), "that the *spiritual children* whom Grace gives to the Church do not believe the Divinity to be enclosed in a Body similar to the Human Body, and do not place His Image in the shape and structure of the Body." This suggests that it is not entirely without foundation that the Manichaeans, insulting the simplicity of the Catholics, asked them (3) "Whether the Divine Essence is therefore limited by a Human Figure? Whether God has hair, nails, nostrils, and bodily organs?" This Error must have reigned among those whom *St. Augustine* calls (4) *the Carnal ones, the little children of the Church*: And one should not be surprised by this, since it was still maintained in Italy in the tenth Century, among the Priests and Monks of the Dioceses of *Verona* and *Vicenza*, as (5) *Ratherius* <note>Ratherius of Verona, a 10th-century bishop and scholar.</note> testifies.

<margin>Their reasons.</margin>
...[di]vine of an organized Body, they did not believe it to be infinite <note term="infinite/immense">The original French uses *immense*, which in 18th-century theology (from the Latin *immensus*) specifically meant "unmeasurable" or "omnipresent"—the quality of being everywhere at once.</note>. When they were asked (6), "If the true God, the Sovereign God, is infinite; they replied that this Question is decided by that of the two contrary Substances, one good, and the other evil. If there is no evil Substance, they said, God is infinite: But if there is such a Substance, He cannot be. Now, the evil Substance exists: Therefore God is not infinite." This is what *Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve, a 4th-century Manichaean bishop known for his debates with St. Augustine.</note> replies to *St. Augustine*.

<margin>This is a consequence of their Principles. If the Divine Nature is extended and corporeal, it cannot be infinite.</margin>
This Error was a necessary consequence of the idea they had of the Divine Nature. God being an extended Substance <note term="extended substance">In philosophy, "extension" refers to something that takes up physical space. The Manichaeans believed God was a physical light-substance rather than a purely spiritual being.</note>, and since two extended Substances cannot be in the same place at the same time, there would have been only God in the Universe if He had been everywhere (7). "If God is a Body," says *Gregory of Nazianzus*, "one must either annihilate all Bodies, or suppose that one Body is within another Body and penetrates it, which is altogether impossible." *St. Augustine* reasoned in the same way (8). "Of whatever nature one supposes Bodies to be, whether terrestrial or celestial, airy or thick, a part is always smaller than the whole, and it is absolutely impossible for two Parts to be at the same time in a place that has only the extension of one." These two Fathers <note>Refers to the "Church Fathers," early influential Christian theologians.</note> intend to show that the Divine Nature cannot be corporeal; and the reasonings they make on this occasion are—to mention it in passing—incompatible with the opinion of the Real Presence of the Body of *Jesus Christ* in the Eucharist <note term="Eucharist">The Christian rite of Holy Communion. The author is pointing out a logical contradiction: if the Church Fathers argue that two physical bodies cannot occupy the same space to defeat the Manichaeans, that same logic would make it impossible for Christ’s physical body to be present within the physical bread and wine.</note>. For, whatever Spirituality one might grant to this Body since its Resurrection, it could not be greater than that which one would attribute to the Divinity if one supposed that He were a Body. This Body would surely be the most subtle of all Bodies. However, *St. Gregory of Nazianzus* and *St. Augustine* maintained that, if the Divinity were a Body, its Parts could not penetrate one another, nor enter into each other. Impenetrability would be a Property of its Essence, because it is a property of all Bodies.

<margin>Reasonings of St. Augustine and Gregory of Nazianzus incompatible with the Presence of the Body of J. Christ in the Eucharist.</margin>
<margin>Our Heretics give to God all possible Infinity according to their Principles.</margin>
The *Manichaeans*, therefore, being unable to admit the Substantial Infinity of God for the reasons I have stated, they nevertheless continued to speak of it as Holy Scripture does. It is thus that, to show— <note>The catchword "trer" at the bottom of the page indicates the next word is "montrer" (to show).</note>

<margin>Eternity of this Earth.</margin>
God being eternal, and residing in a place, it follows that this place must be as eternal as He is. This is also what the Manichaeans said. *St. Augustine*, having asked *Felix* during the Dispute they had together: <margin>(a) Acts against Felix, Ch. 17, Book I.</margin> *(a) Whether God created this Luminous Earth, or if He begat it, or finally if it is eternal*, the Manichaean replied, (5) *It is coeternal with God.* <margin>Consequence that St. Augustine draws from this.</margin> He added that there are three Beings in the Empire of Light who exist by themselves, namely (6) *God the Father, the Earth He inhabits, and the Air that surrounds it.* <margin>(b) Ibid.</margin> *St. Augustine* concluded from this admission *(b)* that God the Father, the Luminous Earth, and the Air of this Earth are consubstantial <note term="consubstantial">Sharing the same fundamental essence or substance; a key term in debates about the Trinity.</note>, and *Felix*, who was a very (7) ignorant Manichaean, agreed to it.

<margin>This Father and his Antagonist both reason poorly.</margin>
We see here an example of what happens only too often in Disputes: both Antagonists reason poorly. *St. Augustine's* conclusion is based on a Proposition denied by all the Philosophers who recognized two eternal Substances, God and *Matter*, but who never believed that *Matter* and God were consubstantial. The idea of coexistence has no necessary connection with that of *Consubstantiality*. On the other hand, *Felix* grants a conclusion that was worthless and directly contrary to the Belief of his Sect, which did not extend Consubstantiality beyond the three Divine Persons.

<margin>(8) One must add to Philippe de Marnix two Modern theologians; one Catholic, namely *Augustin Steuchus*, of Gubbio, Librarian of the Vatican, famous above all for his book, *On Perennial Philosophy*. Per POTENTIAM in quantum ejus potestati subduntur."</note> "God is everywhere by **ESSENCE**, insofar as He is present to all things as the cause of being. By **PRESENCE**, insofar as all things are naked and open to His eyes. By **POWER**, insofar as they are subject to His power." These are the Scholastic views. See Zanchius, *On the Nature of God*, Book II, Chapter VI, Question 2, column 95.</margin>

**Vocabulary:** Manichaeism, Divine Immensity, Philippe de Marnix, Theodore Beza, Michael Servetus, Augustin Steuchus, Conrad Vorstius, Thomas Aquinas, Clementine Homilies, Essence, Power, Majesty

<margin>VI. Land of Darkness, or the place of Matter.</margin>

(3) "It is," he says, "a Mystery known only to Our Lord, who made all things, and who was content to call the Land of Demons THE LEFT; that of God THE RIGHT; the first THE OUTSIDE, and the second THE INSIDE." <note>original: "Quod autem loca Naturis assignari non possunt, hoc est, quod conditio Humana inenarrabile vocat atque ineffabile. It is certain that these *Members of God*, or of the *Light of God*, are a figurative expression, for Mani never attributed a human form or real limbs to the Divinity. Now, nothing is better known in the Kabbalah <note>The Kabbalah is a tradition of Jewish mysticism that seeks to understand the relationship between the eternal, mysterious Infinite and the finite universe.</note> than what are called the (1) <term>SEPHIROTH</term>, which are ten in number. Thus, the Manichaean Kabbalah and the Jewish Kabbalah agree on the substance of the mystery, and differ only on the number of the *Sephiroth*, Mani establishing twelve, and the Kabbalists ten. This difference is a small matter.

# OF MANICHAEUS. BOOK III. CH. IV.
<meta>catchword: Al-</meta>

<margin>He is accused of denying it. Why.</margin>...to strip him of such an essential attribute, because they did not believe that God had created the World from nothing <note>This refers to the doctrine of "creatio ex nihilo," or creation out of nothing, which became a standard orthodox belief.</note>. They were wrong, but others were also wrong to attribute to them a consequence that they themselves disavowed.

<margin>Conditions necessary to base such an accusation.</margin>Before accusing someone of denying *Divine Omnipotence*, one must first fix the idea of it, and then determine what can be the Object of this Power. I say that one must first fix the idea of it. For example, *Hermogenes* <note>Hermogenes was a late 2nd-century teacher who argued that God created the world from eternal matter, as he couldn't reconcile God's goodness with the creation of evil from nothing.</note> defined the *Almighty* (4) as he who has dominion over all things. And, this definition having been established, he maintained that the Catholics <note>In this historical context, "Catholics" refers to the "universal" or orthodox church of the time, as opposed to "heretical" sects.</note> denied the *Omnipotence of God*, because if an eternal Nothingness preceded the Creation of the World, God was for an entire eternity without Dominion. Does one call a King "Almighty" if he has no Subjects? The reasoning of *Hermogenes* is based on the specific notion of the Greek word <term>PANTOCRATOR</term> <note>original: "Pantocrator". From the Greek "pas" (all) and "kratos" (power/rule), often translated as "Almighty" or "Ruler of All."</note>, which is translated as *Almighty*.

<margin>1. Defining the idea of Omnipotence. Ambiguity of this word.</margin>

<margin>It provides grounds to accuse the Orthodox of denying Omnipotence.</margin>*Origen* <note>A prolific early Christian scholar (c. 184–253 AD) whose views on the soul and the universe were later controversial.</note>, who was no small Genius, reasoned on the same Principle. He supposed an eternal Succession of Worlds, created and then destroyed, because without this, God would only have been *Almighty* for five or six thousand years. Whether *Origen* and *Hermogenes* reasoned well or poorly is not what I am examining. I say only that the accusation brought against the Catholics of denying *Omnipotence* was based on a misunderstanding, because, in the idea of the Catholics, *Omnipotence is an absolute Attribute*. It is in God the Power to do all that he wills, all that is in conformity with his Perfections. Whereas in the idea of *Origen*, and according to the notion of the Greek term *Pantocrator*, *Omnipotence is a relative Attribute*, which only began to exist with the World. One must not conclude from this that there are *accidents* <note>In philosophy, an "accident" is a property that a thing can lose without ceasing to be itself; the author argues that being a Creator didn't change God's fundamental nature.</note> in God, because the Creation of the World adds nothing to his Essence, and is only the exercise of his Perfections—an exercise which depends on his Will.

<margin>2. Determining what is possible.</margin>I said in the second place that to accuse someone of denying *Divine Omnipotence*, one must determine what can be the object of this Power, which is to say, what is possible. It is for lack of paying attention to this Rule that people are accused every day of denying *Omnipotence*, because they maintain that God cannot make one and the same thing be both one and many, absent and present, extended and without extension—in a word, that it *be* and *not be*, in the same respects and at the same time. Even if these people were wrong, one would be ill-founded in accusing them of denying *Omnipotence*.

<margin>The Error of the Manichaeans is not in having denied Omnipotence, but in having believed that Creation from nothing is outside the realm of possible things.</margin>
...Divine power, which they acknowledge: Their entire Error would consist in placing among impossible things something which is not so; in finding a contradiction where there is none. This was precisely the Error of the Manichaeans <note>A major religious movement founded by the Persian prophet Mani, which taught a dualistic struggle between a good spiritual world of light and an evil material world of darkness.</note>. We believe that *Creation from nothing* <note>In Latin, *creatio ex nihilo*. This is the theological doctrine that God created the universe out of nothing, rather than from pre-existing matter.</note> is possible: that is to say, we believe that God can bring into existence <term>Substances</term> <note>In this context, the fundamental "stuff" or essence of a thing, rather than its mere attributes.</note> which did not exist: that He has not only the power to create <term>Modes</term> <note>The specific qualities or "ways of being" of a substance, such as its shape or color.</note> within a Substance, but that He can create the Substance itself. Unfortunately, the Manichaeans were biased in favor of the general Error that had always reigned in the World; that is, that *Creation from nothing is outside the realm of possible things*. And having once established this Principle, they did not believe they were stripping God of a real power by denying that He could make something from nothing, because the Impossible is not an object of Power. This is the Cause of their error. But otherwise, the *Omnipotence* of God was an Article of their belief.

<margin>IX. Simplicity is Essential to God.</margin>
IX. *Simplicity is a Perfection essential to the Divine Nature, because it is linked with His Independence, with His Bliss, & with His Immortality.* With His *Independence*, because every composite Being depends on the one who composed it, since nothing can compose or make itself: With His *Bliss*, because every assembly, every mixture of Parts that are of different or contrary natures, being a forced mixture, the Composite could not be at peace. With His *Immortality* for the same reason. Beings joined together by an external Power naturally tend to separate, & can always be separated by the Power that united them. I add that no composite Being can be eternal, because the Substances which compose it must necessarily exist before it. It is for this reason that Theologians maintain that Simplicity is a Property of the Divine Essence. Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the most influential theologians in early Christianity, often called "The Theologian."</note> was well aware of this truth, and alleged several reasons for it in these words, (1) "The First Nature is simple, and exempt from all mixture, because Simplicity is tranquil and peaceful, and is not susceptible to discord: Whereas Composition is the origin of Division, and Division the origin of Dissolution."

<margin>The Manichaeans recognized it.</margin>
Although Manichaeus conceived of the Divinity as an *extended Light*, he nevertheless preserved His *Simplicity*. (2) *The Nature of Light is* ONE AND SIMPLE, says this Heresiarch <note>The founder or leader of a heretical sect.</note>. And elsewhere, *God is* (3) *a* SIMPLE NATURE & *immortal*: And again, (4) *The Essence of Light is* PURE AND SIMPLE.

...[SIM]PLE. If one objects to such formal declarations that *Extension* <note>The quality of taking up space or having physical dimensions.</note> and *Simplicity* <note>In theology, Divine Simplicity is the idea that God is not "made" of different parts or substances, but is a single, indivisible essence.</note> are incompatible, we would respond first that all the Church Fathers <note>The influential early Christian theologians whose writings formed the basis of orthodox doctrine.</note> who believed that the Divine Essence is corporeal <note>Physical or having a body.</note> did not see this consequence, or they denied it. Second, that very skilled modern Metaphysicians deny it as well as they did. <margin>(a) Where mentioned above, p. 246.</margin> *Infinite extension*, says Mr. *(a)* Clarke <note>Samuel Clarke (1675–1729), an English philosopher and clergyman who debated Leibniz and defended the compatibility of Newtonian physics with theology.</note>, *is not at all incompatible with Spirituality and Simplicity*. We will respond in the third place that, even assuming God is a Composite of Parts of Light—as everything in Him is Light, perfectly pure Light, free from all mixture, and existing by itself—this Composition is not subject to any of the inconveniences just mentioned. These are not foreign Parts of different natures brought together by a Superior Power. No Power has united them; no Power can divide them. Their union is as necessary and as eternal as their existence. This is how Manichaeus <note>Also known as Mani, the 3rd-century Persian founder of Manichaeism.</note> might have conceived of things, and it is undoubtedly how the Fathers who believed God to be corporeal conceived of them. Let us confirm what I say with a passage from Plato. <margin>(b) On the Republic, Book X, p. m. 516.</margin> He believed the Soul to be immortal *(b)*, and proved it with very fine reasoning. He believed it to be *simple*, since he believed it to be immortal; but the *Simplicity* he attributed to it meant that it was composed only of parts of the same nature, without any mixture of foreign parts *(5)*. "We do not believe," *he says*, "that the Soul is an assembly of parts of different natures; for that which is composed in such a way could hardly be immortal. It must have received as its portion the most excellent composition."

X. Indivisibility is a consequence of Simplicity, and Manichaeus, by maintaining that the Divine Nature is *simple and immortal*, maintained at the same time that it is *indivisible*. <margin>X. They likewise believed God to be indivisible. (c) See above, p. 486, 487.</margin> Thus he called it *(c)* UNITY, or MONAD <note>From the Greek *monas*, meaning "unit" or "one"; a term used by Pythagoreans and Platonists to describe the ultimate, indivisible source of all things.</note>, par excellence, just as he called *Matter* DUALITY, or DYAD <note>From the Greek *duas*, meaning "two"; representing division, change, and the material world.</note>, because it is not only divisible, but the Parts that compose it are of opposite natures and maintain a perpetual Division therein. He thought of the Nature of God like *Plato*, who usually calls Him *indivisible and the same* <note>original Greek: "ἀμέριστος & ταὐτὸ"</note>, that is to say, *a Nature that cannot be divided*, and *which is always the same.* <note>original Latin: "Individua & Idem."</note>

XI. St. Augustine *(d)* constantly reproaches the Manichaeans for attributing to God the most shameful imperfections, most unworthy of Divinity—namely, those of being susceptible to sins and miseries, and of being PASSIBLE, VIOLABLE, and CORRUPTIBLE. <margin>XI. And impassible. (d) See among others *Confessions*, Book VII, 2. This is St. Augustine’s great argument against the Manichaeans. It recurs everywhere.</margin>

<margin>XII. The Manichaeans recognize the Moral Perfections of the Divinity.</margin>
XII. Regarding Moral Perfections, it would be too obvious a slander to accuse our Heretics of having stripped them from the true God. If they erred in this regard, it was by extending the activity of these Perfections too far; which, though they are infinite in themselves, limit themselves in their exercise, and only deploy as much as the Wisdom of God permits or ordains. His Justice, for example, sets limits to His Mercy, just as His Prudence sets limits to His Power.

<margin>Goodness.</margin>
The Manichaeans thus recognized an infinite GOODNESS in God: Not only did they subscribe to these words of the Lord, <margin>(a) Matt. 19:17. Mark 10:18. An infinitely *Good* Being, they said, can neither do evil, nor will it, nor voluntarily permit it: from which they concluded that there is an evil Nature, which is the necessary Cause of Evils. Thus, the Goodness of God was a trap for them, because they extended its action to the detriment of the Order that the Wisdom of God established in the Government of Intelligent Beings.

...the word *Father* was then present in one of the Evangelists, (1) or that Tertullian, Origen, and Clement of Alexandria did not doubt that Jesus Christ had spoken of his Father.

I have occasionally stated my opinion on a Passage that has excited Controversies among Critics because of the influence it seems to have on Dogma. I return to *Manichaeus*: <margin>Recognized Mercy.</margin> Recognizing Divine *Goodness*, he also recognized *Mercy* or *Clemency*, which is nothing other than *Goodness* insofar as it is exercised upon Sinners and the miserable. He likewise recognized the <margin>Holiness.</margin> *Holiness* of God, whom he calls (2) *the Holy Father*, and whom he (3) *says has an infinite aversion to Iniquity*. (4) *The Divine Substance*, says Fortunatus <note>Fortunatus was a Manichaean elder who famously debated St. Augustine in 392 AD.</note>, *is Holy and without any stain*. This is very just, but one should not have concluded from it—as these profane Heretics dared to do—that the true God is not the one who revealed himself to the Jews. The *Book of Faustus* <note>Faustus of Mileve was a high-ranking Manichaean teacher; his works are known primarily through Augustine's refutation, *Against Faustus*.</note> is filled with blasphemies against the Law under the pretext that several Ordinances seem to him to derogate from the Holiness of God.

<margin>And vindictive Justice.</margin> Although the Manichaeans infinitely exalted His *Goodness*, they did not go so far as to strip Him of His *Justice*, without which Human Malice would soon break all the bonds of Religion. They confessed, therefore, not only that God is *Just*, but that He is (5) *Justice itself* and (6) *the almighty Judge of the world*: (7) *That He is the Author only of Good, but that He is also the just avenger of evils*, (8) *and that He punishes the crimes of the wicked*. They maintained a final Judgment after which Matter and the Demons will be cast into the fire that is never quenched, and the Souls who have not profited from the Grace of the Liberator will be rigorously punished.

These are the ideas the Manichaeans held regarding the Divine Attributes. They are not free from errors, but they are far from being what people are accustomed to representing them as. I have shown them no favor <note>The author suggests he has been a rigorous and impartial historian, neither shielding the Manichaeans from their errors nor inventing new ones for them.</note>. The Reader may be convinced of this by the Passages I have taken care to place in the margin in the Original.

(1) I have no doubt that this latter sentiment is the most true. The word *Father* was not originally in any of the Evangelists, and if it was in the copy of the Gospel according to St. Luke used by Marcion <note>Marcion was a 2nd-century figure who rejected the Old Testament and edited the New Testament to fit his theology; he was often grouped with Manichaeans by later writers.</note>, it had been added. I base this on the testimony of Origen, *Commentary on Matthew*, Vol. XV, p. 376. At that time, one read in that Evangelist only these words, *There is only one who is Good*; but one read in St. Mark and St. Luke, *There is only one who is Good, namely God*. Ibid. p. 379, <note>original Greek: "ὁ δὲ Μάρκος καὶ Λουκᾶς, ... οὐδεὶς ἀγαθὸς εἰ μὴ εἷς, ὁ Θεός."</note> *But Mark and Luke [say] ... none is good but one, that is, God.* Thus the word *Father* was truly added as an explanation, the Ancients having no doubt that Jesus Christ intended to speak of His Father. See *Clement of Alexandria, The Instructor*, Book I, 8. *Origen on Matthew*, cited above. *Justin Martyr*, p. 49. *Epiphanius*, cited above, p. 339. *Novatian, On the Trinity*, Chapter IV, etc. Moreover, this does not exclude the Son of God. *The Father is the only one Good by Himself*, just as He has the Divine Essence by Himself; the Son holds from Him both the Essence and the Perfections of the Essence.

ON MANICHAEUS. BOOK III. CH. V.

### C H A P T E R. V.

->*The Manichaeans confessed the* TRINITY, *and the* CONSUBSTANTIALITY <note>Consubstantiality refers to the doctrine that the persons of the Trinity are of the same "substance" or essence.</note> *of the Divine Persons.*<-

<margin>The Manichaeans recognize THE TRINITY and CONSUBSTANTIALITY. Accused by Socrates of denying the Personality of the Word, which does not seem just.</margin>
**I.** It has just been seen that the Manichaeans were not as heretical as one might think on the Article of the Divine Attributes. One will not be sorry to find them Orthodox, or nearly so, on that of the *Trinity*. It is true that (1) Socrates <note>Socrates Scholasticus (c. 380–439 AD) was a Greek Christian church historian.</note> accuses them of denying the *Personality of the Word* <note>original: "Perfonnalité du Verbe"</note>. But, if this accusation is just, it can only concern some Manichaean Sect that is unknown to us, or it is based on the fact that they conceived the Generation of the Son as an extension of the Substance of the Father. The divine Essence is not divided: It only extends and communicates itself; this is contrary to what the Arians <note>Arians believed that Jesus Christ was a created being, subordinate to God the Father, rather than being of the same substance.</note> say, but we shall see in the sequel that their testimony on this point is highly suspect. However it may be, there are too many proofs that the Manichaeans believed in the Trinity of Divine Persons for us to even suspect them of the contrary. (2) *We serve*, says *Faustus*, *ONE AND THE SAME DIVINITY, under the three names of* FATHER *almighty, of* J. CHRIST HIS SON, *and of the* HOLY SPIRIT. <margin>Confession of Faustus.</margin> This Confession includes both the Trinity of Persons and the Unity of Nature. For it must not be imagined that *Faustus* affected to express himself in terms that hid Sabellianism <note>Sabellianism was a "modalist" heresy that viewed the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit as different roles or modes of a single person, rather than three distinct persons.</note>. St. *Augustine* did not even suspect him of this artifice. Furthermore, far from confounding the Persons, the Heretic considers them as three Majesties, and assigns to each their place in the Universe. St. *Augustine* bears witness to Fortunatus (3), <margin>Admission of St. Augustine.</margin> *that they both held the same belief concerning the Trinity of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.*

<margin>Other testimonies from the same source.</margin>
Since this Article is important, it is well to prove it by incontestable authorities. (1). **You confess**, Saint Augustine says further to the Manichaeans, **that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are united in a nature that is entirely similar.** Never, he says (2) elsewhere, have the Manichaeans dared to deny that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are **of the same substance**. 

<margin>From Photius.</margin>
Photius <note>Photius I (c. 810–893 AD) was the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople and a central figure in the history of the Byzantine Church.</note> confirms these testimonies. (3) **They confess**, he says, **three consubstantial Persons, and of the same Nature, and confess at the same time, one single God, and one single Divinity.** 

<margin>From St. Epiphanius concerning Hierax.</margin>
Saint Epiphanius <note>A 4th-century bishop known for his attacks on various Christian heresies.</note> assures us that Hierax, or Hieracas, one of the twelve first disciples of Manichaeus, (4) "did not fall into the Error" of Origen <note>Origen was a 3rd-century theologian whose views on the hierarchical relationship between the Father and the Son were later criticized.</note> regarding the production of the Son, and that he believed that the Father "truly begot the Son."

<margin>From Photius concerning Agapius.</margin>
(5) Agapius, another disciple of Manichaeus, declares, says Photius, that he confesses **the consubstantial Trinity**. 

<margin>From Facundus of Hermiane.</margin>
I find in Facundus of Hermiane <note>A 6th-century African bishop who participated in the "Three Chapters" controversy.</note> a testimony very advantageous to the Manichaeans on this Article. This African Bishop, wishing to justify Theodore of Mopsuestia <note>A prominent 4th/5th-century theologian whose work became controversial long after his death.</note>, says (6) that he should not be labeled a Manichaean under the pretext that he confesses that the Lord Jesus is **the God Word**, that he is **the Son of God by his own Substance**, and that from before all ages he eternally draws his existence from God the Father. This was therefore consistently the Faith of the Manichaeans, if one excepts perhaps the eternity of the Generation of the Son, on which there may be some doubt.

<margin>II. The Manichaeans led to Consubstantiality by their Principles.</margin>
II. There are Errors which have at least the advantage of being a Preservative against others. All the Heretics who believed in two eternal Substances could not fall into Spinozism <note>The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, which identifies God with the physical universe (pantheism).</note>. Their Error guaranteed them against it. Likewise, those who believed in the eternity of Matter could not be Arians <note>Followers of Arius who believed the Son was a created being made "out of nothing."</note>. Their Principle led them naturally to Consubstantiality. For, assuming on one hand that nothing can be made from nothing—which obliged them to maintain the eternity of Matter—they could not agree with the Arians that the Son of God was drawn from Nothingness. And assuming, on the other hand, that Matter is evil in itself and the cause of all evils, they could not say that the Son of God, who is Holiness and Perfection itself, drew his origin from it. They

<meta>This page continues the exploration of Manichaean Christology, specifically their adherence to the doctrine of consubstantiality—the idea that the Son and Holy Spirit share the same divine essence as the Father. ### OF MANICHAEUS BOOK III. CH. V.

They therefore embraced the System of Divine Emanations, which was apparently that of the Orientals, and believed that the Son and the Holy Spirit came forth from the substance of the Father. They conceived of many other Emanations, but these were incomparably less perfect, as God the Father had communicated His very Substance and all His Perfections only to the two Persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit. The Revelation of the New Testament confirmed them in these ideas, or directed them toward them. This is, if I am not mistaken, the true reason why the *Basilidians*, the *Valentinians*, and the *Manichaeans*—who in other respects held so many Heresies—found themselves Orthodox on the Article of the Trinity and of Consubstantiality <note>The doctrine, central to the Nicene Creed, that the three persons of the Trinity are of the same "substance" or essence.</note>.

<margin>III. Critique of *Victor of Vita*, who accuses the Manichaeans of having been Arians.</margin>
III. Since the Manichaeans had thus preserved the Faith of Consubstantiality, I do not know what to think of the account of *Victor of Vita* <note>A 5th-century bishop of Vita in North Africa, known for his history of the Vandal persecutions.</note>. This Writer asserts, in his (7) *History of the Vandal Persecution*, that *Hunneric* <note>King of the Vandals (reigned 477–484), who was a fervent Arian and persecuted both Catholics and Manichaeans.</note> found the Manichaeans of Africa to be in the same Heresy as himself regarding the Person of Jesus Christ. How can we reconcile this testimony with those of *St. Augustine*, who had died only a few years earlier? *Hunneric* was an Arian, and the Arians held hypotheses entirely opposite to those of the Manichaeans. They even made a point of publishing in their Writings that the sentiment of the Orthodox, regarding the Generation of the Son of God, was nothing but pure Valentinianism or Manichaeism, as (b) *St. Athanasius*, *St. Hilary*, and *St. Epiphanius* testify. *Victor* adds, (8) "that this 
<margin>(a) Athan. de Synod. p. m. 652. Hilar. de Trin. L. VI. Col. m. 25. Epiph. Her. LXIX. n. 7.</margin>
conformity of Errors brought shame upon *Hunneric*, and that, to acquire the reputation of a Religious Prince, he persecuted the Manichaeans with even more violence than the Catholics: that he 
burned several of them; that he drove away a great number, and 
that this proceeding did him much honor." The Spirit of persecution must have been very deeply rooted in the Clerics already, since they offered praise for it at the very time they were suffering from it. For the rest, I suspect that *Victor of Vita* confused Arianism with the subordination and dependence of the Persons of the Son and the Holy Spirit in relation to the Father. To this must perhaps be added the opinion of which I am about to speak, which at its core was not Arian at all.

<margin>IV. It is uncertain if the Manichaeans believed the Generation of the Word to be eternal.</margin>
IV. It is quite a difficult Problem to decide whether the Manichaeans believed that the Word has an eternal Hypostasis <note>A technical theological term referring to the distinct "person" or individual existence of the Word/Son within the Trinity.</note>, or if He only began—

I do not share the opinion of this learned Jesuit. First, it would be dangerous to admit that the Fathers borrowed a Dogma of this importance from Pagan poets or philosophers. One may certainly cite them when one wishes to show that the most abstract Truths of the Christian Religion were not entirely unknown to the Pagans, but one would make them very suspect by admitting they were taken from them. Second, it is certain that the Ancients based themselves on the History of the Creation, as seen in the Passage from *Tertullian* (7) that I cite at the bottom of the page. As long as God does nothing more than conceive within himself the Plan of the Universe, the Word remains in God the Father: he does not come out, and does not become a Hypostasis <term>hypostasis: a Greek theological term for a distinct, individual personhood within the Trinity</term>, until God sets his hand to the work, and requires a Minister to execute his designs. The first verse of *the Gospel according to St. John* also seemed to favor this opinion. *In the beginning was the Word, the Word was with God, and the Word was God. He was in the beginning with God:* they believed they found in these Words that in the beginning, and before God undertook to create the World, the Word—

Second Observation on the words of M. du Pin. This skilled man (2) was mistaken in attributing to the Ancients <note>The "Ancients" refers to the early Church Fathers of the first few centuries.</note> the belief that the *Word, before he had taken flesh, did not perfectly possess the quality of the Word, so that one could say then that he was begotten of the Father.* M. du Pin has confused the qualities of WORD and of SON OF GOD. <margin>V. The Generation of the Word in time was the result of another opinion, namely that the Generation of the Word is an act of the Father's will.</margin>
V. This opinion, so common among the ancient Theologians regarding the timing of the Generation of the Word, was a consequence of another view, stubbornly defended by the Arians <note>Followers of Arius, who held that Jesus Christ was a created being, not co-eternal with God the Father.</note>. This view is that this production is a free operation of the Will of the Father. This sentiment was not correct, but it was not new. I say it was not correct because, as the Divine Essence exists necessarily, it exists by the same necessity in three Persons. Otherwise, there would be no impossibility that the Son and the Holy Spirit might never have had existence, or a real <term>hypostasis</term> <gloss>a technical term for an individual person or distinct substance within the Trinity</gloss>. <margin>VII. Clarification of a calumny by *Euthymius Zigabene* against the *Bogomils*.</margin>
VII. This Question of the Primogeniture <term>Primogeniture: The status of being the first-born. In this theological context, it refers to the debate over whether Christ was the first of God's creations or an eternal being.</term> of the Word provides me a very natural opportunity to clarify and dispel, in passing, an atrocious calumny <note>calumny: A false and malicious statement intended to damage someone's reputation.</note> by the Monk *Euthymius Zigabene* against that Sect called the *Bogomils*, whom the Greeks confuse with the Manichaeans. *Euthymius* accuses them of believing (1) that *Satan not only existed before the Word, but that being older than the Word he* **IS GREATER AND MORE EXCELLENT THAN HIM**. This is certainly a horrible blasphemy, but I dare to assert that it is also a horrible calumny. A Christian Sect—a Sect where people gave themselves to the flames rather than bow the knee before an Image or a Cross—would such a sect make a profession of believing that **SATAN IS GREATER AND MORE EXCELLENT THAN THE SON OF GOD**? However, the man who says so is famous, (2) an Author of esteemed Writings, a Saint of the modern Greeks, a Witness who knew the *Bogomils*, who conferred with a certain *Basil* who was then Head of the Sect, and who perhaps contributed to having him burned alive. Let us uncover the origin, or the pretext, of so dark a calumny; and let us remember once and for all that those who had Heretics burned inherited no less from the Demon the *Spirit of Lying* than the *Spirit of murder and cruelty*.

<margin>Origin and pretext of this calumny.</margin>
One finds, in very Catholic Authors, two very ancient opinions. The first, that the Word did not begin to have his own Hypostasis <term>Hypostasis: A technical term in theology referring to a distinct person or individual existence within the Trinity.</term> until immediately before the Creation of the World. The second, that the Demon is the first of the Intelligences that God created, and over whom he had reigned in Heaven for an infinite number of ages before forming the visible World.

<margin>The Christians divided on the Question of how J. Christ is the Son of God.</margin>
Two reasons oblige me to enter into this discussion. The first is a reason of Equity. We must treat Heretics as we would wish them to treat us, and as we ourselves treat many ancient Doctors. We say, to excuse them, that they lived in times when the difficult matters of Religion were not yet well developed. In terms of the accuracy of ideas and reasoning, they are but the Children of those who honor them as Fathers. What happened to them is what happens to People who find themselves at the birth of Sciences and Arts: their masterpieces are but Rough Sketches to their Posterity. As long as they were Orthodox on the core of the Mystery, we forgive them all the faults they made in the manner of explaining it. This is how charity demands we act toward Men. But if the Rule is good, it must be general. An equitable Man has no double standard: one for his friends, and another for his Enemies. Thus, when I examine the sentiments or the Errors of Heretics, my entire focus is to keep my Judgment

<margin>2. Reason. This Discussion overturns the sophism of the VARIATIONS by the Bishop of Meaux.</margin>
The second reason is self-interested, I admit; but my interest is solely that of Truth and sound Reasoning. Everyone knows the book *The Variations* by the late Bishop of *Meaux* <note>Jacques-Bénigne Bossuet (1627–1704), a prominent French bishop and theologian who famously attacked Protestantism for its internal disagreements.</note>, one of the finest minds of his century, but also one of the greatest declaimers and sophists of our time. He composed this work with the view of overturning the Reformation of Faith and Worship, under the pretext that those who undertook it were not uniform, nor always constant in their sentiments. To strike down this Machine, built with so much artifice and labor against a Reformation whose necessity is evident, one need only recall the variety of opinions among the Ancients on the Question of **HOW JESUS CHRIST IS THE SON OF GOD**. Certainly, if there had been *Bossuets* among the Pagans, and if they had attacked Christianity by the method of *Variations*, they would either have triumphed over it, or this method is nothing but a sophism, invented to surprise the simple-minded and to elude the discussion of Dogmas.

<margin>Confirmation of this proof.</margin>
The defenders of the Bishop of *Meaux*'s sophism will perhaps think to answer me that the *Variations* of the Ancients on the Question at hand should not be imputed to the Church, but to the Heretics, from which it follows that they do no harm to the Authority or the Faith of the Church. I agree that they do no harm to the Truth, which is always independent of Human Opinions, but I maintain that the parallel is just, and that if the argument of the Bishop of *Meaux* is worth anything against the Reformation, it has the same force against Christianity. For 1. It is false that the *Variations* were only among Heretics, since the Fathers—whom one would not dare place in that rank and who were the lights of the primitive Church—did not agree at all on the Article in question, and agree even less with the Decisions of the Oecumenical Councils <term>Oecumenical Councils: Large-scale gatherings of bishops from across the Christian world intended to settle matters of doctrine.</term>, or with those of the modern Scholastics <term>Scholastics: Medieval theologians who used formal logic and philosophy to define Christian doctrines.</term>. 2. Christians emerged either from Judaism or from Paganism, just as the Protestants emerged from the Roman Church. If the Bishop of *Meaux*'s method against the Protestants is good, then it would have been good against the first Christians; and Unbelievers in general, both Jews and Pagans, would have been well-founded in rejecting Christianity without examination, for the reason that those who professed it were divided on the fundamental Article of this Religion—on the Question: **HOW JESUS CHRIST IS THE SON OF GOD**. I believed these Reflections were necessary to explain to the Reader the reason for the discussion into which I am about to enter.

<summary>The author critiques Bishop Bossuet's argument against the Reformation, pointing out that early Christian Fathers also held diverse and conflicting views on Christ's divinity. He argues that theological variation does not invalidate a religious movement, otherwise early Christianity would have been equally vulnerable to such logic.</summary>

### C H A P T E R VI.

*The Church Fathers could not avoid explaining* HOW JESUS CHRIST IS THE SON OF GOD; *hence a prodigious variety of sentiments. Reflections on the number of Bishops at the Council of Nicaea, and on the different Sects found there.*

<margin>
1. That it was impossible for the Fathers not to examine HOW J. Christ is the Son of God.
</margin>
I. When one considers the dreadful Schism <note>The Arian controversy, which divided the Christian world over whether Christ was of the same substance as God the Father.</note> that tore the Church apart at the beginning of the 4th century, one might wish that the Fathers had been content to simply confess that *Jesus Christ is the Son of God*, without explaining the manner in which he is so. Had they agreed on the proposition itself, they might not have been divided over the meaning that should be given to it. But it was not possible to stop there, for the following reasons. 1. One must have some idea of a Dogma <term>Dogma: an official system of principles or tenets concerning faith.</term> that one believes and confesses, since Faith does not have words as its object, but rather the things signified by those words.

<margin>
Reasons.
1. Faith had to be enlightened.
</margin>

<margin>
2. To exclude Error.
</margin>
2. This Proposition, *Jesus is the Son of God*, being susceptible to various meanings, and indeed explained quite differently by many, one could not avoid determining its true significance, or at least excluding the false meanings that were insulting to God, to Reason, and to Faith.

<margin>
3. To respond to the Pagans.
</margin>
3. It was impossible to preach to the Pagans <note>Non-Christians, specifically those practicing the polytheistic religions of the Roman Empire.</note> that *Jesus Christ is the Son of God* without them immediately asking by what right the Christians criticized their own Theology regarding the "Generation of the Gods" while they themselves taught that God has a Son. It was therefore necessary to explain How *Jesus Christ is the Son of God*, and to show the Gentiles that Christian Theology had, on this point, no conformity with their fables.

<margin>
4. To show them that this idea did not come from them.
(a) See Origen, *Against Celsus*, Book VI, p. 308.
</margin>
4. The Fathers were forced by the objections of the Infidels <note>Non-believers; in this context, the pagan critics of Christianity.</note> to resort to explanations. For example, since Pagan authors had said that the *World is the Son of God*, and had made it equal to God, Celsus <gloss>(a)</gloss> <note>Celsus was a 2nd-century Greek philosopher and fierce opponent of early Christianity.</note> took the opportunity to accuse the Christians of having applied to their Jesus what these authors had said of the World. Nothing was more poorly founded than the conjecture of this Epicurean philosopher. Origen <note>A prominent early Christian scholar and theologian from Alexandria.</note> replied to him that if he wanted to find the origin of the Christian Faith among the Pagans, he would have done better to seek it in the Letters of Plato, where that philosopher speaks of a *Son of God* who is not the World, but the Creator of the World, and who has as his Father <gloss>(1)</gloss> *the first God, the Sovereign God, the one who is above all things*. How could one avoid, on such an occasion, showing the differences that exist...

<margin>3. The Doctors felt themselves obliged to delve into the Mysteries.</margin>
Beyond these reasons of necessity, there were others of Propriety—or shall I say, of religious curiosity. The ancient Fathers believed themselves obliged to know and to delve into the mysteries of Christianity. Persuaded that Knowledge <term>Knowledge: translating the French 'Science,' which in this context refers to systematic theological understanding rather than modern natural science.</term>, but especially that of Divine things, is the perfection of the Spirit, they were careful not to limit themselves to the simple faith of Dogmas. Such credulity was excusable only in the Common Folk, for whom it is appropriate to believe, just as it is for the Artisan to work, without knowing the reasons for his Art. <margin>(a) Philocal. Chap. I. p. 11.</margin> (a) "Souls," says Origen, "being unable to acquire the perfection proper to them except through the Knowledge of Divine things, their first and principal Object are those things which concern the Person of God the Father. Next come those which touch upon His only Son, namely, (1) WHAT IS HIS NATURE? IN WHAT MANNER IS HE THE SON OF GOD? *Why did He humble Himself so far as to take on human flesh, and to become Man?*" etc. This, then, was the study and, if I dare say so, the ambition of the true <term>Gnostic: here used in the early sense of a 'Christian intellectual' or one who seeks deep spiritual knowledge, rather than the later heretical sects.</term>. It is this which raised to the rank of THEOLOGIAN men like Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Gregory of Nyssa. They considered Religion just as the Philosophers had considered Nature, and aspired to the happiness of delving into its Mysteries: but unfortunately, it did not go for the Theologians as it did for the Philosophers. The latter maintained peace despite the diversity of their opinions, whereas the former reciprocally anathematized <note>original: "s'anathématiſérent" — to formally curse or excommunicate those with differing views.</note> one another.

<margin>Precept of Petau on this subject, later retracted by himself.</margin>
Modern Doctors have prided themselves on imitating the Ancients. Father Petau <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit theologian known for his work on the history of dogma.</note>, following in their footsteps in this regard, opens a free path to the curiosity of the Human Spirit. I would approve of the maxim of this learned man, if it were not necessary at every moment to bring to it

<margin>II. Surprising variety of opinions on the Question: *How J. Christ is the Son of God.*</margin>
II. It was therefore necessary to explain *How J. Christ is the Son of God*; but it was very difficult for the explanations to be uniform. Among this great multitude of Bishops and Priests dispersed both outside and inside the Empire, it was almost impossible that there should not be a great variety of Opinions. Thus, when the Council of Nicaea <note>The First Council of Nicaea (325 AD) was the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church, called by Emperor Constantine to resolve the Arian controversy regarding the relationship between God the Father and the Son.</note> was assembled to decide the Arian Controversies, CONSTANTINE (3), who wished to hear the Bishops reason and dispute on this matter, was greatly astonished to find so little unanimity among the Doctors, who all gloried in the name of Christians. Eutychius <note>Eutychius of Alexandria, a 10th-century Melkite Patriarch and historian.</note> speaks of *two thousand forty-eight Bishops* (4) *who were, he says, of* DIFFERENT SENTIMENTS, AND OF DIFFERENT RELIGIONS. This great number of Bishops surprises almost as much as their dissensions. The Greeks and Latins, who record the most, count only *three hundred and eighteen*. A word of reflection on this last number will not displease the Reader; these are small points of Ecclesiastical History that serve greatly to make known the character of the Authors.

<margin>III. Reflection on the number of Bishops at the Council of Nicaea. Variation of the most ancient Writers thereupon.</margin>

Finally, *Eutychius* is not essentially at odds with the Greeks. He merely informs us of memorable circumstances that the latter omitted. He counts *two thousand forty-eight Bishops* because he includes in this number both Catholics and Sectarians, whereas the Greeks count among the Fathers of the Council only those who were, or appeared to be, Orthodox, and who signed the Decisions.

V. Let us now examine who these Sectarians were. The first were the (1) MARIAMITES. *They affirmed*, says the Patriarch of Alexandria, *that there are two Gods besides* THE SOVEREIGN GOD, *namely*, CHRIST AND HIS MOTHER. They were Barbarians, whom they named MARIAMITES. I am much mistaken if this account is not a pure fiction, the origin of which is as follows. We know that the word ROUAH (2), which means SPIRIT, is feminine in the Hebrew language, which gave cause for the Nazarenes <note>A group of early Jewish Christians who maintained the practice of the Mosaic Law alongside belief in Christ.</note> to call the Holy Spirit the *Mother of the Savior*. In their Gospel, one read: *THE HOLY SPIRIT, who is MY MOTHER, has just seized me.* This is also what led St. *Epiphanius* to say that the Nazarenes (3) "represented the Holy Spirit under the figure of a woman, but an invisible one." Thus, it is not the Virgin *Mary* that these alleged Heretics placed, with Christ, among the Divine Persons—saving the superiority they reserved for the Father as the SUPREME GOD—it is the HOLY SPIRIT. ### OF MANICHAEISM BOOK III, CH. VI.

<margin>IX. The concept of Sabellianism.</margin>
IX. This is the origin of Sabellianism: here is its nature. *Sabellius* conceived of only one Person in God, of whom the *Word* <note>The "Word" or *Logos* is a theological term for the second person of the Trinity, Jesus Christ.</note> is the *Reason* and *Wisdom*, and of whom the *Holy Spirit* is the *Virtue* or Power. Neither the *Word* nor the *Holy Spirit* were, according to *Sabellius*, "Hypostases" <term>Hypostases: A Greek theological term referring to a distinct person or individual substance within the Trinity.</term>, just as the faculties of reasoning, willing, or acting do not have a separate existence from that of the human soul, and are not persons different from the man himself. This is what can be seen in the *Theological Dogmas* of <margin>(a) *Petau, On the Trinity.* Book I. ch. 6. n. 2.</margin> (a) *Petau*, and in the *Ecclesiastical History* <margin>(b) *Noël Alexandre, Century* III. p. m. 67.</margin> of Father (b) *Alexandre*. Both have followed <margin>(c) *Epiphanius, Heresies* LXII. at the beginning.</margin> (c) Saint *Epiphanius*, who testifies that the Sabellians compared the Divinity to the Sun, in which one distinguishes: 1. the *Substance*, or the body of the Sun; 2. the power of lighting; and 3. the power of heating and animating. *Abulpharage* <note>Also known as Bar Hebraeus, a 13th-century scholar and bishop.</note> confirms much the same as the testimony of St. *Epiphanius*. <margin>There is only one Divine Person, of whom the Word and the Spirit are the Attributes and Properties.</margin> He says (6) "that, according to the Sabellians, what we call the "three Divine Persons are *Existence*, *Wisdom*, and *Life*: that "these are only *respective attributes* of the Divine Essence. He adds "that this sentiment is exactly the same as that "of *Empedocles* on the Divine Attributes, and that it is followed by a "portion of the learned among the Muslims." Thus, the Sabellian Error consisted of annihilating the Personality of the Word and the Holy Spirit; the Trinity being nothing more, in this system, than the Divine Nature considered under the three ideas of *Substance*, of *Thinking Substance*, and of *Substance that wills and acts*. In a word, Sabellianism was, on the subject of the Unity of God, pure Judaism, as <margin>(d) *Basil, Epistle* LXIV.</margin> (d) St. *Basil* puts it so well.

<margin>The union of the Word with Jesus is only an operation of the Word in JESUS.</margin>
