<columns>2</columns>

It is quite true that *Dispensation* <note>Original: *Oikonomia*</note> sometimes signifies the *Incarnation* in the writings of the Church Fathers, but that is not what this word means in either *Hippolytus* or *Tertullian*, who explains it by NUMERUS & DISPOSITIO, meaning the *number* and the *arrangement* of the Persons. Here is what it is: The Fathers claimed that the plurality of Divine Persons did not destroy the Unity of God, firstly because the Son and the Holy Spirit draw their origin from the Father; and secondly because the Son and the Holy Spirit are subordinate to the Father. For example, there will be only one Emperor, but there will be two *Caesars* who govern under the Emperor, who are sons of the Emperor, and who hold

<column-break/>

their origin and their Power from him. That is the *Dispensation*. *The Dispensation of harmony reunites the three Persons into a single God: for there is but one God. The Father commands, the Son obeys, the Holy Spirit teaches knowledge.* <note>Original Greek: Οἰκονομία συμφωνίας συνάγεται εἰς ἕνα Θεόν. εἷς γὰρ ἐστὶν ὁ Θεός· ὁ γὰρ κελεύων πατὴρ, ὁ δὲ ὑπακούων υἱὸς, τὸ δὲ συνέτιζον, ἅγιον πνεῦμα. *Hippolytus, as cited above,* §. XIV. p. 16.</note>

(6) *There are three Persons: Existence, Wisdom, and Life; these are not meanings added to the Divine Essence, but respective Attributes... This is the view adopted by some of the learned Muslims. Abulpharage, Dynasties, p. 81.* <note>Original Latin: *Tres Personas esse Existentiam, Sapientiam & Vitam; nec esse significatus superadditos Essentiæ Divinæ, verum Attributa respectiva. . . Quam Sententiam susceperunt nonnulli ex doctis Mahommedanorum.*</note>

THE WORD is not the SON OF GOD; it is only an Attribute, a Faculty, a property of the Divine Nature.

<meta>This page continues the author’s defense of the Sabellians against the charge of "Patripassianism." ->HISTORY OF DOGMAS<-

<column-break/>

Divine. It is (1) *Jesus Christ as Man, who became the Son of God through the communication of the Word*, as Marcellus <note>Marcellus of Ancyra (died c. 374), a bishop whose opposition to Arianism led him to a position often accused of Sabellianism.</note> says in *Eusebius*. From this comes the fact that the Noetians <note>Followers of Noetus of Smyrna, late 2nd-century theologians who taught that God the Father was himself born and suffered as the Son.</note> reproached the Orthodox, (2) FOR INTRODUCING A STRANGE AND NEW LANGUAGE BY CALLING THE WORD THE SON OF GOD. This title was only suitable for *Jesus as Man*, and *simple Man* regarding his Nature, however great he might be through his Gifts. Sabellianism and Socinianism <note>A 16th-century rationalist Christian movement that denied the full deity of Christ, viewing him as a man invested with divine power.</note> did not differ at all, or differed very little, as several Scholars (3) have observed.

The Sabellians having thus distinguished between *Jesus as Man*, who is *the Christ and the Son of God*, and *the Word*, which is an Attribute of the Father and not his Son, I cannot help but say that one could not justly impute to them the extravagant absurdity THAT ONE AND THE SAME PERSON IS THE FATHER OF HIMSELF AND THE SON OF HIMSELF: THAT THIS PERSON APPEARED SOMETIMES UNDER THE NAME OF THE FATHER AND SOMETIMES UNDER THAT OF THE SON. They never said anything of the kind, and no one had the right to conclude it from their Principles. They placed as much difference between *the Word* and *the Son of God* as there is between an inseparable Attribute of the Divinity and a Man whom it pleases God to overwhelm with extraordinary Gifts. Far from believing that the Word was hypostatically <note>A theological term referring to the union of divine and human natures in the single person of Christ.</note> united to the Son of God, who is Jesus Christ-Man, they believed that the Presence of the Word in Jesus Christ was only a <margin>The communication of the Word to Jesus Christ is only a presence of assistance and operation which must cease.</margin> *presence of assistance and operation*, which must (4) cease when the Redemption of the Faithful is completed by their Resurrection and their Immortality. I hope these clarifications will not displease the Reader. Accurate ideas of things are always agreeable to Minds that love the Truth.

XII. Here is another species of Heretics who appeared at the Council of Nicaea. These are People who said, (a) *that the Word entered through the ear of the Virgin, and that it exited by way of childbirth*. <margin>XII. Other Heretics at the Council of Nicaea. They believe that the Word entered through the ear of the Virgin and exited by way of childbirth. (a) Eutych. as cited above.</margin>

childbirth. This sentiment was that of a certain (5) *Elianus* and his sect. The heresy appears bizarre; it even has something profane about it. *Eutychius* <note>Eutychius of Alexandria (877–940), a Melkite Patriarch and historian.</note> tells us nothing of its origin; apparently, he did not know it. For my part, I conjecture that it came from the Barbarians, like that of the *Mariamites* <note>A sect, sometimes associated with the Collyridians, who were accused of worshipping Mary as a goddess.</note>. Mr. *Asseman* <note>Giuseppe Simone Assemani (1687–1768), a Lebanese Maronite scholar and librarian of the Vatican.</note> informs us that, the Maronite Breviary having been given to some Scholars in Rome to be examined, they were scandalized to find these words: (6) THE WORD OF THE FATHER ENTERED THROUGH THE EAR OF THE BLESSED WOMAN. I am surprised by the sensitivity, or rather the weakness, of these Roman Doctors. They should have been accustomed to this thought, and even to something more. Did they not know, then, that it was in the Hymns of the Church, which were sung in the time of the celebrated *Agobard*? This Bishop of Lyon, who would have dearly liked to correct some of the superstitions of his time, informs us that when the birth of the Savior was celebrated in the West, the singers made the vaults of the churches ring with these edifying words: (7) THE WORD ENTERED THROUGH THE EAR OF THE VIRGIN, AND IT CAME OUT THROUGH THE GOLDEN GATE <note>The "Golden Gate" is a poetic and theological metaphor for the birth canal, intended to emphasize the purity of the Virgin Birth.</note>. I leave it to the reader to guess what this gate is, only to tell him that something more modest is found in a hymn by *St. Ephrem* <note>Ephrem the Syrian (c. 306–373), a prominent Syriac Christian hymnographer and theologian.</note>. (8) *As Death, says this Father, entered through the ear of Eve, so Life entered through the ear of Mary.* *Vossius*, Canon of *Tongres*, who translated the works of *St. Ephrem* from the Greek, remarked that this thought originally came from *Gregory of Neocaesarea*, surnamed *Thaumaturgus* <note>"The Wonder-Worker."</note>, and Mr. *Asseman* tries to authorize it by two passages from Latin authors. The first is from *St. Augustine*. *God, says this Father (9), spoke through his Angel and the Virgin* BECAME PREGNANT THROUGH THE EAR. The second, which is from Pope *Felix* writing to Peter of Antioch, is conceived in these terms: (10) *THE INTIMATE WORD of the Father, THE SUBSTANTIAL WORD, the Word which is God, slipping through the Ears.*

The *Ears of the Holy Virgin* <note>original: "Oreilles de la Sainte Vierge"</note> effected her conception in an ineffable manner. One must have great indulgence to tolerate such unreasonable thoughts in the Ancients; but it required more than just bad taste to insert them into the Hymns of the Church, along with the immodest addition I reported after *Agobard* <note>Agobard of Lyon (c. 779–840), a Carolingian prelate known for his critiques of popular superstitions and liturgical errors.</note>, who was greatly scandalized by it. This is also what horribly scandalized *Mani* <note>The founder of Manichaeism.</note>. He found it dishonorable to the Divinity to make it descend into the womb of a woman, and to make it exit by way of childbirth.

<margin>XIII. Paulianists & Marcionites at the Council of Nicaea.
(a) Eutych. as above.</margin>
XIII. The other Heretics who were present at the Council of Nicaea <note>Held in 325 AD, this was the first ecumenical council of the Christian Church.</note> were *(a)* the followers of *Paul of Samosata* <note>Bishop of Antioch, deposed for heresy in 268; he taught that Jesus was a mere man who became divine.</note>, and those of *Marcion* <note>A 2nd-century teacher who rejected the Old Testament and the God of the Jews.</note>. I was surprised not to see, in the list provided by *Eutychius* <note>Eutychius of Alexandria, a 10th-century Melkite Patriarch and chronicler.</note>, either *Valentinians* <note>Gnostics following the teachings of Valentinus.</note> or *Manichaeans*, as these two Sects were then numerous in the East. For the Manichaeans, the reason is perhaps that they had been proscribed more than thirty years earlier by a Law of *Diocletian*, under the pretext that their Heresy was born among the Persians, a Nation always hostile to the Romans. But it is not the same for the *Valentinians*, who, having arisen within the Empire, enjoyed the same protection as other Christians.

<margin>Why neither Valentinians nor Manichaeans are seen there.</margin>
This leads me to suspect that some of these Heretics hid among the Orthodox under the shadow of the word *Consubstantial* <note>original: "Consubstantiel"; the Greek term "homoousios," meaning "of the same substance," used to define the relationship between God the Father and the Son.</note>. *St. Hilary* (1) informs us that various Sectarians took advantage of this symbolic word and explained it according to their own System. This was, if I am not mistaken, what made it suspicious to *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, the "Father of Church History."</note> and other Bishops who were not Arians. If, therefore, there were such Heretics in the Council, they must have joined the Orthodox and condemned Arianism. What is certain is that (2) *Marcellus of Ancyra* and *Eustathius of Antioch*, his Disciple—neither of whom were in any way Orthodox—declared themselves loudly for *Consubstantiality* against the Arians.

<margin>XIV. Disputes between the Sectarians and the Catholics.</margin>
XIV. *Constantine*, astonished to find the Christian Church so divided on the Question of *How Jesus Christ is the Son of God*, desired that the Bishops of all Parties confer and debate together.

### CHAPTER VII.

->*The opinion of the Arians & their reasons. Reasons of the Orthodox. Opinions of VALENTINUS & MANICHAEUS on the Generation of the Son of God.*<-

<margin>I. The Arians attempt to conflate the Faith of the Church with the opinions of Valentinus or Manichaeus.</margin>
I. I have represented in what confusion the Christian Church found itself, due to the contrary opinions of the Bishops on the Question: HOW *J. Christ is the Son of God*. I have stated the reasons that engaged me in this Discussion. I come now to the examination of the Opinions of *Valentinus* & *Manichaeus* on this Mystery. *Arius* & his Adherents protest *that they do not teach, with* VALENTINUS, *that the Son is a* PROBOLE <note>term: 'Probole' (Greek: προβολή) refers to an emanation or 'casting forth' of a divine being from the Godhead, a concept central to Gnostic systems.</note> *of the Father; nor with* MANICHAEUS, *that he is a* CONSUBSTANTIAL PART <note>term: 'Consubstantial' (Latin: consubstantialis) means of the same substance or essence.</note> *of him*. These words are properly a barb aimed at the Orthodox, whose sentiment the Arians wished to conflate with that of the Valentinians or with that of the Manichaeans.

<margin>II. System of the Arians. They believe the Son of God is a Creature. Praises they give him.</margin>
II. The Arians agreed with the Catholics that the World was drawn from Nothing: but they denied that the Son of God emanates from the Substance of the Father, which obliged them to say that he has no other origin than that of all the Beings that compose the Universe, & that he is a Creature like them. Except for that, they omitted nothing to elevate the condition of the Son of God. (1) "HE IS A CREATURE," they said, "AND A PERFECT CREATURE; this is true: but he is of a completely different order than that of other Creatures. HE WAS MADE; this is also true: but he is like none of the things that were made. He is the most perfect Image of the Perfections of God: He is clothed with

Athanasius, *On the Synods*, page 621. See the Apology of *Eunomius* in Fabricius, *Greek Library*, Vol. VIII, § XV & following. Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VI, at the beginning.

(2) These can be seen in St. Hilary, in the place where he reports the Objections of the Arians against the Passages that the Orthodox alleged to prove the Generation of the Son. <note>original: "Si enim, quod EX IPSO; & quod, EX UTERO & quod, EX PATRE EXIVI ET VENI, velut partem ejus unius Substantiæ; & quasi Prolationis, extendens intelligitur, compositus erit Pater, divisibilis, convertibilis. &c."</note> "For if that which is FROM HIM; and that which is FROM THE WOMB; and that which is I CAME FORTH FROM THE FATHER AND HAVE COME, is understood as a part of that single Substance, and as if an extension of a Prolation, the Father would be composite, divisible, changeable, etc." Hilary, *On the Trinity*, Book VI, col. 100. <margin>They reject Generation & Consubstantiality. Their reasons.</margin>
It was in this way that the Arians tried to emphasize the excellence & the Dignity of the Son of God: but they rejected *Generation*, and consequently *Consubstantiality* <note>term: 'Consubstantiality' (from the Greek 'homoousios') refers to the doctrine that the Father and the Son are of the exact same essence or substance.</note>. the mere name of *Son* is an obvious proof that the Lord has no other origin than the Substance of the Father, because a Father and a Son must necessarily possess the same Nature. 2. That if the Word were created, he would be Son of God in name only, and not in effect. 3. That the attributes of PROPER SON and ONLY SON, which are given to the Lord, show that he is Son of God by nature, and not by creation, by adoption, or by grace. 4. <margin>V. Eusebius’s reflections on that of the Son of God.</margin>
V. <term>Eusebius</term> <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), a historian and bishop known as the "Father of Church History."</note>, after having defended the Generation of the Son against <term>Marcellus</term> <note>Marcellus of Ancyra, a 4th-century bishop accused of Sabellianism, a belief that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are merely different "modes" of one person rather than three distinct persons.</note>, made some reflections on this matter which seem very wise to me, and which I could not resolve to suppress. First, instead of seeking in Nature—as has been done all too often—comparisons more likely to give rise to difficulties than to clarify them, Eusebius (6) recognizes that Divine Generation is beyond all example and all comparison. He remarks (a) secondly,
<margin>1. It must not be clarified through comparisons.</margin>
<margin>(a) *On Ecclesiastical Theology* p. 72.</margin>
> “that the Creation of the Son of God
> “is no less a mystery than his Generation, because
> “one cannot explain how something is made from nothing.
> “That on all sides one was constrained to recognize an
> “incomprehensible Mystery, and to set limits to Human
> “Curiosity.”
<margin>2. It is no more incomprehensible than Creation.</margin>
Nothing is more just than this reflection. Many centuries have passed since Eusebius, but I do not believe that (7) the great minds who came after him have invented anything satisfactory on this matter. Finally, Eusebius ends with this consideration:
<margin>3. It is necessary for salvation to believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God, and not to know how he is so.</margin>
> “GOD said, THIS IS MY SON; LISTEN TO him. Since he commands us to listen to him, let us obey the order of our King. Furthermore, he teaches us what he wants us to know on the subject of his Son in these words of the Gospel (a)
<margin>(a) John III. 16.</margin>
> *God so loved the World, that he gave his only Son, so that whoever believes in him should not perish, but have eternal Life.*
It is therefore necessary to believe in him to have eternal Life. *For he does not say*, (8) THAT HE WHO KNOWS HOW THE SON IS BORN OF THE FATHER WILL HAVE ETERNAL LIFE; BUT HE WHO BELIEVES IN HIM.” <term>Cyril of Jerusalem</term> <note>A 4th-century theologian and Bishop of Jerusalem known for his "Catechetical Lectures."</note> thought and spoke much like Eusebius on the same subject.

> “himself: and that just as there is a
> “real difference between the Understanding
> “of God and his Will, so their
> “substantial images are really
> “distinct from each other, and really
> “distinct from God himself, because
> “nothing is an image of itself.”
Mr. <term>Le Clerc</term> <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), a famous Swiss theologian and scholar known for his critical approach to historical texts and his emphasis on reason.</note> later critiques these hypotheses, and indeed they deserve it. For besides the reflections he makes, does it not follow evidently that the Son, being only the *substantial image of the Divine Understanding*, also has only Understanding as his portion? And by the same reasoning, the Holy Spirit can only have the *Will* as his portion, because he is *the substantial image only of the Will*. After all, what do *substantial images* mean if not *Substances* that are Images of another Substance, for the reason that nothing is an image of itself. It seems to me that after such a great number of useless attempts, it would be time to say that one does not understand how three Persons, really distinct from each other, subsist in a Nature that is <term>numerically one</term> <note>term: 'unique en nombre' (numerically one) is a technical way of saying there is only one God in total, rather than three gods of the same type.</note>, and to leave it at that.

<margin>Definition of the Probole.</margin> PROBOLE signifies, in the ancient Theologians, everything that a Substance produces and pushes, in a way, out of itself. The Latins translate it as *PROLATIO* [prolation or extension], *EMISSIO* [emission], or *EDITIO* [bringing forth]. It is said of the fruits that the Tree bears, and which emerge from its branches. It is also said of the stalk that rises from the root; of the stream that flows from its source; of the rays that emanate from the Sun; and according to (1) *Justin Martyr*, it is also said of that air which comes out of our mouth, and whose different modifications form speech. Finally, it is said of the children whom a Mother brings into the world. In general (2) everything that a Substance produces, whether it separates from it or remains attached to it, is a *Probole*. I believe, however, that the Easterners, who knew the force of Greek terms very well, understood by *Probole* an extension of the Substance, and not a separation, since they opposed it to a *detached part*.

In early theology, this term (from the Greek *probolē*) described the Son being "put forth" or "projected" from the Father, similar to a plant growing from a root.</note>. The Son comes forth from the Essence of the Father just as the *Stem comes forth from the Root*, and the *Stream from its source*: as the *Ray emanates from the Sun*. *The Stem is not the Root: it is however of the same Substance: and although it comes out from it, it always remains attached to it.* It is the same with the Stream and its Source, the Ray and the Sun. <margin>VIII. System of the Valentinians on the Divine Nature and on the production of the Son.</margin>
VIII. Valentinian Theology is too obscure to attempt to fully unravel it here. It is a heap of mysterious enigmas, which were only well-known to the masters of the Sect—assuming even they understood what they were saying. It is true that the *Excerpts from the Doctrine of Theodotus*, for which we are indebted to Clement of Alexandria <note>A Christian theologian and philosopher who taught at the Catechetical School of Alexandria.</note>, clarify a part of it, but there remains a darkness capable of halting the most stubborn curiosity. The passage I am about to relate, which concerns my subject, is not entirely of that nature.

<margin>They do not recognize any incorporeal Substance; they believe God to be an extended and figured Light.
(a) In Eclogae Theodoti.</margin>
The Valentinians did not recognize any entirely incorporeal Substance. *(a)* God himself, according to these Heretics, is a corporeal light, extended and shaped; and the proof they alleged for this was that Scripture speaks of the **Face of God**, and of the **contemplation of this Face**. Now they maintained, *(3)* **that a Face can only belong to a shaped Being, (4) and that nothing can either see or be seen unless it is also shaped and corporeal.** Aside from this, they gave the Divine Essence all possible Perfections. A Light most pure and simple, eternal, immortal, adorned with a form that corresponds to the excellence of its nature; a Light that no one has seen, nor can see, except the only Son. Even the most perfect and sublime Intelligences only contemplate it in this Son, who is the Image that the Light formed of itself when it intended to manifest itself.

<margin>They married him with SIGE, or Silence. Explanation of this enigma.</margin>
Such was the Supreme God, according to the Valentinians. They called him the <term>AGENNETOS</term> <note>original: *Agennetos*. Greek for "First Father" or "Forefather."</note>, the **first Father**, or simply THE FATHER; the *(5)* <term>BYTHOS</term> <note>original: *Bythos*. Greek for "Depth" or "Abyss," representing the unfathomable origin of all things.</note>,

...a lamp whose contained oil, in a single vessel, provides light through two wicks, which are united in the same vessel. The first of these comparisons is constantly cited by the Ancients to show that the <term>Generation of the Son</term> <note>The theological concept of how the Son "comes forth" from the Father without being a separate creation.</note> entails neither division nor diminution of the Essence of the Father. It is found in (6) *Justin Martyr*, in (7) *Tatian*, etc. *A Spirit is born of a Spirit*, (8) says *Tertullian*, *God is born of God, just as a Light is lit by another Light, without the latter suffering any diminution. The <term>Heresiarch</term> <note>The founder of a heretical movement.</note> believed that it is an extreme insult to the Majesty and Holiness of the Son of God to make him descend into the womb of a woman, and then to make him emerge with all the filth that accompanies childbirth. *St. Augustine* (10) is a good witness to what I say.

### CHAPTER VIII.

*The Manichaeans believed in a single God in three Persons, but they did not believe in the equality of those Persons. They placed the SON in the Sun and the Moon, and the HOLY SPIRIT in the Air.*

<margin>I. The Manichaeans believed in three Persons and not three Principles.</margin>
I. I have proved that the Manichaeans recognized the Trinity and the <term>consubstantiality</term> <note>The doctrine that the members of the Trinity are of the same "substance" or essence, rather than being different kinds of being.</note> of the Divine Persons. I have spoken of the Generation of the Son, but I have nothing to say regarding the Article on the Holy Spirit, because the authors I have been able to consult have taught me nothing on this subject. We must therefore now examine what our heretics thought regarding the Distinction of the Persons, their equality or inequality, and the dwelling place of each.

The artifice of the <term>Arians</term> <note>A group that followed the teachings of Arius, who argued that Jesus was a created being and not co-eternal with God the Father.</note> was to confuse, as much as they could, the Orthodox System with that of the <term>Valentinians</term> <note>Followers of Valentinus, a prominent 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who had a complex view of divine emanations.</note> and the Manichaeans. This is a popular argument that has always been used, and will always be used, even though it is based on a very false proposition: namely, that everything a heretic thinks is a heresy. Certainly, even if the Church had thought like *Valentinus* regarding the Trinity, it would not follow that the Church’s belief was an error. On the contrary, one could turn the Arians' objection to the advantage of the Church. For if a heretic like *Valentinus*—who was a scholar, a man of wit, and who appeared as early as the second age after the death of the Apostles—believed in the Generation and Consubstantiality of the Son, could one not conclude with sufficient probability that this sentiment had been, since the time of the Apostles, the sentiment of the Church? However, the Church Fathers, persuaded that it was prudent to distance their System from any conformity with that of the heretics, applied themselves to seeking out the differences that distinguished them. St. Athanasius did this; but, if I am not mistaken, he chose poorly. "(1) We do not introduce," he says, "THREE <term>PRINCIPLES</term> <note>In this context, 'principles' (archai) refers to ultimate, uncreated sources or original causes of existence.</note>, nor THREE FATHERS, as do the Manichaeans and the <term>Marcionites</term> <note>Followers of Marcion, who believed in two distinct gods: a creator of the material world and a superior god of love.</note>, who, to explain the Trinity, use the comparison of three Suns."

<margin>St. Athanasius corrected.</margin>
The accusation is serious, and the Author venerable; however, I do not fear to say it: it is not just. It is possible that the Manichaeans employed the comparison of three Suns:

---

<margin>(1) "For we do not introduce three principles, or three fathers, as do those around Marcion and Manichaeus." <note>original Greek: "Οὐ γὰρ τρεῖς ἀρχὰς, ἢ τρεῖς πατέρας εἰσάγομεν, ὡς οἱ περὶ Μαρκίωνα καὶ Μανιχαῖον."</note></margin>
Athanasius, *Oration IV against the Arians*, page 262.

# ON MANICHAEISM. BOOK III. CH. VIII.
Aaaa 3

...suns: this is not what I deny; but they never claimed that there were three Principles, nor three Fathers, that is to say, three Divine Persons who have existence through themselves. The Divine Nature indeed exists through itself: but the Persons of the Son and of the Holy Spirit exist through the Father. No ancient Writer, as far as I know, has said the contrary.

<margin>The comparison of three suns does not prove it.</margin>
What then was the sentiment of the Manichaeans, and what did the comparison of the three Suns lead to? It was to show, on one hand, the real distinction of the three Persons: and, on the other, their <term>Consubstantiality</term> <note>The doctrine that the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit are of the exact same divine substance or essence.</note>: *Three Suns are three different <term>Hypostases</term>* <note>From the Greek 'hypostasis,' referring to the individual, distinct existence of each person of the Trinity.</note>, they each have their own Subsistence which is proper to them: but they are of the same Nature. If the Manichaeans had said that these three *Suns* exist through themselves, they would indeed have admitted *three Principles and three Fathers*: but if they said that one of these three Suns gave existence to the other two, they admitted only one Father and one Principle.

<margin>Several Fathers made use of the comparison of three Men.</margin>
I will have no trouble agreeing with St. *Athanasius* <note>A 4th-century bishop of Alexandria and a major defender of Trinitarian orthodoxy against Arianism.</note> that the comparison of *three Suns* is worth nothing: but at heart it is nobler, and has nothing more shocking than that of *three men*, which several very Catholic Fathers used to explain the unity of Nature and the particular differences of the three Divine Persons. This is by no means a doubtful fact; it is admitted and proven by Authors very well-versed in Antiquity, and in no way suspected of Heterodoxy <note>Holding non-orthodox or heretical beliefs.</note>. It is true that these two comparisons seem to establish three Gods: For *three Suns are three Suns and three men are three men*. But, besides the fact that the Manichaeans protested that they believed in <term>ONLY ONE GOD</term>; <term>ONE DIVINITY</term> <note>original Latin: "UNUM NUMEN"</note>, says *Faustus*, <term>ONLY ONE DIVINITY</term>, <term>ONE DIVINITY</term> <note>original Greek: "MIAN ΘEOTHTA"</note>, says *Photius*, they defended themselves from the accusation of introducing three Gods by the same reasons as the Orthodox.

<margin>II. How the Fathers defended themselves against establishing three Gods. 1st Reason.</margin>
II. The Arians <note>Followers of Arius who taught that the Son was a created being, subordinate to the Father.</note> reproaching the Catholics for introducing several Gods, and consequently overturning the first foundation of Religion, the latter justified themselves against such a capital accusation by two reasons. The first is that, in multiplying the Persons, they did not multiply the Divine Nature, which always remains <term>ONE</term>, although it subsists in three <term>Hypostases</term>. They considered it as what are called <term>Universal Natures</term> <note>A philosophical concept suggesting that a single essence, like "Humanity," is a real entity shared by individuals, yet remains a single, unified thing.</note>, the Genres and the Species, which are supposed to always keep a perfect unity, even though they are common to several individuals, really distinct and separate from each other. And as it followed from this that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three Gods, in the same way that *Peter*, *James*, and *John* are three Men; the Ancients denied the consequence, maintaining that at heart...

*Peter, James & John* are but one man, because the Human Nature that constitutes them as Men is unique & indivisible. This appears astonishing, but it is undeniable. One can see the clear proofs of this in the works of the celebrated Jesuit (1) *Petavius* <note>Dionysius Petavius (1583–1652), a French Jesuit theologian who wrote extensively on the history of dogmas.</note>.

<margin>
2. A more accurate reason than the first.
There are not several Gods, because there is only one Principle and one Monarch.
</margin>
There was more truth, and without contradiction less inconvenience, in this second response. It is that the plurality of Divine Persons does not destroy the unity of God, (2) because only one of these Persons—namely, the Father—has existence through himself and has no Principle <note>In this context, "Principle" refers to the "arche" or source/origin of existence.</note>. The others derive their origin from him. He is the source from which they emanate and he always maintains over them a sort of Preeminence in his capacity as Father and as Principle. *Eusebius* <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, an early Christian historian and bishop.</note>, who gives this response to *Marcellus of Ancyra*, agrees that if one were to suppose two entirely equal Persons, both having existence through themselves, this would effectively be introducing two Gods, because it would be introducing two Principles. But as the Father has given existence to the Son, and the Son is subordinate to the Father, there is only one God existing through himself, and only one Principle. It was thus that, before *Eusebius*, *(a) Tertullian* among the Latins, *(b) & Hippolytus* among the Greeks had defended the Church from returning to Polytheism; this is what they named *(c)* the <term>DISPENSATION</term> <note>original: "DISPENSATION". This refers to the "Economy" (Oikonomia), the theological concept of how the one God exists as three persons in a structured order.</note>. The Son & the Holy Spirit, drawing their origin from the Father and being subordinate to the Father, the Plurality is reduced to Unity. There is but one *Principle*, and one *Monarch*.

# OF MANICHAEUS. Book III. Ch. VIII.

...the Attributes of the Divine Nature, **excepting however self-origination, self-existence, and absolute independence.** (4) <note>This refers to the "second response" discussed on the previous page regarding the subordination of the Son to the Father.</note> If these two answers justify the Orthodox System against the charge of Polytheism, they also justify the Manichaean System. Let us set forth the origin & the cause of what might have been defective in this latter System. This is necessary to judge Human Errors equitably.

<margin>
III. Origin of the System of Manichaeus regarding the Trinity. The idea of the Platonists on this subject.
</margin>
III. *Manichaeus* found the Trinity in the New Testament, where it is clearly taught. But there were already traces of this Mystery in (5) *Oriental Theology*: & it is from there, if I am not mistaken, that *Plato* had taken the ideas found in his Philosophy.

<margin>
II. Immortal Intelligences are emanations from the supreme Divinity.
</margin>
*Plato* distinguished two Substances: God & Matter. He then distinguished two kinds of Beings; some Spiritual, Intelligent, & Immortal, the others Material & Corporeal. As nothing is made from nothing, Material Beings take their origin from Matter; and spiritual Beings take theirs from the Divinity, of which they are Emanations. God is only the Fashioner of the former, but he is the Father of the latter, (6) because they come forth from him, and they are like a *Portion of his Substance*.

<margin>
Among these Emanations there are two of infinitely superior excellence.
</margin>
All these Emanations are not equal, the Father having communicated his Perfections to them only as much as he judged appropriate and as it suited them. There are only two who participate in the Divinity, and whose Excellence makes them infinitely superior to all the others, the Father having intended to associate them with himself in the Governance of the World. These are the two primary Ministers of the supreme God. Let us listen on this subject to a learned Platonist who flourished at the beginning of the 4th Century. I mean *Chalcidius* <note>A 4th-century philosopher known for his Latin translation and commentary on Plato's Timaeus.</note>, who commented on the *Timaeus*, that difficult Dialogue in which *Plato* sets forth his sentiment on the Divine Nature, on the origin of the World, on that of the Soul, etc. *Plato* thus conceived firstly (7) " **a supreme God**

The difference placed between the Father and the Son is only a <term>Mode</term> <note>French: "Mode"</note>, <term>a mode of existence</term> <note>original: "τρόπος ὑπάρξεως", transliterated as tropos hyparxeos</note>. (a) "When the Apostle," says this ancient Author, "testifies that (b) *Christ is God blessed eternally above all things*, he explains the Mystery of Truth very well and very clearly. Hippolytus cites verses 27 and 28 of Chapter 15 of 1 Corinthians, after which he continues in these terms: (2) *If then all things are subject to Jesus Christ, except for him who subjected all things to him, it follows that he has dominion over all things, and that* THE FATHER HAS DOMINION OVER HIM, SO THAT IN ALL THINGS THERE MAY BE ONLY ONE GOD, TO WHOM THEY ARE ALL SUBJECTED ALONG WITH CHRIST, to whom the Father submitted everything except himself.

Thus, as Manichaeus lived toward the middle of the 3rd century, his Theology could only be consistent with that which was then common in the Church. He believed in the <term>Consubstantiality: The doctrine that the Father and the Son share the same divine essence or "substance."</term> of the *Word* <note>original: "Verbe," referring to the Logos/Christ.</note>, but he believed him subject to the Father, acting only under the orders of the one from whom he holds both his essence and his power. This is why the Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect, in this case, Mani.</note> assigned to the three Divine Persons dwellings proportioned to their dignity. He placed the Father in the supreme Heaven because of his preeminence; the Son in the *Sun*, below the Father; and the Holy Spirit in the *Air*, below the Son. There are some imaginings in this that appear quite bizarre. Let us try to discover their origin, for I am persuaded that Manichaeus was not their author at all.

Now, *Mediator* does not mean here a Person who negotiates a reconciliation between two opposing Parties, but a Person who presides over the Beings of the MIDDLE ORDER—that is to say, over those who hold a middle place between the Divinity, who is eternal in all respects, and mortal Creatures. These Beings are the Intelligences <note>In this context, "Intelligences" refer to spiritual, non-material beings or emanations that govern the cosmos.</note>, who had a beginning but will have no end. # HISTORY OF DOGMAS #

*Psellus* <note>Michael Psellos (c. 1017–1078), a Byzantine philosopher and historian whose works preserved much Neoplatonic and occult lore.</note> is that sublime Intelligence which is called in the *Oracles*, *Noos* <note>original: "Νῆος"; Greek for "Mind" or "Intellect."</note>, MIND, the SPIRIT par excellence, and who stands at the head of the immortal Spirits as their Prince and Chief.

Thus, the name MITHRA was a name common to both the *Sun* and to that *First Intelligence* whom *Plato* calls the *Second God*. Now, as the *Sun* and this *God* are two very different Substances—one being pure *Spirit* and the other *Body*—the most natural reason for a shared name is, in my opinion, that the *Sun* is the Dwelling and the Palace of the First Intelligence. For just as the Hebrews gave the name *Jehovah* to the Ark because the Eternal was thought to dwell there in the midst of his People, so the Persians called the *Sun* by the name of *Mithra* because it is the seat of *Mithra*, that is to say, of the First Intelligence after God.

<margin>
VI. Error of Mr. Huet, who claims that Manichaeus took his opinion from Hermogenes.
</margin>

VI. This thought is certainly more natural and more probable than that of Mr. *Huet* <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French bishop and scholar.</note>, <margin>(a) *Origeniana*. Book II. Question II. §. 18. p. 62.</margin> (*a*) who imagined that our Heresiarch <note>The leader of a heretical sect, here referring to Manichaeus.</note> had borrowed from *Hermogenes* his opinion on the dwelling of the Son of God. It is true that *Hermogenes* <note>A 2nd-century teacher and painter often criticized by early Church Fathers like Tertullian.</note> had taken it into his head that the Lord left his body in the Sun while ascending to Heaven. A passage from (1) *Psalm* 19 gave birth to this folly. One reads in the Septuagint <note>The earliest Greek translation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, *You have placed your Tabernacle in the Sun* (2). <margin>(b) Theodoret, *Compendium of Heretical Fables*. Book 1. 19.</margin> This led some to believe (*b*) that Jesus Christ had deposited his glorified Body there; and others to believe that he transported his mystical Body there, and that the Sun was the dwelling of the Church Triumphant. <margin>(c) Clement of Alexandria, *ibid*.</margin> Among those who held this latter sentiment is placed (*c*) *Pantaenus*, a Teacher of Alexandria, so highly praised by *Clement*, who was one of his successors. <margin>The Sun, according to some Ancients, is the dwelling of the Body of Jesus Christ and of the Blessed.</margin> A modern writer took it upon himself to place Hell where others had put Paradise. There is no extremity to which Human Curiosity will not go to seek out reefs upon which to be shipwrecked. Be that as it may, Mr. *Huet* is certainly mistaken regarding the origin of *Manichaeus's* Error. For, besides the fact that the latter did not believe that Jesus Christ had a physical Body <note>Manichaeism taught Docetism, the belief that Christ's physical form was merely an illusion.</note>, what likelihood is there that he would have borrowed from an African—of whom he had perhaps never heard—that which he found already established among the Sages of his own Nation? In Persia, it was believed that the First of the Intelligences resides in the Sun, and that this beautiful Star (3) *is the dwelling of the Blessed*. <margin>The Persians place Paradise there.</margin> The common prejudice of these peoples led them there. <margin>(a) Cited in Augustine, Book XXI. 2.</margin>

# OF MANICHAEUS BOOK III. CH. VIII. #

<margin>A comparison of the Manichaean imagination with that which places Jesus Christ in the Bread.</margin>
"...the Light." Thus, the Manichaeans, following the ideas of Scripture, placed God the Father in an **invisible and inaccessible Light**; and following after that the ideas of Persian Philosophers, they believed that the Son, who is the Image of the Father, had chosen for his dwelling the visible Light, or the Body of the Sun. If this is a very vain imagination, as it indeed is, it is innocent, and at its core it shocks Reason less than that which encloses Jesus Christ entirely—his Body, his Soul, and his Divinity—under the corruptible Species <note>In theology, "species" refers to the outward appearances of bread and wine (taste, smell, color) that remain after the substance has changed.</note> of Bread and Wine. Moreover, it is at least as well-founded: for if one must explain in the proper and literal sense these words, *This is my Body*, there is without comparison less inconvenience in explaining in the same way those of Psalm 19: *You have set your Tabernacle in the Sun.* <note>original: "In sole posuit tabernaculum suum." This refers to a reading found in the Latin Vulgate Bible; modern translations of Psalm 19:4 usually describe God setting a tent for the sun in the heavens, rather than God dwelling in the sun.</note>

<margin>VII. The Manichaeans placed the Wisdom of Jesus Christ in the Moon. Conjectures on this imagination. (a) As above.</margin>
VII. Before anyone had imagined *Concomitance* <note>The doctrine that because Christ is living, his body, blood, soul, and divinity are all present in both the bread and the wine of the Eucharist, rather than being separated.</note>, theologians placed the Lord's Body in the sign of the Bread, and his Blood in that of the Wine: they thus divided his Flesh and his Blood. The Manichaeans did not divide his Divine Nature, but his Perfections, and placed one in the Sun and the other in the Moon. *The Son*, says Faustus <note>Faustus of Mileve, a prominent 4th-century Manichaean bishop known through the refutations written by Saint Augustine.</note> *(a)*, *dwells in the visible Light, and as he himself is twofold and as he is the Power of God, and the Wisdom of God, we believe that his Power resides in the Sun, and his Wisdom in the Moon.* I wish that Faustus, or at least St. Augustine, who refutes him, had explained this bizarre mystery of Manichaeism to us: but they did not do so, neither one nor the other: Faustus, because he did not have the opportunity; and St. Augustine, perhaps because he did not know it. I have mused upon it, but I could only discover very uncertain conjectures.

<margin>Purification of Souls, by the wisdom and by the virtue of Jesus Christ.</margin>
Our Heretics <note>The Manichaeans.</note> had imagined that Souls, which return to Heaven, first stop in the Moon, as the nearest celestial body, and that after a fairly short stay they pass into the Sun. The Moon was, according to them, a waystation for Souls navigating from Earth to Heaven. They also said that Jesus Christ is the Savior and the Liberator of Souls who keep his commandments. These Principles being supposed, I thought that the Souls, which by the good use they make of the Savior's Grace, make themselves worthy of returning to Heaven, go to receive the first degree of their purification in the Moon, through the Wisdom of Jesus Christ. Is it not *Wisdom*, or the knowledge of Truth, which purifies Spirits? After which they pass into the Sun, where the *Power* <note>The original French uses "Vertu," which in this context implies divine power or efficacy.</note> of Jesus Christ completes their purification.

# HISTORY OF DOGMAS #

Another conjecture on this same subject. The African Manichaeans said (1) that the Sun is composed of a *pure* and benevolent *Fire*, and the Moon of *good Water*. Those in Egypt had other ideas. Now, since all purification is performed by *Fire* and by *Water*, it seems that the Manichaeans made the Souls pass first through the *Water* of the Moon and then through the *Fire* of the Sun, in order to complete their purification which had only begun on Earth. Thus, the Sun and the Moon were the *Purgatories* of Souls. I do not know what the Reader will think of this, but I am quite willing to say what I think. It is that it seems to me incomparably more reasonable to place Purgatory in these Planets than in the bowels of the Earth, or in some unknown Spaces, and to put Souls in the hands of Jesus Christ rather than in those of Demons, who plunge them sometimes into icy Waters and sometimes into burning flames. The *Wisdom* and the *Power* of the Son of God, wherever one places them, are fundamentally the true Purgatory of Souls.

<margin>VIII. The Air, the dwelling of the Holy Spirit.</margin>
VIII. We leave one obscurity to pass into another. The Holy Spirit being THE THIRD MAJESTY, the Manichaeans placed him in the Air, which surrounds the Earth. (2) *We believe*, says Faustus, <note>Faustus of Mileve, a 4th-century Manichaean bishop known for his debates with Saint Augustine.</note> *that the Holy Spirit, who is the* THIRD MAJESTY, *has for his seat all the Air that surrounds us, and that it is by his power, and by his spiritual outpourings, that the Earth conceives and gives birth to* THE PASSIBLE JESUS, <note>The "Passible Jesus" (Jesus Patibilis) is a Manichaean concept representing the divine Light or Life trapped in matter, which "suffers" by being bound to the earth and plants.</note> *who is the Life and Salvation of Men, and who hangs from every Tree.* This is certainly an enigma that is very difficult to explain. I do not believe that Saint Augustine understood it, for everything he says while refuting it clarifies nothing. I leave for now the *Passible Jesus*, of whom I will speak later, to make some Observations on the Sphere of the Holy Spirit.

> *The Word is like the Sun, and the Holy Spirit like the Moon*, which borrows its light from the Sun.

The *Word* communicates its spiritual brilliance to the Divine and intelligent Powers, which compose the first class of Beings in the Universe. The *Holy Spirit* communicates its own to the inferior Beings (4), to the Beings of the second Class, that is to say, to Human Souls. Thus the *Word* presides over the celestial Intelligences, and the *Holy Spirit* over those who are united to Matter. It is through his channel, and by his liberality, that they are enriched with Divine Graces and that they receive the light and the help necessary to defend themselves from Vices. <margin>They had to place him in the Air.</margin> Such being, then, according to Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century historian often cited for his accounts of early Christian and "heretical" beliefs.</note>, the opinion of the Hebrews; as they had to place the *Word* in the Heaven of pure Intelligences, they also had to put the *Holy Spirit* in the *Air*, and bring him closer to the Beings of his Department, so that he might pour out upon them his influences and his spiritual outpourings.

<margin>The Air, the dwelling of Souls according to many Philosophers.</margin>
I remark in the second place, that the *Holy Spirit* having the charge of Human Souls, it was natural to place him in the *Air*, which, according to the opinion of several ancient Philosophers, is the dwelling of Souls. (5)
> *It is there*, says Philo, <note>Philo of Alexandria, a Hellenistic Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize Greek philosophy with Jewish scripture.</note> *that they flutter incessantly.*

(6)
> *The Air*, he says further, *receives and contains the seeds of Souls, which the Creator scatters there by an admirable grace.*

And in another place, (7)
> *There is in the Air the sacred Choir of incorporeal Souls, which are the Ministers and the imitators of the Celestial Virtues. The sacred Oracles call them* ANGELS.

Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus, known for his writings on the soul and his opposition to early Christianity.</note> thinks and speaks much like Philo. (8)
> *Souls*, he says, *are aerial, and it is believed that they draw their substance from the Air.*

If we wish to rely on *Tyrbon*, Mani <note>The founder of Manichaeism.</note> was of this last sentiment. He believed, (9)
> *that the Air is the Soul of Men and of Animals.*

But I am persuaded that *Tyrbon* is mistaken, and that he has confused the *Soul* with *Life*, or our *Air*, which we breathe, with the celestial and pure *Air* which is in the supreme Heaven. Whatever the case may be, many Philosophers placed Souls in the *Air*, and Pythagoras believed, (10) that it is entirely filled with them. Thus, the *Air* being the seat of Souls, according to these Philosophers, and the *Holy Spirit* having the charge of Souls, it is not surprising that they placed him also

<margin>IX. The Holy Spirit is the Active Intellect of the Peripatetics. They placed this Intellect in the Air.</margin>
IX. These first Observations begin to shed some light on the Manichaean System; but the one I am about to add will finish clarifying it. The <term>Peripatetic</term> <note>The Peripatetics were followers of Aristotle's philosophy, known for his systematic approach to logic and nature.</note> Philosophers conceived of two <term>Intellects</term>, or two *Spirits* in the World; one, which they named <term>Active</term> <note>Original Latin: *Intellectum agentem*</note>, and which is separated from Matter: the other, which they called <term>Passive</term> <note>Original Latin: *Intellectum passibilem*</note>, which is united to Matter, and which is the Spirit of Man. *Algazel* <note>Al-Ghazali, a central theologian and philosopher in the Islamic tradition.</note> imagined that this *Active* Intelligence, which illuminates Human Understanding, resides in the *Moon*; but *Avicenna* <note>Ibn Sina, a famous Persian polymath who integrated Aristotelian philosophy with Islamic theology.</note> placed it below the Moon, and in the Elementary World: *Avennazar* and *Averroes* <note>Averroes, or Ibn Rushd, was a medieval Andalusian philosopher known for his commentaries on Aristotle.</note> believed that it only presides over the Human Species. This is certainly the Theology of the Manichaeans. The *Active* Intellect, which resides in the *Air*, is nothing other than the *Holy Spirit*, who communicates his Light to Souls, and who gives them the strength to resist the irregular movements of the Matter to which they are united.

<margin>X. Explanation of a passage from Photius.</margin>
X. I have only one more Remark to make concerning a passage from *Photius* <note>Photius I of Constantinople, a 9th-century patriarch and scholar who documented many ancient works now lost.</note>. He says, in the Extract of *Agapius*, that this famous Manichaean (2) "spoke of the Air as a Divinity, and praised it in his Hymns as if it were <term>a Man and a Column</term>." These are ideas that appear very ill-suited. Is the *Air* a Column? Can a Column be a *man*? Can a *man* be a *God* in a Sect that certainly never deified men? Nothing is more absurd in appearance, but it is far from being so in reality. Let us separate the false from the true, and develop the thought of *Agapius*.

<margin>What the Perfect Air of the Manichaeans is.</margin>
This man celebrated in Hymns the state of blessed Souls when they have reached supreme happiness. There they breathe a <term>Perfect Air</term>, which is not at all mixed with the vapors of Matter; which is not agitated by tempests, nor obscured by clouds and the veils of night. It is the pure *Ether* that the ancient Philosophers believed to be the dwelling of Souls. There they shine with a pure and solid Light, with a Glory that will never be tarnished, and whose stability equals its perfection. It is, so to speak, supported on Columns of eternal duration. These

This is all I have been able to discover until now regarding the System of Manichaeus on the Nature and Attributes of God, and on the Divine Persons.

<margin>III. Other names given to them. That of Numbers.</margin>
III. The Philosophers thus sought terms to express simple and immortal Substances. Pythagoras <note>A famous Greek philosopher and mathematician (c. 570–495 BCE) who believed that numbers were the ultimate reality of the universe.</note> called them NUMBERS. Nothing is more abstract nor more immaterial. Synesius <note>Synesius of Cyrene (c. 373–414), a Neoplatonist philosopher who became a Christian bishop, known for blending Greek philosophy with Christian hymns.</note> imitated him in his Hymns, where he calls God (6) the UNITY OF IMMORTAL NUMBERS and of Immaterial Kings. This means that God is the very simple Principle of pure Intelligences. The same Author says elsewhere to the Son of God, (7) *You are the Unity of Unities, the* NUMBER OF NUMBERS. *You are Unity and Number together. Synesius* seems to copy the very words of Pythagoras, for *Hierocles* <note>Hierocles of Alexandria (5th century CE), a Neoplatonist who wrote a famous commentary on the "Golden Verses" of Pythagoras.</note> mentions a Sacred Book that was attributed to this Philosopher, (8) in which he praised the Divinity and called Him THE NUMBER OF NUMBERS. As for the words of *Synesius*, they signify that the *Word* <note>original: "Verbe," often used to translate the Greek "Logos," referring to the Divine Reason or the second person of the Trinity.</note>, who is Unity in His Nature, is *Number* in relation to His effects, because He is the Author of all Intelligences. All pure Spirit that exists in our world and outside our world emanates from the *Word* or Divine Reason.

<margin>That of Ideas.</margin>
*Plato*, who followed in the footsteps of *Pythagoras*, left aside *Numbers* and substituted *Ideas* for them. Nothing yet is more abstract nor more immaterial. *Synesius*, a faithful follower of *Plato*, did not fail to imitate the expression of this Philosopher and to call God (9) the IDEA OF IDEAS, and immense Beauty.

<margin>And of Words.</margin>
Other Philosophers believed it was better to designate Intelligences by the Attribute of Wisdom and Reason, and named them WORDS <note>original: "Verbes," from the Greek "Logoi." In this context, it refers to spiritual entities or rational principles.</note>. *Plutarch* says somewhere (10) that the WORDS, the *Ideas*, or the *Forms*, and the *Divine Emanations reside in the Heaven and in the Stars. Philo* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who sought to harmonize the Torah with Greek philosophy.</note> (11) gives the name of *Word* to Angels in more than one place. The Valentinians <note>Followers of Valentinus, a prominent 2nd-century Gnostic teacher who developed a complex system of Aeons or divine emanations.</note> (12) called the Son of God and their other *Aeons* in this way indifferently, although they did not place them on a parallel with Him. They defined an *Angel* as (13) *a Word charged with announcing something on behalf of the Sovereign Being, or the Being par excellence.*

<margin>III. Other Names given to them. That of Numbers.</margin>
III. The Philosophers thus sought terms to express simple & immortal Substances. Pythagoras called them NUMBERS (6) <note>In Pythagorean thought, numbers were not just symbols but the actual, immaterial building blocks of reality.</note>. Plato, who followed in the footsteps of Pythagoras, left aside *Numbers* and substituted them with *Ideas*. Nothing, again, more abstract nor more immaterial. *Synesius*, a faithful *Follower of Plato*, did not fail also to imitate the expression of this Philosopher, and to call God (9) the IDEA OF IDEAS, & *immense Beauty*.

<margin>And of Verbs.</margin>

The *Valentinians* (12) <note>A prominent Gnostic sect founded by Valentinus in the 2nd century.</note> indifferently called both the Son of God and their other *Aeons* by this name, although they did not put them on a level with Him. They defined an *Angel* as (13) a *Word* charged with *announcing something on behalf of the Sovereign Being*, or *the Being par excellence*.

<margin>
Explanation of the name Word given to the Son of God by St. John.
(a) John 1:1.
</margin>
It is perhaps in this usage by the philosophers contemporary with *St. John* that one should seek the origin of an expression that is particular to him, and which he nevertheless uses as a common and known expression, since he does not explain it at all. *(a) In the beginning, he says, was the Word.* It is believed that he makes an allusion to the History of Creation by *Moses*, in which God executes everything by the sole force of His command, and that the Evangelist wanted to teach us that *the Word*, which created the Universe, is a *Substantial Word*, and the very Son of God. I do not reject this thought; it does not conflict with mine regarding the use of the term *Word* <note>original: "Parole" or "Verbe."</note>. Pagan, Jewish, and Christian philosophers called pure Spirits *Words*. *St. John* is quite willing to adopt this expression and use it to designate the Divine Nature of the Savior. But in adopting it, because it was as appropriate and familiar as it is noble, he prevents the abuse that might be made of it and distinguishes the Son of God by these two prerogatives, which are unique to Him. The first is that He is the WORD par excellence. *In the beginning was the Word.* The second is that He was not only with *God* like other spirits, BUT THAT HE WAS GOD. *The Word, he says, was with God, and the Word was God.* This is my thought, which I propose to the reader in passing. Let us return to our subject.

Philosophers and theologians, seeking terms to express incorporeal substances, thus designated them by some of their attributes or by some of their operations. They called them *Spirits*, because of the subtlety of their substance, which escapes all the senses; *Intelligences*, because of Thought; *Words*, because of Reason; *Angels*, because of their Ministry; *Eons* or *Aeons* <note>Aeon (from the Greek *Aion*) refers to an eternal age, or in Gnostic thought, a divine power or emanation from God.</note> because of their Immortality and their manner of always subsisting equally, without change and without alteration. In a word, *Aeons* and *Immortals* are synonymous terms.

<margin>Arrian uses it to mean a God.</margin>
...celestial Intelligences. He bases this on the fact that they rendered the Hebrew word *Olam* <note>original: "Holam"; in Hebrew, *Olam* can mean "world," "eternity," or "age."</note> by the word *Aion*, which in their usage signifies not only what we call an *Age*, or a long duration, but the *World* itself. I do not believe this conjecture is well-founded. It is neither the World, nor creatures in general, that the heretics called *Aeons* <note>original: "Aiones."</note>. They were only the Intelligences, and even then, usually the most perfect and sublime ones. Furthermore, although Hellenistic Jews, such as *Philo* for example, used this expression when speaking of Angels, Pagan authors did so as well, and there is no appearance that they took it from the Jews. *Arrian* has his *Epictetus* say, (1) *I am not an* AEON, *but a* MAN: *I am a part of the Universe, as an hour is a part of the day. I must come and pass away like that hour.* AEON means, in this passage, a *God*, an *Immortal*. Note that *Arrian* flourished under *Hadrian*, by whom he was much loved, and under whose reign the partisans—but not the inventors—of the doctrine of *Aeons* arose. Monsieur de *Tillemont* (2) attributes the invention of this doctrine to *Simon Magus* <note>Simon Magus is traditionally considered the first Gnostic, a magician who clashed with the Apostles.</note>, but we shall soon see that he was mistaken.

<margin>V. The innocence of this expression. The Fathers call the Divine Persons "Aeons."</margin>
V. It is right to clear away prejudices that stem less from ignorance than from a poorly understood aversion to heretics. *Clement of Alexandria* (3) rightly said that not all the opinions of sectarians are evil, vain, or contemptible. Let us say the same of their *Ideas* and their *Terms*. However, bias goes so far that one might say that down to the very word *Aeon*, everything is considered heretical, and that one cannot use it without falling into the fantasies of *Simon*, *Menander*, *Valentinus*, and their like. This is prejudice and, if I may dare say so, pure weakness. The Fathers <note>The "Church Fathers" were the influential theologians of the early Christian Church.</note> have no difficulty in naming as *Aeons* not only the celestial Intelligences, but even the *Divine Persons*. If *Valentinus* calls the Divinity (4) the PERFECT AEON, *Synesius* praises Him in his hymns under the glorious title (5) of AEON OF AEONS <note>original: "Σὺ δὲ Ἄναξ Ἀιών Ἀιών" (But You, O King, are the Aeon of Aeons).</note>. He seems to imitate the pseudo-*Dionysius the Areopagite*, who calls God, (6) *the beginning and the measure of ages, the essence of Time, the Aeon of all that exists, and finally the Aeon of Aeons.* <note>original: "Ἀρχὴ καὶ μέτρον αἰώνων... ὁ Αἰὼν αἰώνων" (The beginning and measure of ages... the Aeon of aeons, who exists before the aeons).</note> We have a hymn by *St. Clement of Alexandria* in honor of the Son of God, in which he qualifies Him indifferently as (7) the *Eternal Word* and the *INFINITE AEON* <note>original: "Λόγος αἰώνιος. Αἰὼν ἀπλεῖτος."</note>. The Martyr *Methodius* calls Him (8) <note>original: "Τὸν πρεσβύτατον τῶν Αἰώνων" (The eldest of the Aeons).</note>

(a) John 1:1.
</margin>
It would perhaps be in this usage of the Philosophers contemporary with St. *John* that one should seek the origin of an expression which is peculiar to him, and which he nevertheless uses as a common and well-known expression, since he did not explain it at all. (a) *In the beginning*, he says, *was the Word* <note>original: "Verbe"; translated here as "Word," corresponding to the Greek "Logos," signifying both speech and reason.</note>. It is believed that he is making an allusion to the History of Creation by *Moses*, in which God executes everything by the sole force of his command, and that the Evangelist wanted to teach us that the *Word* which created the Universe is a *Substantial* Word, and the very Son of God. I do not reject this thought; it does not conflict with my own regarding the use of the term *Speech* or *Word*. Pagan, Jewish, and Christian Philosophers called pure Spirits *Words*. St. *John* is willing to adopt this expression and use it to designate the Divine Nature of the Savior. But in adopting it, because it was as appropriate and familiar as it is noble, he prevents the abuse that could be made of it and distinguishes the Son of God by these two prerogatives which are unique to him. The first, that he is the WORD par excellence. *In the beginning was the Word*. The second, that he was not only with God like the other Spirits, but THAT HE WAS GOD. *The Word*, he says, *was with God, and the Word was God*. This is my thought, which I propose to the Reader in passing. Let us return to our subject.

Philosophers and Theologians, seeking terms to express incorporeal Substances, designated them by some of their attributes or some of their operations. They called them *Spirits*, because of the *subtlety* of their Substance, which escapes all the Senses; *Intelligences*, because of *Thought*; *Words*, because of *Reason*; *Angels*, because of their *Ministry*; *Aeons* or *Aiones* <note>original: "Eons" / "Aiones"; from the Greek "Aion," meaning an age, an eternity, or a divine being in Gnostic systems.</note> because of their *Immortality* and their manner of always subsisting equally, without change and without alteration. In a word, *Aeons* and *Immortals* are synonymous terms.

Celestial intelligences. He bases this on the fact that they rendered the Hebrew word *Olam* <note>The Hebrew term *Olam* typically refers to eternity or the world.</note> by that of *Aeon* <note>original: *Aion*</note>, which in their usage signifies not only what we call a *Century*, or a long duration, but the World itself. I do not believe this conjecture is well-founded. It is neither the World nor Creatures in general that the Heretics called *Aeons* <note>original: *Aiones*</note>. These are only the Intelligences, and even ordinarily the most perfect and sublime ones. Moreover, although the Hellenistic Jews, like *Philo*, for example, used this expression when speaking of Angels, the Pagan authors did so too, and there is no appearance that they took it from the Jews. <margin>Arrian uses it to mean a God.</margin> *Arrian* has his *Epictetus* (1) say, *I am not an* AEON, *but a* MAN: *I am a part of the Universe, as an hour is a part of the Day.* <note>original: "Je ne suis pas un EON, mais un HOMME: Je suis une partie de l'Univers, comme une heure est une partie du Jour."</note> I must come and pass like that hour. AEON means in this place a *God*, an *Immortal*. Note that *Arrian* flourished under *Hadrian*, by whom he was much loved, and under whom the Partisans, but not the Inventors, of the Doctrine of *Aeons* arose. M. de *Tillemont* (2) gives the invention of it to *Simon* the Magician <note>Also known as Simon Magus, often cited by early Church historians as the first heretic.</note>, but we will soon see that he was mistaken.

<margin>V. The Innocence of this Expression. The Church Fathers call the Divine Persons Aeons.</margin> V. It is right to erase prejudices, which come less from ignorance than from a misunderstood aversion for Heretics. *Clement of Alexandria* (3) very well said that not all the opinions of Sectarians are bad, nor vain and contemptible. Let us say the same thing of their ideas and their terms. However, prejudice goes so far that one would say that even the word *Aeon* is entirely heretical, and that one cannot use it without falling into the reveries of *Simon*, *Menander*, *Valentinus*, and their like. This is prejudice, and if I dare say, pure weakness. The Fathers make no difficulty in naming *Aeons* not only the celestial Intelligences, but the Divine Persons. If *Valentinus* calls the Divinity (4) the PERFECT AEON, *Synesius* praises him in his Hymns under the glorious title (5) of AEON OF AEONS <note>Greek original: Σὺ δὲ Ἄναξ Αἰῶν' Αἰών — "You, Lord, are the Aeon of Aeons."</note>. Regarding simple Intelligences, the Greek and Latin Fathers quite often call them *Aeons* <term>Aeon: Derived from the Greek "Aion," this term usually refers to an age or eternity, but in this context, it refers to eternal celestial beings or "Intelligences" inhabiting the divine realm.</term>. ### ON MANICHAEISM. Book III. CH. IX.

<margin>Explanation of Ephesians 2:2.</margin>
...think, it seems more natural to me than any other. St. **Paul** says literally: *You walked according to* the AEON of this WORLD <note>original: "Κατὰ τὸν 'Αιῶνα τῶ κόσμυ τότυ"</note> *according to the Prince of the Power of the Air, of those Spirits who work with efficacy in the Children of rebellion.* The advantages of this translation are: 1. that no violence is done to the terms used by St. **Paul**. The AEON of this WORLD is the same thing as the Prince of this World and the God of this Age. 2. One would not be obliged to give the word *Aeon* <term>Aeon: Here used to denote a powerful spiritual being or personification of an age, rather than just a period of time.</term> a sense that is not nearly so simple and natural as that one. 3. The ancient Latin interpreter must have understood it this way; for in the Version used in Africa during the time of St. **Augustine**, one read *according to the* <margin>(a) According to Augustine, Against Fortunatus, Discourse I.</margin> POWER *of this World*; (a) *according to the* GOVERNANCE <note>original: "MAGISTERIUM"</note> *of this World*. *Magisterium* signifies an Order of Magistrates or Superiors. 4. St. **Jerome** does not distance himself from this explanation. It is (9) one of those he proposes. 5. I add to these remarks that of the learned Mr. **Fabricius**, who says regarding these words from the Epistle to the Hebrews: <margin>(b) Heb. 1:2.</margin> (b) *By whom God made the Ages*, (10) *That by the Ages, or the Aeons, one may very well understand the Angels.*

<margin>VI. The Heretics did not take their Aeons from Hesiod.</margin>
VI. These are my reflections on the meaning and origin of this famous name, which was given to Spirits, but which became infamous because of the use the Heretics made of it. Let us now see what we should think about the origin of the System of Aeons. It is an old opinion, and very common among (11) the Fathers, that **Valentinus** <note>Valentinus was a mid-2nd century Gnostic theologian who developed a complex system of thirty divine emanations called Aeons.</note> did nothing but imitate **Hesiod**, and that the *Theogony* of this Poet was the source from which the Heretic took his Aeons and their genealogy. This conjecture has something plausible about it. **Hesiod** begins with *Chaos* and *Night*. One might say these first two Gods resemble quite well the first two Aeons of Valentinus, which are BYTHOS and SIGE: PROFUNDITY and SILENCE. Hesiod's *Theogony* contains the genealogy of thirty Gods, and there are likewise *thirty* Aeons in the theology of Valentinus. However, I cannot—

(10) *In which place it is not absurd to understand the Aeons as Angels.* Fabricius, *Codex Apocryphus of the New Testament*, Vol. I. p. 710.
(11) This is the sentiment of St. Irenaeus, followed by St. Epiphanius and other Ancients, and adopted by Mr. Le Clerc (Bibliot. Ch. Vol. X. p. 190) and generally by the Moderns. Stillingfleet derives

# HISTORY OF DOGMAS

[...could] persuade me that a Philosopher who made profession of Christianity went to draw his Ideas from a Pagan Poem, which was known to everyone, and which is only a tissue of Fables. The Poet borrows the Dogmas of the Philosopher, or the Theologian, and adorns them with ingenious fictions. Orpheus, Homer, and Virgil did so. But will the Philosopher and the Theologian take from the Poet, not only the Dogmas, but the Fictions themselves? Moreover, *Valentinus* <note>A 2nd-century Gnostic theologian who founded the Valentinian school.</note> was a great Platonist, and in this capacity, he could only condemn the fabulous and licentious Theology of the Poets. But here is an Objection, to which I do not know what one can answer.

<margin>Hesiod's Theogony is the Creation of the corporeal World.</margin>
"Hesiod's *Theogony* <note>A poem by Hesiod describing the origins and genealogies of the Greek gods.</note> is nothing other than the Creation of the material and visible World, whose principal parts this Poet has deified, in accordance with Pagan Theology. In the style of the Poets, Theogony is the same thing as *Cosmogony* <note>The study of the origin of the universe.</note> in that of the Philosophers. Thus Hesiod described the formation of the visible World, of which all his Gods are so many essential Parts or Attributes. But the Valentinians wanted to describe the origin of the spiritual World, of the Intelligences who emanate from the Divinity, and who reside outside the enclosure of the Material World. Thus the Theogony of Hesiod and that of the Valentinians are as different as Intelligences are from Bodies, and Originals from their Images."

<margin>VII. The Philosophies of Pythagoras, of Plato, and of the Jewish Kabbalah are the origin of the Aeons.</margin>

The Aeons <term>Aeon: In Gnostic thought, these are divine beings or powers that emanate from the supreme Godhead, representing different aspects of the divine nature.</term> of Tatian <note>A 2nd-century Syrian Christian writer and theologian who became a leader of the ascetic Encratites.</note> are the Intelligible Gods of Aristotle, and the Ideas of Plato. These are precisely the Aeons, their Origin and their Properties. It is from there that the Heretics, who were generally Platonists, took their Doctrine. It is from this source that the Valentinians drew, as (5) Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage, known for his polemics against heresy.</note> has very well remarked. I only suspect that all this Pneumatic Philosophy <term>Pneumatic Philosophy: A system of thought centered on the *pneuma* (spirit), often involving the belief that spiritual reality is the only true reality.</term> came originally from the Chaldeans, from where it passed to the Greeks.

St. *Epiphanius* <note>Epiphanius of Salamis, a 4th-century church father known for his "Panarion," a refutation of various heresies.</note> confirms this latter thought. (1) He says that when the only-begotten Son wished to make God known, (1) *Sige* (Silence) prevented him by the Father's command. However, when I considered that what the Valentinians <note>Followers of Valentinus, who taught that the divine realm consists of a series of paired emanations called Aeons.</note> called *Sige*, they also called *Ennoea* (Thought), I conjectured that *Sige* was the mystical and enigmatic name of *Ennoea*, and that these two words meant the same thing. What gave me this idea is a passage from *Pausanias*, which informs us that the Phoenicians called *Minerva* (2) **SIGA**. Now it is well known that in Pagan Mythology, *Minerva* is nothing other than *Divine Wisdom*. If one admits this conjecture, the Valentinians meant to say that the infinite and incomprehensible Being, in concert with his *Wisdom*, produced **NOUS** and **ALETHEIA**—the Understanding or pure *Spirit* and *Truth*.

<margin>X. Concerning the Aeons Nous and Aletheia, pure Spirit and Truth. Properties of pure Spirit.</margin>
X. One clearly recognizes in these two *Aeons* <term>Aeon: In Gnostic systems, these are divine powers or beings that emanate from the supreme Godhead.</term>, and in those that follow, the Platonism of the Valentinians. It is known that Plato conceived of an Intelligence, which he called **NOUS**, and which was the first Production of the Father and the Principle of all things. It is from this Intelligence that all pure Spirit (*Mens*) in intelligent beings emanates. The privileges of this Spirit are, firstly, to be perfectly simple, indivisible, and unalterable; this is why Plato names it the **SAME** <note>A reference to the "Same" and the "Different" in Plato's *Timaeus*, describing the composition of the World Soul.</note>. Secondly, it knows truths by itself, in an intuitive manner, so to speak, without the help of the Senses, Imagination, or Reasoning. This is seen in the passage from Porphyry <note>A 3rd-century Neoplatonist philosopher and student of Plotinus.</note>, (3) which I cite at the bottom of the page.

<margin>The idea of Truth that accompanies it.</margin>
**NOUS** emanated from the Father along with *Truth*; *Truth* is the inseparable companion and the essential property of the first Intelligence, which alone has the advantage of seeing God, and of seeing in him the eternal Ideas of all things—those models of everything that exists and ever will exist. This is also Platonic. Furthermore, there is a *Metaphysical Truth*, which belongs to beings that are perfectly simple and immutable. Everything that is composed is subject to change.

### OF MANICHAEISM. BOOK III, CH. IX. 581

...judgment and contains falsehood. (4) Nothing is true except that which always exists as the same, and without any alteration. One can see what the pseudo-Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary figure, often associated with the fusion of the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, to whom many mystical and philosophical writings were attributed.</note> says on this subject, who, as far as one can judge, lived at the same time as Valentinus, and who was Egyptian and Platonic like him.

<margin>Logos and Zoe—Reason and Life—make up the universal soul.</margin>
From **NOUS** and **ALETHEIA** were born **LOGOS** and **ZOE**, that is to say, the Word or Reason and Life. This is evidently the Soul of the Universe, of which Life and Reason are the two properties, and which, in the system of Plato, is the second of the Intelligences that proceeded from the Divine Nature. What follows is a mixture of Platonism and Christianity. From the Soul of the Universe descends the Human Soul, which the Valentinians called **MAN**, in accordance with the language of Plato and other Philosophers, who regarded the Body as a part foreign to Man, and as a prison rather than the dwelling place of the Soul. The **CHURCH** is a Christian idea. The Valentinians did not properly compose it of mortal and earthly men, but of immortal souls, and placed it in Heaven, from where souls descend to animate and govern the bodies with which Providence is pleased to clothe them.

<margin>XI. This Doctrine of Aeons is pure Platonism.</margin>
<margin>The first four Aeons make the Tetrad of Pythagoras.</margin>
XI. It is clear, I believe, at present, that the Valentinian Ogdoad <term>Ogdoad: A group of eight primary divine beings or Aeons in Gnostic cosmogony.</term> is nothing other than Platonism. *Bythos* is the infinite and incomprehensible Being: it is God. *Nous* is the first Intelligence that proceeds from it. *Logos* and *Zoe* make up the universal soul, or the second Intelligence, which emanates from God through the channel of the first. *Man* and the *Church* are Human Souls, which derive their origin from the universal soul. All of this is Platonic. The Heretics only added some foreign ideas to it, which served to disguise the system, to give it an air of novelty, and an air of Christianity. I do not believe that the Valentinians denied this, for St. Irenaeus testifies (5) that they claimed their first four Aeons—*Bythos*, *Sige*, *Nous*, and *Aletheia*—were the Tetrad of Pythagoras. We find nothing similar in any ancient author who spoke of the mysteries of Pythagoreanism. Theodore Marcilli, who gathered into his notes on the *Golden Verses* of the Pythagoreans everything he had read on the subject, makes no mention of it. This is why I do...
