<margin>Explanation of this Tetrad.</margin>
I do not doubt that what (1) Thomas Artus d’Embri <note>A 17th-century French writer known for his commentaries on Philostratus and his work on Hermetic philosophy.</note> said of it was taken from St. Irenaeus, who indeed does not contradict the testimony of the Valentinians. On the contrary, he seems to confirm it. The Tetrad <term>Tetrad: From the Greek 'tetraktys,' a group of four; in Pythagoreanism, it represented the source of all existence.</term> of Pythagoras was nothing other than the Divine Nature, or at least a Divine Person with his primary attributes. This is evident from the oath of the Pythagoreans (a).

<margin>Oath of the Pythagoreans. (a) See *Golden Verses*, v. 47.</margin>
> Nay (or Yea), by Him who transmitted to our Soul the Tetrad, 
> The fountain of eternal Nature.
<note>Original Greek: "Οὐ (Aut. Ναὶ) μὰ τὸν ἁμετέρᾳ ψυχᾷ παραδόντα τετρακτὺν Πάγαν ἀενάου Φύσεως."</note>

->*That is to say, I swear by him who taught our Soul the Tetrad, which is the Root of permanent Nature.*<-

(2) *This Tetrad is the Creator of all things, the Intelligible God, who is the Author of the celestial and sensible God, that is to say, of the Sun.* I draw this explanation from Hierocles <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher of the 5th century AD who wrote a famous commentary on the Pythagorean Golden Verses.</note>, whose words I report here. The Reader will permit me to place (3) at the bottom of the page some critical observations on the oath of the Pythagoreans. But what I beg him to note well is that the Valentinians had not taken their *Theogony* <term>Theogony: An account of the origin or genealogy of the gods.</term> from *Hesiod*, though the Church Fathers say so; they took it from the philosophy of Pythagoras; from that of Plato, and to go further back, from that of the Chaldeans.

<margin>XII. Marriages of the Aeons. A mystical idea common to the Platonists.</margin>
XII. One finds some ridicule—though I do not know if it is not more apparent than real—in the method of the Valentinians who made their Aeons some Male and others Female, and who married them together. This language was mystical and very familiar to the Philosophers. Plato, Philo, and the Kabbalists used it. In the style of Philo, *the Husband is nothing other than the active Cause, and the Wife than the passive Cause or the subject.* From this comes the fact that one and the same Being is sometimes Husband and Wife: Husband, by opposition...

...opposition to an inferior Being upon which it acts; and **Wife** in relation to a Superior Being that acts upon it. For example, the Moon is the *Husband* of the Earth because it acts upon the Earth; but she is the **Wife** of the Sun because the Sun acts upon her. It is the same with the **Spirit** (*Mens*), the **Soul**, and the **Body**. The **Soul** is the **Wife** in relation to the **Spirit**, and the *Husband* in relation to the **Body**. So much for natural things. The author of the book titled *The Kabbalah Unveiled* <note>Original title: *Kabbala Denudata*, a major 17th-century work by Christian Knorr von Rosenroth that introduced Jewish mystical texts to a Latin-reading European audience.</note> informs us (4) "that, when dealing with Divine things, the Kabbalists understand by the **Wife** an inclination of the Cause to communicate itself, and to produce Beings similar to itself, but less great and less perfect than the Cause." This is not quite the same thing in the <term>Aeons: In Gnostic systems, these are the various emanations or "levels" of the divine being, often paired in male-female couples called syzygies.</term> of the Valentinians. The **Husband** is the Substance; the **Wife** is (5) only a **Faculty** or an **attribute**, by means of which the Substance produces a certain effect. For example, they will marry God with his **Goodness**, and from this Marriage they will bring forth all Divine Graces. They will similarly marry him with **Justice**, and from it they will bring forth Punishments and Penalties.

<margin>The Wives of the Aeons are only their attributes or their Faculties.</margin>
<margin>The opinion of Ptolemy explained.</margin>
Ptolemy <note>A prominent disciple of Valentinus in the 2nd century AD who modified the Gnostic system into a more structured form.</note>, who changed several things in the System of his Masters, made God (6) **Polygamous**, and gave him two Wives. But if one asks **St. Epiphanius** <note>A 4th-century bishop and heresiologist known for his "Panarion," a massive work attacking various heresies.</note> what these Wives were, he will tell us they are nothing but two (7) **Attributes** or two **Powers** of the Divine Nature, namely (8) **Thought** and **Will**. He tells us that **Thought** was always in God, because he always had the design to produce Beings; but that **Will** was not always there, because otherwise he would have produced them from all Eternity. As long as **Thought** was alone, she was sterile; but as soon as **Will** united with her, everything that **Thought** had conceived actually existed. **St. Epiphanius** (9), who attributes all this to **Ptolemy**, cries out at the extravagance of it; but with the exception of some inaccuracy, I do not see...

### HISTORY OF DOGMAS

...I see nothing so foolish in that. The first two Attributes of the Divine Nature are *Understanding* and *Will*. The Ideas of all things were from all eternity in the Divine *Understanding*; the Design to produce them was there, but they only really existed at the moment that God willed it. This is not poorly thought out.

<margin>XIII. In what sense the Valentinians made God and their Aeons of both sexes.</margin>
XIII. Here is another idea of the <term>Valentinians: Followers of Valentinus (c. 100–160 AD), a prominent Gnostic teacher who taught that the invisible divine world was composed of pairs of male and female principles.</term>, which the Church Fathers turned into ridicule, and which at heart perhaps did not deserve it so much. For under the pretext that the *Wives* of the <term>Aeons: Divine emanations or powers that make up the fullness of God's presence.</term> are not persons different from their *Husbands*, this Sect has been accused of making its Aeons into so many (1) **Hermaphrodites**. We should not believe the Valentinians were foolish enough to assign physical sexes to the Divine Nature, which is the first of the *Aeons*, nor to the spiritual Substances that emanate from it. Let us believe even less that they made them into monsters with two sexes. Otherwise, we would have to attribute the same madness to one of the most learned and polished Bishops of Antiquity, who used the same language as the Valentinians because he was a Philosopher and a Platonist like them.

<margin>Synesius attributes them to God.</margin>
(2) *You are*, he said to God in one of his Hymns, *you are the Root of things past, present, and future. You are the Root of everything that exists. YOU ARE THE FATHER, YOU ARE THE MOTHER, YOU ARE THE MALE, YOU ARE THE FEMALE*: <note>Original Greek: "Σὺ πατὴρ, σὺ δ' ἐσσὶ μήτηρ / Σὺ δ' ἄῤῥην, σὺ δὲ θῆλυς." (You are the father, you are the mother / You are the male, you are the female.) Synesius, Hymn II, v. 90. See also Hymn III, v. 186. Synesius of Cyrene was a 4th-century Neo-Platonist philosopher who became a Christian Bishop.</note> a thought he repeats again in other places. He was nonetheless aware that God is a Spiritual Being, who has no bodily organs, let alone those of generation. Here then is what it means, in relation to God and Spirits, to have both Sexes. It is to unite two Powers, of which one—as the most noble—is represented as the *Male*, and the other—as the less noble—is represented as the *Female*; it is to produce, through the cooperation of these two Powers, *Beings* who participate in them. In a word, it is to unite within oneself and in a perfect <term>Monad: A single, indivisible unit; in philosophy, the ultimate source of all things.</term>, those Powers which are separated in Animals, and to perform alone what can only be done in Nature by the cooperation of the two sexes. I derive this explanation from the pseudo-Hermes Trismegistus, whose words are as follows (3)

### CHAPTER X.

#### On the AEONS of MANI and DIVINE EMANATIONS.

<margin>
Mani conceives of the Aeons as real Persons.
</margin>
I. THE *Aeons of Mani* <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD) was the founder of Manichaeism, a major dualistic religion that saw the universe as a struggle between light and darkness.</note> were not Divine Perfections, but real Persons—perfectly pure Spirits who assist before the Throne of God, who contemplate, adore, and serve him. The question would be to know what origin he gave to them. For we are not sufficiently informed of his System to determine with entire certainty whether he believed them eternal like God, or formed from the pure light of Heaven, or finally emanated from the Divine Substance. Let us examine these three opinions without deciding which was his own.

<margin>
Three opinions on their origin. Mani may have believed them eternal without believing them to be Gods.
</margin>
II. The first will perhaps seem most absurd to us because, according to our Principles, self-existence is inseparable from all possible perfections. IV. The manner in which the system of *Manichaeus* <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism.</note> is represented to us would lead one to judge that he preferred the third sentiment, and that he believed the Aeons were Emanations of the Divinity. But since, according to our Principles, everything that emanates from God must be God, and consequently *Manichaeus* would have multiplied the Divinity to infinity—which he did not intend to do—it is necessary to develop here the Theology of the Ancients on the Article of Divine Emanations. Our Principles are sound: our consequences well-drawn: but their accuracy and necessity have not always been recognized. And to judge the opinions of ancient Heretics soundly and equitably, one must, as I have remarked more than once, go back to the time in which they lived, and compare their sentiments with those that were then accepted, and which are not yet entirely banished from the Faith.

Petau <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a prominent Jesuit theologian and scholar.</note> tells us then (3) *that there are I know not what Beings, who are* WORKS OF GOD, *and who* PROCEED FROM HIS NATURE AND HIS PROPERTIES, AS LIGHT EMANATES FROM THE SUN. These are not Divine Persons. They are Works of God: however, they come out of *his Nature and his Properties*. This is the sentiment of Dionysius the Areopagite <note>A 5th-century Christian theologian whose writings blended Christian doctrine with Neoplatonism.</note>, and that of Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor (c. 580–662 AD), who wrote extensive commentaries on Dionysius.</note> his Commentator. These Writers do not doubt that the Divine Nature is a simple and indivisible Substance: but they do not fail to say that it produces outside itself thinking Substances, which they call EMANATIONS, OR PROCESSIONS. (4) *Procession, says Father Petau, is a certain* EFFUSION (OR DIFFUSION) *and as it were an* EXTENSION OF THE SOVEREIGN AND SIMPLE SUBSTANCE. (5) *It comes out in some way from itself, or at least from its Unity, because it proceeds from Unity to number and to multitude*, as Gregory of Nazianzus <note>A 4th-century Archbishop of Constantinople and one of the "Cappadocian Fathers."</note>, Dionysius himself, and other Fathers commonly express it. These Productions of the Divinity are called (6) *Participating Beings*, because they participate in the Divine Nature. They are (7) BEFORE TIME, AND ABOVE TIME. They are (8) *Works of God, but they are Works that did not begin with Time*. (9) *They* EMANATE FROM ALL ETERNITY FROM THE DIVINE NATURE, *as splendor emanates from the Sun*.

Comparison of the production of Ideas used by Heretics and by Catholics.

VI. It would be difficult to approve this sentiment, and to condemn that which is attributed to Manichaeus <note>Mani (c. 216–274 AD), the founder of Manichaeism, often viewed as a heretic by the early Church.</note>, without falling into partiality and manifest contradiction. It is the same Hypothesis. It is explained the same way, and defended by the same reasons. When the Manichaeans were asked how Intelligences can emanate from God without his Essence being either divided or diminished, they answered first, (10) that no one is foolish enough to admit any reduction or division in the Divine Nature: And secondly, that Spirits emanate from the Divinity, (11) as knowledge and Ideas pass from the Mind of the master into that of his disciples, without the Master's Knowledge suffering any diminution.

IV. The manner in which the system of *Manichaeus* is represented to us would lead one to judge that he preferred the third sentiment, and that he believed the *Aeons* were Emanations of the Divinity. But since, according to our Principles, everything that emanates from God must be God, and consequently Manichaeus would have multiplied the Divinity to infinity—which he did not intend to do—it is necessary to develop here the Theology of the Ancients on the Article of Divine Emanations. Our Principles are sound: our consequences well-drawn: but their correctness and necessity have not always been recognized. And to judge the opinions of the ancient Heretics soundly and equitably, one must, as I have remarked more than once, go back to the time in which they lived, and compare their sentiments with those that were accepted then, and which are not yet entirely banished from the Faith.

For the *Discipline of the secret* <note>The early Christian practice of keeping certain doctrines and rituals hidden from the uninitiated to prevent mockery or misunderstanding.</note> was still unknown in his time. The Christians, accused of profane Mysteries, were careful not to hide their true Mysteries, and did not blush to confess them. Convinced, moreover, of their greatness as well as their truth, they did not believe it necessary to win respect for them by shrouding them in what has been called Holy Darkness. Tatian therefore explains to the Greeks the Mysteries of Christianity, and in particular that of the Generation of the Word. And to show that it occurs without division, and without diminution of the Father's Substance, he first uses the comparison of a Torch, which lights an infinity of others without losing any of its light; and secondly that of Speech (3). *It is thus*, he says, *that when I speak to you, and you hear me, my Reason passes into you, without my being in any way deprived of it.*

Passages from Porphyry, the Oracles of Zoroaster, Philo, and Tatian.

There is, according to these Philosophers, a great difference between *Procession* and *Generation*. *Generation* applies to the Body; *Procession* to Spirits. IX. There is another difficulty that has been raised against the Manichaeans, and which *St. Augustine* did not neglect; it is that if the *Eons* <note>In Gnostic and Manichaean thought, Eons are the various levels of divine beings or powers that emanate from the supreme God.</note> and the *Human Soul* are Emanations of the Divine Nature, they must be beings consubstantial <note>term: consubstantial; explanation: sharing the same fundamental substance or essence, as in the Christian doctrine of the Trinity.</note> with God, and consequently so many Gods. Our Heretics not only disavowed but denied this conclusion, and it must be admitted that they were well-founded according to ancient Theology. Everything that emanates from God is not necessarily God, nor consubstantial with God. Those *Participating Beings*, of whom I spoke following Father *Petau*, were not Gods at all. The reason is that Theologians have distinguished between two types of *Emanations*. Some terminate within the Divine Essence, while others go out from it. The Generation of the Son and the Procession of the Holy *Spirit* terminate within the Divine Essence, but the Procession of *Participating Beings* terminates outside. They emerge, so to speak, from the Essence of God, while the Divine Persons remain within it. A modern scholar has used this same distinction to excuse the Kabbalists <note>Followers of the Jewish mystical tradition known as the Kabbalah.</note>. (1)

> „ One can, he says, conceive of Emanations
> „ in two ways: either as constituting the same Essence
> „ as the subject from which they emanate, or as being separated
> „ from it. Those who conceive of them as constituting the same
> „ Essence run a great risk of falling into Spinozism <note>The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, which was often criticized for pantheism—the idea that God and the universe are the same thing.</note>: but those
> „ who conceive of them as separated say nothing, in my opinion,
> „ that deserves to be blamed. “

After making this distinction, the skillful Professor admits that he subscribes to the sentiment of the celebrated *Thomas Burnet*
<margin>(a) Buddeus, ibid.</margin>
> „ which is that the entire apparatus (2) of the Jewish Kabbalah, which
> „ causes all the Beings of the world to come forth from God, results

> „ emanates from the First Cause, and that everything returns to it: a sentiment
> „ which has nothing dangerous about it, provided it is well understood,
> „ and that one always maintains the distinction between the Creator and the Creature. “

# OF MANICHAEISM. BOOK III. CH. X.

found in *Photius* <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople known for his *Bibliotheca*, which preserved summaries of many lost ancient works.</note>. He asserts that *Agapius*, a famous Manichaean, agrees (3) that *the Soul is consubstantial with God*. But as it is certain that the Sect never recognized more than three Divine Persons, it must be either that *Photius* ranked as a dogma of *Agapius* the consequence he drew from his Principles, or that *Agapius* used the word *consubstantial* <note term="consubstantial">explanation: Sharing the same fundamental essence or "stuff." In strict Trinitarian theology, it implies equality with God, but here the author argues it was used more broadly to mean "made of spirit."</note> in the same sense as Origen. The latter is said to have stated (*a*) "that not only the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but all Intelligent Natures—Angels, Powers, and Man in regard to the Soul—are of the same Substance as God." St. *Jerome* took advantage of this passage to accuse *Origen* of a crime, and by extension *John of Jerusalem*, whom he held a grudge against. But (*b*) Mr. *Huet* <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French scholar and bishop who wrote extensively on Origen.</note> has shown that this Father <note>Meaning St. Jerome.</note> lacked candor, and that all *Origen* meant to say was that Intelligences are spiritual Substances just as God is. They are included under the same category of *Spiritual Substances*, but they are not of the same *specific* nature, being distinguished by essential differences. In a word, everything that is *Spirit* is consubstantial in its quality as Spirit. The Human Soul is, in this respect, consubstantial with the Angels, although it is not of the same Nature. We can now conclude that, according to ancient Theology, there are Divine Emanations that are neither Gods nor consubstantial with God <note>In the sense of being equal to Him.</note>. This is incontestable. All those Philosophers who believed that the Human Soul emanates from God never gave it either the Nature or the Divine Perfections. They viewed Emanations as free productions, to which God communicates only as much of His Perfections as He deems appropriate. The Ebionite <note>An early sect of Jewish Christians.</note> Author of the Discourses falsely attributed to St. *Peter* maintains for this reason that even if the Son of God were begotten of the Father, it would not follow that he was God, (4) *because even though Human Souls come from God, and are of the same Substance, they are nonetheless not Gods*.

found in Photius <note>A 9th-century Patriarch of Constantinople known for his *Bibliotheca*, a collection of summaries of ancient books.</note>. He asserts that *Agapius*, a famous Manichaean, agrees (3) that *the Soul is consubstantial with God*. But as it is certain that the Sect never recognized more than three Divine Persons, it must be that *Photius* either listed the consequence he drew from *Agapius's* principles as one of his dogmas, or that *Agapius* understood the word *consubstantial* <note term="consubstantial">From the Latin *consubstantialis*, meaning "of the same substance." In strict Trinitarian theology, it implies equality in divinity, but here it is used more broadly to mean "sharing a spiritual nature."</note> in the same sense as *Origen*. The latter is said (a) "to have stated that not only the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, but all Intelligent Natures—the Angels, the Powers, and Man in respect to the Soul—are of the same Substance as God." St. *Jerome* took advantage of this passage to accuse *Origen* of a crime, and by extension *John of Jerusalem*, whom he held a grudge against. But (b) Mr. *Huet* <note>Pierre-Daniel Huet (1630–1721), a French scholar and bishop who wrote extensively on Origen.</note> has shown that this Father lacked candor, and that all *Origen* meant to say was that these Intelligences are spiritual Substances just as God is. They are included under the same category of *Spiritual Substances*, but they are not of the same specific nature, being distinguished by essential differences. In a word, everything that is Spirit is consubstantial in its quality as Spirit. The Human Soul is, in this regard, consubstantial with the Angels, although it is not of the same Nature. We can now conclude that, according to ancient Theology, there are Divine Emanations that are neither Gods nor consubstantial with God in a divine sense. This is beyond dispute.

All those Philosophers who believed that the human soul emanates from God never granted it either the Divine Nature or Divine Perfections. They viewed Emanations as free productions, to which God communicates only as much of His Perfections as He sees fit. IX. Another Objection. The Aeons are Gods and consubstantial with God. The Manichaeans deny this, based on ancient Theology. This is only true of immanent Emanations.

IX. There is another difficulty that has been put to the Manichaeans, and which St. *Augustine* did not neglect: it is that if the *Aeons* <note term="Aeons">From the Greek *Aion* (ages); in these systems, they are divine powers or beings that emanate from the supreme God to form the spiritual universe.</note> and the Human Soul are Emanations of the Divine Nature, they are as many Beings consubstantial with God, and consequently as many Gods. Our Heretics not only disavowed but denied this conclusion, and it must be admitted that they were well-founded according to ancient Theology. Everything that emanates from God is not necessarily God, nor consubstantial with God. These *Participating Beings*, of whom I spoke following Father *Petau* <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit scholar who wrote a massive history of theological doctrines.</note>, were not Gods. The reason for this is that Theologians have distinguished two kinds of Emanations. Some terminate within the Divine Essence; others go outside of it. The Generation of the Son and the Procession of the Holy Spirit terminate within the Divine Essence, but the Procession of *Participating Beings* terminates outside. They come out, so to speak, from the Essence of God, in which the Divine Persons remain. A modern scholar used the same distinction to excuse the Kabbalists. (1) "One can," he says, "conceive of Emanations in two ways: either as constituting the same Essence as the subject from which they emanate, or as being separated from it. Those who conceive of them as constituting the same Essence run a great risk of falling into Spinozism <note term="Spinozism">The philosophy of Baruch Spinoza, which suggests that God and the material universe are the same substance—a view often labeled as heresy by his contemporaries.</note>: but those who conceive of them as separate say nothing, in my opinion, that deserves blame." Following this distinction, the skillful Professor admits that he subscribes to the sentiment of the famous *Thomas Burnet*.
